definitionLines: vt. 集合，集会；装配，组装
entries.definition: vt. 集合，集会；装配，组装 vi. 集会，聚集
entries.etymology: early 14c., transitive and intransitive, from Old French assembler "come together, join, unite; gather" (11c.), from Latin assimulare "to make like, liken, compare; copy, imitate; feign, pretend," later "to gather together," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + simulare "to make like" (see simulation). In Middle English and in Old French it also was a euphemism for "to couple sexually." Meaning "to put parts together" in manufacturing is from 1852. Related: Assembled; assembling. Assemble together is redundant.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, transitive and intransitive, 源自 古法语 assembler "come together, join, unite; gather" (11 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 assimulare "to make like, liken, compare; copy, imitate; feign, pretend," later "to gather together," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + simulare "to make like" （参见 simulation). In 中古英语 and in 古法语 it also was a euphemism for "to couple sexually." 义为 "to put parts together" in manufacturing 始于 1852 年. 同源词：Assembled; assembling. Assemble together is redundant.

example.en: Workers assemble the engines by hand at the factory.
example.zh: 工人们在工厂手工组装发动机。

definitionLines: n. 集会，会议；装配，组装
entries.definition: n. 集会，会议；装配，组装
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "a gathering of persons, a group gathered for some purpose," from Old French as(s)emblee "assembly, gathering; union, marriage," noun use of fem. past participle of assembler "to assemble" (see assemble). Meaning "gathering together" is recorded from early 15c.; that of "act of assembling parts or objects" is from 1914, as is assembly line. School sense is recorded from 1932.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "a gathering of persons, a group gathered for some purpose," 源自 古法语 as(s)emblee "assembly, gathering; union, marriage," 为 … 的名词用法 fem. 为 … 的过去分词 assembler "to assemble" （参见 assemble). 义为 "gathering together" 见于 15 世纪初; that of "act of assembling parts or objects" 始于 1914 年, as is assembly line. School sense 见于 1932 年.

example.en: The school held a morning assembly to announce the new policy.
example.zh: 学校举行了晨会，宣布新政策。

entries.etymology: c. 1600, "declare," from Latin assertus, past participle of asserere "claim, maintain, affirm" (see assertion). Related: Asserted; asserting. To assert oneself "stand up for one's rights" is recorded from 1879.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "declare," 源自 拉丁语 assertus, 为 … 的过去分词 asserere "claim, maintain, affirm" （参见 assertion). 同源词：Asserted; asserting. To assert oneself "stand up for one's rights" 见于 1879 年.

example.en: The scientist assert that the new drug was both safe and effective.

definitionLines: vt. 估计，估算；评估，评价， 评定
entries.definition: vt. 估计，估算；评估，评价， 评定
entries.etymology: early 15c., "to fix the amount (of a tax, fine, etc.)," from Anglo-French assesser, from Medieval Latin assessare "fix a tax upon," originally frequentative of Latin assessus "a sitting by," past participle of assidere "to sit beside" (and thus to assist in the office of a judge), from ad- "to" (see ad-) + sedere "to sit" (see sedentary). One of the judge's assistant's jobs was to fix the amount of a fine or tax. Meaning "to estimate the value of property for the purpose of taxing it" is from 1809; transferred sense of "to judge the value of a person, idea, etc." is from 1934. Related: Assessed; assessing.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "to fix the amount (of a tax, fine, etc.)," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 assesser, 源自 中古拉丁语 assessare "fix a tax upon," 原义为 为 … 的反复体 拉丁语 assessus "a sitting by," 为 … 的过去分词 assidere "to sit beside" (and thus to assist in the office of a judge), 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + sedere "to sit" （参见 sedentary). One of the judge's assistant's jobs was to fix the amount of a fine or tax. 义为 "to estimate the value of property for the purpose of taxing it" 始于 1809 年; transferred 语义 "to judge the value of a person, idea, etc." 始于 1934 年. 同源词：Assessed; assessing.

example.en: Managers need to assess employee performance regularly.
example.zh: 管理者需要定期评估员工绩效。

definitionLines: vt. 派给，分配；选定，指定（时 间、地点等）
entries.definition: vt. 派给，分配；选定，指定（时 间、地点等）
entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old French assiginer (13c.) "assign, set (a date, etc.); appoint legally; allot," from Latin assignare "to mark out, to allot by sign, assign, award," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + signare "make a sign," from signum "mark" (see sign). Main original use was in English law, in transferences of personal property. General meaning "to fix, settle, determine, appoint" is from c. 1300. Related: Assigned; assigning.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 assiginer (13 世纪) "assign, set (a date, etc.); appoint legally; allot," 源自 拉丁语 assignare "to mark out, to allot by sign, assign, award," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + signare "make a sign," 源自 signum "mark" （参见 sign). Main original use was in English law, in transferences of personal property. General 意为 "to fix, settle, determine, appoint" 始于 约 1300 年. 同源词：Assigned; assigning.

example.en: The manager will assign specific roles to each team member.
example.zh: 经理将为每位团队成员分配具体职责。

definitionLines: n.（分派的）任务，（指定的）作 业；分配，指派
entries.definition: n.（分派的）任务，（指定的）作 业；分配，指派
entries.etymology: late 14c., "order, request, directive," from Old French assignement "(legal) assignment (of dower, etc.)," from Late Latin assignamentum, noun of action from Latin assignare (see assign). Meaning "appointment to office" is mid-15c.; that of "a task assigned" (to someone) is from c. 1848.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "order, request, directive," 源自 古法语 assignement "(legal) assignment (of dower, etc.)," 源自 晚期拉丁语 assignamentum, 名词 of action 源自 拉丁语 assignare （参见 assign). 义为 "appointment to office" is 15 世纪中期; that of "a task assigned" (to someone) 始于 约 1848 年.

example.en: Each student received a different writing assignment from the teacher.
example.zh: 每个学生从老师那里收到了不同的写作任务。

entries.definition: vt. 吸收；使同化 vi. 同化；吸收
entries.etymology: early 15c., from Latin assimilatus "feigned, pretended, fictitious," past participle of assimilare "to make like," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + simulare "make similar," from similis "like, resembling" (see similar). Originally transitive (with to); intransitive use first recorded 1837. Related: Assimilated; assimilating.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 拉丁语 assimilatus "feigned, pretended, fictitious," 为 … 的过去分词 assimilare "to make like," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + simulare "make similar," 源自 similis "like, resembling" （参见 similar). Originally transitive (with to); intransitive use 首见于 1837 年. 同源词：Assimilated; assimilating.

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Middle French assister "to stand by, help, put, place, assist" (14c.), from Latin assistere "stand by, take a stand near, attend," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + sistere "stand still, take a stand; to set, place, cause to stand," from PIE *si-st-, reduplicated form of root *stā- "to stand" (see stet). Related: Assisted; assisting. Medical assisted suicide attested from 1884.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 中古法语 assister "to stand by, help, put, place, assist" (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 assistere "stand by, take a stand near, attend," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + sistere "stand still, take a stand; to set, place, cause to stand," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *si-st-, reduplicated form of root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). 同源词：Assisted; assisting. Medical assisted suicide attested 自 1884 年起.

example.en: Volunteers were asked to assist the elderly residents with grocery shopping.
example.zh: 志愿者被要求帮助老年居民购买日用品。

entries.definition: a.助手的，辅助的 n. 助手，助理；助教
entries.etymology: mid-15c., assistent "one who helps or aids another," from Middle French assistent, adjective and noun, properly present participle of assister (see assist (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, assistent "one who helps or aids another," 源自 中古法语 assistent, 形容词 and 名词, properly 为 … 的现在分词 assister （参见 assist （动）).

example.en: The surgeon's assistant handed him each instrument during the operation.
example.zh: 外科医生的助手在手术过程中递给他每一件器械。

entries.definition: vt. 联系；联合 vi.交往 n. 合作人，同事
entries.etymology: mid-15c., from Latin associatus past participle of associare "join with," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + sociare "unite with," from socius "companion" (see social (adj.)). Related: Associated; associating. Earlier form of the verb was associen (late 14c.), from Old French associier "associate (with)."
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 拉丁语 associatus 为 … 的过去分词 associare "join with," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + sociare "unite with," 源自 socius "companion" （参见 social （形）). 同源词：Associated; associating. Earlier form of the 动词 was associen (14 世纪晚期), 源自 古法语 associier "associate (with)."

example.en: Many people associate the smell of fresh bread with their grandmother's kitchen.
example.zh: 许多人把新鲜面包的气味与奶奶的厨房联系在一起。

definitionLines: n. 协会，团体；交往；联合，合伙
entries.definition: n. 协会，团体；交往；联合，合伙
entries.etymology: 1530s, "action of coming together," from Medieval Latin associationem (nominative associatio), noun of action from past participle stem of associare (see associate). Meaning "a body of persons with a common purpose" is from 1650s. Meaning "mental connection" is from 1680s; that of "quality or thing called to mind by something else" is from 1810.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "action of coming together," 源自 中古拉丁语 associationem (主格 associatio), 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of associare （参见 associate). 义为 "a body of persons with a common purpose" 始于 1650 年代. 义为 "mental connection" 始于 1680 年代; that of "quality or thing called to mind by something else" 始于 1810 年.

example.en: She joined a professional association for young engineers.
example.zh: 她加入了一个面向年轻工程师的专业协会。

entries.etymology:
early 15c., assumpten "to receive up into heaven" (especially of the Virgin Mary), also assumen "to arrogate," from Latin assumere, adsumere "to take up, take to oneself, take besides, obtain in addition," from ad- "to, up" (see ad-) + sumere "to take," from sub "under" (see sub-) + emere "to take" (see exempt (adj.)).

Meaning "to suppose, to take for granted as the basis of argument" is first recorded 1590s; that of "to take or put on (an appearance, etc.)" is from c. 1600. Related: Assumed; assuming. Early past participle was assumpt. In rhetorical usage, assume expresses what the assumer postulates, often as a confessed hypothesis; presume expresses what the presumer really believes.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, assumpten "to receive up into heaven" (尤指 of the Virgin Mary), also assumen "to arrogate," 源自 拉丁语 assumere, adsumere "to take up, take to oneself, take besides, obtain in addition," 源自 ad- "to, up" （参见 ad-) + sumere "to take," 源自 sub "under" （参见 sub-) + emere "to take" （参见 exempt （形）). 义为 "to suppose, to take for granted as the basis of argument" is 首见于 1590 年代; that of "to take or put on (an appearance, etc.)" 始于 约 1600 年. 同源词：Assumed; assuming. Early past participle was assumpt. In rhetorical usage, assume expresses what the assumer postulates, 常 作为 confessed hypothesis; presume expresses what the presumer really believes.

example.en: Everyone assumed that the project would be completed on time, but it was delayed.
example.zh: 所有人都以为项目会按时完成，但它被推迟了。

definitionLines: n. 假定，设想；担任，承担
entries.definition: n. 假定，设想；担任，承担
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "the reception, uncorrupted, of the Virgin Mary into Heaven," also the Church festival (Aug. 15) commemorating this, Feast of the Assumption, from Old French assumpcion and directly from Latin assumptionem (nominative assumptio) "a taking, receiving," noun of action from past participle stem of assumere "take up, take to oneself" (see assume).

Meaning "minor premise of a syllogism" is late 14c. Meaning "appropriation of a right or possession" is mid-15c. Meaning "action of taking for oneself" is recorded from 1580s; that of "something taken for granted" is from 1620s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "the reception, uncorrupted, of the Virgin Mary into Heaven," also the Church festival (Aug. 15) commemorating this, Feast of the Assumption, 源自 古法语 assumpcion and 直接源自 拉丁语 assumptionem (主格 assumptio) "a taking, receiving," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of assumere "take up, take to oneself" （参见 assume). 义为 "minor premise of a syllogism" is 14 世纪晚期 义为 "appropriation of a right or possession" is 15 世纪中期 义为 "action of taking for oneself" 见于 1580 年代; that of "something taken for granted" 始于 1620 年代.

example.en: The plan rests on the assumption that demand will continue to grow.
example.zh: 该计划建立在需求将继续增长这一假设之上。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French asseurer (12c., Modern French assurer) "to reassure, calm, protect, to render sure," from Vulgar Latin *assecurar, from Latin ad- "to" (see ad-) + securus "safe, secure" (see secure (adj.)). Related: Assured; assuring.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 asseurer (12 世纪, 现代法语 assurer) "to reassure, calm, protect, to render sure," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *assecurar, 源自 拉丁语 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + securus "safe, secure" （参见 secure （形）). 同源词：Assured; assuring.

example.en: He assure his parents that he would call them every week.
example.zh: 他向父母保证每周都会给他们打电话。

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, astonien, from Old French estoner "to stun, daze, deafen, astound," from Vulgar Latin *extonare, from Latin ex- "out" + tonare "to thunder" (see thunder); so, literally "to leave someone thunderstruck." The modern form (influenced by English verbs in -ish, such as distinguish, diminish) is attested from c. 1530.

Related: Astonished; astonishing; astonishingly.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, astonien, 源自 古法语 estoner "to stun, daze, deafen, astound," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *extonare, 源自 拉丁语 ex- "out" + tonare "to thunder" （参见 thunder); so, 字面义为 "to leave someone thunderstruck." The modern form (influenced by English verbs in -ish, such as distinguish, diminish) 见于 约 1530 年. 同源词：Astonished; astonishing; astonishingly.

entries.etymology: coined 1929 in science fiction, popularized from 1961 by U.S. space program, from astro- + nautes "sailor" (see naval). French astronautique (adj.) had been coined 1927 by "J.H. Rosny," pen name of Belgian-born science fiction writer Joseph Henri Honoré Boex (1856-1940) on model of aéronautique, and Astronaut was used in 1880 as the name of a fictional spaceship by English writer Percy Greg (1836-1889) in "Across the Zodiac."
entries.etymologyZh: coined 1929 年 in science fiction, popularized 自 1961 年起 by U.S. space program, 源自 astro- + nautes "sailor" （参见 naval). 法语 astronautique （形） had been coined 1927 年 by "J.H. Rosny," pen name of Belgian-born science fiction writer Joseph Henri Honoré Boex (1856 年-1940 年) on model of aéronautique, and Astronaut was used 于 1880 年 as the name of a fictional spaceship by English writer Percy Greg (1836 年-1889 年) in "Across the Zodiac."

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French astrenomie, from Latin astronomia, from Greek astronomia, literally "star arrangement," from astron "star" (see astro-) + nomos "arranging, regulating," related to nemein "to deal out" (see numismatic). Used earlier than astrology and originally including it.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 astrenomie, 源自 拉丁语 astronomia, 源自 希腊语 astronomia, 字面义为 "star arrangement," 源自 astron "star" （参见 astro-) + nomos "arranging, regulating," related to nemein "to deal out" （参见 numismatic). Used earlier than astrology and 原义为 including it.

example.en: He has been fascinated by astronomy since he first looked through a telescope.
example.zh: 自从他第一次透过望远镜观察，就迷上了天文学。

definitionLines: prep. ［表示地点、位置、场合］ 在，于；［表示时刻、时 节、年龄］在，当；［表示 目标、方向］对，向；［表 示速度、价格等］以； 在……方面
entries.definition: prep. ［表示地点、位置、场合］ 在，于；［表示时刻、时 节、年龄］在，当；［表示 目标、方向］对，向；［表 示速度、价格等］以； 在……方面
entries.etymology:
Old English æt, from Proto-Germanic *at (source also of Old Norse, Gothic at, Old Frisian et, Old High German az), from PIE *ad- "to, near, at" (source also of Latin ad "to, toward" Sanskrit adhi "near;" see ad-).

Lost in German and Dutch, which use their equivalent of to; in Scandinavian, however, to has been lost and at fills its place. In choosing between at church, in church, etc. at is properly distinguished from in or on by involving some practical connection; a worshipper is at church; a tourist is in the church.

The colloquial use of at after where ("where it's at") is attested from 1859. At last is recorded from late 13c.; adverbial phrase at least was in use by 1775. At in Middle English was used freely with prepositions (as in at after, which is in Shakespeare), but this has faded with the exception of at about, which was used in modern times by Trollope, Virginia Woolfe, D.H. Lawrence, and Evelyn Waugh, but nonetheless is regarded as a sign of incompetent writing by my copy editor bosses.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 æt, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *at (source also of 古北欧语, Gothic at, 古弗里西语 et, 古高地德语 az), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *ad- "to, near, at" (source also of 拉丁语 ad "to, toward" 梵语 adhi "near;" 参见 ad-). Lost in 德语 and 荷兰语, which use their equivalent of to; in Scandinavian, however, to has been lost and at fills its place. In choosing between at church, in church, etc. at is properly distinguished 源自 in or on by involving some practical connection; a worshipper is at church; a tourist is in the church. The 口语 use of at after where ("where it's at") 见于 1859 年. At last 见于 13 世纪晚期; adverbial phrase at least was in use 截至 1775 年. At in 中古英语 was used freely with prepositions (as in at after, which is in Shakespeare), but this has faded with the exception of at about, which was used in modern times by Trollope, Virginia Woolfe, D.H. Lawrence, and Evelyn Waugh, but nonetheless is regarded 作为 sign of incompetent writing by my copy editor bosses.

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Latin athleta "a wrestler, athlete, combatant in public games," from Greek athletes "prizefighter, contestant in the games," agent noun from athlein "to contest for a prize," related to athlos "a contest" and athlon "a prize," which is of unknown origin. Before 1750, usually in Latin form. In this sense, Old English had plegmann "play-man." Athlete's foot first recorded 1928, for an ailment that has been around much longer.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 拉丁语 athleta "a wrestler, athlete, combatant in public games," 源自 希腊语 athletes "prizefighter, contestant in the games," agent 名词 源自 athlein "to contest for a prize," related to athlos "a contest" and athlon "a prize," which is 来源不详. Before 1750 年, 通常 in 拉丁语 form. In this sense, 古英语 had plegmann "play-man." Athlete's foot 首见于 1928 年, for an ailment that has been around much longer.

example.en: The athlete trained six hours daily under strict supervision to prepare for the championship.
example.zh: 这位运动员在严格监督下每天训练六小时以备战锦标赛。

entries.definition: a.大西洋的 n. ［the A-］大西洋
entries.etymology: late 14c., occean of Athlant "sea off the west coast of Africa" (early 15c. as occean Atlantyke), from Latin Atlanticus, from Greek Atlantikos "of Atlas," adjectival form of Atlas (genitive Atlantos), in reference to Mount Atlas in Mauritania (see Atlas). Applied to the whole ocean since c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, occean of Athlant "sea off the west coast of Africa" (15 世纪初 as occean Atlantyke), 源自 拉丁语 Atlanticus, 源自 希腊语 Atlantikos "of Atlas," adjectival form of Atlas (属格 Atlantos), in reference to Mount Atlas in Mauritania （参见 Atlas). Applied to the whole ocean 自 约 1600 年.

entries.etymology: 1580s, Titan, son of Iapetus and Clymene, supposed to uphold the pillars of heaven, which was his punishment for being the war leader of the Titans in the struggle with the Olympian gods. The name in Greek perhaps means "The Bearer (of the Heavens)," from a-, copulative prefix, + stem of tlenai "to bear," from PIE root *tele- "to lift, support, weigh." Mount Atlas, in Mauritania, was important in Greek cosmology as a support of the heavens.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, Titan, son of Iapetus and Clymene, supposed to uphold the pillars of heaven, which was his punishment for being the war leader of the Titans in the struggle with the Olympian gods. The name in 希腊语 或许 means "The Bearer (of the Heavens)," 源自 a-, copulative prefix, + stem of tlenai "to bear," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *tele- "to lift, support, weigh." Mount Atlas, in Mauritania, was important in 希腊语 cosmology 作为 support of the heavens.

definitionLines: n. 空气；大气，大气层；气氛
entries.definition: n. 空气；大气，大气层；气氛
entries.etymology:
1630s, atmosphaera (modern form from 1670s), from Modern Latin atmosphaera, from atmo-, comb. form of Greek atmos "vapor, steam" + spharia "sphere" (see sphere). Greek atmos is from PIE *awet-mo-, from root *wet- (1) "to blow" (also "to inspire, spiritually arouse;" see wood (adj.)). First used in English in connection with the Moon, which, as it turns out, practically doesn't have one.
Figurative sense of "surrounding influence, mental or moral environment" is c. 1800.
entries.etymologyZh: 1630 年代, atmosphaera (modern form 源自 1670 年代), 源自 现代 拉丁语 atmosphaera, 源自 atmo-, comb. form of 希腊语 atmos "vapor, steam" + spharia "sphere" （参见 sphere). 希腊语 atmos 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *awet-mo-, 源自 root *wet- (1) "to blow" (also "to inspire, spiritually arouse;" 参见 wood （形）). First used in English in connection with the Moon, which, as it turns out, practically doesn't have one. Figurative 语义 "surrounding influence, mental or moral environment" is 约 1800 年.

example.en: Soft lighting and quiet music created a relaxing atmosphere in the café.
example.zh: 柔和的灯光和轻柔的音乐为咖啡馆营造出轻松的氛围。

entries.etymology: late 15c., as a hypothetical indivisible body, the building block of the universe, from Latin atomus (especially in Lucretius) "indivisible particle," from Greek atomos "uncut, unhewn; indivisible," from a- "not" + tomos "a cutting," from temnein "to cut" (see tome). An ancient term of philosophical speculation (in Leucippus, Democritus), revived 1805 by British chemist John Dalton. In late classical and medieval use also a unit of time, 22,560 to the hour. Atom bomb is from 1945 as both a noun and a verb; compare atomic.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, 作为 hypothetical indivisible body, the building block of the universe, 源自 拉丁语 atomus (尤指 in Lucretius) "indivisible particle," 源自 希腊语 atomos "uncut, unhewn; indivisible," 源自 a- "not" + tomos "a cutting," 源自 temnein "to cut" （参见 tome). An ancient term of philosophical speculation (in Leucippus, Democritus), revived 1805 年 by British chemist John Dalton. In late classical and medieval use also a unit of time, 22,560 to the hour. Atom bomb 始于 1945 年 as both a 名词 and a 动词; 对比 atomic.

example.en: Every element is made up of tiny particles called atoms.
example.zh: 每种元素都由称为原子的微小粒子组成。

entries.etymology:
1670s as a philosophical term (see atomistic); scientific sense dates from 1811, from atom + -ic. Atomic number is from 1821; atomic mass is from 1848. Atomic energy first recorded 1906 in modern sense (as intra-atomic energy from 1903).

Atomic bomb first recorded 1914 in writings of H.G. Wells, who thought of it as a bomb "that would continue to explode indefinitely."

Atomic Age is from 1945. Atomical is from 1640s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1670 年代 作为 philosophical term （参见 atomistic); scientific sense dates 自 1811 年起, 源自 atom + -ic. Atomic number 始于 1821 年; atomic mass 始于 1848 年. Atomic energy 首见于 1906 年 in modern sense (as intra-atomic energy 自 1903 年起). Atomic bomb 首见于 1914 年 in writings of H.G. Wells, who thought of it 作为 bomb "that would continue to explode indefinitely." Atomic Age 始于 1945 年. Atomical 始于 1640 年代.

example.en: The scientists debated the long-term safety of atomic energy as a power source.
example.zh: 科学家们就原子能作为能源的长期安全性展开了辩论。

definitionLines: vt.（to）贴上，系上，附上；使 依附
entries.definition: vt.（to）贴上，系上，附上；使 依附
entries.etymology: mid-14c. (mid-13c. in Anglo-Latin), "to take or seize (property or goods) by law," a legal term, from Old French atachier (11c.), earlier estachier "to attach, fix; stake up, support" (Modern French attacher, also compare Italian attaccare), perhaps from a- "to" + Frankish *stakon "a post, stake" or a similar Germanic word (see stake (n.)). Meaning "to fasten, affix, connect" is from c. 1400. Related: Attached; attaching.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期 (13 世纪中期 in Anglo-拉丁语), "to take or seize (property or goods) by law," a legal term, 源自 古法语 atachier (11 世纪), earlier estachier "to attach, fix; stake up, support" (现代法语 attacher, also 对比 意大利语 attaccare), 或源自 a- "to" + Frankish *stakon "a post, stake" or a similar 日耳曼语 word （参见 stake （名）). 义为 "to fasten, affix, connect" 始于 约 1400 年. 同源词：Attached; attaching.

example.en: Please attach your updated resume to the application email before the deadline tomorrow.
example.zh: 请在明天截止日期前将您更新的简历附在申请邮件中。

definitionLines: vt./n. 攻击，进攻，抨击；（病） 发作
entries.definition: vt./n. 攻击，进攻，抨击；（病） 发作
entries.etymology: c. 1600, from French attaquer (16c.), from Florentine Italian attaccare (battaglia) "join (battle)," thus the word is a doublet of attach, which was used 15c.-17c. also in the sense now reserved to attack. Related: Attacked; attacking.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, 源自 法语 attaquer (16 世纪), 源自 Florentine 意大利语 attaccare (battaglia) "join (battle)," thus the word is a doublet of attach, which was used 15 世纪-17 世纪 also in the sense 现在 reserved to attack. 同源词：Attacked; attacking.

example.en: The rebels planned to attack the government building before sunrise.
example.zh: 叛乱分子计划在日出前袭击政府大楼。

entries.definition: vt. 达到，实现；获得 vi. 达到；获得
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to succeed in reaching," from ataign-, stem of Old French ataindre (11c., Modern French atteindre) "to come up to, reach, attain, endeavor, strive," from Vulgar Latin *attangere, corresponding to Latin attingere "to touch, to arrive at," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + tangere "to touch" (see tangent (adj.)). Latin attingere had a wide range of meanings, including "to attack, to strike, to appropriate, to manage," all somehow suggested by the literal sense "to touch." Related: Attained; attaining.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to succeed in reaching," 源自 ataign-, stem of 古法语 ataindre (11 世纪, 现代法语 atteindre) "to come up to, reach, attain, endeavor, strive," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *attangere, corresponding to 拉丁语 attingere "to touch, to arrive at," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + tangere "to touch" （参见 tangent （形）). 拉丁语 attingere had a wide range of meanings, including "to attack, to strike, to appropriate, to manage," all somehow suggested by the literal sense "to touch." 同源词：Attained; attaining.

example.en: She worked tirelessly to attain her goal of becoming a surgeon.
example.zh: 她不懈努力，以实现成为外科医生的目标。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French attempter (14c.), earlier atenter "to try, attempt, test," from Latin attemptare "to try" (source also of Italian attentare, Old Provençal, Portuguese attentar, Spanish atentar), from ad- "to, upon" (see ad-) + temptare "to try" (see tempt). Related: Attempted; attempting.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 attempter (14 世纪), earlier atenter "to try, attempt, test," 源自 拉丁语 attemptare "to try" (source also of 意大利语 attentare, Old Provençal, 葡萄牙语 attentar, 西班牙语 atentar), 源自 ad- "to, upon" （参见 ad-) + temptare "to try" （参见 tempt). 同源词：Attempted; attempting.

example.en: She made every attempt to finish the report before the deadline.
example.zh: 她尽了一切努力在截止日期前完成报告。

definitionLines: vt. 出席；参加；照顾，护理
entries.definition: vt. 出席；参加；照顾，护理 vi. （to）注意，留意；专心于
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to direct one's mind or energies," from Old French atendre (12c., Modern French attendre) "to expect, wait for, pay attention," and directly from Latin attendere "give heed to," literally "to stretch toward," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + tendere "stretch" (see tenet). The notion is of "stretching" one's mind toward something. Sense of "take care of, wait upon" is from early 14c. Meaning "to pay attention" is early 15c.; that of "to be in attendance" is mid-15c. Related: Attended; attending.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to direct one's mind or energies," 源自 古法语 atendre (12 世纪, 现代法语 attendre) "to expect, wait for, pay attention," and 直接源自 拉丁语 attendere "give heed to," 字面义为 "to stretch toward," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + tendere "stretch" （参见 tenet). The notion is of "stretching" one's mind toward something. 义为 "take care of, wait upon" 始于 14 世纪初 义为 "to pay attention" is 15 世纪初; that of "to be in attendance" is 15 世纪中期 同源词：Attended; attending.

example.en: All employees are required to attend the mandatory training session next Friday.
example.zh: 所有员工须参加下周五的强制培训课程。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "giving heed," from Latin attentionem (nominative attentio) "attention, attentiveness," noun of action from past participle stem of attendere "mental heeding" (see attend). Used with a remarkable diversity of verbs (such as pay, gather, attract, draw, call). As a military cautionary word preparative to giving a command, it is attested from 1792. Attention span is from 1903 (earlier span of attention, 1892).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "giving heed," 源自 拉丁语 attentionem (主格 attentio) "attention, attentiveness," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of attendere "mental heeding" （参见 attend). Attention span 始于 1903 年 (earlier span of attention, 1892 年).

example.en: Please pay attention to the instructions before you begin.
example.zh: 开始之前请注意听指示。

entries.etymology: 1660s, via French attitude (17c.), from Italian attitudine "disposition, posture," also "aptness, promptitude," from Late Latin aptitudinem (nominative aptitudo; see aptitude). Originally 17c. a technical term in art for the posture of a figure in a statue or painting; later generalized to "a posture of the body supposed to imply some mental state" (1725). Sense of "settled behavior reflecting feeling or opinion" is first recorded 1837. Connotations of "antagonistic and uncooperative" developed by 1962 in slang.
entries.etymologyZh: 1660 年代, 经由 法语 attitude (17 世纪), 源自 意大利语 attitudine "disposition, posture," also "aptness, promptitude," 源自 晚期拉丁语 aptitudinem (主格 aptitudo; 参见 aptitude). example.en: His positive attitude toward failure helped him grow from every setback.
example.zh: 他对失败的积极态度帮助他在每次挫折中成长。

definitionLines: n. 律师，（业务或法律事务上 的）代理人
entries.definition: n. 律师，（业务或法律事务上 的）代理人
entries.etymology:
early 14c. (mid-13c. in Anglo-Latin), from Old French atorné "(one) appointed," past participle of aturner "to decree, assign, appoint," from atorner (see attorn). The legal Latin form attornare influenced the spelling in Anglo-French. The sense is of "one appointed to represent another's interests."

In English law, a private attorney was one appointed to act for another in business or legal affairs (usually for pay); an attorney at law or public attorney was a qualified legal agent in the courts of Common Law who prepared the cases for a barrister, who pleaded them (the equivalent of a solicitor in Chancery). So much a term of contempt in England that it was abolished by the Judicature Act of 1873 and merged with solicitor.The double -t- is a mistaken 15c. attempt to restore a non-existent Latin original. Attorney general first recorded 1530s in sense of "legal officer of the state" (late 13c. in Anglo-French), from French, hence the odd plural (subject first, adjective second).

The legal 拉丁语 form attornare influenced the spelling in 盎格鲁-法语. The sense is of "one appointed to represent another's interests." In English law, a private attorney was one appointed to act for another in business or legal affairs (通常 for pay); an attorney at law or public attorney was a qualified legal agent in the courts of Common Law who prepared the cases for a barrister, who pleaded them (the equivalent of a solicitor in Chancery). So much a term of contempt in England that it was abolished by the Judicature Act of 1873 年 and merged with solicitor.The double -t- is a mistaken 15 世纪 attempt to restore a non-existent 拉丁语 original. Attorney general 首见于 1530 年代 in 语义 "legal officer of the state" (13 世纪晚期 in 盎格鲁-法语), 源自 法语, hence the odd plural (subject first, 形容词 second).

example.en: The defendant hired a well-known attorney to represent him in court.
example.zh: 被告聘请了一位知名律师在法庭上为他辩护。

entries.etymology:
early 15c., from Latin attractus, past participle of attrahere "to draw, pull; to attract," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + trahere "draw" (see tract (n.1)).

Originally a medical term for the body's tendency to absorb fluids, nourishment, etc., or for a poultice treatment to "draw out" diseased matter (1560s). Of the ability of people or animals to draw others to them, it is attested from 1560s; of physical forces (magnetism, etc.), from c. 1600 (implied in attraction). Related: Attracted; attracting.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 拉丁语 attractus, 为 … 的过去分词 attrahere "to draw, pull; to attract," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + trahere "draw" （参见 tract (n.1)). Originally a medical term for the body's tendency to absorb fluids, nourishment, etc.，或for a poultice treatment to "draw out" diseased matter (1560 年代). example.zh: 橱窗里色彩鲜艳的陈设吸引了许多好奇的路人驻足观看。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from French attraction, from Latin attractionem (nominative attractio) "a drawing together," noun of action from past participle stem of attrahere (see attract). Originally a medical word, "absorption by the body;" meaning "action of drawing to" is from 1540s (again medical); extended to magnetic, then figuratively to personal (c. 1600) qualities. Meaning "a thing which draws a crowd, interesting or amusing exhibition" is from 1829, a sense that developed in English and soon transferred to the French equivalent of the word.

Meaning "having the quality of drawing people's eye or interest" is from 1580s; sense of "pleasing, alluring" is from c. 1600. Related: Attractively; attractiveness.

entries.etymology: "a sale by increase of bids," 1590s, from Latin auctionem (nominative auctio) "an increasing sale, auction, public sale," noun of action from past participle stem of augere "to increase," from PIE root *aug- (1) "to increase" (see augment). In northern England and Scotland, called a roup. In the U.S., something is sold at auction; in England, by auction.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "the action of hearing," from Old French audience, from Latin audentia "a hearing, listening," from audientum (nominative audiens), present participle of audire "to hear," from PIE compound *au-dh- "to perceive physically, grasp," from root *au- "to perceive" (source also of Greek aisthanesthai "to feel;" Sanskrit avih, Avestan avish "openly, evidently;" Old Church Slavonic javiti "to reveal"). Meaning "formal hearing or reception" is from late 14c.; that of "persons within hearing range, assembly of listeners" is from early 15c. (French audience retains only the older senses). Sense transferred 1855 to "readers of a book." Audience-participation (adj.) first recorded 1940.

entries.etymology: eighth month, 1097, from Latin Augustus (mensis), sixth month of the later Roman calendar, renamed from Sextilis (literally "sixth") in 8 B.C.E. to honor emperor Augustus Caesar, literally "Venerable Caesar" (see august (adj.)). In England, the name replaced native Weodmonað "weed month." One of two months given new names to honor Roman emperors (July being the other), the Romans also gave new imperial names to September (Germanicus) and October (Domitian) but luckily these did not stick.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, from Anglo-French aunte, Old French ante (Modern French tante, from a 13c. variant), from Latin amita "paternal aunt" diminutive of *amma a baby-talk word for "mother" (source also of Greek amma "mother," Old Norse amma "grandmother," Middle Irish ammait "old hag," Hebrew em, Arabic umm "mother").

Extended senses include "an old woman, a gossip" (1580s); "a procuress" (1670s); and "any benevolent woman," in American English, where auntie was recorded since c. 1790 as "a term often used in accosting elderly women." The French word also has become the word for "aunt" in Dutch, German (Tante), and Danish. Swedish has retained the original Germanic (and Indo-European) custom of distinguishing aunts by separate terms derived from "father's sister" (faster) and "mother's sister" (moster). The Old English equivalents were faðu and modrige. In Latin, too, the formal word for "aunt on mother's side" was matertera. Some languages have a separate term for aunts-in-law as opposed to blood relations.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 aunte, 古法语 ante (现代法语 tante, 源自 a 13 世纪 variant), 源自 拉丁语 amita "paternal aunt" 为 … 的指小形式 *amma a baby-talk word for "mother" (source also of 希腊语 amma "mother," 古北欧语 amma "grandmother," Middle 爱尔兰语 ammait "old hag," 希伯来语 em, 阿拉伯语 umm "mother"). Extended senses include "an old woman, a gossip" (1580 年代); "a procuress" (1670 年代); and "any benevolent woman," in American English, where auntie was recorded 自 约 1790 年 as "a term often used in accosting elderly women." The 法语 word also has become the word for "aunt" in 荷兰语, 德语 (Tante), and Danish. Swedish has retained the original 日耳曼语 (and Indo-European) custom of distinguishing aunts by separate terms derived 源自 "father's sister" (faster) and "mother's sister" (moster). The 古英语 equivalents were faðu and modrige. In 拉丁语, too, the formal word for "aunt on mother's side" was matertera. Some languages have a separate term for aunts-in-law as opposed to blood relations.

entries.etymology:
from Latin Terra Australis (16c.), from australis "southern" + -ia. A hypothetical southern continent, known as terra australis incognita, had been proposed since 2c. Dutch explorers called the newfound continent New Holland; the current name was suggested 1814 by Matthew Flinders as an improvement over Terra Australis "as being more agreeable to the ear, and an assimilation to the name of the other great portions of the earth" ["Voyage to Terra Australis"]. In 1817 Gov. Lachlan Macquarie, having read Flinders' suggestion, began using it in official correspondence. The ultimate source is Latin auster "south wind," hence, "the south country."

The Latin sense shift in australis, if it is indeed the same word other Indo-European languages use for east (see aurora), for which Latin uses oriens (see orient), perhaps is based on a false assumption about the orientation of the Italian peninsula, "with shift through 'southeast' explained by the diagonal position of the axis of Italy" [Buck]; see Walde, Alois, "Lateinisches etymologisches Wörterbuch," 3rd. ed., vol. 1, p.87; Ernout, Alfred, and Meillet, Alfred, "Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue latine," 2nd. ed., p.94. Or perhaps the connection is more ancient, and from PIE root *aus- "to shine," source of aurora, which also produces words for "burning," with reference to the "hot" south wind that blows into Italy. Thus auster "(hot) south wind," metaphorically extended to "south."

definitionLines: a. 可信的；真正的，真实的
entries.definition: a. 可信的；真正的，真实的
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "authoritative," from Old French autentique (13c., Modern French authentique) "authentic; canonical," and directly from Medieval Latin authenticus, from Greek authentikos "original, genuine, principal," from authentes "one acting on one's own authority," from autos "self" (see auto-) + hentes "doer, being," from PIE *sene- "to accomplish, achieve." Sense of "entitled to acceptance as factual" is first recorded mid-14c.

Traditionally in modern use, authentic implies that the contents of the thing in question correspond to the facts and are not fictitious; genuine implies that the reputed author is the real one; but this is not always maintained: "The distinction which the 18th c. apologists attempted to establish between genuine and authentic ... does not agree well with the etymology of the latter word, and is not now recognized" [OED].

example.en: The museum only displays authentic artifacts from the dynasty.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, autor "father," from Old French auctor, acteor "author, originator, creator, instigator (12c., Modern French auteur), from Latin auctorem (nominative auctor) "enlarger, founder, master, leader," literally "one who causes to grow," agent noun from auctus, past participle of augere "to increase" (see augment). Meaning "one who sets forth written statements" is from late 14c. The -t- changed to -th- 16c. on mistaken assumption of Greek origin.

definitionLines: a. 有权威的；可相信的
entries.definition: a. 有权威的；可相信的
entries.etymology: c. 1600, "dictatorial" (a sense now restricted to authoritarian), from Medieval Latin authoritativus (see authority). Meaning "possessing authority" is recorded from 1650s; that of "proceeding from proper authority" is from 1809. Related: Authoritatively; authoritativeness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "dictatorial" (a sense 现在 restricted to authoritarian), 源自 中古拉丁语 authoritativus （参见 authority). 义为 "possessing authority" 见于 1650 年代; that of "proceeding from proper authority" 始于 1809 年. 同源词：Authoritatively; authoritativeness.

definitionLines: n. 权力，权威；权威人士，（pl.） 当局
entries.definition: n. 权力，权威；权威人士，（pl.） 当局
entries.etymology:
early 13c., autorite "book or quotation that settles an argument," from Old French auctorité "authority, prestige, right, permission, dignity, gravity; the Scriptures" (12c.; Modern French autorité), from Latin auctoritatem (nominative auctoritas) "invention, advice, opinion, influence, command," from auctor "master, leader, author" (see author (n.)).

Usually spelled with a -c- in English till 16c., when it was dropped in imitation of the French. Meaning "power to enforce obedience" is from late 14c.; meaning "people in authority" is from 1610s. Authorities "those in charge, those with police powers" is recorded from mid-19c.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, autorite "book or quotation that settles an argument," 源自 古法语 auctorité "authority, prestige, right, permission, dignity, gravity; the Scriptures" (12 世纪; 现代法语 autorité), 源自 拉丁语 auctoritatem (主格 auctoritas) "invention, advice, opinion, influence, command," 源自 auctor "master, leader, author" （参见 author （名）). Usually spelled with a -c- in English till 16 世纪, when it was dropped in imitation of the 法语. 义为 "power to enforce obedience" 始于 14 世纪晚期; 意为 "people in authority" 始于 1610 年代. Authorities "those in charge, those with police powers" 见于 19 世纪中期

definitionLines: vt. 使自动化，使自动操作
entries.definition: vt. 使自动化，使自动操作 vi. 自动化，自动操作
entries.etymology: "to convert to automatic operation," 1954, back-formation from automated (q.v.). Ancient Greek verb automatizein meant "to act of oneself, to act unadvisedly." Related: Automating.
entries.etymologyZh: "to convert to automatic operation," 1954 年, back-formation 源自 automated (q.v.). Ancient 希腊语 动词 automatizein meant "to act of oneself, to act unadvisedly." 同源词：Automating.

entries.definition: a.自动的 auto（mobile） n. 汽车
entries.etymology: "self-acting, moving or acting on its own," 1812, from Greek automatos, used of the gates of Olympus and the tripods of Hephaestus (also "without apparent cause, by accident"), from autos "self" (see auto-) + matos "thinking, animated" (see automaton). Of involuntary animal or human actions, from 1748, first used in this sense by English physician and philosopher David Hartley (1705-1757). In reference to a type of firearm, from 1877; specifically of machinery that imitates human-directed action from 1940.
entries.etymologyZh: "self-acting, moving or acting on its own," 1812 年, 源自 希腊语 automatos, used of the gates of Olympus and the tripods of Hephaestus (also "without apparent cause, by accident"), 源自 autos "self" （参见 auto-) + matos "thinking, animated" （参见 automaton). Of involuntary animal or human actions, 自 1748 年起, first used in this sense by English physician and philosopher David Hartley (1705 年-1757 年). In reference to a type of firearm, 自 1877 年起; specifically of machinery that imitates human-directed action 自 1940 年起.

example.en: The factory uses an automatic system to sort packages by size.
example.zh: 工厂使用自动系统按尺寸分拣包裹。

entries.etymology: 1800, from Greek autonomos "having one's own laws," of animals, "feeding or ranging at will," from autos "self" (see auto-) + nomos "law" (see numismatic). Compare privilege. Used mostly in metaphysics and politics; see autonomic.
entries.etymologyZh: 1800 年, 源自 希腊语 autonomos "having one's own laws," of animals, "feeding or ranging at will," 源自 autos "self" （参见 auto-) + nomos "law" （参见 numismatic). 对比 privilege. Used mostly in metaphysics and politics; 参见 autonomic.

entries.etymology: 1620s, of states, from Greek autonomia "independence," noun of quality from autonomos "independent, living by one's own laws," from auto- "self" (see auto-) + nomos "custom, law" (see numismatics). Of persons, from 1803.
entries.etymologyZh: 1620 年代, of states, 源自 希腊语 autonomia "independence," 名词 of quality 源自 autonomos "independent, living by one's own laws," 源自 auto- "self" （参见 auto-) + nomos "custom, law" （参见 numismatics). Of persons, 自 1803 年起.

example.en: The region was granted greater autonomy to manage its own affairs.
example.zh: 该地区获得了更大的自治权来管理自身事务。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., autumpne (modern form from 16c.), from Old French autumpne, automne (13c.), from Latin autumnus (also auctumnus, perhaps influenced by auctus "increase"), which is of unknown origin. Perhaps from Etruscan, but Tucker suggests a meaning "drying-up season" and a root in *auq- (which would suggest the form in -c- was the original) and compares archaic English sere-month "August."

Harvest was the English name for the season until autumn began to displace it 16c. In Britain, the season is popularly August through October; in U.S., September through November. Compare Italian autunno, Spanish otoño, Portuguese outono, all from the Latin word. Unlike the other three seasons, its names across the Indo-European languages leave no evidence that there ever was a common word for it.

Many "autumn" words mean "end, end of summer," or "harvest." Compare also Lithuanian ruduo "autumn," from rudas "reddish," in reference to leaves; Old Irish fogamar, literally "under-winter."
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, autumpne (modern form 源自 16 世纪), 源自 古法语 autumpne, automne (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 autumnus (also auctumnus, 或许 influenced by auctus "increase"), which is 来源不详. Perhaps 源自 Etruscan, but Tucker suggests a 意为 "drying-up season" and a root in *auq- (which would suggest the form in -c- was the original) and compares 古旧 English sere-month "August." Harvest was the English name for the season until autumn began to displace it 16 世纪 In Britain, the season is popularly August through October; in U.S., September through November. 对比 意大利语 autunno, 西班牙语 otoño, 葡萄牙语 outono, all 源自 拉丁语 word. Unlike the other three seasons, its names across the Indo-European languages leave no evidence that there ever was a common word for it. Many "autumn" words mean "end, end of summer," or "harvest." 对比 also Lithuanian ruduo "autumn," 源自 rudas "reddish," in reference to leaves; Old 爱尔兰语 fogamar, 字面义为 "under-winter."

example.en: The leaves turn golden and red every autumn.
example.zh: 每到秋天，树叶都会变成金色和红色。

definitionLines: n. 助动词；辅助者，辅助物
entries.definition: n. 助动词；辅助者，辅助物 a.辅助的；附加的
entries.etymology: c. 1600, from Latin auxiliaris "helpful," from auxilium "aid, help, support," related to auctus, past participle of augere "to increase" (see augment).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, 源自 拉丁语 auxiliaris "helpful," 源自 auxilium "aid, help, support," related to auctus, 为 … 的过去分词 augere "to increase" （参见 augment).

entries.etymology: c. 1300, availen, apparently a French compound formed in English from Old French a- "to" (see ad-) + vailen "to avail," from vaill-, present stem of valoir "be worth," from Latin valere (see valiant). Related: Availed; availing. As a noun, from c. 1400.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, availen, 似乎 a 法语 复合词 formed in English 源自 古法语 a- "to" （参见 ad-) + vailen "to avail," 源自 vaill-, present stem of valoir "be worth," 源自 拉丁语 valere （参见 valiant). 同源词：Availed; availing. 作名词时, 源自 约 1400 年.

definitionLines: a. 可利用的；可得到的
entries.definition: a. 可利用的；可得到的
entries.etymology: mid-15c., "beneficial," also "valid, effective, capable of producing the desired effect," from avail + -able. Meaning "at one's disposal, capable of being made use of" is recorded from 1827.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "beneficial," also "valid, effective, capable of producing the desired effect," 源自 avail + -able. 义为 "at one's disposal, capable of being made use of" 见于 1827 年.

example.en: Tickets are still available for the Friday evening show.
example.zh: 周五晚场的票仍有售。

entries.etymology: c. 1600, "a way of approach" (originally a military word), from Middle French avenue "way of access," from Old French avenue "act of approaching, arrival," noun use of fem. of avenu, past participle of avenir "to come to, arrive," from Latin advenire "to come to," from ad- "to" (see ad-) + venire "to come" (see venue). Meaning shifted to "a way of approach to a country-house," usually bordered by trees, hence, "a broad, tree-lined roadway" (1650s), then to "wide, main street" (by 1846, especially in U.S.).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "a way of approach" (原义为 a military word), 源自 中古法语 avenue "way of access," 源自 古法语 avenue "act of approaching, arrival," 为 … 的名词用法 fem. of avenu, 为 … 的过去分词 avenir "to come to, arrive," 源自 拉丁语 advenire "to come to," 源自 ad- "to" （参见 ad-) + venire "to come" （参见 venue). 义为 shifted to "a way of approach to a country-house," 通常 bordered by trees, hence, "a broad, tree-lined roadway" (1650 年代), 之后 to "wide, main street" (截至 1846 年, 尤指 in U.S.).

example.en: The parade marched down the main avenue in front of thousands of spectators.
example.zh: 游行队伍沿主干道行进，数千名观众在两旁观看。

definitionLines: a. 平均的；平常的，普通的
entries.definition: n.平均，平均数 a. 平均的；平常的，普通的
entries.etymology: late 15c., "financial loss incurred through damage to goods in transit," from French avarie "damage to ship," and Italian avaria; a word from 12c. Mediterranean maritime trade (compare Spanish averia; other Germanic forms, Dutch avarij, German haferei, etc., also are from Romanic languages), which is of uncertain origin. Sometimes traced to Arabic 'arwariya "damaged merchandise." Meaning shifted to "equal sharing of such loss by the interested parties." Transferred sense of "statement of a medial estimate" is first recorded 1735. The mathematical extension is from 1755.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "financial loss incurred through damage to goods in transit," 源自 法语 avarie "damage to ship," and 意大利语 avaria; a word 源自 12 世纪 Mediterranean maritime trade (对比 西班牙语 averia; other 日耳曼语 forms, 荷兰语 avarij, 德语 haferei, etc., also 始于 Romanic languages), which is 来源存疑. Sometimes traced to 阿拉伯语 'arwariya "damaged merchandise." 义为 shifted to "equal sharing of such loss by the interested parties." Transferred 语义 "statement of a medial estimate" is 首见于 1735 年. The mathematical extension 始于 1755 年.

example.en: The average temperature in July is around 35 degrees Celsius here.
example.zh: 这里七月份的平均气温约为摄氏35度。

entries.etymology: c. 1400, from Old French avertir (12c.), "turn, direct; avert; make aware," from Vulgar Latin *advertire, from Latin avertere "to turn away, to drive away," from ab- "from, away" (see ab-) + vertere "to turn" (see versus). Related: Averted; averting.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, 源自 古法语 avertir (12 世纪), "turn, direct; avert; make aware," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *advertire, 源自 拉丁语 avertere "to turn away, to drive away," 源自 ab- "from, away" （参见 ab-) + vertere "to turn" （参见 versus). 同源词：Averted; averting.

definitionLines: n.航空；飞行术；飞机制造业
entries.definition: n.航空；飞行术；飞机制造业
entries.etymology: 1866, from French aviation, noun of action from stem of Latin avis "bird" (see aviary). Coined 1863 by French aviation pioneer Guillaume Joseph Gabriel de La Landelle (1812-1886) in "Aviation ou Navigation aérienne."
entries.etymologyZh: 1866 年, 源自 法语 aviation, 名词 of action 源自 stem of 拉丁语 avis "bird" （参见 aviary). Coined 1863 年 by 法语 aviation pioneer Guillaume Joseph Gabriel de La Landelle (1812 年-1886 年) in "Aviation ou Navigation aérienne."

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Anglo-French avoider "to clear out, withdraw (oneself)," partially Englished from Old French esvuidier "to empty out," from es- "out" (see ex-) + vuidier "to be empty," from voide "empty, vast, wide, hollow, waste" (see void (adj.)). Originally a law term; modern sense of "have nothing to do with" also was in Middle English and corresponds to Old French eviter with which it was perhaps confused. Meaning "escape, evade" first attested 1520s. Related: Avoided; avoiding.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 avoider "to clear out, withdraw (oneself)," partially Englished 源自 古法语 esvuidier "to empty out," 源自 es- "out" （参见 ex-) + vuidier "to be empty," 源自 voide "empty, vast, wide, hollow, waste" （参见 void （形）). Originally a law term; modern 语义 "have nothing to do with" also was in 中古英语 and corresponds to 古法语 eviter with which it was 或许 confused. 义为 "escape, evade" 最早见于 1520 年代. 同源词：Avoided; avoiding.

example.en: Drivers should slow down to avoid skidding on icy roads in winter.
example.zh: 冬天驾驶员应放慢速度以避免在结冰路面打滑。

entries.etymology: mid-13c., awaiten, "to wait for," from Old North French awaitier (Old French agaitier) "to lie in wait for, watch, observe," from a- "to" (see ad-) + waitier "to watch" (see wait (v.)). Originally especially "wait for with hostile intent, wait to ambush or spy upon." Related: Awaited; awaiting.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, awaiten, "to wait for," 源自 Old North 法语 awaitier (古法语 agaitier) "to lie in wait for, watch, observe," 源自 a- "to" （参见 ad-) + waitier "to watch" （参见 wait （动）). Originally 尤指 "wait for with hostile intent, wait to ambush or spy upon." 同源词：Awaited; awaiting.

example.en: A crowd of fans awaited the singer's arrival at the airport.
example.zh: 一群粉丝在机场等候歌手的到来。

entries.definition: a. 醒着的；意识到的 vt. 唤醒，唤起 vi. 醒来，醒悟，觉悟
entries.etymology:
a merger of two Middle English verbs: 1. awaken, from Old English awæcnan (earlier onwæcnan; strong, past tense awoc, past participle awacen) "to awake, arise, originate," from a "on" + wacan "to arise, become awake" (see wake (v.)); and 2. awakien, from Old English awacian (weak, past participle awacode) "to awaken, revive; arise; originate, spring from," from a "on" (see a (2)) + wacian "to be awake, remain awake, watch" (see watch (v.)).

Both originally were intransitive only; the transitive sense being expressed by Middle English awecchen (from Old English aweccan) until later Middle English. In Modern English, the tendency has been to restrict the strong past tense and past participle (awoke, awoken) to the original intransitive sense and the weak inflection (awakened) to the transitive, but this never has been complete (see wake (v.); also compare awaken).
entries.etymologyZh: a merger of two 中古英语 verbs: 1. awaken, 源自 古英语 awæcnan (earlier onwæcnan; strong, past tense awoc, past participle awacen) "to awake, arise, originate," 源自 a "on" + wacan "to arise, become awake" （参见 wake （动）); and 2. awakien, 源自 古英语 awacian (weak, past participle awacode) "to awaken, revive; arise; originate, spring from," 源自 a "on" （参见 a (2)) + wacian "to be awake, remain awake, watch" （参见 watch （动）). Both 原义为 were intransitive only; the transitive sense being expressed by 中古英语 awecchen (源自 古英语 aweccan) until later 中古英语. In 现代英语, the tendency has been to restrict the strong past tense and past participle (awoke, awoken) to the original intransitive sense and the weak inflection (awakened) to the transitive, but this never has been complete （参见 wake （动）; also 对比 awaken).

example.en: She lay awake for hours, unable to fall asleep due to worry.
example.zh: 她忧心忡忡，躺着清醒了好几个小时，无法入睡。

entries.definition: n. 奖，奖品 vt. 授予，奖给
entries.etymology: late 14c., "decide after careful observation," from Anglo-French awarder, from Old North French eswarder (Old French esguarder) "decide, examine" (after careful consideration), from es- "out" (see ex-) + warder "to watch" (see ward (n.)). Related: Awarded; awarding.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "decide after careful observation," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 awarder, 源自 Old North 法语 eswarder (古法语 esguarder) "decide, examine" (after careful consideration), 源自 es- "out" （参见 ex-) + warder "to watch" （参见 ward （名）). 同源词：Awarded; awarding.

example.en: She received the highest award of the evening for her debut performance.
example.zh: 她凭借首次演出获得了当晚的最高奖项。

entries.etymology: late Old English gewær, from Proto-Germanic *ga-waraz (source also of Old Saxon giwar, Middle Dutch gheware, Old High German giwar, German gewahr), from *ga-, intensive prefix, + waraz "wary, cautious" (see wary).
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 gewær, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *ga-waraz (source also of 古撒克逊语 giwar, Middle 荷兰语 gheware, 古高地德语 giwar, 德语 gewahr), 源自 *ga-, intensive prefix, + waraz "wary, cautious" （参见 wary).

example.en: Are you aware of the risks involved in this procedure?
example.zh: 你意识到这个操作所涉及的风险了吗？

entries.etymology: late Old English aweg, earlier on weg "on from this (that) place;" see a- (1) + way (n.). Colloquial use for "without delay" (fire away, also right away) is from earlier sense of "onward in time" (16c.). Intensive use (as in away back) is American English, first attested 1818.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 aweg, earlier on weg "on from this (that) place;" 参见 a- (1) + way （名）. Colloquial use for "without delay" (fire away, also right away) 始于 earlier 语义 "onward in time" (16 世纪). Intensive use (as in away back) is American English, 最早见于 1818 年.

example.en: He moved away from his family after taking a job overseas.
example.zh: 他在海外就职后，离开了家人，远走他乡。

definitionLines: a. 可怕的，引起敬畏的
entries.definition: a. 可怕的，引起敬畏的
entries.etymology: 1590s, "profoundly reverential," from awe (n.) + -some (1). Meaning "inspiring awe" is from 1670s; weakened colloquial sense of "impressive, very good" is recorded by 1961 and was in vogue from after c. 1980. Related: Awesomely; awesomeness.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "profoundly reverential," 源自 awe （名） + -some (1). 义为 "inspiring awe" 始于 1670 年代; weakened 口语 语义 "impressive, very good" is recorded 截至 1961 年 and was in vogue 源自 after 约 1980 年. 同源词：Awesomely; awesomeness.

example.en: The view from the mountaintop was absolutely awesome.
example.zh: 从山顶望去的景色令人叹为观止。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, agheful "worthy of respect or fear," from aghe, an earlier form of awe (n.), + -ful. The Old English word was egefull. Weakened sense "very bad" is from 1809; weakened sense of "exceedingly" is by 1818.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, agheful "worthy of respect or fear," 源自 aghe, an earlier form of awe （名）, + -ful. The 古英语 word was egefull. Weakened sense "very bad" 始于 1809 年; weakened 语义 "exceedingly" is 截至 1818 年.

example.en: The food at that restaurant was awful, and I won't go back.
example.zh: 那家餐厅的食物糟透了，我再也不会去了。

definitionLines: a. 粗笨的，笨拙的；尴尬的，棘 手的
entries.definition: a. 粗笨的，笨拙的；尴尬的，棘 手的 ax（e） n. 斧子
entries.etymology: mid-14c., "in the wrong direction," from awk "back-handed" + adverbial suffix -weard (see -ward). Meaning "clumsy" first recorded 1520s. Related: Awkwardly. Other formations from awk, none of them surviving, were awky, awkly, awkness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "in the wrong direction," 源自 awk "back-handed" + adverbial suffix -weard （参见 -ward). 义为 "clumsy" 首见于 1520 年代. 同源词：Awkwardly. Other formations 源自 awk, none of them surviving, were awky, awkly, awkness.

example.en: There was an awkward silence after his joke fell flat.
example.zh: 他的笑话没人捧场，随后陷入了一阵尴尬的沉默。

entries.etymology: 1540s, "imaginary straight line around which a body (such as the Earth) rotates," from Latin axis "axle, pivot, axis of the earth or sky," from PIE *aks- "axis" (source also of Old English eax, Old High German ahsa "axle;" Greek axon "axis, axle, wagon;" Sanskrit aksah "an axle, axis, beam of a balance;" Lithuanian aszis "axle"). Figurative sense in world history of "alliance between Germany and Italy" (later extended unetymologically to include Japan) is from 1936. Original reference was to a "Rome-Berlin axis" in central Europe. The word later was used in reference to a London-Washington axis (World War II) and a Moscow-Peking axis (early Cold War).
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "imaginary straight line around which a body (such as the Earth) rotates," 源自 拉丁语 axis "axle, pivot, axis of the earth or sky," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *aks- "axis" (source also of 古英语 eax, 古高地德语 ahsa "axle;" 希腊语 axon "axis, axle, wagon;" 梵语 aksah "an axle, axis, beam of a balance;" Lithuanian aszis "axle"). Figurative sense in world history of "alliance between Germany and Italy" (later extended unetymologically to include Japan) 始于 1936 年. Original reference was to a "Rome-Berlin axis" in central Europe. The word later was used in reference to a London-Washington axis (World War II) and a Moscow-Peking axis (early Cold War).

example.en: The graph shows temperature changes plotted along the vertical axis.
example.zh: 图表显示了沿纵轴绘制的温度变化。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., babi, diminutive of baban (see babe + -y (3)). Meaning "childish adult person" is from c. 1600. Meaning "youngest of a group" is from 1897. As a term of endearment for one's lover it is attested perhaps as early as 1839, certainly by 1901; its popularity perhaps boosted by baby vamp "a popular girl," student slang from c. 1922. As an adjective, by 1750.

Baby food is from 1833. Baby blues for "blue eyes" recorded by 1892 (the phrase also was used for "postpartum depression" 1950s-60s). To empty the baby out with the bath (water) is first recorded 1909 in G.B. Shaw (compare German das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten). Baby's breath (noted for sweet smell, which also was supposed to attract cats) as a type of flower is from 1897. French bébé (19c.) is from English.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, babi, 为 … 的指小形式 baban （参见 babe + -y (3)). 义为 "childish adult person" 始于 约 1600 年. 义为 "youngest of a group" 始于 1897 年. 作为 term of endearment for one's lover it is attested perhaps as early as 1839, certainly by 1901; its popularity perhaps boosted by baby vamp "a popular girl," student slang from c. 1922. As an adjective, by 1750. Baby food is from 1833. Baby blues for "blue eyes" recorded by 1892 (the phrase also was used for "postpartum depression" 1950s-60s). To empty the baby out with the bath (water) is first recorded 1909 in G.B. Shaw (compare German das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten). Baby's breath (noted for sweet smell, which also was supposed to attract cats) 作为 type of flower 始于 1897 年. 法语 bébé (19 世纪) 始于 English.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "young man;" also "youthful knight, novice in arms," from Old French bacheler, bachelor, bachelier (11c.) "knight bachelor," a young squire in training for knighthood, also "young man; unmarried man," and as a university title, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Medieval Latin baccalarius "vassal farmer, adult serf without a landholding," one who helps or tends a baccalaria "field or land in the lord's demesne" (according to old French sources, perhaps from an alteration of vacca "a cow" and originally "grazing land" [Kitchin]). Or from Latin baculum "a stick," because the squire would practice with a staff, not a sword. "Perhaps several independent words have become confused in form" [Century Dictionary]. Meaning in English expanded early 14c. to "young unmarried man," late 14c. to "one who has taken the lowest degree in a university." Bachelor party as a pre-wedding ritual is from 1882.

entries.etymology:
Old English bæc "back," from Proto-Germanic *bakam (cognates: Old Saxon and Middle Dutch bak, Old Frisian bek), with no known connections outside Germanic. In other modern Germanic languages the cognates mostly have been ousted in this sense by words akin to Modern English ridge (such as Danish ryg, German Rücken). Many Indo-European languages show signs of once having distinguished the horizontal back of an animal (or a mountain range) from the upright back of a human. In other cases, a modern word for "back" may come from a word related to "spine" (Italian schiena, Russian spina) or "shoulder, shoulder blade" (Spanish espalda, Polish plecy).

To turn (one's) back on (someone or something) "ignore" is from early 14c. Behind (someone's) back "clandestinely" is from late 14c. To know (something) like the back of one's hand, implying familiarity, is first attested 1893. The first attested use of the phrase is from a dismissive speech made to a character in Robert Louis Stevenson's "Catriona":

The story, a sequel to "Kidnapped," has a Scottish setting and context, and the back of my hand to you was noted in the late 19th century as a Scottish expression meaning "I will have nothing to do with you" [see Longmuir's edition of Jamieson's Scottish dictionary]. In English generally, the back of (one's) hand has been used to imply contempt and rejection since at least 1300. Perhaps the connection of a menacing dismissal is what made Stevenson choose that particular anatomical reference.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "inferior in quality;" early 13c., "wicked, evil, vicious," a mystery word with no apparent relatives in other languages.* Possibly from Old English derogatory term bæddel and its diminutive bædling "effeminate man, hermaphrodite, pederast," probably related to bædan "to defile." A rare word before 1400, and evil was more common in this sense until c. 1700. Meaning "uncomfortable, sorry" is 1839, American English colloquial.

Comparable words in the other Indo-European languages tend to have grown from descriptions of specific qualities, such as "ugly," "defective," "weak," "faithless," "impudent," "crooked," "filthy" (such as Greek kakos, probably from the word for "excrement;" Russian plochoj, related to Old Church Slavonic plachu "wavering, timid;" Persian gast, Old Persian gasta-, related to gand "stench;" German schlecht, originally "level, straight, smooth," whence "simple, ordinary," then "bad").

Comparative and superlative forms badder, baddest were common 14c.-18c. and used as recently as Defoe (but not by Shakespeare), but yielded to comparative worse and superlative worst (which had belonged to evil and ill).

As a noun, late 14c., "evil, wickedness." In U.S. place names, sometimes translating native terms meaning "supernaturally dangerous." Ironic use as a word of approval is said to be at least since 1890s orally, originally in African-American vernacular, emerging in print 1928 in a jazz context. It might have emerged from the ambivalence of expressions like bad nigger, used as a term of reproach by whites, but among blacks sometimes representing one who stood up to injustice, but in the U.S. West bad man also had a certain ambivalence:

*Farsi has bad in more or less the same sense as the English word, but this is regarded by linguists as a coincidence. The forms of the words diverge as they are traced back in time (Farsi bad comes from Middle Persian vat), and such accidental convergences exist across many languages, given the vast number of words in each and the limited range of sounds humans can make to signify them. Among other coincidental matches with English are Korean mani "many," Chinese pei "pay," Nahuatl (Aztecan) huel "well," Maya hol "hole."

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, bagge, from Old Norse baggi or a similar Scandinavian source; not found in other Germanic languages, perhaps ultimately of Celtic origin. Disparaging slang for "woman" dates from 1924 (though various specialized senses of this are much older). Meaning "person's area of interest or expertise" is 1964, from African-American vernacular, from jazz sense of "category," probably via notion of putting something in a bag.

To be left holding the bag (and presumably nothing else), "cheated, swindled" is attested by 1793. Many figurative senses, such as the verb meaning "to kill game" (1814) and its colloquial extension to "catch, seize, steal" (1818) are from the notion of the game bag (late 15c.) into which the product of the hunt was placed. To let the cat out of the bag "reveal the secret" is from 1760.

entries.etymology: early 13c., "apparatus for weighing," from Old French balance (12c.) "balance, scales for weighing," also in the figurative sense; from Medieval Latin bilancia, from Late Latin bilanx, from Latin (libra) bilanx "(scale) having two pans," possibly from Latin bis "twice" + lanx "dish, plate, scale of a balance." The accounting sense is from 1580s; the meaning "general harmony between parts" is from 1732; sense of "physical equipoise" is from 1660s. Balance of power in the geopolitical sense is from 1701. Many figurative uses (such as hang in the balance, late 14c.), are from Middle English image of the scales in the hands of personified Justice, Fortune, Fate, etc.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, ballede, probably, with Middle English -ede adjectival suffix + Celtic bal "white patch, blaze" especially on the head of a horse or other animal (from PIE root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, gleam;" see bleach (v.)). entries.etymology:
1570s, "a game played with a large inflated leather ball," from Italian pallone "large ball," from palla "ball," from a Germanic source akin to Langobardic palla (from Proto-Germanic *ball-, from PIE *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell;" see bole) + -one, suffix indicating great size.

Perhaps also borrowed in part from French ballon (16c.), altered (after balle) from Italian pallone. It also meant the ball itself (1590s), which was batted back and forth by means of large wooden paddles strapped to the forearms. In 17c., it also meant "a type of fireworks housed in a pasteboard ball" (1630s) and "round ball used as an architectural ornament" (1650s). Acquired modern meaning after Montgolfier brothers' flights, 1783. As a child's toy, it is attested from 1848; as "outline containing words in a comic engraving" it dates from 1844. Also see -oon.

entries.etymology:
Old English bannan "to summon, command, proclaim," from Proto-Germanic *bannan "proclaim, command, forbid" (source also of Old High German bannan "to command or forbid under threat of punishment," German bannen "banish, expel, curse"), originally "to speak publicly," from PIE root *bha- (2) "to speak" (source also of Old Irish bann "law," Armenian ban "word;" see fame (n.)).

 Main modern sense of "to prohibit" (late 14c.) is from Old Norse cognate banna "to curse, prohibit," and probably in part from Old French ban, which meant "outlawry, banishment," among other things (see banal) and was a borrowing from Germanic. The sense evolution in Germanic was from "speak" to "proclaim a threat" to (in Norse, German, etc.) "curse."

The Germanic root, borrowed in Latin and French, has been productive: banish, bandit, contraband, etc. Related: Banned; banning. Banned in Boston dates from 1920s, in allusion to the excessive zeal and power of that city's Watch and Ward Society.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bannan "to summon, command, proclaim," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bannan "proclaim, command, forbid" (source also of 古高地德语 bannan "to command or forbid under threat of punishment," 德语 bannen "banish, expel, curse"), 原义为 "to speak publicly," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bha- (2) "to speak" (source also of Old 爱尔兰语 bann "law," Armenian ban "word;" 参见 fame （名）). Main modern 语义 "to prohibit" (14 世纪晚期) 始于 古北欧语 同源 banna "to curse, prohibit," and 可能 in part 源自 古法语 ban, which meant "outlawry, banishment," among other things （参见 banal) and was a borrowing 源自 日耳曼语. The sense evolution in 日耳曼语 was 源自 "speak" to "proclaim a threat" to (in Norse, 德语, etc.) "curse." The 日耳曼语 root, borrowed in 拉丁语 and 法语, has been productive: banish, bandit, contraband, etc. 同源词：Banned; banning. Banned in Boston dates 源自 1920 年代, in allusion to the excessive zeal and power of that city's Watch and Ward Society.

example.en: The government decided to ban the sale of single-use plastics.
example.zh: 政府决定禁止销售一次性塑料制品。

entries.etymology: 1590s, borrowed by Spanish or Portuguese from a West African word, possibly Wolof banana. The plant was introduced to the New World from Africa in 1516. Top banana, second banana, etc. are 1950s, from show business slang use of banana for "comedian, especially in a burlesque show." Banana split first attested 1920. Banana oil "nonsense" is slang from c. 1910.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, borrowed by 西班牙语 or 葡萄牙语 源自 a West African word, possibly Wolof banana. The plant was introduced to the New World 源自 Africa 于 1516 年. Top banana, second banana, etc. are 1950 年代, 源自 show business 俚语 use of banana for "comedian, especially in a burlesque show." Banana split 最早见于 1920 年. Banana oil "nonsense" is 俚语 源自 约 1910 年.

entries.definition: n. 条，带；乐队，军乐队；一群， 一伙；波段
entries.etymology: 1520s, "to bind or fasten;" also "to join in a company," from band (n.1) and (n.2) in various noun senses, and partly from French bander. The meaning "to affix an ID band to (a wild animal, etc.)" is attested from 1914. Related: Banded; banding.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "to bind or fasten;" also "to join in a company," 源自 band (n.1) and (n.2) in various 名词 senses, and partly 源自 法语 bander. The 意为 "to affix an ID band to (a wild animal, etc.)" 见于 1914 年. 同源词：Banded; banding.

example.en: The jazz band performed at the festival every summer for five years.
example.zh: 这支爵士乐队连续五年在节日上演出。

entries.etymology: 1590s, from Middle French bandage (16c.), from Old French bander "to bind," from bande "a strip" (see band (n.1)).
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, 源自 中古法语 bandage (16 世纪), 源自 古法语 bander "to bind," 源自 bande "a strip" （参见 band (n.1)).
