entries.definition: n. 巨响，爆炸声；猛击，猛撞 vi. 猛击，猛撞；发出砰的一声， 砰砰作响 vt. 猛击，猛撞
entries.etymology: 1540s, "to strike hard with a loud blow," from a Scandinavian sourse akin to Old Norse banga "to pound, hammer" of echoic origin. Slang meaning "have sexual intercourse with" first recorded 1937. Bang-up "excellent, first-rate," 1820, probably shortened from phrase bang up to the mark. The noun is recorded from late 16c.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "to strike hard with a loud blow," 源自 a Scandinavian sourse akin to 古北欧语 banga "to pound, hammer" of echoic origin. Slang 意为 "have sexual intercourse with" 首见于 1937 年. Bang-up "excellent, first-rate," 1820 年, 可能 shortened 源自 phrase bang up to the mark. The 名词 见于 16 世纪晚期

example.en: The door slammed shut with a loud bang that echoed down the hallway.
example.zh: 门砰地一声猛地关上，声音在走廊里回荡。

entries.etymology: "to act as a banker," 1727, from bank (n.1). As "to deposit in a bank" from 1833. Figurative sense of "to rely on" (i.e. "to put money on") is from 1884, U.S. colloquial. Meaning "to ascend," as of an incline, is from 1892. In aeronautics, from 1911. Related: Banked; banking.
entries.etymologyZh: "to act as a banker," 1727 年, 源自 bank (n.1). As "to deposit in a bank" 自 1833 年起. Figurative 语义 "to rely on" (i.e. "to put money on") 始于 1884 年, U.S. 口语. 义为 "to ascend," as of an incline, 始于 1892 年. In aeronautics, 自 1911 年起. 同源词：Banked; banking.

entries.etymology: "keeper of a bank," 1530s, agent noun formed from bank (n.1), possibly modeled on French banquier (16c.).
entries.etymologyZh: "keeper of a bank," 1530 年代, agent 名词 formed 源自 bank (n.1), possibly modeled on 法语 banquier (16 世纪).

example.en: The banker advised his clients to diversify their investment portfolios.
example.zh: 这位银行家建议客户分散投资组合。

entries.definition: a. 破产的 vt.使破产 n.破产者
entries.etymology: 1560s, from Italian banca rotta, literally "a broken bench,"  from banca "moneylender's shop," literally "bench" (see bank (n.1)) + rotta "broken, defeated, interrupted" from (and remodeled on) Latin rupta, fem. past participle of rumpere "to break" (see rupture (n.)). "[S]o called from the habit of breaking the bench of bankrupts" [Klein]. Earlier in English as a noun, "bankrupt person" (1530s).
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, 源自 意大利语 banca rotta, 字面义为 "a broken bench," 源自 banca "moneylender's shop," 字面义为 "bench" （参见 bank (n.1)) + rotta "broken, defeated, interrupted" 源自 (and remodeled on) 拉丁语 rupta, fem. 为 … 的过去分词 rumpere "to break" （参见 rupture （名）). "[S]o called from the habit of breaking the bench of bankrupts" [Klein]. Earlier in English 作名词时, "bankrupt person" (1530 年代).

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French baniere (Modern French bannière) "flag, banner, standard," from Late Latin bandum "standard," borrowed from a West Germanic cognate of Gothic bandwa "a sign" (see band (n.2)). Figurative use from early 14c. Of newspaper headlines, from 1913.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 baniere (现代法语 bannière) "flag, banner, standard," 源自 晚期拉丁语 bandum "standard," 借自 a West 日耳曼语 同源 of Gothic bandwa "a sign" （参见 band (n.2)). Figurative use 源自 14 世纪初 Of newspaper headlines, 自 1913 年起.

example.en: Protesters marched through the streets carrying a large banner.
example.zh: 抗议者举着一条巨大的横幅游行穿过街道。

entries.etymology: late 15c., "feast, sumptuous entertainment," from French banquet (15c.; in Old French only "small bench"), from Old Italian banchetto, diminutive of banco "bench;" originally a snack eaten on a bench (rather than at table), hence "a slight repast between meals;" the meaning has entirely reversed. As a verb from 1510s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "feast, sumptuous entertainment," 源自 法语 banquet (15 世纪; in 古法语 only "small bench"), 源自 Old 意大利语 banchetto, 为 … 的指小形式 banco "bench;" 原义为 a snack eaten on a bench (rather than at table), hence "a slight repast between meals;" the 意为 has entirely reversed. 作动词时 源自 1510 年代.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to fasten (a gate, etc.) with a bar," from bar (n.1); sense of "to obstruct, prevent" is recorded by 1570s. Expression bar none "without exception" is recorded from 1866.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to fasten (a gate, etc.) with a bar," 源自 bar (n.1); 语义 "to obstruct, prevent" is recorded by 1570 年代. Expression bar none "without exception" 见于 1866 年.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Anglo-French barbour (attested as a surname from early 13c.), from Old French barbeor, barbieor (Modern French barbier, which has a more restricted sense than the English word), from Vulgar Latin *barbatorem, from Latin barba "beard" (see barb (n.)). Originally also regular practitioners of surgery, they were restricted to haircutting and dentistry under Henry VIII.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 barbour (attested 作为 surname 源自 13 世纪初), 源自 古法语 barbeor, barbieor (现代法语 barbier, which has a more restricted sense than the English word), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *barbatorem, 源自 拉丁语 barba "beard" （参见 barb （名）). Originally also regular practitioners of surgery, they were restricted to haircutting and dentistry under Henry VIII.

definitionLines: a.赤裸的，光秃的，空的；极少 的，仅有的
entries.definition: a.赤裸的，光秃的，空的；极少 的，仅有的
entries.etymology: Old English bær "naked, uncovered, unclothed," from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (source also of German bar, Old Norse berr, Dutch baar), from PIE *bhosos (source also of Armenian bok "naked;" Old Church Slavonic bosu, Lithuanian basas "barefoot"). Meaning "sheer, absolute" (c. 1200) is from the notion of "complete in itself."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bær "naked, uncovered, unclothed," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bazaz (source also of 德语 bar, 古北欧语 berr, 荷兰语 baar), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhosos (source also of Armenian bok "naked;" Old Church Slavonic bosu, Lithuanian basas "barefoot"). 义为 "sheer, absolute" (约 1200 年) 始于 the 概念 "complete in itself."

example.en: The walls were bare except for a single painting near the window.
example.zh: 墙壁上空空荡荡，只有窗户旁边挂着一幅画。

entries.etymology: Old English bærlice "openly, clear, public;" see bare (adj.) + -ly (2). Meaning "only, just" is recorded from late 15c.; that of "merely, simply" is from 1570s. In 15c. it also could mean "naked."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bærlice "openly, clear, public;" 参见 bare （形） + -ly (2). 义为 "only, just" 见于 15 世纪晚期; that of "merely, simply" 始于 1570 年代. In 15 世纪 it also could mean "naked."

example.en: He could barely hear the speaker at the back of the vast hall.
example.zh: 他在宽阔大厅的后部几乎听不清演讲者的声音。

entries.definition: v.讨价还价 n. 便宜货；交易
entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French bargaignier (12c., Modern French barguigner) "to haggle over the price," perhaps from Frankish *borganjan "to lend" or some other Germanic source, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *borgan (source also of Old High German borgen; Old English borgian, source of borrow). Another suggestion is that the French word comes from Late Latin barca "a barge," because it "carries goods to and fro." There are difficulties with both suggestions. Related: Bargained; bargaining.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 bargaignier (12 世纪, 现代法语 barguigner) "to haggle over the price," 或源自 Frankish *borganjan "to lend" or some other 日耳曼语 source, 最终源自 原始日耳曼语 *borgan (source also of 古高地德语 borgen; 古英语 borgian, source of borrow). Another suggestion is that the 法语 word comes 源自 晚期拉丁语 barca "a barge," because it "carries goods to and fro." There are difficulties with both suggestions. 同源词：Bargained; bargaining.

example.en: She managed to bargain the price down at the market.
example.zh: 她设法在市场上把价格砍了下来。

entries.definition: vi. 吠；叫骂 n. 树皮；吠声
entries.etymology: in reference to a dog sound, Old English beorcan "to bark," from Proto-Germanic *berkan (source also of Old Norse berkja "to bark"), of echoic origin. Related: Barked; barking. To bark up the wrong tree is U.S. colloquial, first attested 1832, from notion of hounds following the wrong scent.
entries.etymologyZh: in reference to a dog sound, 古英语 beorcan "to bark," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *berkan (source also of 古北欧语 berkja "to bark"), of echoic origin. 同源词：Barked; barking. To bark up the wrong tree is U.S. 口语, 最早见于 1832 年, 源自 概念 hounds following the wrong scent.

example.en: The dog began to bark loudly at the stranger approaching the gate.
example.zh: 狗开始对靠近大门的陌生人大声吠叫。

entries.etymology:
Old English bereærn "barn," literally "barley house," from bere "barley" (see barley) + aern "house," metathesized from *rann, *rasn (source also of Old Norse rann, Gothic razn "house," Old English rest "resting place"). For the formation, compare Old English sealtærn "saltworks," horsern "stable."

Another word for "barn" in Old English was beretun, "barley enclosure" (from tun "enclosure, house"), which accounts for the many Barton place names on the English map, and the common surname. Barn door used figuratively for "broad target" and "great size" since 1540s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bereærn "barn," 字面义为 "barley house," 源自 bere "barley" （参见 barley) + aern "house," metathesized 源自 *rann, *rasn (source also of 古北欧语 rann, Gothic razn "house," 古英语 rest "resting place"). For the formation, 对比 古英语 sealtærn "saltworks," horsern "stable." Another word for "barn" in 古英语 was beretun, "barley enclosure" (源自 tun "enclosure, house"), which accounts for the many Barton place names on the English map, and the common surname. Barn door used figuratively for "broad target" and "great size" 自 1540 年代.

example.en: The farmer stored his grain in a large red barn.
example.zh: 农夫把谷物储存在一间大红色谷仓里。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old French baril (12c.) "barrel, cask, vat," with cognates in all Romance languages (such as Italian barile, Spanish barril), but origin uncertain; perhaps from Gaulish, perhaps somehow related to bar (n.1). Meaning "metal tube of a gun" is from 1640s. Barrel roll in aeronautics is from 1927.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 baril (12 世纪) "barrel, cask, vat," with cognates in all Romance languages (such as 意大利语 barile, 西班牙语 barril), but 来源存疑; 或源自 Gaulish, 或许 somehow related to bar (n.1). 义为 "metal tube of a gun" 始于 1640 年代. Barrel roll in aeronautics 始于 1927 年.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French baraigne, baraing "sterile, barren" (12c.), perhaps originally brahain, of obscure derivation, perhaps from a Germanic language. In England, originally used of women, of land in France. Of land in English from late 14c. As a noun, mid-13c., "a barren woman;" later of land.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 baraigne, baraing "sterile, barren" (12 世纪), 或许 原义为 brahain, of obscure derivation, 或源自 a 日耳曼语 language. In England, 原义为 used of women, of land in France. Of land in English 源自 14 世纪晚期 作名词时, 13 世纪中期, "a barren woman;" later of land.

entries.etymology: early 14c., barere, from Anglo-French barrere, Old French barriere "obstacle, gatekeeper," from barre "bar" (see bar (n.1)). First record of barrier reef is from 1805.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, barere, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 barrere, 古法语 barriere "obstacle, gatekeeper," 源自 barre "bar" （参见 bar (n.1)). First record of barrier reef 始于 1805 年.

example.en: Language differences can be a significant barrier to communication.
example.zh: 语言差异可能是交流的重大障碍。

entries.definition: ．基（础），底（座）；基地 vt.（on）把……建立在……基 础上
entries.etymology: "bottom, foundation, pedestal," early 14c., from Old French bas "depth" (12c.), from Latin basis "foundation," from Greek basis "step, pedestal," from bainein "to step" (see come). The military sense is from 1860. The chemical sense (1810) was introduced in French 1754 by French chemist Guillaume-François Rouelle (1703-1770). Sporting sense of "starting point" ia from 1690s, also "destination of a runner" (1812). As a "safe" spot in a tag-like game, suggested from mid-15c. (as the name of the game later called prisoner's base).
entries.etymologyZh: "bottom, foundation, pedestal," 14 世纪初, 源自 古法语 bas "depth" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 basis "foundation," 源自 希腊语 basis "step, pedestal," 源自 bainein "to step" （参见 come). The military sense 始于 1860 年. The chemical sense (1810 年) was introduced in 法语 1754 年 by 法语 chemist Guillaume-François Rouelle (1703 年-1770 年). Sporting 语义 "starting point" ia 源自 1690 年代, also "destination of a runner" (1812 年). 作为 "safe" spot in a tag-like game, suggested 源自 15 世纪中期 (as the name of the game later called prisoner's base).

example.en: The company decided to base its new strategy on thorough market research.
example.zh: 公司决定将新战略建立在充分市场调研的基础上。

entries.etymology: in the modern sense, 1845, American English, from base (n.) + ball (n.1). Earlier references, such as in Jane Austen's "Northanger Abbey," refer to the game of "rounders," of which baseball is a more elaborate variety. Legendarily invented 1839 by Abner Doubleday in Cooperstown, N.Y. Base was used for "start or finish line of a race" from 1690s; and the sense of "safe spot" found in modern children's game of tag can be traced to 14c. (the sense in baseball is from 1868).
entries.etymologyZh: in the modern sense, 1845 年, American English, 源自 base （名） + ball (n.1). Earlier references, such as in Jane Austen's "Northanger Abbey," refer to the game of "rounders," of which baseball is a more elaborate variety. Legendarily invented 1839 by Abner Doubleday in Cooperstown, N.Y. Base was used for "start or finish line of a race" from 1690s; and the sense of "safe spot" found in modern children's game of tag can be traced to 14 世纪 (the sense in baseball 始于 1868 年).

example.en: He spent his childhood playing baseball in the park with neighborhood kids.
example.zh: 他的童年是在公园里和街坊的孩子们一起打棒球中度过的。

entries.etymology: "lowest story of a building except the cellar," 1730, from base (v.) + -ment.
entries.etymologyZh: "lowest story of a building except the cellar," 1730 年, 源自 base （动） + -ment.

example.en: They stored old furniture in the basement beneath the house.
example.zh: 他们把旧家具存放在房子下面的地下室里。

definitionLines: a.基本的，基础的，根本的；主 要的，首要的
entries.definition: a.基本的，基础的，根本的；主 要的，首要的 n. 基础，基本
entries.etymology: computer language, 1964, initialism (acronym) for Beginners' All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code; invented by Hungarian-born U.S. computer scientist John G. Kemeny (1926-1992) and U.S. computer scientist Thomas E. Kurtz (b.1928).
entries.etymologyZh: computer language, 1964 年, initialism (acronym) for Beginners' All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code; invented by Hungarian-born U.S. computer scientist John G. Kemeny (1926 年-1992 年) and U.S. computer scientist Thomas E. Kurtz (b.1928 年).

example.en: Clean water is one of the most basic needs that all humans share.
example.zh: 清洁的水是所有人共同拥有的最基本需求之一。

entries.etymology: 1903, from basic (adj.) + -ly (2).
entries.etymologyZh: 1903 年, 源自 basic （形） + -ly (2).

example.en: The two plans are basically the same in terms of cost.
example.zh: 这两个方案在成本方面基本上是相同的。

definitionLines: n. 基础，基底；基准，根据
entries.definition: n. 基础，基底；基准，根据
entries.etymology: 1570s, "bottom or foundation (of something material)," from Latin basis "foundation," from Greek basis "a step, stand, base, that whereon one stands," from bainein "go, step" (see come). Transferred and figurative senses (of immaterial things) are from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "bottom or foundation (of something material)," 源自 拉丁语 basis "foundation," 源自 希腊语 basis "a step, stand, base, that whereon one stands," 源自 bainein "go, step" （参见 come). Transferred and figurative senses (of immaterial things) 始于 约 1600 年.

example.en: The team meets on a weekly basis to review progress.
example.zh: 团队每周定期开会回顾进展情况。

entries.etymology: early 13c., from Anglo-French bascat, origin obscure despite much speculation. On one theory from Latin bascauda "kettle, table-vessel," said by the Roman poet Martial to be from Celtic British and perhaps cognate with Latin fascis "bundle, faggot," in which case it probably originally meant "wicker basket." But OED frowns on this, and there is no evidence of such a word in Celtic unless later words in Irish and Welsh, counted as borrowings from English, are original.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 bascat, origin obscure despite much speculation. On one theory 源自 拉丁语 bascauda "kettle, table-vessel," said by the Roman poet Martial to be 源自 Celtic British and 或许 与 … 同源 拉丁语 fascis "bundle, faggot," in which case it 可能 原义为 meant "wicker basket." But OED frowns on this, and there is no evidence of such a word in Celtic unless later words in 爱尔兰语 and Welsh, counted as borrowings 源自 English, are original.

example.en: She filled the basket with fresh fruit from the market.
example.zh: 她把从市场买来的新鲜水果装满了篮子。

entries.etymology: 1892, American English, from basket + ball (n.1). The game was invented 1891 by James A. Naismith (1861-1939), physical education instructor in Springfield, Massachusetts, U.S.
entries.etymologyZh: 1892 年, American English, 源自 basket + ball (n.1). The game was invented 1891 年 by James A. Naismith (1861 年-1939 年), physical education instructor in Springfield, Massachusetts, U.S.

example.zh: 他每个周末都和大学朋友在当地球场打篮球。

example.en: Researchers discovered that bats use echolocation to navigate in complete darkness.

definitionLines: n. 洗澡，沐浴；浴缸，浴盆，浴池
entries.definition: n. 洗澡，沐浴；浴缸，浴盆，浴池
entries.etymology: Old English bæð "immersing in water, mud, etc.," also "quantity of water, etc., for bathing," from Proto-Germanic *batham (source also of Old Norse bað, Middle Dutch bat, German bad), from PIE root *bhe- "to warm" (see fever) + Germanic *-thuz suffix indicating "act, process, condition" (as in birth, death). Original sense was of heating, not immersing in water. The city in Somerset, England (Old English Baðun) was so called from its hot springs. Bath salts attested from 1875 (Dr. Julius Braun, "On the Curative Effects of Baths and Waters").
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bæð "immersing in water, mud, etc.," also "quantity of water, etc., for bathing," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *batham (source also of 古北欧语 bað, Middle 荷兰语 bat, 德语 bad), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhe- "to warm" （参见 fever) + 日耳曼语 *-thuz suffix indicating "act, process, condition" (as in birth, death). Original sense was of heating, not immersing in water. The city in Somerset, England (古英语 Baðun) was so called 源自 its hot springs. Bath salts attested 自 1875 年起 (Dr. Julius Braun, "On the Curative Effects of Baths and Waters").

entries.etymology: 1780, from bath + room (n.). Originally a room with apparatus for bathing, used 20c. in U.S. as a euphemism for a lavatory and often noted as a word that confused British travelers. To  go to the bathroom, euphemism for "relieve oneself; urinate, defecate," from 1920 (in a book for children), but typically used without regard for whether an actual bathroom is involved.

entries.etymology:
1530s, "action of battering," from Middle French batterie, from Old French baterie (12c.) "beating, thrashing, assault," from batre "beat," from Latin battuere "beat" (see batter (v.)).

Meaning shifted in Middle French from "bombardment" ("heavy blows" upon city walls or fortresses) to "unit of artillery" (a sense recorded in English from 1550s). Extension to "electrical cell" (1748, first used by Ben Franklin) is perhaps from the artillery sense via notion of "discharges" of electricity. In Middle English, bateri meant only "forged metal ware." In obsolete baseball jargon battery was the word for "pitcher and catcher" considered as a unit (1867, originally only the pitcher).
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "action of battering," 源自 中古法语 batterie, 源自 古法语 baterie (12 世纪) "beating, thrashing, assault," 源自 batre "beat," 源自 拉丁语 battuere "beat" （参见 batter （动）). 义为 shifted in 中古法语 源自 "bombardment" ("heavy blows" upon city walls or fortresses) to "unit of artillery" (a sense recorded in English 源自 1550 年代). Extension to "electrical cell" (1748 年, first used by Ben Franklin) is 或源自 the artillery sense 经由 概念 "discharges" of electricity. In 中古英语, bateri meant only "forged metal ware." In 已废 baseball jargon battery was the word for "pitcher and catcher" considered 作为 unit (1867 年, 原义为 only the pitcher).

example.en: The remote control stopped working because the battery was dead.

entries.etymology:
Old English beon, beom, bion "be, exist, come to be, become, happen," from Proto-Germanic *biju- "I am, I will be." This "b-root" is from PIE root *bheue- "to be, exist, grow, come into being," and in addition to the words in English it yielded German present first and second person singular (bin, bist, from Old High German bim "I am," bist "thou art"), Latin perfective tenses of esse (fui "I was," etc.), Old Church Slavonic byti "be," Greek phu- "become," Old Irish bi'u "I am," Lithuanian bu'ti "to be," Russian byt' "to be," etc. It also is behind Sanskrit bhavah "becoming," bhavati "becomes, happens," bhumih "earth, world." 

The modern verb to be in its entirety represents the merger of two once-distinct verbs, the "b-root" represented by be and the am/was verb, which was itself a conglomerate. Roger Lass ("Old English") describes the verb as "a collection of semantically related paradigm fragments," while Weekley calls it "an accidental conglomeration from the different Old English dial[ect]s." It is the most irregular verb in Modern English and the most common. Collective in all Germanic languages, it has eight different forms in Modern English:

BE (infinitive, subjunctive, imperative)
AM (present 1st person singular)
ARE (present 2nd person singular and all plural)
IS (present 3rd person singular)
WAS (past 1st and 3rd persons singular)
WERE (past 2nd person singular, all plural; subjunctive)
BEING (progressive & present participle; gerund)
BEEN (perfect participle).

The paradigm in Old English was: SING.PL.1st pres.ic eomic beowe sind(on)we beoð2nd pres.þu eartþu bistge sind(on)ge beoð3rd pres.he ishe biðhie sind(on)hie beoð1st pret.ic wæswe wæron2nd pret.þu wærege waeron3rd pret.heo wæshie wæron1st pret. subj.ic wærewe wæren2nd pret. subj.þu wærege wæren3rd pret. subj.Egcferð wærehie wærenThe "b-root" had no past tense in Old English, but often served as future tense of am/was. In 13c. it took the place of the infinitive, participle and imperative forms of am/was. Later its plural forms (we beth, ye ben, they be) became standard in Middle English and it made inroads into the singular (I be, thou beest, he beth), but forms of are claimed this turf in the 1500s and replaced be in the plural. For the origin and evolution of the am/was branches of this tangle, see am and was.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beon, beom, bion "be, exist, come to be, become, happen," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *biju- "I am, I will be." This "b-root" 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheue- "to be, exist, grow, come into being," and in addition to the words in English it yielded 德语 present first and second person singular (bin, bist, 源自 古高地德语 bim "I am," bist "thou art"), 拉丁语 perfective tenses of esse (fui "I was," etc.), Old Church Slavonic byti "be," 希腊语 phu- "become," Old 爱尔兰语 bi'u "I am," Lithuanian bu'ti "to be," 俄语 byt' "to be," etc. It also is behind 梵语 bhavah "becoming," bhavati "becomes, happens," bhumih "earth, world." The modern 动词 to be in its entirety represents the merger of two once-distinct verbs, the "b-root" represented by be and the am/was 动词, which was itself a conglomerate. The paradigm in 古英语 was: SING.PL.1st pres.ic eomic beowe sind(on)we beoð2nd pres.þu eartþu bistge sind(on)ge beoð3rd pres.he ishe biðhie sind(on)hie beoð1st pret.ic wæswe wæron2nd pret.þu wærege waeron3rd pret.heo wæshie wæron1st pret. subj.ic wærewe wæren2nd pret. subj.þu wærege wæren3rd pret. subj.Egcferð wærehie wærenThe "b-root" had no past tense in 古英语, but 常 served as future tense of am/was. In 13 世纪 it took the place of the infinitive, participle and imperative forms of am/was. For the origin and evolution of the am/was branches of this tangle, 参见 am and was.

entries.etymology: 1530s, "loose, water-worn pebbles of the seashore," probably from Old English bæce, bece "stream," from Proto-Germanic *bakiz. Extended to loose, pebbly shores (1590s), and in dialect around Sussex and Kent beach still has the meaning "pebbles worn by the waves." French grève shows the same evolution. Beach ball first recorded 1940; beach bum first recorded 1950.

entries.etymology:
Old English beam originally "living tree," but by late 10c. also "rafter, post, ship's timber," from Proto-Germanic *baumaz (source also of Old Norse baðmr, Old Frisian bam "tree, gallows, beam," Middle Dutch boom, Old High German boum, German Baum "tree," Gothic bagms), perhaps from PIE verb root *bheue- "to grow" (see be). The shift from *-au- to -ea- is regular in Old English.

Meaning "ray of light" developed in Old English, probably because it was used by Bede to render Latin columna lucis, the Biblical "pillar of fire." Nautical sense of "one of the horizontal transverse timbers holding a ship together" is from early 13c., hence "greatest breadth of a ship," and slang broad in the beam "wide-hipped" (of persons). To be on the beam (1941) was originally an aviator's term for "to follow the course indicated by a radio beam."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beam 原义为 "living tree," but by 10 世纪晚期 also "rafter, post, ship's timber," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *baumaz (source also of 古北欧语 baðmr, 古弗里西语 bam "tree, gallows, beam," Middle 荷兰语 boom, 古高地德语 boum, 德语 Baum "tree," Gothic bagms), 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) 动词 root *bheue- "to grow" （参见 be). The shift 源自 *-au- to -ea- is regular in 古英语. 义为 "ray of light" developed in 古英语, 可能 because it was used by Bede to render 拉丁语 columna lucis, the Biblical "pillar of fire." Nautical 语义 "one of the horizontal transverse timbers holding a ship together" 始于 13 世纪初, hence "greatest breadth of a ship," and 俚语 broad in the beam "wide-hipped" (of persons). To be on the beam (1941 年) was 原义为 an aviator's term for "to follow the course indicated by a radio beam."

example.en: A narrow beam of sunlight broke through the clouds and lit up the valley.
example.zh: 一道细细的阳光穿破云层，照亮了山谷。

entries.etymology:
Old English bean "bean, pea, legume," from Proto-Germanic *bauno (source also of Old Norse baun, Middle Dutch bone, Dutch boon, Old High German bona, German Bohne), and related to Latin faba "bean;" Greek phakos "lentil;" Albanian bathë "horse-bean;" Old Prussian babo, Russian bob "bean," but the original form is obscure; perhaps from a PIE reduplicated base *bha-bha- 

As a metaphor for "something of small value" it is attested from c. 1300. Meaning "head" is U.S. baseball slang c. 1905 (in bean-ball "a pitch thrown at the head"); thus slang verb bean meaning "to hit on the head," attested from 1910.

The notion of lucky or magic beans in English folklore is from the exotic beans or large seeds that wash up occasionally in Cornwall and western Scotland, carried from the Caribbean or South America by the Gulf Stream. They were cherished, believed to ward off the evil eye and aid in childbirth.

Slang bean-counter "accountant" recorded by 1971. To not know beans (American English, 1933) is perhaps from the "of little worth" sense, but may have a connection to colloquial expression recorded around Somerset, to know how many beans make five "be a clever fellow."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bean "bean, pea, legume," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bauno (source also of 古北欧语 baun, Middle 荷兰语 bone, 荷兰语 boon, 古高地德语 bona, 德语 Bohne), and related to 拉丁语 faba "bean;" 希腊语 phakos "lentil;" Albanian bathë "horse-bean;" Old Prussian babo, 俄语 bob "bean," but the original form is obscure; 或源自 a 原始印欧语 (PIE) reduplicated base *bha-bha- 作为 metaphor for "something of small value" it 见于 约 1300 年. 义为 "head" is U.S. baseball 俚语 约 1905 年 (in bean-ball "a pitch thrown at the head"); thus 俚语 动词 bean 意为 "to hit on the head," attested 自 1910 年起. The 概念 lucky or magic beans in English folklore 始于 the exotic beans or large seeds that wash up occasionally in Cornwall and western Scotland, carried 源自 Caribbean or South America by the Gulf Stream. They were cherished, believed to ward off the evil eye and aid in childbirth. Slang bean-counter "accountant" recorded 截至 1971 年. To not know beans (American English, 1933 年) is 或源自 the "of little worth" sense, but may have a connection to 口语 expression recorded around Somerset, to know how many beans make five "be a clever fellow."

entries.etymology:
Old English beran "to bear, bring; bring forth, produce; to endure, sustain; to wear" (class IV strong verb; past tense bær, past participle boren), from Proto-Germanic *beran (source also of Old Saxon beran, Old Frisian bera, Old High German beran, German gebären, Old Norse bera, Gothic bairan "to carry, bear, give birth to"), from PIE root *bher- (1) meaning both "give birth" (though only English and German strongly retain this sense, and Russian has beremennaya "pregnant") and "carry a burden, bring" (see infer).

Ball bearings "bear" the friction. Many senses are from notion of "move onward by pressure." Old English past tense bær became Middle English bare; alternative bore began to appear c. 1400, but bare remained the literary form till after 1600. Past participle distinction of borne for "carried" and born for "given birth" is from late 18c. To bear (something) in mind is from 1530s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beran "to bear, bring; bring forth, produce; to endure, sustain; to wear" (class IV strong 动词; past tense bær, past participle boren), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *beran (source also of 古撒克逊语 beran, 古弗里西语 bera, 古高地德语 beran, 德语 gebären, 古北欧语 bera, Gothic bairan "to carry, bear, give birth to"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bher- (1) 意为 both "give birth" (though only English and 德语 strongly retain this sense, and 俄语 has beremennaya "pregnant") and "carry a burden, bring" （参见 infer). Ball bearings "bear" the friction. Many senses 始于 概念 "move onward by pressure." 古英语 past tense bær became 中古英语 bare; alternative bore began to appear 约 1400 年, but bare remained the literary form till after 1600 年. Past participle distinction of borne for "carried" and born for "given birth" 始于 18 世纪晚期 To bear (something) in mind 始于 1530 年代.

example.en: She could hardly bear the noise from the construction site next door.
example.zh: 她几乎无法忍受隔壁建筑工地的噪音。

entries.etymology:
Old English beard "beard," from West Germanic *barthaz (source also of Old Frisian berd, Middle Dutch baert, Old High German bart, German bart), seemingly from PIE *bhardh-a- "beard" (source also of Old Church Slavonic brada, Lithuanian barzda, and perhaps Latin barba "beard").

Pubic hair sense is from 1600s (but neþir berd "pubic hair" is from late 14c.); in the 1811 "Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue," the phrase beard-splitter is defined as, "A man much given to wenching" (see beaver).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beard "beard," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *barthaz (source also of 古弗里西语 berd, Middle 荷兰语 baert, 古高地德语 bart, 德语 bart), seemingly 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhardh-a- "beard" (source also of Old Church Slavonic brada, Lithuanian barzda, and 或许 拉丁语 barba "beard"). Pubic hair sense 始于 1600 年代 (but neþir berd "pubic hair" 始于 14 世纪晚期); in the 1811 年 "Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue," the phrase beard-splitter is defined as, "A man much given to wenching" （参见 beaver).

example.en: He grew a thick beard during the long winter months.
example.zh: 在漫长的冬季里，他留起了浓密的胡须。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French beste "animal, wild beast," figuratively "fool, idiot" (11c., Modern French bête), from Vulgar Latin *besta, from Latin bestia "beast, wild animal," which is of unknown origin. Used to translate Latin animal. Replaced Old English deor (see deer) as the generic word for "wild creature," only to be ousted 16c. by animal. Of persons felt to be animal-like in various senses from early 13c. Of the figure in the Christian apocalypse story from late 14c.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 beste "animal, wild beast," figuratively "fool, idiot" (11 世纪, 现代法语 bête), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *besta, 源自 拉丁语 bestia "beast, wild animal," which is 来源不详. Used to translate 拉丁语 animal. Replaced 古英语 deor （参见 deer) as the generic word for "wild creature," only to be ousted 16 世纪 by animal. Of persons felt to be animal-like in various senses 源自 13 世纪初 Of the figure in the Christian apocalypse story 源自 14 世纪晚期

example.en: The lion is often called the king of beasts for its strength and majesty.

entries.etymology:
Old English beatan "inflict blows on, thrash" (class VII strong verb; past tense beot, past participle beaten), from Proto-Germanic *bautan (source also of Old Norse bauta, Old High German bozan "to beat"), from PIE root *bhau- "to strike" (see batter (v.)). Of the heart, c. 1200, from notion of it striking against the breast. Meaning "to overcome in a contest" is from 1610s (the source of the sense of "legally avoid, escape" in beat the charges, etc., attested from c. 1920 in underworld slang).

Past tense beat is from c. 1500, probably not from Old English but a shortening of Middle English beted. Dead-beat (originally "tired-out") preserves the old past participle. Meaning "strike cover to rouse or drive game" (c. 1400) is source of beat around the bush (1570s), the metaphoric sense of which has shifted from "make preliminary motions" to "avoid, evade." Command beat it "go away" first recorded 1906 (though "action of feet upon the ground" was a sense of Old English betan). To beat off "masturbate" is recorded by 1960s. For beat generation see beatnik.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beatan "inflict blows on, thrash" (class VII strong 动词; past tense beot, past participle beaten), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bautan (source also of 古北欧语 bauta, 古高地德语 bozan "to beat"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhau- "to strike" （参见 batter （动）). Of the heart, 约 1200 年, 源自 概念 it striking against the breast. 义为 "to overcome in a contest" 始于 1610 年代 (the source of the 语义 "legally avoid, escape" in beat the charges, etc., attested 源自 约 1920 年 in underworld 俚语). Past tense beat 始于 约 1500 年, 可能 not 源自 古英语 but a shortening of 中古英语 beted. Dead-beat (原义为 "tired-out") preserves the old past participle. 义为 "strike cover to rouse or drive game" (约 1400 年) is source of beat around the bush (1570 年代), the metaphoric 语义 which has shifted 源自 "make preliminary motions" to "avoid, evade." Command beat it "go away" 首见于 1906 年 (though "action of feet upon the ground" was a 语义 古英语 betan). To beat off "masturbate" is recorded by 1960 年代. For beat generation 参见 beatnik.

example.en: The underdog team managed to beat the defending champions by a single point.

definitionLines: n. 美，美丽；美人，美丽的东西
entries.definition: n. 美，美丽；美人，美丽的东西
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "physical attractiveness," also "goodness, courtesy," from Anglo-French beute, Old French biauté "beauty, seductiveness, beautiful person" (12c., Modern French beauté), earlier beltet, from Vulgar Latin bellitatem (nominative bellitas) "state of being handsome," from Latin bellus "pretty, handsome, charming," in classical Latin used especially of women and children, or ironically or insultingly of men, perhaps from PIE *dw-en-elo-, diminutive of root *deu- (2) "to do, perform; show favor, revere" (see bene-). Famously defined by Stendhal as la promesse de bonheur "the promise of happiness."

Replaced Old English wlite. Concrete meaning "a beautiful woman" is first recorded late 14c. Beauty sleep "sleep before midnight" is attested by 1850. Beauty spot is from 1650s. Beauty parlor is from 1894.

Beauté du diable (literally "devil's beauty") is used as a French phrase in English from 1825.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "physical attractiveness," also "goodness, courtesy," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 beute, 古法语 biauté "beauty, seductiveness, beautiful person" (12 世纪, 现代法语 beauté), earlier beltet, 源自 通俗拉丁语 bellitatem (主格 bellitas) "state of being handsome," 源自 拉丁语 bellus "pretty, handsome, charming," in classical 拉丁语 used 尤指 of women and children，或ironically or insultingly of men, 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *dw-en-elo-, 为 … 的指小形式 root *deu- (2) "to do, perform; show favor, revere" （参见 bene-). Famously defined by Stendhal as la promesse de bonheur "the promise of happiness." Replaced 古英语 wlite. Concrete 意为 "a beautiful woman" is 首见于 14 世纪晚期 Beauty sleep "sleep before midnight" is attested 截至 1850 年. Beauty spot 始于 1650 年代. Beauty parlor 始于 1894 年. Beauté du diable (字面义为 "devil's beauty") is used 作为 法语 phrase in English 自 1825 年起.

entries.etymology: Old English bedd "bed, couch, resting place, garden plot," from Proto-Germanic *badjam "sleeping place dug in the ground" (source also of Old Frisian, Old Saxon bed, Middle Dutch bedde, Old Norse beðr, Old High German betti, German Bett, Gothic badi "bed"), from PIE root *bhedh- "to dig, pierce" (source also of Hittite beda- "to pierce, prick," Greek bothyros "pit," Latin fossa "ditch," Lithuanian bedre "to dig," Breton bez "grave"). Both "sleeping" and "gardening" senses are in Old English. Meaning "bottom of a lake, sea, watercourse" is from 1580s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bedd "bed, couch, resting place, garden plot," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *badjam "sleeping place dug in the ground" (source also of 古弗里西语, 古撒克逊语 bed, Middle 荷兰语 bedde, 古北欧语 beðr, 古高地德语 betti, 德语 Bett, Gothic badi "bed"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhedh- "to dig, pierce" (source also of Hittite beda- "to pierce, prick," 希腊语 bothyros "pit," 拉丁语 fossa "ditch," Lithuanian bedre "to dig," Breton bez "grave"). entries.etymology:
stinging insect, Old English beo "bee," from Proto-Germanic *bion (source also of Old Norse by, Old High German bia, Middle Dutch bie), possibly from PIE root *bhi- "quiver." Used metaphorically for "busy worker" since 1530s.

Sense of "meeting of neighbors to unite their labor for the benefit of one of their number," 1769, American English, probably is from comparison to the social activity of the insect; this was extended to other senses (such as spelling bee, first attested 1809; Raising-bee (1814) for building construction; also hanging bee "a lynching"). To have a bee in (one's) bonnet (1825), said of one who is harebrained or has an intense new notion or fancy, is said in Jamieson to be Scottish, perhaps from earlier expressions such as head full of bees (1510s), denoting mad mental activity.

To have a bee in (one's) bonnet (1825 年), said of one who is harebrained or has an intense new notion or fancy, is said in Jamieson to be 苏格兰语, 或源自 earlier expressions such as head full of bees (1510 年代), denoting mad mental activity.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old French buef "ox; beef; ox hide" (11c., Modern French boeuf), from Latin bovem (nominative bos, genitive bovis) "ox, cow," from PIE root *gwou- "cow, ox, bull" (see cow (n.)). Original plural was beeves.

entries.etymology:
Old English beor "strong drink, beer, mead," a word of much-disputed and ambiguous origin, cognate with Old Frisian biar, Middle Dutch and Dutch bier, Old High German bior, German Bier.

Probably a 6c. West Germanic monastic borrowing of Vulgar Latin biber "a drink, beverage" (from Latin infinitive bibere "to drink;" see imbibe). Another suggestion is that it comes from Proto-Germanic *beuwoz-, from *beuwo- "barley." The native Germanic word for the beverage was the one that yielded ale (q.v.).

They did have words for it, however. Greek brytos, used in reference to Thracian or Phrygian brews, was related to Old English breowan "brew;" Latin zythum is from Greek zythos, first used of Egyptian beer and treated as an Egyptian word but perhaps truly Greek and related to zyme "leaven." French bière is from Germanic. Spanish cerveza is from Latin cervesia "beer," perhaps related to Latin cremor "thick broth."

Old Church Slavonic pivo, source of the general Slavic word for "beer," is originally "a drink" (compare Old Church Slavonic piti "drink"). French bière is a 16c. borrowing from German. U.S. slang beer goggles, through which every potential romantic partner looks desirable, is from 1986.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beor "strong drink, beer, mead," a word of much-disputed and ambiguous origin, 与 … 同源 古弗里西语 biar, Middle 荷兰语 and 荷兰语 bier, 古高地德语 bior, 德语 Bier. Probably a 6 世纪 West 日耳曼语 monastic borrowing of 通俗拉丁语 biber "a drink, beverage" (源自 拉丁语 infinitive bibere "to drink;" 参见 imbibe). Another suggestion is that it comes 源自 原始日耳曼语 *beuwoz-, 源自 *beuwo- "barley." The 本族 日耳曼语 word for the beverage was the one that yielded ale (q.v.). They did have words for it, however. 希腊语 brytos, used in reference to Thracian or Phrygian brews, was related to 古英语 breowan "brew;" 拉丁语 zythum 始于 希腊语 zythos, first used of Egyptian beer and treated 作为 Egyptian word but 或许 truly 希腊语 and related to zyme "leaven." 法语 bière 始于 日耳曼语. 西班牙语 cerveza 始于 拉丁语 cervesia "beer," 或许 related to 拉丁语 cremor "thick broth." Old Church Slavonic pivo, source of the general Slavic word for "beer," is 原义为 "a drink" (对比 Old Church Slavonic piti "drink"). 法语 bière is a 16 世纪 borrowing 源自 德语. U.S. 俚语 beer goggles, through which every potential romantic partner looks desirable, 始于 1986 年.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, perhaps from Old English bedecian "to beg," from Proto-Germanic *beth-; or possibly from Anglo-French begger, from Old French begart (see beggar). The Old English word for "beg" was wædlian, from wædl "poverty." Of trained dogs, 1816.

As a courteous mode of asking (beg pardon, etc.), first attested c. 1600. To beg the question translates Latin petitio principii, and means "to assume something that hasn't been proven as a basis of one's argument," thus "asking" one's opponent to give something unearned, though more of the nature of taking it for granted without warrant.

Of trained dogs, 1816 年. 作为 courteous mode of asking (beg pardon, etc.), 最早见于 约 1600 年. To beg the question translates 拉丁语 petitio principii, and means "to assume something that hasn't been proven as a basis of one's argument," thus "asking" one's opponent to give something unearned, though more of the nature of taking it for granted without warrant.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French begart, originally a member of the Beghards, lay brothers of mendicants in the Low Countries, from Middle Dutch beggaert "mendicant," of uncertain origin, with pejorative suffix (see -ard). Compare Beguine. Early folk etymology connected the English word with bag. Form with -ar attested from 14c., but begger was more usual 15c.-17c. The feminine form beggestere is attested as a surname from c. 1300. Beggar's velvet was an old name for "dust bunnies." "Beggers should be no choosers" is in Heywood (1562).

entries.etymology: Old English beginnan "to begin, attempt, undertake," a rare word beside the more usual form onginnan (class III strong verb; past tense ongann, past participle ongunnen); from bi- (see be-) + West Germanic *ginnan, of obscure meaning and found only in compounds, perhaps "to open, open up" (compare Old High German in-ginnan "to cut open, open up," also "begin, undertake"), with sense evolution from "open" to "begin." Cognates elsewhere in Germanic include Old Frisian biginna "to begin," Middle Dutch beghinnen, Old High German beginnan, German beginnen, Old Frisian bijenna "to begin," Gothic duginnan.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beginnan "to begin, attempt, undertake," a rare word beside the more usual form onginnan (class III strong 动词; past tense ongann, past participle ongunnen); 源自 bi- （参见 be-) + West 日耳曼语 *ginnan, of obscure 意为 and found only in compounds, 或许 "to open, open up" (对比 古高地德语 in-ginnan "to cut open, open up," also "begin, undertake"), with sense evolution 源自 "open" to "begin." Cognates elsewhere in 日耳曼语 include 古弗里西语 biginna "to begin," Middle 荷兰语 beghinnen, 古高地德语 beginnan, 德语 beginnen, 古弗里西语 bijenna "to begin," Gothic duginnan.

definitionLines: n. 相信；信仰，信条，信念
entries.definition: n. 相信；信仰，信条，信念
entries.etymology:
late 12c., bileave, replacing Old English geleafa "belief, faith," from West Germanic *ga-laubon "to hold dear, esteem, trust" (source also of Old Saxon gilobo, Middle Dutch gelove, Old High German giloubo, German Glaube), from *galaub- "dear, esteemed," from intensive prefix *ga- + *leubh- "to care, desire, like, love" (see love (v.)). The prefix was altered on analogy of the verb believe. The distinction of the final consonant from that of believe developed 15c.

Belief used to mean "trust in God," while faith meant "loyalty to a person based on promise or duty" (a sense preserved in keep one's faith, in good (or bad) faith and in common usage of faithful, faithless, which contain no notion of divinity). But faith, as cognate of Latin fides, took on the religious sense beginning in 14c. translations, and belief had by 16c. become limited to "mental acceptance of something as true," from the religious use in the sense of "things held to be true as a matter of religious doctrine" (a sense attested from early 13c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪晚期, bileave, replacing 古英语 geleafa "belief, faith," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *ga-laubon "to hold dear, esteem, trust" (source also of 古撒克逊语 gilobo, Middle 荷兰语 gelove, 古高地德语 giloubo, 德语 Glaube), 源自 *galaub- "dear, esteemed," 源自 intensive prefix *ga- + *leubh- "to care, desire, like, love" （参见 love （动）). The prefix was altered on analogy of the 动词 believe. The distinction of the final consonant 源自 that of believe developed 15 世纪 Belief used to mean "trust in God," while faith meant "loyalty to a person based on promise or duty" (a sense preserved in keep one's faith, in good (or bad) faith and in common usage of faithful, faithless, which contain no 概念 divinity). But faith, as 同源 of 拉丁语 fides, took on the religious sense beginning in 14 世纪 translations, and belief had by 16 世纪 become limited to "mental acceptance of something as true," 源自 religious use in the 语义 "things held to be true as a matter of religious doctrine" (a sense attested 源自 13 世纪初).

example.en: His strong belief in hard work shaped every decision he made.
example.zh: 他对勤劳的坚定信念影响着他所做的每一个决定。

entries.definition: vt. 相信，认力 vi. 相信，信任，信奉
entries.etymology:
Old English belyfan "to believe," earlier geleafa (Mercian), gelefa (Northumbrian), gelyfan (West Saxon) "believe," from Proto-Germanic *ga-laubjan "to believe," perhaps literally "hold dear, love" (source also of Old Saxon gilobian "believe," Dutch geloven, Old High German gilouben, German glauben), ultimately a compound based on PIE *leubh- "to care, desire, love" (see belief).

Spelling beleeve is common till 17c.; then altered, perhaps by influence of relieve, etc. To believe on instead of in was more common in 16c. but now is a peculiarity of theology; believe of also sometimes was used in 17c. Related: Believed (formerly occasionally beleft); believing. Expression believe it or not attested by 1874; Robert Ripley's newspaper cartoon of the same name is from 1918. Emphatic you better believe attested from 1854.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 belyfan "to believe," earlier geleafa (Mercian), gelefa (Northumbrian), gelyfan (West Saxon) "believe," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *ga-laubjan "to believe," 或许 字面义为 "hold dear, love" (source also of 古撒克逊语 gilobian "believe," 荷兰语 geloven, 古高地德语 gilouben, 德语 glauben), ultimately a 复合词 based on 原始印欧语 (PIE) *leubh- "to care, desire, love" （参见 belief). Spelling beleeve is common till 17 世纪; 之后 altered, 或许 by influence of relieve, etc. To believe on instead of in was more common in 16 世纪 but 现在 is a peculiarity of theology; believe of also 有时 was used in 17 世纪 同源词：Believed (formerly occasionally beleft); believing. Expression believe it or not attested 截至 1874 年; Robert Ripley's newspaper cartoon of the same name 始于 1918 年. Emphatic you better believe attested 自 1854 年起.

example.en: Most scientists firmly believe that climate change is driven by human activity.

entries.etymology: Old English belle, common North Sea Germanic (cognates: Middle Dutch belle, Middle Low German belle) but not found elsewhere in Germanic (except as a borrowing), from PIE root *bhel- (4) "to sound, roar." Statistical bell curve was coined 1870s in French. Of glasses in the shape of a bell from 1640s. Bell pepper is from 1707, so called for its shape. Bell, book, and candle is a reference to a form of excommunication. To ring a bell "awaken a memory" (1934) is perhaps a reference to Pavlovian experiments.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 belle, common North Sea 日耳曼语 (cognates: Middle 荷兰语 belle, Middle Low 德语 belle) but not found elsewhere in 日耳曼语 (except 作为 borrowing), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhel- (4) "to sound, roar." Statistical bell curve was coined 1870 年代 in 法语. Of glasses in the shape of a bell 源自 1640 年代. Bell pepper 始于 1707 年, so called for its shape. Bell, book, and candle is a reference to a form of excommunication. To ring a bell "awaken a memory" (1934 年) is 或许 a reference to Pavlovian experiments.

entries.etymology:
Old English belg, bylig (West Saxon), bælg (Anglian) "leather bag, purse, bellows," from Proto-Germanic *balgiz "bag" (source also of Old Norse belgr "bag, bellows," bylgja "billow," Gothic balgs "wineskin"), from PIE *bholgh-, from root *bhelgh- "to swell," an extension of *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell" (see bole). Meaning shifted to "abdomen of a human or animal" (late 13c.) as the old plural form of the noun emerged as a separate word (see bellows). Meaning "bulging part or concave surface of anything" is 1590s. The West Germanic root had a figurative or extended sense of "anger, arrogance" (as in Old English bolgenmod "enraged;" belgan (v.) "to become angry"), probably from the notion of "swelling."

Indo-European languages commonly use the same word for both the external belly and the internal (stomach, womb, etc.), but the distinction of external and internal is somewhat present in English belly/stomach; Greek gastr- (see gastric) in classical language denoted the paunch or belly, while modern science uses it only in reference to the stomach as an organ.

As a personal name from 12c. From c. 1200 as a symbol of gluttony. Belly-naked in Middle English was "stripped to the belly, completely naked." Fastidious avoidance of belly in speech and writing (compensated for by stretching the senses of imported stomach and abdomen, baby-talk tummy and misappropriated midriff) began late 18c. and the word was banished from Bibles in many early 19c. editions. Belly-punch (n.) is attested from 1811.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 belg, bylig (West Saxon), bælg (Anglian) "leather bag, purse, bellows," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *balgiz "bag" (source also of 古北欧语 belgr "bag, bellows," bylgja "billow," Gothic balgs "wineskin"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bholgh-, 源自 root *bhelgh- "to swell," an extension of *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell" （参见 bole). 义为 shifted to "abdomen of a human or animal" (13 世纪晚期) as the old plural form of the 名词 emerged 作为 separate word （参见 bellows). 义为 "bulging part or concave surface of anything" is 1590 年代. The West 日耳曼语 root had a figurative or extended 语义 "anger, arrogance" (as in 古英语 bolgenmod "enraged;" belgan （动） "to become angry"), 可能 源自 概念 "swelling." Indo-European languages commonly use the same word for both the external belly and the internal (stomach, womb, etc.), but the distinction of external and internal is somewhat present in English belly/stomach; 希腊语 gastr- （参见 gastric) in classical language denoted the paunch or belly, while modern science uses it only in reference to the stomach 作为 organ. 作为 personal name 源自 12 世纪 From 约 1200 年 作为 symbol of gluttony. Belly-naked in 中古英语 was "stripped to the belly, completely naked." Fastidious avoidance of belly in speech and writing (compensated for by stretching the senses of imported stomach and abdomen, baby-talk tummy and misappropriated midriff) began 18 世纪晚期 and the word was banished 源自 Bibles in many 19 世纪初 editions. Belly-punch （名） 见于 1811 年.

example.en: The baby laughed as his mother tickled his belly.
example.zh: 当妈妈挠他肚子时，婴儿笑了起来。

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "to go along with, properly relate to," from be- intensive prefix, + longen "to go," from Old English langian "pertain to, to go along with," which is of unknown origin. Senses of "be the property of" and "be a member of" first recorded late 14c. Cognate with Middle Dutch belanghen, Dutch belangen, German belangen. Replaced earlier Old English gelang, with completive prefix ge-.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "to go along with, properly relate to," 源自 be- intensive prefix, + longen "to go," 源自 古英语 langian "pertain to, to go along with," which is 来源不详. Senses of "be the property of" and "be a member of" 首见于 14 世纪晚期 Cognate with Middle 荷兰语 belanghen, 荷兰语 belangen, 德语 belangen. Replaced earlier 古英语 gelang, with completive prefix ge-.

example.en: This ancient manuscript belongs to the national museum's permanent collection.
example.zh: 这份古老的手稿属于国家博物馆的永久馆藏。

entries.etymology: "goods, effects, possessions," 1817, from plural of verbal noun from belong.
entries.etymologyZh: "goods, effects, possessions," 1817 年, 源自 为 … 的复数 verbal 名词 源自 belong.

entries.etymology: late 14c., from past participle of verb belove (c. 1200), from be- + loven "to love" (see love (v.)). Noun meaning "one who is beloved" is from 1520s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 为 … 的过去分词 动词 belove (约 1200 年), 源自 be- + loven "to love" （参见 love （动）). Noun 意为 "one who is beloved" 始于 1520 年代.

example.en: She kept the beloved letters from her grandmother in a box.
example.zh: 她把祖母写给她的珍爱信件保存在一个盒子里。

entries.etymology: early 14c., biloogh, from be- "by, about" + logh, lou, lowe "low" (see low (adj.)). Apparently a variant of earlier a-lowe (influenced by other adverbs in be-; see before), the parallel form to an-high (now on high). Beneath was the usual word; below was very rare in Middle English and gained currency only in 16c. It is frequent in Shakespeare. As a preposition from 1570s. According to Fowler, below is the opposite of above and concerns difference of level and suggests comparison of independent things. Under is the opposite of over and is concerned with superposition and subjection and suggests some interrelation.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, biloogh, 源自 be- "by, about" + logh, lou, lowe "low" （参见 low （形）). Apparently a 为 … 的变体 earlier a-lowe (influenced by other adverbs in be-; 参见 before), the parallel form to an-high (现在 on high). Beneath was the usual word; below was very rare in 中古英语 and gained currency only in 16 世纪 It is frequent in Shakespeare. 作为 preposition 源自 1570 年代. According to Fowler, below is the opposite of above and concerns difference of level and suggests comparison of independent things. Under is the opposite of over and is concerned with superposition and subjection and suggests some interrelation.

entries.etymology:
Old English belt "belt, girdle," from Proto-Germanic *baltjaz (source also of Old High German balz, Old Norse balti, Swedish bälte), an early Germanic borrowing from Latin balteus "girdle, sword belt," said by Varro to be an Etruscan word.

As a mark of rank or distinction, mid-14c.; references to boxing championship belts date from 1812. Mechanical sense is from 1795. Transferred sense of "broad stripe encircling something" is from 1660s. Below the belt "unfair" (1889) is from pugilism. To get something under (one's) belt is to get it into one's stomach. To tighten (one's) belt "endure privation" is from 1887.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 belt "belt, girdle," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *baltjaz (source also of 古高地德语 balz, 古北欧语 balti, Swedish bälte), an early 日耳曼语 borrowing 源自 拉丁语 balteus "girdle, sword belt," said by Varro to be an Etruscan word. 作为 mark of rank or distinction, 14 世纪中期; references to boxing championship belts date 自 1812 年起. Mechanical sense 始于 1795 年. Transferred 语义 "broad stripe encircling something" 始于 1660 年代. Below the belt "unfair" (1889 年) 始于 pugilism. To get something under (one's) belt is to get it into one's stomach. To tighten (one's) belt "endure privation" 始于 1887 年.

definitionLines: n. 长凳，条凳；工作台；台，座
entries.definition: n. 长凳，条凳；工作台；台，座
entries.etymology: Old English benc "long seat," from Proto-Germanic *bankiz "bank of earth," perhaps here "man-made earthwork," later "bench, table" (source also of Old Frisian bank "bench," Old Norse bekkr, Danish bænk, Middle Dutch banc, Old High German banch), from PIE root *bheg- "to break." Used for "office of a judge" since late 13c. Sporting sense "reserve of players" (in baseball, North American football, etc.) is by 1909, from literal sense of place where players sit when not in action (by 1889).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 benc "long seat," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bankiz "bank of earth," 或许 here "man-made earthwork," later "bench, table" (source also of 古弗里西语 bank "bench," 古北欧语 bekkr, Danish bænk, Middle 荷兰语 banc, 古高地德语 banch), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheg- "to break." Used for "office of a judge" 自 13 世纪晚期 Sporting sense "reserve of players" (in baseball, North American football, etc.) is 截至 1909 年, 源自 literal 语义 place where players sit when not in action (截至 1889 年).

example.en: The carpenter set his tools on the bench before starting work.
example.zh: 木匠开始工作前把工具放在工作台上。

entries.definition: n. 弯曲，曲折处 vt. 折弯；使屈服
entries.etymology:
Old English bendan "to bend a bow; confine with a string, fetter," causative of bindan "to bind," from Proto-Germanic base *band- "string, band" (source also of Old Norse benda "to join, strain, strive, bend"), from PIE root *bhendh- "to bind" (source also of Gothic bindan, Old High German bintan, Sanskrit badhnati "binds," Lithuanian bendras "partner;" Old Persian bandaka- "subject").

Modern sense (early 14c.) is via notion of bending a bow to string it. Cognate with band, bind, and bond. Related: Bended; bent; bending.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bendan "to bend a bow; confine with a string, fetter," 为 … 的使役形式 bindan "to bind," 源自 原始日耳曼语 base *band- "string, band" (source also of 古北欧语 benda "to join, strain, strive, bend"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhendh- "to bind" (source also of Gothic bindan, 古高地德语 bintan, 梵语 badhnati "binds," Lithuanian bendras "partner;" Old 波斯语 bandaka- "subject"). 现代 sense (14 世纪初) is 经由 概念 bending a bow to string it. Cognate with band, bind, and bond. 同源词：Bended; bent; bending.

example.en: You need to bend your knees slightly when lifting heavy objects to protect your back.
example.zh: 提举重物时，你需要稍微弯曲膝盖以保护脊背。

entries.definition: prep. 在……下方，在……之下 ad. 在下方

example.en: The roots of the old tree spread far beneath the surface of the ground.
example.zh: 那棵老树的根系在地面之下延伸很远。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "helpful, advantageous," from Middle French bénéficial and directly from Latin beneficialis "pertaining to a favor," from beneficium (see benefice). Related: Beneficially.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "helpful, advantageous," 源自 中古法语 bénéficial and 直接源自 拉丁语 beneficialis "pertaining to a favor," 源自 beneficium （参见 benefice). 同源词：Beneficially.

example.en: Regular exercise is beneficial to both physical and mental health.
example.zh: 定期锻炼对身心健康都有益。

entries.definition: n. 利益，恩惠 vt. 有利于，受益于 vi. （from） 得益于
entries.etymology: late 14c., "good or noble deed," also "advantage, profit," from Anglo-French benfet "well-done," from Latin benefactum "good deed," from bene facere (see benefactor). Meaning "performance or entertainment to raise money for some charitable cause" is from 1680s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "good or noble deed," also "advantage, profit," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 benfet "well-done," 源自 拉丁语 benefactum "good deed," 源自 bene facere （参见 benefactor). 义为 "performance or entertainment to raise money for some charitable cause" 始于 1680 年代.

example.en: Exercise benefits both the body and the mind in many ways.
example.zh: 锻炼在许多方面对身体和心智都有益处。

entries.etymology: Old English be sidan "by the side of" (only as two words), from be- + sidan dative of side (n.). By 1200, formed as one word and used as both adverb and preposition. The alternative Middle English meaning "outside" led to the sense preserved in beside oneself "out of one's wits" (late 15c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 be sidan "by the side of" (only as two words), 源自 be- + sidan dative of side （名）. By 1200 年, formed as one word and used as both 副词 and preposition. The alternative 中古英语 意为 "outside" led to the sense preserved in beside oneself "out of one's wits" (15 世纪晚期).

entries.definition: ad. 而且，还有 prep.除……之外
entries.etymology: attested from c. 1200 (common after c. 1400), from beside + adverbial genitive -s. Once sharing all the senses of beside, now properly limited to "in addition to, otherwise."
entries.etymologyZh: attested 源自 约 1200 年 (common after 约 1400 年), 源自 beside + adverbial 属格 -s. Once sharing all the senses of beside, 现在 properly limited to "in addition to, otherwise."

entries.definition: a.最好的 ad. 最，最好
entries.etymology:
Old English beste, reduced by assimilation of -t- from earlier Old English betst "best, first, in the best manner," originally superlative of bot "remedy, reparation," the root word now only surviving in to boot (see boot (n.2)), though its comparative, better, and superlative, best, have been transferred to good (and in some cases well). From Proto-Germanic root *bat-, with comparative *batizon and superlative *batistaz (source also of Old Frisian, Old Saxon, Middle Dutch best, Old High German bezzist, German best, Old Norse beztr, Gothic batists).

Best-seller as short for "best-selling book" is from 1902, apparently originally in the publishing trade; best friend was in Chaucer (late 14c.). Best girl is first attested 1881, American English; best man is 1814, originally Scottish, replacing groomsman. To be able to do something with the best of them is recorded by 1748.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beste, reduced by assimilation of -t- 源自 earlier 古英语 betst "best, first, in the best manner," 原义为 superlative of bot "remedy, reparation," the root word 现在 only surviving in to boot （参见 boot (n.2)), though its comparative, better, and superlative, best, have been transferred to good (and in some cases well). From 原始日耳曼语 root *bat-, with comparative *batizon and superlative *batistaz (source also of 古弗里西语, 古撒克逊语, Middle 荷兰语 best, 古高地德语 bezzist, 德语 best, 古北欧语 beztr, Gothic batists). Best-seller as short for "best-selling book" 始于 1902 年, 似乎 原义为 in the publishing trade; best friend was in Chaucer (14 世纪晚期). Best girl is 最早见于 1881 年, American English; best man is 1814 年, 原义为 苏格兰语, replacing groomsman. To be able to do something with the best of them is recorded 截至 1748 年.

example.en: He always does his best to help others, no matter how busy he is.
example.zh: 无论多忙，他总是尽力帮助他人。

entries.definition: vt. 以……打赌，与……打赌 vi. 赌，打赌 n. 打赌；赌注，赌金
entries.etymology: 1590s, as both a verb and noun, in the argot of petty criminals, of unknown origin; probably a shortening of abet or else from obsolete beet "to make good," from Old English bætan "make better, arouse, stimulate," from Proto-Germanic *baitjan, in which case the verb would be the original. The original notion is perhaps "to improve" a contest by wagering on it, or it is from the "bait" sense in abet. Used since 1852 in various American English slang assertions (compare you bet "be assured," 1857). Related: Betting.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, as both a 动词 and 名词, in the argot of petty criminals, 来源不详; 可能 a shortening of abet or else 源自 已废 beet "to make good," 源自 古英语 bætan "make better, arouse, stimulate," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *baitjan, in which case the 动词 would be the original. The original notion is 或许 "to improve" a contest by wagering on it，或it 始于 the "bait" sense in abet. Used 自 1852 年 in various American English 俚语 assertions (对比 you bet "be assured," 1857 年). 同源词：Betting.

example.en: I bet you ten dollars that he arrives late again.
example.zh: 我跟你赌十美元他又要迟到。

entries.etymology: late 13c., bitrayen "mislead, deceive, betray," from be- + obsolete Middle English tray, from Old French traine "betrayal, deception, deceit," from trair (Modern French trahir) "betray, deceive," from Latin tradere "hand over," from trans- "across" (see trans-) + dare "to give" (see date (n.1)). Related: Betrayed; betraying.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, bitrayen "mislead, deceive, betray," 源自 be- + 已废 中古英语 tray, 源自 古法语 traine "betrayal, deception, deceit," 源自 trair (现代法语 trahir) "betray, deceive," 源自 拉丁语 tradere "hand over," 源自 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + dare "to give" （参见 date (n.1)). 同源词：Betrayed; betraying.

example.en: He would never betray his closest friends, no matter what.
example.zh: 无论如何，他都不会背叛他最亲密的朋友。

entries.definition: a. 较好的，更好的 ad.更好 vt. 改良，改善
entries.etymology: Old English bettra, earlier betera, from Proto-Germanic *batizo-, from PIE *bhad- "good;" see best. Comparative adjective of good in the older Germanic languages (compare Old Frisian betera, Old Saxon betiro, Old Norse betr, Danish bedre, Old High German bezziro, German besser, Gothic batiza). In English it superseded bet in the adverbial sense by 1600. Better half "wife" is first attested 1570s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bettra, earlier betera, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *batizo-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhad- "good;" 参见 best. Comparative 形容词 of good in the older 日耳曼语 languages (对比 古弗里西语 betera, 古撒克逊语 betiro, 古北欧语 betr, Danish bedre, 古高地德语 bezziro, 德语 besser, Gothic batiza). In English it superseded bet in the adverbial sense 截至 1600 年. Better half "wife" is 最早见于 1570 年代.

example.en: New trade policies helped better living standards for rural families.
example.zh: 新贸易政策帮助提升了农村家庭的生活水平。

entries.etymology: mid-13c., from Anglo-French beverage, Old French bevrage, from Old French boivre "to drink" (Modern French boire; from Latin bibere "to imbibe;" see imbibe) + -age, suffix forming mass or abstract nouns (see -age).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 beverage, 古法语 bevrage, 源自 古法语 boivre "to drink" (现代法语 boire; 源自 拉丁语 bibere "to imbibe;" 参见 imbibe) + -age, suffix forming mass or abstract nouns （参见 -age).

definitionLines: vt. 使迷惑，使不知所措
entries.definition: vt. 使迷惑，使不知所措
entries.etymology: 1680s, from be- "thoroughly" + archaic wilder "lead astray, lure into the wilds," probably a back-formation from wilderness. An earlier word with the same sense was bewhape (early 14c.). Related: Bewildered; bewildering; bewilderingly.
entries.etymologyZh: 1680 年代, 源自 be- "thoroughly" + 古旧 wilder "lead astray, lure into the wilds," 可能 a back-formation 源自 wilderness. An earlier word with the same sense was bewhape (14 世纪初). 同源词：Bewildered; bewildering; bewilderingly.

definitionLines: prep. 在……那边，在……以 外；超出，超过
entries.definition: prep. 在……那边，在……以 外；超出，超过 ad. 在那边，在远处
entries.etymology: Old English begeondan "beyond, from the farther side," from be- "by," here probably indicating position, + geond "yonder" (prep.); see yond. A compound not found elsewhere in Germanic.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 begeondan "beyond, from the farther side," 源自 be- "by," here 可能 indicating position, + geond "yonder" （介）; 参见 yond. A 复合词 not found elsewhere in 日耳曼语.

entries.etymology: 1520s, from French biais "slant, slope, oblique," also figuratively, "expedient, means" (13c., originally in Old French a past participle adjective, "sideways, askance, against the grain"), which is of unknown origin, probably from Old Provençal biais, with cognates in Old Catalan and Sardinian; possibly from Vulgar Latin *(e)bigassius, from Greek epikarsios "athwart, crosswise, at an angle," from epi- "upon" + karsios "oblique," from PIE *krs-yo-, from root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)). It became a noun in Old French. "[A] technical term in the game of bowls, whence come all the later uses of the word" [OED]. Transferred sense of "predisposition, prejudice" is from 1570s in English.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, 源自 法语 biais "slant, slope, oblique," also figuratively, "expedient, means" (13 世纪, 原义为 in 古法语 a past participle 形容词, "sideways, askance, against the grain"), which is 来源不详, 可能 源自 Old Provençal biais, with cognates in Old Catalan and Sardinian; possibly 源自 通俗拉丁语 *(e)bigassius, 源自 希腊语 epikarsios "athwart, crosswise, at an angle," 源自 epi- "upon" + karsios "oblique," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *krs-yo-, 源自 root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" （参见 shear （动）). It became a 名词 in 古法语. "[A] technical term in the game of bowls, whence come all the later uses of the word" [OED]. Transferred 语义 "predisposition, prejudice" 始于 1570 年代 in English.

example.en: The study revealed a clear bias against female candidates in hiring.
example.zh: 研究揭示了招聘中对女性候选人存在明显偏见。

entries.etymology:
early 14c., from Anglo-Latin biblia, Old French bible (13c.) "the Bible," also any large book generally, from Medieval and Late Latin biblia "the Bible" (neuter plural interpreted as feminine singular), from phrase biblia sacra "holy books," a translation of Greek ta biblia to hagia "the holy books." The Latin word is from Greek biblion "paper, scroll," the ordinary word for "book," originally a diminutive of byblos "Egyptian papyrus."

The Greek word perhaps is from Byblos, the name of the Phoenician port from which Egyptian papyrus was exported to Greece (modern Jebeil, in Lebanon; compare parchment). Or the place name might be from the Greek word, which then would be probably of Egyptian origin. The Christian scripture was referred to in Greek as Ta Biblia as early as c. 223. Bible replaced Old English biblioðece (see bibliothek) as the ordinary word for "the Scriptures." Figurative sense of "any authoritative book" is from 1804. Bible-thumper "strict Christian" is from 1870. Bible belt in reference to the swath of the U.S. South then dominated by fundamentalist Christians is from 1926; likely coined by H.L. Mencken in the "American Mercury."
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, 源自 Anglo-拉丁语 biblia, 古法语 bible (13 世纪) "the Bible," also any large book generally, 源自 Medieval and 晚期拉丁语 biblia "the Bible" (neuter plural interpreted as feminine singular), 源自 phrase biblia sacra "holy books," a translation of 希腊语 ta biblia to hagia "the holy books." The 拉丁语 word 始于 希腊语 biblion "paper, scroll," the ordinary word for "book," 原义为 a 为 … 的指小形式 byblos "Egyptian papyrus." The 希腊语 word 或许 始于 Byblos, the name of the Phoenician port 源自 which Egyptian papyrus was exported to Greece (modern Jebeil, in Lebanon; 对比 parchment). Or the place name might be 源自 希腊语 word, which 之后 would be 可能 of Egyptian origin. The Christian scripture was referred to in 希腊语 as Ta Biblia as early as 约 223 年. Bible replaced 古英语 biblioðece （参见 bibliothek) as the ordinary word for "the Scriptures." Figurative 语义 "any authoritative book" 始于 1804 年. Bible-thumper "strict Christian" 始于 1870 年. Bible belt in reference to the swath of the U.S. South 之后 dominated by fundamentalist Christians 始于 1926 年; likely coined by H.L. Mencken in the "American Mercury."

entries.etymology: 1868, coined from bi- "two" + Greek kyklos "circle, wheel" (see cycle (n.)), on the pattern of tricycle; both the word and the vehicle superseding earlier velocipede. The English word probably is not from French, though often said to be (many French sources say the French word is from English). The assumption apparently is because Pierre Lallement, employee of a French carriage works, improved Macmillan's 1839 pedal velocipede in 1865 and took the invention to America. See also pennyfarthing. As a verb, from 1869.
entries.etymologyZh: 1868 年, coined 源自 bi- "two" + 希腊语 kyklos "circle, wheel" （参见 cycle （名）), on the pattern of tricycle; both the word and the vehicle superseding earlier velocipede. The English word 可能 is not 源自 法语, though 常 said to be (many 法语 sources say the 法语 word 始于 English). The assumption 似乎 is because Pierre Lallement, employee of a 法语 carriage works, improved Macmillan's 1839 年 pedal velocipede 于 1865 年 and took the invention to America. See also pennyfarthing. 作动词时, 自 1869 年起.

entries.definition: vt. 出价，投标 n1. 出价，投标
entries.etymology:
probably an early Middle English mutual influence or confusion of two old words: The sense in bid farewell is from Old English biddan "to ask, entreat, beg, pray, beseech; order" (class V strong verb, past tense bæd, past participle beden), from Proto-Germanic *bidjan "to pray, entreat" (source also of German bitten "to ask," attested in Old High German from 8c., also Old Saxon bidjan, Old Frisian bidda, Old Norse biðja, Gothic bidjan). This, according to Kluge and Watkins, is from a PIE root *gwhedh- "to ask, pray" (see bead (n.)).

To bid at an auction, meanwhile, is from Old English beodan "offer, proclaim" (class II strong verb; past tense bead, past participle boden), from Proto-Germanic *beudan "to stretch out, reach out, offer, present," (source also of German bieten "to offer," Old High German biatan, also Old Saxon biodan, Old Frisian biada, Old Norse bjoða, Gothic anabiudan "to command"). This is from PIE root *bheudh- "to be aware, make aware" (see bode (v.)). As a noun, 1788, from the verb.

This, according to Kluge and Watkins, 始于 a 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *gwhedh- "to ask, pray" （参见 bead （名）). To bid at an auction, meanwhile, 始于 古英语 beodan "offer, proclaim" (class II strong 动词; past tense bead, past participle boden), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *beudan "to stretch out, reach out, offer, present," (source also of 德语 bieten "to offer," 古高地德语 biatan, also 古撒克逊语 biodan, 古弗里西语 biada, 古北欧语 bjoða, Gothic anabiudan "to command"). This 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheudh- "to be aware, make aware" （参见 bode （动）). 作名词时, 1788 年, 源自 动词.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, northern England dialect, "powerful, strong," of obscure origin, possibly from a Scandinavian source (compare Norwegian dialectal bugge "great man"). Old English used micel in many of the same senses. Meaning "of great size" is late 14c.; that of "grown up" is attested from 1550s. Sense of "important" is from 1570s. Meaning "generous" is U.S. colloquial by 1913.

Big band as a musical style is from 1926. Slang big head "conceit" is first recorded 1850. Big business "large commercial firms collectively" is 1905; big house "penitentiary" is U.S. underworld slang first attested 1915 (in London, "a workhouse," 1851). In financial journalism, big ticket items so called from 1956. Big lie is from Hitler's grosse Lüge.

Big band 作为 musical style 始于 1926 年. Slang big head "conceit" is 首见于 1850 年. Big business "large commercial firms collectively" is 1905 年; big house "penitentiary" is U.S. underworld 俚语 最早见于 1915 年 (in London, "a workhouse," 1851 年). In financial journalism, big ticket items so called 自 1956 年起. Big lie 始于 Hitler's grosse Lüge.

entries.etymology:
1680s, from French billion (originally byllion in Chuquet's unpublished "Le Triparty en la Science des Nombres," 1484; copied by De la Roche, 1520); see bi- "two" + million. A million million in Britain and Germany (numeration by groups of sixes), which was the original sense; subsequently altered in French to "a thousand million" (numeration by groups of threes) and picked up in that form in U.S., "due in part to French influence after the Revolutionary War" [David E. Smith, "History of Mathematics," 1925]. France then reverted to the original meaning in 1948. British usage is truer to the etymology, but U.S. sense is said to be increasingly common there in technical writing.

For a time in Britain gillion (1961), based on giga-, was tried as "a thousand million" to avoid ambiguity.

A million million in Britain and Germany (numeration by groups of sixes), which was the original sense; subsequently altered in 法语 to "a thousand million" (numeration by groups of threes) and picked up in that form in U.S., "due in part to French influence after the Revolutionary War" [David E. Smith, "History of Mathematics," 1925 年]. France 之后 reverted to the original 意为 于 1948 年. entries.etymology: Old English bindan "to tie up with bonds" (literally and figuratively), also "to make captive; to cover with dressings and bandages" (class III strong verb; past tense band, past participle bunden), from Proto-Germanic *bindan (source also of Old Saxon bindan, Old Norse  and Old Frisian binda, Old High German binten "to bind," German binden, Gothic bindan), from PIE root *bhendh- "to bind" (see bend (v.)). Intransitive sense of "stick together" is from 1670s. Of books, from c. 1400.

Intransitive 语义 "stick together" 始于 1670 年代. Of books, 源自 约 1400 年.

entries.etymology:
early 13c., from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse *byrðr (replacing cognate Old English gebyrd "birth, descent, race; offspring; nature; fate"), from Proto-Germanic *gaburthis (source also of Old Frisian berd, Old Saxon giburd, Dutch geboorte, Old High German giburt, German geburt, Gothic gabaurþs), from PIE *bhrto past participle of root *bher- (1) "to carry, to bear" (source also of Sanskrit bhrtih "a bringing, maintenance," Latin fors, genitive fortis "chance;" see bear (v.)).

Suffix -th is for "process" (as in bath, death). Meaning "parentage, lineage, extraction" (revived from Old English) is from mid-13c. Birth control is from 1914; birth rate from 1859. Birth certificate is from 1842.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 a Scandinavian source such as 古北欧语 *byrðr (replacing 同源 古英语 gebyrd "birth, descent, race; offspring; nature; fate"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *gaburthis (source also of 古弗里西语 berd, 古撒克逊语 giburd, 荷兰语 geboorte, 古高地德语 giburt, 德语 geburt, Gothic gabaurþs), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhrto 为 … 的过去分词 root *bher- (1) "to carry, to bear" (source also of 梵语 bhrtih "a bringing, maintenance," 拉丁语 fors, 属格 fortis "chance;" 参见 bear （动）). entries.etymology:
Old English bitan (class I strong verb; past tense bat, past participle biten), from Proto-Germanic *bitan (source also of Old Saxon bitan, Old Norse and Old Frisian bita, Middle Dutch biten, Dutch bijten, German beissen, Gothic beitan "to bite"), from PIE root *bheid- "to split, crack" (see fissure).

To bite the bullet is said to be 1700s military slang, from old medical custom of having the patient bite a lead bullet during an operation to divert attention from pain and reduce screaming. Figurative use from 1891; the custom itself attested from 1840s. To bite (one's) tongue "refrain from speaking" is 1590s. To bite the dust "die" is 1750 (Latin had the same image; compare Virgil's procubuit moriens et humum semel ore momordit). To bite off more than one can chew (c. 1880) is U.S. slang, from plug tobacco.

To bite the bullet is said to be 1700 年代 military 俚语, 源自 old medical custom of having the patient bite a lead bullet during an operation to divert attention 源自 pain and reduce screaming. Figurative use 自 1891 年起; the custom itself attested 源自 1840 年代. To bite (one's) tongue "refrain from speaking" is 1590s. To bite the dust "die" is 1750 (Latin had the same image; compare Virgil's procubuit moriens et humum semel ore momordit). To bite off more than one can chew (约 1880 年) is U.S. 俚语, 源自 plug tobacco.

entries.etymology: Old English biter "bitter, sharp, cutting; angry, embittered; cruel," from Proto-Germanic *bitras- (source also of Old Saxon bittar, Old Norse bitr, Dutch bitter, Old High German bittar, German bitter, Gothic baitrs "bitter"), from PIE root *bheid- "to split" (source also of Old English bitan "to bite;" see bite (v.)). Evidently the meaning drifted in prehistoric times from "biting, of pungent taste," to "acrid-tasting." Used figuratively in Old English of states of mind and words. Related: Bitterly.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 biter "bitter, sharp, cutting; angry, embittered; cruel," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bitras- (source also of 古撒克逊语 bittar, 古北欧语 bitr, 荷兰语 bitter, 古高地德语 bittar, 德语 bitter, Gothic baitrs "bitter"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheid- "to split" (source also of 古英语 bitan "to bite;" 参见 bite （动）). entries.etymology: 1640s, from French bizarre "odd, fantastic" (16c.), from Italian bizarro "irascible, tending to quick flashes of anger" (13c.), from bizza "fit of anger, quick flash of anger" (13c.). The sense in Italian evolved to "unpredictable, eccentric," then "strange, weird," in which sense it was taken into French and then English. Older derivation from Basque bizar "a beard" is no longer considered tenable.

The sense in 意大利语 evolved to "unpredictable, eccentric," 之后 "strange, weird," in which sense it was taken into 法语 and 之后 English. Older derivation 源自 Basque bizar "a beard" is no longer considered tenable.

example.en: The artist was known for her bizarre sculptures made of trash.
