entries.definition: a./n.黑，黑色；黑暗 n. 黑色；黑人
entries.etymology:
Old English blæc "dark," from Proto-Germanic *blakaz "burned" (source also of Old Norse blakkr "dark," Old High German blah "black," Swedish bläck "ink," Dutch blaken "to burn"), from PIE *bhleg- "to burn, gleam, shine, flash" (source also of Greek phlegein "to burn, scorch," Latin flagrare "to blaze, glow, burn"), from root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn;" see bleach (v.).

The same root produced Old English blac "bright, shining, glittering, pale;" the connecting notions being, perhaps, "fire" (bright) and "burned" (dark). The usual Old English word for "black" was sweart (see swart). According to OED: "In ME. it is often doubtful whether blac, blak, blake, means 'black, dark,' or 'pale, colourless, wan, livid.' " Used of dark-skinned people in Old English.

Of coffee, first attested 1796. Meaning "fierce, terrible, wicked" is late 14c. The color of sin and sorrow since at least c. 1300; sense of "with dark purposes, malignant" emerged 1580s (as in black magic). Black face in reference to a performance style originated in U.S., is from 1868. Black flag, flown (especially by pirates) as a signal of "no mercy," from 1590s. Black dog "melancholy" attested from 1826. Black belt is from 1875 in reference to districts of the U.S. South with heaviest African population; 1870 with reference to fertility of soil; 1913 in judo sense. Black power is from 1966, associated with Stokely Carmichael. Black English "English as spoken by African-Americans," is by 1969.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 blæc "dark," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blakaz "burned" (source also of 古北欧语 blakkr "dark," 古高地德语 blah "black," Swedish bläck "ink," 荷兰语 blaken "to burn"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhleg- "to burn, gleam, shine, flash" (source also of 希腊语 phlegein "to burn, scorch," 拉丁语 flagrare "to blaze, glow, burn"), 源自 root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn;" 参见 bleach （动）. The same root produced 古英语 blac "bright, shining, glittering, pale;" the connecting notions being, 或许, "fire" (bright) and "burned" (dark). The usual 古英语 word for "black" was sweart （参见 swart). According to OED: "In ME. it is often doubtful whether blac, blak, blake, means 'black, dark,' or 'pale, colourless, wan, livid.' " Used of dark-skinned people in 古英语. Of coffee, 最早见于 1796 年. 义为 "fierce, terrible, wicked" is 14 世纪晚期 The color of sin and sorrow 自 at least 约 1300 年; 语义 "with dark purposes, malignant" emerged 1580 年代 (as in black magic). Black face in reference to a performance style originated in U.S., 始于 1868 年. Black flag, flown (尤指 by pirates) 作为 signal of "no mercy," 源自 1590 年代. Black dog "melancholy" attested 自 1826 年起. Black belt 始于 1875 年 in reference to districts of the U.S. South with heaviest African population; 1870 年 with reference to fertility of soil; 1913 年 in judo sense. Black power 始于 1966 年, associated with Stokely Carmichael. Black English "English as spoken by African-Americans," is 截至 1969 年.

entries.etymology: Old English blæd "a leaf," but also "a leaf-like part" (of spade, oar, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *bladaz (source also of Old Frisian bled "leaf," German Blatt, Old Saxon, Danish, Dutch blad, Old Norse blað), from PIE *bhle-to-, suffixed form (past participle) of *bhel- (3) "to thrive, bloom," possibly identical with *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell" (see bole). Extended in Middle English to shoulders (c. 1300) and swords (early 14c.). The modern use in reference to grass may be a Middle English revival, by influence of Old French bled "corn, wheat" (11c., perhaps from Germanic). The cognate in German, Blatt, is the general word for "leaf;" Laub is used collectively as "foliage." Old Norse blað was used of herbs and plants, lauf in reference to trees. This might have been the original distinction in Old English, too. Of men from 1590s; in later use often a reference to 18c. gallants, but the original exact sense, and thus signification, is uncertain.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 blæd "a leaf," but also "a leaf-like part" (of spade, oar, etc.), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bladaz (source also of 古弗里西语 bled "leaf," 德语 Blatt, 古撒克逊语, Danish, 荷兰语 blad, 古北欧语 blað), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhle-to-, suffixed form (past participle) of *bhel- (3) "to thrive, bloom," possibly identical with *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell" （参见 bole). Extended in 中古英语 to shoulders (约 1300 年) and swords (14 世纪初). The modern use in reference to grass may be a 中古英语 revival, by influence of 古法语 bled "corn, wheat" (11 世纪, 或源自 日耳曼语). The 同源 in 德语, Blatt, is the general word for "leaf;" Laub is used collectively as "foliage." 古北欧语 blað was used of herbs and plants, lauf in reference to trees. This might have been the original distinction in 古英语, too. Of men 源自 1590 年代; in later use 常 a reference to 18 世纪 gallants, but the original exact sense, and thus signification, is uncertain.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "find fault with;" c. 1300, "lay blame on," from Old French blasmer (12c., Modern French blâmer) "to rebuke, reprimand, condemn, criticize," from Vulgar Latin *blastemare, from Late Latin blasphemare "revile, reproach" (see blaspheme). Replaced Old English witan with long "i." Related: Blamed; blaming.

entries.etymology:
early 13c., "white, pale, colorless," from Old French blanc "white, shining," from Frankish *blank "white, gleaming," or some other West Germanic source (compare Old Norse blakkr, Old English blanca "white horse;" Old High German blanc, blanch; German blank "shining, bright"), from Proto-Germanic *blangkaz "to shine, dazzle," extended form of PIE root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" (see bleach (v.)).

Meaning "having empty spaces" evolved c. 1400. Sense of "void of expression" (a blank look) is from 1550s. Spanish blanco, Italian bianco are said to be from Germanic. Related: Blankly, blankness.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "white, pale, colorless," 源自 古法语 blanc "white, shining," 源自 Frankish *blank "white, gleaming," or some other West 日耳曼语 source (对比 古北欧语 blakkr, 古英语 blanca "white horse;" 古高地德语 blanc, blanch; 德语 blank "shining, bright"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blangkaz "to shine, dazzle," extended form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" （参见 bleach （动）). 义为 "having empty spaces" evolved 约 1400 年. 义为 "void of expression" (a blank look) 始于 1550 年代. 西班牙语 blanco, 意大利语 bianco are said to be 源自 日耳曼语. 同源词：Blankly, blankness.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "bed-clothing; white woolen stuff," from Old French blanchet "light wool or flannel cloth; an article made of this material," diminutive of blanc "white" (see blank (adj.), which had a secondary sense of "a white cloth." Wet blanket (1830) is from the notion of a person who throws a damper on social situations like a wet blanket smothers a fire. In U.S. history, a blanket Indian (1859) was one using the traditional garment instead of wearing Western dress.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "bed-clothing; white woolen stuff," 源自 古法语 blanchet "light wool or flannel cloth; an article made of this material," 为 … 的指小形式 blanc "white" （参见 blank （形）, which had a secondary 语义 "a white cloth." Wet blanket (1830 年) 始于 the 概念 a person who throws a damper on social situations like a wet blanket smothers a fire. In U.S. history, a blanket Indian (1859 年) was one using the traditional garment instead of wearing Western dress.

example.en: She wrapped herself in a thick blanket to keep warm on the cold night.
example.zh: 在寒冷的夜晚，她用厚毯子把自己裹起来保暖。

entries.definition: vt. 炸掉，摧毁 n. 爆炸，爆破；一阵（风）
entries.etymology:
Old English blæst "blowing, breeze, puff of wind," from Proto-Germanic *bles- (source also of Old Norse blastr, Old High German blast "a blowing, blast," German blasen, Gothic blesan "to blow"), from PIE *bhle- "to blow," probably a variant of root *bhel- (2) "to blow, inflate, swell" (see bole).

Meaning "explosion" is from 1630s; that of "noisy party, good time" is from 1953, American English slang. Sense of "strong current of air for iron-smelting" (1690s) led to blast furnace and transferred sense in full blast "the extreme" (1839). Blast was the usual word for "a smoke of tobacco" c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 blæst "blowing, breeze, puff of wind," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bles- (source also of 古北欧语 blastr, 古高地德语 blast "a blowing, blast," 德语 blasen, Gothic blesan "to blow"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhle- "to blow," 可能 a 为 … 的变体 root *bhel- (2) "to blow, inflate, swell" （参见 bole). 义为 "explosion" 始于 1630 年代; that of "noisy party, good time" 始于 1953 年, American English 俚语. 义为 "strong current of air for iron-smelting" (1690 年代) led to blast furnace and transferred sense in full blast "the extreme" (1839 年). Blast was the usual word for "a smoke of tobacco" 约 1600 年.

example.en: Workers used dynamite to blast the old bridge.
example.zh: 工人们用炸药炸毁了那座旧桥。

entries.etymology: Old English bledan "to let blood," in Middle English and after, "to let blood from surgically;" also "to emit blood," from Proto-Germanic *blodjan "emit blood" (source also of Old Norse blæða, German bluten), from *bhlo-to- "swell, gush, spurt" (see blood (n.)). Meaning "extort money from" is from 1670s. Of dyes or paints, from 1862. Related: Bled; bleeding.

entries.definition: v.混合，掺杂，调和 n. 混合；混合物
entries.etymology: c. 1300, blenden, "to mix, mingle, stir up a liquid," in northern writers, from or akin to rare Old English blandan "to mix," blondan (Mercian) or Old Norse blanda "to mix," or a combination of the two; from Proto-Germanic *blandan "to mix," which comes via a notion of "to make cloudy" from an extended Germanic form of the PIE root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" (see bleach (v.); also blind (adj.)). Compare Old Saxon and Old High German blantan, Gothic blandan, Middle High German blenden "to mix;" German Blendling "bastard, mongrel," and outside Germanic, Lithuanian blandus "troubled, turbid, thick;" Old Church Slavonic blesti "to go astray." Figurative use from early 14c. Related: Blended; blending.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, blenden, "to mix, mingle, stir up a liquid," in northern writers, 源自 or akin to rare 古英语 blandan "to mix," blondan (Mercian) or 古北欧语 blanda "to mix," or a combination of the two; 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blandan "to mix," which comes 经由 a 概念 "to make cloudy" 源自 an extended 日耳曼语 form of the 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" （参见 bleach （动）; also blind （形）). 对比 古撒克逊语 and 古高地德语 blantan, Gothic blandan, Middle High 德语 blenden "to mix;" 德语 Blendling "bastard, mongrel," and outside 日耳曼语, Lithuanian blandus "troubled, turbid, thick;" Old Church Slavonic blesti "to go astray." Figurative use 源自 14 世纪初 同源词：Blended; blending.

example.en: The chef likes to blend different spices to create unique flavors.
example.zh: 这位厨师喜欢混合不同香料来创造独特的风味。

entries.etymology: Old English bletsian, bledsian, Northumbrian bloedsian "to consecrate, make holy, give thanks," from Proto-Germanic *blodison "hallow with blood, mark with blood," from *blotham "blood" (see blood (n.)). Originally a blood sprinkling on pagan altars. This word was chosen in Old English bibles to translate Latin benedicere and Greek eulogein, both of which have a ground sense of "to speak well of, to praise," but were used in Scripture to translate Hebrew brk "to bend (the knee), worship, praise, invoke blessings." L.R. Palmer ("The Latin Language") writes, "There is nothing surprising in the semantic development of a word denoting originally a special ritual act into the more generalized meanings to 'sacrifice,' 'worship,' 'bless,'" and compares Latin immolare (see immolate). Meaning shifted in late Old English toward "pronounce or make happy," by resemblance to unrelated bliss. No cognates in other languages. Related: Blessed; blessing.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bletsian, bledsian, Northumbrian bloedsian "to consecrate, make holy, give thanks," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blodison "hallow with blood, mark with blood," 源自 *blotham "blood" （参见 blood （名）). Originally a blood sprinkling on pagan altars. This word was chosen in 古英语 bibles to translate 拉丁语 benedicere and 希腊语 eulogein, both of which have a ground 语义 "to speak well of, to praise," but were used in Scripture to translate 希伯来语 brk "to bend (the knee), worship, praise, invoke blessings." L.R. Palmer ("The Latin Language") writes, "There is nothing surprising in the semantic development of a word denoting originally a special ritual act into the more generalized meanings to 'sacrifice,' 'worship,' 'bless,'" and compares 拉丁语 immolare （参见 immolate). 义为 shifted in late 古英语 toward "pronounce or make happy," by resemblance to unrelated bliss. No cognates in other languages. 同源词：Blessed; blessing.

example.en: The priest stepped forward to bless the congregation at the end of the service.
example.zh: 礼拜结束时，牧师走上前为会众祝福。

entries.definition: a. 盲的，瞎的；盲目的 vt. 使失明；蒙蔽
entries.etymology:
Old English blind "blind," also "dark, enveloped in darkness, obscure; unintelligent, lacking mental perception," probably from Proto-Germanic *blinda- "blind" (source also of Dutch and German blind, Old Norse blindr, Gothic blinds "blind"), perhaps, via notion of "to make cloudy, deceive," from an extended Germanic form of the PIE root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" (see bleach (v.)). Compare Lithuanian blendzas "blind," blesti "to become dark." The original sense would be not "sightless" but rather "confused," which perhaps underlies such phrases as blind alley (Chaucer's lanes blynde), which is older than the sense of "closed at one end" (1610s).

In reference to doing something without seeing it first, by 1840. Of aviators flying without instruments or without clear observation, from 1919. Related: Blinded; blinding. Blindman's bluff is from 1580s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 blind "blind," also "dark, enveloped in darkness, obscure; unintelligent, lacking mental perception," 可能 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blinda- "blind" (source also of 荷兰语 and 德语 blind, 古北欧语 blindr, Gothic blinds "blind"), 或许, 经由 概念 "to make cloudy, deceive," 源自 an extended 日耳曼语 form of the 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" （参见 bleach （动）). 对比 Lithuanian blendzas "blind," blesti "to become dark." The original sense would be not "sightless" but rather "confused," which 或许 underlies such phrases as blind alley (Chaucer's lanes blynde), which is older than the sense of "closed at one end" (1610s). In reference to doing something without seeing it first, by 1840. Of aviators flying without instruments or without clear observation, from 1919. Related: Blinded; blinding. Blindman's bluff 始于 1580 年代.

example.en: The explosion blinded him temporarily and he could not see for several minutes.
example.zh: 爆炸使他暂时失明，他好几分钟都看不见。

entries.definition: vt. 眨眼；使闪烁 vi.眨眼；闪烁 7•闪光；眨眼；瞬间
entries.etymology:
1580s, perhaps from Middle Dutch blinken "to glitter," which is of uncertain origin, possibly, with German blinken "to gleam, sparkle, twinkle," from a nasalized form of base found in Old English blican "to shine, glitter" (see bleach (v.)).

Middle English had blynke (c. 1300) in the sense "a brief gleam or spark," perhaps a variant of blench "to move suddenly or sharply; to raise one's eyelids" (c. 1200), perhaps from the rare Old English blencan "deceive." Related: Blinked; blinking. The last, as a euphemism for a stronger word, is attested by 1914.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, 或源自 Middle 荷兰语 blinken "to glitter," which is 来源存疑, possibly, with 德语 blinken "to gleam, sparkle, twinkle," 源自 a nasalized form of base found in 古英语 blican "to shine, glitter" （参见 bleach （动）). 中古英语 had blynke (约 1300 年) in the sense "a brief gleam or spark," 或许 a 为 … 的变体 blench "to move suddenly or sharply; to raise one's eyelids" (约 1200 年), 或源自 the rare 古英语 blencan "deceive." 同源词：Blinked; blinking. The last, 作为 euphemism for a stronger word, is attested 截至 1914 年.

example.en: She blinked several times, trying to adjust to the bright light.
example.zh: 她眨了几下眼，试图适应强烈的光线。

entries.definition: vt.阻塞，封锁； n. 街区，街段；大块（木料、石 料、金属、冰等）；阻塞物， 路障
entries.etymology:
"solid piece," c. 1300, from Old French bloc "log, block" of wood (13c.), via Middle Dutch bloc "trunk of a tree" or Old High German bloh, from a common Germanic source, from PIE *bhlugo-, from *bhelg- "a thick plank, beam" (see balk).

Meaning "mould for a hat" is from 1570s. Slang sense of "head" is from 1630s. Extended sense of "obstruction" is first recorded 1640s. In cricket from 1825; in U.S. football from 1912. The meaning in city block is 1796, from the notion of a "compact mass" of buildings; slang meaning "fashionable promenade" is 1869.
entries.etymologyZh: "solid piece," 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 bloc "log, block" of wood (13 世纪), 经由 Middle 荷兰语 bloc "trunk of a tree" or 古高地德语 bloh, 源自 a common 日耳曼语 source, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhlugo-, 源自 *bhelg- "a thick plank, beam" （参见 balk). 义为 "mould for a hat" 始于 1570 年代. Slang 语义 "head" 始于 1630 年代. Extended 语义 "obstruction" is 首见于 1640 年代. In cricket 自 1825 年起; in U.S. football 自 1912 年起. The 意为 in city block is 1796 年, 源自 概念 a "compact mass" of buildings; 俚语 意为 "fashionable promenade" is 1869 年.

entries.etymology: 1998, short for weblog (which is attested from 1994, though not in the sense "online journal"), from (World Wide) Web + log. Joe Bloggs (c. 1969) was British slang for "any hypothetical person" (compare U.S. equivalent Joe Blow); earlier blog meant "a servant boy" in one of the college houses (c. 1860, see Partridge, who describes this use as a "perversion of bloke"), and, as a verb, "to defeat" in schoolboy slang. The Blogger online publishing service was launched in 1999.

entries.etymology:
Old English blod "blood," from Proto-Germanic *blodam "blood" (source also of Old Frisian blod, Old Saxon blôd, Old Norse bloð, Middle Dutch bloet, Dutch bloed, Old High German bluot, German Blut, Gothic bloþ), from PIE *bhlo-to-, perhaps meaning "to swell, gush, spurt," or "that which bursts out" (compare Gothic bloþ "blood," bloma "flower"), in which case it would be from suffixed form of *bhle-, extended form of root *bhel- (3) "to thrive, bloom" (see folio).

There seems to have been an avoidance in Germanic, perhaps from taboo, of other PIE words for "blood," such as *esen- (source of poetic Greek ear, Old Latin aser, Sanskrit asrk, Hittite eshar); also *krew-, which seems to have had a sense of "blood outside the body, gore from a wound" (source of Latin cruour "blood from a wound," Greek kreas "meat"), which came to mean simply "blood" in the Balto-Slavic group and some other languages.

Inheritance and relationship senses (also found in Latin sanguis, Greek haima) emerged in English by mid-13c. Meaning "person of one's family, race, kindred" is late 14c. As the seat of passions, it is recorded from c. 1300. Slang meaning "hot spark, a man of fire" [Johnson] is from 1560s. Blood pressure attested from 1862. Blood money is from 1530s; originally money paid for causing the death of another.

Blood type is from 1928. That there were different types of human blood was discovered c. 1900 during early experiments in transfusion. To get blood from a stone "do the impossible" is from 1660s. Expression blood is thicker than water attested by 1803, in reference to family ties of those separated by distance. New (or fresh) blood, in reference to members of an organization or group is from 1880.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 blod "blood," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blodam "blood" (source also of 古弗里西语 blod, 古撒克逊语 blôd, 古北欧语 bloð, Middle 荷兰语 bloet, 荷兰语 bloed, 古高地德语 bluot, 德语 Blut, Gothic bloþ), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhlo-to-, 或许 意为 "to swell, gush, spurt," or "that which bursts out" (对比 Gothic bloþ "blood," bloma "flower"), in which case it would be 源自 suffixed form of *bhle-, extended form of root *bhel- (3) "to thrive, bloom" （参见 folio). There seems to have been an avoidance in 日耳曼语, 或源自 taboo, of other 原始印欧语 (PIE) words for "blood," such as *esen- (source of poetic 希腊语 ear, Old 拉丁语 aser, 梵语 asrk, Hittite eshar); also *krew-, which seems to have had a 语义 "blood outside the body, gore from a wound" (source of 拉丁语 cruour "blood from a wound," 希腊语 kreas "meat"), which came to mean simply "blood" in the Balto-Slavic group and some other languages. Inheritance and relationship senses (also found in 拉丁语 sanguis, 希腊语 haima) emerged in English by 13 世纪中期 义为 "person of one's family, race, kindred" is 14 世纪晚期 As the seat of passions, it 见于 约 1300 年. Slang 意为 "hot spark, a man of fire" [Johnson] 始于 1560 年代. Blood pressure attested 自 1862 年起. Blood money 始于 1530 年代; 原义为 money paid for causing the death of another. Blood type 始于 1928 年. That there were different types of human blood was discovered 约 1900 年 during early experiments in transfusion. To get blood 源自 a stone "do the impossible" 始于 1660 年代. Expression blood is thicker than water attested 截至 1803 年, in reference to family ties of those separated by distance. New (or fresh) blood, in reference to members of an organization or group 始于 1880 年.

example.zh: 护士从病人手臂上抽血化验。

entries.etymology: also blood-shed, c. 1500, "the shedding of (one's) blood," from verbal phrase (attested in late Old English), from blood (n.) + shed (v.). The sense of "slaughter" is much older (early 13c., implied in bloodshedding).
entries.etymologyZh: also blood-shed, 约 1500 年, "the shedding of (one's) blood," 源自 verbal phrase (见于 late 古英语), 源自 blood （名） + shed （动）. The 语义 "slaughter" is much older (13 世纪初, implied in bloodshedding).

entries.etymology: mid-13c., blomen, from the noun (see bloom (n.1)). Related: Bloomed; blooming.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, blomen, 源自 名词 （参见 bloom (n.1)). 同源词：Bloomed; blooming.

example.en: The cherry trees were in full bloom, and nearly every branch was covered with open flowers.
example.zh: 樱花树正在盛开，几乎每根枝条都开满了花。

entries.definition: vi. 开花；兴旺 n. 花；开花期；兴旺期；
entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old English blostm, blostma "blossom, flower, fruit," from Proto-Germanic *blo-s- (source also of Middle Low German blosom, Dutch bloesem, German Blust), from PIE *bhlow-, extended form of *bhel- (3) "to thrive, bloom" (see folio). This is the native word, now largely superseded by bloom (n.1) and flower (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古英语 blostm, blostma "blossom, flower, fruit," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blo-s- (source also of Middle Low 德语 blosom, 荷兰语 bloesem, 德语 Blust), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhlow-, extended form of *bhel- (3) "to thrive, bloom" （参见 folio). This is the 本族 word, 现在 largely superseded by bloom (n.1) and flower （名）.

example.en: The cherry trees blossom every spring along the riverside path.
example.zh: 每年春天，沿河小路两旁的樱花树都会盛开。

entries.etymology: 1828 (from 1822 as a French word in English), from French blouse, "workman's or peasant's smock" (1788), origin unknown. Perhaps akin to Provençal (lano) blouso "short (wool)" [Gamillscheg]. Another suggestion [Klein] is that it is from Medieval Latin pelusia, from Pelusium, a city in Upper Egypt, supposedly a clothing manufacturing center in the Middle Ages.

entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "to stumble about blindly," 源自 a Scandinavian source akin to 古北欧语 blundra "shut one's eyes," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhlendh- （参见 blind). 义为 "make a stupid mistake" is 首见于 1711 年. 同源词：Blundered; blundering.

entries.definition: vt.使模糊不清；使暗淡 vi. 变模糊 n. 模糊不清的事物
entries.etymology: 1540s, "smear on the surface of writing;" perhaps akin to blear. Extended sense of "confused dimness" is from 1860.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "smear on the surface of writing;" 或许 akin to blear. Extended 语义 "confused dimness" 始于 1860 年.

example.en: Tears began to blur her vision as she read the farewell letter.
example.zh: 她读着告别信，泪水开始使她的视线模糊起来。

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., bluschen, blischen, probably from Old English blyscan "blush, become red, glow" (glossing Latin rutilare), akin to blyse "torch," from Proto-Germanic *blisk- "to shine, burn," which also yielded words in Low German (Dutch blozen "to blush") and Scandinavian (Danish blusse "to blaze; to blush"); ultimately from PIE *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" (see bleach (v.)).

For vowel evolution, see bury. Earliest recorded senses were "to shine brightly; to look, stare." Sense of "turn red in the face" (with shame, modesty, etc.) is from c. 1400. Related: Blushed; blushing.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, bluschen, blischen, 可能 源自 古英语 blyscan "blush, become red, glow" (glossing 拉丁语 rutilare), akin to blyse "torch," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *blisk- "to shine, burn," which also yielded words in Low 德语 (荷兰语 blozen "to blush") and Scandinavian (Danish blusse "to blaze; to blush"); 最终源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhel- (1) "to shine, flash, burn" （参见 bleach （动）). For vowel evolution, 参见 bury. Earliest recorded senses were "to shine brightly; to look, stare." 义为 "turn red in the face" (with shame, modesty, etc.) 始于 约 1400 年. 同源词：Blushed; blushing.

definitionLines: n. 板，木板，纸板；董事会，理事 会
entries.definition: n. 板，木板，纸板；董事会，理事 会 v. 上船/车/飞机
entries.etymology:
verb senses derived from various senses of board (n.1) and board (n.2) include "come alongside" (a ship), mid-15c. (from n.2); "put boards on, frame with boards," late 14c. (implied in boarded, from n.1); "
to get onto" (a ship), 1590s, transferred from mid-19c. to stages, railway cars, aircraft, etc. (from n.2). Meaning "to be supplied with food and lodging" is from 1550s (from n.1 in transferred sense). Transitive meaning "provide with daily meals and lodging" is from 1590s. Related: Boarded; boarding.
entries.etymologyZh: 动词 senses derived 源自 various senses of board (n.1) and board (n.2) include "come alongside" (a ship), 15 世纪中期 (源自 n.2); "put boards on, frame with boards," 14 世纪晚期 (implied in boarded, 源自 n.1); " to get onto" (a ship), 1590 年代, transferred 源自 19 世纪中期 to stages, railway cars, aircraft, etc. (源自 n.2). 义为 "to be supplied with food and lodging" 始于 1550 年代 (源自 n.1 in transferred sense). Transitive 意为 "provide with daily meals and lodging" 始于 1590 年代. 同源词：Boarded; boarding.

definitionLines: vt. 吹嘘；以拥有……而自豪
entries.definition: vi. （of/about） 夸耀，说大话 vt. 吹嘘；以拥有……而自豪 n. 自吹自擂
entries.etymology:
mid-13c., "arrogance, presumption, pride, vanity;" c. 1300, "a brag, boastful speech," from Anglo-French bost "ostentation," probably via Scandinavian (compare Norwegian baus "proud, bold, daring"), from Proto-Germanic *bausia "to blow up, puff up, swell" (source also of Middle High German bus "swelling," dialectal German baustern "to swell;" Middle Dutch bose, Dutch boos "evil, wicked, angry," Old High German bosi "worthless, slanderous," German böse "evil, bad, angry"), from PIE *bhou-, variant of root *beu-, *bheu- "to grow, swell" (see bull (n.2)).

The notion apparently is of being "puffed up" with pride; compare Old English belgan "to become angry, offend, provoke," belg "anger, arrogance," from the same root as bellows and belly (n.). Related: Boasted; boasting. An Old English word for "boasting" was micelsprecende, "big talk."
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, "arrogance, presumption, pride, vanity;" 约 1300 年, "a brag, boastful speech," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 bost "ostentation," 可能 经由 Scandinavian (对比 Norwegian baus "proud, bold, daring"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bausia "to blow up, puff up, swell" (source also of Middle High 德语 bus "swelling," 方言 德语 baustern "to swell;" Middle 荷兰语 bose, 荷兰语 boos "evil, wicked, angry," 古高地德语 bosi "worthless, slanderous," 德语 böse "evil, bad, angry"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhou-, 为 … 的变体 root *beu-, *bheu- "to grow, swell" （参见 bull (n.2)). The notion 似乎 is of being "puffed up" with pride; 对比 古英语 belgan "to become angry, offend, provoke," belg "anger, arrogance," 源自 same root as bellows and belly （名）. 同源词：Boasted; boasting. An 古英语 word for "boasting" was micelsprecende, "big talk."

example.en: He tends to boast about his expensive car whenever he meets new people.
example.zh: 每当他遇到新朋友时，总喜欢炫耀他那辆昂贵的汽车。

entries.etymology: Old English bat "boat, ship, vessel," from Proto-Germanic *bait- (source also of Old Norse batr, Dutch boot, German Boot), possibly from PIE root *bheid- "to split" (see fissure) if the notion is of making a boat by hollowing out a tree trunk; or it may be an extension of the name for some part of a ship. French bateau "boat" is from Old English or Norse. Spanish batel, Italian battello, Medieval Latin batellus likewise probably are from Germanic.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bat "boat, ship, vessel," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bait- (source also of 古北欧语 batr, 荷兰语 boot, 德语 Boot), possibly 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheid- "to split" （参见 fissure) if the notion is of making a boat by hollowing out a tree trunk; or it may be an extension of the name for some part of a ship. 法语 bateau "boat" 始于 古英语 or Norse. 西班牙语 batel, 意大利语 battello, 中古拉丁语 batellus likewise 可能 始于 日耳曼语.

example.en: They crossed the lake on a small wooden boat.
example.zh: 他们乘坐一艘小木船渡过了湖面。

definitionLines: n. 身体，躯体；主体；物体；尸 体；（一）群，（一）批
entries.definition: n. 身体，躯体；主体；物体；尸 体；（一）群，（一）批
entries.etymology:
Old English bodig "trunk, chest" (of a man or animal); related to Old High German botah, of unknown origin. Not elsewhere in Germanic, and the word has died out in German (replaced by leib, originally "life," and körper, from Latin). In English, extension to "person" is from late 13c. Meaning "main part" of anything was in late Old English, hence its use in reference to vehicles (1520s).

Contrasted with soul since at least mid-13c. Meaning "corpse" (short for dead body) is from late 13c. Transferred to matter generally in Middle English (as in heavenly body, late 14c.). Body politic "the nation, the state" first recorded 1520s, legalese, with French word order. Body image was coined 1935. Body language is attested from 1967, perhaps from French langage corporel (1966). Phrase over my dead body attested by 1833.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bodig "trunk, chest" (of a man or animal); related to 古高地德语 botah, 来源不详. Not elsewhere in 日耳曼语, and the word has died out in 德语 (replaced by leib, 原义为 "life," and körper, 源自 拉丁语). In English, extension to "person" 始于 13 世纪晚期 义为 "main part" of anything was in late 古英语, hence its use in reference to vehicles (1520 年代). Contrasted with soul 自 at least 13 世纪中期 义为 "corpse" (short for dead body) 始于 13 世纪晚期 Transferred to matter generally in 中古英语 (as in heavenly body, 14 世纪晚期). Body politic "the nation, the state" 首见于 1520 年代, legalese, with 法语 word order. Body image was coined 1935 年. Body language 见于 1967 年, 或源自 法语 langage corporel (1966 年). Phrase over my dead body attested 截至 1833 年.

example.en: Regular stretching keeps the body flexible and reduces injury risk.
example.zh: 定期拉伸能保持身体柔韧性，降低受伤风险。

entries.etymology:
early 13c., from Old French bolir "boil, bubble up, ferment, gush" (12c., Modern French bouillir), from Latin bullire "to bubble, seethe," from PIE base *beu- "to swell" (see bull (n.2)). The native word is seethe. Figurative sense of "to agitate the feelings" is from 1640s.
Related: Boiled; boiling. Boiling point is recorded from 1773.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 古法语 bolir "boil, bubble up, ferment, gush" (12 世纪, 现代法语 bouillir), 源自 拉丁语 bullire "to bubble, seethe," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) base *beu- "to swell" （参见 bull (n.2)). The 本族 word is seethe. Figurative 语义 "to agitate the feelings" 始于 1640 年代. 同源词：Boiled; boiling. Boiling point 见于 1773 年.

example.en: Boil the pasta for ten minutes before draining the water.
example.zh: 将意大利面煮十分钟，然后倒掉水。

entries.etymology: 1540s, agent noun from boil (v.). Meaning "vessel for boiling" is from 1725; steam engine sense is from 1757.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, agent 名词 源自 boil （动）. 义为 "vessel for boiling" 始于 1725 年; steam engine sense 始于 1757 年.

definitionLines: a. 勇敢的；冒失的；醒目的； （线、字等）粗的
entries.definition: a. 勇敢的；冒失的；醒目的； （线、字等）粗的
entries.etymology:
Old English beald (West Saxon), bald (Anglian) "bold, brave, confident, strong," from Proto-Germanic *balthaz (source also of Old High German bald "bold, swift," in names such as Archibald, Leopold, Theobald; Gothic balþei "boldness;" Old Norse ballr "frightful, dangerous"), perhaps from PIE *bhol-to- suffixed form of *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell" (see bole).

Of flavors (coffee, etc.) from 1829. The noun meaning "those who are bold" is from c. 1300. Old French and Provençal baut "bold," Italian baldo "bold, daring, fearless" are Germanic loan-words.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 beald (West Saxon), bald (Anglian) "bold, brave, confident, strong," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *balthaz (source also of 古高地德语 bald "bold, swift," in names such as Archibald, Leopold, Theobald; Gothic balþei "boldness;" 古北欧语 ballr "frightful, dangerous"), 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhol-to- suffixed form of *bhel- (2) "to blow, swell" （参见 bole). Of flavors (coffee, etc.) 自 1829 年起. The 名词 意为 "those who are bold" 始于 约 1300 年. 古法语 and Provençal baut "bold," 意大利语 baldo "bold, daring, fearless" are 日耳曼语 loan-words.

example.en: She made a bold decision to quit her stable job and start a company.
example.zh: 她做出了一个大胆的决定，辞去稳定的工作去创业。

entries.definition: n. 螺栓，插销；霹雳 vt. 闩门，关窗，拴住
entries.etymology:
Old English bolt "short, stout arrow with a heavy head;" also "crossbow for throwing bolts," from Proto-Germanic *bultas (source also of Old Norse bolti, Danish bolt, Dutch bout, German Bolzen), perhaps from PIE root *bheld- "to knock, strike" (source also of Lithuanian beldu "I knock," baldas "pole for striking").

Applied since Middle English to other short metal rods (especially those with knobbed ends). From the notion of an arrow's flight comes the lightning bolt (1530s). A bolt of canvas (c. 1400) was so called for its shape. Adverbial phrase bolt upright is from late 14c.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bolt "short, stout arrow with a heavy head;" also "crossbow for throwing bolts," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bultas (source also of 古北欧语 bolti, Danish bolt, 荷兰语 bout, 德语 Bolzen), 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheld- "to knock, strike" (source also of Lithuanian beldu "I knock," baldas "pole for striking"). Applied 自 中古英语 to other short metal rods (尤指 those with knobbed ends). From the 概念 an arrow's flight comes the lightning bolt (1530 年代). A bolt of canvas (约 1400 年) was so called for its shape. Adverbial phrase bolt upright 始于 14 世纪晚期

example.en: He tightened every bolt before the machine started.
example.zh: 机器启动前他拧紧了每一颗螺栓。

entries.definition: n. 炸弹 vt. 轰炸
entries.etymology: 1580s, from French bombe, from Italian bomba, probably from Latin bombus "a deep, hollow noise; a buzzing or booming sound," from Greek bombos "deep and hollow sound," echoic. Originally of mortar shells, etc.; modern sense of "explosive device placed by hand or dropped from airplane" is 1909. Meaning "old car" is from 1953. Meaning "success" is from 1954 (late 1990s slang the bomb "the best" is probably a fresh formation); opposite sense of "a failure" is from 1963. The bomb "atomic bomb" is from 1945.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, 源自 法语 bombe, 源自 意大利语 bomba, 可能 源自 拉丁语 bombus "a deep, hollow noise; a buzzing or booming sound," 源自 希腊语 bombos "deep and hollow sound," echoic. Originally of mortar shells, etc.; modern 语义 "explosive device placed by hand or dropped from airplane" is 1909 年. 义为 "old car" 始于 1953 年. 义为 "success" 始于 1954 年 (late 1990 年代 俚语 the bomb "the best" is 可能 a fresh formation); opposite 语义 "a failure" 始于 1963 年. The bomb "atomic bomb" 始于 1945 年.

example.en: Enemy aircraft dropped a bomb on the bridge during the war.
example.zh: 战争期间，敌机在这座桥上投下了一枚炸弹。

definitionLines: n. 契约，公债，债券；联结，联系
entries.definition: n. 契约，公债，债券；联结，联系
entries.etymology: early 13c., "anything that binds," phonetic variant of band (n.1). For vowel change, see long (adj.); also influenced by Old English bonda "householder," literally "dweller" (see bondage). Legalistic sense first recorded 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "anything that binds," phonetic 为 … 的变体 band (n.1). For vowel change, 参见 long （形）; also influenced by 古英语 bonda "householder," 字面义为 "dweller" （参见 bondage). Legalistic sense 首见于 1590 年代.

example.en: Shared memories create a strong emotional bond between old friends.
example.zh: 共同的回忆在老朋友之间建立起强烈的情感纽带。

entries.etymology: Old English ban "bone, tusk," from Proto-Germanic *bainam (source also of Old Frisian ben, Old Norse bein, Danish ben, German Bein). No cognates outside Germanic (the common PIE root is *os-; see osseous); the Norse, Dutch, and German cognates also mean "shank of the leg," and this is the main meaning in Modern German, but English never seems to have had this sense.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ban "bone, tusk," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bainam (source also of 古弗里西语 ben, 古北欧语 bein, Danish ben, 德语 Bein). No cognates outside 日耳曼语 (the common 原始印欧语 (PIE) root is *os-; 参见 osseous); the Norse, 荷兰语, and 德语 cognates also mean "shank of the leg," and this is the main 意为 in 现代 德语, but English never seems to have had this sense.

example.en: The doctor confirmed that the bone in her wrist had fully healed.
example.zh: 医生确认她手腕上的骨头已经完全愈合了。

definitionLines: n. 奖金；红利；额外津贴
entries.definition: n. 奖金；红利；额外津贴
entries.etymology: 1773, "Stock Exchange Latin" [Weekley], from Latin bonus "good" (adj.); see bene-. The correct noun form would be bonum. In U.S. history the bonus army was tens of thousands of World War I veterans and followers who marched on Washington, D.C., in 1932 demanding early redemption of their service bonus certificates (which carried a maximum value of $625).
entries.etymologyZh: 1773 年, "Stock Exchange Latin" [Weekley], 源自 拉丁语 bonus "good" （形）; 参见 bene-. The correct 名词 form would be bonum. In U.S. history the bonus army was tens of thousands of World War I veterans and followers who marched on Washington, D.C., 于 1932 年 demanding early redemption of their service bonus certificates (which carried a maximum value of $625).

example.en: Employees who exceeded their targets received a generous year-end bonus.
example.zh: 超额完成目标的员工获得了丰厚的年终奖金。

entries.definition: n. 书，书籍 vt. 预订
entries.etymology: Old English boc "book, writing, written document," traditionally from Proto-Germanic *bokiz "beech" (source also of German Buch "book" Buche "beech;" see beech), the notion being of beechwood tablets on which runes were inscribed, but it may be from the tree itself (people still carve initials in them). The Old English word originally meant any written document. Latin and Sanskrit also have words for "writing" that are based on tree names ("birch" and "ash," respectively). Meaning "libretto of an opera" is from 1768. A betting book is from 1856.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 boc "book, writing, written document," traditionally 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bokiz "beech" (source also of 德语 Buch "book" Buche "beech;" 参见 beech), the notion being of beechwood tablets on which runes were inscribed, but it may be 源自 tree itself (people still carve initials in them). The 古英语 word 原义为 meant any written document. 拉丁语 and 梵语 also have words for "writing" that are based on tree names ("birch" and "ash," respectively). 义为 "libretto of an opera" 始于 1768 年. A betting book 始于 1856 年.

example.en: I need to book a flight ticket before prices go up next week.
example.zh: 我需要在下周价格上涨之前预订一张机票。

entries.etymology: 1859, from book (n.) + diminutive ending -let.
entries.etymologyZh: 1859 年, 源自 book （名） + diminutive ending -let.

entries.etymology: also book-mark, 1840, from book (n.) + mark (n.1). Bookmarker is older (1838). As a verb, by 1900. Related: Bookmarked; bookmarking.
entries.etymologyZh: also book-mark, 1840 年, 源自 book （名） + mark (n.1). Bookmarker is older (1838 年). 作动词时, 截至 1900 年. 同源词：Bookmarked; bookmarking.

definitionLines: v./n. 隆隆声；繁荣，兴隆起来
entries.definition: v./n. 隆隆声；繁荣，兴隆起来
entries.etymology: mid-15c., earliest use was for bees and wasps, probably echoic of humming. The meaning "make a loud noise" is 15c. Compare bomb. Meaning "to burst into prosperity" (of places, businesses, etc.) is 1871, American English. Related: Boomed; booming. Boom box first attested 1978.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, earliest use was for bees and wasps, 可能 echoic of humming. The 意为 "make a loud noise" is 15 世纪 对比 bomb. 义为 "to burst into prosperity" (of places, businesses, etc.) is 1871 年, American English. 同源词：Boomed; booming. Boom box 最早见于 1978 年.

example.en: The local tourism industry began to boom after the new airport opened.
example.zh: 新机场开通后，当地旅游业开始繁荣起来。

entries.etymology: 1815, literal and figurative, American English, of unknown origin. Related: Boosted; boosting. As a noun by 1825.
entries.etymologyZh: 1815 年, literal and figurative, American English, 来源不详. 同源词：Boosted; boosting. 作名词时 截至 1825 年.

example.en: Lower interest rates are expected to boost consumer spending this quarter.
example.zh: 预计较低的利率将在本季度促进消费支出。

entries.etymology: mid-12c., from Old Danish boþ "temporary dwelling," from East Norse *boa "to dwell," from Proto-Germanic *bowan-, from PIE root *bheue- "to be, exist, grow" (see be). See also bound (adj.2). Compare German Bude "booth, stall," Middle Dutch boode, Lithuanian butas "house," Old Irish both "hut," Bohemian bouda, Polish buda, some probably borrowed from East Norse, some formed from the PIE root.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪中期, 源自 Old Danish boþ "temporary dwelling," 源自 East Norse *boa "to dwell," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bowan-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bheue- "to be, exist, grow" （参见 be). See also bound (adj.2). 对比 德语 Bude "booth, stall," Middle 荷兰语 boode, Lithuanian butas "house," Old 爱尔兰语 both "hut," Bohemian bouda, Polish buda, some 可能 借自 East Norse, some formed 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root.

example.en: She stepped into the phone booth to make a quick call.
example.zh: 她走进电话亭打了个简短的电话。

definitionLines: vi. 交界，与……毗邻；与…… 相似
entries.definition: n. 边缘；边界，边境 vi. 交界，与……毗邻；与…… 相似
entries.etymology: mid-14c., from Old French bordure "seam, edge of a shield, border," from Frankish *bord or a similar Germanic source (compare Old English bord "side;" see board (n.2)). The geopolitical sense first attested 1530s, in Scottish (replacing earlier march), from The Borders, name of the district adjoining the boundary between England and Scotland.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 bordure "seam, edge of a shield, border," 源自 Frankish *bord or a similar 日耳曼语 source (对比 古英语 bord "side;" 参见 board (n.2)). The geopolitical sense 最早见于 1530 年代, in 苏格兰语 (replacing earlier march), 源自 The Borders, name of the district adjoining the boundary between England and Scotland.

example.en: Soldiers guard the border between the two countries day and night.
example.zh: 士兵日夜守卫着两国之间的边境。

definitionLines: vt. 钻洞，打眼，钻探；使厌烦
entries.definition: vt. 钻洞，打眼，钻探；使厌烦 n. 令人讨厌的人/物
entries.etymology: thing which causes ennui or annoyance, 1778; of persons by 1812; from bore (v.1).
entries.etymologyZh: thing which causes ennui or annoyance, 1778 年; of persons 截至 1812 年; 源自 bore (v.1).

example.en: His endless complaints began to bore everyone in the room.
example.zh: 他没完没了的抱怨开始让房间里的每个人都感到厌烦。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "action of piercing," from bore (v.). From 1853 in reference to animals that bore; 1840 in the sense "wearying, causing ennui."
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "action of piercing," 源自 bore （动）. From 1853 年 in reference to animals that bore; 1840 年 in the sense "wearying, causing ennui."

example.en: The two-hour lecture was so boring that half the students fell asleep.
example.zh: 这场长达两小时的讲座太无聊了，有一半学生睡着了。

entries.etymology: Old English borgian "to lend, be surety for," from Proto-Germanic *borg "pledge" (source also of Old English borg "pledge, security, bail, debt," Old Norse borga "to become bail for, guarantee," Middle Dutch borghen "to protect, guarantee," Old High German boragen "to beware of," German borgen "to borrow; to lend"), from PIE root *bhergh- (1) "to hide, protect" (see bury). entries.etymology:
mid-13c., boie "servant, commoner, knave, boy," of unknown origin. Possibly from Old French embuie "one fettered," from Vulgar Latin *imboiare, from Latin boia "leg iron, yoke, leather collar," from Greek boeiai dorai "ox hides." (Words for "boy" double as "servant, attendant" across the Indo-European map -- compare Italian ragazzo, French garçon, Greek pais, Middle English knave, Old Church Slavonic otroku -- and often it is difficult to say which meaning came first.)

But it also appears to be identical with East Frisian boi "young gentleman," and perhaps with Dutch boef "knave," from Middle Dutch boeve, perhaps from Middle Low German buobe. This suggests a gradational relationship to babe. For a different conjecture:

Used slightingly of young men in Middle English; meaning "male negro slave or Asian personal servant of any age" attested from c. 1600. Exclamation oh, boy attested from 1892.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, boie "servant, commoner, knave, boy," 来源不详. Possibly 源自 古法语 embuie "one fettered," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *imboiare, 源自 拉丁语 boia "leg iron, yoke, leather collar," 源自 希腊语 boeiai dorai "ox hides." (Words for "boy" double as "servant, attendant" across the Indo-European map -- 对比 意大利语 ragazzo, 法语 garçon, 希腊语 pais, 中古英语 knave, Old Church Slavonic otroku -- and 常 it is difficult to say which 意为 came first.) But it also appears to be identical with East Frisian boi "young gentleman," and 或许 with 荷兰语 boef "knave," 源自 Middle 荷兰语 boeve, 或源自 Middle Low 德语 buobe. This suggests a gradational relationship to babe. For a different conjecture: Used slightingly of young men in 中古英语; 意为 "male negro slave or Asian personal servant of any age" attested 源自 约 1600 年. Exclamation oh, boy attested 自 1892 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English brægen "brain," from Proto-Germanic *bragnam (source also of Middle Low German bregen, Old Frisian and Dutch brein), from PIE root *mregh-m(n)o- "skull, brain" (source also of Greek brekhmos "front part of the skull, top of the head"). But Liberman writes that brain "has no established cognates outside West Germanic ..." and is not connected to the Greek word. More probably, he writes, its etymon is PIE *bhragno "something broken."

The custom of using the plural to refer to the substance (literal or figurative), as opposed to the organ, dates from 16c. Figurative sense of "intellectual power" is from late 14c.; meaning "a clever person" is first recorded 1914. Brain teaser is from 1923. Brain stem first recorded 1879, from German. Brain drain is attested from 1963. An Old English word for "head" was brægnloca, which might be translated as "brain locker." In Middle English, brainsick (Old English brægenseoc) meant "mad, addled."

But Liberman writes that brain "has no established cognates outside West Germanic ..." and is not connected to the 希腊语 word. More 可能, he writes, its etymon is 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhragno "something broken." The custom of using the plural to refer to the substance (literal or figurative), as opposed to the organ, dates 源自 16 世纪 Figurative 语义 "intellectual power" 始于 14 世纪晚期; 意为 "a clever person" is 首见于 1914 年. Brain teaser 始于 1923 年. Brain stem 首见于 1879 年, 源自 德语. Brain drain 见于 1963 年. An 古英语 word for "head" was brægnloca, which might be translated as "brain locker." In 中古英语, brainsick (古英语 brægenseoc) meant "mad, addled."

Meaning "local office of a business" is first recorded 1817, from earlier sense of "component part of a system" (1690s).

entries.etymology:
Old English bræs "brass, bronze," originally in reference to an alloy of copper and tin (now bronze), later and in modern use an alloy of two parts copper, one part zinc. A mystery word, with no known cognates beyond English. Perhaps akin to French brasser "to brew," because it is an alloy. It also has been compared to Old Swedish brasa "fire," but no sure connection can be made. Yet another theory connects it with Latin ferrum "iron," itself of obscure origin.

As brass was unknown in antiquity, use of the word in Bible translations, etc., likely means "bronze." The Romans were the first to deliberately make it. Words for "brass" in other languages (such as German Messing, Old English mæsling, French laiton, Italian ottone) also tend to be difficult to explain.

The meaning "effrontery, impudence" is from 1620s. Slang sense of "high officials" is first recorded 1899. The brass tacks that you get down to (1897) probably are the ones used to measure cloth on the counter of a dry goods store, suggesting precision. Slang brass balls "toughness, courage" (emphatically combining two metaphors for the same thing) attested by 1960s.

It also has been compared to Old Swedish brasa "fire," but no sure connection can be made. Yet another theory connects it with 拉丁语 ferrum "iron," itself of obscure origin. entries.etymology:
late 15c., from Middle French brave, "splendid, valiant," from Italian bravo "brave, bold," originally "wild, savage," possibly from Medieval Latin bravus "cutthroat, villain," from Latin pravus "crooked, depraved;" a less likely etymology being from Latin barbarus (see barbarous). A Celtic origin (Irish breagh, Cornish bray) also has been suggested.

Old English words for this, some with overtones of "rashness," included modig (now "moody"), beald ("bold"), cene ("keen"), dyrstig ("daring"). Brave new world is from the title of Aldous Huxley's 1932 satirical utopian novel; he lifted the phrase from Shakespeare ("Tempest" v.i.183).

A Celtic origin (爱尔兰语 breagh, Cornish bray) also has been suggested. 古英语 words for this, some with overtones of "rashness," included modig (现在 "moody"), beald ("bold"), cene ("keen"), dyrstig ("daring"). Brave new world 始于 the title of Aldous Huxley's 1932 年 satirical utopian novel; he lifted the phrase 源自 Shakespeare ("Tempest" v.i.183).

Figurative sense of "a breaking of rules, etc." was in Old English Breach of contract is at least from 1660s.

entries.etymology:
Old English bread "bit, crumb, morsel; bread," cognate with Old Norse brauð, Danish brød, Old Frisian brad, Middle Dutch brot, Dutch brood, German Brot. According to one theory [Watkins, etc.] from Proto-Germanic *brautham, which would be from the root of brew (v.) and refer to the leavening.

But OED argues at some length for the basic sense being not "cooked food" but "piece of food," and the Old English word deriving from a Proto-Germanic *braudsmon- "fragments, bits" (cognate with Old High German brosma "crumb," Old English breotan "to break in pieces") and being related to the root of break (v.). It cites  Slovenian kruh "bread," literally "a piece."

Either way, by c. 1200 it had replaced the usual Old English word for "bread," which was hlaf (see loaf (n.)). Slang meaning "money" dates from 1940s, but compare breadwinner. Bread-and-butter in the figurative sense of "basic needs" is from 1732. Bread and circuses (1914) is from Latin, in reference to food and entertainment provided by governments to keep the populace happy. "Duas tantum res anxius optat, Panem et circenses" [Juvenal, Sat. x.80].
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bread "bit, crumb, morsel; bread," 与 … 同源 古北欧语 brauð, Danish brød, 古弗里西语 brad, Middle 荷兰语 brot, 荷兰语 brood, 德语 Brot. According to one theory [Watkins, etc.] 源自 原始日耳曼语 *brautham, which would be 源自 root of brew （动） and refer to the leavening. But OED argues at some length for the basic sense being not "cooked food" but "piece of food," and the 古英语 word deriving 源自 a 原始日耳曼语 *braudsmon- "fragments, bits" (与 … 同源 古高地德语 brosma "crumb," 古英语 breotan "to break in pieces") and being related to the root of break （动）. It cites Slovenian kruh "bread," 字面义为 "a piece." Either way, by 约 1200 年 it had replaced the usual 古英语 word for "bread," which was hlaf （参见 loaf （名）). Slang 意为 "money" dates 源自 1940 年代, but 对比 breadwinner. Bread-and-butter in the figurative 语义 "basic needs" 始于 1732 年. Bread and circuses (1914 年) 始于 拉丁语, in reference to food and entertainment provided by governments to keep the populace happy. "Duas tantum res anxius optat, Panem et circenses" [Juvenal, Sat. x.80].

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "act of breaking," from break (v.). Sense of "short interval between spells of work" (originally between lessons at school) is from 1861. Meaning "stroke of luck" is attested by 1911, probably an image from billiards (where the break that starts the game is attested from 1865). Meaning "stroke of mercy" is from 1914. Musical sense, "improvised passage, solo" is attested from 1920s in jazz.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "act of breaking," 源自 break （动）. 义为 "short interval between spells of work" (原义为 between lessons at school) 始于 1861 年. 义为 "stroke of luck" is attested 截至 1911 年, 可能 an image 源自 billiards (where the break that starts the game 见于 1865 年). 义为 "stroke of mercy" 始于 1914 年. Musical sense, "improvised passage, solo" 见于 1920 年代 in jazz.

entries.etymology:
mid-15c., from break (v.) + fast (n.). An Old English word for it was undernmete (see undern), also morgenmete "morning meal.". The verb is recorded from 1670s. Related: Breakfasted; breakfasting.

Spanish almuerzo "lunch," but formerly and still locally "breakfast," is from Latin admorsus, past participle of admordere "to bite into," from ad- "to" + mordere "to bite." In common with almuerzo, words for "breakfast" tend over time to shift in meaning toward "lunch;" compare French déjeuner "breakfast," later "lunch" (equivalent of Spanish desayuno "breakfast"), both from Vulgar Latin *disieiunare "to breakfast," from Latin dis- "apart, in a different direction from" + ieiunare, jejunare "fast" (see jejune; also compare dine). German Frühstück is from Middle High German vruostücke, literally "early bit."
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 break （动） + fast （名）. An 古英语 word for it was undernmete （参见 undern), also morgenmete "morning meal.". The 动词 见于 1670 年代. 同源词：Breakfasted; breakfasting. 西班牙语 almuerzo "lunch," but formerly and still locally "breakfast," 始于 拉丁语 admorsus, 为 … 的过去分词 admordere "to bite into," 源自 ad- "to" + mordere "to bite." In common with almuerzo, words for "breakfast" tend over time to shift in 意为 toward "lunch;" 对比 法语 déjeuner "breakfast," later "lunch" (equivalent of 西班牙语 desayuno "breakfast"), both 源自 通俗拉丁语 *disieiunare "to breakfast," 源自 拉丁语 dis- "apart, in a different direction from" + ieiunare, jejunare "fast" （参见 jejune; also 对比 dine). 德语 Frühstück 始于 Middle High 德语 vruostücke, 字面义为 "early bit."

entries.etymology: 1918, in a military sense, from break (v.) + through (adv.). The verbal phrase is attested from c. 1400. Meaning "abrupt solution or progress" is from 1930s, on the notion of a successful attack.

entries.etymology: Old English breost "breast, bosom; mind, thought, disposition," from Proto-Germanic *breustam "breast" (source also of Old Saxon briost, Old Frisian briast, Old Norse brjost, Dutch borst, German brust, Gothic brusts), perhaps literally "swelling" and from PIE root *bhreus- "to swell, sprout" (source also of Middle Irish bruasach "having a broad, strong chest," Old Irish bruinne "breast"). The spelling conforms to the Scottish and northern England dialectal pronunciation. Figurative sense of "seat of the emotions" was in Old English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 breost "breast, bosom; mind, thought, disposition," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *breustam "breast" (source also of 古撒克逊语 briost, 古弗里西语 briast, 古北欧语 brjost, 荷兰语 borst, 德语 brust, Gothic brusts), 或许 字面义为 "swelling" and 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhreus- "to swell, sprout" (source also of Middle 爱尔兰语 bruasach "having a broad, strong chest," Old 爱尔兰语 bruinne "breast"). The spelling conforms to the 苏格兰语 and northern England 方言 pronunciation. Figurative 语义 "seat of the emotions" was in 古英语.

entries.etymology: Old English bræð "odor, scent, stink, exhalation, vapor" (Old English word for "air exhaled from the lungs" was æðm), from Proto-Germanic *bræthaz "smell, exhalation" (source also of Old High German bradam, German Brodem "breath, steam"), from PIE root *gwhre- "to breathe, smell."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bræð "odor, scent, stink, exhalation, vapor" (古英语 word for "air exhaled from the lungs" was æðm), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bræthaz "smell, exhalation" (source also of 古高地德语 bradam, 德语 Brodem "breath, steam"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *gwhre- "to breathe, smell."

entries.etymology: Old English bredan "bring young to birth, carry," also "cherish, keep warm," from West Germanic *brodjan (source also of Old High German bruoten, German brüten "to brood, hatch"), from *brod- "fetus, hatchling," from PIE *bhreue- "burn, heat" (see brood (n.)). Original notion of the word was incubation, warming to hatch. Sense of "grow up, be reared" (in a clan, etc.) is late 14c. Related: Bred; breeding.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bredan "bring young to birth, carry," also "cherish, keep warm," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *brodjan (source also of 古高地德语 bruoten, 德语 brüten "to brood, hatch"), 源自 *brod- "fetus, hatchling," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhreue- "burn, heat" （参见 brood （名）). Original 概念 the word was incubation, warming to hatch. 义为 "grow up, be reared" (in a clan, etc.) is 14 世纪晚期 同源词：Bred; breeding.

entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, "north or northeast wind," 源自 Old 西班牙语 briza "cold northeast wind;" in West Indies and 西班牙语 Main, the sense shifting to "northeast trade wind," 之后 "fresh wind from the sea." The 俚语 for "something easy" is American English, 约 1928 年.

entries.etymology: Old English breowan "to brew" (class II strong verb, past tense breaw, past participle browen), from Proto-Germanic *breuwan "to brew" (source also of Old Norse brugga, Old Frisian briuwa, Middle Dutch brouwen, Old High German briuwan, German brauen "to brew"), from PIE root *bhreuə- "to bubble, boil, effervesce" (source also of Sanskrit bhurnih "violent, passionate," Greek phrear "well, spring, cistern," Latin fervere "to boil, foam," Thracian Greek brytos "fermented liquor made from barley," Russian bruja "current," Old Irish bruth "heat;" Old English beorma "yeast;" Old High German brato "roast meat"), the original sense thus being "make a drink by boiling." Related: Brewed; brewing.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 breowan "to brew" (class II strong 动词, past tense breaw, past participle browen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *breuwan "to brew" (source also of 古北欧语 brugga, 古弗里西语 briuwa, Middle 荷兰语 brouwen, 古高地德语 briuwan, 德语 brauen "to brew"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhreuə- "to bubble, boil, effervesce" (source also of 梵语 bhurnih "violent, passionate," 希腊语 phrear "well, spring, cistern," 拉丁语 fervere "to boil, foam," Thracian 希腊语 brytos "fermented liquor made from barley," 俄语 bruja "current," Old 爱尔兰语 bruth "heat;" 古英语 beorma "yeast;" 古高地德语 brato "roast meat"), the original sense thus being "make a drink by boiling." 同源词：Brewed; brewing.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "thing stolen," from Old French bribe "bit, piece, hunk; morsel of bread given to beggars" (14c., compare Old French bribeor "vagrant, beggar"), from briber, brimber "to beg," a general Romanic word (Gamillscheg marks it as Rotwelsch, i.e. "thieves' jargon"), of uncertain origin; old sources suggest Celtic (compare Breton breva "to break"). Shift of meaning to "gift given to influence corruptly" is by mid-15c.

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Old French briche "brick," probably from a Germanic source akin to Middle Dutch bricke "a tile," literally "a broken piece," from the verbal root of break (v.). Meaning "a good, honest fellow" is from 1840, probably on notion of squareness (as in fair and square) though most extended senses of brick (and square) applied to persons in English are not meant to be complimentary. Brick wall in the figurative sense of "impenetrable barrier" is from 1886.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 古法语 briche "brick," 可能 源自 a 日耳曼语 source akin to Middle 荷兰语 bricke "a tile," 字面义为 "a broken piece," 源自 verbal root of break （动）. 义为 "a good, honest fellow" 始于 1840 年, 可能 on 概念 squareness (as in fair and square) though most extended senses of brick (and square) applied to persons in English are not meant to be complimentary. entries.etymology: Old English bryd "bride, betrothed or newly married woman," from Proto-Germanic *bruthiz "woman being married" (source also of Old Frisian breid, Dutch bruid, Old High German brut, German Braut "bride"). Gothic cognate bruþs, however, meant "daughter-in-law," and the form of the word borrowed from Old High German into Medieval Latin (bruta) and Old French (bruy) had only this sense. In ancient Indo-European custom, the married woman went to live with her husband's family, so the only "newly wed female" in such a household would have been the daughter-in-law. On the same notion, some trace the word itself to the PIE verbal root *bru- "to cook, brew, make broth," as this likely was the daughter-in-law's job.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bryd "bride, betrothed or newly married woman," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bruthiz "woman being married" (source also of 古弗里西语 breid, 荷兰语 bruid, 古高地德语 brut, 德语 Braut "bride"). Gothic 同源 bruþs, however, meant "daughter-in-law," and the form of the word 借自 古高地德语 into 中古拉丁语 (bruta) and 古法语 (bruy) had only this sense. In ancient Indo-European custom, the married woman went to live with her husband's family, so the only "newly wed female" in such a household would have been the daughter-in-law. On the same notion, some trace the word itself to the PIE verbal root *bru- "to cook, brew, make broth," as this likely was the daughter-in-law's job.

Meaning "quick-witted" is from 1741.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bryht, by metathesis 源自 beorht "bright; splendid; clear-sounding; beautiful; divine," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *berhta- "bright" (source also of 古撒克逊语 berht, 古北欧语 bjartr, 古高地德语 beraht, Gothic bairhts "bright"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhereg- "to gleam, white" (source also of 梵语 bhrajate "shines, glitters," Lithuanian breksta "to dawn," Welsh berth "bright, beautiful"). 义为 "quick-witted" 始于 1741 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English bringan "to bring, bring forth, produce, present, offer" (past tense brohte, past participle broht), from Proto-Germanic *brengan (source also of Old Frisian brenga, Middle Dutch brenghen, Old High German bringan, Gothic briggan); no exact cognates outside Germanic, but it appears to be from PIE root *bhrengk-, compound based on root *bher- (1) "to carry" (source also of Latin ferre; see infer).

The tendency to conjugate this as a strong verb on the model of sing, drink, etc., is ancient: Old English also had a rare strong past participle form, brungen, corresponding to modern colloquial brung. To bring down the house figuratively (1754) is to elicit applause so thunderous it collapses the roof.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bringan "to bring, bring forth, produce, present, offer" (past tense brohte, past participle broht), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *brengan (source also of 古弗里西语 brenga, Middle 荷兰语 brenghen, 古高地德语 bringan, Gothic briggan); no exact cognates outside 日耳曼语, but it appears to be 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhrengk-, 复合词 based on root *bher- (1) "to carry" (source also of 拉丁语 ferre; 参见 infer). The tendency to conjugate this 作为 strong 动词 on the model of sing, drink, etc., is ancient: 古英语 also had a rare strong past participle form, brungen, corresponding to modern 口语 brung. To bring down the house figuratively (1754 年) is to elicit applause so thunderous it collapses the roof.

entries.etymology: mid-14c. (mid-13c. in surnames), "commercial agent, factor," also "an agent in sordid business," from Anglo-French brocour "small trader," from abrokur "retailer of wine, tapster;" perhaps from Portuguese alborcar "barter," but more likely from Old French brocheor, from brochier "to broach, tap, pierce (a keg)," from broche "pointed tool" (see broach (n.)), giving original sense of "wine dealer," hence "retailer, middleman, agent." In Middle English, used contemptuously of peddlers and pimps, "one who buys and sells public office" (late 14c. in Anglo-French), "intermediary in love or marriage" (late 14c.).

entries.etymology:
1721, "alloy of copper and tin," from French bronze, from Italian bronzo, from Medieval Latin bronzium. Perhaps cognate (via notion of color) with Venetian bronza "glowing coals," or German brunst "fire." Perhaps influenced by Latin Brundisium the Italian town of Brindisi (Pliny writes of aes Brundusinum). Perhaps ultimately from Persian birinj "copper."

In Middle English, the distinction between bronze (copper-tin alloy) and brass (copper-zinc alloy) was not clear, and both were called bras. A bronze medal was given to a third-place finisher since at least 1852. The archaeological Bronze Age (1865) falls between the Stone and Iron ages, and is a reference to the principal material for making weapons and ornaments.

Perhaps influenced by 拉丁语 Brundisium the 意大利语 town of Brindisi (Pliny writes of aes Brundusinum). Perhaps 最终源自 波斯语 birinj "copper." In 中古英语, the distinction between bronze (copper-tin alloy) and brass (copper-zinc alloy) was not clear, and both were called bras. entries.etymology:
Old English brom "broom, brushwood," the common flowering shrub whose twigs were tied together to make a tool for sweeping, from Proto-Germanic *bræmaz "thorny bush" (source also of Dutch braam, German Brombeere "blackberry"), from PIE root *bh(e)rem- "to project, a point."

Traditionally, both the flowers and sweeping with broom twigs were considered unlucky in May (Suffolk, Sussex, Wiltshire, etc.). The witch's flying broomstick originally was one among many such objects (pitchfork, trough, bowl), but the broomstick became fixed as the popular tool of supernatural flight via engravings from a famous Lancashire witch trial of 1612.

entries.etymology:
Old English broþor, from Proto-Germanic *brothar (source also of Old Norse broðir, Danish broder, Old Frisian brother, Dutch broeder, German Bruder, Gothic bróþar), from PIE root *bhrater (source also of Sanskrit bhrátár-, Old Persian brata, Greek phratér, Latin frater, Old Irish brathir, Welsh brawd, Lithuanian broterelis, Old Prussian brati, Old Church Slavonic bratru, Czech bratr "brother").

A highly stable word across the Indo-European languages. In the few cases where other words provide the sense, it is where the cognate of brother had been applied widely to "member of a fraternity," or where there was need to distinguish "son of the same mother" and "son of the same father." E.g. Greek adelphos, probably originally an adjective with frater and meaning, specifically, "brother of the womb" or "brother by blood;" and Spanish hermano "brother," from Latin germanus "full brother." As a familiar term of address from one man to another, it is attested from 1912 in U.S. slang; the specific use among blacks is recorded from 1973.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 broþor, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *brothar (source also of 古北欧语 broðir, Danish broder, 古弗里西语 brother, 荷兰语 broeder, 德语 Bruder, Gothic bróþar), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhrater (source also of 梵语 bhrátár-, Old 波斯语 brata, 希腊语 phratér, 拉丁语 frater, Old 爱尔兰语 brathir, Welsh brawd, Lithuanian broterelis, Old Prussian brati, Old Church Slavonic bratru, Czech bratr "brother"). A highly stable word across the Indo-European languages. In the few cases where other words provide the sense, it is where the 同源 of brother had been applied widely to "member of a fraternity," or where there was need to distinguish "son of the same mother" and "son of the same father." E.g. 希腊语 adelphos, 可能 原义为 an 形容词 with frater and 意为, specifically, "brother of the womb" or "brother by blood;" and 西班牙语 hermano "brother," 源自 拉丁语 germanus "full brother." 作为 familiar term of address 源自 one man to another, it 见于 1912 年 in U.S. 俚语; the specific use among blacks 见于 1973 年.

entries.etymology:
early 14c., browes, brues "brow, forehead, eyebrow," earlier brouwes (c. 1300), bruwen (c. 1200), from Old English bru, probably originally "eyebrow," but extended to "eyelash," then "eyelid" by association of the hair of the eyebrow with the hair of the eyelid, the eyebrows then becoming Old English oferbrua "overbrows" (early Middle English uvere breyhes or briges aboue þe eiges).

The general word for "eyebrow" in Middle English was  brew, breowen (c. 1200), from Old English bræw (West Saxon), *brew (Anglian), from Proto-Germanic *bræwi- "blinker, twinkler" (source also of Old Frisian bre, Old Saxon brawa, Middle Dutch brauwe "eyelid," Old High German brawa"eyebrow," Old Norse bra "eyebrow," Gothic brahw "twinkle, blink," in phrase in brahwa augins "in the twinkling of an eye").

Old English bru is from Proto-Germanic *brus- "eyebrow" (source also of Old Norse brun), from PIE *bhru- "eyebrow" (source also of Sanskrit bhrus "eyebrow," Greek ophrys, Old Church Slavonic bruvi, Lithuanian bruvis "brow," Old Irish bru "edge"). The -n- in the Old Norse (brun) and German (braune) forms of the word are from a genitive plural inflection.

Words for "eyelid," "eyelash," and "eyebrow" changed about maddeningly in Old and Middle English (and in all the West Germanic languages). By 1530s, brow had been given an extended sense of "forehead," especially with reference to movements and expressions that showed emotion or attitude.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "feed on buds," from Middle French brouster, from Old French broster "to sprout, bud," from brost "young shoot, twig," probably from Proto-Germanic *brust- "bud, shoot," from PIE *bhreus- "to swell, sprout" (see breast (n.)). Lost its final -t in English on the mistaken notion that the letter was a past participle inflection. Figurative extension to "peruse" (books) is 1870s, American English. Related: Browsed; browsing.

entries.etymology:
Old English brun "dark, dusky," developing a definite color sense only 13c., from Proto-Germanic *brunaz (source also of Old Norse brunn, Danish brun, Old Frisian and Old High German brun, Dutch bruin, German braun), from PIE *bher- (3) "shining, brown" (source also of Lithuanian beras "brown"), related to *bheros "dark animal" (compare beaver, bear (n.), and Greek phrynos "toad," literally "the brown animal").

The Old English word also had a sense of "brightness, shining," preserved only in burnish. The Germanic word was adopted into Romanic (Middle Latin brunus, Italian and Spanish bruno, French brun). Brown Bess, slang name for old British Army flintlock musket, first recorded 1785.

The 古英语 word also had a 语义 "brightness, shining," preserved only in burnish. The 日耳曼语 word was adopted into Romanic (Middle 拉丁语 brunus, 意大利语 and 西班牙语 bruno, 法语 brun). entries.etymology:
mid-13c., from Anglo-French buquet "bucket, pail," from Old French buquet "bucket," which is from Frankish or some other Germanic source, or a diminutive of cognate Old English buc "pitcher, bulging vessel," originally "belly" (buckets were formerly of leather as well as wood), both from West Germanic *buh- (source also of Dutch buik, Old High German buh, German Bauch "belly"), possibly from a variant of PIE root *beu-, *bheu- "to grow, swell" (see bull (n.2)).

Kick the bucket "to die" (1785) perhaps is from unrelated Old French buquet "balance," a beam from which slaughtered animals were hung; perhaps reinforced by the notion of suicide by hanging after standing on an upturned bucket (but Farmer calls attention to bucket "a Norfolk term for a pulley").

entries.etymology: early 15c., "leather pouch," from Middle French bougette, diminutive of Old French bouge "leather bag, wallet, pouch," from Latin bulga "leather bag," of Gaulish origin (compare Old Irish bolg "bag," Breton bolc'h "flax pod"), from PIE *bhelgh- (see belly (n.)). entries.etymology:
"insect," 1620s (earliest reference is to bedbugs), of unknown origin, probably but not certainly from or influenced by Middle English bugge "something frightening, scarecrow" (late 14c.), a meaning obsolete since the "insect" sense arose except in bugbear (1570s) and bugaboo (q.v.).

Probably connected with Scottish bogill "goblin, bugbear," or obsolete Welsh bwg "ghost, goblin" (compare Welsh bwgwl "threat," earlier "fear," Middle Irish bocanách "supernatural being"). Some speculate that these words are from a root meaning "goat" (see buck (n.1)) and represent originally a goat-like spectre. Compare also bogey (n.1) and German bögge, böggel-mann "goblin." Perhaps influenced in meaning by Old English -budda used in compounds for "beetle" (compare Low German budde "louse, grub," Middle Low German buddech "thick, swollen"). 

Meaning "defect in a machine" (1889) may have been coined c. 1878 by Thomas Edison (perhaps with the notion of an insect getting into the works). Meaning "person obsessed by an idea" (such as firebug) is from 1841, perhaps from notion of persistence. Sense of "microbe, germ" is from 1919. Bugs "crazy" is from c. 1900. Bug juice as a slang name for drink is from 1869, originally "bad whiskey." The 1811 slang dictionary has bug-hunter "an upholsterer." Bug-word "word or words meant to irritate and vex" is from 1560s.
entries.etymologyZh: "insect," 1620 年代 (earliest reference is to bedbugs), 来源不详, 可能 but not certainly 源自 or influenced by 中古英语 bugge "something frightening, scarecrow" (14 世纪晚期), a 意为 已废 自 the "insect" sense arose except in bugbear (1570 年代) and bugaboo (q.v.). Probably connected with 苏格兰语 bogill "goblin, bugbear," or 已废 Welsh bwg "ghost, goblin" (对比 Welsh bwgwl "threat," earlier "fear," Middle 爱尔兰语 bocanách "supernatural being"). Some speculate that these words 始于 a root 意为 "goat" （参见 buck (n.1)) and represent 原义为 a goat-like spectre. 对比 also bogey (n.1) and 德语 bögge, böggel-mann "goblin." Perhaps influenced in 意为 by 古英语 -budda used in compounds for "beetle" (对比 Low 德语 budde "louse, grub," Middle Low 德语 buddech "thick, swollen"). 义为 "defect in a machine" (1889 年) may have been coined 约 1878 年 by Thomas Edison (或许 with the 概念 an insect getting into the works). 义为 "person obsessed by an idea" (such as firebug) 始于 1841 年, 或源自 概念 persistence. 义为 "microbe, germ" 始于 1919 年. Bugs "crazy" 始于 约 1900 年. Bug juice 作为 俚语 name for drink 始于 1869 年, 原义为 "bad whiskey." The 1811 年 俚语 dictionary has bug-hunter "an upholsterer." Bug-word "word or words meant to irritate and vex" 始于 1560 年代.

example.en: The developer spent hours tracking down a bug that caused the app to crash.
example.zh: 开发者花了数小时追踪一个导致应用崩溃的程序漏洞。

entries.etymology: late Old English byldan "construct a house," verb form of bold "house," from Proto-Germanic *buthlam (source also of Old Saxon bodl, Old Frisian bodel "building, house"), from PIE *bhu- "to dwell," from root *bheue- "to be, exist, grow" (see be). Rare in Old English; in Middle English it won out over more common Old English timbran (see timber). Modern spelling is unexplained. Figurative use from mid-15c. Of physical things other than buildings from late 16c. Related: Builded (archaic); built; building.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 byldan "construct a house," 动词 form of bold "house," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *buthlam (source also of 古撒克逊语 bodl, 古弗里西语 bodel "building, house"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhu- "to dwell," 源自 root *bheue- "to be, exist, grow" （参见 be). Rare in 古英语; in 中古英语 it won out over more common 古英语 timbran （参见 timber). 现代 spelling is unexplained. Figurative use 源自 15 世纪中期 Of physical things other than buildings 源自 16 世纪晚期 同源词：Builded (古旧); built; building.

example.en: It takes years to build a friendship strong enough to survive real hardship.
example.zh: 建立一段能经受真正磨难的友谊需要数年时间。

entries.etymology: "a structure," c. 1300, verbal noun from build (v.).
entries.etymologyZh: "a structure," 约 1300 年, verbal 名词 源自 build （动）.

example.en: The old building in the city center was converted into a museum.
example.zh: 市中心的一栋旧建筑被改造成了一座博物馆。

entries.etymology: 1560s, "an onion," from Middle French bulbe (15c.), from Latin bulbus "bulb, bulbous root, onion," from Greek bolbos "plant with round swelling on underground stem." Expanded by 1800 to "swelling in a glass tube" (thermometer bulb, light bulb, etc.).
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, "an onion," 源自 中古法语 bulbe (15 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 bulbus "bulb, bulbous root, onion," 源自 希腊语 bolbos "plant with round swelling on underground stem." Expanded 截至 1800 年 to "swelling in a glass tube" (thermometer bulb, light bulb, etc.).

definitionLines: n. 体积，容积；大块，大批；大部 分，主体
entries.definition: n. 体积，容积；大块，大批；大部 分，主体
entries.etymology:
mid-15c., "a heap," earlier "ship's cargo" (mid-14c.), from a Scandinavian source akin to Old Norse bulki "a heap; ship's cargo," thus "goods loaded loose" (perhaps literally "rolled-up load"), from Proto-Germanic *bul-, from PIE root *bhel- (2) "to blow, inflate, swell" (see bole).

Meaning extended by confusion with obsolete bouk "belly" (from Old English buc "body, belly," from Proto-Germanic *bukaz; see bucket), which led to sense of "size," first attested mid-15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "a heap," earlier "ship's cargo" (14 世纪中期), 源自 a Scandinavian source akin to 古北欧语 bulki "a heap; ship's cargo," thus "goods loaded loose" (或许 字面义为 "rolled-up load"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bul-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhel- (2) "to blow, inflate, swell" （参见 bole). 义为 extended by confusion with 已废 bouk "belly" (源自 古英语 buc "body, belly," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bukaz; 参见 bucket), which led to 语义 "size," 最早见于 15 世纪中期

example.en: The bulk of the company's revenue comes from online sales.
example.zh: 公司收入的大部分来自网络销售。

entries.etymologyZh: "push through roughly," 1884 年, 源自 bull (n.1). 同源词：Bulled; bulling.

example.en: The farmer separated the bull from the cows before milking time.

entries.etymology: 1550s, from Middle French boulette "cannonball, small ball," diminutive of boule "a ball" (13c.), from Latin bulla "round thing, knob" (see bull (n.2)). Earliest version of bite the bullet recorded 1891, probably with a sense of giving someone a soft lead bullet to clench in the teeth during a painful operation.
entries.etymologyZh: 1550 年代, 源自 中古法语 boulette "cannonball, small ball," 为 … 的指小形式 boule "a ball" (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 bulla "round thing, knob" （参见 bull (n.2)). entries.etymology: 1765, from French bulletin (16c.), modeled on Italian bulletino, diminutive of bulletta "document, voting slip," itself a diminutive of Latin bulla (see bull (n.2)) with equivalent of Old French -elet (see -let). The word was used earlier in English in the Italian form (mid-17c.). Popularized by their use in the Napoleonic Wars as the name for dispatches sent from the front and meant for the home public (which led to the proverbial expression as false as a bulletin). Bulletin board is from 1831.
entries.etymologyZh: 1765 年, 源自 法语 bulletin (16 世纪), modeled on 意大利语 bulletino, 为 … 的指小形式 bulletta "document, voting slip," itself a 为 … 的指小形式 拉丁语 bulla （参见 bull (n.2)) with equivalent of 古法语 -elet （参见 -let). The word was used earlier in English in the 意大利语 form (17 世纪中期). Popularized by their use in the Napoleonic Wars as the name for dispatches sent 源自 front and meant for the home public (which led to the proverbial expression as false 作为 bulletin). Bulletin board 始于 1831 年.

example.en: The school posted a bulletin about the change in exam schedule.
example.zh: 学校张贴了一份关于考试时间变更的公告。

entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "protuberance caused by a blow;" 1610 年代 as "a dull, solid blow;" 参见 bump （动）. The dancer's bump and grind attested 自 1940 年起.

entries.etymology:
early 14c., "protuberance on the body, swelling," perhaps echoic of the sound of hitting and connected to bump (compare, possibly in similar relationship, hump/hunch).

The sense of "cluster" is mid-15c.; connection with the earlier sense is obscure, and this may be a separate word, perhaps through a nasalized form of Old French bouge (2), 15c., from Flemish boudje diminutive of boud "bundle." Meaning "a lot, a group" is from 1620s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "protuberance on the body, swelling," 或许 echoic of the sound of hitting and connected to bump (对比, possibly in similar relationship, hump/hunch). The 语义 "cluster" is 15 世纪中期; connection with the earlier sense is obscure, and this may be a separate word, 或许 through a nasalized form of 古法语 bouge (2), 15 世纪, 源自 Flemish boudje 为 … 的指小形式 boud "bundle." 义为 "a lot, a group" 始于 1620 年代.

entries.etymology: early 14c., "bound collection of things," from Middle Dutch bondel, diminutive of bond, from binden "to bind," or perhaps a merger of this word and Old English byndele "binding," from Proto-Germanic *bundilin (source also of German bündel "to bundle"), from PIE root *bhendh- "tie" (see bend (v.)). Meaning "a lot of money" is from 1899. To be a bundle of nerves "very anxious" is from 1938.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "bound collection of things," 源自 Middle 荷兰语 bondel, 为 … 的指小形式 bond, 源自 binden "to bind," or 或许 a merger of this word and 古英语 byndele "binding," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bundilin (source also of 德语 bündel "to bundle"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhendh- "tie" （参见 bend （动）). 义为 "a lot of money" 始于 1899 年.
