entries.etymology: 1690s, "desk with drawers, writing desk," from French bureau "office; desk, writing table," originally "cloth covering for a desk," from burel "coarse woolen cloth" (as a cover for writing desks), Old French diminutive of bure "dark brown cloth," which is perhaps either from Latin burrus "red," or from Late Latin burra "wool, shaggy garment." Offices being full of such desks, the meaning expanded 1720 to "division of a government." Meaning "chest of drawers" is from 1770, said to be American English but early in British use.

entries.etymologyZh: 1818 年, 源自 法语 bureaucratie, coined by 法语 economist Jean Claude Marie Vincent de Gournay (1712 年-1759 年) on model of democratie, aristocratie, 源自 bureau "office," 字面义为 "desk" （参见 bureau) + 希腊语 suffix -kratia denoting "power of" （参见 -cracy).

entries.etymology: "act of burying," late 13c.; earlier "tomb" (c. 1200), false singular from Old English byrgels "tomb," from byrgan "to bury" + suffix -els; a compound also found in Old Saxon burgisli, suggesting a Proto-Germanic *burgisli-, from PIE root *bhergh- (1) "to hide, protect" (see bury). The Germanic suffix *-isli- (also in Old English hydels "hiding place," fætels "bag") became obsolete and was felt as a plural of the Latin-derived suffix -al (2) forming nouns of action from verbs (survival, approval, etc.).
entries.etymologyZh: "act of burying," 13 世纪晚期; earlier "tomb" (约 1200 年), false singular 源自 古英语 byrgels "tomb," 源自 byrgan "to bury" + suffix -els; a 复合词 also found in 古撒克逊语 burgisli, suggesting a 原始日耳曼语 *burgisli-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhergh- (1) "to hide, protect" （参见 bury). The 日耳曼语 suffix *-isli- (also in 古英语 hydels "hiding place," fætels "bag") became 已废 and was felt 作为 为 … 的复数 the 拉丁语-derived suffix -al (2) forming nouns of action 源自 verbs (survival, approval, etc.).

entries.definition: v. 燃烧，烧毁 v. /n. 灼伤，烧伤
entries.etymology:
12c., combination of Old Norse brenna "to burn, light," and two originally distinct Old English verbs: bærnan "to kindle" (transitive) and beornan "to be on fire" (intransitive), all from Proto-Germanic *brennan/*brannjan (source also of Middle Dutch bernen, Dutch branden, Old High German brinnan, German brennen, Gothic -brannjan "to set on fire"). This perhaps is from PIE 
*gwher- "to heat, warm" (see warm (adj.)), or from PIE *bhre-n-u, from root *bhreue- "to boil forth, well up" (see brew (v.)). Related: Burned/burnt (see -ed); burning.

Figuratively (of passions, battle, etc.) in Old English. Meaning "cheat, swindle, victimize" is first attested 1650s. In late 18c, slang, burned meant "infected with venereal disease." To burn one's bridges (behind one) "behave so as to destroy any chance of returning to a status quo" (attested by 1892 in Mark Twain), perhaps ultimately is from reckless cavalry raids in the American Civil War. Slavic languages have historically used different and unrelated words for the transitive and intransitive senses of "set fire to"/"be on fire:" for example Polish palić/gorzeć, Russian žeč'/gorel.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪, combination of 古北欧语 brenna "to burn, light," and two 原义为 distinct 古英语 verbs: bærnan "to kindle" (transitive) and beornan "to be on fire" (intransitive), all 源自 原始日耳曼语 *brennan/*brannjan (source also of Middle 荷兰语 bernen, 荷兰语 branden, 古高地德语 brinnan, 德语 brennen, Gothic -brannjan "to set on fire"). This 或许 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *gwher- "to heat, warm" （参见 warm （形）)，或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhre-n-u, 源自 root *bhreue- "to boil forth, well up" （参见 brew （动）). 同源词：Burned/burnt （参见 -ed); burning. Figuratively (of passions, battle, etc.) in 古英语. 义为 "cheat, swindle, victimize" is 最早见于 1650 年代. In late 18c, 俚语, burned meant "infected with venereal disease." To burn one's bridges (behind one) "behave so as to destroy any chance of returning to a status quo" (attested by 1892 in Mark Twain), perhaps ultimately is from reckless cavalry raids in the American Civil War. Slavic languages have historically used different and unrelated words for the transitive and intransitive senses of "set fire to"/"be on fire:" for example Polish palić/gorzeć, Russian žeč'/gorel.

example.en: The candle will burn out if you leave it unattended.
example.zh: 如果你不管它，蜡烛会燃烧殆尽。

entries.definition: vi./n. 破裂，爆炸 vi. （into）突然发生，突然发作
entries.etymology:
Old English berstan (intransitive) "break suddenly, shatter under pressure" (class III strong verb; past tense bærst, past participle borsten), from a West Germanic metathesis of Proto-Germanic *brest- (source also of Old Saxon brestan, Old Frisian bersta, Middle Dutch berstan, Low German barsten, Dutch barsten, Old High German brestan, German bersten "to burst"), from PIE root *bhres- "to burst, break, crack."

The forms reverted to brest- in Middle English from influence of Old Norse brestan/brast/brosten, from the same Germanic root, but it was re-metathesized late 16c. and emerged in the modern form, though brast was common as past tense through 17c. and survives in dialect.

Of extended or distended surfaces from 1530s. Figuratively, in reference to being over-full of excitement, anticipation, etc., from 1630s. Transitive sense ("to cause to break") is from late 13c. Meaning "to issue suddenly and abundantly" is from c. 1300 (literal), mid-13c. (figurative). Meaning "break into sudden activity or expression" is from 1680s. Related: Bursting.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 berstan (intransitive) "break suddenly, shatter under pressure" (class III strong 动词; past tense bærst, past participle borsten), 源自 a West 日耳曼语 metathesis of 原始日耳曼语 *brest- (source also of 古撒克逊语 brestan, 古弗里西语 bersta, Middle 荷兰语 berstan, Low 德语 barsten, 荷兰语 barsten, 古高地德语 brestan, 德语 bersten "to burst"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhres- "to burst, break, crack." The forms reverted to brest- in 中古英语 源自 influence of 古北欧语 brestan/brast/brosten, 源自 same 日耳曼语 root, but it was re-metathesized 16 世纪晚期 and emerged in the modern form, though brast was common as past tense through 17 世纪 and survives in dialect. Of extended or distended surfaces 源自 1530 年代. Figuratively, in reference to being over-full of excitement, anticipation, etc., 源自 1630 年代. Transitive sense ("to cause to break") 始于 13 世纪晚期 义为 "to issue suddenly and abundantly" 始于 约 1300 年 (literal), 13 世纪中期 (figurative). 义为 "break into sudden activity or expression" 始于 1680 年代. 同源词：Bursting.

example.en: The crowd burst into cheers when the final whistle confirmed the home team's victory.
example.zh: 终场哨声确认主队获胜时，人群突然爆发出欢呼声。

entries.etymology:
Old English byrgan "to raise a mound, hide, bury, inter," akin to beorgan "to shelter," from Proto-Germanic *burzjan- "protection, shelter" (source also of Old Saxon bergan, Dutch bergen, Old Norse bjarga, Swedish berga, Old High German bergan "protect, shelter, conceal," German bergen, Gothic bairgan "to save, preserve"), from PIE root *bhergh- (1) "to hide, protect" (source also of Old Church Slavonic brego "I preserve, guard"). Related: Buried; burying. Burying-ground "cemetery" attested from 1711.

The Old English -y- was a short "oo" sound, like modern French -u-. Under normal circumstances it transformed into Modern English -i- (in bridge, kiss, listen, sister, etc.), but in bury and a few other words (as in merry, knell) it retained a Kentish change to "e" that took place in the late Old English period. In the West Midlands, meanwhile, the Old English -y- sound persisted, slightly modified over time, giving the standard modern pronunciation of blush, much, church.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 byrgan "to raise a mound, hide, bury, inter," akin to beorgan "to shelter," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *burzjan- "protection, shelter" (source also of 古撒克逊语 bergan, 荷兰语 bergen, 古北欧语 bjarga, Swedish berga, 古高地德语 bergan "protect, shelter, conceal," 德语 bergen, Gothic bairgan "to save, preserve"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhergh- (1) "to hide, protect" (source also of Old Church Slavonic brego "I preserve, guard"). 同源词：Buried; burying. Burying-ground "cemetery" attested 自 1711 年起. The 古英语 -y- was a short "oo" sound, like modern 法语 -u-. Under normal circumstances it transformed into 现代英语 -i- (in bridge, kiss, listen, sister, etc.), but in bury and a few other words (as in merry, knell) it retained a Kentish change to "e" that took place in the late 古英语 period. In the West Midlands, meanwhile, the 古英语 -y- sound persisted, slightly modified over time, giving the standard modern pronunciation of blush, much, church.

example.en: They decided to bury the time capsule in the schoolyard.
example.zh: 他们决定把时间胶囊埋在校园里。

entries.etymology: 1832, abbreviation of omnibus (q.v.). The modern English noun is nothing but a Latin dative plural ending. To miss the bus, in the figurative sense of "lose an opportunity," is from 1901, Australian English (OED has a figurative miss the omnibus from 1886). Busman's holiday "leisure time spent doing what one does for a living" (1893) is probably a reference to London bus drivers riding the buses on their days off.
entries.etymologyZh: 1832 年, abbreviation of omnibus (q.v.). The modern English 名词 is nothing but a 拉丁语 dative plural ending. To miss the bus, in the figurative 语义 "lose an opportunity," 始于 1901 年, Australian English (OED has a figurative miss the omnibus 自 1886 年起). Busman's holiday "leisure time spent doing what one does for a living" (1893 年) is 可能 a reference to London bus drivers riding the buses on their days off.

entries.etymology:
"many-stemmed woody plant," Old English bysc, from West Germanic *busk "bush, thicket" (source also of Old Saxon and Old High German busc, Dutch bosch, bos, German Busch). Influenced by or combined with cognate words from Scandinavian (such as Old Norse buskr, Danish busk, but this might be from West Germanic) and Old French (busche "firewood," apparently of Frankish origin), and also perhaps Anglo-Latin bosca "firewood," from Medieval Latin busca (whence Italian bosco, Spanish bosque, French bois), which apparently also was borrowed from West Germanic; compare Boise.

In British American colonies, applied from 1650s to the uncleared districts, hence "country," as opposed to town (1780); probably originally from Dutch bosch in the same sense, because it seems to appear first in English in former Dutch colonies. Meaning "pubic hair" (especially of a woman) is from 1745. To beat the bushes (mid-15c.) is a way to rouse birds so that they fly into the net which others are holding, which originally was the same thing as beating around the bush (see beat (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: "many-stemmed woody plant," 古英语 bysc, 源自 West 日耳曼语 *busk "bush, thicket" (source also of 古撒克逊语 and 古高地德语 busc, 荷兰语 bosch, bos, 德语 Busch). Influenced by or combined with 同源 words 源自 Scandinavian (such as 古北欧语 buskr, Danish busk, but this might be 源自 West 日耳曼语) and 古法语 (busche "firewood," 似乎 of Frankish origin), and also 或许 Anglo-拉丁语 bosca "firewood," 源自 中古拉丁语 busca (whence 意大利语 bosco, 西班牙语 bosque, 法语 bois), which 似乎 also was 借自 West 日耳曼语; 对比 Boise. In British American colonies, applied 源自 1650 年代 to the uncleared districts, hence "country," as opposed to town (1780 年); 可能 原义为 源自 荷兰语 bosch in the same sense, because it seems to appear first in English in former 荷兰语 colonies. 义为 "pubic hair" (尤指 of a woman) 始于 1745 年. To beat the bushes (15 世纪中期) is a way to rouse birds so that they fly into the net which others are holding, which 原义为 was the same thing as beating around the bush （参见 beat （动）).

example.en: A rabbit darted out from behind a bush and crossed the garden path.
example.zh: 一只兔子从灌木后面蹿出，穿过花园小路。

definitionLines: n. 生意，业务；事务，职责；公 司，行业
entries.definition: n. 生意，业务；事务，职责；公 司，行业
entries.etymology:
Old English bisignes (Northumbrian) "care, anxiety, occupation," from bisig "careful, anxious, busy, occupied, diligent" (see busy (adj.)) + -ness. Middle English sense of "state of being much occupied or engaged" (mid-14c.) is obsolete, replaced by busyness.

Sense of "a person's work, occupation" is first recorded late 14c. (in late Old English bisig (adj.) appears as a noun with the sense "occupation, state of employment"). Meaning "what one is about at the moment" is from 1590s. Sense of "trade, commercial engagements" is first attested 1727. In 17c. it also could mean "sexual intercourse." Modern two-syllable pronunciation is 17c.

Business card first attested 1840; business letter from 1766. Business end "the practical or effective part" (of something) is American English, by 1874. Phrase business as usual attested from 1865. To mean business "be intent on serious action" is from 1856. To mind (one's) own business is from 1620s. Johnson's dictionary also has busiless "At leisure; without business; unemployed."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bisignes (Northumbrian) "care, anxiety, occupation," 源自 bisig "careful, anxious, busy, occupied, diligent" （参见 busy （形）) + -ness. 中古英语 语义 "state of being much occupied or engaged" (14 世纪中期) is 已废, replaced by busyness. 义为 "a person's work, occupation" is 首见于 14 世纪晚期 (in late 古英语 bisig （形） appears 作名词时 with the sense "occupation, state of employment"). 义为 "what one is about at the moment" 始于 1590 年代. 义为 "trade, commercial engagements" is 最早见于 1727 年. In 17 世纪 it also could mean "sexual intercourse." 现代 two-syllable pronunciation is 17 世纪 Business card 最早见于 1840 年; business letter 自 1766 年起. Business end "the practical or effective part" (of something) is American English, 截至 1874 年. Phrase business as usual attested 自 1865 年起. To mean business "be intent on serious action" 始于 1856 年. To mind (one's) own business is from 1620s. Johnson's dictionary also has busiless "At leisure; without business; unemployed."

example.en: After years of effort, he turned his small blog into a profitable online business.
example.zh: 经过多年努力，他把自己的小博客变成了一个盈利的网络业务。

entries.etymology: "to burst," 1806, variant of burst (v.); for loss of -r-, compare ass (n.2). Meaning "go bankrupt" is from 1834. Meaning "break into" is from 1859. The slang meaning "demote" (especially in a military sense) is from 1918; that of "place under arrest" is from 1953 (earlier "to raid" from Prohibition). In card games, "to go over a score of 21," from 1939. Related: Busted; busting.
entries.etymologyZh: "to burst," 1806 年, 为 … 的变体 burst （动）; for loss of -r-, 对比 ass (n.2). 义为 "go bankrupt" 始于 1834 年. 义为 "break into" 始于 1859 年. The 俚语 意为 "demote" (尤指 in a military sense) 始于 1918 年; that of "place under arrest" 始于 1953 年 (earlier "to raid" 源自 Prohibition). In card games, "to go over a score of 21," 自 1939 年起. 同源词：Busted; busting.

definitionLines: a. 忙，忙碌；热闹的，繁忙的； （电话）占线
entries.definition: a. 忙，忙碌；热闹的，繁忙的； （电话）占线
entries.etymology:
Old English bisig "careful, anxious," later "continually employed or occupied," cognate with Old Dutch bezich, Low German besig; no known connection with any other Germanic or Indo-European language. Still pronounced as in Middle English, but for some unclear reason the spelling shifted to -u- in 15c.

The notion of "anxiousness" has drained from the word since Middle English. Often in a bad sense in early Modern English, "prying, meddlesome" (preserved in busybody). The word was a euphemism for "sexually active" in 17c. Of telephone lines, 1893. Of display work, "excessively detailed, visually cluttered," 1903.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bisig "careful, anxious," later "continually employed or occupied," 与 … 同源 古荷兰语 bezich, Low 德语 besig; no known connection with any other 日耳曼语 or Indo-European language. Still pronounced as in 中古英语, but for some unclear reason the spelling shifted to -u- in 15 世纪 The 概念 "anxiousness" has drained 源自 word 自 中古英语. Often in a bad sense in early 现代英语, "prying, meddlesome" (preserved in busybody). The word was a euphemism for "sexually active" in 17 世纪 Of telephone lines, 1893 年. Of display work, "excessively detailed, visually cluttered," 1903 年.

example.en: The hospital emergency room was busy all night after the accident.
example.zh: 事故发生后，医院急诊室整晚都非常忙碌。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Anglo-French boucher, from Old French bochier "butcher, executioner" (12c., Modern French boucher), probably literally "slaughterer of goats," from bouc "male goat," from Frankish *bukk or some other Germanic source (see buck (n.1)) or Celtic *bukkos "he-goat." Figurative sense of "brutal murderer" is attested from 1520s. Butcher-knife attested from 18c. Related: Butcherly. Old English had flæscmangere "butcher" ('flesh-monger').
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 boucher, 源自 古法语 bochier "butcher, executioner" (12 世纪, 现代法语 boucher), 可能 字面义为 "slaughterer of goats," 源自 bouc "male goat," 源自 Frankish *bukk or some other 日耳曼语 source （参见 buck (n.1)) or Celtic *bukkos "he-goat." Figurative 语义 "brutal murderer" 见于 1520 年代. Butcher-knife attested 源自 18 世纪 同源词：Butcherly. 古英语 had flæscmangere "butcher" ('flesh-monger').

entries.etymology:
Old English butere "butter," general West Germanic (compare Old Frisian, Old High German butera, German Butter, Dutch boter), an early loan-word from Latin butyrum "butter" (source of Italian burro, Old French burre, French beurre), from Greek boutyron, perhaps literally "cow-cheese," from bous "ox, cow" (see cow (n.)) + tyros "cheese" (see tyrosine); but this might be a folk etymology of a Scythian word.

The product was used from an early date in India, Iran and northern Europe, but not in ancient Greece and Rome. Herodotus described it (along with cannabis) among the oddities of the Scythians. Butter-knife attested from 1818.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 butere "butter," general West 日耳曼语 (对比 古弗里西语, 古高地德语 butera, 德语 Butter, 荷兰语 boter), an early loan-word 源自 拉丁语 butyrum "butter" (source of 意大利语 burro, 古法语 burre, 法语 beurre), 源自 希腊语 boutyron, 或许 字面义为 "cow-cheese," 源自 bous "ox, cow" （参见 cow （名）) + tyros "cheese" （参见 tyrosine); but this might be a folk etymology of a Scythian word. The product was used 源自 an early date in India, Iran and northern Europe, but not in ancient Greece and Rome. Herodotus described it (along with cannabis) among the oddities of the Scythians. Butter-knife attested 自 1818 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English buttorfleoge, evidently butter (n.) + fly (n.), but of obscure signification. Perhaps based on the old notion that the insects (or witches disguised as butterflies) consume butter or milk that is left uncovered. Or, less creatively, simply because the pale yellow color of many species' wings suggests the color of butter. Another theory connects it to the color of the insect's excrement, based on Dutch cognate boterschijte. An overview of words for "butterfly" in various languages can be found here. Also see papillon.

Applied to persons from c. 1600, originally in reference to vain and gaudy attire; by 1806 in reference to transformation from early lowly state; in reference to flitting tendencies by 1873. The swimming stroke so called from 1936. Butterflies "light stomach spasms caused by anxiety" is from 1908.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 buttorfleoge, 显然 butter （名） + fly （名）, but of obscure signification. Perhaps based on the old notion that the insects (or witches disguised as butterflies) consume butter or milk that is left uncovered. Or, less creatively, simply because the pale yellow color of many species' wings suggests the color of butter. Another theory connects it to the color of the insect's excrement, based on 荷兰语 同源 boterschijte. An overview of words for "butterfly" in various languages can be found here. Also 参见 papillon. Applied to persons 源自 约 1600 年, 原义为 in reference to vain and gaudy attire; 截至 1806 年 in reference to transformation 源自 early lowly state; in reference to flitting tendencies 截至 1873 年. The swimming stroke so called 自 1936 年起. Butterflies "light stomach spasms caused by anxiety" 始于 1908 年.

example.en: A colorful butterfly landed on the flower and stayed still.
example.zh: 一只色彩鲜艳的蝴蝶停在花朵上一动不动。

entries.definition: n. 扣子；按钮 vt. 扣，扣紧
entries.etymology:
c. 1300 (surname Botouner "button-maker" attested from mid-13c.), from Old French boton "a button," originally "a bud" (12c., Modern French bouton), from bouter, boter "to thrust," common Romanic (Spanish boton, Italian bottone), ultimately from Germanic (see butt (v.)). Thus a button is, etymologically, something that pushes up, or thrusts out.

Meaning "point of the chin" is pugilistic slang, by 1921. A button as something you push to create an effect by closing an (electrical) circuit is attested from 1840s. Button-pusher as "deliberately annoying or provocative person" is attested by 1990 (in reference to Bill Gates, in "InfoWorld" magazine, Nov. 19). In the 1980s it meant "photographer."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年 (surname Botouner "button-maker" attested 源自 13 世纪中期), 源自 古法语 boton "a button," 原义为 "a bud" (12 世纪, 现代法语 bouton), 源自 bouter, boter "to thrust," common Romanic (西班牙语 boton, 意大利语 bottone), 最终源自 日耳曼语 （参见 butt （动）). Thus a button is, etymologically, something that pushes up，或thrusts out. 义为 "point of the chin" is pugilistic 俚语, 截至 1921 年. A button as something you push to create an effect by closing an (electrical) circuit 见于 1840 年代. Button-pusher as "deliberately annoying or provocative person" is attested 截至 1990 年 (in reference to Bill Gates, in "InfoWorld" magazine, Nov. 19). In the 1980 年代 it meant "photographer."

entries.etymology:
Old English bycgan (past tense bohte) "to buy, pay for, acquire; redeem, ransom; procure; get done," from Proto-Germanic *bugjan (source also of Old Saxon buggjan, Old Norse byggja, Gothic bugjan), which is of unknown origin and not found outside Germanic.

The surviving spelling is southwest England dialect; the word was generally pronounced in Old English and Middle English with a -dg- sound as "budge," or "bidge." Meaning "believe, accept as true" first recorded 1926. Related: Bought; buying. To buy time "prevent further deterioration but make no improvement" is attested from 1946.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 bycgan (past tense bohte) "to buy, pay for, acquire; redeem, ransom; procure; get done," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *bugjan (source also of 古撒克逊语 buggjan, 古北欧语 byggja, Gothic bugjan), which is 来源不详 and not found outside 日耳曼语. The surviving spelling is southwest England dialect; the word was generally pronounced in 古英语 and 中古英语 with a -dg- sound as "budge," or "bidge." 义为 "believe, accept as true" 首见于 1926 年. 同源词：Bought; buying. To buy time "prevent further deterioration but make no improvement" 见于 1946 年.

example.en: I need to buy some groceries at the supermarket on my way home today.
example.zh: 我今天回家路上需要在超市买一些杂货。

entries.etymology: late 15c., echoic of bees and other insects. Aviation sense of "fly low and close" is by 1941 (see buzz (n.)). Related: Buzzed; buzzing. Buzz off (1914) originally meant "to ring off on the telephone," from the use of buzzers to signal a call or message on old systems. As a command, it originally would have been telling someone to get off the line.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, echoic of bees and other insects. Aviation 语义 "fly low and close" is 截至 1941 年 （参见 buzz （名）). 同源词：Buzzed; buzzing. Buzz off (1914 年) 原义为 meant "to ring off on the telephone," 源自 use of buzzers to signal a call or message on old systems. 作为 command, it 原义为 would have been telling someone to get off the line.

entries.etymology: also by-pass, 1848, of certain pipes in a gasworks, from by + pass (n.). First used 1922 for "road for the relief of congestion;" figurative sense is from 1928. The heart operation was first so called 1957.
entries.etymologyZh: also by-pass, 1848 年, of certain pipes in a gasworks, 源自 by + pass （名）. First used 1922 年 for "road for the relief of congestion;" figurative sense 始于 1928 年. The heart operation was first so called 1957 年.

entries.definition: n. 旁观者；看热闹的人
entries.etymology: 1610s, from by + agent noun from stand (v.). They have been innocent at least since 1829. Stander-by is from 1540s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, 源自 by + agent 名词 源自 stand （动）. They have been innocent at least 自 1829 年. Stander-by 始于 1540 年代.

entries.etymology:
1826,  "light, horse-drawn carriage," shortening of cabriolet (1763), from French  cabriolet (18c.), diminutive of cabrioler "leap, caper" (16c./17c.), from Italian capriolare "jump in the air," from capriola, properly "the leap of a kid," from Latin capreolus "wild goat, roebuck," from PIE *kap-ro- "he-goat, buck" (source also of Old Irish gabor, Welsh gafr, Old English hæfr, Old Norse hafr "he-goat"). The carriages had springy suspensions.

Extended to hansoms and other types of carriages, then extended to similar-looking parts of locomotives (1851). Applied especially to public horse carriages, then to automobiles-for-hire (1899) when these began to replace them.
entries.etymologyZh: 1826 年, "light, horse-drawn carriage," shortening of cabriolet (1763 年), 源自 法语 cabriolet (18 世纪), 为 … 的指小形式 cabrioler "leap, caper" (16 世纪/17 世纪), 源自 意大利语 capriolare "jump in the air," 源自 capriola, properly "the leap of a kid," 源自 拉丁语 capreolus "wild goat, roebuck," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *kap-ro- "he-goat, buck" (source also of Old 爱尔兰语 gabor, Welsh gafr, 古英语 hæfr, 古北欧语 hafr "he-goat"). The carriages had springy suspensions. Extended to hansoms and other types of carriages, 之后 extended to similar-looking parts of locomotives (1851 年). Applied 尤指 to public horse carriages, 之后 to automobiles-for-hire (1899 年) when these began to replace them.

example.en: She hailed a cab outside the airport and asked to be taken downtown.
example.zh: 她在机场外拦了一辆出租车，要求去市中心。

entries.etymology: mid-14c., from Old French cabane "hut, cabin," from Old Provençal cabana, from Late Latin capanna "hut" (source of Spanish cabana, Italian capanna), of doubtful origin. French cabine (18c.), Italian cabino are English loan-words. Meaning "room or partition of a vessel" (set aside for use of officers) is from late 14c. Cabin fever first recorded by 1918 in the "need to get out and about" sense; earlier (1820s) it was a term for typhus.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 cabane "hut, cabin," 源自 Old Provençal cabana, 源自 晚期拉丁语 capanna "hut" (source of 西班牙语 cabana, 意大利语 capanna), of doubtful origin. 法语 cabine (18 世纪), 意大利语 cabino are English loan-words. 义为 "room or partition of a vessel" (set aside for use of officers) 始于 14 世纪晚期 Cabin fever 首见于 截至 1918 年 in the "need to get out and about" sense; earlier (1820 年代) it was a term for typhus.

example.en: They spent the weekend in a cozy wooden cabin near the lake.
example.zh: 他们在湖边一间温馨的小木屋里度过了周末。

entries.etymology:
1540s, "secret storehouse, treasure chamber," from Middle French cabinet "small room" (16c.), diminutive of Old French cabane "cabin" (see cabin); perhaps influenced by (or rather, from) Italian gabbinetto, diminutive of gabbia, from Latin cavea "stall, stoop, cage, den for animals" (see cave (n.)).

Meaning "case for safe-keeping" (of papers, liquor, etc.) is from 1540s, gradually shading to mean a piece of furniture that does this. Sense of "private room where advisors meet" (c. 1600) led to modern political meaning (1640s); perhaps originally short for cabinet council (1630s); compare board (n.1) in its evolution from place where some group meets to the word for the group that meets there.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "secret storehouse, treasure chamber," 源自 中古法语 cabinet "small room" (16 世纪), 为 … 的指小形式 古法语 cabane "cabin" （参见 cabin); 或许 influenced by (or rather, 源自) 意大利语 gabbinetto, 为 … 的指小形式 gabbia, 源自 拉丁语 cavea "stall, stoop, cage, den for animals" （参见 cave （名）). 义为 "case for safe-keeping" (of papers, liquor, etc.) 始于 1540 年代, gradually shading to mean a piece of furniture that does this. 义为 "private room where advisors meet" (约 1600 年) led to modern political 意为 (1640 年代); 或许 原义为 short for cabinet council (1630 年代); 对比 board (n.1) in its evolution 源自 place where some group meets to the word for the group that meets there.

example.en: She stored the medicine in the bathroom cabinet out of reach of children.
example.zh: 她把药物存放在浴室橱柜里，放在孩子够不到的地方。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old North French cable, from Medieval Latin capulum "lasso, rope, halter for cattle," from Latin capere "to take, seize" (see capable). Technically, in nautical use, a rope 10 or more inches around, to hold the ship when at anchor; in non-nautical use, a rope of wire (not hemp or fiber). Given a new range of senses in 19c.: Meaning "message received by telegraphic cable" is from 1883 (short for cable message). Cable car is from 1879. Cable television first attested 1963; shortened form cable is from 1972.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 Old North 法语 cable, 源自 中古拉丁语 capulum "lasso, rope, halter for cattle," 源自 拉丁语 capere "to take, seize" （参见 capable). Technically, in nautical use, a rope 10 or more inches around, to hold the ship when at anchor; in non-nautical use, a rope of wire (not hemp or fiber). Given a new range of senses in 19 世纪: 义为 "message received by telegraphic cable" 始于 1883 年 (short for cable message). Cable car 始于 1879 年. Cable television 最早见于 1963 年; shortened form cable 始于 1972 年.

example.en: Workers laid the underwater cable to connect the two islands.
example.zh: 工人们铺设了水下电缆，将两座岛屿连接起来。

entries.etymology: 1802, from French café "coffee, coffeehouse," from Italian caffe "coffee" (see coffee). The beverage was introduced in Venice by 1615 and in France from 1650s by merchants and travelers who had been to Turkey and Egypt. The first public café might have been the one opened in Marseilles in 1660.
entries.etymologyZh: 1802 年, 源自 法语 café "coffee, coffeehouse," 源自 意大利语 caffe "coffee" （参见 coffee). The beverage was introduced in Venice 截至 1615 年 and in France 源自 1650 年代 by merchants and travelers who had been to Turkey and Egypt. The first public café might have been the one opened in Marseilles 于 1660 年.

example.en: She reads every morning at the cafe near her office.
example.zh: 她每天早上在办公室附近的咖啡馆里读书。

entries.etymology: 1839, American English, from Mexican Spanish cafeteria "coffee store," from café "coffee" (see coffee) + Spanish -tería "place where something is done" (usually business). The ending came to be understood popularly as meaning "help-yourself" (as though café + -teria) and was extended to new formation with that sense from c. 1923.
entries.etymologyZh: 1839 年, American English, 源自 Mexican 西班牙语 cafeteria "coffee store," 源自 café "coffee" （参见 coffee) + 西班牙语 -tería "place where something is done" (通常 business). The ending came to be understood popularly as 意为 "help-yourself" (as though café + -teria) and was extended to new formation with that sense 源自 约 1923 年.

entries.etymology: early 13c., from Old French cage "cage, prison; retreat, hideout" (12c.), from Latin cavea "hollow place, enclosure for animals, coop, hive, stall, dungeon, spectators' seats in the theater" (source also of Italian gabbia "basket for fowls, coop;" see cave (n.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 古法语 cage "cage, prison; retreat, hideout" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 cavea "hollow place, enclosure for animals, coop, hive, stall, dungeon, spectators' seats in the theater" (source also of 意大利语 gabbia "basket for fowls, coop;" 参见 cave （名）).

example.en: The zookeeper cleaned the lion's cage every morning.
example.zh: 动物园管理员每天早上清洁狮子的笼子。

entries.etymology:
early 13c., from Old Norse kaka "cake," from West Germanic *kokon- (source also of Middle Dutch koke, Dutch koek, Old High German huohho, German Kuchen). Not now believed to be related to Latin coquere "to cook," as formerly supposed. Replaced its Old English cognate, coecel.

Originally (until early 15c.) "a flat, round loaf of bread." Piece of cake "something easy" is from 1936. The let them eat cake story is found in Rousseau's "Confessions," in reference to an incident c. 1740, long before Marie Antoinette, though it has been associated with her since c. 1870; it apparently was a chestnut in the French royal family that had been told of other princesses and queens before her.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 古北欧语 kaka "cake," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *kokon- (source also of Middle 荷兰语 koke, 荷兰语 koek, 古高地德语 huohho, 德语 Kuchen). Not 现在 believed to be related to 拉丁语 coquere "to cook," as formerly supposed. Replaced its 古英语 同源, coecel. Originally (until 15 世纪初) "a flat, round loaf of bread." Piece of cake "something easy" 始于 1936 年. The let them eat cake story is found in Rousseau's "Confessions," in reference to an incident 约 1740 年, long before Marie Antoinette, though it has been associated with her 自 约 1870 年; it 似乎 was a chestnut in the 法语 royal family that had been told of other princesses and queens before her.

entries.etymology: coined 1808 by English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy (1778-1829), who first succeeded in isolating it, from Latin calx (genitive calcis) "limestone" (see chalk (n.)) + metallic element ending -ium.
entries.etymologyZh: coined 1808 年 by English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy (1778 年-1829 年), who first succeeded in isolating it, 源自 拉丁语 calx (属格 calcis) "limestone" （参见 chalk （名）) + metallic element ending -ium.

example.en: Drinking milk every day helps children build strong bones because of its high calcium content.
example.zh: 每天喝牛奶有助于儿童建立强壮的骨骼，因为牛奶含钙量高。

entries.etymology: 1560s, "to compute, to estimate by mathematical means," from Latin calculatus, past participle of calculare "to reckon, compute," from calculus (see calculus). Meaning "to plan, devise" is from 1650s. Replaced earlier calculen (mid-14c.), from Old French calculer. Related: Calculable.

example.en: Scientists used a formula to calculate the distance between the two stars.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "mathematician, one who calculates," from Latin calculator, from calculatus, past participle of calculare "to reckon, compute," from calculus (see calculus). Of mechanical adding machine contraptions, from 1784. Of electronic ones, from 1946.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "mathematician, one who calculates," 源自 拉丁语 calculator, 源自 calculatus, 为 … 的过去分词 calculare "to reckon, compute," 源自 calculus （参见 calculus). Of mechanical adding machine contraptions, 自 1784 年起. Of electronic ones, 自 1946 年起.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "system of division of the year;" mid-14c. as "table showing divisions of the year;" from Old French calendier "list, register," from Latin calendarium "account book," from calendae/kalendae "calends" the first day of the Roman month -- when debts fell due and accounts were reckoned.

This is from calare "to announce solemnly, call out," as the priests did in proclaiming the new moon that marked the calends, from PIE root kele- (2) "to call, shout" (see claim (v.)). In Rome, new moons were not calculated mathematically but rather observed by the priests from the Capitol; when they saw it, they would "declare" the number of days till the nones (five or seven, depending on the month). The word was taken by the early Church for its register list of saints and their feast days.

Sometimes used in a general sense, "to insert between others" (1824). The -ar spelling in English is 17c. to differentiate it from the now obscure calender "cloth-presser."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "system of division of the year;" 14 世纪中期 as "table showing divisions of the year;" 源自 古法语 calendier "list, register," 源自 拉丁语 calendarium "account book," 源自 calendae/kalendae "calends" the first day of the Roman month -- when debts fell due and accounts were reckoned. This 始于 calare "to announce solemnly, call out," as the priests did in proclaiming the new moon that marked the calends, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root kele- (2) "to call, shout" （参见 claim （动）). In Rome, new moons were not calculated mathematically but rather observed by the priests 源自 Capitol; when they saw it, they would "declare" the number of days till the nones (five or seven, depending on the month). The word was taken by the early Church for its register list of saints and their feast days. Sometimes used in a general sense, "to insert between others" (1824 年). The -ar spelling in English is 17 世纪 to differentiate it 源自 现在 obscure calender "cloth-presser."

entries.etymology:
Old English ceallian "to call, shout," less common than clipian; replaced by related Old Norse kalla "to cry loudly," from Proto-Germanic *kall- (source also of Dutch kallen "to talk," Old High German kallon "to call"), from PIE root *gal- (2) "to call, scream, shriek, shout" (source also of Sanskrit garhati "bewail, criticize;" Latin gallus "cock;" Old High German klaga, German Klage "complaint, grievance, lament, accusation;" Old English clacu "affront;" Old Church Slavonic glasu "voice," glagolu "word;" Welsh galw "call"). Related: Called; calling.

Meaning "to give a name to" is mid-13c. Coin-toss sense is from 1801. Meaning "to visit" (Middle English) was literally "to stand at the door and call."  Telephone/telegraph sense is from 1889. To call out someone to fight (1823) corresponds to French provoquer. To call it a day is from 1834.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ceallian "to call, shout," less common than clipian; replaced by related 古北欧语 kalla "to cry loudly," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *kall- (source also of 荷兰语 kallen "to talk," 古高地德语 kallon "to call"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *gal- (2) "to call, scream, shriek, shout" (source also of 梵语 garhati "bewail, criticize;" 拉丁语 gallus "cock;" 古高地德语 klaga, 德语 Klage "complaint, grievance, lament, accusation;" 古英语 clacu "affront;" Old Church Slavonic glasu "voice," glagolu "word;" Welsh galw "call"). 同源词：Called; calling. 义为 "to give a name to" is 13 世纪中期 Coin-toss sense 始于 1801 年. 义为 "to visit" (中古英语) was 字面义为 "to stand at the door and call." Telephone/telegraph sense 始于 1889 年. To call out someone to fight (1823 年) corresponds to 法语 provoquer. To call it a day 始于 1834 年.

example.en: She decided to call her doctor as soon as she felt worse.

entries.definition: a. 平静，镇静，沉着 v.（使）镇静，（使）镇定 n. 平静，风平浪静
entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French calme "tranquility, quiet," traditionally from Old Italian calma, from Late Latin cauma "heat of the mid-day sun" (in Italy, a time when everything rests and is still), from Greek kauma "heat" (especially of the sun), from kaiein "to burn" (see caustic). Spelling influenced by Latin calere "to be hot." Figurative application to social or mental conditions is 16c.

example.en: She forced herself to stay calm even as the situation grew increasingly chaotic.

entries.etymology:
Old English camel, perhaps via Old North French camel (Old French chamel, Modern French chameau), from Latin camelus, from Greek kamelos, from Hebrew or Phoenician gamal, perhaps related to Arabic jamala "to bear."

Another Old English word for the beast was olfend, apparently based on confusion of camels with elephants in a place and time when both were known only from travelers' vague descriptions. The Arabian have one hump (the lighter variety is the dromedary); the Bactrian have two.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 camel, 或许 经由 Old North 法语 camel (古法语 chamel, 现代法语 chameau), 源自 拉丁语 camelus, 源自 希腊语 kamelos, 源自 希伯来语 or Phoenician gamal, 或许 related to 阿拉伯语 jamala "to bear." Another 古英语 word for the beast was olfend, 似乎 based on confusion of camels with elephants in a place and time when both were known only 源自 travelers' vague descriptions. The Arabian have one hump (the lighter variety is the dromedary); the Bactrian have two.

entries.etymology:
1708, "vaulted building," from Latin camera "vaulted room" (source of Italian camera, Spanish camara, French  chambre), from Greek kamara "vaulted chamber."

The word also was used early 18c. as a short form of Modern Latin camera obscura "dark chamber" (a black box with a lens that could project images of external objects), contrasted with camera lucida (Latin for "light chamber"), which uses prisms to produce on paper beneath the instrument an image, which can be traced. It became the word for "picture-taking device" when modern photography began, c. 1840 (extended to television filming devices 1928). Camera-shy is attested from 1890. Old Church Slavonic komora, Lithuanian kamara, Old Irish camra all are borrowings from Latin.
entries.etymologyZh: 1708 年, "vaulted building," 源自 拉丁语 camera "vaulted room" (source of 意大利语 camera, 西班牙语 camara, 法语 chambre), 源自 希腊语 kamara "vaulted chamber." The word also was used 18 世纪初 作为 short form of 现代 拉丁语 camera obscura "dark chamber" (a black box with a lens that could project images of external objects), contrasted with camera lucida (拉丁语 for "light chamber"), which uses prisms to produce on paper beneath the instrument an image, which can be traced. It became the word for "picture-taking device" when modern photography began, 约 1840 年 (extended to television filming devices 1928 年). Camera-shy 见于 1890 年. Old Church Slavonic komora, Lithuanian kamara, Old 爱尔兰语 camra all are borrowings 源自 拉丁语.

entries.etymologyZh: "tasteless," 1909 年, homosexual 俚语, 来源存疑, 或源自 17 世纪中期 法语 camper "to portray, pose" (as in se camper "put oneself in a bold, provocative pose"); popularized 1964 年 by Susan Sontag's essay "Notes on Camp." Campy 见于 1959 年.

entries.etymology: 1640s, "operation of an army in the field," during a single season, in a particular region, or in a definite enterprise; from French campagne "campaign," literally "open country," from Old French champagne "countryside, open country" (suited to military maneuvers), from Late Latin campania "level country" (source of Italian campagna, Spanish campaña, Portuguese campanha), from Latin campus "a field" (see campus). Old armies spent winters in quarters and took to the "open field" to seek battle in summer. Extension of meaning to "political activity before an election, marked by organized action in influencing the voters" [DAE] is American English, 1809.

entries.etymology:
Old English canne "a cup, container," from Proto-Germanic *kanna (source also of Old Saxon, Old Norse, Swedish kanna, Middle Dutch kanne, Dutch kan, Old High German channa, German Kanne). Probably an early borrowing from Late Latin canna "container, vessel," from Latin canna "reed," also "reed pipe, small boat;" but the sense evolution is difficult.

Modern "air-tight vessel of tinned iron" is from 1867 (can-opener is from 1877). Slang meaning "toilet" is c. 1900, said to be a shortening of piss-can. Meaning "buttocks" is from c. 1910.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 canne "a cup, container," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *kanna (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古北欧语, Swedish kanna, Middle 荷兰语 kanne, 荷兰语 kan, 古高地德语 channa, 德语 Kanne). Probably an early borrowing 源自 晚期拉丁语 canna "container, vessel," 源自 拉丁语 canna "reed," also "reed pipe, small boat;" but the sense evolution is difficult. 现代 "air-tight vessel of tinned iron" 始于 1867 年 (can-opener 始于 1877 年). entries.etymology: early 15c., from French canal, chanel "water channel, tube, pipe, gutter" (12c.), from Latin canalis "water pipe, groove, channel," noun use of adjective from canna "reed" (see cane (n.)). Originally in English "a pipe for liquid," its sense transferred by 1670s to "artificial waterway."

entries.etymology: late 14c., "cross out with lines," from Anglo-French canceler, from Latin cancellare "to make resemble a lattice," which in Late Latin took on a sense "cross out something written" by marking it with crossed lines, from cancelli, plural of cancellus "lattice, grating," diminutive of cancer "crossed bars, lattice," a variant of carcer "prison" (see incarceration). Figurative use, "to nullify an obligation" is from mid-15c. Related: Canceled (also cancelled); cancelling.

example.en: The airline decided to cancel all flights due to the severe storm.

entries.etymology:
Old English cancer "spreading sore, cancer" (also canceradl), from Latin cancer "a crab," later, "malignant tumor," from Greek karkinos, which, like the Modern English word, has three meanings: crab, tumor, and the zodiac constellation (late Old English), from PIE root *qarq- "to be hard" (like the shell of a crab); source also of Sanskrit karkatah "crab," karkarah "hard;" and perhaps cognate with PIE root *qar-tu- "hard, strong," source of English hard.

Greek physicians Hippocrates and Galen, among others, noted similarity of crabs to some tumors with swollen veins. Meaning "person born under the zodiac sign of Cancer" is from 1894. The sun being in Cancer at the summer solstice, the constellation had association in Latin writers with the south and with summer heat. Cancer stick "cigarette" is from 1959.

entries.etymology: c. 1600s, from Latin candidatus "one aspiring to office," originally "white-robed," past participle of candidare "to make white or bright," from candidus (see candid). Office-seekers in ancient Rome wore white togas.
entries.etymologyZh: c. 1600 年代, 源自 拉丁语 candidatus "one aspiring to office," 原义为 "white-robed," 为 … 的过去分词 candidare "to make white or bright," 源自 candidus （参见 candid). Office-seekers in ancient Rome wore white togas.

example.en: Only one candidate passed all three rounds of interviews.

entries.etymology:
Old English candel "lamp, lantern, candle," an early ecclesiastical borrowing from Latin candela "a light, torch, candle made of tallow or wax," from candere "to shine," from PIE root *kand- "to glow, to shine, to shoot out light" (source also of Sanskrit cand- "to give light, shine," candra- "shining, glowing, moon;" Greek kandaros "coal;" Welsh cann "white;" Middle Irish condud "fuel").

Candles were unknown in ancient Greece (where oil lamps sufficed), but common from early times among Romans and Etruscans. Candles on birthday cakes seems to have been originally a German custom. To hold a candle to originally meant "to help in a subordinate capacity," from the notion of an assistant or apprentice holding a candle for light while the master works (compare Old English taporberend "acolyte"). To burn the candle at both ends is recorded from 1730.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 candel "lamp, lantern, candle," an early ecclesiastical borrowing 源自 拉丁语 candela "a light, torch, candle made of tallow or wax," 源自 candere "to shine," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *kand- "to glow, to shine, to shoot out light" (source also of 梵语 cand- "to give light, shine," candra- "shining, glowing, moon;" 希腊语 kandaros "coal;" Welsh cann "white;" Middle 爱尔兰语 condud "fuel"). Candles were unknown in ancient Greece (where oil lamps sufficed), but common 源自 early times among Romans and Etruscans. Candles on birthday cakes seems to have been 原义为 a 德语 custom. To hold a candle to 原义为 meant "to help in a subordinate capacity," 源自 概念 an assistant or apprentice holding a candle for light while the master works (对比 古英语 taporberend "acolyte"). To burn the candle at both ends 见于 1730 年.

entries.etymology: late 13c., "crystalized sugar," from Old French çucre candi "sugar candy," ultimately from Arabic qandi, from Persian qand "cane sugar," probably from Sanskrit khanda "piece (of sugar)," perhaps from Dravidian (compare Tamil kantu "candy," kattu "to harden, condense").

example.en: The children received a bag of candy as a treat after the Halloween parade.

entries.etymology: c. 1400, "tube for projectiles," from Anglo-French canon, Old French canon (14c.), from Italian cannone "large tube, barrel," augmentative of Latin canna "reed, tube" (see cane (n.)). Meaning "large ordnance piece," the main modern sense, is from 1520s. Spelling not differentiated from canon till c. 1800. Cannon fodder (1891) translates German kanonenfutter (compare Shakespeare's food for powder in "I Hen. IV").
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "tube for projectiles," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 canon, 古法语 canon (14 世纪), 源自 意大利语 cannone "large tube, barrel," 为 … 的扩大形式 拉丁语 canna "reed, tube" （参见 cane （名）). 义为 "large ordnance piece," the main modern sense, 始于 1520 年代. entries.etymology:
"sturdy cloth made from hemp or flax," mid-14c., from Anglo-French canevaz, Old North French canevach, Old French chanevaz, literally "made of hemp, hempen," noun use of Vulgar Latin adjective *cannapaceus "made of hemp," from Latin cannabis, from Greek kannabis "hemp," a Scythian or Thracian word (see cannabis).

Latin adjectives in -aceus sometimes were made in Romanic languages into nouns of augmentative or pejorative force. Especially as a surface for oil paintings from c. 1700; hence "an oil painting" (1764).
entries.etymologyZh: "sturdy cloth made from hemp or flax," 14 世纪中期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 canevaz, Old North 法语 canevach, 古法语 chanevaz, 字面义为 "made of hemp, hempen," 为 … 的名词用法 通俗拉丁语 形容词 *cannapaceus "made of hemp," 源自 拉丁语 cannabis, 源自 希腊语 kannabis "hemp," a Scythian or Thracian word （参见 cannabis). 拉丁语 adjectives in -aceus 有时 were made in Romanic languages into nouns of augmentative or pejorative force. Especially 作为 surface for oil paintings 源自 约 1700 年; hence "an oil painting" (1764 年).

example.en: She stretched a fresh canvas across the frame before starting her oil painting.
example.zh: 她在开始油画创作前，将一块新帆布绷在画框上。

entries.etymology:
late Old English cæppe "hood, head-covering, cape," from Late Latin cappa "a cape, hooded cloak" (source of Spanish capa, Old North French cape, French chape), possibly a shortened from capitulare "headdress," from Latin caput "head" (see head (n.)).

Meaning "women's head covering" is early 13c. in English; extended to men late 14c. Figurative thinking cap is from 1839 (considering cap is 1650s). Of cap-like coverings on the ends of anything (such as hub-cap) from mid-15c. Meaning "contraceptive device" is first recorded 1916. That of "cap-shaped piece of copper lined with gunpowder and used to ignite a firearm" is c. 1826; extended to paper version used in toy pistols, 1872 (cap-pistol is from 1879).

The Late Latin word apparently originally meant "a woman's head-covering," but the sense was transferred to "hood of a cloak," then to "cloak" itself, though the various senses co-existed. Old English took in two forms of the Late Latin word, one meaning "head-covering," the other "ecclesiastical dress" (see cape (n.1)). In most Romance languages, a diminutive of Late Latin cappa has become the usual word for "head-covering" (such as French chapeau).
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 cæppe "hood, head-covering, cape," 源自 晚期拉丁语 cappa "a cape, hooded cloak" (source of 西班牙语 capa, Old North 法语 cape, 法语 chape), possibly a shortened 源自 capitulare "headdress," 源自 拉丁语 caput "head" （参见 head （名）). 义为 "women's head covering" is 13 世纪初 in English; extended to men 14 世纪晚期 Figurative thinking cap 始于 1839 年 (considering cap is 1650 年代). Of cap-like coverings on the ends of anything (such as hub-cap) 源自 15 世纪中期 义为 "contraceptive device" is 首见于 1916 年. That of "cap-shaped piece of copper lined with gunpowder and used to ignite a firearm" is 约 1826 年; extended to paper version used in toy pistols, 1872 年 (cap-pistol 始于 1879 年). The 晚期拉丁语 word 似乎 原义为 meant "a woman's head-covering," but the sense was transferred to "hood of a cloak," 之后 to "cloak" itself, though the various senses co-existed. 古英语 took in two forms of the 晚期拉丁语 word, one 意为 "head-covering," the other "ecclesiastical dress" （参见 cape (n.1)). In most Romance languages, a 为 … 的指小形式 晚期拉丁语 cappa has become the usual word for "head-covering" (such as 法语 chapeau).

definitionLines: n. 能力，才能；性能，容量
entries.definition: n. 能力，才能；性能，容量
entries.etymology: 1580s, from capable + -ity. Capabilities "undeveloped faculty or property" is attested from 1778.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, 源自 capable + -ity. Capabilities "undeveloped faculty or property" 见于 1778 年.

example.en: The new software has the capability to process thousands of requests per second.
example.zh: 这款新软件具备每秒处理数千个请求的能力。

definitionLines: a. 能干的，有能力的，有才能的
entries.definition: a. 能干的，有能力的，有才能的
entries.etymology: 1560s, from Middle French capable or directly from Late Latin capabilis "receptive; able to grasp or hold," used by theologians, from Latin capax "able to hold much, broad, wide, roomy;" also "receptive, fit for;" adjectival form of capere "to grasp, lay hold, take, catch; undertake; take in, hold; be large enough for; comprehend," from PIE *kap- "to grasp" (source also of Sanskrit kapati "two handfuls;" Greek kaptein "to swallow, gulp down;" Lettish kampiu "seize;" Old Irish cacht "servant-girl," literally "captive;" Welsh caeth "captive, slave;" Gothic haban "have, hold;" Old English hæft "handle," habban "to have, hold," Modern English have). Related: Capably.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, 源自 中古法语 capable or 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 capabilis "receptive; able to grasp or hold," used by theologians, 源自 拉丁语 capax "able to hold much, broad, wide, roomy;" also "receptive, fit for;" adjectival form of capere "to grasp, lay hold, take, catch; undertake; take in, hold; be large enough for; comprehend," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *kap- "to grasp" (source also of 梵语 kapati "two handfuls;" 希腊语 kaptein "to swallow, gulp down;" Lettish kampiu "seize;" Old 爱尔兰语 cacht "servant-girl," 字面义为 "captive;" Welsh caeth "captive, slave;" Gothic haban "have, hold;" 古英语 hæft "handle," habban "to have, hold," 现代英语 have). 同源词：Capably.

example.en: She is perfectly capable of handling the project on her own.
example.zh: 她完全有能力独立完成这个项目。

definitionLines: n. 容量，容积；能量；能力；接受 力
entries.definition: n. 容量，容积；能量；能力；接受 力
entries.etymology: early 15c., from Middle French capacité "ability to hold" (15c.), from Latin capacitatem (nominative capacitas) "breadth, capacity, capability of holding much," noun of state from capax (genitive capacis) "able to hold much," from capere "to take" (see capable). Meaning "largest audience a place can hold" is 1908.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 中古法语 capacité "ability to hold" (15 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 capacitatem (主格 capacitas) "breadth, capacity, capability of holding much," 名词 of state 源自 capax (属格 capacis) "able to hold much," 源自 capere "to take" （参见 capable). 义为 "largest audience a place can hold" is 1908 年.

example.en: The new stadium has a seating capacity of over fifty thousand people.
example.zh: 新体育场的座位容量超过五万人。

entries.definition: n. 首都；资本，资金 a. 主要的，基本的
entries.etymology:
early 13c., "of or pertaining to the head," from Old French capital, from Latin capitalis "of the head," hence "capital, chief, first," from caput (genitive capitis) "head" (see capitulum). Meaning "main, principal, chief, dominant, most important" is from early 15c. in English. Capital letter for an upper case one is attested from late 14c. The modern informal sense of "excellent, first-rate" is dated from 1762 in OED (as an exclamation of approval, OED's first example is 1875), perhaps from earlier use of the word in reference to ships, "first-rate, powerful enough to be in the line of battle," attested from 1650s, fallen into disuse after 1918. 

A capital crime (1520s) is one that affects the life or "head;" capital had a sense of "deadly, mortal" from late 14c. in English, a sense also found in Latin. The felt connection between "head" and "life, mortality" also existed in Old English: as in heafodgilt "deadly sin, capital offense," heafdes þolian "to forfeit life." Capital punishment was in Blackstone (1765) and classical Latin capitis poena. Capital gain is recorded from 1921. Capital goods is recorded from 1899. Related: Capitally.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "of or pertaining to the head," 源自 古法语 capital, 源自 拉丁语 capitalis "of the head," hence "capital, chief, first," 源自 caput (属格 capitis) "head" （参见 capitulum). 义为 "main, principal, chief, dominant, most important" 始于 15 世纪初 in English. Capital letter for an upper case one 见于 14 世纪晚期 The modern informal 语义 "excellent, first-rate" is dated 自 1762 年起 in OED (作为 exclamation of approval, OED's first example is 1875 年), 或源自 earlier use of the word in reference to ships, "first-rate, powerful enough to be in the line of battle," attested 源自 1650 年代, fallen into disuse after 1918 年. A capital crime (1520 年代) is one that affects the life or "head;" capital had a 语义 "deadly, mortal" 源自 14 世纪晚期 in English, a sense also found in 拉丁语. The felt connection between "head" and "life, mortality" also existed in 古英语: as in heafodgilt "deadly sin, capital offense," heafdes þolian "to forfeit life." Capital punishment was in Blackstone (1765 年) and classical 拉丁语 capitis poena. Capital gain 见于 1921 年. Capital goods 见于 1899 年. 同源词：Capitally.

example.en: Beijing is the capital of China and a major cultural center.
example.zh: 北京是中国的首都，也是重要的文化中心。

entries.etymology: 1650s, from French capsule "a membranous sac" (16c.), from Latin capsula "small box or chest," diminutive of capsa "box, case, chest" (see case (n.2)). Medicinal sense is 1875; shortened form cap is from 1942. Sense in space capsule is first recorded 1954. As an adjective from 1938. Related: Capsular.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, 源自 法语 capsule "a membranous sac" (16 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 capsula "small box or chest," 为 … 的指小形式 capsa "box, case, chest" （参见 case (n.2)). Medicinal sense is 1875 年; shortened form cap 始于 1942 年. Sense in space capsule is 首见于 1954 年. 作形容词时 自 1938 年起. 同源词：Capsular.

definitionLines: n. 首领，队长；船长，舰长；陆军 上尉，海军上校
entries.definition: n. 首领，队长；船长，舰长；陆军 上尉，海军上校
entries.etymology:
late 14c., capitayn, "a leader, chief, one who stands at the head of others," from Old French capitaine "captain, leader," from Late Latin capitaneus "chief," noun use of adjective capitaneus "prominent, chief," from Latin caput (genitive capitis) "head" (see capitulum).

Military sense of "officer who commands a company" (rank between major and lieutenant) is from 1560s; naval sense of "officer who commands a man-of-war" is from 1550s, extended to "master or commander of a vessel of any kind" by 1704. Sporting sense is first recorded 1823.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, capitayn, "a leader, chief, one who stands at the head of others," 源自 古法语 capitaine "captain, leader," 源自 晚期拉丁语 capitaneus "chief," 为 … 的名词用法 形容词 capitaneus "prominent, chief," 源自 拉丁语 caput (属格 capitis) "head" （参见 capitulum). Military 语义 "officer who commands a company" (rank between major and lieutenant) 始于 1560 年代; naval 语义 "officer who commands a man-of-war" 始于 1550 年代, extended to "master or commander of a vessel of any kind" 截至 1704 年. Sporting sense is 首见于 1823 年.

example.en: The captain ordered the crew to abandon the sinking ship immediately.
example.zh: 船长命令船员立即弃船。

entries.definition: a.被俘虏的；被迷住的 ^.俘虏；迷恋者
entries.etymology: late 14c., "imprisoned, enslaved," from Latin captivus "caught, taken prisoner," from captus, past participle of capere "to take, hold, seize" (see capable). As a noun from c. 1400; an Old English noun was hæftling, from hæft "taken, seized."
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "imprisoned, enslaved," 源自 拉丁语 captivus "caught, taken prisoner," 源自 captus, 为 … 的过去分词 capere "to take, hold, seize" （参见 capable). 作名词时 源自 约 1400 年; an 古英语 名词 was hæftling, 源自 hæft "taken, seized."

definitionLines: vt. 捕获，捉拿；夺取，攻占
entries.definition: vt. 捕获，捉拿；夺取，攻占
entries.etymology: 1540s, from Middle French capture "a taking," from Latin captura "a taking" (especially of animals), from captus (see captive).
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, 源自 中古法语 capture "a taking," 源自 拉丁语 captura "a taking" (尤指 of animals), 源自 captus （参见 captive).

example.en: Police managed to capture the suspect after a brief chase through the alley.
example.zh: 警方在小巷中短暂追捕后成功抓获了嫌疑人。

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "wheeled vehicle," from Anglo-French carre, Old North French carre, from Vulgar Latin *carra, related to Latin carrum, carrus (plural carra), originally "two-wheeled Celtic war chariot," from Gaulish karros, a Celtic word (compare Old Irish and Welsh carr "cart, wagon," Breton karr "chariot"), from PIE *krsos, from root *kers- "to run" (see current (adj.)).

"From 16th to 19th c. chiefly poetic, with associations of dignity, solemnity, or splendour ..." [OED]. Used in U.S. by 1826 of railway freight carriages and of passenger coaches on a railway by 1830; by 1862 of a streetcar or tramway car. Extension to "automobile" is by 1896, but from 1831 to the first decade of 20c. the cars meant "railroad train." Car bomb first 1972, in reference to Northern Ireland. The Latin word also is the source of Italian and Spanish carro, French char.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "wheeled vehicle," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 carre, Old North 法语 carre, 源自 通俗拉丁语 *carra, related to 拉丁语 carrum, carrus (plural carra), 原义为 "two-wheeled Celtic war chariot," 源自 Gaulish karros, a Celtic word (对比 Old 爱尔兰语 and Welsh carr "cart, wagon," Breton karr "chariot"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *krsos, 源自 root *kers- "to run" （参见 current （形）). "From 16th to 19th c. chiefly poetic, with associations of dignity, solemnity, or splendour ..." [OED]. Used in U.S. 截至 1826 年 of railway freight carriages and of passenger coaches on a railway 截至 1830 年; 截至 1862 年 of a streetcar or tramway car. Extension to "automobile" is 截至 1896 年, but 自 1831 年起 to the first decade of 20 世纪 the cars meant "railroad train." Car bomb first 1972 年, in reference to Northern Ireland. The 拉丁语 word also is the source of 意大利语 and 西班牙语 carro, 法语 char.

example.en: She parked her car in the underground garage and walked to the office.
example.zh: 她把车停在地下停车场，然后步行去办公室。

entries.etymology:
non-metallic element, 1789, coined 1787 in French by Lavoisier as charbone, from Latin carbonem (nominative carbo) "a coal, glowing coal; charcoal," from PIE root *ker- (4) "heat, fire, to burn" (source also of Latin cremare "to burn;" Sanskrit kudayati "singes;" Lithuanian kuriu "to heat," karštas "hot," krosnis "oven;" Old Church Slavonic kurjo "to smoke," krada "fireplace, hearth;" Russian ceren "brazier;" Old High German harsta "roasting;" Gothic hauri "coal;" Old Norse hyrr "fire;" Old English heorð "hearth").

Carbon 14, long-lived radioactive isotope used in dating organic deposits, is from 1936. Carbon dating (using carbon 14) is recorded from 1958. Carbon cycle is attested from 1912. Carbon footprint was in use by 2001. Carbon paper (soon to be obsolete) is from 1895.
