entries.etymology:
Old English ceace, cece "jaw, jawbone," in late Old English also "the fleshy wall of the mouth." Perhaps from the root of Old English ceowan "chew" (see chew (v.)), or from Proto-Germanic *kaukon (source also of Middle Low German kake "jaw, jawbone," Middle Dutch kake "jaw," Dutch kaak), not found outside West Germanic.

Words for "cheek," "jaw," and "chin" tend to run together in IE languages (compare PIE *genw-, source of Greek genus "jaw, cheek," geneion "chin," and English chin); Aristotle considered the chin as the front of the "jaws" and the cheeks as the back of them. The other Old English word for "cheek" was ceafl (see jowl (n.1)).

In reference to the buttocks from c. 1600. Sense of "insolence" is from 1840, perhaps from a notion akin to that which led to jaw "insolent speech," mouth off, etc. To turn the other cheek is an allusion to Matt. v:39 and Luke vi:29.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ceace, cece "jaw, jawbone," in late 古英语 also "the fleshy wall of the mouth." Perhaps 源自 root of 古英语 ceowan "chew" （参见 chew （动）)，或源自 原始日耳曼语 *kaukon (source also of Middle Low 德语 kake "jaw, jawbone," Middle 荷兰语 kake "jaw," 荷兰语 kaak), not found outside West 日耳曼语. Words for "cheek," "jaw," and "chin" tend to run together in IE languages (对比 原始印欧语 (PIE) *genw-, source of 希腊语 genus "jaw, cheek," geneion "chin," and English chin); Aristotle considered the chin as the front of the "jaws" and the cheeks as the back of them. The other 古英语 word for "cheek" was ceafl （参见 jowl (n.1)). In reference to the buttocks 源自 约 1600 年. 义为 "insolence" 始于 1840 年, 或源自 a notion akin to that which led to jaw "insolent speech," mouth off, etc. To turn the other cheek is an allusion to Matt. v:39 and Luke vi:29.

example.en: Tears rolled down her cheek as she said goodbye.
example.zh: 告别时，泪水顺着她的脸颊流下来。

entries.definition: n. /n.喝彩，欢呼 vt. 使高兴，使振作
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "the face," especially as expressing emotion, from Anglo-French chere "the face," Old French chiere "face, countenance, look, expression," from Late Latin cara "face" (source also of Spanish cara), possibly from Greek kara "head," from PIE root *ker- (1) "head, horn" (see horn (n.)). From mid-13c. as "frame of mind, state of feeling, spirit; mood, humor."

By late 14c. the meaning had extended metaphorically to "mood, mental condition," as reflected in the face. This could be in a good or bad sense ("The feend ... beguiled her with treacherye, and brought her into a dreerye cheere," "Merline," c. 1500), but a positive sense (probably short for good cheer) has predominated since c. 1400. Meaning "shout of encouragement" first recorded 1720, perhaps nautical slang (compare earlier verbal sense, "to encourage by words or deeds," early 15c.). The antique English greeting what cheer (mid-15c.) was picked up by Algonquian Indians of southern New England from the Puritans and spread in Indian languages as far as Canada.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "the face," 尤指 as expressing emotion, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 chere "the face," 古法语 chiere "face, countenance, look, expression," 源自 晚期拉丁语 cara "face" (source also of 西班牙语 cara), possibly 源自 希腊语 kara "head," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ker- (1) "head, horn" （参见 horn （名）). From 13 世纪中期 as "frame of mind, state of feeling, spirit; mood, humor." By 14 世纪晚期 the 意为 had extended metaphorically to "mood, mental condition," as reflected in the face. This could be in a good or bad sense ("The feend ... beguiled her with treacherye, and brought her into a dreerye cheere," "Merline," 约 1500 年), but a positive sense (可能 short for good cheer) has predominated 自 约 1400 年. 义为 "shout of encouragement" 首见于 1720 年, 或许 nautical 俚语 (对比 earlier verbal sense, "to encourage by words or deeds," 15 世纪初). The antique English greeting what cheer (15 世纪中期) was picked up by Algonquian Indians of southern New England 源自 Puritans and spread in Indian languages as far as Canada.

example.en: The crowd cheered loudly as the team scored the winning goal.
example.zh: 当球队打入制胜球时，人群大声欢呼。

entries.etymology: c. 1400, "full of cheer," from cheer (n.) + -ful. Meaning "elevating the spirits" is from mid-15c. Related: Cheerfully; cheerfulness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "full of cheer," 源自 cheer （名） + -ful. 义为 "elevating the spirits" 始于 15 世纪中期 同源词：Cheerfully; cheerfulness.

definitionLines: n. 化学制品/产品/物质/成分
entries.definition: a.化学的 n. 化学制品/产品/物质/成分
entries.etymology: 1570s, "relating to chemistry," from chemic "of alchemy" (a worn-down derivative of Medieval Latin alchimicus; see alchemy) + -al (1). In early use also of alchemy. Related: Chemically.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "relating to chemistry," 源自 chemic "of alchemy" (a worn-down 为 … 的派生形式 中古拉丁语 alchimicus; 参见 alchemy) + -al (1). In early use also of alchemy. 同源词：Chemically.

example.en: Exposure to certain chemical compounds can damage the liver over time.
example.zh: 长期接触某些化学化合物可能会损害肝脏。

entries.etymology: 1560s, chymist, "alchemist," from Middle French chimiste, from Medieval Latin chimista, reduced from alchimista (see alchemy). Modern spelling is from c. 1790. Meaning "chemical scientist" is from 1620s; meaning "dealer in medicinal drugs" (mostly in British English) is from 1745.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, chymist, "alchemist," 源自 中古法语 chimiste, 源自 中古拉丁语 chimista, reduced 源自 alchimista （参见 alchemy). 现代 spelling 始于 约 1790 年. 义为 "chemical scientist" 始于 1620 年代; 意为 "dealer in medicinal drugs" (mostly in British English) 始于 1745 年.

entries.etymology: c. 1600, "alchemy," from chemist + -ry; also see chemical (adj.). The meaning "natural physical process" is 1640s, and the scientific study not so called until 1788. The figurative sense of "instinctual attraction or affinity" is attested slightly earlier, from the alchemical sense.

entries.etymology:
13c., from Old French esches "chessmen," plural of eschec "game of chess, chessboard; checkmate" (see check (n.1)), from the key move of the game. Modern French still distinguishes échec "check, blow, rebuff, defeat," from plural échecs "chess."

The original word for "chess" is Sanskrit chaturanga "four members of an army" -- elephants, horses, chariots, foot soldiers. This is preserved in Spanish ajedrez, from Arabic (al) shat-ranj, from Persian chatrang, from the Sanskrit word.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪, 源自 古法语 esches "chessmen," 为 … 的复数 eschec "game of chess, chessboard; checkmate" （参见 check (n.1)), 源自 key move of the game. 现代法语 still distinguishes échec "check, blow, rebuff, defeat," 源自 plural échecs "chess." The original word for "chess" is 梵语 chaturanga "four members of an army" -- elephants, horses, chariots, foot soldiers. This is preserved in 西班牙语 ajedrez, 源自 阿拉伯语 (al) shat-ranj, 源自 波斯语 chatrang, 源自 梵语 word.

entries.etymology: Old English cest "box, coffer, casket," from Proto-Germanic *kista (source also of Old Norse and Old High German kista, Old Frisian, Middle Dutch, German kiste, Dutch kist), an early borrowing from Latin cista "chest, box," from Greek kiste "a box, basket," from PIE *kista "woven container." Meaning extended to "thorax" 1520s, replacing breast (n.), on the metaphor of the ribs as a box for the organs. Chest of drawers is from 1590s.

Chest of drawers 始于 1590 年代.

entries.etymology:
Old English ceowan "to bite, gnaw, chew," from West Germanic *keuwwan (source also of Middle Low German keuwen, Dutch kauwen, Old High German kiuwan, German kauen), from PIE root *gyeu- "to chew" (source also of Old Church Slavonic živo "to chew," Lithuanian žiaunos "jaws," Persian javidan "to chew").

Figurative sense of "to think over" is from late 14c.; to chew the rag "discusss some matter" is from 1885, apparently originally British army slang. Related: Chewed; chewing. To chew (someone) out (1948) probably is military slang from World War II. Chewing gum is by 1843, American English, originally hardened secretions of the spruce tree.

Figurative 语义 "to think over" 始于 14 世纪晚期; to chew the rag "discusss some matter" 始于 1885 年, 似乎 原义为 British army 俚语. 同源词：Chewed; chewing. To chew (someone) out (1948 年) 可能 is military 俚语 源自 World War II. Chewing gum is 截至 1843 年, American English, 原义为 hardened secretions of the spruce tree.

entries.etymology:
Old English cicen (plural cicenu) "young fowl," which by early Middle English had came to mean "young chicken," then later any chicken, from Proto-Germanic *kiukinam (source also of Middle Dutch kiekijen, Dutch kieken, Old Norse kjuklingr, Swedish kyckling, German Küken "chicken"), from root *keuk- (echoic of the bird's sound and possibly also the root of cock (n.1)) + diminutive suffixes.

Applied to the young of other bird species from early 13c. Adjective sense of "cowardly" is at least as old as 14c. (compare hen-herte "a chicken-hearted person," mid-15c.). As the name of a game of danger to test courage, it is first recorded 1953. Chicken feed "paltry sum of money" is by 1897, American English slang; literal use (it is made from the from lowest quality of grain) by 1834. Chicken lobster "young lobster," is from c. 1960s, American English, apparently from chicken in its sense of "young." Generic words for "chicken" in Indo-European tend to be extended uses of "hen" words, as hens are more numerous among domestic fowl, but occasionally they are from words for the young, as in English and in Latin pullus.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "highest in rank or power; most important or prominent; supreme, best," from Old French chief "chief, principal, first" (10c., Modern French chef), from Vulgar Latin *capum (also source of Spanish and Portuguese cabo, Italian capo, Provençal cap), from Latin caput "head," also "leader, guide, chief person; summit; capital city" (see capitulum).

entries.etymology:
Old English cild "fetus, infant, unborn or newly born person," from Proto-Germanic *kiltham (source also of Gothic kilþei "womb," inkilþo "pregnant;" Danish kuld "children of the same marriage;" Old Swedish kulder "litter;" Old English cildhama "womb," lit. "child-home"); no certain cognates outside Germanic. "App[arently] originally always used in relation to the mother as the 'fruit of the womb'" [Buck]. Also in late Old English, "a youth of gentle birth" (archaic, usually written childe). In 16c.-17c. especially "girl child." 

The wider sense "young person before the onset of puberty" developed in late Old English. Phrase with child "pregnant" (late 12c.) retains the original sense. The sense extension from "infant" to "child" also is found in French enfant, Latin infans. Meaning "one's own child; offspring of parents" is from late 12c. (the Old English word was bearn; see bairn). Figurative use from late 14c. Most Indo-European languages use the same word for "a child" and "one's child," though there are exceptions (such as Latin liberi/pueri).

The difficulty with the plural began in Old English, where the nominative plural was at first cild, identical with the singular, then c.975 a plural form cildru (genitive cildra) arose, probably for clarity's sake, only to be re-pluraled late 12c. as children, which is thus a double plural. Middle English plural cildre survives in Lancashire dialect childer and in Childermas.

Child abuse is attested by 1963; child-molester from 1950. Child care is from 1915. Child's play, figurative of something easy, is in Chaucer (late 14c.).

entries.etymology: Old English ciele, cele "cold, coolness, chill, frost," from Proto-Germanic *kal- "to be cold," from PIE root *gel- "cold" (see cold). According to OED, the word seems to have been obsolete after c. 1400 (displaced by cold) and the modern use is a back-formation since c. 1600 from the verb.

entries.etymology: late 13c., "furnace;" early 14c., "chimney stack of a fireplace;" late 14c., "fireplace in a residential space;" from Old French cheminee "fireplace; room with a fireplace; hearth; chimney stack" (12c., Modern French cheminée), from Late Latin (camera) caminata "fireplace; room with a fireplace," from Latin caminatus, adjective of caminus "furnace, forge; hearth, oven; flue," from Greek kaminos "furnace, oven, brick kiln." Jamieson [1808] notes that in vulgar use in Scotland it always is pronounced "chimley." Chimney sweep attested from 1610s, earlier chimney sweeper (c. 1500).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "furnace;" 14 世纪初, "chimney stack of a fireplace;" 14 世纪晚期, "fireplace in a residential space;" 源自 古法语 cheminee "fireplace; room with a fireplace; hearth; chimney stack" (12 世纪, 现代法语 cheminée), 源自 晚期拉丁语 (camera) caminata "fireplace; room with a fireplace," 源自 拉丁语 caminatus, 形容词 of caminus "furnace, forge; hearth, oven; flue," 源自 希腊语 kaminos "furnace, oven, brick kiln." entries.etymology:
Old English cin, cinn "chin" (but in some compounds suggesting an older, broader sense of "jawbone"); a general Germanic word (compare Old Saxon and Old High German kinni; Old Norse kinn; German Kinn "chin;" Gothic kinnus "cheek"), from PIE root *genu-, probably originally "jaw, jawbone," but also forming words for "chin, cheek" (source also of Sanskrit hanuh "jaw," Avestan zanu- "chin;" Armenian cnawt "jawbone, cheek;" Lithuanian žándas "jawbone;" Greek genus "chin, lower jaw," geneion "chin;" Old Irish gin "mouth," Welsh gen "jawbone, chin").

The West Germanic words generally mean "chin," but there are traces of earlier use as "jaw," such as Old English cinbane "jawbone," and the words for "cheek," "chin," and "jaw" naturally overlap and interchange; compare cheek (n.), which originally meant "jaw," and Latin maxilla, which gave Italian mascella "jaw," but Spanish mejilla "cheek."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 cin, cinn "chin" (but in some compounds suggesting an older, broader 语义 "jawbone"); a general 日耳曼语 word (对比 古撒克逊语 and 古高地德语 kinni; 古北欧语 kinn; 德语 Kinn "chin;" Gothic kinnus "cheek"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *genu-, 可能 原义为 "jaw, jawbone," but also forming words for "chin, cheek" (source also of 梵语 hanuh "jaw," Avestan zanu- "chin;" Armenian cnawt "jawbone, cheek;" Lithuanian žándas "jawbone;" 希腊语 genus "chin, lower jaw," geneion "chin;" Old 爱尔兰语 gin "mouth," Welsh gen "jawbone, chin"). The West 日耳曼语 words generally mean "chin," but there are traces of earlier use as "jaw," such as 古英语 cinbane "jawbone," and the words for "cheek," "chin," and "jaw" naturally overlap and interchange; 对比 cheek （名）, which 原义为 meant "jaw," and 拉丁语 maxilla, which gave 意大利语 mascella "jaw," but 西班牙语 mejilla "cheek."

entries.etymology: Asian country name, 1550s, of uncertain origin, probably ultimately from Sanskrit Cina-s "the Chinese" (earliest European usage is in Italian, by Marco Polo), perhaps from Qin dynasty, which ruled 3c. B.C.E. Latinized as Sina, hence sinologist. The Chinese word for the country is Chung-kuo (Wade-Giles), Zhongguo (Pinyin).

entries.definition: a.中国（人/话）的 n.中国人，汉语
entries.etymology: 1570s, from China + -ese. As a noun from c. 1600. Chinee (n.) is a vulgar back-formation from this word on the mistaken notion that the word is a plural. As an adjective, Chinish also was used 16c. Chinese fire-drill "chaotic situation of many people rushing around futilely" is attested by 1962, U.S. military slang, perhaps with roots in World War II U.S. Marine Corps slang. The game Chinese checkers is attested from 1938.

Chinee （名） is a vulgar back-formation 源自 this word on the mistaken notion that the word is a plural. 作形容词时, Chinish also was used 16 世纪 汉语 fire-drill "chaotic situation of many people rushing around futilely" is attested 截至 1962 年, U.S. military 俚语, 或许 with roots in World War II U.S. Marine Corps 俚语. The game 汉语 checkers 见于 1938 年.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "to chip" (intransitive, of stone); from Old English forcippian "to pare away by cutting, cut off," verbal form of cipp "small piece of wood" (see chip (n.)). Transitive meaning "to cut up, cut or trim" is from late 15c. Sense of "break off fragments" is 18c. To chip in "contribute" (1861) is  American English, perhaps from card-playing. Related: Chipped; chipping. Chipped beef attested from 1826.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "to chip" (intransitive, of stone); 源自 古英语 forcippian "to pare away by cutting, cut off," verbal form of cipp "small piece of wood" （参见 chip （名）). Transitive 意为 "to cut up, cut or trim" 始于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "break off fragments" is 18 世纪 To chip in "contribute" (1861 年) is American English, 或源自 card-playing. 同源词：Chipped; chipping. Chipped beef attested 自 1826 年起.

entries.etymology:
c. 1600, from Nahuatl (Aztecan) xocolatl, possibly from xocolia "to make bitter" + atl "water." Brought to Spain by 1520, from thence to the rest of Europe. Originally a drink; as a paste or cake made of ground, roasted, sweetened cacao seeds, 1640s.

As a color from 1776. Chocolate chip is from 1940; chocolatier is attested from 1888.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, 源自 Nahuatl (Aztecan) xocolatl, possibly 源自 xocolia "to make bitter" + atl "water." Brought to Spain 截至 1520 年, 源自 thence to the rest of Europe. Originally a drink; 作为 paste or cake made of ground, roasted, sweetened cacao seeds, 1640 年代. 作为 color 自 1776 年起. Chocolate chip 始于 1940 年; chocolatier 见于 1888 年.

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "that which is choice," from choice (adj.) blended with earlier chois (n.) "action of selecting" (c. 1300); "power of choosing" (early 14c.), "someone or something chosen" (late 14c.), from Old French chois "one's choice; fact of having a choice" (12c., Modern French choix), from verb choisir "to choose, distinguish, discern; recognize, perceive, see," from Frankish or some other Germanic source related to Old English ceosan "to choose, taste, try;" see choose. Late Old English chis "fastidious, choosy," from or related to ceosan, probably also contributed to the development of choice. 
Replaced Old English cyre "choice, free will," from the same base, probably because the imported word was closer to choose [see note in OED].
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "that which is choice," 源自 choice （形） blended with earlier chois （名） "action of selecting" (约 1300 年); "power of choosing" (14 世纪初), "someone or something chosen" (14 世纪晚期), 源自 古法语 chois "one's choice; fact of having a choice" (12 世纪, 现代法语 choix), 源自 动词 choisir "to choose, distinguish, discern; recognize, perceive, see," 源自 Frankish or some other 日耳曼语 source related to 古英语 ceosan "to choose, taste, try;" 参见 choose. Late 古英语 chis "fastidious, choosy," 源自 or related to ceosan, 可能 also contributed to the development of choice. Replaced 古英语 cyre "choice, free will," 源自 same base, 可能 because the imported word was closer to choose [参见 note in OED].

example.en: With so many options, making a choice was harder than expected.
example.zh: 选项太多，做出选择比预期的难。

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, transitive, "to strangle;" late 14c., "to make to suffocate," of persons as well as swallowed objects, a shortening of acheken (c. 1200), from Old English aceocian "to choke, suffocate" (with intensive a-), probably from root of ceoke "jaw, cheek" (see cheek (n.)).

Intransitive sense from c. 1400. Meaning "gasp for breath" is from early 15c. Figurative use from c. 1400, in early use often with reference to weeds stifling the growth of useful plants (a Biblical image). Meaning "to fail in the clutch" is attested by 1976, American English. Related: Choked; choking. Choke-cherry (1785) supposedly so called for its astringent qualities. Johnson also has choke-pear "Any aspersion or sarcasm, by which another person is put to silence." Choked up "overcome with emotion and unable to speak" is attested by 1896. The baseball batting sense is by 1907.

entries.etymology: Old English ceosan "choose, seek out, select; decide, test, taste, try; accept, approve" (class II strong verb; past tense ceas, past participle coren), from Proto-Germanic *keus- (source also of Old Frisian kiasa, Old Saxon kiosan, Dutch kiezen, Old High German kiosan, German kiesen, Old Norse kjosa, Gothic kiusan "choose," Gothic kausjan "to taste, test"), from PIE root *geus- "to taste, relish" (see gusto). Only remotely related to choice. Variant spelling chuse is Middle English, very frequent 16c.-18c. The irregular past participle leveled out to chosen by 1200.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ceosan "choose, seek out, select; decide, test, taste, try; accept, approve" (class II strong 动词; past tense ceas, past participle coren), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *keus- (source also of 古弗里西语 kiasa, 古撒克逊语 kiosan, 荷兰语 kiezen, 古高地德语 kiosan, 德语 kiesen, 古北欧语 kjosa, Gothic kiusan "choose," Gothic kausjan "to taste, test"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *geus- "to taste, relish" （参见 gusto). Only remotely related to choice. Variant spelling chuse is 中古英语, very frequent 16 世纪-18 世纪 The irregular past participle leveled out to chosen 截至 1200 年.

example.en: It was hard to choose between the two equally good options.
example.zh: 在两个同样好的选项之间做出选择很难。

entries.etymology:
title given to Jesus of Nazareth, Old English crist (by 830, perhaps 675), from Latin Christus, from Greek khristos "the anointed" (translation of Hebrew mashiah; see messiah), noun use of verbal adjective of khriein "to rub, anoint" (see chrism). The Latin term drove out Old English Hæland "healer, savior," as the preferred descriptive term for Jesus.

A title, treated as a proper name in Old English, but not regularly capitalized until 17c. Pronunciation with long -i- is result of Irish missionary work in England, 7c.-8c. The ch- form, regular since c. 1500 in English, was rare before. Capitalization of the word begins 14c. but is not fixed until 17c. The 17c. mystical sect of the Familists edged it toward a verb with Christed "made one with Christ."
entries.etymologyZh: title given to Jesus of Nazareth, 古英语 crist (by 830, 或许 675), 源自 拉丁语 Christus, 源自 希腊语 khristos "the anointed" (translation of 希伯来语 mashiah; 参见 messiah), 为 … 的名词用法 verbal 形容词 of khriein "to rub, anoint" （参见 chrism). The 拉丁语 term drove out 古英语 Hæland "healer, savior," as the preferred descriptive term for Jesus. A title, treated 作为 proper name in 古英语, but not regularly capitalized until 17 世纪 Pronunciation with long -i- is result of 爱尔兰语 missionary work in England, 7 世纪-8 世纪 The ch- form, regular 自 约 1500 年 in English, was rare before. Capitalization of the word begins 14 世纪 but is not fixed until 17 世纪 The 17 世纪 mystical sect of the Familists edged it toward a 动词 with Christed "made one with Christ."

entries.etymology:
late Old English Cristes mæsse, from Christ (and retaining the original vowel sound) + mass (n.2).

Written as one word from mid-14c. As a verb from 1590s. Father Christmas first attested in a carol attributed to Richard Smart, Rector of Plymtree (Devon) from 1435-77. Christmas tree in modern sense first attested 1835 in American English, from German Weihnachtsbaum. Christmas cards first designed 1843, popular by 1860s. Christmas Eve is Middle English Cristenmesse Even (c. 1300).
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 Cristes mæsse, 源自 Christ (and retaining the original vowel sound) + mass (n.2). Written as one word 源自 14 世纪中期 作动词时 源自 1590 年代. Father Christmas 最早见于 in a carol attributed to Richard Smart, Rector of Plymtree (Devon) 自 1435 年起-77. Christmas tree in modern sense 最早见于 1835 年 in American English, 源自 德语 Weihnachtsbaum. Christmas cards first designed 1843 年, popular by 1860 年代. Christmas Eve is 中古英语 Cristenmesse Even (约 1300 年).

entries.etymology: early 15c., of diseases, "lasting a long time," from Middle French chronique, from Latin chronicus, from Greek khronikos "of time, concerning time," from khronos "time" (see chrono-). Vague disapproving sense (from 17c.) is from association with diseases and later addictions.

example.en: He has suffered from chronic back pain for over ten years.
example.zh: 他已经遭受慢性背痛超过十年了。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, cronicle, from Anglo-French cronicle, from Old French cronique "chronicle" (Modern French chronique), from Latin chronica (neuter plural mistaken for fem. singular), from Greek ta khronika (biblia) "the (books of) annals, chronology," neuter plural of khronikos "of time, concerning time," from khronos "time" (see chrono-). Ending modified in Anglo-French, perhaps by influence of article. Old English had cranic "chronicle," cranicwritere "chronicler." The classical -h- was restored in English from 16c.

entries.etymology:
Old English cirice, circe "church, public place of worship; Christians collectively," from Proto-Germanic *kirika (source also of Old Saxon kirika, Old Norse kirkja, Old Frisian zerke, Middle Dutch kerke, Dutch kerk, Old High German kirihha, German Kirche), probably [see note in OED] from Greek kyriake (oikia), kyriakon doma "Lord's (house)," from kyrios "ruler, lord," from PIE root *keue- "to swell" ("swollen," hence "strong, powerful"); see cumulus. Phonetic spelling from c. 1200, established by 16c. For vowel evolution, see bury. As an adjective from 1570s.

Greek kyriakon (adj.) "of the Lord" was used of houses of Christian worship since c.300, especially in the East, though it was less common in this sense than ekklesia or basilike. An example of the direct Greek-to-Germanic progress of many Christian words, via the Goths; it probably was used by West Germanic people in their pre-Christian period.

Also picked up by Slavic, probably via Germanic (Old Church Slavonic criky, Russian cerkov). Finnish kirkko, Estonian kirrik are from Scandinavian. Romance and Celtic languages use variants of Latin ecclesia (such as French église, 11c.).

Church-bell was in late Old English. Church-goer is from 1680s. Church key is early 14c.; slang use for "can or bottle opener" is by 1954, probably originally U.S. college student slang. Church-mouse, proverbial in many languages for its poverty, is 1731 in English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 cirice, circe "church, public place of worship; Christians collectively," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *kirika (source also of 古撒克逊语 kirika, 古北欧语 kirkja, 古弗里西语 zerke, Middle 荷兰语 kerke, 荷兰语 kerk, 古高地德语 kirihha, 德语 Kirche), 可能 [参见 note in OED] 源自 希腊语 kyriake (oikia), kyriakon doma "Lord's (house)," 源自 kyrios "ruler, lord," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *keue- "to swell" ("swollen," hence "strong, powerful"); 参见 cumulus. Phonetic spelling 源自 约 1200 年, established by 16 世纪 For vowel evolution, 参见 bury. 作形容词时 源自 1570 年代. 希腊语 kyriakon （形） "of the Lord" was used of houses of Christian worship 自 约 300 年, 尤指 in the East, though it was less common in this sense than ekklesia or basilike. An example of the direct 希腊语-to-日耳曼语 progress of many Christian words, 经由 the Goths; it 可能 was used by West 日耳曼语 people in their pre-Christian period. Also picked up by Slavic, 可能 经由 日耳曼语 (Old Church Slavonic criky, 俄语 cerkov). Finnish kirkko, Estonian kirrik 始于 Scandinavian. Romance and Celtic languages use variants of 拉丁语 ecclesia (such as 法语 église, 11 世纪). Church-bell was in late 古英语. Church-goer 始于 1680 年代. Church key is 14 世纪初; 俚语 use for "can or bottle opener" is 截至 1954 年, 可能 原义为 U.S. college student 俚语. Church-mouse, proverbial in many languages for its poverty, is 1731 年 in English.

entries.etymology: 1730, from Spanish cigarro (source also of French cigare), probably from Maya sicar "to smoke rolled tobacco leaves," from si'c "tobacco;" or from or influenced by Spanish cigarra "grasshopper, cicada" (on resemblance of shape), from Vulgar Latin *cicala (source also of French cigale, Italian cigala). Cigar-box is from 1819; cigar-store from 1839; the wooden cigar-store Indian is from 1879, American English, but wooden images of feathered Indians or Negroes are mentioned outside tobacconists' shops in England by 1852, and are said to have been in earlier use on the Continent.

entries.etymology: 1899, "a movie hall," from French cinéma, shortened from cinématographe "motion picture projector and camera," coined 1890s by Lumiere brothers, who invented it, from Latinized form of Greek kinemat-, comb. form of kinema "movement," from kinein "to move" (see cite) + graphein "to write" (see -graphy). Meaning "movies collectively, especially as an art form" recorded by 1914. Cinéma vérité is 1963, from French.
entries.etymologyZh: 1899 年, "a movie hall," 源自 法语 cinéma, shortened 源自 cinématographe "motion picture projector and camera," coined 1890 年代 by Lumiere brothers, who invented it, 源自 Latinized form of 希腊语 kinemat-, comb. form of kinema "movement," 源自 kinein "to move" （参见 cite) + graphein "to write" （参见 -graphy). 义为 "movies collectively, especially as an art form" recorded 截至 1914 年. Cinéma vérité is 1963 年, 源自 法语.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "figure of a circle," from Old French cercle "circle, ring (for the finger); hoop of a helmet or barrel" (12c.), from Latin circulus "circular figure; small ring, hoop; circular orbit" (also source of Italian cerchio), diminutive of circus "ring" (see circus).

Replaced Old English trendel and hring. Late Old English used circul, from Latin, but only in an astronomical sense. Meaning "group of persons surrounding a center of interest" is from 1714 (it also was a secondary sense of Latin circulus); that of "coterie" is from 1640s (a sense also found in Latin circulus). To come full circle is in Shakespeare.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "figure of a circle," 源自 古法语 cercle "circle, ring (for the finger); hoop of a helmet or barrel" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 circulus "circular figure; small ring, hoop; circular orbit" (also source of 意大利语 cerchio), 为 … 的指小形式 circus "ring" （参见 circus). Replaced 古英语 trendel and hring. Late 古英语 used circul, 源自 拉丁语, but only in an astronomical sense. 义为 "group of persons surrounding a center of interest" 始于 1714 年 (it also was a secondary 语义 拉丁语 circulus); that of "coterie" 始于 1640 年代 (a sense also found in 拉丁语 circulus). To come full circle is in Shakespeare.

example.en: Draw a circle with a compass and label its center point.
example.zh: 用圆规画一个圆并标出其圆心。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "a going around; a line going around," from Old French circuit (14c.) "a circuit; a journey (around something)," from Latin circuitus "a going around," from stem of circuire, circumire "go around," from circum "round" (see circum-) + ire "to go" (see ion). Electrical sense is from 1746. Of judicial assignments, from 1570s; of venues for itinerant entertainers, from 1834. Circuit breaker is recorded from 1874. Related: Circuital.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "a going around; a line going around," 源自 古法语 circuit (14 世纪) "a circuit; a journey (around something)," 源自 拉丁语 circuitus "a going around," 源自 stem of circuire, circumire "go around," 源自 circum "round" （参见 circum-) + ire "to go" （参见 ion). Electrical sense 始于 1746 年. Of judicial assignments, 源自 1570 年代; of venues for itinerant entertainers, 自 1834 年起. Circuit breaker 见于 1874 年. 同源词：Circuital.

example.en: The technician repaired the broken circuit in the control panel.
example.zh: 技术员修复了控制面板中损坏的电路。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Anglo-French circuler, Old French circuler "circular" (14c., Modern French circulaire), from Latin circularis, from circulus (see circle (n.)). The metaphoric circular firing squad is attested by 1990.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 circuler, 古法语 circuler "circular" (14 世纪, 现代法语 circulaire), 源自 拉丁语 circularis, 源自 circulus （参见 circle （名）). The metaphoric circular firing squad is attested 截至 1990 年.

entries.etymology: 1540s (late 15c. as a past participle adjective), as a chemical term for alternating vaporization and condensation, from Latin circulatus, past participle of circulare "to form a circle," from circulus (see circle (n.)). Meaning "to move around, revolve" is from 1670s; of blood, from 1650s; of persons, "to mingle in a social gathering," from 1863. Sense of "to pass about freely" is from 1660s; of newspapers from 1885. Related: Circulated; circulating.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代 (15 世纪晚期 作为 past participle 形容词), 作为 chemical term for alternating vaporization and condensation, 源自 拉丁语 circulatus, 为 … 的过去分词 circulare "to form a circle," 源自 circulus （参见 circle （名）). 义为 "to move around, revolve" 始于 1670 年代; of blood, 源自 1650 年代; of persons, "to mingle in a social gathering," 自 1863 年起. 义为 "to pass about freely" 始于 1660 年代; of newspapers 自 1885 年起. 同源词：Circulated; circulating.

example.en: Fresh air needs to circulate freely through the building to prevent mold.
example.zh: 新鲜空气需要在建筑内自由流通以防止发霉。

entries.etymology:
early 13c., "conditions surrounding and accompanying an event," from Old French circonstance "circumstance, situation," also literally, "outskirts" (13c., Modern French circonstance), from Latin circumstantia "surrounding condition," neuter plural of circumstans (genitive circumstantis), present participle of circumstare "stand around, surround, encompass, occupy, take possession of" from circum "around" (see circum-) + stare "to stand" from PIE root *stā- "to stand" (see stet). The Latin word is a loan-translation of Greek peristasis.

Meaning "a person's surroundings, environment" is from mid-14c. Meaning "a detail" is from c. 1300; sense of "that which is non-essential" is from 1590s. Obsolete sense of "formality about an important event" (late 14c.) lingers in Shakespeare's phrase pomp and circumstance ("Othello" III, iii).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "conditions surrounding and accompanying an event," 源自 古法语 circonstance "circumstance, situation," also 字面义为, "outskirts" (13 世纪, 现代法语 circonstance), 源自 拉丁语 circumstantia "surrounding condition," neuter 为 … 的复数 circumstans (属格 circumstantis), 为 … 的现在分词 circumstare "stand around, surround, encompass, occupy, take possession of" 源自 circum "around" （参见 circum-) + stare "to stand" 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). The 拉丁语 word is a loan-translation of 希腊语 peristasis. 义为 "a person's surroundings, environment" 始于 14 世纪中期 义为 "a detail" 始于 约 1300 年; 语义 "that which is non-essential" 始于 1590 年代. Obsolete 语义 "formality about an important event" (14 世纪晚期) lingers in Shakespeare's phrase pomp and circumstance ("Othello" III, iii).

example.en: Under no circumstance should you share your password with anyone else.
example.zh: 在任何情况下都不应将密码分享给他人。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., in reference to ancient Rome, from Latin circus "ring, circular line," which was applied by Romans to circular arenas for performances and contests and oval courses for racing (especially the Circus Maximus), from or cognate with Greek kirkos "a circle, a ring," from PIE *kirk- from root *(s)ker- (3) "to turn, bend" (see ring (n.)).

In reference to modern large arenas for performances from 1791; sense then extended to the performing company, hence "traveling show" (originally traveling circus, 1838). Extended in World War I to squadrons of military aircraft. Meaning "lively uproar, chaotic hubbub" is from 1869. Sense in Picadilly Circus and other place names is from early 18c. sense "buildings arranged in a ring," also "circular road." The adjective form is circensian.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, in reference to ancient Rome, 源自 拉丁语 circus "ring, circular line," which was applied by Romans to circular arenas for performances and contests and oval courses for racing (尤指 the Circus Maximus), 源自 or 与 … 同源 希腊语 kirkos "a circle, a ring," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *kirk- 源自 root *(s)ker- (3) "to turn, bend" （参见 ring （名）). In reference to modern large arenas for performances 自 1791 年起; sense 之后 extended to the performing company, hence "traveling show" (原义为 traveling circus, 1838 年). Extended in World War I to squadrons of military aircraft. 义为 "lively uproar, chaotic hubbub" 始于 1869 年. Sense in Picadilly Circus and other place names 始于 18 世纪初 sense "buildings arranged in a ring," also "circular road." The 形容词 form is circensian.

example.en: The children were thrilled to see lions and acrobats at the traveling circus.
example.zh: 孩子们看到巡回马戏团里的狮子和杂技演员，兴奋不已。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "to summon," from Old French citer "to summon" (14c.), from Latin citare "to summon, urge, call; put in sudden motion, call forward; rouse, excite," frequentative of ciere "to move, set in motion, stir, rouse, call, invite" from PIE root *keie- "to set in motion, to move to and fro" (source also of Sanskrit cyavate "stirs himself, goes;" Greek kinein "to move, set in motion; change, stir up," kinymai "move myself;" Gothic haitan "call, be called;" Old English hatan "command, call"). Sense of "calling forth a passage of writing" is first attested 1530s. Related: Cited; citing.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "to summon," 源自 古法语 citer "to summon" (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 citare "to summon, urge, call; put in sudden motion, call forward; rouse, excite," 为 … 的反复体 ciere "to move, set in motion, stir, rouse, call, invite" 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *keie- "to set in motion, to move to and fro" (source also of 梵语 cyavate "stirs himself, goes;" 希腊语 kinein "to move, set in motion; change, stir up," kinymai "move myself;" Gothic haitan "call, be called;" 古英语 hatan "command, call"). 义为 "calling forth a passage of writing" is 最早见于 1530 年代. 同源词：Cited; citing.

example.en: The lawyer decided to cite several important cases to support her argument.
example.zh: 律师决定引用几个重要案例来支持她的论点。

entries.etymology: early 14c., "inhabitant of a city," from Anglo-French citezein (spelling subsequently altered, probably by influence of denizen), from Old French citeien "city-dweller, town-dweller, citizen" (12c., Modern French citoyen), from cite (see city) + -ain (see -ian). Replaced Old English burhsittend and ceasterware. Sense of "inhabitant of a country" is late 14c. Citizen's arrest recorded from 1941; citizen's band (radio) from 1947. Citizen of the world (late 15c.) translates Greek kosmopolites.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "inhabitant of a city," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 citezein (spelling subsequently altered, 可能 by influence of denizen), 源自 古法语 citeien "city-dweller, town-dweller, citizen" (12 世纪, 现代法语 citoyen), 源自 cite （参见 city) + -ain （参见 -ian). Replaced 古英语 burhsittend and ceasterware. 义为 "inhabitant of a country" is 14 世纪晚期 Citizen's arrest recorded from 1941; citizen's band (radio) 自 1947 年起. Citizen of the world (15 世纪晚期) translates 希腊语 kosmopolites.

example.en: Every citizen has the right to vote in a democratic society.
example.zh: 在民主社会中，每一位公民都有投票权。

entries.etymology:
early 13c., in medieval usage a cathedral town, but originally "any settlement," regardless of size (distinction from town is 14c., though in English it always seems to have ranked above borough), from Old French cite "town, city" (10c., Modern French cité), from earlier citet, from Latin civitatem (nominative civitas; in Late Latin sometimes citatem) originally "citizenship, condition or rights of a citizen, membership in the community," later "community of citizens, state, commonwealth" (used, for instance of the Gaulish tribes), from civis "townsman," from PIE root *kei- "to lie; bed, couch; homestead; beloved, dear" (see cemetery).

The sense has been transferred from the inhabitants to the place. The Latin word for "city" was urbs, but a resident was civis. Civitas seems to have replaced urbs as Rome (the ultimate urbs) lost its prestige. Loss of Latin -v- is regular in French in some situations (compare alleger from alleviare; neige from nivea; jeune from juvenis. A different sound evolution from the Latin word yielded Italian citta, Catalan ciutat, Spanish ciudad, Portuguese cidade.

Replaced Old English burh (see borough). London is the city from 1550s. As an adjective from c. 1300. City hall first recorded 1670s to fight city hall is 1913, American English; city slicker first recorded 1916 (see slick); both American English. City limits is from 1825. The newspaper city desk attested from 1878. Inner city first attested 1968. City state (also city-state) is attested from 1877.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, in medieval usage a cathedral town, but 原义为 "any settlement," regardless of size (distinction 源自 town is 14 世纪, though in English it always seems to have ranked above borough), 源自 古法语 cite "town, city" (10 世纪, 现代法语 cité), 源自 earlier citet, 源自 拉丁语 civitatem (主格 civitas; in 晚期拉丁语 有时 citatem) 原义为 "citizenship, condition or rights of a citizen, membership in the community," later "community of citizens, state, commonwealth" (used, for instance of the Gaulish tribes), 源自 civis "townsman," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *kei- "to lie; bed, couch; homestead; beloved, dear" （参见 cemetery). The sense has been transferred 源自 inhabitants to the place. The 拉丁语 word for "city" was urbs, but a resident was civis. Civitas seems to have replaced urbs as Rome (the ultimate urbs) lost its prestige. Loss of 拉丁语 -v- is regular in 法语 in some situations (对比 alleger 源自 alleviare; neige 源自 nivea; jeune 源自 juvenis. A different sound evolution 源自 拉丁语 word yielded 意大利语 citta, Catalan ciutat, 西班牙语 ciudad, 葡萄牙语 cidade. Replaced 古英语 burh （参见 borough). London is the city 源自 1550 年代. 作形容词时 源自 约 1300 年. City hall 首见于 1670 年代 to fight city hall is 1913 年, American English; city slicker 首见于 1916 年 （参见 slick); both American English. City limits 始于 1825 年. The newspaper city desk attested 自 1878 年起. Inner city 最早见于 1968 年. City state (also city-state) 见于 1877 年.

example.en: The city plans to build three new subway lines by 2030.
example.zh: 该城市计划在2030年前建成三条新地铁线路。

definitionLines: a. 公民的，市民的；市的
entries.definition: a. 公民的，市民的；市的
entries.etymology: 1540s, originally mostly in civic crown (Latin corona civica), a chaplet of oak leaves awarded to one who saved the life of a fellow citizen in battle, from Latin civicus "of a citizen," adjectival derivation of civis "townsman" (see city). Sense of "having to do with citizens" is from 1790.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, 原义为 mostly in civic crown (拉丁语 corona civica), a chaplet of oak leaves awarded to one who saved the life of a fellow citizen in battle, 源自 拉丁语 civicus "of a citizen," adjectival derivation of civis "townsman" （参见 city). 义为 "having to do with citizens" 始于 1790 年.

example.en: Voting is considered a fundamental civic duty in a democracy.
example.zh: 在民主国家，投票被视为一项基本的公民义务。

definitionLines: a. 市民的，公民的，国民的；民 间的；民事的，根据民法的； 文职的；有礼貌的
entries.definition: a. 市民的，公民的，国民的；民 间的；民事的，根据民法的； 文职的；有礼貌的
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "relating to civil law or life; pertaining to the internal affairs of a state," from Old French civil "civil, relating to civil law" (13c.) and directly from Latin civilis "relating to a citizen, relating to public life, befitting a citizen," hence by extension "popular, affable, courteous;" alternative adjectival derivation of civis "townsman" (see city).

The sense of "polite" was in classical Latin, from the courteous manners of citizens, as opposed to those of soldiers. But English did not pick up this nuance of the word until late 16c. "Courteous is thus more commonly said of superiors, civil of inferiors, since it implies or suggests the possibility of incivility or rudeness" [OED]. Civil case (as opposed to criminal) is recorded from 1610s. Civil liberty is by 1640s. Civil service is from 1772, originally in reference to the East India Company.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "relating to civil law or life; pertaining to the internal affairs of a state," 源自 古法语 civil "civil, relating to civil law" (13 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 civilis "relating to a citizen, relating to public life, befitting a citizen," hence by extension "popular, affable, courteous;" alternative adjectival derivation of civis "townsman" （参见 city). The 语义 "polite" was in classical 拉丁语, 源自 courteous manners of citizens, as opposed to those of soldiers. But English did not pick up this nuance of the word until 16 世纪晚期 "Courteous is thus more commonly said of superiors, civil of inferiors, since it implies or suggests the possibility of incivility or rudeness" [OED]. Civil case (as opposed to criminal) 见于 1610 年代. Civil liberty is by 1640 年代. Civil service 始于 1772 年, 原义为 in reference to the East India Company.

example.en: The new law protects the civil rights of all residents.
example.zh: 新法律保护所有居民的公民权利。

definitionLines: a. 平民的，民间的，民用的
entries.definition: n. 平民，百姓 a. 平民的，民间的，民用的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "judge or authority on civil law," from Old French civilien "of the civil law," created from Latin civilis "relating to a citizen, relating to public life, befitting a citizen; popular, affable, courteous" (see civil). Sense of "non-military person" is attested by 1819 (earlier in this sense was civilian, attested from c. 1600 as "non-soldier"). The adjective is from 1640s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "judge or authority on civil law," 源自 古法语 civilien "of the civil law," created 源自 拉丁语 civilis "relating to a citizen, relating to public life, befitting a citizen; popular, affable, courteous" （参见 civil). 义为 "non-military person" is attested 截至 1819 年 (earlier in this sense was civilian, attested 源自 约 1600 年 as "non-soldier"). The 形容词 始于 1640 年代.

example.en: The conflict resulted in heavy civilian casualties in the city.
example.zh: 这场冲突导致城市中大量平民伤亡。

entries.etymology: 1704, "law which makes a criminal process civil," from civilize + -ation. Sense of "civilized condition" first recorded 1772, probably from French civilisation, to be an opposite to barbarity and a distinct word from civility. Sense of a particular human society in a civilized condition, considered as a whole over time, is from 1857. Related: Civilizational.
entries.etymologyZh: 1704 年, "law which makes a criminal process civil," 源自 civilize + -ation. 义为 "civilized condition" 首见于 1772 年, 可能 源自 法语 civilisation, to be an opposite to barbarity and a distinct word 源自 civility. 义为 a particular human society in a civilized condition, considered 作为 whole over time, 始于 1857 年. 同源词：Civilizational.

example.en: Ancient Egypt made remarkable contributions to human civilization.
example.zh: 古埃及为人类文明作出了卓越贡献。

entries.etymology: c. 1600, "to bring out of barbarism," from French civiliser, verb from Old French civil (adj.), from Latin civilis "relating to a citizen, relating to public life, befitting a citizen; popular, affable, courteous" (see civil). Meaning "become civilized" is from 1868. Related: Civilized; civilizing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "to bring out of barbarism," 源自 法语 civiliser, 动词 源自 古法语 civil （形）, 源自 拉丁语 civilis "relating to a citizen, relating to public life, befitting a citizen; popular, affable, courteous" （参见 civil). 义为 "become civilized" 始于 1868 年. 同源词：Civilized; civilizing.

definitionLines: vt. 声称，主张；要求，认领， 索赔
entries.definition: vt. 声称，主张；要求，认领， 索赔 n. 权利；要求；主张
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "to call, call out; to ask or demand by virtue of right or authority," from accented stem of Old French clamer "to call, name, describe; claim; complain; declare," from Latin clamare "to cry out, shout, proclaim," from PIE *kele- (2) "to shout," imitative (compare Sanskrit usakala "cock," literally "dawn-calling;" Latin calare "to announce solemnly, call out;" Middle Irish cailech "cock;" Greek kalein "to call," kelados "noise," kledon "report, fame;" Old High German halan "to call;" Old English hlowan "to low, make a noise like a cow;" Lithuanian kalba "language"). Related: Claimed; claiming.

Meaning "to maintain as true" is from 1864; specific sense "to make a claim" (on an insurance company) is from 1897. Claim properly should not stray too far from its true meaning of "to demand recognition of a right."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to call, call out; to ask or demand by virtue of right or authority," 源自 accented stem of 古法语 clamer "to call, name, describe; claim; complain; declare," 源自 拉丁语 clamare "to cry out, shout, proclaim," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *kele- (2) "to shout," imitative (对比 梵语 usakala "cock," 字面义为 "dawn-calling;" 拉丁语 calare "to announce solemnly, call out;" Middle 爱尔兰语 cailech "cock;" 希腊语 kalein "to call," kelados "noise," kledon "report, fame;" 古高地德语 halan "to call;" 古英语 hlowan "to low, make a noise like a cow;" Lithuanian kalba "language"). 同源词：Claimed; claiming. 义为 "to maintain as true" 始于 1864 年; specific sense "to make a claim" (on an insurance company) 始于 1897 年. Claim properly should not stray too far 源自 its true 意为 of "to demand recognition of a right."

example.en: The suspect claimed he was at home all night, but no one could confirm his alibi.
example.zh: 嫌疑人声称他整晚都在家，但没有人能证实他的不在场证明。

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Gaelic clann "family, stock, offspring," akin to Old Irish cland "offspring, tribe," both from Latin planta "offshoot" (see plant (n.)). The Goidelic branch of Celtic (including Gaelic) had no initial p-, so it substituted k- or c- for Latin p-. The same Latin word in (non-Goidelic) Middle Welsh became plant "children."
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 Gaelic clann "family, stock, offspring," akin to Old 爱尔兰语 cland "offspring, tribe," both 源自 拉丁语 planta "offshoot" （参见 plant （名）). The Goidelic branch of Celtic (including Gaelic) had no initial p-, so it substituted k- or c- for 拉丁语 p-. The same 拉丁语 word in (non-Goidelic) Middle Welsh became plant "children."

entries.etymology: Old English clæppan "to throb, beat," common Germanic, echoic (cognate with Old Frisian klapa "to beat," Old Norse klappa, Old High German klaphon, German klappen, Old Saxon klapunga). Meaning "to strike or knock" is from c. 1300. Meaning "to make a sharp noise" is late 14c. Of hands, to beat them together to get attention or express joy, from late 14c. To clap (someone) on the back is from 1520s. Related: Clapped; clapping.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 clæppan "to throb, beat," common 日耳曼语, echoic (与 … 同源 古弗里西语 klapa "to beat," 古北欧语 klappa, 古高地德语 klaphon, 德语 klappen, 古撒克逊语 klapunga). 义为 "to strike or knock" 始于 约 1300 年. 义为 "to make a sharp noise" is 14 世纪晚期 Of hands, to beat them together to get attention or express joy, 源自 14 世纪晚期 To clap (someone) on the back 始于 1520 年代. 同源词：Clapped; clapping.

entries.definition: vi. 澄清，阐明 v.使明晰
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "make illustrious, make known," from Old French clarifiier "clarify, make clear, explain" (12c.), from Late Latin clarificare "to make clear," also "to glorify," from Latin clarificus "brilliant," from clarus "clear, distinct" (see clear (adj.)) + root of facere "to make, do" (see factitious).

Meaning "make clear, purify" is from early 15c. in English; intransitive sense of "grow or become clear" is from 1590s. Figurative sense of "to free from obscurity" is from 1823. Related: Clarified; clarifying.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "make illustrious, make known," 源自 古法语 clarifiier "clarify, make clear, explain" (12 世纪), 源自 晚期拉丁语 clarificare "to make clear," also "to glorify," 源自 拉丁语 clarificus "brilliant," 源自 clarus "clear, distinct" （参见 clear （形）) + root of facere "to make, do" （参见 factitious). 义为 "make clear, purify" 始于 15 世纪初 in English; intransitive 语义 "grow or become clear" 始于 1590 年代. Figurative 语义 "to free from obscurity" 始于 1823 年. 同源词：Clarified; clarifying.

example.en: Could you clarify what you mean by that statement?
example.zh: 您能澄清一下您那句话的含义吗？

entries.etymology: c. 1500, "to make a loud, sharp sound," of imitative origin, or a blend of clap and crash. Compare Dutch kletsen "splash, clash," German klatschen, Danish klaske "clash, knock about." Figurative sense, in reference to non-physical strife or battle, is first attested 1620s. Of things, "to come into collision," from 1650s; of colors, "to go badly together," first recorded 1894. Related: Clashed; clashing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年, "to make a loud, sharp sound," of imitative origin，或a blend of clap and crash. 对比 荷兰语 kletsen "splash, clash," 德语 klatschen, Danish klaske "clash, knock about." Figurative sense, in reference to non-physical strife or battle, is 最早见于 1620 年代. Of things, "to come into collision," 源自 1650 年代; of colors, "to go badly together," 首见于 1894 年. 同源词：Clashed; clashing.

example.en: The two rival groups clashed violently outside the stadium after the game.
example.zh: 两个对立团体在比赛结束后在体育场外发生激烈冲突。

definitionLines: n. 种类，等级，阶级；班，班级， 年级；（一节）课
entries.definition: n. 种类，等级，阶级；班，班级， 年级；（一节）课
entries.etymology:
c. 1600, "group of students," from French classe (14c.), from Latin classis "a class, a division; army, fleet," especially "any one of the six orders into which Servius Tullius divided the Roman people for the purpose of taxation;" traditionally originally "the people of Rome under arms" (a sense attested in English from 1650s), and thus akin to calare "to call (to arms)," from PIE root *kele- (2) "to shout" (see claim (v.)). In early use in English also in Latin form classis.

School and university sense of "course, lecture" (1650s) is from the notion of a form or lecture reserved to scholars who had attained a certain level. Natural history sense is from 1753. Meaning "a division of society according to status" (upper, lower, etc.) is from 1772. Meaning "high quality" is from 1847. Class-consciousness (1903) is from German klassenbewusst.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "group of students," 源自 法语 classe (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 classis "a class, a division; army, fleet," 尤指 "any one of the six orders into which Servius Tullius divided the Roman people for the purpose of taxation;" traditionally 原义为 "the people of Rome under arms" (a sense 见于 English 源自 1650 年代), and thus akin to calare "to call (to arms)," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *kele- (2) "to shout" （参见 claim （动）). In early use in English also in 拉丁语 form classis. School and university 语义 "course, lecture" (1650 年代) 始于 the 概念 a form or lecture reserved to scholars who had attained a certain level. Natural history sense 始于 1753 年. 义为 "a division of society according to status" (upper, lower, etc.) 始于 1772 年. 义为 "high quality" 始于 1847 年. Class-consciousness (1903 年) 始于 德语 klassenbewusst.

example.en: The teacher asked the entire class to submit their essays by Friday afternoon.
example.zh: 老师要求全班同学在周五下午之前提交作文。

entries.etymology: 1610s, "of the highest class; approved as a model," from French classique (17c.), from Latin classicus "relating to the (highest) classes of the Roman people," hence, "superior," from classis (see class). Originally in English, "of the first class;" meaning "belonging to standard authors of Greek and Roman antiquity" is attested from 1620s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "of the highest class; approved as a model," 源自 法语 classique (17 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 classicus "relating to the (highest) classes of the Roman people," hence, "superior," 源自 classis （参见 class). Originally in English, "of the first class;" 意为 "belonging to standard authors of Greek and Roman antiquity" 见于 1620 年代.

example.en: Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice is an enduring classic of English fiction.
example.zh: 简·奥斯汀的《傲慢与偏见》是英国小说中的一部永恒经典。

entries.etymology:
1590s, "of the highest rank" (originally in literature), from classic + -al (1). Classical music (1836) was defined originally against romantic music.

But already by 1880s it was acknowledged the term had a double sense: Music that had withstood the test of time, as well as music of a style contrasted to "romantic." Later (early 20c.) it was contrasted to jazz (in this sense more often with reference to the orchestras than to the music itself). Still later in contrast to popular music generally (mid-20c.). Classical history is the history of ancient Greece and Rome; ancient history is the history of mankind from the earliest reliable records to the fall of Rome (476 C.E.).
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "of the highest rank" (原义为 in literature), 源自 classic + -al (1). Classical music (1836 年) was defined 原义为 against romantic music. But already by 1880 年代 it was acknowledged the term had a double sense: Music that had withstood the test of time, as well as music of a style contrasted to "romantic." Later (20 世纪初) it was contrasted to jazz (in this sense more 常 with reference to the orchestras than to the music itself). Still later in contrast to popular music generally (20 世纪中期). Classical history is the history of ancient Greece and Rome; ancient history is the history of mankind 源自 earliest reliable records to the fall of Rome (476 C.E.).

example.en: She prefers classical music to modern pop songs.
example.zh: 她更喜欢古典音乐，而非现代流行歌曲。

entries.etymology: 1772, "action of classifying," noun of action from Latin stem of classify, or from French classification. Meaning "result of classifying" is from 1789.
entries.etymologyZh: 1772 年, "action of classifying," 名词 of action 源自 拉丁语 stem of classify，或源自 法语 classification. 义为 "result of classifying" 始于 1789 年.

example.en: The classification of these insects is based on their wing structure.
example.zh: 这些昆虫的分类是基于它们的翅膀结构。

entries.etymology: 1782, from French classifier, from classe (see class (n.)) + -fier (see -fy). Related: Classified; classifying.
entries.etymologyZh: 1782 年, 源自 法语 classifier, 源自 classe （参见 class （名）) + -fier （参见 -fy). 同源词：Classified; classifying.

example.en: Scientists classify animals based on their physical characteristics and DNA.
example.zh: 科学家根据动物的身体特征和DNA对其进行分类。

entries.etymology: "one of the same class at school or college," 1713, from class (n.) + mate (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: "one of the same class at school or college," 1713 年, 源自 class （名） + mate （名）.

entries.etymology: also class-room, 1811, from class (n.) + room (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: also class-room, 1811 年, 源自 class （名） + room （名）.

definitionLines: n. 子句，从句；（章程、条约等 的）条，项；条款
entries.definition: n. 子句，从句；（章程、条约等 的）条，项；条款
entries.etymology: c. 1200, "a sentence, a brief statement, a short passage," from Old French clause "stipulation" (in a legal document), 12c., from Medieval Latin clausa "conclusion," used in the sense of classical Latin clausula "the end, a closing, termination," also "end of a sentence or a legal argument," from clausa, fem. noun from past participle of claudere "to close, to shut, to conclude" (see close (v.)). Grammatical sense is from c. 1300. Legal meaning "distinct condition, stipulation, or proviso" is recorded from late 14c. in English. The sense of "ending" seems to have fallen from the word between Latin and French.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "a sentence, a brief statement, a short passage," 源自 古法语 clause "stipulation" (in a legal document), 12 世纪, 源自 中古拉丁语 clausa "conclusion," used in the 语义 classical 拉丁语 clausula "the end, a closing, termination," also "end of a sentence or a legal argument," 源自 clausa, fem. 名词 源自 为 … 的过去分词 claudere "to close, to shut, to conclude" （参见 close （动）). Grammatical sense 始于 约 1300 年. Legal 意为 "distinct condition, stipulation, or proviso" 见于 14 世纪晚期 in English. The 语义 "ending" seems to have fallen 源自 word between 拉丁语 and 法语.

example.en: The lawyer pointed out a clause in the contract that could cause problems.
example.zh: 律师指出合同中有一个可能引发问题的条款。

entries.etymology: Old English clawu, earlier clea, "claw, talon, iron hook," from Proto-Germanic *klawo (source also of Old Frisian klawe "claw, hoe," Middle Dutch klouwe, Dutch klauw, Old High German klawa, German Klaue "claw"). Claw-foot in reference to furniture is from 1823; claw-and-ball attested from 1893. Claw-hammer attested from 1769.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 clawu, earlier clea, "claw, talon, iron hook," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *klawo (source also of 古弗里西语 klawe "claw, hoe," Middle 荷兰语 klouwe, 荷兰语 klauw, 古高地德语 klawa, 德语 Klaue "claw"). Claw-foot in reference to furniture 始于 1823 年; claw-and-ball attested 自 1893 年起. Claw-hammer attested 自 1769 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English clæg "stiff, sticky earth; clay," from Proto-Germanic *klaijaz (source also of Old High German kliwa "bran," German Kleie, Old Frisian klai "clay," Old Saxon klei, Middle Dutch clei, Danish klæg "clay;" also Old English clæman, Old Norse kleima, Old High German kleiman "to cover with clay"), from PIE root *glei- "clay" (source also of Greek gloios "sticky matter;" Latin gluten "glue;" Old Church Slavonic glina "clay," glenu "slime, mucus;" Old Irish glenim "I cleave, adhere").

in Scripture, the stuff from which the body of the first man was formed; hence "human body" (especially when dead). Clay pigeon is from 1888. Feet of clay "fundamental weakness" is from Dan. ii:33.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 clæg "stiff, sticky earth; clay," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *klaijaz (source also of 古高地德语 kliwa "bran," 德语 Kleie, 古弗里西语 klai "clay," 古撒克逊语 klei, Middle 荷兰语 clei, Danish klæg "clay;" also 古英语 clæman, 古北欧语 kleima, 古高地德语 kleiman "to cover with clay"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *glei- "clay" (source also of 希腊语 gloios "sticky matter;" 拉丁语 gluten "glue;" Old Church Slavonic glina "clay," glenu "slime, mucus;" Old 爱尔兰语 glenim "I cleave, adhere"). in Scripture, the stuff 源自 which the body of the first man was formed; hence "human body" (尤指 when dead). Clay pigeon 始于 1888 年. Feet of clay "fundamental weakness" 始于 Dan. ii:33.

example.en: The children shaped animals out of soft clay during art class.
example.zh: 孩子们在美术课上用软黏土捏出各种动物。

definitionLines: a. 明亮的，清澈的；晴朗的
vt. 清除；澄清；晴朗起来
entries.definition: a. 明亮的，清澈的；晴朗的 a./ad. 清楚，清晰 vt. 清除；澄清；晴朗起来
entries.etymology:
late 13c., "bright," from Old French cler "clear" (of sight and hearing), "light, bright, shining; sparse" (12c., Modern French clair), from Latin clarus "clear, loud," of sounds; figuratively "manifest, plain, evident," in transferred use, of sights, "bright, distinct;" also "illustrious, famous, glorious" (source of Italian chiaro, Spanish claro), from PIE *kle-ro-, from root *kele- (2) "to shout" (see claim (v.)).

The sense evolution involves an identification of the spreading of sound and the spreading of light (compare English loud, used of colors; German hell "clear, bright, shining," of pitch, "distinct, ringing, high"). Of complexion, from c. 1300; of the weather, from late 14c.; of meanings or explanations, "manifest to the mind, comprehensible," c. 1300. (An Old English word for this was sweotol "distinct, clear, evident.") Sense of "free from encumbrance," apparently nautical, developed c. 1500. Phrase in the clear attested from 1715. Clear-sighted is from 1580s (clear-eyed is from 1529s); clear-headed is from 1709.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "bright," 源自 古法语 cler "clear" (of sight and hearing), "light, bright, shining; sparse" (12 世纪, 现代法语 clair), 源自 拉丁语 clarus "clear, loud," of sounds; figuratively "manifest, plain, evident," in transferred use, of sights, "bright, distinct;" also "illustrious, famous, glorious" (source of 意大利语 chiaro, 西班牙语 claro), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *kle-ro-, 源自 root *kele- (2) "to shout" （参见 claim （动）). The sense evolution involves an identification of the spreading of sound and the spreading of light (对比 English loud, used of colors; 德语 hell "clear, bright, shining," of pitch, "distinct, ringing, high"). Of complexion, 源自 约 1300 年; of the weather, 源自 14 世纪晚期; of meanings or explanations, "manifest to the mind, comprehensible," 约 1300 年. (An 古英语 word for this was sweotol "distinct, clear, evident.") 义为 "free from encumbrance," 似乎 nautical, developed 约 1500 年. Phrase in the clear attested 自 1715 年起. Clear-sighted 始于 1580 年代 (clear-eyed 始于 1529 年代); clear-headed 始于 1709 年.

example.en: His instructions were clear enough for even beginners to follow without help.

entries.etymology:
"man ordained in the ministry," c. 1200, from Old English cleric and Old French clerc "clergyman, priest; scholar, student," both from Church Latin clericus "a priest," noun use of adjective meaning "priestly, belonging to the clerus" (see cleric).

Modern bureaucratic usage is a reminder of the dark ages when clergy alone could read and write and were employed for that skill by secular authorities. In late Old English the word can mean "king's scribe; keeper of accounts;" by c. 1200 clerk took on a secondary sense in Middle English (as the cognate word did in Old French) of "anyone who can read or write." This led to the sense "assistant in a business" (c. 1500), originally a keeper of accounts, later, especially in American English, "a retail salesman" (1790). Related: Clerkship.

In late 古英语 the word can mean "king's scribe; keeper of accounts;" by 约 1200 年 clerk took on a secondary sense in 中古英语 (as the 同源 word did in 古法语) of "anyone who can read or write." This led to the sense "assistant in a business" (约 1500 年), 原义为 a keeper of accounts, later, 尤指 in American English, "a retail salesman" (1790 年). 同源词：Clerkship.

entries.etymology:
1580s, "handy, dexterous," apparently from East Anglian dialectal cliver "expert at seizing," perhaps from East Frisian klüfer "skillful," or Norwegian dialectic klover "ready, skillful," and perhaps influenced by Old English clifer "claw, hand" (early usages seem to refer to dexterity). Or perhaps akin to Old Norse kleyfr "easy to split" and from a root related to cleave "to split." Extension to intellect is first recorded 1704.

The meaning has narrowed since, but clever also often in old use and dialect meant "well-shaped, attractive-looking" and in 19c. American English sometimes "good-natured, agreeable." Related: Cleverly; cleverness.

Or 或许 akin to 古北欧语 kleyfr "easy to split" and 源自 a root related to cleave "to split." Extension to intellect is 首见于 1704 年. The 意为 has narrowed 自, but clever also 常 in old use and dialect meant "well-shaped, attractive-looking" and in 19 世纪 American English 有时 "good-natured, agreeable." 同源词：Cleverly; cleverness.

example.en: She came up with a clever solution to fix the broken system.

entries.etymology: 1580s, of imitative origin (compare Dutch and East Frisian klikken "to click; Old French clique "tick of a clock"). The figurative sense, in reference usually to persons, "hit it off at once, become friendly upon meeting" is from 1915, perhaps based on the sound of a key in a lock. Related: Clicked; clicking.

definitionLines: n. 顾客；委托人；当事人
entries.definition: n. 顾客；委托人；当事人
entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Anglo-French clyent (c. 1300), from Latin clientem (nominative cliens) "follower, retainer," perhaps a variant of present participle of cluere "listen, follow, obey" (see listen); or, more likely, from clinare "to incline, bend," from suffixed form of PIE root *klei- "to lean" (see lean (v.)).

The ground sense apparently is of one who leans on another for protection. In ancient Rome, a plebeian under protection of a patrician (called patronus in this relationship; see patron); in English originally "a lawyer's customer," by c. 1600 extended to any customer.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 clyent (约 1300 年), 源自 拉丁语 clientem (主格 cliens) "follower, retainer," 或许 a 为 … 的变体 为 … 的现在分词 cluere "listen, follow, obey" （参见 listen); or, more likely, 源自 clinare "to incline, bend," 源自 suffixed form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *klei- "to lean" （参见 lean （动）). The ground sense 似乎 is of one who leans on another for protection. In ancient Rome, a plebeian under protection of a patrician (called patronus in this relationship; 参见 patron); in English 原义为 "a lawyer's customer," by 约 1600 年 extended to any customer.

example.en: The lawyer met with her client to discuss the terms of the contract.

entries.etymology:
Old English clif "rock, promontory, steep slope," from Proto-Germanic *kliban (source also of Old Saxon clif, Old Norse klif, Middle Dutch klippe, Dutch klip, Old High German klep, German Klippe "cliff, promontory, steep rock").

Clift has been a variant spelling since 15c. and was common in early Modern English, influenced by or merged with clift, a variant of cleft (n.). Cliff-dweller first attested 1889, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 clif "rock, promontory, steep slope," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *kliban (source also of 古撒克逊语 clif, 古北欧语 klif, Middle 荷兰语 klippe, 荷兰语 klip, 古高地德语 klep, 德语 Klippe "cliff, promontory, steep rock"). Clift has been a variant spelling 自 15 世纪 and was common in early 现代英语, influenced by or merged with clift, a 为 … 的变体 cleft （名）. Cliff-dweller 最早见于 1889 年, American English.

example.en: Hikers were warned to stay away from the edge of the cliff.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "horizontal zone of the earth," Scottish, from Old French climat "region, part of the earth," from Latin clima (genitive climatis) "region; slope of the Earth," from Greek klima "region, zone," literally "an inclination, slope," thus "slope of the Earth from equator to pole," from root of klinein "to slope, to lean" (see lean (v.)).

The angle of sun on the slope of the Earth's surface defined the zones assigned by early geographers. Early references in English, however, are in astrology works, as each of the seven (then) climates was held to be under the influence of one of the planets. Shift from "region" to "weather associated with a region" perhaps began in Middle English, certainly by c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "horizontal zone of the earth," 苏格兰语, 源自 古法语 climat "region, part of the earth," 源自 拉丁语 clima (属格 climatis) "region; slope of the Earth," 源自 希腊语 klima "region, zone," 字面义为 "an inclination, slope," thus "slope of the Earth from equator to pole," 源自 root of klinein "to slope, to lean" （参见 lean （动）). The angle of sun on the slope of the Earth's surface defined the zones assigned by early geographers. Early references in English, however, are in astrology works, as each of the seven (之后) climates was held to be under the influence of one of the planets. Shift 源自 "region" to "weather associated with a region" 或许 began in 中古英语, certainly by 约 1600 年.

example.en: Scientists warn that the climate crisis threatens all life on Earth.
example.zh: 科学家警告说，气候危机威胁着地球上的所有生命。

entries.etymology:
1580s, in the rhetorical sense (a chain of reasoning in graduating steps from weaker to stronger), from Late Latin climax (genitive climacis), from Greek klimax "propositions rising in effectiveness," literally "ladder," from root of klinein "to slope," from PIE root *klei- "to lean" (see lean (v.)).

The rhetorical meaning evolved in English through "series of steps by which a goal is achieved," to "escalating steps," to (1789) "high point of intensity or development," a usage credited by the OED to "popular ignorance." The meaning "sexual orgasm" is recorded by 1880 (also in terms such as climax of orgasm), said to have been promoted from c. 1900 by birth-control pioneer Marie Stopes (1880-1958) and others as a more accessible word than orgasm (n.).

The rhetorical 意为 evolved in English through "series of steps by which a goal is achieved," to "escalating steps," to (1789 年) "high point of intensity or development," a usage credited by the OED to "popular ignorance." The 意为 "sexual orgasm" is recorded 截至 1880 年 (also in terms such as climax of orgasm), said to have been promoted 源自 约 1900 年 by birth-control pioneer Marie Stopes (1880 年-1958 年) and others 作为 more accessible word than orgasm （名）.

entries.etymology: Old English climban "raise oneself using hands and feet; rise gradually, ascend; make an ascent of" (past tense clamb, past participle clumben, clumbe), from West Germanic *klimban "go up by clinging" (source also of Dutch klimmen "to climb," Old High German klimban, German klimmen). A strong verb in Old English, weak by 16c. Most other Germanic languages long ago dropped the -b. Meaning "to mount as if by climbing" is from mid-14c. Figurative sense of "rise slowly by effort" is from mid-13c. Related: Climbed; climbing.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 climban "raise oneself using hands and feet; rise gradually, ascend; make an ascent of" (past tense clamb, past participle clumben, clumbe), 源自 West 日耳曼语 *klimban "go up by clinging" (source also of 荷兰语 klimmen "to climb," 古高地德语 klimban, 德语 klimmen). A strong 动词 in 古英语, weak by 16 世纪 Most other 日耳曼语 languages long ago dropped the -b. 义为 "to mount as if by climbing" 始于 14 世纪中期 Figurative 语义 "rise slowly by effort" 始于 13 世纪中期 同源词：Climbed; climbing.

entries.etymology:
Old English clingan "hold fast, adhere closely; congeal, shrivel" (strong verb, past tense clang, past participle clungen), from Proto-Germanic *klingg- (source also of Danish klynge "to cluster;" Old High German klinga "narrow gorge;" Old Norse klengjask "press onward;" Danish klinke, Dutch klinken "to clench;" German Klinke "latch").

The main sense shifted in Middle English to "adhere to" (something else), "stick together." Of persons in embrace, c. 1600. Figuratively (to hopes, outmoded ideas, etc.), from 1580s. Of clothes from 1792. Related: Clung; clinging.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 clingan "hold fast, adhere closely; congeal, shrivel" (strong 动词, past tense clang, past participle clungen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *klingg- (source also of Danish klynge "to cluster;" 古高地德语 klinga "narrow gorge;" 古北欧语 klengjask "press onward;" Danish klinke, 荷兰语 klinken "to clench;" 德语 Klinke "latch"). The main sense shifted in 中古英语 to "adhere to" (something else), "stick together." Of persons in embrace, 约 1600 年. Figuratively (to hopes, outmoded ideas, etc.), 源自 1580 年代. Of clothes 自 1792 年起. 同源词：Clung; clinging.

example.en: The frightened child clung to her mother and refused to let go.

entries.etymology:
1620s, from French clinique (17c.), from Latin clinicus "physician that visits patients in their beds," from Greek klinike (techne) "(practice) at the sickbed," from klinikos "of the bed," from kline "bed, couch, that on which one lies," from suffixed form of PIE root *kli- "lean, slope" (see lean (v.)).

Originally in English "bedridden person;" sense of "hospital" is 1884, from German Klinik in this sense, itself from French clinique, via the notion of "bedside medical education." The modern sense is thus reversed from the classical, when the "clinic" came to the patient. General sense of "conference for group instruction in something" is from 1919.
entries.etymologyZh: 1620 年代, 源自 法语 clinique (17 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 clinicus "physician that visits patients in their beds," 源自 希腊语 klinike (techne) "(practice) at the sickbed," 源自 klinikos "of the bed," 源自 kline "bed, couch, that on which one lies," 源自 suffixed form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *kli- "lean, slope" （参见 lean （动）). Originally in English "bedridden person;" 语义 "hospital" is 1884 年, 源自 德语 Klinik in this sense, itself 源自 法语 clinique, 经由 the 概念 "bedside medical education." The modern sense is thus reversed 源自 classical, when the "clinic" came to the patient. General 语义 "conference for group instruction in something" 始于 1919 年.

entries.etymology: 1780, "pertaining to hospital patients or hospital care," from clinic + -al (2). Meaning "coldly dispassionate" (like a medical report) is recorded from 1928. Related: Clinically.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "to shut, cover in," from Old French clos- (past participle stem of clore "to shut, to cut off from"), 12c., from Latin clausus, past participle of claudere "to shut, close; to block up, make inaccessible; put an end to; shut in, enclose, confine" (always -clusus, -cludere in compounds).

The Latin word might be from the possible PIE root *klau- "hook, peg, crooked or forked branch" (used as a bar or bolt in primitive structures); source also of Latin clavis "key," clavus "nail," claustrum "bar, bolt, barrier," claustra "dam, wall, barricade, stronghold;" Greek kleidos (genitive) "bar, bolt, key," klobos "cage;" Old Irish clo "nail," Middle Irish clithar "hedge, fence;" Old Church Slavonic ključi "hook, key," ključiti "shut;" Lithuanian kliuti "to catch, be caught on," kliaudziu "check, hinder," kliuvu "clasp, hang;" Old High German sliozan "shut," German schließen "to shut," Schlüssel "key."

Also partly from Old English beclysan "close in, shut up." Intransitive sense "become shut" is from late 14c. Meaning "draw near to" is from 1520s. Intransitive meaning "draw together, come together" is from 1550s, hence the idea in military verbal phrase close ranks (mid-17c.), later with figurative extensions. Meaning "bring to an end, finish" is from c. 1400; intransitive sense "come to an end" is from 1826. Of stock prices, from 1860. Meaning "bring together the parts of" (a book, etc.) is from 1560s. Related: Closed; closing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "to shut, cover in," 源自 古法语 clos- (past participle stem of clore "to shut, to cut off from"), 12 世纪, 源自 拉丁语 clausus, 为 … 的过去分词 claudere "to shut, close; to block up, make inaccessible; put an end to; shut in, enclose, confine" (always -clusus, -cludere in compounds). The 拉丁语 word might be 源自 possible 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *klau- "hook, peg, crooked or forked branch" (used 作为 bar or bolt in primitive structures); source also of 拉丁语 clavis "key," clavus "nail," claustrum "bar, bolt, barrier," claustra "dam, wall, barricade, stronghold;" 希腊语 kleidos (属格) "bar, bolt, key," klobos "cage;" Old 爱尔兰语 clo "nail," Middle 爱尔兰语 clithar "hedge, fence;" Old Church Slavonic ključi "hook, key," ključiti "shut;" Lithuanian kliuti "to catch, be caught on," kliaudziu "check, hinder," kliuvu "clasp, hang;" 古高地德语 sliozan "shut," 德语 schließen "to shut," Schlüssel "key." Also partly 源自 古英语 beclysan "close in, shut up." Intransitive sense "become shut" 始于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "draw near to" 始于 1520 年代. Intransitive 意为 "draw together, come together" 始于 1550 年代, hence the idea in military verbal phrase close ranks (17 世纪中期), later with figurative extensions. 义为 "bring to an end, finish" 始于 约 1400 年; intransitive sense "come to an end" 始于 1826 年. Of stock prices, 自 1860 年起. 义为 "bring together the parts of" (a book, etc.) 始于 1560 年代. 同源词：Closed; closing.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Old French closet "small enclosure, private room," diminutive of clos "enclosure," from Latin clausum "closed space, enclosure, confinement," from neuter past participle of claudere "to shut" (see close (v.)). In Matt. vi:6 it renders Latin cubiculum "bedchamber, bedroom," Greek tamieion "chamber, inner chamber, secret room;" thus originally in English "a private room for study or prayer." Modern sense of "small side-room for storage" is first recorded 1610s.

The adjective is from 1680s, "private, secluded;" meaning "secret, unknown" recorded from 1952, first of alcoholism, but by 1970s used principally of homosexuality; the phrase come out of the closet "admit something openly" first recorded 1963, and lent new meanings to the word out.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 closet "small enclosure, private room," 为 … 的指小形式 clos "enclosure," 源自 拉丁语 clausum "closed space, enclosure, confinement," 源自 neuter 为 … 的过去分词 claudere "to shut" （参见 close （动）). In Matt. vi:6 it renders 拉丁语 cubiculum "bedchamber, bedroom," 希腊语 tamieion "chamber, inner chamber, secret room;" thus 原义为 in English "a private room for study or prayer." 现代 语义 "small side-room for storage" is 首见于 1610 年代. The 形容词 始于 1680 年代, "private, secluded;" 意为 "secret, unknown" recorded 自 1952 年起, first of alcoholism, but by 1970 年代 used principally of homosexuality; the phrase come out of the closet "admit something openly" 首见于 1963 年, and lent new meanings to the word out.

entries.etymology: Old English claþ "a cloth, sail, cloth covering, woven or felted material to wrap around one," hence, also, "garment," from Proto-Germanic *kalithaz (source also of Old Frisian klath "cloth," Middle Dutch cleet, Dutch kleed "garment, dress," Middle High German kleit, German Kleid "garment"), of obscure origin. As an adjective from 1590s. The cloth "the clerical profession" is from 17c. in reference to characteristic dress.
