entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "physical strength," from Old French force "force, strength; courage, fortitude; violence, power, compulsion" (12c.), from Vulgar Latin *fortia (source also of Old Spanish forzo, Spanish fuerza, Italian forza), noun use of neuter plural of Latin fortis "strong, mighty; firm, steadfast; brave, bold" (see fort).

Meanings "power to convince the mind" and "power exerted against will or consent" are from mid-14c. Meaning "body of armed men, a military organization" first recorded late 14c. (also in Old French). Physics sense is from 1660s; force field attested by 1920. Related: Forces.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "physical strength," 源自 古法语 force "force, strength; courage, fortitude; violence, power, compulsion" (12 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *fortia (source also of Old 西班牙语 forzo, 西班牙语 fuerza, 意大利语 forza), 为 … 的名词用法 neuter 为 … 的复数 拉丁语 fortis "strong, mighty; firm, steadfast; brave, bold" （参见 fort). Meanings "power to convince the mind" and "power exerted against will or consent" 始于 14 世纪中期 义为 "body of armed men, a military organization" 首见于 14 世纪晚期 (also in 古法语). Physics sense 始于 1660 年代; force field attested 截至 1920 年. 同源词：Forces.

example.en: The tight deadline forced him to work through the night without any rest.
example.zh: 紧迫的截止日期迫使他彻夜工作，没有休息。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "to scheme," from fore- "before" + casten in the sense of "contrive, plan, prepare" (late 14c.; see cast (v.)). Meaning "predict events" first attested late 15c. (cast (v.) "to perceive, notice" is from late 14c.). Related: Forecasting.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "to scheme," 源自 fore- "before" + casten in the 语义 "contrive, plan, prepare" (14 世纪晚期; 参见 cast （动）). 义为 "predict events" 最早见于 15 世纪晚期 (cast （动） "to perceive, notice" 始于 14 世纪晚期). 同源词：Forecasting.

example.en: The meteorologist issued a forecast of heavy snow for the weekend.
example.zh: 气象学家发布了本周末大雪的预报。

entries.etymology: Middle English forhed, from Old English forheafod "forehead, brow," from fore- + heafod (see head (n.)). Similar formation in Dutch voorhoofd, German Vorhaupt, Danish forhoved.
entries.etymologyZh: 中古英语 forhed, 源自 古英语 forheafod "forehead, brow," 源自 fore- + heafod （参见 head （名）). Similar formation in 荷兰语 voorhoofd, 德语 Vorhaupt, Danish forhoved.

definitionLines: a.外国的，对外的；外国产的， 外国来的
entries.definition: a.外国的，对外的；外国产的， 外国来的
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, ferren, foran, foreyne, in reference to places, "outside the boundaries of a country;" of persons, "born in another country," from Old French forain "strange, foreign; outer, external, outdoor; remote, out-of-the-way" (12c.), from Medieval Latin foraneus "on the outside, exterior," from Latin foris (adv.) "outside," literally "out of doors," related to foris "a door," from PIE *dhwor-ans-, from root *dhwer- "door, doorway" (see door).

English spelling altered 17c., perhaps by influence of reign, sovereign. Sense of "alien to one's nature, not connected with, extraneous" attested late 14c. Meaning "pertaining to another country" (as in foreign policy) is from 1610s. Replaced native fremd. Related: Foreignness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, ferren, foran, foreyne, in reference to places, "outside the boundaries of a country;" of persons, "born in another country," 源自 古法语 forain "strange, foreign; outer, external, outdoor; remote, out-of-the-way" (12 世纪), 源自 中古拉丁语 foraneus "on the outside, exterior," 源自 拉丁语 foris （副） "outside," 字面义为 "out of doors," related to foris "a door," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *dhwor-ans-, 源自 root *dhwer- "door, doorway" （参见 door). English spelling altered 17 世纪, 或许 by influence of reign, sovereign. 义为 "alien to one's nature, not connected with, extraneous" attested 14 世纪晚期 义为 "pertaining to another country" (as in foreign policy) 始于 1610 年代. Replaced 本族 fremd. 同源词：Foreignness.

example.en: She has a talent for learning foreign languages quickly and accurately.
example.zh: 她有快速而准确地学习外语的天赋。

entries.etymology:
early 15c., foreyner; see foreign + -er (1).

In American English from 1620s through mid-19c., however, it was used of a person from a different colony or state. Earlier as a noun in English was simple foreign (early 14c.), probably from Old French, which used the adjective as a noun meaning "foreigner;" also "outskirts; the outside world; latrine, privy." Spelling furriner, representing pronunciation, is from 1832, originally in Irish dialect pieces but by 1840s picked up by American dialect writers (Thomas Chandler Haliburton).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, foreyner; 参见 foreign + -er (1). In American English 源自 1620 年代 through 19 世纪中期, however, it was used of a person 源自 a different colony or state. Earlier 作名词时 in English was simple foreign (14 世纪初), 可能 源自 古法语, which used the 形容词 作名词时 意为 "foreigner;" also "outskirts; the outside world; latrine, privy." Spelling furriner, representing pronunciation, 始于 1832 年, 原义为 in 爱尔兰语 dialect pieces but by 1840 年代 picked up by American dialect writers (Thomas Chandler Haliburton).

example.en: The city has become a popular destination for foreigner tourists in recent years.
example.zh: 近年来，这座城市已成为外国游客的热门目的地。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from fore- + runner. Middle English literal rendition of Latin praecursor, used in reference to John the Baptist as the forerunner of Christ. Old English had foreboda and forerynel.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 fore- + runner. 中古英语 literal rendition of 拉丁语 praecursor, used in reference to John the Baptist as the forerunner of Christ. 古英语 had foreboda and forerynel.

entries.etymology: Old English foreseon "have a premonition," from fore- "before" + seon "to see, see ahead" (see see (v.)). Perhaps modeled on Latin providere. Related: Foresaw; foreseeing; foreseen. Similar formation in Dutch voorzien, German vorsehen.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 foreseon "have a premonition," 源自 fore- "before" + seon "to see, see ahead" （参见 参见 （动）). Perhaps modeled on 拉丁语 providere. 同源词：Foresaw; foreseeing; foreseen. Similar formation in 荷兰语 voorzien, 德语 vorsehen.

definitionLines: n.先见，远见；预见；深谋远虑
entries.definition: n.先见，远见；预见；深谋远虑
entries.etymology: also fore-sight, early 14c., "insight obtained beforehand;" also "prudence," from fore- + sight (n.). Perhaps modeled on Latin providentia. Compare German Vorsicht "attention, caution, cautiousness."
entries.etymologyZh: also fore-sight, 14 世纪初, "insight obtained beforehand;" also "prudence," 源自 fore- + sight （名）. Perhaps modeled on 拉丁语 providentia. 对比 德语 Vorsicht "attention, caution, cautiousness."

entries.etymology:
late 13c., "extensive tree-covered district," especially one set aside for royal hunting and under the protection of the king, from Old French forest "forest, wood, woodland" (Modern French forêt), probably ultimately from Late Latin/Medieval Latin forestem silvam "the outside woods," a term from the Capitularies of Charlemagne denoting "the royal forest." This word comes to Medieval Latin, perhaps via a Germanic source akin to Old High German forst, from Latin foris "outside" (see foreign). If so, the sense is "beyond the park," the park (Latin parcus; see park (n.)) being the main or central fenced woodland.

Another theory traces it through Medieval Latin forestis, originally "forest preserve, game preserve," from Latin forum in legal sense "court, judgment;" in other words "land subject to a ban" [Buck]. Replaced Old English wudu (see wood (n.)). Spanish and Portuguese floresta have been influenced by flor "flower."
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "extensive tree-covered district," 尤指 one set aside for royal hunting and under the protection of the king, 源自 古法语 forest "forest, wood, woodland" (现代法语 forêt), 可能 最终源自 晚期拉丁语/中古拉丁语 forestem silvam "the outside woods," a term 源自 Capitularies of Charlemagne denoting "the royal forest." This word comes to 中古拉丁语, 或许 经由 a 日耳曼语 source akin to 古高地德语 forst, 源自 拉丁语 foris "outside" （参见 foreign). If so, the sense is "beyond the park," the park (拉丁语 parcus; 参见 park （名）) being the main or central fenced woodland. Another theory traces it through 中古拉丁语 forestis, 原义为 "forest preserve, game preserve," 源自 拉丁语 forum in legal sense "court, judgment;" in other words "land subject to a ban" [Buck]. Replaced 古英语 wudu （参见 wood （名）). 西班牙语 and 葡萄牙语 floresta have been influenced by flor "flower."

example.en: Hundreds of species of birds live deep in the tropical forest.
example.zh: 数百种鸟类生活在热带雨林深处。

entries.etymology: late 14c., for ever; from for + ever. Often written as one word from late 17c. As a noun by 1858. Emphatic forevermore is from 1819.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, for ever; 源自 for + ever. Often written as one word 源自 17 世纪晚期 作名词时 截至 1858 年. Emphatic forevermore 始于 1819 年.

example.en: She promised to love him forever, no matter what happened.
example.zh: 她承诺无论发生什么都永远爱他。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "a smithy," from Old French forge "forge, smithy" (12c.), earlier faverge, from Latin fabrica "workshop, smith's shop," hence also "a trade, an industry;" also "a skillful production, a crafty device," from faber (genitive fabri) "workman in hard materials, smith" (see fabric). As the heating apparatus itself (a furnace fitted with a bellows), from late 15c. Forge-water (1725), in which heated iron has been dipped, was used popularly as a medicine in 18c.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "a smithy," 源自 古法语 forge "forge, smithy" (12 世纪), earlier faverge, 源自 拉丁语 fabrica "workshop, smith's shop," hence also "a trade, an industry;" also "a skillful production, a crafty device," 源自 faber (属格 fabri) "workman in hard materials, smith" （参见 fabric). As the heating apparatus itself (a furnace fitted with a bellows), 源自 15 世纪晚期 Forge-water (1725 年), in which heated iron has been dipped, was used popularly 作为 medicine in 18 世纪

example.en: The criminal had forged the signature on the legal documents.
example.zh: 罪犯伪造了法律文件上的签名。

entries.etymology: Old English forgietan "lose the power of recalling to the mind; fail to remember; neglect inadvertently," from for-, used here probably with privative force, "away, amiss, opposite" + gietan "to grasp" (see get). To "un-get," hence "to lose" from the mind. A common Germanic construction (compare Old Saxon fargetan, Old Frisian forjeta, Dutch vergeten, Old High German firgezzan, German vergessen "to forget"). The physical sense would be "to lose (one's) grip on," but that is not recorded in any historical Germanic language. Figurative sense of "lose care for" is from late 13c. Related: Forgetting; forgot; forgotten.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 forgietan "lose the power of recalling to the mind; fail to remember; neglect inadvertently," 源自 for-, used here 可能 with privative force, "away, amiss, opposite" + gietan "to grasp" （参见 get). To "un-get," hence "to lose" 源自 mind. A common 日耳曼语 construction (对比 古撒克逊语 fargetan, 古弗里西语 forjeta, 荷兰语 vergeten, 古高地德语 firgezzan, 德语 vergessen "to forget"). The physical sense would be "to lose (one's) grip on," but that is not recorded in any historical 日耳曼语 language. Figurative 语义 "lose care for" 始于 13 世纪晚期 同源词：Forgetting; forgot; forgotten.

example.en: Did you forget to bring the signed permission slip for the field trip?
example.zh: 你忘带野外考察的签名许可单了吗？

entries.etymology:
Old English forgiefan "give, grant, allow; remit (a debt), pardon (an offense)," also "give up" and "give in marriage" (past tense forgeaf, past participle forgifen); from for-, here probably "completely," + giefan "give" (see give (v.)).

The sense of "to give up desire or power to punish" (late Old English) is from use of such a compound as a Germanic loan-translation of Vulgar Latin *perdonare (Old Saxon fargeban, Dutch vergeven, German vergeben "to forgive," Gothic fragiban "to grant;" and see pardon (n.)). Related: Forgave; forgiven; forgiving.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 forgiefan "give, grant, allow; remit (a debt), pardon (an offense)," also "give up" and "give in marriage" (past tense forgeaf, past participle forgifen); 源自 for-, here 可能 "completely," + giefan "give" （参见 give （动）). The 语义 "to give up desire or power to punish" (late 古英语) 始于 use of such a 复合词 作为 日耳曼语 loan-translation of 通俗拉丁语 *perdonare (古撒克逊语 fargeban, 荷兰语 vergeven, 德语 vergeben "to forgive," Gothic fragiban "to grant;" and 参见 pardon （名）). 同源词：Forgave; forgiven; forgiving.

example.en: She finally found the strength to forgive him for his mistakes.
example.zh: 她终于鼓起勇气原谅了他的错误。

entries.etymology:
Old English forca, force "pitchfork, forked instrument, forked weapon," from a Germanic borrowing (Old Frisian forke, Dutch vork, Old Norse forkr, Danish fork) of Latin furca "pitchfork; fork used in cooking," a word of uncertain origin. Old English also had forcel "pitchfork." From c. 1200 as "forked stake or post" (as a gallows or prop).

Table forks are said to have been not used among the nobility in England until 15c. and not common until early 17c. The word is first attested in this sense in English in an inventory from 1430, probably from Old North French forque (Old French furche, Modern French fourche), from the Latin word. Of rivers, from 1753; of roads, from 1839. As a bicycle part from 1871. As a chess attack on two pieces simultaneously by one (usually a knight), it dates from 1650s. In old slang, forks "the two forefingers" is from 1812.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 forca, force "pitchfork, forked instrument, forked weapon," 源自 a 日耳曼语 borrowing (古弗里西语 forke, 荷兰语 vork, 古北欧语 forkr, Danish fork) of 拉丁语 furca "pitchfork; fork used in cooking," a word 来源存疑. 古英语 also had forcel "pitchfork." From 约 1200 年 as "forked stake or post" (作为 gallows or prop). Table forks are said to have been not used among the nobility in England until 15 世纪 and not common until 17 世纪初 The word is 最早见于 in this sense in English in an inventory 自 1430 年起, 可能 源自 Old North 法语 forque (古法语 furche, 现代法语 fourche), 源自 拉丁语 word. Of rivers, 自 1753 年起; of roads, 自 1839 年起. 作为 bicycle part 自 1871 年起. 作为 chess attack on two pieces simultaneously by one (通常 a knight), it dates 源自 1650 年代. In old 俚语, forks "the two forefingers" 始于 1812 年.

example.en: Turn left at the fork where the road splits into two.
example.zh: 在道路一分为二的岔口处左转。

definitionLines: n. 形状，形式，方式；类型，结 构；表格，格式
entries.definition: n. 形状，形式，方式；类型，结 构；表格，格式 vt.形成，构成，组成
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, forme, fourme, "semblance, image, likeness," from Old French forme, fourme, "physical form, appearance; pleasing looks; shape, image; way, manner" (12c.), from Latin forma "form, contour, figure, shape; appearance, looks; a fine form, beauty; an outline, a model, pattern, design; sort, kind condition," a word of unknown origin. One theory holds that it is from or cognate with Greek morphe "form, beauty, outward appearance" (see Morpheus) via Etruscan [Klein].

From c. 1300 as "physical shape (of something), contour, outline," of a person, "shape of the body;" also "appearance, likeness;" also "the imprint of an object." From c. 1300 as "correct or appropriate way of doing something; established procedure; traditional usage; formal etiquette." Mid-14c. as "instrument for shaping; a mould;" late 14c. as "way in which something is done," also "pattern of a manufactured object." Used widely from late 14c. in theology and Platonic philosophy with senses "archetype of a thing or class; Platonic essence of a thing; the formative principle." From c. 1300 in law, "a legal agreement; terms of agreement," later "a legal document" (mid-14c.). Meaning "a document with blanks to be filled in" is from 1855. From 1590s as "systematic or orderly arrangement;" from 1610s as "mere ceremony." From 1550s as "a class or rank at school" (from sense "a fixed course of study," late 14c.). Form-fitting (adj.) in reference to clothing is from 1893.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, forme, fourme, "semblance, image, likeness," 源自 古法语 forme, fourme, "physical form, appearance; pleasing looks; shape, image; way, manner" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 forma "form, contour, figure, shape; appearance, looks; a fine form, beauty; an outline, a model, pattern, design; sort, kind condition," a word 来源不详. One theory holds that it 始于 or 与 … 同源 希腊语 morphe "form, beauty, outward appearance" （参见 Morpheus) 经由 Etruscan [Klein]. From 约 1300 年 as "physical shape (of something), contour, outline," of a person, "shape of the body;" also "appearance, likeness;" also "the imprint of an object." From 约 1300 年 as "correct or appropriate way of doing something; established procedure; traditional usage; formal etiquette." Mid-14 世纪 as "instrument for shaping; a mould;" 14 世纪晚期 as "way in which something is done," also "pattern of a manufactured object." Used widely 源自 14 世纪晚期 in theology and Platonic philosophy with senses "archetype of a thing or class; Platonic essence of a thing; the formative principle." From 约 1300 年 in law, "a legal agreement; terms of agreement," later "a legal document" (14 世纪中期). 义为 "a document with blanks to be filled in" 始于 1855 年. From 1590 年代 as "systematic or orderly arrangement;" 源自 1610 年代 as "mere ceremony." From 1550 年代 as "a class or rank at school" (源自 sense "a fixed course of study," 14 世纪晚期). Form-fitting （形） in reference to clothing 始于 1893 年.

example.en: The government moved to form a new committee dedicated to environmental protection.
example.zh: 政府着手组建一个专门负责环境保护的新委员会。

definitionLines: a. 正式的；礼仪上的；形式的
entries.definition: a. 正式的；礼仪上的；形式的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "pertaining to form or arrangement;" also, in philosophy and theology, "pertaining to the form or essence of a thing," from Old French formal, formel "formal, constituent" (13c.) and directly from Latin formalis, from forma "a form, figure, shape" (see form (n.)). From early 15c. as "in due or proper form, according to recognized form," As a noun, c. 1600 (plural) "things that are formal;" as a short way to say formal dance, recorded by 1906 among U.S. college students.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "pertaining to form or arrangement;" also, in philosophy and theology, "pertaining to the form or essence of a thing," 源自 古法语 formal, formel "formal, constituent" (13 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 formalis, 源自 forma "a form, figure, shape" （参见 form （名）). From 15 世纪初 as "in due or proper form, according to recognized form," 作名词时, 约 1600 年 (plural) "things that are formal;" 作为 short way to say formal dance, recorded 截至 1906 年 among U.S. college students.

example.en: Guests are expected to wear formal attire at the ceremony.
example.zh: 出席典礼的来宾须着正式服装。

definitionLines: vt. 安排……的格局（或规格），
entries.definition: n. 形式，格式 vt. 安排……的格局（或规格）， ［计］格式化（磁盘）
entries.etymology: 1840, "shape and size" (of a book), via French format (18c.), ultimately from Modern Latin liber formatus "a book formed" in a certain shape and size, from past participle of formare "to form," from forma "form, shape" (see form (n.)). Extended to computers by 1955.
entries.etymologyZh: 1840 年, "shape and size" (of a book), 经由 法语 format (18 世纪), 最终源自 现代 拉丁语 liber formatus "a book formed" in a certain shape and size, 源自 为 … 的过去分词 formare "to form," 源自 forma "form, shape" （参见 form （名）). Extended to computers 截至 1955 年.

example.en: Please submit your report in PDF format to ensure compatibility across devices.
example.zh: 请以PDF格式提交报告，以确保跨设备兼容性。

entries.definition: a.在前的，以前的 n.前者
entries.etymology: "earlier in time," mid-12c., comparative of forme "first, earliest in time or order," from Old English forma "first," from Proto-Germanic *fruma-, *furma-, from PIE *pre-mo-, suffixed (superlative) form of root *per- (1) "forward, through; before; first" (see per). Probably patterned on formest (see foremost); it is an unusual case of a comparative formed from a superlative (the Old English -m is a superlative suffix). As "first of two," 1580s.
entries.etymologyZh: "earlier in time," 12 世纪中期, comparative of forme "first, earliest in time or order," 源自 古英语 forma "first," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *fruma-, *furma-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *pre-mo-, suffixed (superlative) form of root *per- (1) "forward, through; before; first" （参见 per). Probably patterned on formest （参见 foremost); it is an unusual case of a comparative formed 源自 a superlative (the 古英语 -m is a superlative suffix). As "first of two," 1580 年代.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "causing fear," from Middle French formidable (15c.), from Latin formidabilis "causing fear, terrible," from formidare "to fear," from formido "fearfulness, fear, terror, dread." Sense has softened somewhat over time, in the direction of "so great (in strength, size, etc.) as to discourage effort." Related: Formidably.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "causing fear," 源自 中古法语 formidable (15 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 formidabilis "causing fear, terrible," 源自 formidare "to fear," 源自 formido "fearfulness, fear, terror, dread." Sense has softened somewhat over time, in the direction of "so great (in strength, size, etc.) as to discourage effort." 同源词：Formidably.

entries.etymology: 1630s, "words used in a ceremony or ritual" (earlier as a Latin word in English), from Latin formula "form, draft, contract, regulation;" in law, "a rule, method;" literally "small form," diminutive of forma "form" (see form (n.)). Modern sense is colored by Carlyle's use (1837) of the word in a sense of "rule slavishly followed without understanding" [OED]. From 1706 as "a prescription, a recipe;" mathematical use is from 1796; chemistry sense is from 1842. In motor racing, "class or specification of a car" (usually by engine size), 1927.
entries.etymologyZh: 1630 年代, "words used in a ceremony or ritual" (earlier 作为 拉丁语 word in English), 源自 拉丁语 formula "form, draft, contract, regulation;" in law, "a rule, method;" 字面义为 "small form," 为 … 的指小形式 forma "form" （参见 form （名）). 现代 sense is colored by Carlyle's use (1837 年) of the word in a 语义 "rule slavishly followed without understanding" [OED]. entries.definition: vt. 用公式表示；系统地阐述或 提出
entries.etymology: "to express in a formula," 1837, from formula + -ate (2). Won out over formulize (1842); formularize (1845). Related: Formulated; formulating.
entries.etymologyZh: "to express in a formula," 1837 年, 源自 formula + -ate (2). Won out over formulize (1842 年); formularize (1845 年). 同源词：Formulated; formulating.

example.en: The committee needs to formulate a clear strategy before the deadline.
example.zh: 委员会需要在截止日期前制定出一套明确的策略。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "fortified place, stronghold," from Old French fort "fort, fortress; strong man," noun use of adjective meaning "strong, stout, sturdy; hard, severe, difficult; hard to understand; dreadful, terrible; fortified" (10c.), from Latin fortis "strong, mighty; firm, steadfast; brave, spirited," from Old Latin forctus, possibly from PIE root *bhergh- (2) "high, elevated," with derivatives referring to hills and hill-forts (see barrow (n.2)). Or possibly from *dher- (2) "to hold firmly, support." Figurative use of hold the fort attested from 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "fortified place, stronghold," 源自 古法语 fort "fort, fortress; strong man," 为 … 的名词用法 形容词 意为 "strong, stout, sturdy; hard, severe, difficult; hard to understand; dreadful, terrible; fortified" (10 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 fortis "strong, mighty; firm, steadfast; brave, spirited," 源自 Old 拉丁语 forctus, possibly 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhergh- (2) "high, elevated," with derivatives referring to hills and hill-forts （参见 barrow (n.2)). Or possibly 源自 *dher- (2) "to hold firmly, support." Figurative use of hold the fort attested 源自 1590 年代.

entries.etymology: Old English forð "forward, onward, further; continually;" as a preposition, "during," perfective of fore, from Proto-Germanic *furtha- "forward" (source also of Old Frisian, Old Saxon forth "forward, onward," Old Norse forð, Dutch voort, German fort), from extended form of PIE root *per- (1) "forward, through" (see per). The construction in and so forth was in Old English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 forð "forward, onward, further; continually;" 作为 preposition, "during," perfective of fore, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *furtha- "forward" (source also of 古弗里西语, 古撒克逊语 forth "forward, onward," 古北欧语 forð, 荷兰语 voort, 德语 fort), 源自 extended form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *per- (1) "forward, through" （参见 per). The construction in and so forth was in 古英语.

entries.etymology: "about to happen or appear," late 15c., present participle adjective from Middle English forthcomen, from Old English forðcuman "to come forth, come to pass;" see forth + come (v.). Meaning "informative, responsive" is from 1835. A once-common verb formation; English also had forthbring, forthcall, forthdo, forthgo, forthpass, forthset, all now obsolete.
entries.etymologyZh: "about to happen or appear," 15 世纪晚期, present participle 形容词 源自 中古英语 forthcomen, 源自 古英语 forðcuman "to come forth, come to pass;" 参见 forth + come （动）. 义为 "informative, responsive" 始于 1835 年. A once-common 动词 formation; English also had forthbring, forthcall, forthdo, forthgo, forthpass, forthset, all 今废.

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Middle French fortitude, from Latin fortitudo "strength, force, firmness, manliness," from fortis "strong, brave" (see fort).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 中古法语 fortitude, 源自 拉丁语 fortitudo "strength, force, firmness, manliness," 源自 fortis "strong, brave" （参见 fort).

entries.etymology: "period of two weeks," 17c. contraction of Middle English fourteniht, from Old English feowertyne niht, literally "fourteen nights," preserving the ancient Germanic custom of reckoning by nights (mentioned by Tacitus in "Germania" xi). Related: Fortnightly.
entries.etymologyZh: "period of two weeks," 17 世纪 contraction of 中古英语 fourteniht, 源自 古英语 feowertyne niht, 字面义为 "fourteen nights," preserving the ancient 日耳曼语 custom of reckoning by nights (mentioned by Tacitus in "Germania" xi). 同源词：Fortnightly.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "having good fortune; bringing good fortune," from Latin fortunatus "prospered, prosperous; lucky, happy," past participle of fortunare "to make prosperous," from fortuna (see fortune). Fortunate Islands "mythical abode of the blessed dead, in the Western Ocean" (early 15c.; late 14c. as Ilondes of fortune) translates Latin Fortunatae Insulae.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "having good fortune; bringing good fortune," 源自 拉丁语 fortunatus "prospered, prosperous; lucky, happy," 为 … 的过去分词 fortunare "to make prosperous," 源自 fortuna （参见 fortune). Fortunate Islands "mythical abode of the blessed dead, in the Western Ocean" (15 世纪初; 14 世纪晚期 as Ilondes of fortune) translates 拉丁语 Fortunatae Insulae.

example.en: We were fortunate to find a parking spot right in front of the venue.
example.zh: 我们很幸运，在场馆正门前找到了一个停车位。

entries.etymology: "by (good) fortune," 1540s, from fortunate + -ly (2).
entries.etymologyZh: "by (good) fortune," 1540 年代, 源自 fortunate + -ly (2).

example.en: Fortunately, the fire was discovered early and no one was hurt.
example.zh: 幸运的是，火灾被早早发现，没有人受伤。

definitionLines: n. 命运，运气；财富，财产
entries.definition: n. 命运，运气；财富，财产
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "chance, luck as a force in human affairs," from Old French fortune "lot, good fortune, misfortune" (12c.), from Latin fortuna "chance, fate, good luck," from fors (genitive fortis) "chance, luck," possibly ultimately from PIE root *bher- (1) "to carry" (see infer). If so, the sense might be "that which is brought."

Sense of "owned wealth" is first found in Spenser; probably it evolved from senses of "one's condition or standing in life," hence "position as determined by wealth," then "wealth, large estate" itself. Often personified as a goddess; her wheel betokens vicissitude. Soldier of fortune first attested 1660s. Fortune 500 "most profitable American companies" is 1955, from the list published annually in "Fortune" magazine. Fortune-hunter "one who seeks to marry for wealth" is from 1680s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "chance, luck as a force in human affairs," 源自 古法语 fortune "lot, good fortune, misfortune" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 fortuna "chance, fate, good luck," 源自 fors (属格 fortis) "chance, luck," possibly 最终源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bher- (1) "to carry" （参见 infer). If so, the sense might be "that which is brought." 义为 "owned wealth" is first found in Spenser; 可能 it evolved 源自 senses of "one's condition or standing in life," hence "position as determined by wealth," 之后 "wealth, large estate" itself. Often personified 作为 goddess; her wheel betokens vicissitude. Soldier of fortune 最早见于 1660 年代. Fortune 500 "most profitable American companies" is 1955 年, 源自 list published annually in "Fortune" magazine. Fortune-hunter "one who seeks to marry for wealth" 始于 1680 年代.

example.en: He made a fortune by investing in technology stocks early.
example.zh: 他通过早期投资科技股赚取了大量财富。

entries.etymology:
early 12c., feowerti, from Old English feowertig, Northumbrian feuortig "forty," from feower "four" (see four) + tig "group of ten" (see -ty (1)). Compare Old Saxon fiwartig, Old Frisian fiuwertich, Dutch veertig, Old High German fiorzug, German vierzig, Old Norse fjorir tigir, Gothic fidwor tigjus.

Forty winks "short sleep" is attested from 1821; in early use associated with, and perhaps coined by, English eccentric and lifestyle reformer William Kitchiner M.D. (1775-1827). Forty-niner in U.S. history was an adventurer to California (usually from one of the eastern states) in search of fortune during the gold rush of 1849.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪初, feowerti, 源自 古英语 feowertig, Northumbrian feuortig "forty," 源自 feower "four" （参见 four) + tig "group of ten" （参见 -ty (1)). 对比 古撒克逊语 fiwartig, 古弗里西语 fiuwertich, 荷兰语 veertig, 古高地德语 fiorzug, 德语 vierzig, 古北欧语 fjorir tigir, Gothic fidwor tigjus. Forty winks "short sleep" 见于 1821 年; in early use associated with, and 或许 coined by, English eccentric and lifestyle reformer William Kitchiner M.D. (1775 年-1827 年). Forty-niner in U.S. history was an adventurer to California (通常 源自 one of the eastern states) in search of fortune during the gold rush of 1849 年.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "place of assembly in ancient Rome," from Latin forum "marketplace, open space, public place," apparently akin to foris, foras "out of doors, outside," from PIE root *dhwer- "door, doorway" (see door). Sense of "assembly, place for public discussion" first recorded 1680s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "place of assembly in ancient Rome," 源自 拉丁语 forum "marketplace, open space, public place," 似乎 akin to foris, foras "out of doors, outside," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *dhwer- "door, doorway" （参见 door). 义为 "assembly, place for public discussion" 首见于 1680 年代.

example.en: The university held an open forum on climate policy last Friday.
example.zh: 大学上周五举行了一场关于气候政策的公开论坛。

definitionLines: a.前部的，向前的；进步的，激 进的
entries.definition: a.前部的，向前的；进步的，激 进的 ad. 向前，前进；向将来 vt. 转交，转递
entries.etymology: Old English forewearde "toward the front, in front; toward the future; at the beginning;" see fore + -ward. Adjectival sense of "early" is from 1520s; that of "presumptuous" is attested from 1560s. The Old English adjective meant "inclined to the front; early; former."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 forewearde "toward the front, in front; toward the future; at the beginning;" 参见 fore + -ward. Adjectival 语义 "early" 始于 1520 年代; that of "presumptuous" 见于 1560 年代. The 古英语 形容词 meant "inclined to the front; early; former."

example.en: She stepped forward to accept the award on behalf of the team.
example.zh: 她上前代表团队领奖。

entries.etymology:
1610s, "any thing dug up;" 1650s (adj.) "obtained by digging" (of coal, salt, etc.), from French fossile (16c.), from Latin fossilis "dug up," from fossus, past participle of fodere "to dig," from PIE root *bhedh- "to dig, pierce."

Restricted noun sense of "geological remains of a plant or animal" is from 1736 (the adjective in the sense "pertaining to fossils" is from 1660s); slang meaning "old person" first recorded 1859. Fossil fuel (1833) preserves the earlier, broader sense.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "any thing dug up;" 1650 年代 （形） "obtained by digging" (of coal, salt, etc.), 源自 法语 fossile (16 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 fossilis "dug up," 源自 fossus, 为 … 的过去分词 fodere "to dig," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhedh- "to dig, pierce." Restricted 名词 语义 "geological remains of a plant or animal" 始于 1736 年 (the 形容词 in the sense "pertaining to fossils" 始于 1660 年代); 俚语 意为 "old person" 首见于 1859 年. Fossil fuel (1833 年) preserves the earlier, broader sense.

example.en: The museum's new exhibit features a rare dinosaur fossil.
example.zh: 博物馆的新展览展出了一块珍稀恐龙化石。

entries.etymology: "discovered," late 14c., past participle adjective from find (v.). Expression and found attached to the wages or charges in old advertisements for job openings, travelling berths, etc., indicates that meals are provided. It comes from the expression to find one's self "to provide for one's self." "When a laborer engages to provide himself with victuals, he is said to find himself, or to receive day wages"  [Bartlett, "Dictionary of Americanisms," 1848]. Hence, so much and found for "wages + meals provided."
entries.etymologyZh: "discovered," 14 世纪晚期, past participle 形容词 源自 find （动）. Expression and found attached to the wages or charges in old advertisements for job openings, travelling berths, etc., indicates that meals are provided. It comes 源自 expression to find one's self "to provide for one's self." "When a laborer engages to provide himself with victuals, he is said to find himself，或to receive day wages" [Bartlett, "Dictionary of Americanisms," 1848]. Hence, so much and found for "wages + meals provided."

example.en: Scientists found through repeated trials that the drug cut symptoms by half.
example.zh: 科学家们通过反复试验发现，这种药物将症状减轻了一半。

definitionLines: n. 成立，建立，创办；地基，基 础；根据；基金会
entries.definition: n. 成立，建立，创办；地基，基 础；根据；基金会
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "action of founding," from Old French fondacion "foundation" (14c.) or directly from Late Latin fundationem (nominative fundatio) "a founding," noun of action from past participle stem of Latin fundare "to lay a bottom or foundation" (see found (v.1)). The Latin word is glossed in Old English by staþol.

Specialized sense of "establishment of an institution with an endowment to pay for it" is from late 14c.; meaning "that which is founded" (a college, hospital, etc.) is from 1510s; meaning "funds endowed for benevolent or charitable purposes" is from early 15c. Sense of "solid base of a structure" is from early 15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "action of founding," 源自 古法语 fondacion "foundation" (14 世纪) or 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 fundationem (主格 fundatio) "a founding," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of 拉丁语 fundare "to lay a bottom or foundation" （参见 found (v.1)). The 拉丁语 word is glossed in 古英语 by staþol. Specialized 语义 "establishment of an institution with an endowment to pay for it" 始于 14 世纪晚期; 意为 "that which is founded" (a college, hospital, etc.) 始于 1510 年代; 意为 "funds endowed for benevolent or charitable purposes" 始于 15 世纪初 义为 "solid base of a structure" 始于 15 世纪初

example.en: A strong foundation in mathematics is essential for studying engineering.
example.zh: 扎实的数学基础对学习工程学至关重要。

entries.etymology:
early 15c., "spring of water that collects in a pool," from Old French fontaine "natural spring" (12c.), from Medieval Latin fontana "fountain, a spring" (source of Spanish and Italian fontana), from post-classical noun use of fem. of Latin fontanus "of a spring," from fons (genitive fontis) "spring (of water)," from PIE root *dhen- (1) "to run, flow" (source also of Sanskrit dhanayati, Old Persian danuvatiy "flows, runs").

The extended sense of "artificial jet of water" (and the structures that make them) is first recorded c. 1500. Hence also fountain-pen (by 1823), so called for the reservoir that supplies a continuous flow of ink. "A French fountain-pen is described in 1658 and Miss Burney used one in 1789" [Weekley]. Fountain of youth, and the story of Ponce de Leon's quest for it, seem to have been introduced in American English by Hawthorne's "Dr. Heidegger's Experiment" (January 1837).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "spring of water that collects in a pool," 源自 古法语 fontaine "natural spring" (12 世纪), 源自 中古拉丁语 fontana "fountain, a spring" (source of 西班牙语 and 意大利语 fontana), 源自 post-classical 为 … 的名词用法 fem. of 拉丁语 fontanus "of a spring," 源自 fons (属格 fontis) "spring (of water)," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *dhen- (1) "to run, flow" (source also of 梵语 dhanayati, Old 波斯语 danuvatiy "flows, runs"). The extended 语义 "artificial jet of water" (and the structures that make them) is 首见于 约 1500 年. Hence also fountain-pen (截至 1823 年), so called for the reservoir that supplies a continuous flow of ink. "A French fountain-pen is described in 1658 and Miss Burney used one in 1789" [Weekley]. Fountain of youth, and the story of Ponce de Leon's quest for it, seem to have been introduced in American English by Hawthorne's "Dr. Heidegger's Experiment" (January 1837 年).

example.en: Children played around the fountain in the center of the plaza.
example.zh: 孩子们在广场中央的喷泉周围嬉戏。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old English feowertyne; see four + -teen. Compare Old Saxon fiertein, Old Frisian fiuwertine, Dutch veertien, Old High German fiorzehan, German vierzehn, Danish fjorten, Gothic fidwortaihun.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 古英语 feowertyne; 参见 four + -teen. 对比 古撒克逊语 fiertein, 古弗里西语 fiuwertine, 荷兰语 veertien, 古高地德语 fiorzehan, 德语 vierzehn, Danish fjorten, Gothic fidwortaihun.

entries.definition: num.第四 n. 四分之一
entries.etymology:
mid-15c., alteration (by influence of four), of ferthe, from Old English feorða "fourth," from Proto-Germanic *fe(d)worthon- (source also of Old Saxon fiortho, Old Norse fiorðe, Dutch vierde, Old High German fiordo, German vierte); see four + -th (1).  As a noun from 1590s, both of fractions and in music.

Among the old Quakers, who rejected the pagan weekday names, fourth day was Wednesday, often a secondary day of meeting for worship. Fourth-dimension attested from 1844. The theatrical fourth wall is from 1807. The celebration of the Fourth of July as the epoch of American independence is attested from 1777.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, alteration (by influence of four), of ferthe, 源自 古英语 feorða "fourth," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *fe(d)worthon- (source also of 古撒克逊语 fiortho, 古北欧语 fiorðe, 荷兰语 vierde, 古高地德语 fiordo, 德语 vierte); 参见 four + -th (1). 作名词时 源自 1590 年代, both of fractions and in music. Among the old Quakers, who rejected the pagan weekday names, fourth day was Wednesday, 常 a secondary day of meeting for worship. Fourth-dimension attested 自 1844 年起. The theatrical fourth wall 始于 1807 年. The celebration of the Fourth of July as the epoch of American independence 见于 1777 年.

entries.etymology: name of an Algonquian people (confederated with the Sac after 1760), translating French renards, which itself may be a translation of an Iroquoian term meaning "red fox people." Their name for themselves is /meškwahki:-haki/ "red earths." French renard "fox" is from Reginhard, the name of the fox in old Northern European fables (as in Low German Reinke de Vos, but Chaucer in The Nun's Priest's Tale calls him Daun Russell); it is Germanic and means literally "strong in council, wily."
entries.etymologyZh: name of an Algonquian people (confederated with the Sac after 1760 年), translating 法语 renards, which itself may be a translation of an Iroquoian term 意为 "red fox people." Their name for themselves is /meškwahki:-haki/ "red earths." 法语 renard "fox" 始于 Reginhard, the name of the fox in old Northern European fables (as in Low 德语 Reinke de Vos, but Chaucer in The Nun's Priest's Tale calls him Daun Russell); it is 日耳曼语 and means 字面义为 "strong in council, wily."

entries.etymology: 1510s, "liable to sin, morally weak;" c. 1600, "liable to break;" a back-formation from fragility, or else from Middle French fragile (Old French fragele, 14c.), from Latin fragilis "easily broken," from root of frangere "to break" (see fraction). Transferred sense of "of frail constitution" (of persons) is from 1858.
entries.etymologyZh: 1510 年代, "liable to sin, morally weak;" 约 1600 年, "liable to break;" a back-formation 源自 fragility，或else 源自 中古法语 fragile (古法语 fragele, 14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 fragilis "easily broken," 源自 root of frangere "to break" （参见 fraction). Transferred 语义 "of frail constitution" (of persons) 始于 1858 年.

example.en: Handle this glassware carefully because it is extremely fragile.
example.zh: 拿这个玻璃器皿要小心，因为它非常易碎。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "small piece or part," from Latin fragmentum "a fragment, remnant," literally "a piece broken off," from root of frangere "to break" (see fraction).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "small piece or part," 源自 拉丁语 fragmentum "a fragment, remnant," 字面义为 "a piece broken off," 源自 root of frangere "to break" （参见 fraction).

example.en: Archaeologists found fragments of ancient pottery at the site.
example.zh: 考古学家在遗址发现了古代陶器的碎片。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., from Latin fragrantem (nominative fragrans) "sweet-smelling," present participle of fragrare "smell strongly, emit (a sweet) odor," from Proto-Italic *fragro-, from PIE root *bhrag- "to smell" (source also of Old Irish broimm "break wind," Middle High German bræhen "to smell," Middle Dutch bracke, Old High German braccho "hound, setter;" see brach). Usually of pleasing or agreeable smells, but sometimes ironic. Related: Fragrantly.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 拉丁语 fragrantem (主格 fragrans) "sweet-smelling," 为 … 的现在分词 fragrare "smell strongly, emit (a sweet) odor," 源自 Proto-Italic *fragro-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bhrag- "to smell" (source also of Old 爱尔兰语 broimm "break wind," Middle High 德语 bræhen "to smell," Middle 荷兰语 bracke, 古高地德语 braccho "hound, setter;" 参见 brach). Usually of pleasing or agreeable smells, but 有时 ironic. 同源词：Fragrantly.

definitionLines: n. 框架，框子；骨架，体格
entries.definition: n. 框架，框子；骨架，体格 vt. 装框子
entries.etymology:
Old English framian "to profit, be helpful, avail, benefit," from fram (adj., adv.) "active, vigorous, bold," originally "going forward," from fram (prep.) "forward; from" (see from). Influenced by related Old English fremman "help forward, promote; do, perform, make, accomplish," and Old Norse fremja "to further, execute." Compare German frommen "avail, profit, benefit, be of use."

Sense focused in Middle English from "make ready" (mid-13c.) to "prepare timber for building" (late 14c.). Meaning "compose, devise" is first attested 1540s. The criminal slang sense of "blame an innocent person" (1920s) is probably from earlier sense of "plot in secret" (1900), perhaps ultimately from meaning "fabricate a story with evil intent," which is first attested 1510s. Related: Framed; framing.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 framian "to profit, be helpful, avail, benefit," 源自 fram (adj., adv.) "active, vigorous, bold," 原义为 "going forward," 源自 fram （介） "forward; from" （参见 源自). Influenced by related 古英语 fremman "help forward, promote; do, perform, make, accomplish," and 古北欧语 fremja "to further, execute." 对比 德语 frommen "avail, profit, benefit, be of use." Sense focused in 中古英语 源自 "make ready" (13 世纪中期) to "prepare timber for building" (14 世纪晚期). 义为 "compose, devise" is 最早见于 1540 年代. The criminal 俚语 语义 "blame an innocent person" (1920 年代) is 可能 源自 earlier 语义 "plot in secret" (1900 年), 或许 最终源自 意为 "fabricate a story with evil intent," which is 最早见于 1510 年代. 同源词：Framed; framing.

example.en: The carpenter built a wooden frame for the painting before hanging it.
example.zh: 木匠在挂画之前为这幅画做了一个木框。

entries.etymology: 1640s, "structure for enclosing or supporting," from frame (n.) + work (n.). Figurative sense "adjusted arrangement" is from 1816.
entries.etymologyZh: 1640 年代, "structure for enclosing or supporting," 源自 frame （名） + work （名）. Figurative sense "adjusted arrangement" 始于 1816 年.

example.en: The new policy fits within the legal framework of the country.
example.zh: 新政策符合该国的法律框架。

entries.etymology: French coin, late 14c., frank, from French franc; a name said to have been given because Medieval Latin Francorum Rex, "King of the Franks" (see Frank), was inscribed on gold coins first made during the reign of Jean le Bon (1350-64). Used of different gold and silver coins over the years; as the name of an official monetary unit of France from 1795.

entries.etymology:
one of the Germanic tribal people (Salian Franks) situated on the lower Rhine from 3c. that conquered Romano-Celtic northern Gaul c.500 C.E.; from their territory and partly from their language grew modern France and French. Old English franc, franca "freeman, noble; Frank, Frenchman," from Medieval Latin francus, a Late Latin borrowing of Frankish *Frank, the people's self-designation (cognate with Old High German Franko, the Latin word also is the source of Spanish and Italian names Franco).

The origin of the ethnic name is uncertain; it traditionally is said to be from the old Germanic word *frankon "javelin, lance" (compare Old English franca "lance, javelin"), their preferred weapon, but the reverse may be the case. Compare also Saxon, traditionally from root of Old English seax "knife." The adjectival sense of "free, at liberty" (see frank (adj.)) probably developed from the tribal name, not the other way round. It was noted by 1680s that, in the Levant, this was the name given to anyone of Western nationality (compare Feringhee and lingua franca).

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "insane," unexplained variant of Middle English frentik (see frenetic). Compare franzy, dialectal form of frenzy. Transferred meaning "affected by wild excitement" is from late 15c. Of the adverbial forms, frantically (1749) is later than franticly (1540s).

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "criminal deception" (mid-13c. in Anglo-Latin); from Old French fraude "deception, fraud" (13c.), from Latin fraudem (nominative fraus) "a cheating, deceit," of persons "a cheater, deceiver." Not in Watkins; perhaps ultimately from PIE *dhreugh- "to deceive" (source also of Sanskrit dhruti- "deception; error"). Meaning "a fraudulent production, something intended to deceive" is from 1650s. The meaning "impostor, deceiver, pretender; humbug" is attested from 1850. Pious fraud (1560s) is properly "deception practiced for the sake of what is deemed a good purpose;" colloquially used as "person who talks piously but is not pious at heart."

The 意为 "impostor, deceiver, pretender; humbug" 见于 1850 年. entries.etymology:
Old English freo "free, exempt from, not in bondage, acting of one's own will," also "noble; joyful," from Proto-Germanic *frija- "beloved; not in bondage" (source also of Old Frisian fri, Old Saxon vri, Old High German vri, German frei, Dutch vrij, Gothic freis "free"), from PIE *priy-a- "dear, beloved," from root *pri- "to love" (source also of Sanskrit priyah "own, dear, beloved," priyate "loves;" Old Church Slavonic prijati "to help," prijatelji "friend;" Welsh rhydd "free").

The primary Germanic sense seems to have been "beloved, friend, to love;" which in some languages (notably Germanic and Celtic) developed also a sense of "free," perhaps from the terms "beloved" or "friend" being applied to the free members of one's clan (as opposed to slaves; compare Latin liberi, meaning both "free persons" and "children of a family"). For the older sense in Germanic, compare Gothic frijon "to love;" Old English freod "affection, friendship, peace," friga "love," friðu "peace;" Old Norse friðr "peace, personal security; love, friendship," German Friede "peace;" Old English freo "wife;" Old Norse Frigg "wife of Odin," literally "beloved" or "loving;" Middle Low German vrien "to take to wife," Dutch vrijen, German freien "to woo."

Meaning "clear of obstruction" is from mid-13c.; sense of "unrestrained in movement" is from c. 1300; of animals, "loose, at liberty, wild," late 14c. Meaning "liberal, not parsimonious" is from c. 1300. Sense of "characterized by liberty of action or expression" is from 1630s; of art, etc., "not holding strictly to rule or form," from 1813. Of nations, "not subject to foreign rule or to despotism," recorded in English from late 14c. (Free world "non-communist nations" attested from 1950 on notion of "based on principles of civil liberty.") Sense of "given without cost" is 1580s, from notion of "free of cost."

Free lunch, originally offered in bars to draw in customers, by 1850, American English. Free pass on railways, etc., attested by 1850. Free speech in Britain was used of a privilege in Parliament since the time of Henry VIII. In U.S., in reference to a civil right to expression, it became a prominent phrase in the debates over the Gag Rule (1836). Free enterprise recorded from 1832; free trade is from 1823; free market from 1630s. Free will is from early 13c. Free school is from late 15c. Free association in psychology is from 1899. Free love "sexual liberation" attested from 1822 (the doctrine itself is much older), American English. Free and easy "unrestrained" is from 1690s.

entries.etymology:
Old English freodom "power of self-determination, state of free will; emancipation from slavery, deliverance;" see free (adj.) + -dom. Meaning "exemption from arbitrary or despotic control, civil liberty" is from late 14c. Meaning "possession of particular privileges" is from 1570s. Similar formation in Old Frisian fridom, Dutch vrijdom, Middle Low German vridom. Freedom-rider recorded 1961 in reference to civil rights activists in U.S. trying to integrate bus lines.

Freedom fighter attested by 1903 (originally with reference to Cuba). Freedom-loving (adj.) is from 1841.

entries.etymology: Middle English frely, from Old English freolice "of one's own accord, readily;" see free (adj.) + -ly (2). Meaning "unstintedly; plentifully" is from c. 1300; that of "without constraint, under free conditions" is from 1590s. Similar formation in Middle Low German vrilike, Dutch vrijelijk "freely," German freilich "to be sure."

entries.etymology:
alteration of freese, friese, from Middle English fresen, from Old English freosan (intransitive) "turn to ice" (class II strong verb; past tense freas, past participle froren), from Proto-Germanic *freusan "to freeze" (source also of Dutch vriezen, Old Norse frjosa, Old High German friosan, German frieren "to freeze," and related to Gothic frius "frost"), from Proto-Germanic *freus-, equivalent to PIE root *preus- "to freeze," also "to burn" (source also of Sanskrit prusva, Latin pruina "hoarfrost," Welsh rhew "frost," Sanskrit prustah "burnt," Albanian prus "burning coals," Latin pruna "a live coal").

Of weather, "be cold enough to freeze," 13c. Meaning "perish from cold" is c. 1300. Transitive sense "harden into ice, congeal as if by frost" first recorded late 14c.; figurative sense late 14c., "make hard or unfeeling." Intransitive meaning "become rigid or motionless" attested by 1720. Sense of "fix at a certain level" is from 1933; of assets, "make non-transactable," from 1922. Freeze frame is from 1960, originally "a briefly Frozen Shot after the Jingle to allow ample time for Change over at the end of a T.V. 'Commercial.' " ["ABC of Film & TV," 1960].

entries.definition: a. 法国（人）的，法语的 n. 法国人，法语
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, frensh, frenche, "pertaining to France or the French," from Old English frencisc "French," originally "of the Franks," from franca, the people name (see Frank). A similar contraction of -ish is in Dutch, Scotch, Welsh, suggesting the habit applies to the names of only the intimate neighbors.

In some provincial forms of English it could mean simply "foreign." Used in many combination-words, often dealing with food or sex: French dressing (by 1860); French toast (1630s); French letter "condom" (c. 1856, perhaps on resemblance of sheepskin and parchment), french (v.) "perform oral sex on," and French kiss (1923) all probably stem from the Anglo-Saxon equation of Gallic culture and sexual sophistication, a sense first recorded 1749 in the phrase French novel. (In late 19c.-early 20c., a French kiss was a kiss on each cheek.) French-Canadian is from 1774; french doors is by 1847. To take French leave, "depart without telling the host," is 1771, from a social custom then prevalent. However, this is said to be called in France filer à l'anglaise, literally "to take English leave."

A similar contraction of -ish is in 荷兰语, Scotch, Welsh, suggesting the habit applies to the names of only the intimate neighbors. In some provincial forms of English it could mean simply "foreign." entries.etymology: 1550s, "state of being crowded" (now obsolete); 1640s, "fact of occurring often;" from Latin frequentia "an assembling in great numbers, a crowding; crowd, multitude, throng," from frequentem (see frequent). Sense in physics, "rate of recurrence," especially of a vibration, is from 1831. In radio electronics, frequency modulation (1922, abbreviated F.M.) as a system of broadcasting is distinguished from amplitude modulation (or A.M.).

Sense in physics, "rate of recurrence," 尤指 of a vibration, 始于 1831 年. In radio electronics, frequency modulation (1922 年, abbreviated F.M.) 作为 system of broadcasting is distinguished 源自 amplitude modulation (or A.M.).

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "ample, profuse," from Old French frequent, or directly from Latin frequentem (nominative frequens) "often, regular, repeated; in great numbers, crowded, numerous, filled, full, populous," which is of uncertain origin. Watkins says probably from PIE *bhrekw- "to cram together," and compares Greek phrassein "to fence in," Latin farcire "to cram." Meaning "common, usual" is from 1530s; that of "happening at short intervals, often recurring" is from c. 1600.

entries.etymology: 1560s, "a chafing, rubbing," from Middle French friction (16c.) and directly from Latin frictionem (nominative frictio) "a rubbing, rubbing down," noun of action from past participle stem of fricare "to rub, rub down," which is of uncertain origin. Watkins suggests possibly from PIE root *bhreie- "to rub, break." Sense of "resistance to motion" is from 1722; figurative sense of "disagreement, clash, lack of harmony, mutual irritation" first recorded 1761. Related: Frictional.

entries.etymology:
sixth day of the week, Old English frigedæg "Friday, Frigga's day," from Frige, genitive of *Frigu (see Frigg), Germanic goddess of married love. The day name is a West Germanic translation of Latin dies Veneris "day of (the planet) Venus," which itself translated Greek Aphrodites hemera.

Compare Old Norse frijadagr, Old Frisian frigendei, Middle Dutch vridach, Dutch vrijdag, German Freitag "Friday," and the Latin-derived cognates Old French vendresdi, French vendredi, Spanish viernes. In Germanic religion, Freya (q.v.) corresponds more closely in character to Venus than Frigg does, and some early Icelandic writers used Freyjudagr for "Friday."

A fast-day in the Church, hence Friday face (17c.) for a gloomy countenance. Black Friday as the name for the busy shopping day after U.S. Thanksgiving holiday is said to date from 1960s and perhaps was coined by those who had the job of controlling the crowds, not by the merchants; earlier it was used principally of Fridays when financial markets crashed (1866, 1869, 1873).

entries.etymology:
Old English freond "one attached to another by feelings of personal regard and preference," from Proto-Germanic *frijand- "lover, friend" (source also of Old Norse frændi, Old Danish frynt, Old Frisian friund, Dutch vriend, Middle High German friunt, German Freund, Gothic frijonds "friend"), from PIE *priy-ont-, "loving," present participle form of root *pri- "to love" (see free (adj.)).

Meaning "a Quaker" (a member of the Society of Friends) is from 1670s. Feond ("fiend," originally "enemy") and freond often were paired alliteratively in Old English; both are masculine agent nouns derived from present participle of verbs, but they are not directly related to one another (see fiend). Related: Friends.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 freond "one attached to another by feelings of personal regard and preference," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *frijand- "lover, friend" (source also of 古北欧语 frændi, Old Danish frynt, 古弗里西语 friund, 荷兰语 vriend, Middle High 德语 friunt, 德语 Freund, Gothic frijonds "friend"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *priy-ont-, "loving," present participle form of root *pri- "to love" （参见 free （形）). 义为 "a Quaker" (a member of the Society of Friends) 始于 1670 年代. Feond ("fiend," 原义为 "enemy") and freond 常 were paired alliteratively in 古英语; both are masculine agent nouns derived 源自 为 … 的现在分词 verbs, but they are not directly related to one another （参见 fiend). 同源词：Friends.

example.en: She has been my closest friend since we met in college ten years ago.
example.zh: 自从十年前我们在大学相识，她就一直是我最亲密的朋友。

entries.etymology: Old English freondlic "well-disposed, kindly;" see friend (n.) + -ly (1). Related: Friendlily; friendliness. As an adverb Old English had freondliche, but by 14c. as the inflections wore off in English it had become indistinguishable from the adjective. Probably owing to that it is rare in modern use; friendfully (mid-15c.) and the correct but ungainly friendlily (1670s) never caught on.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 freondlic "well-disposed, kindly;" 参见 friend （名） + -ly (1). 同源词：Friendlily; friendliness. 作为 副词 古英语 had freondliche, but by 14 世纪 as the inflections wore off in English it had become indistinguishable 源自 形容词. example.en: The locals were extremely friendly and helped us find our way.

entries.etymology:
late 13c., "forehead," from Old French front "forehead, brow" (12c.), from Latin frontem (nominative frons) "forehead, brow, front; countenance, expression (especially as an indicator of truthfulness or shame); facade of a building, forepart; external appearance; vanguard, front rank," a word of "no plausible etymology" (de Vaan). Perhaps literally "that which projects," from PIE *bhront-, from root *bhren- "to project, stand out" (see brink). Or from PIE *ser- (4), "base of prepositions and preverbs with the basic meaning 'above, over, up, upper'" [Watkins, not in Pokorny].

Sense "foremost part of anything" emerged in the English word mid-14c.; sense of "the face as expressive of temper or character" is from late 14c. (hence frontless "shameless," c. 1600). The military sense of "foremost part of an army" (mid-14c.) led to the meaning "field of operations in contact with the enemy" (1660s); home front is from 1919. Meaning "organized body of political forces" is from 1926.


Sense of "public facade" is from 1891; that of "something serving as a cover for illegal activities" is from 1905. Adverbial phrase in front is from 1610s. Meteorological sense first recorded 1921.

entries.etymology: Old English forst, frost "frost, a freezing, frozen precipitation, extreme cold," from Proto-Germanic *frustaz- "frost" (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Old High German frost, Middle Dutch and Dutch vorst), related to freosan "to freeze," from suffixed form of PIE *preus- "to freeze; burn" (see freeze (v.)). Both forms of the word were common in English till late 15c.; the triumph of frost may be due to its similarity to the forms in other Germanic languages. A black frost (late 14c.) is one which kills plants (turns them black) but is not accompanied by visible frozen dew.

Figurative transitive sense "look with displeasure" is from 1570s. Related: Frowned; frowning.

definitionLines: n. 水果，果实；成果，结果

entries.etymology:
late 12c., "any vegetable product useful to humans or animals," from Old French fruit "fruit, fruit eaten as dessert; harvest; virtuous action" (12c.), from Latin fructus "an enjoyment, delight, satisfaction; proceeds, produce, fruit, crops," from frug-, stem of frui "to use, enjoy," from suffixed form of PIE *bhrug- "agricultural produce," also "to enjoy" (see brook (v.)). The Latin word also is the source of Spanish fruto, Italian frutto, German Frucht, Swedish frukt-.

Originally in English meaning all products of the soil (vegetables, nuts, grain, acorns); modern narrower sense is from early 13c. Also "income from agricultural produce, revenue or profits from the soil" (mid-14c.), hence, "profit," the classical sense preserved in fruits of (one's) labor. Meaning "offspring, progeny, child" is from mid-13c.; that of "any consequence, outcome, or result" is from late 14c. Meaning "odd person, eccentric" is from 1910; that of "male homosexual" is from 1935, underworld slang. The term also is noted in 1931 as tramp slang for "a girl or woman willing to oblige," probably from the fact of being "easy picking." Fruit salad recorded from 1861; fruit-cocktail from 1900; fruit-bat by 1869.

The 拉丁语 word also is the source of 西班牙语 fruto, 意大利语 frutto, 德语 Frucht, Swedish frukt-. Fruit salad recorded 自 1861 年起; fruit-cocktail 自 1900 年起; fruit-bat 截至 1869 年.

entries.etymology: late 13c., "cook (something) in a shallow pan over a fire," from Old French frire "to fry" (13c.), from Latin frigere "to roast or fry," from PIE *bher- (4) "to cook, bake" (source also of Sanskrit bhrjjati "roasts," bharjanah "roasting;" Persian birishtan "to roast;" Greek phrygein "to roast, bake"). Intransitive sense is from late 14c. U.S. slang meaning "execute in the electric chair" is U.S. slang from 1929. As a noun, "fried meat," from 1630s. Related: Fried; frying. Frying pan recorded from mid-14c.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, feuel, feul "fuel, material for burning," also figurative, from Old French foaille "fuel for heating," from Medieval Latin legal term focalia "right to demand material for making fire, right of cutting fuel," from classical Latin focalia "brushwood for fuel," from neuter plural of Latin focalis "pertaining to a hearth," from focus "hearth, fireplace" (see focus (n.)). Figurative use from 1570s. Of food, as fuel for the body, 1876. As "combustible liquid for an internal combustion engine" from 1886. A French derivative is fouailler "woodyard." Fuel-oil is from 1882.

entries.etymology:
Old English full "containing all that can be received; having eaten or drunk to repletion; filled; perfect, entire, utter," from Proto-Germanic *fulla- "full" (source also of Old Saxon full, Old Frisian ful, Dutch vol, Old High German fol, German voll, Old Norse fullr, Gothic fulls), from PIE *pele- (1) "to fill" (see poly-). Related: Fuller; fullest.

The adverb is Old English ful "very, fully, entirely, completely" and was common in Middle English (full well, full many, etc.); sense of "quite, exactly, precisely" is from 1580s. Full moon, one with its whole disc illuminated, was Old English fulles monan; first record of full-blood in reference to racial purity is from 1812. Full house is 1710 in the theatrical sense, 1887 in the poker sense (three of a kind and a pair, earlier full-hand, 1850). Full-dress (adj.) "appropriate to a formal occasion" is from 1761, from the noun phrase.

Full moon, one with its whole disc illuminated, was 古英语 fulles monan; first record of full-blood in reference to racial purity 始于 1812 年. Full house is 1710 年 in the theatrical sense, 1887 年 in the poker sense (three of a kind and a pair, earlier full-hand, 1850 年). Full-dress （形） "appropriate to a formal occasion" 始于 1761 年, 源自 名词 phrase.

definitionLines: n. 玩笑，乐趣；有趣的人/事
entries.definition: n. 玩笑，乐趣；有趣的人/事
entries.etymology: "diversion, amusement, mirthful sport," 1727, earlier "a cheat, trick" (c. 1700), from verb fun (1680s) "to cheat, hoax," which is of uncertain origin, probably a variant of Middle English fonnen "befool" (c. 1400; see fond). Scantly recorded in 18c. and stigmatized by Johnson as "a low cant word." Older senses are preserved in phrase to make fun of (1737) and funny money "counterfeit bills" (1938, though this use of the word may be more for the sake of the rhyme). See also funny. Fun and games "mirthful carryings-on" is from 1906.

entries.etymology: 1530s, "one's proper work or purpose; power of acting in a specific proper way," from Middle French fonction (16c.) and directly from Latin functionem (nominative functio) "a performance, an execution," noun of action from funct-, past participle stem of fungi "perform, execute, discharge," from PIE root *bheug- (2) "to use, enjoy" (see brook (v.)). Meaning "official ceremony" is from 1630s, originally in church use. Use in mathematics probably was begun by Leibnitz (1692). In reference to computer operations, 1947.

entries.etymology: 1670s, "a bottom, the bottom; foundation, groundwork," from French fond "a bottom, floor, ground" (12c.), also "a merchant's basic stock or capital," from Latin fundus "bottom, foundation, piece of land," from PIE root *bhudh- "bottom, base" (source also of Sanskrit budhnah, Greek pythmen "foundation, bottom," Old English botm "lowest part;" see bottom (n.)). example.en: Access to clean drinking water is a fundamental human right recognized by the United Nations.
example.zh: 获得清洁饮用水是联合国所认可的一项基本人权。

entries.etymology: "ceremony of burying a dead person," 1510s, probably short for funeral service, etc., from funeral (adj.).

example.en: The whole village gathered for the funeral of the beloved elder.
example.zh: 全村人聚集在一起，为这位受人爱戴的长者举行葬礼。

definitionLines: a.滑稽的，可笑的，有趣的；稀 奇的，古的

entries.etymology: "humorous," 1756, from fun (n.) + -y (2). Meaning "strange, odd, causing perplexity" is by 1806, said to be originally U.S. Southern (marked as colloquial in Century Dictionary). The two senses of the word led to the retort question "funny ha-ha or funny peculiar," which is attested by 1916. Related: Funnier; funniest. Funny farm "mental hospital" is slang from 1962. Funny bone "elbow end of the humerus" (where the ulnar nerve passes relatively unprotected) is from 1826, so called for the tingling sensation when struck. Funny-man was originally (1854) a circus or stage clown.

example.en: The comedian's funny impression of the politician left the audience in tears of laughter.
example.zh: 这位喜剧演员对那位政客的滑稽模仿令观众笑到流泪。

entries.etymology:
late 14c. "trimming or lining of a garment" (implied c. 1300 in surname Furhode "fur hood"), probably from Old French forrer, fourrer "cover with fur, line (clothing)," in general "to cover, fill with," from fuerre "sheath, scabbard" (via notion of "covering"), from Frankish *fodr or another Germanic source, from Proto-Germanic *fodram "sheath" (source also of Old Frisian foder "coat lining," Old High German fotar "a lining," German Futter, Gothic fodr "sword sheath"), from PIE root *pa- "to protect, feed" (see food (n.)).

First applied c. 1400 to the hairy pelt of an animal, whether still on the animal or not. The Old French noun might have had the sense "hide, fur, pelt" (and thus might serve as the immediate source of the English noun), but this is not attested. Absent this, the sense transfer from the lining to the material that goes to make it probably happened in English. As an adjective from 1590s.

First applied 约 1400 年 to the hairy pelt of an animal, whether still on the animal or not. The 古法语 名词 might have had the sense "hide, fur, pelt" (and thus might serve as the immediate source of the English 名词), but this is not attested. Absent this, the sense transfer 源自 lining to the material that goes to make it 可能 happened in English. 作形容词时 源自 1590 年代.

example.en: The coat was lined with soft fur to keep the wearer warm in winter.
example.zh: 这件外套内衬软毛皮，能让穿者在冬天保暖。

definitionLines: v. 供应，提供；陈设，布置
entries.definition: v. 供应，提供；陈设，布置
entries.etymology: mid-15c., "fit out, equip, to provision" (a castle, ship, person); "provide (soldiers)," from Old French furniss-/forniss-, present participle stem of furnir/fornir "accomplish, carry out; equip, fit out; provide" (12c.), from Vulgar Latin *fornire, alteration of *fromire, from West Germanic *frumjan "forward movement, advancement" (source also of Old High German frumjan "to do, execute, provide"), from Proto-Germanic *fram- "forwards" (see from). General meaning "to provide" (something) is from 1520s; specifically "provide furniture for a room or house" from 1640s. Related: Furnished; furnishing.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "fit out, equip, to provision" (a castle, ship, person); "provide (soldiers)," 源自 古法语 furniss-/forniss-, present participle stem of furnir/fornir "accomplish, carry out; equip, fit out; provide" (12 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *fornire, alteration of *fromire, 源自 West 日耳曼语 *frumjan "forward movement, advancement" (source also of 古高地德语 frumjan "to do, execute, provide"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *fram- "forwards" （参见 源自). General 意为 "to provide" (something) 始于 1520 年代; specifically "provide furniture for a room or house" 源自 1640 年代. 同源词：Furnished; furnishing.

entries.etymology: 1520s, "act of supplying or providing," from Middle French fourniture "a supply; act of furnishing," from Old French forneture (13c.), from fornir "to furnish" (see furnish). Sense of "chairs, tables, etc.; household stuff; movables required or ornamental in a dwelling-place" (1570s) is unique to English; most other European languages derive their words for this from Latin mobile "movable."
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "act of supplying or providing," 源自 中古法语 fourniture "a supply; act of furnishing," 源自 古法语 forneture (13 世纪), 源自 fornir "to furnish" （参见 furnish). 义为 "chairs, tables, etc.; household stuff; movables required or ornamental in a dwelling-place" (1570 年代) is unique to English; most other European languages derive their words for this 源自 拉丁语 mobile "movable."

example.en: All the furniture in the living room was made of solid oak.
example.zh: 客厅里所有的家具都是实心橡木制成的。

definitionLines: ad.（far 的比较级）；更远地，更 大程度上；而且，此外；进一 步地；
a. 另外的，更多的；更远的
entries.definition: ad.（far 的比较级）；更远地，更 大程度上；而且，此外；进一 步地； a. 另外的，更多的；更远的 vt. 促进，增进
entries.etymology:
Old English furðor, forðor "to a more advanced position, forward, onward, beyond, more distant; farther away; later, afterward; to a greater degree or extent, in addition; moreover," etymologically representing either "forth-er" or "fore-ther." The former would be from furðum (see forth) + comparative suffix *-eron-, *-uron- (compare inner, outer).

Alternative etymology (Watkins) traces it to Proto-Germanic *furthera-, from PIE *pr-tero- (source also of Greek proteros "former"), representing the root *per- (1) "forward, through" (see per) + comparative suffix also found in after, other. Senses of "in addition, to a greater extent" are later metaphoric developments.

It replaced or absorbed farrer, ferrer as comparative of far (itself a comparative but no longer felt as one). Farrer itself displaced Old English fierr in this job; farrer survived until 17c., then was reduced to dialect by rival farther. "The primary sense of further, farther is 'more forward, more onward'; but this sense is practically coincident with that of the comparative degree of far, where the latter word refers to real or attributed motion in some particular direction." [OED]

Senses of "in addition, to a greater extent" are later metaphoric developments. It replaced or absorbed farrer, ferrer as comparative of far (itself a comparative but no longer felt as one). "The primary sense of further, farther is 'more forward, more onward'; but this sense is practically coincident with that of the comparative degree of far, where the latter word refers to real or attributed motion in some particular direction." [OED]

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from further (adv.) + more. There also was a farthermore in Middle English. Related: Furthermost.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 further （副） + more. There also was a farthermore in 中古英语. 同源词：Furthermost.

example.en: The plan was expensive; furthermore, it was unlikely to succeed.
example.zh: 这个计划代价高昂；此外，它也不太可能成功。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "fierce passion," from Old French furie, fuire "rage, frenzy" (14c.), from Latin furia "violent passion, rage, madness," from or related to furere "to rage, be mad," which is of uncertain origin. "Many etymologies have been proposed, but none is clearly the best" [de Vaan]. Romans used Furiæ to translate Greek Erinyes, the collective name for the avenging deities sent from Tartarus to punish criminals (in later accounts three in number and female). Hence, in English, figuratively, "an angry woman" (late 14c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "fierce passion," 源自 古法语 furie, fuire "rage, frenzy" (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 furia "violent passion, rage, madness," 源自 or related to furere "to rage, be mad," which is 来源存疑. Romans used Furiæ to translate 希腊语 Erinyes, the collective name for the avenging deities sent 源自 Tartarus to punish criminals (in later accounts three in number and female). Hence, in English, figuratively, "an angry woman" (14 世纪晚期).

example.en: She left the meeting in a fury, slamming the door behind her.
example.zh: 她怒气冲冲地离开了会议室，随手摔上了门。

entries.etymology: 1680s, "to melt, make liquid by heat" (transitive), back-formation from fusion. Intransitive sense, "to become liquid," attested from 1800. Figurative sense of "blend different things, blend or unite as if by melting together" is recorded by 1817. Intransitive figurative sense "become intermingled or blended" is by 1873. Related: Fused; fusing.
entries.etymologyZh: 1680 年代, "to melt, make liquid by heat" (transitive), back-formation 源自 fusion. Intransitive sense, "to become liquid," attested 自 1800 年起. Figurative 语义 "blend different things, blend or unite as if by melting together" is recorded 截至 1817 年. Intransitive figurative sense "become intermingled or blended" is 截至 1873 年. 同源词：Fused; fusing.

entries.etymology: 1550s, "act of melting by heat," from Middle French fusion or directly from Latin fusionem (nominative fusio) "an outpouring, effusion," noun of action from fusus, past participle of fundere "to pour, melt" (see found (v.2)). Meaning "union or blending of different things; state of being united or blended" is by 1776; used especially in 19c, of politics, in early 20c. of psychology, atoms, and jazz (in nuclear physics sense, first recorded 1947; in musical sense, by 1972).
entries.etymologyZh: 1550 年代, "act of melting by heat," 源自 中古法语 fusion or 直接源自 拉丁语 fusionem (主格 fusio) "an outpouring, effusion," 名词 of action 源自 fusus, 为 … 的过去分词 fundere "to pour, melt" （参见 found (v.2)). 义为 "union or blending of different things; state of being united or blended" is 截至 1776 年; used 尤指 in 19c, of politics, in 20 世纪初 of psychology, atoms, and jazz (in nuclear physics sense, 首见于 1947 年; in musical sense, 截至 1972 年).

entries.etymology: "trifling bustle," 1701, originally colloquial, perhaps an alteration of force (n.), or "echoic of the sound of something sputtering or bubbling" [OED], or from Danish fjas "foolery, nonsense." First attested in Anglo-Irish writers, but there are no obvious connections to words in Irish. To make a fuss was earlier to keep a fuss (1726). Fuss and feathers "bustle and display" is from 1848, American English, suggestive of a game cock or a peacock, originally of U.S. Army Gen. Winfield Scott (1786-1866) in the Mexican war.

entries.etymology:
late 15c., "that which has been acquired" (possessions, resources, wealth), from Middle French gain, from Old French gaaigne "gain, profit, advantage; work, business; booty; arable land" (12c.), from gaaignier "to gain, earn; capture, win" (see gain (v.)). Meaning "any incremental increase" (in weight, etc.) is by 1851. Related: Gains.

The original French word enfolded the notions of "profit from agriculture" and "booty, prey." Neither the verb nor the noun gain is in Middle English, which however had gainage "profit derived from agriculture" (late 14c., from Old French gaaignage); gaineier "farmer" (late 13c. as a surname); gainerie "a farm" (mid-15c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "that which has been acquired" (possessions, resources, wealth), 源自 中古法语 gain, 源自 古法语 gaaigne "gain, profit, advantage; work, business; booty; arable land" (12 世纪), 源自 gaaignier "to gain, earn; capture, win" （参见 gain （动）). 义为 "any incremental increase" (in weight, etc.) is 截至 1851 年. 同源词：Gains. The original 法语 word enfolded the notions of "profit from agriculture" and "booty, prey." Neither the 动词 nor the 名词 gain is in 中古英语, which however had gainage "profit derived from agriculture" (14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 gaaignage); gaineier "farmer" (13 世纪晚期 作为 surname); gainerie "a farm" (15 世纪中期).

example.en: She traveled abroad for a year to gain more experience in her field.
example.zh: 她出国旅行了一年，以在自己的领域获得更多经验。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., from French galaxie or directly from Late Latin galaxias "the Milky Way" as a feature in the night sky (in classical Latin via lactea or circulus lacteus)from Greek galaxias (adj.), in galaxias kyklos, literally "milky circle," from gala (genitive galaktos) "milk" (see lacto-). The technical astronomical sense in reference to the discrete stellar aggregate including the sun and all visible stars emerged by 1848. Figurative sense of "brilliant assembly of persons" is from 1580s. Milky Way is a translation of Latin via lactea.
Originally ours was the only one known. Astronomers began to speculate by mid-19c. that some of the spiral nebulae they could see in telescopes were actually immense and immensely distant structures the size and shape of the Milky Way. But the matter was not settled in the affirmative until the 1920s.

Astronomers began to speculate by 19 世纪中期 that some of the spiral nebulae they could 参见 in telescopes were actually immense and immensely distant structures the size and shape of the Milky Way. entries.etymology:
mid-15c., "covered walk or passageway, narrow and partly open passageway along a wall," from Old French galerie "a long portico" (14c.), from Medieval Latin galeria, of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of galilea "church porch," which is probably from Latin Galilaea "Galilee," the northernmost region of Palestine (see Galilee); church porches sometimes were so called, perhaps from being at the far end of the church:

Sense of "building to house art" first recorded 1590s. In reference to theaters, of the section with the highest, cheapest seats; hence "people who occupy a (theater) gallery" (contrasted with "gentlemen of the pit") first by Lovelace, 1640s, hence to play to the gallery (1867).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "covered walk or passageway, narrow and partly open passageway along a wall," 源自 古法语 galerie "a long portico" (14 世纪), 源自 中古拉丁语 galeria, 来源不详. Perhaps an alteration of galilea "church porch," which is 可能 源自 拉丁语 Galilaea "Galilee," the northernmost region of Palestine （参见 Galilee); church porches 有时 were so called, 或源自 being at the far end of the church: 义为 "building to house art" 首见于 1590 年代. example.en: Her paintings are currently on display at a downtown art gallery.

entries.etymology: English measure of capacity (containing four quarts), usually for liquids, late 13c., from Old North French galon, corresponding to Old French jalon, name of a liquid measure roughly equivalent to a modern gallon," which is related to (perhaps augmentative of) jale "bowl," from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin diminutive form galleta "bucket, pail," also "a measure of wine," a word of unknown origin, perhaps from Gaulish galla "vessel."
entries.etymologyZh: English measure of capacity (containing four quarts), 通常 for liquids, 13 世纪晚期, 源自 Old North 法语 galon, corresponding to 古法语 jalon, name of a liquid measure roughly equivalent to a modern gallon," which is related to (perhaps augmentative of) jale "bowl," from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin diminutive form galleta "bucket, pail," also "a measure of wine," a word of unknown origin, perhaps from Gaulish galla "vessel."

entries.etymology: "risk something of value on a game of chance," 1726 (implied in gambling), from a dialectal survival of Middle English gammlen, variant of gamenen "to play, jest, be merry," from Old English gamenian "to play, joke, pun," from gamen (see game (n.)), with form as in fumble, etc. Or possibly gamble is from a derivative of gamel "to play games" (1590s), itself likely a frequentative from game. Originally regarded as a slang word. The intrusive -b- may be from confusion with unrelated gambol (v.). Transitive meaning "to squander in gambling" is from 1808. Related: Gambled; gambling.
