entries.etymology:
Old English læfan "to allow to remain in the same state or condition; to let remain, allow to survive; to have left (of a deceased person, in reference to heirs, etc.); to bequeath (a heritage)," from Proto-Germanic *laibijan (source also of Old Frisian leva "to leave," Old Saxon farlebid "left over"), causative of *liban "remain" (source of Old English belifan, German bleiben, Gothic bileiban "to remain"), from root *laf- "remnant, what remains," from PIE *leip- "to stick, adhere;" also "fat" (cognates: Greek lipos "fat;" Old English lifer "liver," life).

The Germanic root seems to have had only the sense "remain, continue" (which was in Old English as well but has since become obsolete), which also is in Greek lipares "persevering, importunate." But this usually is regarded as a development from the primary PIE sense of "adhere, be sticky" (compare Lithuanian lipti, Old Church Slavonic lipet "to adhere," Greek lipos "grease," Sanskrit rip-/lip- "to smear, adhere to."

Originally a strong verb (past participle lifen), it early switched to a weak form. Meaning "go away, take one's departure, depart from; leave behind" (c. 1200) comes from notion of "leave behind" (as in to leave the earth "to die;" to leave the field "retreat"). From c. 1200 as "to stop, cease; give up, relinquish, abstain from having to do with; discontinue, come to an end;" also "to omit, neglect; to abandon, forsake, desert; divorce;" also "allow (someone) to go."

Colloquial use for "let, allow" is by 1840, said by OED to be chiefly American English. Not related to leave (n.). To leave out "omit" is from late 15c. To leave (something) alone is from c. 1400; to leave (something) be is from 1825. To leave (something/nothing) to be desired is from 1780. To leave it at that is from 1902. Leave off is from c. 1400 as "cease, desist" (transitive); early 15c. as "stop, make an end" (intransitive).

The 日耳曼语 root seems to have had only the sense "remain, continue" (which was in 古英语 as well but has 自 become 已废), which also is in 希腊语 lipares "persevering, importunate." entries.etymology:
early 15c., "drawing, painting," from Latin pictura "painting," from pictus, past participle of pingere "to make pictures, to paint, to embroider," (see paint (v.)). Picture window is from 1938. Picture post-card first recorded 1899. Phrase every picture tells a story first attested 1900, in advertisements for an illustrated life of Christ. To be in (or out of) the picture in the figurative sense dates to 1900.

Expression a picture is worth a thousand words, attested from 1918, probably was from the publication trade (the notion that a picture was worth 1,000 words is in printers' publications by 1911). The phrase also was in use in the form worth a million words, the form used by American newspaper editor Arthur Brisbane (1864-1936) in an editorial much-read c. 1916 titled "What is a Good Newspaper" in the "New York Evening Journal." In part it read, "After news and humor come good pictures. In this day of hurry we learn through the eye, and one picture may be worth a million words." It seems to have emerged into general use via the medium of advertising (which scaled down the number and also gave the expression its spurious origin story as "a Japanese proverb" or some such thing, by 1919). Earlier various acts or deeds (and in one case "the arrow") were said to be worth a thousand words.

mid-15c. "of or pertaining to the law," from Old French légal "legal" (14c.) or directly from Latin legalis "pertaining to the law," from lex (genitive legis) "an enactment; a precept, regulation, principle, rule; formal proposition for a law, motion, bill; a contract, arrangement, contrivance. entries.etymology:
early 14c., "narrative dealing with a happening or an event," from Old French legende (12c., Modern French légende) and directly from Medieval Latin legenda "legend, story," especially lives of saints, which were formerly read at matins and in refectories of religious houses, literally "(things) to be read," on certain days in church, etc., from Latin legendus, neuter plural gerundive of legere "to read; to gather, pluck, select" (see lecture (n.)).

Extended sense of "nonhistorical or mythical story," with or without saints, wonders, and miracles is first recorded late 14c. Meaning "writing or inscription" (especially on a coin or medal) is from 1610s; on a map, illustration, etc., from 1903. To be a legend in (one's) own time is from 1958.

Extended 语义 "nonhistorical or mythical story," with or without saints, wonders, and miracles is 首见于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "writing or inscription" (尤指 on a coin or medal) 始于 1610 年代; on a map, illustration, etc., 自 1903 年起. To be a legend in (one's) own time 始于 1958 年.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "lawfully begotten, born of parents legally married," from Middle French legitimer and directly from Medieval Latin legitimatus, past participle of legitimare "make lawful, declare to be lawful," from Latin legitimus "lawful," originally "fixed by law, in line with the law," from lex (genitive legis) "law" (see legal). Transferred sense of "genuine, real" is attested from 1550s. Related: Legitimately; legitimateness. The older adjective in English was legitime "lawful, of legitimate birth" (late 14c.), from Old French legitime, from Latin legitimus.

Transferred 语义 "genuine, real" 见于 1550 年代. 同源词：Legitimately; legitimateness. The older 形容词 in English was legitime "lawful, of legitimate birth" (14 世纪晚期), 源自 古法语 legitime, 源自 拉丁语 legitimus.

entries.etymology:
Old English lengðu "property of being long or extended in one direction; distance along a line," from Proto-Germanic *langitho, abstract noun from *langaz "long" (root of Old English lang; see long (adj.)) + *-itho, abstract noun suffix (see -th (2)). Cognate with Old Norse lengd, Old Frisian lengethe, Dutch lengte.

Figurative sense of "the distance one goes, extremity to which something is carried" is from 1690s. Phrase at length "to full extent" is attested from c. 1500. As "the length of a swimming pool," 1912. From the notion of "a piece or portion of the extent of anything" come the theater slang sense "a 42-line portion of an actor's part" and the sporting sense "the length of a horse, car, etc. in a race" used as a unit of measure (1650s).

Cognate with 古北欧语 lengd, 古弗里西语 lengethe, 荷兰语 lengte. Figurative 语义 "the distance one goes, extremity to which something is carried" 始于 1690 年代. Phrase at length "to full extent" 见于 约 1500 年. As "the length of a swimming pool," 1912 年. From the 概念 "a piece or portion of the extent of anything" come the theater 俚语 sense "a 42-line portion of an actor's part" and the sporting sense "the length of a horse, car, etc. in a race" used 作为 unit of measure (1650 年代).

entries.definition: a./ad. 较少（的），更少（的），更 小（的）
entries.etymology: Old English læs (adv.), læssa (adj.), comparative of læs "small;" from Proto-Germanic *lais-izo "smaller" (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian les "less;" Middle Dutch lise "soft, gentle," German leise "soft"), from PIE root *leis- (2) "small" (source also of Lithuanian liesas "thin"). Formerly also "younger," as a translation of Latin minor, a sense now obsolete except in James the Less. Used as a comparative of little, but not related to it. The noun is Old English læsse.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 læs （副）, læssa （形）, comparative of læs "small;" 源自 原始日耳曼语 *lais-izo "smaller" (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古弗里西语 les "less;" Middle 荷兰语 lise "soft, gentle," 德语 leise "soft"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *leis- (2) "small" (source also of Lithuanian liesas "thin"). Formerly also "younger," 作为 translation of 拉丁语 minor, a sense 今废 except in James the Less. Used 作为 comparative of little, but not related to it. The 名词 is 古英语 læsse.

entries.etymology: early 13c., "a reading aloud from the Bible," also "something to be learned by a student," from Old French leçon, from Latin lectionem (nominative lectio) "a reading," noun of action from past participle stem of legere "to read" (see lecture (n.)). Transferred sense of "an occurrence from which something can be learned" is from 1580s.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "a reading aloud from the Bible," also "something to be learned by a student," 源自 古法语 leçon, 源自 拉丁语 lectionem (主格 lectio) "a reading," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of legere "to read" （参见 lecture （名）). Transferred 语义 "an occurrence from which something can be learned" 始于 1580 年代.

example.en: Losing the championship taught him a valuable lesson about teamwork.
example.zh: 失去冠军头衔让他学到了关于团队合作的宝贵一课。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, contracted from Middle English phrase les te "less that," from Old English phrase þy læs þe "whereby less that," from þy, instrumental case of demonstrative article þæt "that" + læs (see less) + þe "the." The þy was dropped and the remaining two words contracted into leste.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, contracted 源自 中古英语 phrase les te "less that," 源自 古英语 phrase þy læs þe "whereby less that," 源自 þy, instrumental case of demonstrative article þæt "that" + læs （参见 less) + þe "the." The þy was dropped and the remaining two words contracted into leste.

entries.etymology:
Old English lætan "to allow to remain; let go, leave, depart from; leave undone; to allow; bequeath," also "to rent" (class VII strong verb; past tense let, past participle læten), from Proto-Germanic *letan (source also of Old Saxon latan, Old Frisian leta, Dutch laten, German lassen, Gothic letan "to leave, let"), from PIE *le- (2) "to let go, slacken" (source also of Latin lassus "faint, weary," Lithuanian leisti "to let, to let loose;" see lenient). If that derivation is correct, the primary sense would be "let go through weariness, neglect."

Of blood, from late Old English. To let (something) slip originally (1520s) was a reference to hounds on a leash; figurative use from 1540s. To let (someone) off "allow to go unpunished" is from 1814. To let on "reveal, divulge" is from 1725; to let up "cease, stop" is from 1787. Let alone "not to mention" is from 1812.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 lætan "to allow to remain; let go, leave, depart from; leave undone; to allow; bequeath," also "to rent" (class VII strong 动词; past tense let, past participle læten), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *letan (source also of 古撒克逊语 latan, 古弗里西语 leta, 荷兰语 laten, 德语 lassen, Gothic letan "to leave, let"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *le- (2) "to let go, slacken" (source also of 拉丁语 lassus "faint, weary," Lithuanian leisti "to let, to let loose;" 参见 lenient). If that derivation is correct, the primary sense would be "let go through weariness, neglect." Of blood, 源自 late 古英语. To let (something) slip 原义为 (1520 年代) was a reference to hounds on a leash; figurative use 源自 1540 年代. To let (someone) off "allow to go unpunished" 始于 1814 年. To let on "reveal, divulge" 始于 1725 年; to let up "cease, stop" 始于 1787 年. Let alone "not to mention" 始于 1812 年.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "a bed," also "bed-like vehicle carried on men's shoulders" (early 14c.), from Anglo-French litere "portable bed," Old French litiere "litter, stretcher, bier; straw, bedding," from Medieval Latin lectaria "litter" (altered in French by influence of lit "bed"), from Latin lectus "bed, couch," from PIE *legh-to-, from root *legh- "to lie" (see lie (v.2)).

Meaning extended early 15c. to "straw used for bedding" (early 14c. in Anglo-French) and late 15c. to "offspring of an animal at one birth" (in one bed); sense of "scattered oddments, disorderly debris" is first attested 1730, probably from Middle English verb literen "provide with bedding" (late 14c.), with notion of strewing straw. Litter by 19c. had come to mean both the straw bedding and the animal waste in it after use.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "a bed," also "bed-like vehicle carried on men's shoulders" (14 世纪初), 源自 盎格鲁-法语 litere "portable bed," 古法语 litiere "litter, stretcher, bier; straw, bedding," 源自 中古拉丁语 lectaria "litter" (altered in 法语 by influence of lit "bed"), 源自 拉丁语 lectus "bed, couch," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *legh-to-, 源自 root *legh- "to lie" （参见 lie (v.2)). 义为 extended 15 世纪初 to "straw used for bedding" (14 世纪初 in 盎格鲁-法语) and 15 世纪晚期 to "offspring of an animal at one birth" (in one bed); 语义 "scattered oddments, disorderly debris" is 最早见于 1730 年, 可能 源自 中古英语 动词 literen "provide with bedding" (14 世纪晚期), with 概念 strewing straw. Litter by 19 世纪 had come to mean both the straw bedding and the animal waste in it after use.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "tool to indicate a horizontal line," from Old French livel "a level" (13c.), ultimately from Latin libella "a balance, level," diminutive of libra "balance, scale, unit of weight," from PIE *lithra- "a scale." Cognate Spanish nivel, Modern French niveau are from the same source but altered by dissimilation. Meaning "horizontality" is from c. 1400. Meaning "position as marked by a horizontal line" is from 1530s. Phrase on the level "fair, honest" is from 1872; earlier it meant "moderate, without great ambition" (1790).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "tool to indicate a horizontal line," 源自 古法语 livel "a level" (13 世纪), 最终源自 拉丁语 libella "a balance, level," 为 … 的指小形式 libra "balance, scale, unit of weight," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *lithra- "a scale." Cognate 西班牙语 nivel, 现代法语 niveau 始于 the same source but altered by dissimilation. 义为 "horizontality" 始于 约 1400 年. 义为 "position as marked by a horizontal line" 始于 1530 年代. Phrase on the level "fair, honest" 始于 1872 年; earlier it meant "moderate, without great ambition" (1790 年).

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old French levier (Modern French leveur) "a lifter, a lever," agent noun from lever "to raise," from Latin levare "to raise," from levis "light" in weight, from PIE root *legwh- "light, having little weight; easy, agile, nimble" (source also of Sanskrit laghuh "quick, small;" Greek elakhys "small," elaphros "light;" Old Church Slavonic liguku, Lithuanian lengvas "light;" Old Irish laigiu "smaller, worse;" Gothic leihts, Old English leoht "light" (adj.)). As a verb, 1856, from the noun.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "bound or obliged by law," probably from Anglo-French *liable, from Old French lier "to bind, tie up, fasten, tether; bind by obligation," from Latin ligare "to bind, to tie" (see ligament). With -able. General sense of "exposed to" (something undesirable) is from 1590s. Incorrect use for "likely" is attested by 1886.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "bound or obliged by law," 可能 源自 盎格鲁-法语 *liable, 源自 古法语 lier "to bind, tie up, fasten, tether; bind by obligation," 源自 拉丁语 ligare "to bind, to tie" （参见 ligament). With -able. General 语义 "exposed to" (something undesirable) 始于 1590 年代. Incorrect use for "likely" is attested 截至 1886 年.

entries.etymology: 1640s, from French liaison "a union, a binding together" (13c.), from Late Latin ligationem (nominative ligatio) "a binding," from past participle stem of Latin ligare "to bind" (see ligament). Originally a cookery term for a thickening agent for sauces. Sense of "intimate relations" is from 1806. Military sense of "cooperation between branches, allies, etc." is from 1816. The noun meaning "one who is concerned with liaison of units, etc." is short for liaison officer.

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "generous," also, late 14c., "selfless; noble, nobly born; abundant," and, early 15c., in a bad sense "extravagant, unrestrained," from Old French liberal "befitting free men, noble, generous, willing, zealous" (12c.), from Latin liberalis "noble, gracious, munificent, generous," literally "of freedom, pertaining to or befitting a free man," from liber "free, unrestricted, unimpeded; unbridled, unchecked, licentious," from PIE *leudh-ero-, probably originally "belonging to the people" (though the precise semantic development is obscure; compare frank (adj.)), and a suffixed form of the base *leudh- "people" (source also of Old Church Slavonic ljudu, Lithuanian liaudis, Old English leod, German Leute "nation, people;" Old High German liut "person, people").

With the meaning "free from restraint in speech or action," liberal was used 16c.-17c. as a term of reproach. It revived in a positive sense in the Enlightenment, with a meaning "free from prejudice, tolerant," which emerged 1776-88.

In reference to education, explained by Fowler as "the education designed for a gentleman (Latin liber a free man) & ... opposed on the one hand to technical or professional or any special training, & on the other to education that stops short before manhood is reached" (see liberal arts). Purely in reference to political opinion, "tending in favor of freedom and democracy" it dates from c. 1801, from French libéral, originally applied in English by its opponents (often in French form and with suggestions of foreign lawlessness) to the party favorable to individual political freedoms. But also (especially in U.S. politics) tending to mean "favorable to government action to effect social change," which seems at times to draw more from the religious sense of "free from prejudice in favor of traditional opinions and established institutions" (and thus open to new ideas and plans of reform), which dates from 1823.

With the 意为 "free from restraint in speech or action," liberal was used 16 世纪-17 世纪 作为 term of reproach. It revived in a positive sense in the Enlightenment, with a 意为 "free from prejudice, tolerant," which emerged 1776 年-88. In reference to education, explained by Fowler as "the education designed for a gentleman (Latin liber a free man) & ... opposed on the one hand to technical or professional or any special training, & on the other to education that stops short before manhood is reached" （参见 liberal arts). Purely in reference to political opinion, "tending in favor of freedom and democracy" it dates 源自 约 1801 年, 源自 法语 libéral, 原义为 applied in English by its opponents (常 in 法语 form and with suggestions of foreign lawlessness) to the party favorable to individual political freedoms. But also (尤指 in U.S. politics) tending to mean "favorable to government action to effect social change," which seems at times to draw more 源自 religious 语义 "free from prejudice in favor of traditional opinions and established institutions" (and thus open to new ideas and plans of reform), which dates 自 1823 年起.

entries.etymology: 1620s, from Latin liberatus, past participle of liberare "set free," from liber "free" (see liberal). Meaning "to free an occupied territory from the enemy" (often used ironically) is from 1942. Related: Liberated; liberating.
entries.etymologyZh: 1620 年代, 源自 拉丁语 liberatus, 为 … 的过去分词 liberare "set free," 源自 liber "free" （参见 liberal). 义为 "to free an occupied territory from the enemy" (常 used ironically) 始于 1942 年. 同源词：Liberated; liberating.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "free choice, freedom to do as one chooses," from Old French liberté "freedom, liberty, free will" (14c.), from Latin libertatem (nominative libertas) "freedom, condition of a free man; absence of restraint; permission," from liber "free" (see liberal)Nautical sense of "leave of absence" is from 1758. To take liberties "go beyond the bounds of propriety" is from 1620s. Sense of "privileges by grant" (14c.) led to sense of "a person's private land" (mid-15c.), which yielded sense in 18c. in both England and America of "a district within a county but having its own justice of the peace," and also "a district adjacent to a city and in some degree under its municipal jurisdiction" (as in Northern Liberties of Philadelphia). Also compare Old French libertés "local rights, laws, taxes."

To take liberties "go beyond the bounds of propriety" 始于 1620 年代. 义为 "privileges by grant" (14 世纪) led to 语义 "a person's private land" (15 世纪中期), which yielded sense in 18 世纪 in both England and America of "a district within a county but having its own justice of the peace," and also "a district adjacent to a city and in some degree under its municipal jurisdiction" (as in Northern Liberties of Philadelphia). Also 对比 古法语 libertés "local rights, laws, taxes."

entries.etymology: "custodian of a library," 1713; see library + -an. Earlier form was library-keeper (1640s), and librarian was used earlier in a sense "scribe" (1660s).
entries.etymologyZh: "custodian of a library," 1713 年; 参见 library + -an. Earlier form was library-keeper (1640 年代), and librarian was used earlier in a sense "scribe" (1660 年代).

entries.etymology: place for books, late 14c., from Anglo-French librarie, Old French librairie "collection of books" (14c.), noun use of adj. librarius "concerning books," from Latin librarium "chest for books," from liber (genitive libri) "book, paper, parchment," originally "the inner bark of trees," probably a derivative of PIE root *leub(h)- "to strip, to peel" (see leaf). The equivalent word in most Romance languages now means "bookseller's shop." Old English had bochord, literally "book hord."

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "liberty (to do something), leave," from Old French licence "freedom, liberty, power, possibility; permission," (12c.), from Latin licentia "freedom, liberty, license," from licentem (nominative licens), present participle of licere "to be allowed, be lawful," from PIE root *leik- "to offer, bargain" (source also of Lettish likstu "I come to terms"). Meaning "formal (usually written) permission from authority to do something" (marry, hunt, drive, etc.) is first attested early 15c. Meaning "excessive liberty, disregard of propriety" is from mid-15c. There have been attempts to confine license to verbal use and licence to noun use (compare advise/advice, devise/device.

entries.etymology: mid-13c., from Old English hlid "lid, cover, opening, gate," from Proto-Germanic *khlithan (source also of Old Norse hlið "gate, gap," Swedish lid "gate," Old French hlid, Middle Dutch lit, Dutch lid, Old High German hlit "lid, cover"), from PIE root *klei- "to lean" (see lean (v.)), with here perhaps the sense of "that which bends over." Meaning "eyelid" is from early 13c. Slang sense of "hat, cap" is attested from 1896. Slang phrase put a lid on "clamp down on, silence, end" is from 1906.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "one who takes the place of another," from Old French lieu tenant "substitute, deputy," literally "placeholder," from lieu "place" (see lieu) + tenant, present participle of tenir "to hold" (see tenant). The notion is of a "substitute" for higher authority. Specific military sense of "officer next in rank to a captain" is from 1570s. Pronunciation with lef- is common in Britain, and spellings to reflect it date back to 14c., but the origin of this is a mystery (OED rejects suggestion that it comes from old confusion of -u- and -v-).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "one who takes the place of another," 源自 古法语 lieu tenant "substitute, deputy," 字面义为 "placeholder," 源自 lieu "place" （参见 lieu) + tenant, 为 … 的现在分词 tenir "to hold" （参见 tenant). The notion is of a "substitute" for higher authority. Specific military 语义 "officer next in rank to a captain" 始于 1570 年代. Pronunciation with lef- is common in Britain, and spellings to reflect it date back to 14 世纪, but the origin of this is a mystery (OED rejects suggestion that it comes 源自 old confusion of -u- and -v-).

example.en: The young lieutenant was put in charge of leading his platoon through the jungle.
example.zh: 这位年轻的中尉被任命带领他的排穿越丛林。

definitionLines: n. 生命；寿命，一生；生活， 生计；生物
entries.definition: n. 生命；寿命，一生；生活， 生计；生物
entries.etymology:
Old English life (dative lif) "existence, lifetime, way of life, condition of being a living thing, opposite of death," from Proto-Germanic *libam (source also of Old Norse lif "life, body," Dutch lijf "body," Old High German lib "life," German Leib "body"), properly "continuance, perseverance," from PIE *leip- "to remain, persevere, continue; stick, adhere" (see leave (v.)). Much of the modern range of meanings was present in Old English. Meaning "property which distinguishes living from non-living matter" is from 1560s. Sense of "vitality, energy" is from 1580s. Extended 1703 to "term of duration (of inanimate objects)."

Life-jacket is from 1840; life-preserver from 1630s of anything that is meant to save a life, 1803 of devices worn to prevent drowning. Life-saver is from 1883, figurative use from 1909, as a brand of hard sugar candy, from 1912, so called for shape. Life-form is from 1861. Life cycle is from 1855.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 life (dative lif) "existence, lifetime, way of life, condition of being a living thing, opposite of death," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *libam (source also of 古北欧语 lif "life, body," 荷兰语 lijf "body," 古高地德语 lib "life," 德语 Leib "body"), properly "continuance, perseverance," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *leip- "to remain, persevere, continue; stick, adhere" （参见 leave （动）). Much of the modern range of meanings was present in 古英语. 义为 "property which distinguishes living from non-living matter" 始于 1560 年代. 义为 "vitality, energy" 始于 1580 年代. Extended 1703 年 to "term of duration (of inanimate objects)." Life-jacket 始于 1840 年; life-preserver 源自 1630 年代 of anything that is meant to save a life, 1803 年 of devices worn to prevent drowning. Life-saver 始于 1883 年, figurative use 自 1909 年起, 作为 brand of hard sugar candy, 自 1912 年起, so called for shape. Life-form 始于 1861 年. Life cycle 始于 1855 年.

example.en: Regular exercise can significantly improve the quality of your life.
example.zh: 定期锻炼能显著提高你的生活质量。

entries.etymology: also life-style, 1929, from life (n.) + style (n.); originally a specific term used by Austrian psychologist Alfred Adler (1870-1937); broader sense is by 1961.
entries.etymologyZh: also life-style, 1929 年, 源自 life （名） + style （名）; 原义为 a specific term used by Austrian psychologist Alfred Adler (1870 年-1937 年); broader sense is 截至 1961 年.

example.en: Adopting a healthier lifestyle can reduce the risk of many chronic diseases.
example.zh: 采用更健康的生活方式可以降低许多慢性病的风险。

entries.etymology: also life-time, early 13c., from life (n.) + time (n.). One word from 19c. Old English had lifdæg in same sense, literally "life day."
entries.etymologyZh: also life-time, 13 世纪初, 源自 life （名） + time （名）. One word 源自 19 世纪 古英语 had lifdæg in same sense, 字面义为 "life day."

example.en: He dedicated his lifetime to protecting endangered species.
example.zh: 他将毕生精力献给了保护濒危物种的事业。

definitionLines: v. 提起，举起；消散，（云雾） 升起
n. 举起；升起；电梯，升降机； 搭便车
entries.definition: v. 提起，举起；消散，（云雾） 升起 n. 举起；升起；电梯，升降机； 搭便车
entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old Norse lypta "to raise," from Proto-Germanic *luftijan (source also of Middle Low German lüchten, Dutch lichten, German lüften "to lift;" Old English lyft "heaven, air," see loft). The meaning "steal" (as in shop-lift) is first recorded 1520s. Related: Lifted; lifting.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古北欧语 lypta "to raise," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *luftijan (source also of Middle Low 德语 lüchten, 荷兰语 lichten, 德语 lüften "to lift;" 古英语 lyft "heaven, air," 参见 loft). The 意为 "steal" (as in shop-lift) is 首见于 1520 年代. 同源词：Lifted; lifting.

example.en: It took three workers to lift the heavy machine into place.
example.zh: 需要三名工人才能把那台重机器抬到位置上。

definitionLines: n. 光，光亮，光线；灯，灯光
a.轻的；轻捷的，轻快的； 淡（色）的；明亮的
entries.definition: n. 光，光亮，光线；灯，灯光 vt. 点，点燃；照亮，照耀 a.轻的；轻捷的，轻快的； 淡（色）的；明亮的
entries.etymology:
"brightness, radiant energy," Old English leht, earlier leoht "light, daylight," from Proto-Germanic *leukhtam (source also of Old Saxon lioht, Old Frisian liacht, Middle Dutch lucht, Dutch licht, Old High German lioht, German Licht, Gothic liuhaþ "light"), from PIE *leuk- "light, brightness" (source also of Sanskrit rocate "shines;" Armenian lois "light," lusin "moon;" Greek leukos "bright, shining, white;" Latin lucere "to shine," lux "light," lucidus "clear;" Old Church Slavonic luci "light;" Lithuanian laukas "pale;" Welsh llug "gleam, glimmer;" Old Irish loche "lightning," luchair "brightness;" Hittite lukezi "is bright").

The -gh- was an Anglo-French scribal attempt to render the Germanic hard -h- sound, which has since disappeared from this word. The figurative spiritual sense was in Old English; the sense of "mental illumination" is first recorded mid-15c. Meaning "something used for igniting" is from 1680s. Meaning "a consideration which puts something in a certain view (as in in light of) is from 1680s. Something that's a joy and a delight has been the light of (someone's) eyes since Old English:

To see the light "come into the world" is from 1680s; later in a Christian sense.
entries.etymologyZh: "brightness, radiant energy," 古英语 leht, earlier leoht "light, daylight," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *leukhtam (source also of 古撒克逊语 lioht, 古弗里西语 liacht, Middle 荷兰语 lucht, 荷兰语 licht, 古高地德语 lioht, 德语 Licht, Gothic liuhaþ "light"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *leuk- "light, brightness" (source also of 梵语 rocate "shines;" Armenian lois "light," lusin "moon;" 希腊语 leukos "bright, shining, white;" 拉丁语 lucere "to shine," lux "light," lucidus "clear;" Old Church Slavonic luci "light;" Lithuanian laukas "pale;" Welsh llug "gleam, glimmer;" Old 爱尔兰语 loche "lightning," luchair "brightness;" Hittite lukezi "is bright"). The -gh- was an 盎格鲁-法语 scribal attempt to render the 日耳曼语 hard -h- sound, which has 自 disappeared 源自 this word. The figurative spiritual sense was in 古英语; the 语义 "mental illumination" is 首见于 15 世纪中期 义为 "something used for igniting" 始于 1680 年代. 义为 "a consideration which puts something in a certain view (as in in light of) is from 1680s. Something that's a joy and a delight has been the light of (someone's) eyes since Old English: To see the light "come into the world" 始于 1680 年代; later in a Christian sense.

example.en: The room was filled with warm light from the fireplace.
example.zh: 房间里充满了壁炉散发出的温暖光芒。

definitionLines: n. 照明；照明设备；舞台灯光； 点火
entries.definition: n. 照明；照明设备；舞台灯光； 点火
entries.etymology: "shining, illumination," Old English lihting, from leoht (see light (n.)).
entries.etymologyZh: "shining, illumination," 古英语 lihting, 源自 leoht （参见 light （名）).

example.en: The director adjusted the lighting to create a warmer atmosphere on stage.
example.zh: 导演调整了灯光，以在舞台上营造更温馨的氛围。

entries.definition: n. 闪电 a.闪电般的，快速的
entries.etymology: late 13c., present participle of lightnen "make bright," extended form of Old English lihting, from leht (see light (n.)). Meaning "cheap, raw whiskey" is attested from 1781, also sometimes "gin." Lightning bug is attested from 1778. Lightning rod from 1790.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, 为 … 的现在分词 lightnen "make bright," extended form of 古英语 lihting, 源自 leht （参见 light （名）). 义为 "cheap, raw whiskey" 见于 1781 年, also 有时 "gin." Lightning bug 见于 1778 年. Lightning rod 自 1790 年起.

example.en: A bolt of lightning struck the old oak tree during the storm.
example.zh: 暴风雨中一道闪电击中了那棵老橡树。

entries.definition: v. 喜爱，喜欢；想要 prep. 像，同……一样 a. 同样的，相似的
entries.etymology:
"having the same characteristics or qualities" (as another), Middle English shortening of Old English gelic "like, similar," from Proto-Germanic *galika- "having the same form," literally "with a corresponding body" (source also of Old Saxon gilik, Dutch gelijk, German gleich, Gothic galeiks "equally, like"), a compound of *ga- "with, together" + Germanic base *lik- "body, form; like, same" (source also of Old English lic "body," German Leiche "corpse," Danish lig, Swedish lik, Dutch lijk "body, corpse"). Analogous, etymologically, to Latin conform. The modern form (rather than *lich) may be from a northern descendant of the Old English word's Norse cognate, glikr.

Formerly with comparative liker and superlative likest (still in use 17c.). The preposition (c. 1200) and the adverb (c. 1300) both are from the adjective. As a conjunction, first attested early 16c. The word has been used as a postponed filler ("going really fast, like") from 1778; as a presumed emphatic ("going, like, really fast") from 1950, originally in counterculture slang and bop talk. Phrase more like it "closer to what is desired" is from 1888.
entries.etymologyZh: "having the same characteristics or qualities" (as another), 中古英语 shortening of 古英语 gelic "like, similar," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *galika- "having the same form," 字面义为 "with a corresponding body" (source also of 古撒克逊语 gilik, 荷兰语 gelijk, 德语 gleich, Gothic galeiks "equally, like"), a 由 … 复合而成 *ga- "with, together" + 日耳曼语 base *lik- "body, form; like, same" (source also of 古英语 lic "body," 德语 Leiche "corpse," Danish lig, Swedish lik, 荷兰语 lijk "body, corpse"). Analogous, etymologically, to 拉丁语 conform. The modern form (rather than *lich) may be 源自 a northern descendant of the 古英语 word's Norse 同源, glikr. Formerly with comparative liker and superlative likest (still in use 17 世纪). The preposition (约 1200 年) and the 副词 (约 1300 年) both 始于 the 形容词. 作为 conjunction, 最早见于 16 世纪初 The word has been used 作为 postponed filler ("going really fast, like") 自 1778 年起; 作为 presumed emphatic ("going, like, really fast") 自 1950 年起, 原义为 in counterculture 俚语 and bop talk. Phrase more like it "closer to what is desired" 始于 1888 年.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "resemblance, similarity," from likely + -hood. Meaning "probability" is from mid-15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "resemblance, similarity," 源自 likely + -hood. 义为 "probability" 始于 15 世纪中期

example.en: There is a high likelihood that the project will be completed on time.
example.zh: 该项目按时完成的可能性很高。

entries.definition: a. 可能的，有希望的 ad.大概，多半
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, perhaps from Old Norse likligr "likely," from likr "like" (see like (adj.)). Old English had cognate geliclic. Meaning "having the appearance of being strong and capable" is from mid-15c., though now mostly confined to American English; according to OED this sense is perhaps influenced by like (v.). Sense of "good-looking" is from late 15c. Meaning "probably" is attested from late 14c., now principally in American English.

As an adverb, late 14c., from the adjective.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 或源自 古北欧语 likligr "likely," 源自 likr "like" （参见 like （形）). 古英语 had 同源 geliclic. 义为 "having the appearance of being strong and capable" 始于 15 世纪中期, though 现在 mostly confined to American English; according to OED this sense is 或许 influenced by like （动）. 义为 "good-looking" 始于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "probably" 见于 14 世纪晚期, 现在 principally in American English. 作为 副词, 14 世纪晚期, 源自 形容词.

example.en: She is likely to arrive late because of the traffic.
example.zh: 由于交通拥堵，她可能会迟到。

definitionLines: ad. 同样地，照样地；又，也
entries.definition: ad. 同样地，照样地；又，也
entries.etymology: mid-15c., from the phrase in like wise "in the same manner" (mid-15c.), from like (adj.) + wise (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 phrase in like wise "in the same manner" (15 世纪中期), 源自 like （形） + wise （名）.

example.en: She donated to the charity, and her husband did likewise.
example.zh: 她向慈善机构捐款，她丈夫也同样如此。

example.en: The surgeon carefully repaired the broken limb with a metal plate.
example.zh: 外科医生用金属板仔细修复了断裂的肢体。

entries.definition: n. 界线，限度；（pL.）范围 vt. 限制，限定
entries.etymology: c. 1400, "boundary, frontier," from Old French limite "a boundary," from Latin limitem (nominative limes) "a boundary, limit, border, embankment between fields," related to limen "threshold." Originally of territory; general sense from early 15c. Colloquial sense of "the very extreme, the greatest degree imaginable" is from 1904.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "boundary, frontier," 源自 古法语 limite "a boundary," 源自 拉丁语 limitem (主格 limes) "a boundary, limit, border, embankment between fields," related to limen "threshold." Originally of territory; general sense 源自 15 世纪初 Colloquial 语义 "the very extreme, the greatest degree imaginable" 始于 1904 年.

example.en: The city ordinance limits the total height of new buildings to twelve floors.
example.zh: 市政法令将新建筑物的总高度限定在十二层。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French limitacion and directly from Latin limitationem (nominative limitatio), noun of action from past participle stem of limitare (see limit (v.)). Phrase statute of limitations attested by 1768.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 limitacion and 直接源自 拉丁语 limitationem (主格 limitatio), 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of limitare （参见 limit （动）). Phrase statute of limitations attested 截至 1768 年.

example.en: Every technology has its own limitation that engineers must work around.
example.zh: 每项技术都有其自身的局限性，工程师必须设法克服。

entries.etymology: 1550s, past participle adjective from limit (v.); as a stand-alone for limited express train, by 1883. Limited edition is from 1920; limited monarchy from 1640s; limited war is from 1948. In British company names, Limited (abbrev. Ltd.), 1855, is short for limited liability company, one in which the liability of partners is limited, usually to the amount of their capital investment.
entries.etymologyZh: 1550 年代, past participle 形容词 源自 limit （动）; 作为 stand-alone for limited express train, 截至 1883 年. Limited edition 始于 1920 年; limited monarchy 源自 1640 年代; limited war 始于 1948 年. In British company names, Limited (abbrev. Ltd.), 1855 年, is short for limited liability company, one in which the liability of partners is limited, 通常 to the amount of their capital investment.

example.en: The hospital has limited resources to treat all the patients.
example.zh: 医院的资源有限，无法救治所有患者。

entries.definition: a. 柔软的，易曲的 vi. 跛行
entries.etymology: 1560s, of unknown origin, perhaps related to Middle English lympen "to fall short" (c. 1400), which is probably from Old English lemphealt "halting, lame, limping," which has a lone cognate in the rare Middle High German limphin, and perhaps is from a PIE root meaning "slack, loose, to hang down" (source also of Sanskrit lambate "hangs down," Middle High German lampen "to hang down"). Related: Limped; limping. As a noun, 1818, from the verb.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, 来源不详, 或许 related to 中古英语 lympen "to fall short" (约 1400 年), which is 可能 源自 古英语 lemphealt "halting, lame, limping," which has a lone 同源 in the rare Middle High 德语 limphin, and 或许 始于 a 原始印欧语 (PIE) root 意为 "slack, loose, to hang down" (source also of 梵语 lambate "hangs down," Middle High 德语 lampen "to hang down"). 同源词：Limped; limping. 作名词时, 1818 年, 源自 动词.

definitionLines: n. 线，线条；界线；行，行列； 航线，交通线，通讯线
entries.definition: n. 线，线条；界线；行，行列； 航线，交通线，通讯线 v. 排队，排列
entries.etymology:
a Middle English merger of Old English line "cable, rope; series, row, row of letters; rule, direction," and Old French ligne "guideline, cord, string; lineage, descent;" both from Latin linea "linen thread, string, line," from phrase linea restis "linen cord," from fem. of lineus (adj.) "of linen," from linum "linen" (see linen).

Oldest sense is "rope, cord, string;" extended late 14c. to "a thread-like mark" (from sense "cord used by builders for making things level," mid-14c.), also "track, course, direction." Sense of "things or people arranged in a straight line" is from 1550s. That of "cord bearing hooks used in fishing" is from c. 1300. Meaning "one's occupation, branch of business" is from 1630s, probably from misunderstood KJV translation of 2 Cor. x:16, "And not to boast in another mans line of things made ready to our hand," where line translates Greek kanon, literally "measuring rod." Meaning "class of goods in stock" is from 1834. Meaning "telegraph wire" is from 1847 (later "telephone wire").

Meaning "policy or set of policies of a political faction" is 1892, American English, from notion of a procession of followers; this is the sense in party line. In British army, the Line (1802) is the regular, numbered troops, as distinguished from guards and auxiliaries. In the Navy (1704, as in ship of the line) it refers to the battle line. Lines "words of an actor's part" is from 1882. Lines of communication were originally transverse trenches in siegeworks.
entries.etymologyZh: a 中古英语 merger of 古英语 line "cable, rope; series, row, row of letters; rule, direction," and 古法语 ligne "guideline, cord, string; lineage, descent;" both 源自 拉丁语 linea "linen thread, string, line," 源自 phrase linea restis "linen cord," 源自 fem. of lineus （形） "of linen," 源自 linum "linen" （参见 linen). Oldest sense is "rope, cord, string;" extended 14 世纪晚期 to "a thread-like mark" (源自 sense "cord used by builders for making things level," 14 世纪中期), also "track, course, direction." 义为 "things or people arranged in a straight line" 始于 1550 年代. That of "cord bearing hooks used in fishing" 始于 约 1300 年. 义为 "one's occupation, branch of business" 始于 1630 年代, 可能 源自 misunderstood KJV translation of 2 Cor. x:16, "And not to boast in another mans line of things made ready to our hand," where line translates 希腊语 kanon, 字面义为 "measuring rod." 义为 "class of goods in stock" 始于 1834 年. 义为 "telegraph wire" 始于 1847 年 (later "telephone wire"). 义为 "policy or set of policies of a political faction" is 1892 年, American English, 源自 概念 a procession of followers; this is the sense in party line. In British army, the Line (1802 年) is the regular, numbered troops, as distinguished 源自 guards and auxiliaries. In the Navy (1704 年, as in ship of the line) it refers to the battle line. Lines "words of an actor's part" 始于 1882 年. Lines of communication were 原义为 transverse trenches in siegeworks.

example.en: A long line of people waited outside the store before it opened.
example.zh: 开门前，门外排着一长队人。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, lenger "reside, dwell," northern England frequentative of lengen "to tarry," from Old English lengan "prolong, lengthen," from Proto-Germanic *langjan "to make long" (source also of Old Frisian lendza, Old High German lengan, Dutch lengen "to lengthen"), source of Old English lang (see long (adj.)). Sense of "delay going, depart slowly and unwillingly" is from 1520s. Related: Lingered; lingering.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, lenger "reside, dwell," northern England 为 … 的反复体 lengen "to tarry," 源自 古英语 lengan "prolong, lengthen," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *langjan "to make long" (source also of 古弗里西语 lendza, 古高地德语 lengan, 荷兰语 lengen "to lengthen"), source of 古英语 lang （参见 long （形）). 义为 "delay going, depart slowly and unwillingly" 始于 1520 年代. 同源词：Lingered; lingering.

entries.definition: n. 环，链环；联系 v.连接，联系
entries.etymology: early 15c., "one of a series of rings or loops which form a chain; section of a cord," probably from Old Norse *hlenkr or a similar Scandinavian source (compare Old Norse hlekkr "link," Old Swedish lænker "chain, link," Norwegian lenke, Danish lænke), from Proto-Germanic *khlink- (source also of German lenken "to bend, turn, lead," gelenk "articulation, joint, link," Old English hlencan (plural) "armor"), from PIE root *kleng- "to bend, turn." Missing link between man and apes dates to 1880.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "one of a series of rings or loops which form a chain; section of a cord," 可能 源自 古北欧语 *hlenkr or a similar Scandinavian source (对比 古北欧语 hlekkr "link," Old Swedish lænker "chain, link," Norwegian lenke, Danish lænke), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *khlink- (source also of 德语 lenken "to bend, turn, lead," gelenk "articulation, joint, link," 古英语 hlencan (plural) "armor"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *kleng- "to bend, turn." Missing link between man and apes dates to 1880 年.

example.en: Researchers have found a clear link between poor sleep and memory problems.
example.zh: 研究人员发现睡眠不足与记忆问题之间存在明显联系。

entries.etymology:
late 12c., from Old French lion "lion," figuratively "hero," from Latin leonem (nominative leo) "lion; the constellation leo," from Greek leon (genitive leontos), from a non-Indo-European language, perhaps Semitic (compare Hebrew labhi "lion," plural lebaim; Egyptian labai, lawai "lioness").

A general Germanic borrowing from Latin (compare Old English leo, Anglian lea; Old Frisian lawa; Middle Dutch leuwe, Dutch leeuw; Old High German lewo, German Löwe); it is found in most European languages, often via Germanic (Old Church Slavonic livu, Polish lew, Czech lev, Old Irish leon, Welsh llew). Used figuratively from c. 1200 in an approving sense, "one who is fiercely brave," and a disapproving one, "tyrannical leader, greedy devourer." Lion's share "the greatest portion" is attested from 1701.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 lion "lion," figuratively "hero," 源自 拉丁语 leonem (主格 leo) "lion; the constellation leo," 源自 希腊语 leon (属格 leontos), 源自 a non-Indo-European language, 或许 Semitic (对比 希伯来语 labhi "lion," plural lebaim; Egyptian labai, lawai "lioness"). A general 日耳曼语 borrowing 源自 拉丁语 (对比 古英语 leo, Anglian lea; 古弗里西语 lawa; Middle 荷兰语 leuwe, 荷兰语 leeuw; 古高地德语 lewo, 德语 Löwe); it is found in most European languages, 常 经由 日耳曼语 (Old Church Slavonic livu, Polish lew, Czech lev, Old 爱尔兰语 leon, Welsh llew). Used figuratively 源自 约 1200 年 in an approving sense, "one who is fiercely brave," and a disapproving one, "tyrannical leader, greedy devourer." Lion's share "the greatest portion" 见于 1701 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English lippa, from Proto-Germanic *lepjon (source also of Old Frisian lippa, Middle Dutch lippe, Dutch lip, Old High German lefs, German Lefze, Swedish läpp, Danish læbe), from PIE *leb- "to lick; lip" (source also of Latin labium).

French lippe is from a Germanic source. Transferred sense of "edge or margin of a cup, etc." is from 1590s. Slang sense "saucy talk" is from 1821, probably from move the lip (1570s) "utter even the slightest word (against someone)." To bite (one's) lip "show vexation" is from early 14c. Stiff upper lip as a sign of courage is from 1833. Lip gloss is attested from 1939; lip balm from 1877. Related: Lips.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 lippa, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *lepjon (source also of 古弗里西语 lippa, Middle 荷兰语 lippe, 荷兰语 lip, 古高地德语 lefs, 德语 Lefze, Swedish läpp, Danish læbe), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *leb- "to lick; lip" (source also of 拉丁语 labium). 法语 lippe 始于 a 日耳曼语 source. Transferred 语义 "edge or margin of a cup, etc." 始于 1590 年代. Slang sense "saucy talk" 始于 1821 年, 可能 源自 move the lip (1570 年代) "utter even the slightest word (against someone)." To bite (one's) lip "show vexation" 始于 14 世纪初 Stiff upper lip 作为 sign of courage 始于 1833 年. Lip gloss 见于 1939 年; lip balm 自 1877 年起. 同源词：Lips.

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French liquide "liquid, running," from Latin liquidus "fluid, liquid, moist," figuratively "flowing, continuing," from liquere "be fluid," related to liqui "to melt, flow," from PIE *wleik- "to flow, run." Of sounds, from 1630s (the Latin word also was used of sounds). Financial sense of "capable of being converted to cash" is first recorded 1818.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, likur "any matter in a liquid state," from Old French licor "fluid, liquid; sap; oil" (Modern French liqueur), from Latin liquorem (nominative liquor) "liquidity, fluidity," also "a liquid, the sea," from liquere "be fluid, liquid" (see liquid (adj.)). Narrowed sense of "fermented or distilled drink" (especially wine) first recorded c. 1300. To liquor up "get drunk" is from 1845. The form in English has been assimilated to Latin, but the pronunciation has not changed.

entries.etymology: Old English hlysnan "to listen," from Proto-Germanic *khlusinon (source also of Dutch luisteren, Old High German hlosen "to listen," German lauschen "to listen"), from PIE root *kleu- "hearing, to hear" (source also of Sanskrit srnoti "hears," srosati "hears, obeys;" Avestan sraothra "ear;" Middle Persian srod "hearing, sound;" Lithuanian klausau "to hear," slove "splendor, honor;" Old Church Slavonic slusati "to hear," slava "fame, glory," slovo "word;" Greek klyo "hear, be called," kleos "report, rumor, fame glory," kleio "make famous;" Latin cluere "to hear oneself called, be spoken of;" Old Irish ro-clui-nethar "hears," clunim "I hear," clu "fame, glory," cluada "ears;" Welsh clywaf "I hear;" Old English hlud "loud," hleoðor "tone, tune;" Old High German hlut "sound;" Gothic hiluþ "listening, attention"). The -t- probably is by influence of Old English hlystan (see list (v.2)). For vowel evolution, see bury. As a noun from 1788 (on the listen "alert").

The -t- 可能 is by influence of 古英语 hlystan （参见 list (v.2)). For vowel evolution, 参见 bury. 作名词时 自 1788 年起 (on the listen "alert").

Erroneously used in reference to metaphors, hyperbole, etc., even by writers like Dryden and Pope, to indicate "what follows must be taken in the strongest admissible sense" (1680s), which is opposite to the word's real meaning and a long step down the path to the modern misuse of it.

definitionLines: n. 文学，文学作品；文献
entries.definition: n. 文学，文学作品；文献
entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Latin literatura/litteratura "learning, a writing, grammar," originally "writing formed with letters," from litera/littera "letter" (see letter (n.1)). Originally "book learning" (it replaced Old English boccræft), the meaning "literary production or work" is first attested 1779 in Johnson's "Lives of the English Poets" (he didn't include this definition in his dictionary, however); that of "body of writings from a period or people" is first recorded 1812.

Meaning "the whole of the writing on a particular subject" is from 1860; sense of "printed matter generally" is from 1895. The Latin word also is the source of Spanish literatura, Italian letteratura, German Literatur.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 拉丁语 literatura/litteratura "learning, a writing, grammar," 原义为 "writing formed with letters," 源自 litera/littera "letter" （参见 letter (n.1)). Originally "book learning" (it replaced 古英语 boccræft), the 意为 "literary production or work" is 最早见于 1779 年 in Johnson's "Lives of the English Poets" (he didn't include this definition in his dictionary, however); that of "body of writings from a period or people" is 首见于 1812 年. 义为 "the whole of the writing on a particular subject" 始于 1860 年; 语义 "printed matter generally" 始于 1895 年. The 拉丁语 word also is the source of 西班牙语 literatura, 意大利语 letteratura, 德语 Literatur.

definitionLines: a. 小，幼小；矮小，渺小；不多 的，少到几乎没有的
entries.definition: a. 小，幼小；矮小，渺小；不多 的，少到几乎没有的 ad./n. 不多，几乎没有
entries.etymology:
Old English lytel "not large, not much; short in distance or time; unimportant," also used in late Old English as a noun, "small piece; a short time," from Proto-Germanic *lutilla- (source also of Old Saxon luttil, Dutch luttel, Old High German luzzil, German lützel, Gothic leitils "little"), perhaps originally a diminutive of the root of Old English lyt "little, few," from PIE *leud- "small." "Often synonymous with small, but capable of emotional implications which small is not" [OED].

Phrase the little woman "wife" attested from 1795. Little people "the faeries" is from 1726; as "children," it is attested from 1752; as "ordinary people" (opposed to the great), it is attested from 1827. Little Neck clams (1884) are so called for Little Neck, Long Island, a "neck" of land on the island's North Shore. Little by little is from late 15c. (litylle be litille). Little green men "space aliens" is from 1950. Little black dress is from 1939.

Little Orphan Annie originally was (as Little Orphant Annie) the character in James Whitcomb Riley's 1885 poem, originally titled "Elf Child." The U.S. newspaper comic strip created by Harold Gray (1894-1968) debuted in 1924 in the New York "Daily News."

entries.definition: ci. 住，居住；生活，过活，生存 vt.过生活 a. 活的，有生命的；实况播送的
entries.etymology: Old English lifian (Anglian), libban (West Saxon) "to be, to live, have life; to experience," also "to supply oneself with food, to pass life (in some condition)," from Proto-Germanic *liben (source also of Old Norse lifa "to live, remain," Old Frisian libba, German leben, Gothic liban "to live"), from PIE root *leip- "to remain, continue" (source also of Greek liparein "to persist, persevere;" see leave). Meaning "to make a residence, dwell" is from c. 1200. Related: Lived; living.To live it up "live gaily and extravagantly" is from 1903. To live up to "act in accordance with" is 1690s, from earlier live up "live on a high (moral or mental) level" (1680s). To live (something) down "outwear (some slander or embarrassment)" is from 1842. To live with "cohabit as husband and wife" is attested from 1749; sense of "to put up with" is attested from 1937. Expression live and learn is attested from c. 1620.

To live up to "act in accordance with" is 1690 年代, 源自 earlier live up "live on a high (moral or mental) level" (1680 年代). To live (something) down "outwear (some slander or embarrassment)" 始于 1842 年. To live with "cohabit as husband and wife" 见于 1749 年; 语义 "to put up with" 见于 1937 年. Expression live and learn 见于 约 1620 年.

definitionLines: n. 负荷，负担；（一）担，（一）车
entries.definition: v.装，装载，装填 n. 负荷，负担；（一）担，（一）车
entries.etymology:
"that which is laid upon a person or beast, burden," c. 1200, from Old English lad "way, course, carrying," from Proto-Germanic *laitho (source also of Old High German leita, German leite, Old Norse leið "way, course"); related to Old English lædan "to guide," from PIE *leit- (2) "to go forth" (see lead (v.1)). Sense shifted 13c. to supplant words based on lade, to which it is not etymologically connected; original association with "guide" is preserved in lodestone. Meaning "amount customarily loaded at one time" is from c. 1300.

Figurative sense of "burden weighing on the mind, heart, or soul" is first attested 1590s. Meaning "amount of work" is from 1946. Colloquial loads "lots, heaps" is attested from c. 1600. Phrase take a load off (one's) feet "sit down, relax" is from 1914, American English. Get a load of "take a look at" is American English colloquial, attested from 1929.

Sense shifted 13 世纪 to supplant words based on lade, to which it is not etymologically connected; original association with "guide" is preserved in lodestone. 义为 "amount customarily loaded at one time" 始于 约 1300 年. entries.etymology: late 13c., from Old English hlaf "portion of bread baked in a mass of definite form," from Proto-Germanic *khlaibuz (source also of Old Norse hleifr, Swedish lev, Old Frisian hlef, Old High German hleib, German Laib, Gothic hlaifs "bread, loaf"), of uncertain origin, perhaps connected to Old English hlifian "to raise higher, tower," on the notion of the bread rising as it bakes, but it is unclear whether "loaf" or "bread" is the original sense. Finnish leipä, Old Church Slavonic chlebu, Lithuanian klepas probably are Germanic loan words. Meaning "chopped meat shaped like a bread loaf" is attested from 1787.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, 源自 古英语 hlaf "portion of bread baked in a mass of definite form," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *khlaibuz (source also of 古北欧语 hleifr, Swedish lev, 古弗里西语 hlef, 古高地德语 hleib, 德语 Laib, Gothic hlaifs "bread, loaf"), 来源存疑, 或许 connected to 古英语 hlifian "to raise higher, tower," on the 概念 the bread rising as it bakes, but it is unclear whether "loaf" or "bread" is the original sense. entries.definition: n. 贷款 v./n. 借出
entries.etymology:
mid-13c., from Old Norse lan, related to lja "to lend," from Proto-Germanic *laikhwniz (source also of Old Frisian len "thing lent," Middle Dutch lene, Dutch leen "loan, fief," Old High German lehan, German Lehn "fief, feudal tenure"), originally "to let have, to leave (to someone)," from PIE *leikw- "to leave" (see relinquish).

The Norse word also is cognate with Old English læn "gift," which did not survive into Middle English, but its derived verb lænan is the source of lend (v.). As a verb, loan is attested from 1540s, perhaps earlier, and formerly was current, but has now been supplanted in England by lend, though it survives in American English.

Loan word (1874) is a translation of German Lehnwort; loan-translation "word or phrase that has been translated literally from another language and which keeps its original connotation" is attested by 1933, from German Lehnübersetzung. Slang loan shark first attested 1900.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, 源自 古北欧语 lan, related to lja "to lend," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *laikhwniz (source also of 古弗里西语 len "thing lent," Middle 荷兰语 lene, 荷兰语 leen "loan, fief," 古高地德语 lehan, 德语 Lehn "fief, feudal tenure"), 原义为 "to let have, to leave (to someone)," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *leikw- "to leave" （参见 relinquish). The Norse word also is 与 … 同源 古英语 læn "gift," which did not survive into 中古英语, but its derived 动词 lænan is the source of lend （动）. 作动词时, loan 见于 1540 年代, 或许 earlier, and formerly was current, but has 现在 been supplanted in England by lend, though it survives in American English. Loan word (1874 年) is a translation of 德语 Lehnwort; loan-translation "word or phrase that has been translated literally from another language and which keeps its original connotation" is attested 截至 1933 年, 源自 德语 Lehnübersetzung. Slang loan shark 最早见于 1900 年.

example.en: She took out a loan to pay for her university education.
example.zh: 她贷款支付大学学费。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "cloister, covered walk," from Medieval Latin laubia, lobia "covered walk in a monastery," from a Germanic source (compare Old High German louba "hall, roof;" see lodge (n.)). Meaning "large entrance hall in a public building" is from 1590s. Political sense of "those who seek to influence legislation" is attested by 1790s in American English, in reference to the custom of influence-seekers gathering in large entrance-halls outside legislative chambers.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "cloister, covered walk," 源自 中古拉丁语 laubia, lobia "covered walk in a monastery," 源自 a 日耳曼语 source (对比 古高地德语 louba "hall, roof;" 参见 lodge （名）). 义为 "large entrance hall in a public building" 始于 1590 年代. Political 语义 "those who seek to influence legislation" is attested by 1790 年代 in American English, in reference to the custom of influence-seekers gathering in large entrance-halls outside legislative chambers.

example.en: Environmental groups plan to lobby Congress for stricter emissions standards.
example.zh: 环保团体计划游说国会制定更严格的排放标准。

definitionLines: a. 地方的，当地的；局部的
entries.definition: a. 地方的，当地的；局部的
entries.etymology: "pertaining to position," late 14c. (originally medical, "confined to a particular part of the body"), from Old French local (13c.) and directly from Late Latin localis "pertaining to a place," from Latin locus "place" (see locus). The meaning "limited to a particular place" is from c. 1500. Local color is from 1721, originally a term in painting; meaning "anything picturesque" is from c. 1900.
entries.etymologyZh: "pertaining to position," 14 世纪晚期 (原义为 medical, "confined to a particular part of the body"), 源自 古法语 local (13 世纪) and 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 localis "pertaining to a place," 源自 拉丁语 locus "place" （参见 locus). The 意为 "limited to a particular place" 始于 约 1500 年. Local color 始于 1721 年, 原义为 a term in painting; 意为 "anything picturesque" 始于 约 1900 年.

example.en: The local newspaper was the first to break the story about the factory closure.
example.zh: 当地报纸最先报道了工厂关闭的消息。

definitionLines: vt. 找出，查出；设置在，位于
entries.definition: vt. 找出，查出；设置在，位于
entries.etymology: 1650s, "to establish oneself in a place, settle," from Latin locatus, past participle of locare "to place, put, set, dispose, arrange," from locus "a place" (see locus). Sense of "mark the limits of a place" (especially a land grant) is attested from 1739 in American English; this developed to "establish (something) in a place" (1807) and "to find out the place of" (1882, American English). Related: Located; locating.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, "to establish oneself in a place, settle," 源自 拉丁语 locatus, 为 … 的过去分词 locare "to place, put, set, dispose, arrange," 源自 locus "a place" （参见 locus). 义为 "mark the limits of a place" (尤指 a land grant) 见于 1739 年 in American English; this developed to "establish (something) in a place" (1807 年) and "to find out the place of" (1882 年, American English). 同源词：Located; locating.

example.en: The new hospital will be located in the city center.
example.zh: 新医院将位于市中心。

definitionLines: n. 位置，地点；定位，测量
entries.definition: n. 位置，地点；定位，测量
entries.etymology: "position, place," 1590s, from Latin locationem (nominative locatio), noun of action from past participle stem of locare (see locate); Hollywood sense of "place outside a film studio where a scene is filmed" is from 1914.
entries.etymologyZh: "position, place," 1590 年代, 源自 拉丁语 locationem (主格 locatio), 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of locare （参见 locate); Hollywood 语义 "place outside a film studio where a scene is filmed" 始于 1914 年.

example.en: The new hospital was built in a central location for easy access.
example.zh: 新医院建在一个中心位置，方便人们前往。

entries.etymology: "to fasten with a lock," c. 1300, from Old English lucan "to lock, to close" (class II strong verb; past tense leac, past participle locen), from the same root as lock (n.1). Cognate with Old Frisian luka "to close," Old Saxon lukan, Old High German luhhan, Old Norse luka, Gothic galukan. Meaning "to embrace closely" is from 1610s. Related: Locked; locking. Slang lock horns "fight" is from 1839.
entries.etymologyZh: "to fasten with a lock," 约 1300 年, 源自 古英语 lucan "to lock, to close" (class II strong 动词; past tense leac, past participle locen), 源自 same root as lock (n.1). Cognate with 古弗里西语 luka "to close," 古撒克逊语 lukan, 古高地德语 luhhan, 古北欧语 luka, Gothic galukan. 义为 "to embrace closely" 始于 1610 年代. 同源词：Locked; locking. Slang lock horns "fight" 始于 1839 年.

example.en: Make sure to lock the door before you leave the office tonight.
example.zh: 今晚离开办公室前，务必锁好门。

entries.definition: vt. 供临时住宿 vi. 暂宿，借宿
entries.etymology:
mid-13c. in surnames and place names; late 13c. as "small building or hut," from Old French loge "arbor, covered walk; hut, cabin, grandstand at a tournament," from Frankish *laubja "shelter" (cognate with Old High German louba "porch, gallery," German Laube "bower, arbor"), from Proto-Germanic *laubja- "shelter," likely originally "shelter of foliage," or "roof made from bark," from root of leaf (n.).

"Hunter's cabin" sense is first recorded late 14c. Sense of "local branch of a society" is first recorded 1680s, from mid-14c. logge "workshop of masons." Also used of certain American Indian buildings, hence lodge-pole (1805). Feste of Logges (c. 1400) was a Middle English rendition of the Old Testament Jewish Feast of Tabernacles.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期 in surnames and place names; 13 世纪晚期 as "small building or hut," 源自 古法语 loge "arbor, covered walk; hut, cabin, grandstand at a tournament," 源自 Frankish *laubja "shelter" (与 … 同源 古高地德语 louba "porch, gallery," 德语 Laube "bower, arbor"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *laubja- "shelter," likely 原义为 "shelter of foliage," or "roof made from bark," 源自 root of leaf （名）. "Hunter's cabin" sense is 首见于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "local branch of a society" is 首见于 1680 年代, 源自 14 世纪中期 logge "workshop of masons." Also used of certain American Indian buildings, hence lodge-pole (1805 年). Feste of Logges (约 1400 年) was a 中古英语 rendition of the Old Testament Jewish Feast of Tabernacles.

entries.etymology: "exalted, of high rank," early 15c.; also "with a high purpose," from loft + -y (2). From early 14c. as a surname. Literal sense of "high" is attested from 1580s. Related: Loftily; loftiness.
entries.etymologyZh: "exalted, of high rank," 15 世纪初; also "with a high purpose," 源自 loft + -y (2). From 14 世纪初 作为 surname. Literal 语义 "high" 见于 1580 年代. 同源词：Loftily; loftiness.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "branch of philosophy that treats of forms of thinking," from Old French logique (13c.), from Latin (ars) logica, from Greek logike (techne) "reasoning (art)," from fem. of logikos "pertaining to speaking or reasoning," from logos "reason, idea, word" (see logos). Meaning "logical argumentation" is from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "branch of philosophy that treats of forms of thinking," 源自 古法语 logique (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 (ars) logica, 源自 希腊语 logike (techne) "reasoning (art)," 源自 fem. of logikos "pertaining to speaking or reasoning," 源自 logos "reason, idea, word" （参见 logos). 义为 "logical argumentation" 始于 约 1600 年.

example.en: His argument lacks logic and fails to convince anyone.
example.zh: 他的论点缺乏逻辑，无法说服任何人。

definitionLines: a. 逻辑（上）的，符合逻辑的
entries.definition: a. 逻辑（上）的，符合逻辑的 10g0 n. 商标，徽标
entries.etymology: early 15c., "based on reason," from logic + -al (1). Meaning "pertaining to logic" is c. 1500. Attested from 1860 as "following as a reasonable consequence." Related: Logically.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "based on reason," 源自 logic + -al (1). 义为 "pertaining to logic" is 约 1500 年. Attested 自 1860 年起 as "following as a reasonable consequence." 同源词：Logically.

example.en: It seems logical to assume that demand will rise when prices fall.
example.zh: 假设价格下降时需求会上升，这似乎是符合逻辑的。

definitionLines: a. 孤独，寂寞；荒凉，人迹稀少
entries.definition: a. 孤独，寂寞；荒凉，人迹稀少
entries.etymology: c. 1600, "solitary, lone," from lone + -ly (1). Meaning "dejected for want of company" is from 1811. Lonely heart (n.) "a lonely-hearted person" is from 1922. Lonely hearted (adj.) is attested from 1820.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "solitary, lone," 源自 lone + -ly (1). 义为 "dejected for want of company" 始于 1811 年. Lonely heart （名） "a lonely-hearted person" 始于 1922 年. Lonely hearted （形） 见于 1820 年.

example.en: Living far from family made her feel lonely and isolated.
example.zh: 远离家人让她感到孤独和与世隔绝。

entries.definition: a.长的，长远的；长期的 ad. 长久地，长期地 vi.渴望，极想
entries.etymology:
"that extends considerably from end to end," Old English lang "long," from Proto-Germanic *langgaz (source also of Old Frisian and Old Saxon lang, Old High German and German lang, Old Norse langr, Middle Dutch lanc, Dutch lang, Gothic laggs "long").

The Germanic words are perhaps from PIE *dlonghos- (source also of Latin longus, Old Persian darga-, Persian dirang, Sanskrit dirghah, Greek dolikhos "long," Greek endelekhes "perpetual," Latin indulgere "to indulge"), from root *del- "long."

The adverb is from Old English lange, longe, from the adjective. No longer "not as formerly" is from c. 1300; to be not long for this world "soon to die" is from 1714.

The word illustrates the Old English tendency for short "a" to become short "o" before -n- (also retained in bond/band and West Midlands dialectal lond from land and hond from hand).

Long vowels (c. 1000) originally were pronounced for an extended time. Sporting long ball is from 1744, originally in cricket. Long jump as a sporting event is attested from 1864. A ship's long-boat so called from 1510s. Long knives, name Native Americans gave to white settlers (originally in Virginia/Kentucky) is from 1774.
Long in the tooth (1841 of persons) is from horses showing age by recession of gums. Long time no see, imitative of American Indian speech, is first recorded 1900. To be long on something, "have a lot" of it, is from 1900, American English slang.
entries.etymologyZh: "that extends considerably from end to end," 古英语 lang "long," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *langgaz (source also of 古弗里西语 and 古撒克逊语 lang, 古高地德语 and 德语 lang, 古北欧语 langr, Middle 荷兰语 lanc, 荷兰语 lang, Gothic laggs "long"). The 日耳曼语 words are 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *dlonghos- (source also of 拉丁语 longus, Old 波斯语 darga-, 波斯语 dirang, 梵语 dirghah, 希腊语 dolikhos "long," 希腊语 endelekhes "perpetual," 拉丁语 indulgere "to indulge"), 源自 root *del- "long." The 副词 始于 古英语 lange, longe, 源自 形容词. No longer "not as formerly" 始于 约 1300 年; to be not long for this world "soon to die" 始于 1714 年. The word illustrates the 古英语 tendency for short "a" to become short "o" before -n- (also retained in bond/band and West Midlands 方言 lond 源自 land and hond 源自 hand). Long vowels (约 1000 年) 原义为 were pronounced for an extended time. Sporting long ball 始于 1744 年, 原义为 in cricket. Long jump 作为 sporting event 见于 1864 年. A ship's long-boat so called 源自 1510 年代. Long knives, name Native Americans gave to white settlers (原义为 in Virginia/Kentucky) 始于 1774 年. Long in the tooth (1841 年 of persons) 始于 horses showing age by recession of gums. Long time no 参见, imitative of American Indian speech, is 首见于 1900 年. To be long on something, "have a lot" of it, 始于 1900 年, American English 俚语.

example.en: After years abroad, she longed to return to her hometown and see her parents.
example.zh: 在海外多年后，她渴望回到故乡看望父母。

entries.etymology: 1610s, from Late Latin longaevitatem (nominative longaevitas) "great age, long life," from Latin longaevus "long-lived," from longus (see long (adj.)) + aevum "lifetime, age" (see eon).
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, 源自 晚期拉丁语 longaevitatem (主格 longaevitas) "great age, long life," 源自 拉丁语 longaevus "long-lived," 源自 longus （参见 long （形）) + aevum "lifetime, age" （参见 eon).

entries.etymology: late 14c., "length," from Latin longitudo "length, duration," from longus (see long (adj.)). For origins, see latitude.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "length," 源自 拉丁语 longitudo "length, duration," 源自 longus （参见 long （形）). For origins, 参见 latitude.

entries.definition: vi. /n. （at）看，注视 v. 好像，显得 n. 脸色，外表
entries.etymology:
Old English locian "use the eyes for seeing, gaze, look, behold, spy," from West Germanic *lokjan (source also of Old Saxon lokon "see, look, spy," Middle Dutch loeken "to look," Old High German luogen, German dialectal lugen "to look out"), of unknown origin, perhaps cognate with Breton lagud "eye." In Old English, usually with on; the use of at began 14c. Meaning "seek, search out" is c. 1300; meaning "to have a certain appearance" is from c. 1400. Of objects, "to face in a certain direction," late 14c.

Look after "take care of" is from late 14c., earlier "to seek" (c. 1300), "to look toward" (c. 1200). Look into "investigate" is from 1580s; look up "research in books or papers" is from 1690s. To look down upon in the figurative sense is from 1711; to look down one's nose is from 1921. To look forward "anticipate" is c. 1600; meaning "anticipate with pleasure" is mid-19c. To not look back "make no pauses" is colloquial, first attested 1893. In look sharp (1711) sharp originally was an adverb, "sharply."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 locian "use the eyes for seeing, gaze, look, behold, spy," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *lokjan (source also of 古撒克逊语 lokon "see, look, spy," Middle 荷兰语 loeken "to look," 古高地德语 luogen, 德语 方言 lugen "to look out"), 来源不详, 或许 与 … 同源 Breton lagud "eye." In 古英语, 通常 with on; the use of at began 14 世纪 义为 "seek, search out" is 约 1300 年; 意为 "to have a certain appearance" 始于 约 1400 年. Of objects, "to face in a certain direction," 14 世纪晚期 Look after "take care of" 始于 14 世纪晚期, earlier "to seek" (约 1300 年), "to look toward" (约 1200 年). Look into "investigate" 始于 1580 年代; look up "research in books or papers" 始于 1690 年代. To look down upon in the figurative sense 始于 1711 年; to look down one's nose 始于 1921 年. To look forward "anticipate" is 约 1600 年; 意为 "anticipate with pleasure" is 19 世纪中期 To not look back "make no pauses" is 口语, 最早见于 1893 年. In look sharp (1711 年) sharp 原义为 was an 副词, "sharply."

example.en: You look exhausted today; you should rest after this meeting.
example.zh: 你今天看起来筋疲力尽，这个会议结束后应该好好休息。

definitionLines: z。朦胧地出现；隐约可见；可 怕地出现
entries.definition: z。朦胧地出现；隐约可见；可 怕地出现
entries.etymology: weaving machine, Old English geloma "utensil, tool," from ge-, perfective prefix, + -loma, of unknown origin (compare Old English andloman (plural) "apparatus, furniture"). Originally "implement or tool of any kind" (as in heirloom); thus, "the penis" (c. 1400-1600). Specific meaning "a machine in which yarn or thread is woven into fabric" is from c. 1400.
entries.etymologyZh: weaving machine, 古英语 geloma "utensil, tool," 源自 ge-, perfective prefix, + -loma, 来源不详 (对比 古英语 andloman (plural) "apparatus, furniture"). Originally "implement or tool of any kind" (as in heirloom); thus, "the penis" (约 1400 年-1600 年). Specific 意为 "a machine in which yarn or thread is woven into fabric" 始于 约 1400 年.

example.en: Dark storm clouds began to loom on the horizon.
example.zh: 黑暗的乌云开始在地平线上隐约显现。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "loop of cloth, rope, leather, etc.," probably of Celtic origin (compare Gaelic lub "bend," Irish lubiam), influenced by or blended with Old Norse hlaup "a leap, run" (see leap (v.)). In reference to magnetic recording tape or film, first recorded 1931. Computer programming sense first attested 1947.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "loop of cloth, rope, leather, etc.," 可能 of Celtic origin (对比 Gaelic lub "bend," 爱尔兰语 lubiam), influenced by or blended with 古北欧语 hlaup "a leap, run" （参见 leap （动）). In reference to magnetic recording tape or film, 首见于 1931 年. Computer programming sense 最早见于 1947 年.

entries.etymology:
early 13c., "not securely fixed;" c. 1300, "unbound," from Old Norse lauss "loose, free, vacant, dissolute," cognate with Old English leas "devoid of, false, feigned, incorrect," from Proto-Germanic *lausaz (source also of Danish løs "loose, untied," Swedish lös "loose, movable, detached," Middle Dutch, German los "loose, free," Gothic laus "empty, vain"), from PIE *leu- "to loosen, divide, cut apart" (see lose). Meaning "not clinging, slack" is mid-15c. Meaning "not bundled" is late 15c. Sense of "unchaste, immoral" is recorded from late 15c. Meaning "at liberty, free from obligation" is 1550s. Sense of "rambling, disconnected" is from 1680s. Figurative sense of loose cannon was in use by 1896, probably from celebrated image in a popular story by Hugo:

Loose end in reference to something unfinished, undecided, unguarded is from 1540s; to be at loose ends is from 1807. Phrase on the loose "free, unrestrained" is from 1749 (upon the loose).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "not securely fixed;" 约 1300 年, "unbound," 源自 古北欧语 lauss "loose, free, vacant, dissolute," 与 … 同源 古英语 leas "devoid of, false, feigned, incorrect," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *lausaz (source also of Danish løs "loose, untied," Swedish lös "loose, movable, detached," Middle 荷兰语, 德语 los "loose, free," Gothic laus "empty, vain"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *leu- "to loosen, divide, cut apart" （参见 lose). 义为 "not clinging, slack" is 15 世纪中期 义为 "not bundled" is 15 世纪晚期 义为 "unchaste, immoral" 见于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "at liberty, free from obligation" is 1550 年代. 义为 "rambling, disconnected" 始于 1680 年代. Figurative 语义 loose cannon was in use 截至 1896 年, 可能 源自 celebrated image in a popular story by Hugo: Loose end in reference to something unfinished, undecided, unguarded 始于 1540 年代; to be at loose ends 始于 1807 年. Phrase on the loose "free, unrestrained" 始于 1749 年 (upon the loose).

example.en: Pull the rope tight — it's too loose to hold anything.
example.zh: 把绳子拉紧——它太松了，什么都固定不住。

entries.etymology: late 14c., losnen, later lousen (early 15c.), from loose (v.) + -en (1). Related: Loosened; loosening.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, losnen, later lousen (15 世纪初), 源自 loose （动） + -en (1). 同源词：Loosened; loosening.

example.en: Please loosen the rope so the boat can drift away from the dock.
example.zh: 请把绳子松开，这样船就能从码头漂走了。

entries.etymology: mid-13c., laverd, loverd, from Old English hlaford "master of a household, ruler, superior," also "God" (translating Latin Dominus, though Old English drihten was used more often), earlier hlafweard, literally "one who guards the loaves," from hlaf "bread, loaf" (see loaf (n.)) + weard "keeper, guardian" (see ward (n.)). Compare lady (literally "bread-kneader"), and Old English hlafæta "household servant," literally "loaf-eater." Modern monosyllabic form emerged 14c. As an interjection from late 14c. Lord's Prayer is from 1540s. Lord of the Flies translates Beelzebub (q.v.) and was name of 1954 book by William Golding. To drink like a lord is from 1620s.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, laverd, loverd, 源自 古英语 hlaford "master of a household, ruler, superior," also "God" (translating 拉丁语 Dominus, though 古英语 drihten was used more 常), earlier hlafweard, 字面义为 "one who guards the loaves," 源自 hlaf "bread, loaf" （参见 loaf （名）) + weard "keeper, guardian" （参见 ward （名）). 对比 lady (字面义为 "bread-kneader"), and 古英语 hlafæta "household servant," 字面义为 "loaf-eater." 现代 monosyllabic form emerged 14 世纪 作为 interjection 源自 14 世纪晚期 Lord's Prayer 始于 1540 年代. Lord of the Flies translates Beelzebub (q.v.) and was name of 1954 年 book by William Golding. To drink like a lord 始于 1620 年代.

entries.etymology: "a truck; a long, flat wagon," 1838, British railroad word, probably from verb lurry "to pull, tug" (1570s), of uncertain origin. Meaning "large motor vehicle for carrying goods" is first attested 1911.
entries.etymologyZh: "a truck; a long, flat wagon," 1838 年, British railroad word, 可能 源自 动词 lurry "to pull, tug" (1570 年代), 来源存疑. 义为 "large motor vehicle for carrying goods" is 最早见于 1911 年.

definitionLines: vt. 丢，丢失，丧失；失败，输； 迷（路）
entries.definition: vt. 丢，丢失，丧失；失败，输； 迷（路）
entries.etymology:
Old English losian "be lost, perish," from los "destruction, loss," from Proto-Germanic *lausa- (source also of Old Norse los "the breaking up of an army;" Old English forleosan "to lose, destroy," Old Frisian forliasa, Old Saxon farliosan, Middle Dutch verliesen, Old High German firliosan, German verlieren), from PIE root *leu- "to loosen, divide, cut apart, untie, separate" (source also of Sanskrit lunati "cuts, cuts off," lavitram "sickle;" Greek lyein "to loosen, untie, slacken," lysus "a loosening;" Latin luere "to loose, release, atone for, expiate").

Replaced related leosan (a class II strong verb whose past participle loren survives in forlorn and lovelorn), from Proto-Germanic *leusanan (source also of Old High German virliosan, German verlieren, Old Frisian urliasa, Gothic fraliusan "to lose").

Transitive sense of "to part with accidentally" is from c. 1200. Meaning "fail to maintain" is from mid-15c. Meaning "to be defeated" (in a game, etc.) is from 1530s. Meaning "to cause (someone) to lose his way" is from 1640s. To lose (one's) mind "become insane" is attested from c. 1500. To lose out "fail" is 1858, American English. Related: Lost; losing.

Replaced related leosan (a class II strong 动词 whose past participle loren survives in forlorn and lovelorn), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *leusanan (source also of 古高地德语 virliosan, 德语 verlieren, 古弗里西语 urliasa, Gothic fraliusan "to lose"). Transitive 语义 "to part with accidentally" 始于 约 1200 年. 义为 "fail to maintain" 始于 15 世纪中期 义为 "to be defeated" (in a game, etc.) 始于 1530 年代. 义为 "to cause (someone) to lose his way" 始于 1640 年代. To lose (one's) mind "become insane" 见于 约 1500 年. To lose out "fail" is 1858 年, American English. 同源词：Lost; losing.

definitionLines: n. 丧失，丢失；亏损，损失；失败
entries.definition: n. 丧失，丢失；亏损，损失；失败
entries.etymology: Old English los "loss, destruction," from Proto-Germanic *lausa- (see lose). The modern word, however, probably evolved 14c. with a weaker sense, from lost, the original past participle of lose. Phrase at a loss (1590s) originally refers to hounds losing the scent. To cut (one's) losses is from 1885, originally in finance.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 los "loss, destruction," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *lausa- （参见 lose). The modern word, however, 可能 evolved 14 世纪 with a weaker sense, 源自 lost, the original 为 … 的过去分词 lose. Phrase at a loss (1590 年代) 原义为 refers to hounds losing the scent. To cut (one's) losses 始于 1885 年, 原义为 in finance.

example.en: The company reported a net loss of two million dollars this year.
example.zh: 该公司今年报告了净亏损两百万美元。

definitionLines: 《.失去的；错过的，浪费掉的； 无望的，迷路的
entries.definition: 《.失去的；错过的，浪费掉的； 无望的，迷路的
entries.etymology: "defeated," c. 1300; "wasted, spent in vain," c. 1500; also "no longer to be found" (1520s), from past participle of lose. Lost Cause in reference to the Southern U.S. bid for independence is from the title of E.A. Pollard's history of the CSA and the rebellion (1866). Lost Generation in reference to the period 1914-18 first attested 1926 in Hemingway's "The Sun Also Rises," where he credits it to Gertrude Stein. Lost-and-found as the name of a department where misplaced articles are brought or sought is by 1907.
