definitionLines: a. 较小的，较少的，较次要的
entries.definition: a. 较小的，较少的，较次要的 n. 辅修学科 vi.辅修
entries.etymology:
early 13c., menour "Franciscan" (see minor (n.)), from Latin minor "less, lesser, smaller, junior," figuratively "inferior, less important," formed as a masculine/feminine form of minus on the mistaken assumption that minus was a neuter comparative, from PIE root *mei- (2) "small" (see minus).

Some English usages are via Old French menor "less, smaller, lower; underage, younger," from Latin minor. Meaning "underage" is from 1570s. Meaning "lesser" in English is from early 15c.; that of "less important" is from 1620s. The musical sense is from 1690s. In the baseball sense, minor league is from 1884; the figurative extension is first recorded 1926.

Some English usages are 经由 古法语 menor "less, smaller, lower; underage, younger," 源自 拉丁语 minor. 义为 "underage" 始于 1570 年代. 义为 "lesser" in English 始于 15 世纪初; that of "less important" 始于 1620 年代. The musical sense 始于 1690 年代. In the baseball sense, minor league 始于 1884 年; the figurative extension is 首见于 1926 年.

example.en: The delay caused only minor inconvenience, lasting less than five minutes.
example.zh: 延误只造成了轻微的不便，持续不到五分钟。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "condition of being smaller," from Middle French minorité (15c.), or directly from Medieval Latin minoritatem (nominative minoritas), from Latin minor (see minor (adj.)). Meaning "state of being under legal age" is from 1540s; that of "smaller number or part" is from 1736. The meaning "group of people separated from the rest of a community by race, religion, language, etc." is from 1919, originally in an Eastern European context.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "condition of being smaller," 源自 中古法语 minorité (15 世纪)，或直接源自 中古拉丁语 minoritatem (主格 minoritas), 源自 拉丁语 minor （参见 minor （形）). 义为 "state of being under legal age" 始于 1540 年代; that of "smaller number or part" 始于 1736 年. The 意为 "group of people separated from the rest of a community by race, religion, language, etc." 始于 1919 年, 原义为 in an Eastern European context.

example.en: The policy was criticized for failing to protect the rights of ethnic minority groups.
example.zh: 该政策因未能保护少数民族群体的权利而受到批评。

entries.etymology: "to stamp metal to make coins," 1540s, from mint (n.2). Related: Minted; minting. Minter "one who stamps coins to create money" is from early 12c.
entries.etymologyZh: "to stamp metal to make coins," 1540 年代, 源自 mint (n.2). 同源词：Minted; minting. Minter "one who stamps coins to create money" 始于 12 世纪初

entries.definition: a. 減的，负的 prep. 减去 n. 减号，负号
entries.etymology:
late 15c., "with subtraction of," from Latin minus "less," neuter of minor "smaller," from PIE *mi-nu-, suffixed form of root *mei- (2) "small" (source also of Latin minuere "to diminish, reduce, lessen," Greek meion "less, smaller," Old English minsian "to diminish," Sanskrit miyate "diminishes, declines," Russian men'she "less").

Mathematical use in expressions of calculation did not exist in the word in classical Latin and is probably from North Sea medieval commercial usage of Latin plus and minus to indicate surplus or deficiency of weight or measure. Origin of the "minus sign" is disputed.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "with subtraction of," 源自 拉丁语 minus "less," neuter of minor "smaller," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *mi-nu-, suffixed form of root *mei- (2) "small" (source also of 拉丁语 minuere "to diminish, reduce, lessen," 希腊语 meion "less, smaller," 古英语 minsian "to diminish," 梵语 miyate "diminishes, declines," 俄语 men'she "less"). Mathematical use in expressions of calculation did not exist in the word in classical 拉丁语 and is 可能 源自 North Sea medieval commercial usage of 拉丁语 plus and minus to indicate surplus or deficiency of weight or measure. Origin of the "minus sign" is disputed.

definitionLines: n. 分，分钟；一会儿，片刻
entries.definition: n. 分，分钟；一会儿，片刻
entries.etymology: "sixtieth part of an hour or degree," late 14c., from Old French minut (13c.) or directly from Medieval Latin minuta "minute, short note," from Latin minuta, noun use of fem. of minutus "small, minute" (see minute (adj.)). In Medieval Latin, pars minuta prima "first small part" was used by mathematician Ptolemy for one-sixtieth of a circle, later of an hour (next in order was secunda minuta, which became second (n.)). German Minute, Dutch minuut also are from French. Used vaguely for "short time" from late 14c. As a measure expressing distance (travel time) by 1886. Minute hand is attested from 1726.
entries.etymologyZh: "sixtieth part of an hour or degree," 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 minut (13 世纪) or 直接源自 中古拉丁语 minuta "minute, short note," 源自 拉丁语 minuta, 为 … 的名词用法 fem. of minutus "small, minute" （参见 minute （形）). In 中古拉丁语, pars minuta prima "first small part" was used by mathematician Ptolemy for one-sixtieth of a circle, later of an hour (next in order was secunda minuta, which became second （名）). 德语 Minute, 荷兰语 minuut also 始于 法语. Used vaguely for "short time" 源自 14 世纪晚期 作为 measure expressing distance (travel time) 截至 1886 年. Minute hand 见于 1726 年.

example.en: Please hold on a minute while I transfer your call to the manager.
example.zh: 请稍等片刻，我将把您的电话转接给经理。

definitionLines: n. 奇迹，令人惊奇的人/事
entries.definition: n. 奇迹，令人惊奇的人/事
entries.etymology:
mid-12c., "a wondrous work of God," from Old French miracle (11c.) "miracle, story of a miracle, miracle play," from Latin miraculum "object of wonder" (in Church Latin, "marvelous event caused by God"), from mirari "to wonder at, marvel, be astonished," figuratively "to regard, esteem," from mirus "wonderful, astonishing, amazing," earlier *smeiros, from PIE *smei- "to smile, laugh" (source also of Sanskrit smerah "smiling," Greek meidan "to smile," Old Church Slavonic smejo "to laugh;" see smile (v.)).

From mid-13c. as "extraordinary or remarkable feat," without regard to deity. Replaced Old English wundortacen, wundorweorc. The Greek words rendered as miracle in the English bibles were semeion "sign," teras "wonder," and dynamis "power," in Vulgate translated respectively as signum, prodigium, and virtus. The Latin word is the source of Spanish milagro, Italian miracolo.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪中期, "a wondrous work of God," 源自 古法语 miracle (11 世纪) "miracle, story of a miracle, miracle play," 源自 拉丁语 miraculum "object of wonder" (in 教会拉丁语, "marvelous event caused by God"), 源自 mirari "to wonder at, marvel, be astonished," figuratively "to regard, esteem," 源自 mirus "wonderful, astonishing, amazing," earlier *smeiros, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *smei- "to smile, laugh" (source also of 梵语 smerah "smiling," 希腊语 meidan "to smile," Old Church Slavonic smejo "to laugh;" 参见 smile （动）). From 13 世纪中期 as "extraordinary or remarkable feat," without regard to deity. Replaced 古英语 wundortacen, wundorweorc. The 希腊语 words rendered as miracle in the English bibles were semeion "sign," teras "wonder," and dynamis "power," in Vulgate translated respectively as signum, prodigium, and virtus. The 拉丁语 word is the source of 西班牙语 milagro, 意大利语 miracolo.

example.en: It was a miracle that all the passengers survived the crash.
example.zh: 所有乘客在坠机中幸存下来，这真是一个奇迹。

definitionLines: a. 不可思议的，奇迹的
entries.definition: a. 不可思议的，奇迹的
entries.etymology: mid-15c., from Middle French miraculeux, from Medieval Latin miraculosus, from Latin miraculum "miracle, marvel, wonder" (see miracle). Related:  Miraculously (early 15c.); miraculousness.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 中古法语 miraculeux, 源自 中古拉丁语 miraculosus, 源自 拉丁语 miraculum "miracle, marvel, wonder" （参见 miracle). 同源词：Miraculously (15 世纪初); miraculousness.

entries.etymology:
early 13c., from Old French mireoir "a reflecting glass, looking glass; observation, model, example," earlier miradoir (11c.), from mirer "look at" (oneself in a mirror), "observe, watch, contemplate," from Vulgar Latin *mirare "to look at," variant of Latin mirari "to wonder at, admire" (see miracle).

The Spanish cognate, mirador (from mirar "to look, look at, behold"), has come to mean "watch tower." Latin speculum "mirror" is the source of words for "mirror" in neighboring languages: Italian specchio, Spanish espejo, Old High German spiegal, German Spiegel, Dutch spiegel, Danish spejl, Swedish spegel. An ancient Germanic group of words for "mirror" is represented by Gothic skuggwa, Old Norse skuggsja, Old High German scucar, which are related to Old English scua "shade, shadow."

Figurative usage is attested from c. 1300. Used in divination since classical and biblical times; mirrors in modern England are the subject of at least 14 known superstitions, according to folklorists. Belief that breaking one brings bad luck is attested from 1777. Mirror ball attested from 1968.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 古法语 mireoir "a reflecting glass, looking glass; observation, model, example," earlier miradoir (11 世纪), 源自 mirer "look at" (oneself in a mirror), "observe, watch, contemplate," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *mirare "to look at," 为 … 的变体 拉丁语 mirari "to wonder at, admire" （参见 miracle). The 西班牙语 同源, mirador (源自 mirar "to look, look at, behold"), has come to mean "watch tower." 拉丁语 speculum "mirror" is the source of words for "mirror" in neighboring languages: 意大利语 specchio, 西班牙语 espejo, 古高地德语 spiegal, 德语 Spiegel, 荷兰语 spiegel, Danish spejl, Swedish spegel. An ancient 日耳曼语 group of words for "mirror" is represented by Gothic skuggwa, 古北欧语 skuggsja, 古高地德语 scucar, which are related to 古英语 scua "shade, shadow." Figurative usage 见于 约 1300 年. Used in divination 自 classical and biblical times; mirrors in modern England are the subject of at least 14 known superstitions, according to folklorists. Belief that breaking one brings bad luck 见于 1777 年. Mirror ball attested 自 1968 年起.

example.en: She checked her hair in the mirror before leaving the house.
example.zh: 她在出门前对着镜子检查了一下头发。

entries.etymology: 1710, "bad management, neglect;" see mis- (1) + conduct (n.). Meaning "wrong conduct" is attested from 1729.
entries.etymologyZh: 1710 年, "bad management, neglect;" 参见 mis- (1) + conduct （名）. 义为 "wrong conduct" 见于 1729 年.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "full of misery, causing wretchedness" (of conditions), from Old French miserable "prone to pity, merciful," and directly from Latin miserabilis "pitiable, miserable, deplorable, lamentable," from miserari "to pity, lament, deplore," from miser "wretched" (see miser). Of persons, "existing in a state of misery" it is attested from 1520s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "full of misery, causing wretchedness" (of conditions), 源自 古法语 miserable "prone to pity, merciful," and 直接源自 拉丁语 miserabilis "pitiable, miserable, deplorable, lamentable," 源自 miserari "to pity, lament, deplore," 源自 miser "wretched" （参见 miser). Of persons, "existing in a state of misery" it 见于 1520 年代.

example.en: The refugees lived in miserable conditions with little food or shelter.
example.zh: 难民们生活在悲惨的条件下，几乎没有食物和住所。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "condition of external unhappiness," from Old French misere "miserable situation, misfortune, distress" (12c.), from Latin miseria "wretchedness," from miser (see miser). Meaning "condition of one in great sorrow or mental distress" is from 1530s. Meaning "bodily pain" is 1825, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "condition of external unhappiness," 源自 古法语 misere "miserable situation, misfortune, distress" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 miseria "wretchedness," 源自 miser （参见 miser). 义为 "condition of one in great sorrow or mental distress" 始于 1530 年代. 义为 "bodily pain" is 1825 年, American English.

example.en: The novel captures the misery of people living through war and famine.
example.zh: 这部小说记录了人们在战争与饥荒中所承受的苦难。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., from mis- (1) + fortune. Related: Misfortunate.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 mis- (1) + fortune. 同源词：Misfortunate.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "to go astray;" see mis- (1) + guide (v.). Transitive sense of "to guide in the wrong direction" is first attested c. 1500. Related: Misguided; misguiding.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "to go astray;" 参见 mis- (1) + guide （动）. Transitive 语义 "to guide in the wrong direction" is 最早见于 约 1500 年. 同源词：Misguided; misguiding.

definitionLines: vt. 把……带错路；使误入歧 途；使误解
entries.definition: vt. 把……带错路；使误入歧 途；使误解
entries.etymology: Old English mislædan "to mislead," common Germanic compound (compare Middle Low German, Middle Dutch misleiden, Old High German misseleiten, German missleiten, Danish mislede); see mis- (1) + lead (v.). Related: misleading; misled.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 mislædan "to mislead," common 日耳曼语 复合词 (对比 Middle Low 德语, Middle 荷兰语 misleiden, 古高地德语 misseleiten, 德语 missleiten, Danish mislede); 参见 mis- (1) + lead （动）. 同源词：misleading; misled.

definitionLines: vt. 未击中，没达到；未看到，未 注意到；没赶上；遗漏，省 去；惦念
entries.definition: 小姐；［M-］……小姐 vt. 未击中，没达到；未看到，未 注意到；没赶上；遗漏，省 去；惦念
entries.etymology:
Old English missan "fail to hit, miss (a mark); fail in what was aimed at; escape (someone's notice)," influenced by Old Norse missa "to miss, to lack;" both from Proto-Germanic *missjan "to go wrong" (source also of Old Frisian missa, Middle Dutch, Dutch missen, German missen "to miss, fail"), from *missa- "in a changed manner," hence "abnormally, wrongly," from PIE root *mei- (1) "to change" (root of mis- (1); see mutable). Related: Missed; missing.

Meaning "to fail to get what one wanted" is from mid-13c. Sense of "to escape, avoid" is from 1520s; that of "to perceive with regret the absence or loss of (something or someone)" is from late 15c. Sense of "to not be on time for" is from 1823; to miss the boat in the figurative sense of "be too late for" is from 1929, originally nautical slang.  To miss out (on) "fail to get" is from 1929.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 missan "fail to hit, miss (a mark); fail in what was aimed at; escape (someone's notice)," influenced by 古北欧语 missa "to miss, to lack;" both 源自 原始日耳曼语 *missjan "to go wrong" (source also of 古弗里西语 missa, Middle 荷兰语, 荷兰语 missen, 德语 missen "to miss, fail"), 源自 *missa- "in a changed manner," hence "abnormally, wrongly," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *mei- (1) "to change" (root of mis- (1); 参见 mutable). 同源词：Missed; missing. 义为 "to fail to get what one wanted" 始于 13 世纪中期 义为 "to escape, avoid" 始于 1520 年代; that of "to perceive with regret the absence or loss of (something or someone)" 始于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "to not be on time for" 始于 1823 年; to miss the boat in the figurative 语义 "be too late for" 始于 1929 年, 原义为 nautical 俚语. To miss out (on) "fail to get" 始于 1929 年.

entries.etymology: "thing thrown or discharged as a weapon," is 1650s, from missile (adj.), 1610s, "capable of being thrown," chiefly in phrase missile weapon, from French missile and directly from Latin missilis "that may be thrown or hurled" (also, in plural, as a noun, "weapons that can be thrown, darts, javelins"), from missus "a throwing, hurling," past participle of mittere "to send" (see mission). Sense of "self-propelled rocket or bomb" is first recorded 1738; the modern remote guidance projectile so called from 1945.
entries.etymologyZh: "thing thrown or discharged as a weapon," is 1650 年代, 源自 missile （形）, 1610 年代, "capable of being thrown," chiefly in phrase missile weapon, 源自 法语 missile and 直接源自 拉丁语 missilis "that may be thrown or hurled" (also, in plural, 作名词时, "weapons that can be thrown, darts, javelins"), 源自 missus "a throwing, hurling," 为 … 的过去分词 mittere "to send" （参见 mission). 义为 "self-propelled rocket or bomb" is 首见于 1738 年; the modern remote guidance projectile so called 自 1945 年起.

entries.etymology: "not present, absent," 1520s, from present participle of miss (v.). Military sense of "not present after a battle but not known to have been killed or captured" is from 1845. Missing link first attested 1851 in Lyell. Missing person is from 1876.
entries.etymologyZh: "not present, absent," 1520 年代, 源自 为 … 的现在分词 miss （动）. Military 语义 "not present after a battle but not known to have been killed or captured" 始于 1845 年. Missing link 最早见于 1851 年 in Lyell. Missing person 始于 1876 年.

example.en: Rescue teams are still searching for the three missing climbers on the north face.
example.zh: 救援队仍在北壁搜寻三名失踪的登山者。

entries.etymology:
1590s, "a sending abroad," originally of Jesuits, from Latin missionem (nominative missio) "act of sending, a despatching; a release, a setting at liberty; discharge from service, dismissal," noun of action from past participle stem of mittere "to send," oldest form probably *smittere, of unknown origin.

Diplomatic sense of "body of persons sent to a foreign land on commercial or political business" is from 1620s. In American English, sometimes "an embassy" (1805). Meaning "dispatch of an aircraft on a military operation" (1929, American English) later extended to spacecraft flights (1962), hence, mission control (1964). As a style of furniture, said to be imitative of furniture in the buildings of original Spanish missions to North America, it is attested from 1900.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "a sending abroad," 原义为 of Jesuits, 源自 拉丁语 missionem (主格 missio) "act of sending, a despatching; a release, a setting at liberty; discharge from service, dismissal," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of mittere "to send," oldest form 可能 *smittere, 来源不详. Diplomatic 语义 "body of persons sent to a foreign land on commercial or political business" 始于 1620 年代. In American English, 有时 "an embassy" (1805 年). 义为 "dispatch of an aircraft on a military operation" (1929 年, American English) later extended to spacecraft flights (1962 年), hence, mission control (1964 年). 作为 style of furniture, said to be imitative of furniture in the buildings of original 西班牙语 missions to North America, it 见于 1900 年.

example.en: The peacekeeping troops were sent abroad to fulfill their mission.
example.zh: 维和部队被派往国外执行他们的使命。

entries.definition: n. 传教的；传教士的 n.传教士
entries.etymology: 1650s, from missionary (adj.). Missionary position attested by 1963, said to have been coined by Kinsey (1948), who identified its origin in work done by Polish anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski in Melanesia in the 1920s; allegedly from the term used by South Pacific peoples to describe what Christian missionaries promoted to replace their local variations. By late 1960s it became the general term for this type of sex, formerly also known as the English-American position.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, 源自 missionary （形）. Missionary position attested 截至 1963 年, said to have been coined by Kinsey (1948 年), who identified its origin in work done by Polish anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski in Melanesia in the 1920 年代; allegedly 源自 term used by South Pacific peoples to describe what Christian missionaries promoted to replace their local variations. By late 1960 年代 it became the general term for this type of sex, formerly also known as the English-American position.

example.en: The missionary spent years spreading the gospel in remote villages.
example.zh: 这位传教士在偏远村庄传播福音多年。

entries.etymology: Old English mist "dimness (of eyesight), mist" (earliest in compounds, such as misthleoðu "misty cliffs," wælmist "mist of death"), from Proto-Germanic *mikhstaz (source also of Middle Low German mist, Dutch mist, Icelandic mistur, Norwegian and Swedish mist), perhaps from PIE *meigh- "to urinate" (source also of Greek omikhle, Old Church Slavonic migla, Sanskrit mih, megha "cloud, mist;" see micturition).Also in Old English in sense of "dimness of the eyes, either by illness or tears," and in figurative sense of "things that obscure mental vision."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 mist "dimness (of eyesight), mist" (earliest in compounds, such as misthleoðu "misty cliffs," wælmist "mist of death"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *mikhstaz (source also of Middle Low 德语 mist, 荷兰语 mist, Icelandic mistur, Norwegian and Swedish mist), 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *meigh- "to urinate" (source also of 希腊语 omikhle, Old Church Slavonic migla, 梵语 mih, megha "cloud, mist;" 参见 micturition).Also in 古英语 in 语义 "dimness of the eyes, either by illness or tears," and in figurative 语义 "things that obscure mental vision."

example.en: A thin mist covered the valley in the early morning light.
example.zh: 清晨的光线中，一层薄雾笼罩着山谷。

entries.definition: n. 错误，过失，误会 vt. 误解，弄错，错认
entries.etymology: early 14c., "to commit an offense;" late 14c., "to misunderstand, misinterpret," from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse mistaka "take in error, miscarry," from mis- "wrongly" (see mis- (1)) + taka "take" (see take (v.)). Related: Mistook; mistaking.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "to commit an offense;" 14 世纪晚期, "to misunderstand, misinterpret," 源自 a Scandinavian source such as 古北欧语 mistaka "take in error, miscarry," 源自 mis- "wrongly" （参见 mis- (1)) + taka "take" （参见 take （动）). 同源词：Mistook; mistaking.

example.en: Sending the wrong file was an easy mistake to make.
example.zh: 发错文件是一个很容易犯的错误。

entries.etymology: early 14c., "female teacher, governess," from Old French maistresse "mistress (lover); housekeeper; governess, female teacher" (Modern French maîtresse), fem. of maistre "master" (see master (n.)). Sense of "a woman who employs others or has authority over servants" is from early 15c. Sense of "kept woman of a married man" is from early 15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "female teacher, governess," 源自 古法语 maistresse "mistress (lover); housekeeper; governess, female teacher" (现代法语 maîtresse), fem. of maistre "master" （参见 master （名）). 义为 "a woman who employs others or has authority over servants" 始于 15 世纪初 义为 "kept woman of a married man" 始于 15 世纪初

entries.etymology: c. 1200; see mis- (1) + understand. Related: Misunderstood; misunderstanding.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年; 参见 mis- (1) + understand. 同源词：Misunderstood; misunderstanding.

definitionLines: vt. 混合，掺和；混淆，混乱
entries.definition: vt. 混合，掺和；混淆，混乱
entries.etymology: 1530s, back-formation from Middle English myxte (early 15c.) "composed of more than one element, of mixed nature," from Anglo-French mixte, from Latin mixtus, past participle of miscere "to mix, mingle, blend; fraternize with; throw into confusion," from PIE *meik- "to mix" (source also of Sanskrit misrah "mixed," Greek misgein, mignynai "to mix, mix up, mingle; to join, bring together; join (battle); make acquainted with," Old Church Slavonic mešo, mesiti "to mix," Russian meshat, Lithuanian maišau "to mix, mingle," Welsh mysgu). Also borrowed in Old English as miscian. Related: Mixed; mixing.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, back-formation 源自 中古英语 myxte (15 世纪初) "composed of more than one element, of mixed nature," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 mixte, 源自 拉丁语 mixtus, 为 … 的过去分词 miscere "to mix, mingle, blend; fraternize with; throw into confusion," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *meik- "to mix" (source also of 梵语 misrah "mixed," 希腊语 misgein, mignynai "to mix, mix up, mingle; to join, bring together; join (battle); make acquainted with," Old Church Slavonic mešo, mesiti "to mix," 俄语 meshat, Lithuanian maišau "to mix, mingle," Welsh mysgu). Also borrowed in 古英语 as miscian. 同源词：Mixed; mixing.

example.en: The chef decided to mix fresh herbs into the sauce for extra flavor.
example.zh: 厨师决定将新鲜香草混入酱汁以增添风味。

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Old French misture and directly from Latin mixtura "a mixing," from mixtus (see mix (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 古法语 misture and 直接源自 拉丁语 mixtura "a mixing," 源自 mixtus （参见 mix （动）).

example.en: The medicine is a mixture of two active compounds in equal parts.
example.zh: 这种药物是两种等量活性化合物的混合物。

entries.definition: n. 呻吟；哀悼；呼啸 vi.发出呻吟声；抱怨，悼 vt.呻吟
entries.etymology: c. 1200, "lamentation, mourning, weeping; complaining, the expressing of complaints; a complaint; lover's complaint; accusation, charge," probably from an unrecorded Old English *man "complaint," related to Old English mænan "complain, moan," also "tell, intend, signify" (see mean (v.1)); but OED discounts this connection. Meaning "long, low inarticulate murmur from some prolonged pain" is first recorded 1670s, "with onomatopoeic suggestion" [OED].
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "lamentation, mourning, weeping; complaining, the expressing of complaints; a complaint; lover's complaint; accusation, charge," 可能 源自 an unrecorded 古英语 *man "complaint," related to 古英语 mænan "complain, moan," also "tell, intend, signify" （参见 mean (v.1)); but OED discounts this connection. 义为 "long, low inarticulate murmur from some prolonged pain" is 首见于 1670 年代, "with onomatopoeic suggestion" [OED].

entries.etymology: city in Alabama, U.S., attested c. 1540 in Spanish as Mauvila, referring to an Indian group and perhaps from Choctaw (Muskogean) moeli "to paddle." Related: Mobilian.
entries.etymologyZh: city in Alabama, U.S., attested 约 1540 年 in 西班牙语 as Mauvila, referring to an Indian group and 或源自 Choctaw (Muskogean) moeli "to paddle." 同源词：Mobilian.

example.en: The company operates a mobile workforce that can be deployed across different regions.
example.zh: 该公司拥有一支可跨地区部署的流动劳动力队伍。

definitionLines: vt. 动员，调动；集合，组织
entries.definition: vt. 动员，调动；集合，组织 vi. 动员起来
entries.etymology: 1833 in the military sense; 1838 as "render capable of movement, bring into circulation," from French mobiliser, from mobile "movable" (see mobile). Related: Mobilized; mobilizing.
entries.etymologyZh: 1833 年 in the military sense; 1838 年 as "render capable of movement, bring into circulation," 源自 法语 mobiliser, 源自 mobile "movable" （参见 mobile). 同源词：Mobilized; mobilizing.

entries.definition: vt. 嘲弄；模仿 vi. 嘲弄，嘲笑
entries.etymology: mid-15c., mokken, "make fun of," also "to trick, delude, make a fool of, treat with scorn;" from Old French mocquer "deride, jeer," a word of unknown origin. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *muccare "to blow the nose" (as a derisive gesture), from Latin mucus; or possibly from Middle Dutch mocken "to mumble" or Middle Low German mucken "grumble." Or perhaps simply imitative of such speech. Related: Mocked; mocking; mockingly. Replaced Old English bysmerian. Sense of "imitating," as in mockingbird and mock turtle (1763), is from notion of derisive imitation.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, mokken, "make fun of," also "to trick, delude, make a fool of, treat with scorn;" 源自 古法语 mocquer "deride, jeer," a word 来源不详. Perhaps 源自 通俗拉丁语 *muccare "to blow the nose" (作为 derisive gesture), 源自 拉丁语 mucus; or possibly 源自 Middle 荷兰语 mocken "to mumble" or Middle Low 德语 mucken "grumble." Or 或许 simply imitative of such speech. 同源词：Mocked; mocking; mockingly. Replaced 古英语 bysmerian. 义为 "imitating," as in mockingbird and mock turtle (1763 年), 始于 概念 derisive imitation.

example.en: The team switched to a remote working mode during the pandemic.
example.zh: 疫情期间，团队转换为远程办公模式。

definitionLines: n. 样式；模型，原型；模特儿；模 范，典型
entries.definition: n. 样式；模型，原型；模特儿；模 范，典型 vt. 作……的模型；（after/on/ upon） 模仿，依…•…仿造
entries.etymology:
1570s, "likeness made to scale; architect's set of designs," from Middle French modelle (16c., Modern French modèle), from Italian modello "a model, mold," from Vulgar Latin *modellus, from Latin modulus "a small measure, standard," diminutive of modus "manner, measure" (see mode (n.1)).

Sense of "thing or person to be imitated" is 1630s. Meaning "motor vehicle of a particular design" is from 1900 (such as Model T, 1908; Ford's other early models included C, F, and B). Sense of "artist's model" is first recorded 1690s; that of "fashion model" is from 1904. German, Swedish modell, Dutch, Danish model are from French or Italian.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "likeness made to scale; architect's set of designs," 源自 中古法语 modelle (16 世纪, 现代法语 modèle), 源自 意大利语 modello "a model, mold," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *modellus, 源自 拉丁语 modulus "a small measure, standard," 为 … 的指小形式 modus "manner, measure" （参见 mode (n.1)). 义为 "thing or person to be imitated" is 1630 年代. 义为 "motor vehicle of a particular design" 始于 1900 年 (such as Model T, 1908 年; Ford's other early models included C, F, and B). Sense of "artist's model" is first recorded 1690s; that of "fashion model" 始于 1904 年. 德语, Swedish modell, 荷兰语, Danish model 始于 法语 or 意大利语.

example.en: She served as a model for young designers around the world.
example.zh: 她是全球年轻设计师的榜样。

definitionLines: a. 中等的，适度的；温和的， 稳健的
entries.definition: a. 中等的，适度的；温和的， 稳健的
entries.etymology: late 14c., originally of weather and other physical conditions, from Latin moderatus "within bounds, observing moderation;" figuratively "modest, restrained," past participle of moderari "to regulate, mitigate, restrain, temper, set a measure, keep (something) within measure," related to modus "measure," from PIE *med-es-, from base *med- (see medical (adj.)). The notion is "keeping within due measure." In English, of persons from early 15c.; of opinions from 1640s; of prices from 1904. Related: Moderateness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 原义为 of weather and other physical conditions, 源自 拉丁语 moderatus "within bounds, observing moderation;" figuratively "modest, restrained," 为 … 的过去分词 moderari "to regulate, mitigate, restrain, temper, set a measure, keep (something) within measure," related to modus "measure," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *med-es-, 源自 base *med- （参见 medical （形）). The notion is "keeping within due measure." In English, of persons 源自 15 世纪初; of opinions 源自 1640 年代; of prices 自 1904 年起. 同源词：Moderateness.

example.en: Doctors recommend moderate exercise for people with heart conditions.
example.zh: 医生建议有心脏病的人进行适度的锻炼。

definitionLines: a. 现代的，近代的；新式的
entries.definition: a. 现代的，近代的；新式的
entries.etymology:
c. 1500, "now existing;" 1580s, "of or pertaining to present or recent times;" from Middle French moderne (15c.) and directly from Late Latin modernus "modern" (Priscian, Cassiodorus), from Latin modo "just now, in a (certain) manner," from modo (adv.) "to the measure," ablative of modus "manner, measure" (see mode (n.1)). Extended form modern-day attested from 1909.

In Shakespeare, often with a sense of "every-day, ordinary, commonplace." Slang abbreviation mod first attested 1960. Modern art is from 1807 (by contrast to ancient); modern dance first attested 1912; first record of modern jazz is from 1954. Modern conveniences first recorded 1926.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年, "now existing;" 1580 年代, "of or pertaining to present or recent times;" 源自 中古法语 moderne (15 世纪) and 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 modernus "modern" (Priscian, Cassiodorus), 源自 拉丁语 modo "just now, in a (certain) manner," 源自 modo （副） "to the measure," ablative of modus "manner, measure" （参见 mode (n.1)). Extended form modern-day attested 自 1909 年起. In Shakespeare, 常 with a 语义 "every-day, ordinary, commonplace." Slang abbreviation mod 最早见于 1960 年. 现代 art 始于 1807 年 (by contrast to ancient); modern dance 最早见于 1912 年; first record of modern jazz 始于 1954 年. 现代 conveniences 首见于 1926 年.

example.en: Modern technology has transformed how people communicate globally.
example.zh: 现代技术彻底改变了人们全球沟通的方式。

entries.etymology: 1748, from modern + -ize, or from French moderniser. Related: Modernized; modernizing; modernizer.
entries.etymologyZh: 1748 年, 源自 modern + -ize，或源自 法语 moderniser. 同源词：Modernized; modernizing; modernizer.

definitionLines: a. 端庄的，朴素的；谦虚的， 谦逊的；适度的
entries.definition: a. 端庄的，朴素的；谦虚的， 谦逊的；适度的
entries.etymology: 1560s, "having moderate self-regard," from Middle French modeste (14c.), from Latin modestus "keeping due measure" (see modesty). Of women, "not improper or lewd," 1590s; of female attire, 1610s. Of demands, etc., c. 1600. Related: Modestly.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, "having moderate self-regard," 源自 中古法语 modeste (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 modestus "keeping due measure" （参见 modesty). Of women, "not improper or lewd," 1590 年代; of female attire, 1610 年代. Of demands, etc., 约 1600 年. 同源词：Modestly.

example.en: Despite his fame, he remained modest and never boasted about his achievements.
example.zh: 尽管名声显赫，他依然谦虚，从不炫耀自己的成就。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "freedom from exaggeration, self-control," from Middle French modestie or directly from Latin modestia "moderation, sense of honor, correctness of conduct," from modestus "moderate, keeping measure, sober, gentle, temperate," from modus "measure, manner" (see mode (n.1)). Meaning "quality of having a moderate opinion of oneself" is from 1550s; that of "womanly propriety" is from 1560s.

entries.definition: vt. 修改，修饰；更改 vi.修改
entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French modifier (14c.), from Latin modificare "to limit, measure off, restrain," from modus "measure, manner" (see mode (n.1)) + root of facere "to make" (see factitious). Related: Modified; modifying.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 modifier (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 modificare "to limit, measure off, restrain," 源自 modus "measure, manner" （参见 mode (n.1)) + root of facere "to make" （参见 factitious). 同源词：Modified; modifying.

example.en: We had to modify the original design slightly so that it would meet the new safety standards.
example.zh: 我们不得不对原设计稍作改动，以便它能符合新的安全标准。

entries.etymology: 1580s, "allotted measure," from Middle French module (1540s) or directly from Latin modulus "small measure," diminutive of modus "measure, manner" (see mode (n.1)). Meaning "interchangeable part" first recorded 1955; that of "separate section of a spacecraft" is from 1961.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "allotted measure," 源自 中古法语 module (1540 年代) or 直接源自 拉丁语 modulus "small measure," 为 … 的指小形式 modus "measure, manner" （参见 mode (n.1)). 义为 "interchangeable part" 首见于 1955 年; that of "separate section of a spacecraft" 始于 1961 年.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "moist, wet; well-irrigated," from Old French moiste "damp, wet, soaked" (13c., Modern French moite), from Vulgar Latin *muscidus "moldy," also "wet," from Latin mucidus "slimy, moldy, musty," from mucus "slime" (see mucus). Alternative etymology [Diez] is from Latin musteus "fresh, green, new," literally "like new wine," from musteum "new wine" (see must (n.1)). If this wasn't the source, it influenced the form of the other word in Old French. Related: Moistly; moistness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "moist, wet; well-irrigated," 源自 古法语 moiste "damp, wet, soaked" (13 世纪, 现代法语 moite), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *muscidus "moldy," also "wet," 源自 拉丁语 mucidus "slimy, moldy, musty," 源自 mucus "slime" （参见 mucus). Alternative etymology [Diez] 始于 拉丁语 musteus "fresh, green, new," 字面义为 "like new wine," 源自 musteum "new wine" （参见 must (n.1)). If this wasn't the source, it influenced the form of the other word in 古法语. 同源词：Moistly; moistness.

example.en: The soil was moist and perfect for planting seeds.
example.zh: 土壤湿润，非常适合播种。

entries.etymology: mid-14c., from Old French moistour "moisture, dampness, wetness" (13c., Modern French moiteur), from moiste (see moist).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 moistour "moisture, dampness, wetness" (13 世纪, 现代法语 moiteur), 源自 moiste （参见 moist).

example.en: The old basement walls were covered with moisture after heavy rain.
example.zh: 大雨过后，旧地下室的墙壁上布满了湿气。

entries.etymology: 1794, "extremely minute particle," from French molécule (1670s), from Modern Latin molecula, diminutive of Latin moles "mass, barrier" (see mole (3)). For ending see -cule. A vague meaning at first; the vogue for the word (used until late 18c. only in Latin form) can be traced to the philosophy of Descartes. First used of Modern Latin molecula in modern scientific sense by Amedeo Avogadro (1811).
entries.etymologyZh: 1794 年, "extremely minute particle," 源自 法语 molécule (1670 年代), 源自 现代 拉丁语 molecula, 为 … 的指小形式 拉丁语 moles "mass, barrier" （参见 mole (3)). For ending 参见 -cule. First used of 现代 拉丁语 molecula in modern scientific sense by Amedeo Avogadro (1811 年).

example.en: A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
example.zh: 一个水分子由两个氢原子和一个氧原子组成。

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "very brief portion of time, instant," in moment of time, from Old French moment (12c.) "moment, minute; importance, weight, value" or directly from Latin momentum "movement, motion; moving power; alteration, change;" also "short time, instant" (also source of Spanish, Italian momento), contraction of *movimentum, from movere "to move" (see move (v.)). Some (but not OED) explain the sense evolution of the Latin word by notion of a particle so small it would just "move" the pointer of a scale, which led to the transferred sense of "minute time division." Sense of "importance, 'weight' " is attested in English from 1520s.

Phrase never a dull moment first recorded 1889 in Jerome K. Jerome's "Three Men in a Boat." Phrase moment of truth first recorded 1932 in Hemingway's "Death in the Afternoon," from Spanish el momento de la verdad, the final sword-thrust in a bull-fight.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "very brief portion of time, instant," in moment of time, 源自 古法语 moment (12 世纪) "moment, minute; importance, weight, value" or 直接源自 拉丁语 momentum "movement, motion; moving power; alteration, change;" also "short time, instant" (also source of 西班牙语, 意大利语 momento), contraction of *movimentum, 源自 movere "to move" （参见 move （动）). Some (but not OED) explain the sense evolution of the 拉丁语 word by 概念 a particle so small it would just "move" the pointer of a scale, which led to the transferred 语义 "minute time division." 义为 "importance, 'weight' " is 见于 English 源自 1520 年代. Phrase never a dull moment 首见于 1889 年 in Jerome K. Jerome's "Three Men in a Boat." Phrase moment of truth first recorded 1932 in Hemingway's "Death in the Afternoon," 源自 西班牙语 el momento de la verdad, the final sword-thrust in a bull-fight.

example.en: At that moment, the fire alarm went off and everyone evacuated immediately.
example.zh: 就在那一刻，火警响了，所有人立刻疏散。

entries.etymology: "lasting a moment," mid-15c., from Latin momentarius "of brief duration," from momentum (see moment).
entries.etymologyZh: "lasting a moment," 15 世纪中期, 源自 拉丁语 momentarius "of brief duration," 源自 momentum （参见 moment).

entries.etymology:
second day of the week, Old English mondæg, monandæg "Monday," literally "day of the moon," from mona (genitive monan; see moon (n.)) + dæg (see day). Common Germanic (Old Norse manandagr, Old Frisian monendei, Dutch maandag, German Montag) loan-translation of Late Latin Lunæ dies, source of the day name in Romance languages (French lundi, Italian lunedi, Spanish lunes), itself a loan-translation of Greek selenes hemera. The name for this day in Slavic tongues generally means "day after Sunday."

Phrase Monday morning quarterback is attested from 1932, Monday being the first day back at work after the weekend, when school and college football games were played. Black Monday (mid-14c.) is the Monday after Easter day, though how it got its reputation for bad luck is a mystery. Saint Monday (1753) was "used with reference to the practice among workmen of being idle Monday, as a consequence of drunkenness on the Sunday" before [OED]. Clergymen, meanwhile, when indisposed complained of feeling Mondayish (1804) in reference to effects of Sunday's labors.
entries.etymologyZh: second day of the week, 古英语 mondæg, monandæg "Monday," 字面义为 "day of the moon," 源自 mona (属格 monan; 参见 moon （名）) + dæg （参见 day). Common 日耳曼语 (古北欧语 manandagr, 古弗里西语 monendei, 荷兰语 maandag, 德语 Montag) loan-translation of 晚期拉丁语 Lunæ dies, source of the day name in Romance languages (法语 lundi, 意大利语 lunedi, 西班牙语 lunes), itself a loan-translation of 希腊语 selenes hemera. The name for this day in Slavic tongues generally means "day after Sunday." Phrase Monday morning quarterback 见于 1932 年, Monday being the first day back at work after the weekend, when school and college football games were played. Black Monday (14 世纪中期) is the Monday after Easter day, though how it got its reputation for bad luck is a mystery. Saint Monday (1753 年) was "used with reference to the practice among workmen of being idle Monday, as a consequence of drunkenness on the Sunday" before [OED]. Clergymen, meanwhile, when indisposed complained of feeling Mondayish (1804 年) in reference to effects of Sunday's labors.

entries.etymology: "pertaining to money," 1802, from Late Latin monetarius "pertaining to money," originally "of a mint," from Latin moneta "mint, coinage" (see money). Related: Monetarily.
entries.etymologyZh: "pertaining to money," 1802 年, 源自 晚期拉丁语 monetarius "pertaining to money," 原义为 "of a mint," 源自 拉丁语 moneta "mint, coinage" （参见 money). 同源词：Monetarily.

example.en: The central bank announced a new monetary policy to control inflation.
example.zh: 中央银行宣布了一项新的货币政策以控制通货膨胀。

entries.etymology:
mid-13c., "coinage, metal currency," from Old French monoie "money, coin, currency; change" (Modern French monnaie), from Latin moneta "place for coining money, mint; coined money, money, coinage," from Moneta, a title or surname of the Roman goddess Juno, in or near whose temple money was coined; perhaps from monere "advise, warn" (see monitor (n.)), with the sense of "admonishing goddess," which is sensible, but the etymology is difficult. Extended early 19c. to include paper money.

To make money "earn pay" is first attested mid-15c. Highwayman's threat your money or your life first attested 1841. Phrase in the money (1902) originally meant "one who finishes among the prize-winners" (in a horse race, etc.). The challenge to put (one's) money where (one's) mouth is is first recorded 1942, American English. money-grub "one who is sordidly intent on amassing money" is from 1768. The image of money burning a hole in someone's pocket is attested from 1520s.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, "coinage, metal currency," 源自 古法语 monoie "money, coin, currency; change" (现代法语 monnaie), 源自 拉丁语 moneta "place for coining money, mint; coined money, money, coinage," 源自 Moneta, a title or surname of the Roman goddess Juno, in or near whose temple money was coined; 或源自 monere "advise, warn" （参见 monitor （名）), with the 语义 "admonishing goddess," which is sensible, but the etymology is difficult. Extended 19 世纪初 to include paper money. To make money "earn pay" is 最早见于 15 世纪中期 Highwayman's threat your money or your life first attested 1841. Phrase in the money (1902) originally meant "one who finishes among the prize-winners" (in a horse race, etc.). The challenge to put (one's) money where (one's) mouth is is first recorded 1942, American English. money-grub "one who is sordidly intent on amassing money" is from 1768. The image of money burning a hole in someone's pocket 见于 1520 年代.

example.en: She saved enough money to buy a new laptop for college.
example.zh: 她存了足够的钱来为大学购置一台新笔记本电脑。

definitionLines: n. 班长；监测器，显示器
entries.definition: n. 班长；监测器，显示器
entries.etymology:
1540s, "senior pupil at a school charged with keeping order, etc.," from Latin monitor "one who reminds, admonishes, or checks," also "an overseer, instructor, guide, teacher," agent noun from monere "to admonish, warn, advise," related to memini "I remember, I am mindful of," and to mens "mind," from PIE root *men- "to think" (see mind (n.)).

The type of lizard so called because it is supposed to give warning of crocodiles (1826). Meaning "squat, slow-moving type of ironclad warship" (1862) so called from name of the first vessel of this design, chosen by the inventor, Swedish-born U.S. engineer John Ericsson (1803-1889), because it was meant to "admonish" the Confederate leaders in the U.S. Civil War. Broadcasting sense of "a device to continuously check on the technical quality of a transmission" (1931) led to special sense of "a TV screen displaying the picture from a particular camera."
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "senior pupil at a school charged with keeping order, etc.," 源自 拉丁语 monitor "one who reminds, admonishes, or checks," also "an overseer, instructor, guide, teacher," agent 名词 源自 monere "to admonish, warn, advise," related to memini "I remember, I am mindful of," and to mens "mind," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *men- "to think" （参见 mind （名）). The type of lizard so called because it is supposed to give warning of crocodiles (1826 年). 义为 "squat, slow-moving type of ironclad warship" (1862 年) so called 源自 name of the first vessel of this design, chosen by the inventor, Swedish-born U.S. engineer John Ericsson (1803 年-1889 年), because it was meant to "admonish" the Confederate leaders in the U.S. Civil War. Broadcasting 语义 "a device to continuously check on the technical quality of a transmission" (1931 年) led to special 语义 "a TV screen displaying the picture from a particular camera."

example.en: The class monitor reminded students to keep quiet during the exam.
example.zh: 班长提醒学生在考试期间保持安静。

entries.etymology:
1520s, likely from an unrecorded Middle Low German *moneke or Middle Dutch *monnekijn, a colloquial word for "monkey," originally a diminutive of some Romanic word, compare French monne (16c.); Middle Italian monnicchio, from Old Italian monna; Spanish mona "ape, monkey." In a 1498 Low German version of the popular medieval beast story Roman de Renart ("Reynard the Fox"), Moneke is the name given to the son of Martin the Ape; transmission of the word to English might have been via itinerant entertainers from the German states.

The Old French form of the name is Monequin (recorded as Monnekin in a 14c. version from Hainault), which could be a diminutive of some personal name, or it could be from the general Romanic word, which may be ultimately from Arabic maimun "monkey," literally "auspicious," a euphemistic usage because the sight of apes was held by the Arabs to be unlucky [Klein]. The word would have been influenced in Italian by folk etymology from monna "woman," a contraction of ma donna "my lady."
Monkey has been used affectionately for "child" since c. 1600. As a type of modern popular dance, it is attested from 1964. Monkey business attested from 1883. Monkey suit "fancy uniform" is from 1886. Monkey wrench is attested from 1858; its figurative sense of "something that obstructs operations" is from the notion of one getting jammed in the gears of machinery (compare spanner in the works). To make a monkey of someone is attested from 1900. To have a monkey on one's back "be addicted" is 1930s narcotics slang, though the same phrase in the 1860s meant "to be angry." There is a story in the Sinbad cycle about a tormenting ape-like creature that mounts a man's shoulders and won't get off, which may be the root of the term. In 1890s British slang, to have a monkey up the chimney meant "to have a mortgage on one's house." The three wise monkeys ("see no evil," etc.) are attested from 1926.

In a 1498 年 Low 德语 version of the popular medieval beast story Roman de Renart ("Reynard the Fox"), Moneke is the name given to the son of Martin the Ape; transmission of the word to English might have been 经由 itinerant entertainers 源自 德语 states. entries.etymology:
"exclusive control of a commodity or trade," 1530s, from Latin monopolium, from Greek monopolion "right of exclusive sale," from mono- + polein "to sell," from PIE root *pel- (5) "to sell" (source also of Sanskrit panate "barters, purchases," Lithuanian pelnas "gain," Old Church Slavonic splenu, Russian polon "prey, booty," Old Norse falr, Dutch veil, German feil "for sale, venal").

Alternative form monopole (1540s, from the Old French form of the word) was common in 16c. The popular board game, invented by Charles Darrow, is from 1935. Monopoly money "unreal currency" is attested from 1972, in reference to the paper used in the game.

entries.etymology: early 14c., "malformed animal or human, creature afflicted with a birth defect," from Old French monstre, mostre "monster, monstrosity" (12c.), and directly from Latin monstrum "divine omen, portent, sign; abnormal shape; monster, monstrosity," figuratively "repulsive character, object of dread, awful deed, abomination," from root of monere "warn" (see monitor (n.)). Abnormal or prodigious animals were regarded as signs or omens of impending evil. Extended by late 14c. to imaginary animals composed of parts of creatures (centaur, griffin, etc.). Meaning "animal of vast size" is from 1520s; sense of "person of inhuman cruelty or wickedness" is from 1550s. As an adjective, "of extraordinary size," from 1837. In Old English, the monster Grendel was an aglæca, a word related to aglæc "calamity, terror, distress, oppression."

entries.etymology: Old English monað, from Proto-Germanic *menoth- (source also of Old Saxon manoth, Old Frisian monath, Middle Dutch manet, Dutch maand, Old High German manod, German Monat, Old Norse manaðr, Gothic menoþs "month"), related to *menon- "moon" (see moon (n.); the month was calculated from lunar phases). entries.etymology:
Old English mona, from Proto-Germanic *menon- (source also of Old Saxon and Old High German mano, Old Frisian mona, Old Norse mani, Danish maane, Dutch maan, German Mond, Gothic mena "moon"), from PIE *me(n)ses- "moon, month" (source also of Sanskrit masah "moon, month;" Avestan ma, Persian mah, Armenian mis "month;" Greek mene "moon," men "month;" Latin mensis "month;" Old Church Slavonic meseci, Lithuanian menesis "moon, month;" Old Irish mi, Welsh mis, Breton miz "month"), probably from root *me- "to measure," in reference to the moon's phases as the measure of time.

A masculine noun in Old English. In Greek, Italic, Celtic, Armenian the cognate words now mean only "month." Greek selene (Lesbian selanna) is from selas "light, brightness (of heavenly bodies)." Old Norse also had tungl "moon," ("replacing mani in prose" - Buck), evidently an older Germanic word for "heavenly body," cognate with Gothic tuggl, Old English tungol "heavenly body, constellation," of unknown origin or connection. Hence Old Norse tunglfylling "lunation," tunglœrr "lunatic" (adj.).

Extended 1665 to satellites of other planets. To shoot the moon "leave without paying rent" is British slang from c. 1823; card-playing sense perhaps influenced by gambler's shoot the works (1922) "go for broke" in shooting dice. The moon race and the U.S. space program of the 1960s inspired a number of coinages, including, from those skeptical of the benefits to be gained, moondoggle (based on boondoggle). The man in the moon is mentioned since early 14c.; he carries a bundle of thorn-twigs and is accompanied by a dog. Some Japanese, however, see a rice-cake-making rabbit in the moon.

definitionLines: a. 道德的，道义的，有道德的
entries.definition: a. 道德的，道义的，有道德的 n.寓意，教育意义
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "pertaining to character or temperament" (good or bad), from Old French moral (14c.) and directly from Latin moralis "proper behavior of a person in society," literally "pertaining to manners," coined by Cicero ("De Fato," II.i) to translate Greek ethikos (see ethics) from Latin mos (genitive moris) "one's disposition," in plural, "mores, customs, manners, morals," of uncertain origin. Perhaps sharing a PIE root with English mood (n.1).

Meaning "morally good, conforming to moral rules," is first recorded late 14c. of stories, 1630s of persons. Original value-neutral sense preserved in moral support, moral victory (with sense of "pertaining to character as opposed to physical action"). Related: Morally.

Meaning "goodness" is attested from 1590s.

entries.etymology:
Old English mara "greater, more, stronger, mightier," used as a comparative of micel "great" (see mickle), from Proto-Germanic *maizon- (source also of Old Saxon mera, Old Norse meiri, Old Frisian mara, Middle Dutch mere, Old High German mero, German mehr), from PIE *meis- (source also of Avestan mazja "greater," Old Irish mor "great," Welsh mawr "great," Greek -moros "great," Oscan mais "more"), from root *me- (3) "big." Sometimes used as an adverb in Old English ("in addition"), but Old English generally used related ma "more" as adverb and noun. This became Middle English mo, but more in this sense began to predominate in later Middle English.

More or less "in a greater or lesser degree" is from early 13c.; appended to a statement to indicate approximation, from 1580s.

entries.etymology: mid-13c., morn, morewen (see morn) + suffix -ing, on pattern of evening. Originally the time just before sunrise. As an adjective from 1530s. Morning after in reference to a hangover is from 1884; in reference to a type of contraception, attested from 1867. Morning sickness as a symptom of pregnancy is from 1793 (Old English had morgenwlætung). Morning glory is from 1814, in reference to the time the flowers open. Morning star "Venus in the east before sunrise" is from 1530s (Old English had morgensteorra "morn-star"). As a greeting, short for good morning, attested by 1895.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "deadly," also "doomed to die," from Old French mortel "destined to die; deserving of death," from Latin mortalis "subject to death, mortal, of a mortal, human," from mors (genitive mortis) "death," from PIE base *mer- "to die," with derivatives referring to death and human beings" (source also of Sanskrit mrtih "death," martah "mortal man;" Avestan miryeite "dies," Old Persian martiya- "man;" Armenian meranim "die;" Latin mori "to die;" Lithuanian mirtis "mortal man;" Greek brotos "mortal" (hence ambrotos "immortal"); Old Church Slavonic mrutvu "dead;" Old Irish marb, Welsh marw "died;" Old English morþ "murder"). The most widespread Indo-European root for "to die," forming the common word for it except in Greek and Germanic. Watkins says it is "possibly" the same as PIE *mer- "rub, pound, wear away" (see morbid).

entries.etymology: late 14c., morgage, "conveyance of property as security for a loan or agreement," from Old French morgage (13c.), mort gaige, literally "dead pledge" (replaced in modern French by hypothèque), from mort "dead" (see mortal (adj.)) + gage "pledge" (see wage (n.)). So called because the deal dies either when the debt is paid or when payment fails. Old French mort is from Vulgar Latin *mortus "dead," from Latin mortuus, past participle of mori "to die" (see mortal (adj.)). The -t- restored in English based on Latin.

entries.etymology:
Old English mus "small rodent," also "muscle of the arm," from Proto-Germanic *mus (source also of Old Norse, Old Frisian, Middle Dutch, Danish, Swedish mus, Dutch muis, German Maus "mouse"), from PIE *mus- (source also of Sanskrit mus "mouse, rat," Old Persian mush "mouse," Old Church Slavonic mysu, Latin mus, Lithuanian muse "mouse," Greek mys "mouse, muscle").

Plural form mice (Old English mys) shows effects of i-mutation. Contrasted with man (n.) from 1620s. Meaning "black eye" (or other discolored lump) is from 1842. Computer sense is from 1965, though applied to other things resembling a mouse in shape since 1750, mainly nautical.

Computer sense 始于 1965 年, though applied to other things resembling a mouse in shape 自 1750 年, mainly nautical.

entries.etymology: Old English muþ "mouth, opening, door, gate," from Proto-Germanic *munthaz (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian muth, Old Norse munnr, Danish mund, Middle Dutch mont, Dutch mond, Old High German mund, German Mund, Gothic munþs "mouth"), with characteristic loss of nasal consonant in Old English (compare tooth, goose), from PIE *mnto-s (source also of Latin mentum "chin"). In the sense of "outfall of a river" it is attested from late Old English; as the opening of anything with capacity (a bottle, cave, etc.) it is recorded from c. 1200. Mouth-organ attested from 1660s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 muþ "mouth, opening, door, gate," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *munthaz (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古弗里西语 muth, 古北欧语 munnr, Danish mund, Middle 荷兰语 mont, 荷兰语 mond, 古高地德语 mund, 德语 Mund, Gothic munþs "mouth"), with characteristic loss of nasal consonant in 古英语 (对比 tooth, goose), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *mnto-s (source also of 拉丁语 mentum "chin"). In the 语义 "outfall of a river" it 见于 late 古英语; as the opening of anything with capacity (a bottle, cave, etc.) it 见于 约 1200 年. Mouth-organ attested 源自 1660 年代.

definitionLines: vt. 移动，搬动，迁移；感动
entries.definition: vt. 移动，搬动，迁移；感动 vi. 动，走动；搬家，迁移 n. 动，动作，行动
entries.etymology:
late 13c., from Anglo-French mover, Old French movoir "to move, get moving, set out; set in motion; introduce" (Modern French mouvoir), from Latin movere "move, set in motion; remove; disturb" (past participle motus, frequentative motare), from PIE root *meue- "to push away" (source also of Sanskrit kama-muta "moved by love" and probably mivati "pushes, moves;" Lithuanian mauti "push on;" Greek ameusasthai "to surpass," amyno "push away").

Intransitive sense developed in Old French and came thence to English, though it now is rare in French. Meaning "to affect with emotion" is from c. 1300; that of "to prompt or impel toward some action" is from late 14c. Sense of "to change one's place of residence" is from 1707. Meaning "to propose (something) in an assembly, etc.," is first attested mid-15c.  Related: Moved; moving.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 mover, 古法语 movoir "to move, get moving, set out; set in motion; introduce" (现代法语 mouvoir), 源自 拉丁语 movere "move, set in motion; remove; disturb" (past participle motus, frequentative motare), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *meue- "to push away" (source also of 梵语 kama-muta "moved by love" and 可能 mivati "pushes, moves;" Lithuanian mauti "push on;" 希腊语 ameusasthai "to surpass," amyno "push away"). Intransitive sense developed in 古法语 and came thence to English, though it 现在 is rare in 法语. 义为 "to affect with emotion" 始于 约 1300 年; that of "to prompt or impel toward some action" 始于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "to change one's place of residence" 始于 1707 年. 义为 "to propose (something) in an assembly, etc.," is 最早见于 15 世纪中期 同源词：Moved; moving.

example.en: They decided to move to a bigger apartment after the baby was born.
example.zh: 宝宝出生后，他们决定搬到更大的公寓。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French movement "movement, exercise; start, instigation" (Modern French mouvement), from Medieval Latin movimentum, from Latin movere (see move (v.)). In the musical sense of "major division of a piece" it is attested from 1776; in the political/social sense, from 1828. Related: Movements.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 movement "movement, exercise; start, instigation" (现代法语 mouvement), 源自 中古拉丁语 movimentum, 源自 拉丁语 movere （参见 move （动）). In the musical 语义 "major division of a piece" it 见于 1776 年; in the political/social sense, 自 1828 年起. 同源词：Movements.

example.en: The civil rights movement of the 1960s changed laws across the United States.
example.zh: 20世纪60年代的民权运动改变了美国各地的法律。

entries.etymology: 1912 (perhaps 1908), shortened form of moving picture in the cinematographic sense (1896). As an adjective from 1913. Movie star attested from 1913. Another early name for it was photoplay.

example.en: We watched an exciting action movie at the theater last weekend.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, worn down by loss of unaccented last syllable from Middle English muchel "large, much," from Old English micel "great in amount or extent," from Proto-Germanic *mekilaz, from PIE *meg- "great" (see mickle). As a noun and an adverb, from c. 1200. For vowel evolution, see bury.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, worn down by loss of unaccented last syllable 源自 中古英语 muchel "large, much," 源自 古英语 micel "great in amount or extent," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *mekilaz, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *meg- "great" （参见 mickle). 作名词时 and an 副词, 源自 约 1200 年. For vowel evolution, 参见 bury.

example.en: The exam questions were much harder than anyone had expected.

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., cognate with and probably from Middle Low German mudde, Middle Dutch modde "thick mud," from Proto-Germanic *mud- from PIE *(s)meu-/*mu- [Buck], found in many words denoting "wet" or "dirty" (source also of Greek mydos "damp, moisture," Old Irish muad "cloud," Polish muł "slime," Sanskrit mutra- "urine," Avestan muthra- "excrement, filth"); related to German Schmutz "dirt," which also is used for "mud" in roads, etc., to avoid dreck, which originally meant "excrement." Welsh mwd is from English. Replaced native fen.

Meaning "lowest or worst of anything" is from 1580s. As a word for "coffee," it is hobo slang from 1925; as a word for "opium" from 1922. To throw or hurl mud "make disgraceful accusations" is from 1762. To say (one's) name is mud and mean "(one) is discredited" is first recorded 1823, from mud in obsolete sense of "a stupid twaddling fellow" (1708). Mud in your eye as a toast recorded from 1912, American English. Mud puppy "salamander" is from 1889, American English; mud bath is from 1798; mud pie is from 1788.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 与 … 同源 and 可能 源自 Middle Low 德语 mudde, Middle 荷兰语 modde "thick mud," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *mud- 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *(s)meu-/*mu- [Buck], found in many words denoting "wet" or "dirty" (source also of 希腊语 mydos "damp, moisture," Old 爱尔兰语 muad "cloud," Polish muł "slime," 梵语 mutra- "urine," Avestan muthra- "excrement, filth"); related to 德语 Schmutz "dirt," which also is used for "mud" in roads, etc., to avoid dreck, which 原义为 meant "excrement." To throw or hurl mud "make disgraceful accusations" 始于 1762 年. To say (one's) name is mud and mean "(one) is discredited" is 首见于 1823 年, 源自 mud in 已废 语义 "a stupid twaddling fellow" (1708 年). Mud in your eye 作为 toast recorded 自 1912 年起, American English. Mud puppy "salamander" 始于 1889 年, American English; mud bath 始于 1798 年; mud pie 始于 1788 年.

example.en: His boots were covered in thick mud after the hike through the muddy trail.

entries.etymology: 1640s, "involving many parts," from French multiple (14c.), from Late Latin multiplus "manifold," from Latin multi- "many, much" (see multi-) + -plus "-fold" (see -plus). entries.etymology:
1540s, from Middle French municipal, from Latin municipalis "of a citizen of a free town, of a free town," also "of a petty town, provincial," from municipium "free town, city whose citizens have the privileges of Roman citizens but are governed by their own laws," from municeps "citizen, inhabitant of a free town." Second element is root of capere "assume, take" (see capable). First element is from munus (plural munia) "service performed for the community, duty, work," also "public spectacle paid for by the magistrate, (gladiatorial) entertainment, gift," from Old Latin moenus "service, duty, burden," from PIE *moi-n-es-, generally taken as a suffixed form of root *mei- (1) "to change, go, move" (Watkins; see mutable); but Tucker says "more probably" from the other PIE root 
*mei- meaning "bind," so that munia = "obligations" and communis = "bound together."

Second element is root of capere "assume, take" （参见 capable). entries.etymology: late 14c., "expression of discontent by grumbling," from Old French murmure "murmur, sound of human voices; trouble, argument" (12c.), noun of action from murmurer "to murmur," from Latin murmurare "to murmur, mutter," from murmur (n.) "a hum, muttering, rushing," probably from a PIE reduplicative base *mor-mor, of imitative origin (source also of Sanskrit murmurah "crackling fire," Greek mormyrein "to roar, boil," Lithuanian murmlenti "to murmur"). Meaning "softly spoken words" is from 1670s.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Middle French muscle "muscle, sinew" (14c.) and directly from Latin musculus "a muscle," literally "little mouse," diminutive of mus "mouse" (see mouse (n.)).

So called because the shape and movement of some muscles (notably biceps) were thought to resemble mice. The analogy was made in Greek, too, where mys is both "mouse" and "muscle," and its comb. form gives the medical prefix myo-. Compare also Old Church Slavonic mysi "mouse," mysica "arm;" German Maus "mouse; muscle," Arabic 'adalah "muscle," 'adal "field mouse." In Middle English, lacerte, from the Latin word for "lizard," also was used as a word for a muscle.

Hence muscular and mousy are relatives, and a Middle English word for "muscular" was lacertous, "lizardy." Figurative sense of "force, violence, threat of violence" is 1930, American English. Muscle car "hot rod" is from 1969.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 中古法语 muscle "muscle, sinew" (14 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 musculus "a muscle," 字面义为 "little mouse," 为 … 的指小形式 mus "mouse" （参见 mouse （名）). So called because the shape and movement of some muscles (notably biceps) were thought to resemble mice. In 中古英语, lacerte, 源自 拉丁语 word for "lizard," also was used 作为 word for a muscle. Hence muscular and mousy are relatives, and a 中古英语 word for "muscular" was lacertous, "lizardy." entries.etymology: 1610s, "the university building in Alexandria," from Latin museum "library, study," from Greek mouseion "place of study, library or museum, school of art or poetry," originally "a seat or shrine of the Muses," from Mousa "Muse" (see muse (n.)). Earliest use in reference to English institutions was of libraries (such as the British Museum); sense of "building to display objects" first recorded 1680s.

entries.definition: n. 蘑菇 vi. 迅速生长
entries.etymology:
mid-15c., muscheron, musseroun (attested 1327 as a surname, John Mussheron), from Anglo-French musherun, Old French meisseron (11c., Modern French mousseron), perhaps from Late Latin mussirionem (nominative mussirio), though this might as well be borrowed from French. Barnhart says "of uncertain origin." Klein calls it "a word of pre-Latin origin, used in the North of France;" OED says it usually is held to be a derivative of French mousse "moss" (from Germanic), and Weekley agrees, saying it is properly "applied to variety which grows in moss," but Klein says they have "nothing in common." For the final -m Weekley refers to grogram, vellum, venom. Modern spelling is from 1560s.

Used figuratively for something or someone that makes a sudden appearance in full form from 1590s. In reference to the shape of clouds after explosions, etc., it is attested from 1916, though the actual phrase mushroom cloud does not appear until 1955.

Barnhart says "of uncertain origin." Klein calls it "a word of pre-Latin origin, used in the North of France;" OED says it 通常 is held to be a 为 … 的派生形式 法语 mousse "moss" (源自 日耳曼语), and Weekley agrees, saying it is properly "applied to variety which grows in moss," but Klein says they have "nothing in common." For the final -m Weekley refers to grogram, vellum, venom. 现代 spelling 始于 1560 年代. Used figuratively for something or someone that makes a sudden appearance in full form 源自 1590 年代. entries.etymology:
mid-13c., musike, from Old French musique (12c.) and directly from Latin musica "the art of music," also including poetry (also source of Spanish musica, Italian musica, Old High German mosica, German Musik, Dutch muziek, Danish musik), from Greek mousike (techne) "(art) of the Muses," from fem. of mousikos "pertaining to the Muses," from Mousa "Muse" (see muse (n.)). Modern spelling from 1630s. In classical Greece, any art in which the Muses presided, but especially music and lyric poetry.

The use of letters to denote music pitch probably is at least as old as ancient Greece, as their numbering system was ill-suited to the job. Natural scales begin at C (not A) because in ancient times the minor mode was more often used than the major one, and the natural minor scale begins at A.

Music box is from 1773, originally "barrel organ;" music hall is from 1842, especially "hall licensed for musical entertainment" (1857). To face the music "accept the consequences" is from 1850; the exact image is uncertain, one theory ties it to stage performers, another to cavalry horses having to be taught to stay calm while the regimental band plays. To make (beautiful) music with someone "have sexual intercourse" is from 1967.
