entries.etymology: early 15c., "pertaining to music; tuneful, harmonious; adept at making music," from Middle French musical (14c.) and directly from Medieval Latin musicalis, from Latin musica (see music). Musical box is from 1829. Children's game musical chairs is attested from 1877, hence use of musical as a modifier meaning "changing rapidly from one to another possessor" (1924). Related: Musically.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "pertaining to music; tuneful, harmonious; adept at making music," 源自 中古法语 musical (14 世纪) and 直接源自 中古拉丁语 musicalis, 源自 拉丁语 musica （参见 music). Musical box 始于 1829 年. Children's game musical chairs 见于 1877 年, hence use of musical 作为 modifier 意为 "changing rapidly from one to another possessor" (1924 年). 同源词：Musically.

example.en: She comes from a very musical family and plays the violin.
example.zh: 她来自一个很有音乐天赋的家庭，会拉小提琴。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "one skilled in music," from Old French musicien (14c.), or a native formation from music + -ian. Sense of "professional musical performer" first recorded mid-15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "one skilled in music," 源自 古法语 musicien (14 世纪)，或a 本族 formation 源自 music + -ian. 义为 "professional musical performer" 首见于 15 世纪中期

example.en: The musician practiced scales for two hours every morning before breakfast.
example.zh: 这位音乐家每天早饭前练两个小时音阶。

definitionLines: auz. v. 必须，应当；必定，谅必
entries.definition: auz. v. 必须，应当；必定，谅必
entries.etymology: Old English moste, past tense of motan "have to, be able to," from Proto-Germanic *mot- "ability, leisure (to do something)" (source also of Old Saxon motan "to be obliged to, have to," Old Frisian mota, Middle Low German moten, Dutch moeten, German müssen "to be obliged to," Gothic gamotan "to have room to, to be able to"), perhaps from PIE root *med- "to measure, to take appropriate measures" (see medical (adj.)). Used as present tense from c. 1300, from the custom of using past subjunctive as a moderate or polite form of the present.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 moste, 为 … 的过去时 motan "have to, be able to," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *mot- "ability, leisure (to do something)" (source also of 古撒克逊语 motan "to be obliged to, have to," 古弗里西语 mota, Middle Low 德语 moten, 荷兰语 moeten, 德语 müssen "to be obliged to," Gothic gamotan "to have room to, to be able to"), 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *med- "to measure, to take appropriate measures" （参见 medical （形）). Used as present tense 源自 约 1300 年, 源自 custom of using past subjunctive 作为 moderate or polite form of the present.

example.en: She must have left early because her coat was already gone.
example.zh: 她肯定早早离开了，因为她的外套已经不见了。

entries.etymology: late 14c., mewet "silent," from Old French muet "dumb, mute" (12c.), diminutive of mut, mo, from Latin mutus "silent, speechless, dumb," probably from imitative base *meue- (source also of Sanskrit mukah "dumb," Greek myein "to be shut," of the mouth). Form assimilated in 16c. to Latin mutus.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, mewet "silent," 源自 古法语 muet "dumb, mute" (12 世纪), 为 … 的指小形式 mut, mo, 源自 拉丁语 mutus "silent, speechless, dumb," 可能 源自 imitative base *meue- (source also of 梵语 mukah "dumb," 希腊语 myein "to be shut," of the mouth). Form assimilated in 16 世纪 to 拉丁语 mutus.

entries.definition: vi. 咕哝；喃喃自语 n. 咕哝；喃喃自语
entries.etymology: early 14c., moteren "to mumble," from a common PIE imitative *mut- "to grunt, mutter" (source also of Old Norse muðla "to murmur," Latin muttire "to mutter," Old High German mutilon "to murmur, mutter; to drizzle"), with frequentative suffix -er. Related: Muttered; muttering.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, moteren "to mumble," 源自 a common 原始印欧语 (PIE) imitative *mut- "to grunt, mutter" (source also of 古北欧语 muðla "to murmur," 拉丁语 muttire "to mutter," 古高地德语 mutilon "to murmur, mutter; to drizzle"), with frequentative suffix -er. 同源词：Muttered; muttering.

example.en: He began to mutter complaints under his breath during the long meeting.
example.zh: 他在漫长的会议中开始低声咕哝着抱怨。

entries.etymology:
late 15c., originally of feelings, from Middle French mutuel (14c.), from Latin mutuus "reciprocal, done in exchange," from PIE root *mei- (1) "to change, exchange" (see mutable).

Mutual Admiration Society (1851) seems to have been coined by Thoreau. Mutual fund is recorded from 1950. The Cold War's mutual assured destruction attested from 1966. (Assured destruction was an early 1960s term in U.S. military policy circles in reference to nuclear weapons as a deterrent, popularized c. 1964 by Robert McNamara, U.S. Secretary of Defense under Lyndon Johnson, e.g. statement before House Armed Services Committee, Feb. 18, 1965; the mutual perhaps first added by Donald Brennan, conservative defense analyst and a public critic of the policy, who also noted the acronym MAD.)
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, 原义为 of feelings, 源自 中古法语 mutuel (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 mutuus "reciprocal, done in exchange," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *mei- (1) "to change, exchange" （参见 mutable). Mutual Admiration Society (1851 年) seems to have been coined by Thoreau. Mutual fund 见于 1950 年. The Cold War's mutual assured destruction attested 自 1966 年起. (Assured destruction was an early 1960 年代 term in U.S. military policy circles in reference to nuclear weapons 作为 deterrent, popularized 约 1964 年 by Robert McNamara, U.S. Secretary of Defense under Lyndon Johnson, e.g. statement before House Armed Services Committee, Feb. 18, 1965 年; the mutual 或许 first added by Donald Brennan, conservative defense analyst and a public critic of the policy, who also noted the acronym MAD.)

example.en: The two countries signed a mutual defense agreement last year.
example.zh: 两国去年签署了一项相互防御协议。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, mi, reduced form of mine used before words beginning in consonants except h- (my father, but mine enemy), and from 14c. before all nouns. As interjection, by 1825, probably a shortened form of my God!
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, mi, reduced form of mine used before words beginning in consonants except h- (my father, but mine enemy), and 源自 14 世纪 before all nouns. As interjection, 截至 1825 年, 可能 a shortened form of my God!

entries.etymology: c. 1500, alteration of meself, from Old English phrase (ic) me self, where me is "a kind of ethical dative" [OED], altered in Middle Ages from meself on analogy of herself, with her- felt as genitive; though analogous hisself remains bad form.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年, alteration of meself, 源自 古英语 phrase (ic) me self, where me is "a kind of ethical dative" [OED], altered in Middle Ages 源自 meself on analogy of herself, with her- felt as 属格; though analogous hisself remains bad form.

definitionLines: a. 神秘的，可疑的，难以理解的
entries.definition: a. 神秘的，可疑的，难以理解的
entries.etymology: 1610s, "full of mystery," from Latin mysterium (see mystery (n.1)) + -ous. Related: Mysteriously; mysteriousness. Earlier in same sense was mysterial (early 15c.), from Late Latin mysterialis.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "full of mystery," 源自 拉丁语 mysterium （参见 mystery (n.1)) + -ous. 同源词：Mysteriously; mysteriousness. Earlier in same sense was mysterial (15 世纪初), 源自 晚期拉丁语 mysterialis.

example.en: She gave him a mysterious smile and walked away without a word.
example.zh: 她神秘地对他一笑，一言不发地走开了。

entries.etymology: 1830, from French Mythe (1818) and directly from Modern Latin mythus, from Greek mythos "speech, thought, story, myth, anything delivered by word of mouth," of unknown origin.General sense of "untrue story, rumor" is from 1840.
entries.etymologyZh: 1830 年, 源自 法语 Mythe (1818 年) and 直接源自 现代 拉丁语 mythus, 源自 希腊语 mythos "speech, thought, story, myth, anything delivered by word of mouth," 来源不详.General 语义 "untrue story, rumor" 始于 1840 年.

example.en: The ancient Greeks told a myth about how the gods punished human pride.
example.zh: 古希腊人讲述了一个关于众神惩罚人类傲慢的神话。

entries.definition: n. 钉；指甲，爪 vt. 钉，使牢固
entries.etymology:
Old English negel "metal pin," nægl "fingernail (handnægl), toenail," from Proto-Germanic *naglaz (source also of Old Norse nagl "fingernail," nagli "metal nail;" Old Saxon and Old High German nagel, Old Frisian neil, Middle Dutch naghel, Dutch nagel, German Nagel "fingernail, small metal spike"), from PIE root *(o)nogh "nail" (source also of Greek onyx "claw, fingernail;" Latin unguis "nail, claw;" Old Church Slavonic noga "foot," noguti "nail, claw;" Lithuanian naga "hoof," nagutis "fingernail;" Old Irish ingen, Old Welsh eguin "nail, claw").

The "fingernail" sense seems to be the original one. Nail polish attested from 1891. To bite one's nails as a sign of anxiety is attested from 1570s. Nail-biting is from 1805. Hard as nails is from 1828. To hit the nail on the head "say or do just the right thing" is first recorded 1520s. Phrase on the nail "on the spot, exactly" is from 1590s, of obscure origin; OED says it is not even certain it belongs to this sense of nail.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 negel "metal pin," nægl "fingernail (handnægl), toenail," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *naglaz (source also of 古北欧语 nagl "fingernail," nagli "metal nail;" 古撒克逊语 and 古高地德语 nagel, 古弗里西语 neil, Middle 荷兰语 naghel, 荷兰语 nagel, 德语 Nagel "fingernail, small metal spike"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *(o)nogh "nail" (source also of 希腊语 onyx "claw, fingernail;" 拉丁语 unguis "nail, claw;" Old Church Slavonic noga "foot," noguti "nail, claw;" Lithuanian naga "hoof," nagutis "fingernail;" Old 爱尔兰语 ingen, Old Welsh eguin "nail, claw"). The "fingernail" sense seems to be the original one. Nail polish attested 自 1891 年起. To bite one's nails 作为 sign of anxiety 见于 1570 年代. Nail-biting 始于 1805 年. Hard as nails 始于 1828 年. To hit the nail on the head "say or do just the right thing" is 首见于 1520 年代. Phrase on the nail "on the spot, exactly" 始于 1590 年代, of obscure origin; OED says it is not even certain it belongs to this 语义 nail.

entries.etymology: 1650s, "natural, simple, artless," from French naïve, fem. of naïf, from Old French naif "naive, natural, genuine; just born; foolish, innocent; unspoiled, unworked" (13c.), from Latin nativus "not artificial," also "native, rustic," literally "born, innate, natural" (see native (adj.)). Related: Naively.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, "natural, simple, artless," 源自 法语 naïve, fem. of naïf, 源自 古法语 naif "naive, natural, genuine; just born; foolish, innocent; unspoiled, unworked" (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 nativus "not artificial," also "native, rustic," 字面义为 "born, innate, natural" （参见 本族 （形）). 同源词：Naively.

example.en: It was naive of her to trust a stranger with all her personal information.
example.zh: 她把个人信息全部告诉一个陌生人，实在是太天真了。

definitionLines: a. 裸体的；毫无遮掩的
entries.definition: a. 裸体的；毫无遮掩的
entries.etymology:
Old English nacod "nude, bare; empty," also "not fully clothed," from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz (source also of Old Frisian nakad, Middle Dutch naket, Dutch naakt, Old High German nackot, German nackt, Old Norse nökkviðr, Old Swedish nakuþer, Gothic naqaþs "naked"), from PIE root *nogw- "naked" (source also of Sanskrit nagna, Hittite nekumant-, Old Persian *nagna-, Greek gymnos, Latin nudus, Lithuanian nuogas, Old Church Slavonic nagu-, Russian nagoi, Old Irish nocht, Welsh noeth "bare, naked"). Related: Nakedly; nakedness. Applied to qualities, actions, etc., from late 14c. (first in "The Cloud of Unknowing"); phrase naked truth is from 1585, in Alexander Montgomerie's "The Cherry and the Slae":

Phrase naked as a jaybird (1943) was earlier naked as a robin (1879, in a Shropshire context); the earliest known comparative based on it was naked as a needle (late 14c.). Naked eye is from 1660s, unnecessary in the world before telescopes and microscopes.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 nacod "nude, bare; empty," also "not fully clothed," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *nakwadaz (source also of 古弗里西语 nakad, Middle 荷兰语 naket, 荷兰语 naakt, 古高地德语 nackot, 德语 nackt, 古北欧语 nökkviðr, Old Swedish nakuþer, Gothic naqaþs "naked"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *nogw- "naked" (source also of 梵语 nagna, Hittite nekumant-, Old 波斯语 *nagna-, 希腊语 gymnos, 拉丁语 nudus, Lithuanian nuogas, Old Church Slavonic nagu-, 俄语 nagoi, Old 爱尔兰语 nocht, Welsh noeth "bare, naked"). 同源词：Nakedly; nakedness. Applied to qualities, actions, etc., 源自 14 世纪晚期 (first in "The Cloud of Unknowing"); phrase naked truth 始于 1585 年, in Alexander Montgomerie's "The Cherry and the Slae": Phrase naked 作为 jaybird (1943 年) was earlier naked 作为 robin (1879 年, in a Shropshire context); the earliest known comparative based on it was naked 作为 needle (14 世纪晚期). Naked eye 始于 1660 年代, unnecessary in the world before telescopes and microscopes.

example.en: The truth was laid naked for everyone in the room to see.
example.zh: 真相在房间里所有人面前毫无遮掩地暴露出来。

definitionLines: n. 名字，名称；名声，名望；名义
vt. 给…•…取名；列举；任命，提 名
entries.definition: n. 名字，名称；名声，名望；名义 vt. 给…•…取名；列举；任命，提 名
entries.etymology:
Old English nama, noma "name, reputation," from Proto-Germanic *namon (source also of Old Saxon namo, Old Frisian nama, Old High German namo, German Name, Middle Dutch name, Dutch naam, Old Norse nafn, Gothic namo "name"), from PIE *nomn- (source also of Sanskrit nama; Avestan nama; Greek onoma, onyma; Latin nomen; Old Church Slavonic ime, genitive imene; Russian imya; Old Irish ainm; Old Welsh anu "name").

Meaning "famous person" is from 1610s. Meaning "one's reputation" is from c. 1300. As a modifier meaning "well-known," first attested 1938. Name brand is from 1944; name-calling attested from 1846; name-dropper first recorded 1947. name-tag is from 1903; name-child attested from 1845. The name of the game "the essential thing or quality" is from 1966; to have one's name in lights "be a famous performer" is from 1929.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 nama, noma "name, reputation," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *namon (source also of 古撒克逊语 namo, 古弗里西语 nama, 古高地德语 namo, 德语 Name, Middle 荷兰语 name, 荷兰语 naam, 古北欧语 nafn, Gothic namo "name"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *nomn- (source also of 梵语 nama; Avestan nama; 希腊语 onoma, onyma; 拉丁语 nomen; Old Church Slavonic ime, 属格 imene; 俄语 imya; Old 爱尔兰语 ainm; Old Welsh anu "name"). 义为 "famous person" 始于 1610 年代. 义为 "one's reputation" 始于 约 1300 年. 作为 modifier 意为 "well-known," 最早见于 1938 年. Name brand 始于 1944 年; name-calling attested 自 1846 年起; name-dropper 首见于 1947 年. name-tag 始于 1903 年; name-child attested 自 1845 年起. The name of the game "the essential thing or quality" 始于 1966 年; to have one's name in lights "be a famous performer" 始于 1929 年.

example.en: The committee formally voted to name the new building after the founder.
example.zh: 委员会正式投票决定以创始人的名字命名新楼。

entries.etymology: "particularly, especially" (i.e. "by name"), late 12c., from name (n.) + -ly (2).
entries.etymologyZh: "particularly, especially" (i.e. "by name"), 12 世纪晚期, 源自 name （名） + -ly (2).

example.en: Only one person can make this decision, namely the CEO.
example.zh: 只有一个人能做这个决定，即首席执行官。

entries.definition: vt. 叙述；给……作旁白 vi. 叙述；讲述
entries.etymology: 1748, back-formation from narration or else from Latin narratus, past participle of narrare "to tell, relate, recount." "Richardson and Johnson call it Scottish" [OED], a stigma which kept it from general use until 19c. A few mid-17c. instances are traceable to Spanish narrar. Related: Narrated; narrating.
entries.etymologyZh: 1748 年, back-formation 源自 narration or else 源自 拉丁语 narratus, 为 … 的过去分词 narrare "to tell, relate, recount." "Richardson and Johnson call it Scottish" [OED], a stigma which kept it 源自 general use until 19 世纪 A few 17 世纪中期 instances are traceable to 西班牙语 narrar. 同源词：Narrated; narrating.

definitionLines: a. 叙事的，叙述的；叙事体的
entries.definition: n. 叙述；故事；讲述 a. 叙事的，叙述的；叙事体的
entries.etymology: mid-15c., from Middle French narratif, from Late Latin narrativus "suited to narration," from Latin narrat-, stem of narrare (see narration).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 中古法语 narratif, 源自 晚期拉丁语 narrativus "suited to narration," 源自 拉丁语 narrat-, stem of narrare （参见 narration).

example.en: The film follows a narrative that spans three generations of one family.
example.zh: 这部电影跟随一个跨越三代家庭的叙事展开。

definitionLines: a. 狭的，狭窄的；狭隘的
entries.definition: a. 狭的，狭窄的；狭隘的
entries.etymology: Old English nearu "narrow, constricted, limited; petty; causing difficulty, oppressive; strict, severe," from West Germanic *narwaz "narrowness" (source also of Frisian nar, Old Saxon naru, Middle Dutch nare, Dutch naar); not found in other Germanic languages and of unknown origin. The narrow seas (c. 1400) were the waters between Great Britain and the continent and Ireland. Related: Narrowness.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 nearu "narrow, constricted, limited; petty; causing difficulty, oppressive; strict, severe," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *narwaz "narrowness" (source also of Frisian nar, 古撒克逊语 naru, Middle 荷兰语 nare, 荷兰语 naar); not found in other 日耳曼语 languages and 来源不详. The narrow seas (约 1400 年) were the waters between Great Britain and the continent and Ireland. 同源词：Narrowness.

example.en: The road became very narrow as it wound up the mountain.
example.zh: 这条路蜿蜒而上，变得非常狭窄。

definitionLines: a. 令人厌恶的；难弄的；恶劣 的；污秽的
entries.definition: a. 令人厌恶的；难弄的；恶劣 的；污秽的
entries.etymology:
c. 1400, "foul, filthy, dirty, unclean," of unknown origin; perhaps [Barnhart] from Old French nastre "miserly, envious, malicious, spiteful," shortened form of villenastre "infamous, bad," from vilein "villain" + -astre, pejorative suffix, from Latin -aster.

Alternative etymology [OED] is from Dutch nestig "dirty," literally "like a bird's nest." Likely reinforced in either case by a Scandinavian source (compare Swedish dialectal naskug "dirty, nasty"), which also might be the source of the Middle English word. Of weather, from 1630s; of things generally, "unpleasant, offensive," from 1705. Of people, "ill-tempered," from 1825. Noun meaning "something nasty" is from 1935. Related: Nastily; nastiness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "foul, filthy, dirty, unclean," 来源不详; 或许 [Barnhart] 源自 古法语 nastre "miserly, envious, malicious, spiteful," shortened form of villenastre "infamous, bad," 源自 vilein "villain" + -astre, pejorative suffix, 源自 拉丁语 -aster. Alternative etymology [OED] 始于 荷兰语 nestig "dirty," 字面义为 "like a bird's nest." Likely reinforced in either case by a Scandinavian source (对比 Swedish 方言 naskug "dirty, nasty"), which also might be the source of the 中古英语 word. Of weather, 源自 1630 年代; of things generally, "unpleasant, offensive," 自 1705 年起. Of people, "ill-tempered," 自 1825 年起. Noun 意为 "something nasty" 始于 1935 年. 同源词：Nastily; nastiness.

example.en: The kitchen was in a nasty state after the party last night.
example.zh: 昨晚聚会过后，厨房乱得一塌糊涂。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old French nacion "birth, rank; descendants, relatives; country, homeland" (12c.) and directly from Latin nationem (nominative natio) "birth, origin; breed, stock, kind, species; race of people, tribe," literally "that which has been born," from natus, past participle of nasci "be born" (Old Latin gnasci; see genus). Political sense has gradually predominated, but earliest English examples inclined toward the racial meaning "large group of people with common ancestry." Older sense preserved in application to North American Indian peoples (1640s). Nation-building first attested 1907 (implied in nation-builder).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 nacion "birth, rank; descendants, relatives; country, homeland" (12 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 nationem (主格 natio) "birth, origin; breed, stock, kind, species; race of people, tribe," 字面义为 "that which has been born," 源自 natus, 为 … 的过去分词 nasci "be born" (Old 拉丁语 gnasci; 参见 genus). Political sense has gradually predominated, but earliest English examples inclined toward the racial 意为 "large group of people with common ancestry." Older sense preserved in application to North American Indian peoples (1640 年代). Nation-building 最早见于 1907 年 (implied in nation-builder).

example.en: Leaders from every nation were invited to attend the global climate summit.
example.zh: 来自每个国家的领导人都受邀出席全球气候峰会。

entries.etymology: 1590s, from Middle French national (from Old French nation), and also from nation + -al (1). As a noun, "citizen of a (particular) nation," from 1887. National anthem first recorded 1819, in Shelley. Related: Nationally.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, 源自 中古法语 national (源自 古法语 nation), and 亦源自 nation + -al (1). 作名词时, "citizen of a (particular) nation," 自 1887 年起. National anthem 首见于 1819 年, in Shelley. 同源词：Nationally.

example.en: The government launched a national campaign to promote recycling habits.
example.zh: 政府发起了一场全国性的运动来推广回收习惯。

definitionLines: n. /a. 民族主义者（的）；国家主
entries.definition: n. /a. 民族主义者（的）；国家主
entries.etymology: "one devoted to his nation," 1715, from national in a now obsolete sense of "patriotic" (1711) + -ist. Related: Nationalistic; nationalistically.
entries.etymologyZh: "one devoted to his nation," 1715 年, 源自 national in a 今废 语义 "patriotic" (1711 年) + -ist. 同源词：Nationalistic; nationalistically.

entries.etymology: 1690s, "national quality," from national + -ity (in some usages perhaps from French nationalité. As "fact of belonging to or being a citizen of a particular state," from 1828, gradually shading into "race, ethnicity." Meaning "separate existence as a nation" is recorded from 1832. Related: Nationalities.
entries.etymologyZh: 1690 年代, "national quality," 源自 national + -ity (in some usages 或源自 法语 nationalité. As "fact of belonging to or being a citizen of a particular state," 自 1828 年起, gradually shading into "race, ethnicity." 义为 "separate existence as a nation" 见于 1832 年. 同源词：Nationalities.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "natural, hereditary, connected with something in a natural way," from Old French natif "native, born in; raw, unspoiled" (14c.) and directly from Latin nativus "innate, produced by birth," from natus, past participle of nasci (Old Latin gnasci) "be born," related to gignere "beget," from PIE root *gene-/*gen- "to give birth, beget," with derivatives referring to familial and tribal groups (see genus). From late 15c. as "born in a particular place." From early 15c. as "of one's birth," also used from mid-15c. in sense of "bound; born in servitude or serfdom," also, as a noun "a bondsman, serf." Native American attested from 1956.

definitionLines: a. 自然界的，天生的；天赋的， 固有的
entries.definition: a. 自然界的，天生的；天赋的， 固有的
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, naturel, "of one's inborn character; hereditary, by birth;" early 14c. as "of the world of nature (especially as opposed to man)," from Old French naturel "of nature, conforming to nature; by birth," and directly from Latin naturalis "by birth, according to nature," from natura "nature" (see nature).

From late 15c. as "not miraculous, in conformity with nature." Meaning "easy, free from affectation" is attested from c. 1600. Of things, "not artificially created," c. 1600. As a euphemism for "illegitimate, bastard" (of children), it is first recorded c. 1400, on notion of blood kinship (but not legal status).

Natural science is from late 14c.; natural law is from early 15c. Natural order "apparent order in nature" is from 1690s. Natural childbirth first attested 1933. Natural life, usually in reference to the duration of life, is from late 15c. Natural history is from 1560s (see history). To die of natural causes is from 1570s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, naturel, "of one's inborn character; hereditary, by birth;" 14 世纪初 as "of the world of nature (especially as opposed to man)," 源自 古法语 naturel "of nature, conforming to nature; by birth," and 直接源自 拉丁语 naturalis "by birth, according to nature," 源自 natura "nature" （参见 nature). From 15 世纪晚期 as "not miraculous, in conformity with nature." 义为 "easy, free from affectation" 见于 约 1600 年. Of things, "not artificially created," 约 1600 年. 作为 euphemism for "illegitimate, bastard" (of children), it is 首见于 约 1400 年, on 概念 blood kinship (but not legal status). Natural science 始于 14 世纪晚期; natural law 始于 15 世纪初 Natural order "apparent order in nature" 始于 1690 年代. Natural childbirth 最早见于 1933 年. Natural life, 通常 in reference to the duration of life, 始于 15 世纪晚期 Natural history 始于 1560 年代 （参见 history). To die of natural causes 始于 1570 年代.

definitionLines: n. 自然，自然界；性质，本性， 天性
entries.definition: n. 自然，自然界；性质，本性， 天性
entries.etymology:
late 13c., "restorative powers of the body, bodily processes; powers of growth;" from Old French nature "nature, being, principle of life; character, essence," from Latin natura "course of things; natural character, constitution, quality; the universe," literally "birth," from natus "born," past participle of nasci "to be born," from PIE *gene- "to give birth, beget" (see genus).

From late 14c. as "creation, the universe;" also "heredity, birth, hereditary circumstance; essential qualities, innate disposition" (as in human nature); "nature personified, Mother Nature." Specifically as "material world beyond human civilization or society" from 1660s. Nature and nurture have been contrasted since 1874.

From 14 世纪晚期 as "creation, the universe;" also "heredity, birth, hereditary circumstance; essential qualities, innate disposition" (as in human nature); "nature personified, Mother Nature." example.en: It is in a dog's nature to be loyal to its owner above all else.

definitionLines: n. 航海，航空，导航，领航，航行
entries.definition: n. 航海，航空，导航，领航，航行
entries.etymology: 1530s, from Middle French navigation (14c.) or directly from Latin navigationem (nominative navigatio) "a sailing, navigation, voyage," noun of action from past participle stem of navigare "to sail, sail over, go by sea, steer a ship," from navis "ship" (see naval) + root of agere "to drive" (see act (n.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, 源自 中古法语 navigation (14 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 navigationem (主格 navigatio) "a sailing, navigation, voyage," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of navigare "to sail, sail over, go by sea, steer a ship," 源自 navis "ship" （参见 naval) + root of agere "to drive" （参见 act （名）).

entries.etymology: early 14c., "fleet of ships," especially for purposes of war, from Old French navie "fleet; ship," from Latin navigia, plural of navigium "vessel, boat," from navis "ship" (see naval). Meaning "a nation's collective, organized sea power" is from 1530s. The Old English words were sciphere (usually of Viking invaders) and scipfierd (usually of the home defenses). Navy blue was the color of the British naval uniform. Navy bean attested from 1856, so called because they were grown to be used by the Navy.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "fleet of ships," 尤指 for purposes of war, 源自 古法语 navie "fleet; ship," 源自 拉丁语 navigia, 为 … 的复数 navigium "vessel, boat," 源自 navis "ship" （参见 naval). 义为 "a nation's collective, organized sea power" 始于 1530 年代. The 古英语 words were sciphere (通常 of Viking invaders) and scipfierd (通常 of the home defenses). Navy blue was the color of the British naval uniform. Navy bean attested 自 1856 年起, so called because they were grown to be used by the Navy.

ad. 接近，靠近；大约，差不多

entries.etymology: Old English near "closer, nearer," comparative of neah, neh"nigh." Influenced by Old Norse naer "near," it came to be used as a positive form mid-13c., and new comparative nearer developed 1500s (see nigh). As an adjective from c. 1300. Originally an adverb but now supplanted in most such senses by nearly; it has in turn supplanted correct nigh as an adjective. Related: Nearness. In near and dear (1620s) it refers to nearness of kinship. Near East first attested 1891, in Kipling. Near beer "low-alcoholic brew" is from 1908.

Originally an 副词 but 现在 supplanted in most such senses by nearly; it has in turn supplanted correct nigh 作形容词时. 同源词：Nearness. In near and dear (1620 年代) it refers to nearness of kinship. definitionLines: 整洁的，简洁的；优美的， 精致的；利索的
entries.definition: 整洁的，简洁的；优美的， 精致的；利索的
entries.etymology:
1540s, "clean, free from dirt," from Anglo-French neit, Middle French net "clear, pure" (12c.), from Latin nitidus "well-favored, elegant, trim," literally "gleaming," from nitere "to shine," from PIE root *nei- "to shine" (source also of Middle Irish niam "gleam, splendor," niamda "shining;" Old Irish noib "holy," niab "strength;" Welsh nwyfiant "gleam, splendor").

Meaning "inclined to be tidy" is from 1570s. Of liquor, "straight," c. 1800, from meaning "unadulterated" (of wine), which is first attested 1570s. Informal sense of "very good" first recorded 1934 in American English; variant neato is teenager slang, first recorded 1968. Related: Neatly; neatness.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "clean, free from dirt," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 neit, 中古法语 net "clear, pure" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 nitidus "well-favored, elegant, trim," 字面义为 "gleaming," 源自 nitere "to shine," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *nei- "to shine" (source also of Middle 爱尔兰语 niam "gleam, splendor," niamda "shining;" Old 爱尔兰语 noib "holy," niab "strength;" Welsh nwyfiant "gleam, splendor"). 义为 "inclined to be tidy" 始于 1570 年代. Of liquor, "straight," 约 1800 年, 源自 意为 "unadulterated" (of wine), which is 最早见于 1570 年代. Informal 语义 "very good" 首见于 1934 年 in American English; variant neato is teenager 俚语, 首见于 1968 年. 同源词：Neatly; neatness.

definitionLines: a. 必须的，必要的；必然的
entries.definition: a. 必须的，必要的；必然的
entries.etymology: late 14c. "needed, required, essential, indispensable," from Old French necessaire "necessary, urgent, compelling" (13c.), and directly from Latin necessarius "unavoidable, indispensable, necessary," from necesse "unavoidable, indispensable," originally "no backing away," from ne- "not" + cedere "to withdraw, go away, yield" (see cede). The root sense is of that from which there is no evasion, that which is inevitable. Necessary house "privy" is from c. 1600. Necessary evil is from 1540s (the original reference was to "woman").
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期 "needed, required, essential, indispensable," 源自 古法语 necessaire "necessary, urgent, compelling" (13 世纪), and 直接源自 拉丁语 necessarius "unavoidable, indispensable, necessary," 源自 necesse "unavoidable, indispensable," 原义为 "no backing away," 源自 ne- "not" + cedere "to withdraw, go away, yield" （参见 cede). The root sense is of that 源自 which there is no evasion, that which is inevitable. Necessary house "privy" 始于 约 1600 年. Necessary evil 始于 1540 年代 (the original reference was to "woman").

entries.etymology:
Old English hnecca "neck, nape, back of the neck" (a fairly rare word) from Proto-Germanic *hnekk- "the nape of the neck" (source also of Old Frisian hnekka, Middle Dutch necke, Dutch nek, Old Norse hnakkr, Old High German hnach, German Nacken "neck"), with no certain cognates outside Germanic, though Klein's sources suggest PIE *knok- "high point, ridge" (source of Old Irish cnocc, Welsh cnwch, Old Breton cnoch "hill").

The more usual Old English words were hals (the general Germanic word, cognate with Gothic, Old Norse, Danish, Swedish, Dutch, German hals), cognate with Latin collum (see collar (n.)); and sweora, swira "neck, nape," probably also from a PIE root meaning "column" (cognate with Old English swer "column," Sanskrit svaru- "post").

Transferred senses attested from c. 1400. Phrase neck of the woods (American English) is attested from 1780 in the sense of "narrow stretch of woods;" 1839 with meaning "settlement in a wooded region." To stick one's neck out "take a risk" is first recorded 1919, American English. Horses running neck and neck is attested from 1799.

entries.definition: n./v. 必须，必要；缺少 auz. v. 需要，必须
entries.etymology:
Old English nied (West Saxon), ned (Mercian) "necessity, compulsion, duty; hardship, distress; errand, business," originally "violence, force," from Proto-Germanic *nauthiz/*naudiz (source also of Old Saxon nod, Old Norse nauðr, Old Frisian ned, Middle Dutch, Dutch nood, Old High German not, German Not, Gothic nauþs "need"), probably cognate with Old Prussian nautin "need," and perhaps with Old Church Slavonic nazda, Russian nuzda, Polish nędza "misery, distress," from PIE *nau- (1) "death, to be exhausted" (see narwhal).

The more common Old English word for "need, necessity, want" was ðearf, but they were connected via a notion of "trouble, pain," and the two formed a compound, niedðearf "need, necessity, compulsion, thing needed." Nied also might have been influenced by Old English neod "desire, longing," which often was spelled the same. Common in Old English compounds, such as niedfaru "compulsory journey," a euphemism for "death;" niedhæmed "rape," the second element being an Old English word meaning "sexual intercourse;" niedling "slave." Meaning "extreme poverty, destitution" is from c. 1200.

The more common 古英语 word for "need, necessity, want" was ðearf, but they were connected 经由 a 概念 "trouble, pain," and the two formed a 复合词, niedðearf "need, necessity, compulsion, thing needed." Nied also might have been influenced by 古英语 neod "desire, longing," which 常 was spelled the same. Common in 古英语 compounds, such as niedfaru "compulsory journey," a euphemism for "death;" niedhæmed "rape," the second element being an 古英语 word 意为 "sexual intercourse;" niedling "slave." 义为 "extreme poverty, destitution" 始于 约 1200 年.

example.en: A cactus needs very little water to survive in the desert.

entries.etymology: Old English nædl, from Proto-Germanic *næthlo (source also of Old Saxon nathla, Old Norse nal, Old Frisian nedle, Old High German nadala, German Nadel, Gothic neþla "needle"), literally "a tool for sewing," from PIE *net-la-, from root *(s)ne- "to sew, to spin" (source also of Sanskrit snayati "wraps up," Greek nein "to spin," Latin nere "to spin," German nähen "to sew," Old Church Slavonic niti "thread," Old Irish snathat "needle," Welsh nyddu "to sew," nodwydd "needle") + instrumental suffix *-tla.Meaning "piece of magnetized steel in a compass" is from late 14c. (on a dial or indicator from 1928); the surgical instrument so called from 1727; phonographic sense from 1902; sense of "leaf of a fir or pine tree" first attested 1797. Needledom "the world of sewing" is from 1847. Needle's eye, figurative of a minute opening, often is a reference to Matt. xix:24.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 nædl, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *næthlo (source also of 古撒克逊语 nathla, 古北欧语 nal, 古弗里西语 nedle, 古高地德语 nadala, 德语 Nadel, Gothic neþla "needle"), 字面义为 "a tool for sewing," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *net-la-, 源自 root *(s)ne- "to sew, to spin" (source also of 梵语 snayati "wraps up," 希腊语 nein "to spin," 拉丁语 nere "to spin," 德语 nähen "to sew," Old Church Slavonic niti "thread," Old 爱尔兰语 snathat "needle," Welsh nyddu "to sew," nodwydd "needle") + instrumental suffix *-tla.义为 "piece of magnetized steel in a compass" 始于 14 世纪晚期 (on a dial or indicator 自 1928 年起); the surgical instrument so called 自 1727 年起; phonographic sense 自 1902 年起; 语义 "leaf of a fir or pine tree" 最早见于 1797 年. Needledom "the world of sewing" 始于 1847 年. Needle's eye, figurative of a minute opening, 常 is a reference to Matt. xix:24.

definitionLines: a.否定的，消极的，反面的； 负的，阴性的
entries.definition: a.否定的，消极的，反面的； 负的，阴性的
entries.etymology:
c. 1400, "expressing denial," from Old French negatif (13c.) and directly from Latin negativus "that which denies," from negat-, past participle stem of negare "deny, say no" (see deny). Meaning "expressing negation" is from c. 1500; that of "characterized by absence" is from 1560s. Algebraic sense is from 1670s. The electricity sense is from 1755.

Related: Negatively.

entries.etymology: "to communicate in search of mutual agreement," 1590s, back-formation from negotiation, or else from Latin negotiatus, past participle of negotiari. In the sense of "tackle successfully" (1862), it at first meant "to clear on horseback a hedge, fence, or other obstacle" and "originated in the hunting-field; those who hunt the fox like also to hunt jocular verbal novelties" [Gowers, 1965]. Related: Negotiated; negotiating.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old French neveu (Old North French nevu) "grandson, descendant," from Latin nepotem (nominative nepos) "sister's son, grandson, descendant," in post-Augustan Latin, "nephew," from PIE *nepot- "grandchild," and in a general sense, "male descendant other than son" (source also of Sanskrit napat "grandson, descendant;" Old Persian napat- "grandson;" Old Lithuanian nepuotis "grandson;" Dutch neef; German Neffe "nephew;" Old Irish nia, genitive niath "son of a sister," Welsh nei). Used in English in all the classical senses until meaning narrowed in 17c., and also as a euphemism for "the illegitimate son of an ecclesiastic" (1580s). The Old English cognate, nefa "nephew, stepson, grandson, second cousin" survived to 16c.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "god of the sea," from Latin Neptunus, son of Saturn, brother of Jupiter, the Roman god of the sea (later identified with Greek Poseidon), probably from PIE root *nebh- "cloud" (source of Latin nebula "fog, mist, cloud;" see nebula), via a sense of "moist, wet." entries.etymology:
late 14c., nerf "sinew, tendon," from Old French nerf and directly from Medieval Latin nervus "nerve," from Latin nervus "sinew, tendon; cord, bowstring," metathesis of pre-Latin *neuros, from PIE *(s)neu- "tendon, sinew" (source also of Sanskrit snavan- "band, sinew," Armenian neard "sinew," Greek neuron "sinew, tendon," in Galen "nerve"). Sense of "fibers that convey impulses between the brain and the body" is from c. 1600.

Secondary senses developed from meaning "strength, vigor, energy" (c. 1600), from the "sinew" sense. Hence figurative sense of "feeling, courage," first attested c. 1600; that of "courage, boldness" is from 1809; bad sense "impudence, cheek" is from 1887. Latin nervus also had a figurative sense of "vigor, force, power, strength," as did Greek neuron. From the neurological sense come Nerves "condition of nervousness," attested from 1792; to get on someone's nerves, from 1895. War of nerves "psychological warfare" is from 1915.

Secondary senses developed 源自 意为 "strength, vigor, energy" (约 1600 年), 源自 "sinew" sense. Hence figurative 语义 "feeling, courage," 最早见于 约 1600 年; that of "courage, boldness" 始于 1809 年; bad sense "impudence, cheek" 始于 1887 年. 拉丁语 nervus also had a figurative 语义 "vigor, force, power, strength," as did 希腊语 neuron. From the neurological sense come Nerves "condition of nervousness," attested 自 1792 年起; to get on someone's nerves, 自 1895 年起. War of nerves "psychological warfare" 始于 1915 年.

definitionLines: a.神经的；神经过敏的，紧张不
entries.definition: a.神经的；神经过敏的，紧张不
entries.etymology: c. 1400, "affecting the sinews," from Latin nervosus "sinewy, vigorous," from nervus "sinew, nerve" (see nerve). Meaning "of or belonging to the nerves" in the modern sense is from 1660s. Meaning "suffering disorder of the nervous system" is from 1734; illogical sense "restless, agitated, lacking nerve" is 1740. Widespread popular use as a euphemism for mental forced the medical community to coin neurological to replace it in the older sense. Nervous wreck first attested 1862. Related: Nervously; nervousness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "affecting the sinews," 源自 拉丁语 nervosus "sinewy, vigorous," 源自 nervus "sinew, nerve" （参见 nerve). 义为 "of or belonging to the nerves" in the modern sense 始于 1660 年代. 义为 "suffering disorder of the nervous system" 始于 1734 年; illogical sense "restless, agitated, lacking nerve" is 1740 年. entries.etymology:
Old English nest "bird's nest, snug retreat," also "young bird, brood," from Proto-Germanic *nistaz (source also of Middle Low German, Middle Dutch nest, German Nest), from PIE *nizdo- (source also of Sanskrit nidah "resting place, nest," Latin nidus "nest," Old Church Slavonic gnezdo, Old Irish net, Welsh nyth, Breton nez "nest"), probably from *ni "down" + *sed- (1) "to sit" (see sedentary).

Used since Middle English in reference to various accumulations of things (such as a nest of drawers, early 18c.). Nest egg "retirement savings" is from 1700, originally "a real or artificial egg left in a nest to induce the hen to go on laying there" (c. 1600).

entries.etymology:
Old English næfre "never," compound of ne "not, no" (from PIE root *ne- "no, not;" see un- (1)) + æfre "ever" (see ever). Early used as an emphatic form of not (as still in never mind). Old English, unlike its modern descendant, had the useful custom of attaching ne to words to create their negatives, as in nabban for na habban "not to have."

Italian giammai, French jamais, Spanish jamas are from Latin iam "already" + magis "more;" thus literally "at any time, ever," originally with a negative, but this has been so thoroughly absorbed in sense as to be formally omitted.

Phrase never say die "don't despair" is from 1818. Never Never Land is first attested in Australia as a name for the uninhabited northern part of Queensland (1884), perhaps so called because anyone who had gone there once never wished to return. Meaning "imaginary, illusory or utopian place" first attested 1900 in American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 næfre "never," 由 … 复合而成 ne "not, no" (源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ne- "no, not;" 参见 un- (1)) + æfre "ever" （参见 ever). Early used 作为 emphatic form of not (as still in never mind). 古英语, unlike its modern descendant, had the useful custom of attaching ne to words to create their negatives, as in nabban for na habban "not to have." 意大利语 giammai, 法语 jamais, 西班牙语 jamas 始于 拉丁语 iam "already" + magis "more;" thus 字面义为 "at any time, ever," 原义为 with a negative, but this has been so thoroughly absorbed in sense as to be formally omitted. Phrase never say die "don't despair" 始于 1818 年. Never Never Land is 最早见于 in Australia 作为 name for the uninhabited northern part of Queensland (1884 年), 或许 so called because anyone who had gone there once never wished to return. 义为 "imaginary, illusory or utopian place" 最早见于 1900 年 in American English.

definitionLines: 一 a. 新的，新近的；新来的；不熟 悉的，没经验的
entries.definition: 一 a. 新的，新近的；新来的；不熟 悉的，没经验的
entries.etymology:
Old English neowe, niowe, earlier niwe "new, fresh, recent, novel, unheard-of, different from the old; untried, inexperienced," from Proto-Germanic *newjaz (source also of Old Saxon niuwi, Old Frisian nie, Middle Dutch nieuwe, Dutch nieuw, Old High German niuwl, German neu, Danish and Swedish ny, Gothic niujis "new"), from PIE *newo- "new" (source also of Sanskrit navah, Persian nau, Hittite newash, Greek neos, Lithuanian naujas, Old Church Slavonic novu, Russian novyi, Latin novus, Old Irish nue, Welsh newydd "new").

The adverb is Old English niwe, from the adjective. New math in reference to a system of teaching mathematics based on investigation and discovery is from 1958. New World (adj.) to designate phenomena of the Western Hemisphere first attested 1823, in Lord Byron; the noun phrase is recorded from 1550s. New Deal in the FDR sense attested by 1932. New school in reference to the more advanced or liberal faction of something is from 1806. New Left (1960) was a coinage of U.S. political sociologist C. Wright Mills (1916-1962). New light in reference to religions is from 1640s. New frontier, in U.S. politics, "reform and social betterment," is from 1934 but associated with John F. Kennedy's use of it in 1960.

The 副词 is 古英语 niwe, 源自 形容词. New math in reference to a system of teaching mathematics based on investigation and discovery 始于 1958 年. New World （形） to designate phenomena of the Western Hemisphere 最早见于 1823 年, in Lord Byron; the 名词 phrase 见于 1550 年代. New Deal in the FDR sense attested 截至 1932 年. New school in reference to the more advanced or liberal faction of something 始于 1806 年. New Left (1960 年) was a coinage of U.S. political sociologist C. Wright Mills (1916 年-1962 年). New light in reference to religions 始于 1640 年代. New frontier, in U.S. politics, "reform and social betterment," 始于 1934 年 but associated with John F. Kennedy's use of it 于 1960 年.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "new things," plural of new (n.) "new thing," from new (adj.); after French nouvelles, used in Bible translations to render Medieval Latin nova (neuter plural) "news," literally "new things." Sometimes still regarded as plural, 17c.-19c. Meaning "tidings" is early 15c. Meaning "radio or television program presenting current events" is from 1923. Bad news "unpleasant person or situation" is from 1926. Expression no news, good news can be traced to 1640s. Expression news to me is from 1889.  

The News in the Virginia city Newport News is said to derive from the name of one of its founders, William Newce.

definitionLines: ad. 其次，然后，下次；居后
entries.definition: ad. 其次，然后，下次；居后 a.紧接的，其次的；贴近的
entries.etymology: Old English niehsta, nyhsta (West Saxon), nesta (Anglian) "nearest, closest," superlative of neah (West Saxon), neh (Anglian) "nigh;" from Proto-Germanic *nekh- "near" + superlative suffix *-istaz. Cognate with Old Norse næstr, Dutch naast "next," Old High German nahisto "neighbor," German nächst "next." Adverbial and prepositional use from c. 1200. Phrase the next person "a typical person" is from 1857.

definitionLines: a. 好的，美的，令人愉快的

entries.etymology:
late 13c., "foolish, stupid, senseless," from Old French nice (12c.) "careless, clumsy; weak; poor, needy; simple, stupid, silly, foolish," from Latin nescius "ignorant, unaware," literally "not-knowing," from ne- "not" (see un-) + stem of scire "to know" (see science). "The sense development has been extraordinary, even for an adj." [Weekley] -- from "timid" (pre-1300); to "fussy, fastidious" (late 14c.); to "dainty, delicate" (c. 1400); to "precise, careful" (1500s, preserved in such terms as a nice distinction and nice and early); to "agreeable, delightful" (1769); to "kind, thoughtful" (1830).

By 1926, it was pronounced "too great a favorite with the ladies, who have charmed out of it all its individuality and converted it into a mere diffuser of vague and mild agreeableness." [Fowler]

"The sense development has been extraordinary, even for an adj." [Weekley] -- 源自 "timid" (pre-1300 年); to "fussy, fastidious" (14 世纪晚期); to "dainty, delicate" (约 1400 年); to "precise, careful" (1500 年代, preserved in such terms 作为 nice distinction and nice and early); to "agreeable, delightful" (1769 年); to "kind, thoughtful" (1830 年). By 1926 年, it was pronounced "too great a favorite with the ladies, who have charmed out of it all its individuality and converted it into a mere diffuser of vague and mild agreeableness." [Fowler]

entries.etymology:
whitish metal element, 1755, coined in 1754 by Swedish mineralogist Axel von Cronstedt (1722-1765) from shortening of Swedish kopparnickel "copper-colored ore" (from which it was first obtained), a half-translation of German Kupfernickel, literally "copper demon," from Kupfer (see copper) + Nickel "demon, goblin, rascal" (a pet form of masc. proper name Nikolaus, compare English Old Nick "the devil;" see Nicholas); the ore so called by miners because it looked like copper but yielded none.

Meaning "coin made partly of nickel" is from 1857, when the U.S. introduced one-cent coins made of nickel to replace the old bulky copper pennies. Application to five-cent piece (originally one part nickel, three parts copper) is from 1883, American English; in earlier circulation there were silver half-dimes. To nickel-and-dime (someone) is from 1964 (nickels and dimes "very small amounts of money" is attested from 1893).
