entries.definition: ad. 一次，一度；曾经 conj.一旦……就…… n.一次
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, anes, from ane "one" (see one ) + adverbial genitive. Replaced Old English æne. Spelling changed as pronunciation shifted from two syllables to one after c. 1300. Pronunciation change to "wuns" parallels that of one. As an emphatic, meaning "once and for all," it is attested from c. 1300, but this now is regarded as a Pennsylvania German dialect formation. Meaning "in a past time" (but not necessarily just one time) is from mid-13c.

Once upon a time as the beginning of a story is recorded from 1590s. At once originally (early 13c.) meant "simultaneously," later "in one company" (c. 1300), and preserved the sense of "one" in the word; the phrase typically appeared as one word, atones; the modern meaning "immediately" is attested from 1530s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, anes, 源自 ane "one" （参见 one ) + adverbial 属格. Replaced 古英语 æne. Spelling changed as pronunciation shifted 源自 two syllables to one after 约 1300 年. Pronunciation change to "wuns" parallels that of one. 作为 emphatic, 意为 "once and for all," it 见于 约 1300 年, but this 现在 is regarded 作为 Pennsylvania 德语 dialect formation. 义为 "in a past time" (but not necessarily just one time) 始于 13 世纪中期 Once upon a time as the beginning of a story 见于 1590 年代. At once 原义为 (13 世纪初) meant "simultaneously," later "in one company" (约 1300 年), and preserved the 语义 "one" in the word; the phrase typically appeared as one word, atones; the modern 意为 "immediately" 见于 1530 年代.

entries.definition: num. 一，一个 pron. 一个人；任何人 a. 一个的；某一 …•…的；同 …的
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, from Old English an (adjective, pronoun, noun) "one," from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (source also of Old Norse einn, Danish een, Old Frisian an, Dutch een, German ein, Gothic ains), from PIE *oi-no- "one, unique" (source also of Greek oinos "ace (on dice);" Latin unus "one;" Old Persian aivam; Old Church Slavonic -inu, ino-; Lithuanian vienas; Old Irish oin; Breton un "one").

Originally pronounced as it still is in only, and in dialectal good 'un, young 'un, etc.; the now-standard pronunciation "wun" began c. 14c. in southwest and west England (Tyndale, a Gloucester man, spells it won in his Bible translation), and it began to be general 18c. Use as indefinite pronoun influenced by unrelated French on and Latin homo.

One and only "sweetheart" is from 1906. One of those things "unpredictable occurrence" is from 1934. Slang one-arm bandit "a type of slot machine" is recorded by 1938. One-night stand is 1880 in performance sense; 1963 in sexual sense. One of the boys "ordinary amiable fellow" is from 1893. One-track mind is from 1927. Drinking expression one for the road is from 1950 (as a song title).

entries.etymology:
early 12c., from Anglo-French union, Old French oignon "onion" (formerly also oingnon), and directly from Latin unionem (nominative unio), colloquial rustic Roman for "a kind of onion," also "pearl" (via notion of a string of onions), literally "one, unity;" sense connection is the successive layers of an onion, in contrast with garlic or cloves.

Old English had ynne (in ynne-leac), from the same Latin source, which also produced Irish inniun, Welsh wynwyn and similar words in Germanic. In Dutch, the ending in -n was mistaken for a plural inflection and new singular ui formed. The usual Indo-European name is represented by Greek kromion, Irish crem, Welsh craf, Old English hramsa, Lithuanian kremuse.

The usual Latin word was cepa, a loan from an unknown language; it is the source of Old French cive, Old English cipe, and, via Late Latin diminutive cepulla, Italian cipolla, Spanish cebolla, Polish cebula. German Zwiebel also is from this source, but altered by folk etymology in Old High German (zwibolla) from words for "two" and "ball." Onion ring is attested from 1952.

Onion dome attested from 1956; onion grass from 1883; onion skin as a type of paper from 1892. Onions, the surname, is attested from mid-12c. (Ennian), from Old Welsh Enniaun, ultimately from Latin Annianus, which was associated with Welsh einion "anvil."

In 荷兰语, the ending in -n was mistaken for a plural inflection and new singular ui formed. The usual Indo-European name is represented by 希腊语 kromion, 爱尔兰语 crem, Welsh craf, 古英语 hramsa, Lithuanian kremuse. The usual 拉丁语 word was cepa, a loan 源自 an unknown language; it is the source of 古法语 cive, 古英语 cipe, and, 经由 晚期拉丁语 diminutive cepulla, 意大利语 cipolla, 西班牙语 cebolla, Polish cebula. 德语 Zwiebel also 始于 this source, but altered by folk etymology in 古高地德语 (zwibolla) 源自 words for "two" and "ball." Onion ring 见于 1952 年. Onion dome attested 自 1956 年起; onion grass 自 1883 年起; onion skin 作为 type of paper 自 1892 年起. Onions, the surname, 见于 12 世纪中期 (Ennian), 源自 Old Welsh Enniaun, 最终源自 拉丁语 Annianus, which was associated with Welsh einion "anvil."

entries.definition: ad. 只，仅仅 a. 唯一的
entries.etymology: Old English ænlic, anlic "only, unique, solitary," literally "one-like," from an "one" (see one) + -lic "-like" (see -ly (1)). Use as an adverb and conjunction developed in Middle English. Distinction of only and alone (now usually in reference to emotional states) is unusual; in many languages the same word serves for both. German also has a distinction in allein/einzig. Phrase only-begotten (mid-15c.) is biblical, translating Latin unigenitus, Greek monogenes. The Old English form was ancenned.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ænlic, anlic "only, unique, solitary," 字面义为 "one-like," 源自 an "one" （参见 one) + -lic "-like" （参见 -ly (1)). Use 作为 副词 and conjunction developed in 中古英语. Distinction of only and alone (现在 通常 in reference to emotional states) is unusual; in many languages the same word serves for both. 德语 also has a distinction in allein/einzig. Phrase only-begotten (15 世纪中期) is biblical, translating 拉丁语 unigenitus, 希腊语 monogenes. The 古英语 form was ancenned.

entries.etymology:
Old English open "not closed down, raised up" (of gates, eyelids, etc.), also "exposed, evident, well-known, public," often in a bad sense, "notorious, shameless;" from Proto-Germanic *upana, literally "put or set up" (source also of Old Norse opinn, Swedish öppen, Danish aaben, Old Saxon opan, Old Frisian epen, Old High German offan, German offen "open"), from PIE *upo "up from under, over" (source also of Latin sub, Greek hypo; see sub-). Related to up, and throughout Germanic the word has the appearance of a past participle of *up (v.), but no such verb has been found. The source of words for "open" in many Indo-European languages seems to be an opposite of the word for "closed, shut" (such as Gothic uslukan).

Of physical spaces, "unobstructed, unencumbered," c. 1200; of rooms with unclosed entrances, c. 1300; of wounds, late 14c. Transferred sense of "frank, candid" is attested from early 14c. Of shops, etc., "available for business," it dates from 1824. Open door in reference to international trading policies is attested from 1856. Open season is first recorded 1896, of game; and figuratively 1914 of persons. Open book in the figurative sense of "person easy to understand" is from 1853. Open house "hospitality for all visitors" is first recorded 1824. Open-and-shut "simple, straightforward" first recorded 1841 in New Orleans. Open marriage, one in which the partners sleep with whomever they please, is from 1972. Open road (1817, American English) originally meant a public one; romanticized sense of "traveling as an expression of personal freedom" first recorded 1856, in Whitman.

Related to up, and throughout 日耳曼语 the word has the appearance of a 为 … 的过去分词 *up （动）, but no such 动词 has been found. The source of words for "open" in many Indo-European languages seems to be an opposite of the word for "closed, shut" (such as Gothic uslukan). Of physical spaces, "unobstructed, unencumbered," 约 1200 年; of rooms with unclosed entrances, 约 1300 年; of wounds, 14 世纪晚期 Transferred 语义 "frank, candid" 见于 14 世纪初 Of shops, etc., "available for business," it dates 自 1824 年起. entries.etymology: Old English openung "act of opening" (a door, mouth, etc.), "disclosure, manifestation," verbal noun from present participle of open (v.). Meaning "vacant space, hole, aperture, doorway" is attested from c. 1200. Meaning "act of opening (a place, to the public)" is from late 14c. Sense of "action of beginning (something)" is from 1712; meaning "first performance of a play" is 1855; "start of an art exhibit" is from 1905. Sense of "opportunity, chance" is from 1793.

entries.etymology: "a drama sung" [Klein], 1640s, from Italian opera, literally "a work, labor, composition," from Latin opera "work, effort" (Latin plural regarded as feminine singular), secondary (abstract) noun from operari "to work," from opus (genitive operis) "a work" (see opus). Defined in "Elson's Music Dictionary" as, "a form of musical composition evolved shortly before 1600, by some enthusiastic Florentine amateurs who sought to bring back the Greek plays to the modern stage." As a branch of dramatic art, it is attested from 1759. First record of opera glass "small binoculars for use at the theater" is from 1738. Soap opera is first recorded 1939, as a disparaging reference to daytime radio dramas sponsored by soap manufacturers.

entries.definition: vi. 操作，运转；动手术，开刀 vt. 操作，操纵，进行
entries.etymology: c. 1600, "to be in effect," back-formation from operation, or else from Latin operatus, past participle of operari "to work, labor, toil, take pains" (in Late Latin "to have effect, be active, cause"). Surgical sense is first attested 1799. Meaning "to work machinery" is from 1864 in American English. Related: Operated; operating. Operating system in the computer sense is from 1961.

Surgical sense is 最早见于 1799 年. 义为 "to work machinery" 始于 1864 年 in American English. 同源词：Operated; operating. Operating system in the computer sense 始于 1961 年.

definitionLines: n. 操作，工作，运转；手术；运算
entries.definition: n. 操作，工作，运转；手术；运算
entries.etymology: late 14c., "action, performance, work," also "the performance of some science or art," from Old French operacion "operation, working, proceedings," from Latin operationem (nominative operatio) "a working, operation," from past participle stem of operari "to work, labor" (in Late Latin "to have effect, be active, cause"), from opera "work, effort," related to opus (genitive operis) "a work" (see opus). The surgical sense is first attested 1590s. Military sense of "series of movements and acts" is from 1749.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "placed on the other side of (something)," from Old French oposite "opposite, contrary" (13c.), from Latin oppositus "standing against, opposed, opposite," past participle of opponere "set against" (see opponent). Meaning "contrary in nature or character" is from 1570s. As a noun from late 14c. As a preposition from 1758. As an adverb from 1817. Related: Oppositely.

entries.etymology: 1759 (in translations of Voltaire), from French optimisme (1737), from Modern Latin optimum, used by Gottfried Leibniz (in "Théodicée," 1710) to mean "the greatest good," from Latin optimus "the best" (see optimum). The doctrine holds that the actual world is the "best of all possible worlds," in which the creator accomplishes the most good at the cost of the least evil.Launched out of philosophical jargon and into currency by Voltaire's satire on it in "Candide." General sense of "belief that good ultimately will prevail in the world" first attested 1841 in Emerson; meaning "tendency to take a hopeful view of things" first recorded 1819 in Shelley.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, from Old English conjunction oþþe "either, or," related to Old Frisian ieftha, Middle Dutch ofte, Old Norse eða, Old High German odar, German oder, Gothic aiþþau "or." This was extended in early Middle English (and Old High German) with an -r ending, perhaps by analogy with "choice between alternative" words that ended thus (such as either, whether), then reduced to oþþr, at first in unstressed situations (commonly thus in Northern and Midlands English by 1300), and finally reduced to or, though other survived in this sense until 16c.

The contraction took place in the second term of an alternative, such as either ... or, a common construction in Old English, where both words originally were oþþe (see nor).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古英语 conjunction oþþe "either, or," related to 古弗里西语 ieftha, Middle 荷兰语 ofte, 古北欧语 eða, 古高地德语 odar, 德语 oder, Gothic aiþþau "or." This was extended in early 中古英语 (and 古高地德语) with an -r ending, 或许 by analogy with "choice between alternative" words that ended thus (such as either, whether), 之后 reduced to oþþr, at first in unstressed situations (commonly thus in Northern and Midlands English 截至 1300 年), and finally reduced to or, though other survived in this sense until 16 世纪 The contraction took place in the second term of an alternative, such as either ... or, a common construction in 古英语, where both words 原义为 were oþþe （参见 nor).

entries.etymology: late 14c., "a message from a god, expressed by divine inspiration," from Old French oracle "temple, house of prayer; oracle" (12c.) and directly from Latin oraculum "divine announcement, oracle; place where oracles are given," from orare "pray, plead" (see orator), with material instrumental suffix -culo-. In antiquity, "the agency or medium of a god," also "the place where such divine utterances were given." This sense is attested in English from c. 1400.

entries.etymology:
1620s, from Late Latin oralis, from Latin os (genitive oris) "mouth, opening, face, entrance," from PIE *os- "mouth" (source also of Sanskrit asan "mouth," asyam "mouth, opening," Avestan ah-, Hittite aish, Middle Irish a "mouth," Old Norse oss "mouth of a river," Old English or "beginning, origin, front").

Psychological meaning "of the mouth as the focus of infantile sexual energy" (as in oral fixation) is from 1910. The sexual sense is first recorded 1948, in Kinsey. As a noun, "oral examination," attested from 1876. Related: Orally (c. 1600); orality. Os was the usual word for "mouth" in Latin, but as the vowel distinction was lost it became similar in sound to os "bone" (see osseous). Thus bucca, originally "cheek" but used colloquially as "mouth," became the usual word for "mouth" (see bouche).

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, of the fruit, from Old French orange, orenge (12c., Modern French orange), from Medieval Latin pomum de orenge, from Italian arancia, originally narancia (Venetian naranza), alteration of Arabic naranj, from Persian narang, from Sanskrit naranga-s "orange tree," of uncertain origin. Not used as a color word until 1540s.

Loss of initial n- probably due to confusion with definite article (as in une narange, una narancia), but perhaps influenced by French or "gold." The name of the town of Orange in France (see Orangemen) perhaps was deformed by the name of the fruit. Orange juice is attested from 1723.

The tree's original range probably was northern India. The Persian orange, grown widely in southern Europe after its introduction in Italy 11c., was bitter; sweet oranges were brought to Europe 15c. from India by Portuguese traders and quickly displaced the bitter variety, but only Modern Greek still seems to distinguish the bitter (nerantzi) from the sweet (portokali "Portuguese") orange. Portuguese, Spanish, Arab, and Dutch sailors planted citrus trees along trade routes to prevent scurvy. On his second voyage in 1493, Christopher Columbus brought the seeds of oranges, lemons and citrons to Haiti and the Caribbean. Introduced in Florida (along with lemons) in 1513 by Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de Leon. Introduced to Hawaii 1792.

In ancient Rome, it referred to the place in the theater reserved for senators and other dignitaries. Meaning "group of musicians performing at a concert, opera, etc." first recorded 1720; "part of theater in front of the stage" is from 1768.

entries.etymology:
early 13c., "body of persons living under a religious discipline," from Old French ordre "position, estate; rule, regulation; religious order" (11c.), from earlier ordene, from Latin ordinem (nominative ordo) "row, rank, series, arrangement," originally "a row of threads in a loom," from Italic root *ord- "to arrange, arrangement" (source of ordiri "to begin to weave;" compare primordial), of unknown origin.

Meaning "a rank in the (secular) community" is first recorded c. 1300; meaning "command, directive" is first recorded 1540s, from the notion of "to keep in order." Military and honorary orders grew our of the fraternities of Crusader knights. Business and commerce sense is attested from 1837. In natural history, as a classification of living things, it is first recorded 1760. Meaning "condition of a community which is under the rule of law" is from late 15c.

Phrase in order to (1650s) preserves etymological notion of "sequence." The word reflects a medieval notion: "a system of parts subject to certain uniform, established ranks or proportions," and was used of everything from architecture to angels. Old English expressed many of the same ideas with endebyrdnes. In short order "without delay" is from 1834, American English; order of battle is from 1769.

entries.etymology:
fusion of late Old English organe, and Old French orgene (12c.), both meaning "musical instrument," both from Latin organa, plural of organum "a musical instrument," from Greek organon "implement, tool for making or doing; musical instrument; organ of sense, organ of the body," literally "that with which one works," from PIE *werg-ano-, from root *werg- "to do" (source also of Greek ergon "work," orgia "religious performances;" Armenian gorc "work;" Avestan vareza "work, activity;" Gothic waurkjan, Old English wyrcan "to work," Old English weorc "deed, action, something done;" Old Norse yrka "work, take effect").

Applied vaguely in late Old English to musical instruments; by late 14c. the sense of the word (used in both singular and plural form) narrowed to the musical instrument now known by that name (involving pipes supplied with wind by a bellows and worked by means of keys), though Augustine (c. 400) knew this as a specific sense of Latin organa. The meaning "body part adapted to a certain function" is attested from late 14c., from a Medieval Latin sense of Latin organum. Organist is first recorded 1590s; organ-grinder is attested from 1806.

Applied vaguely in late 古英语 to musical instruments; by 14 世纪晚期 the 语义 the word (used in both singular and plural form) narrowed to the musical instrument 现在 known by that name (involving pipes supplied with wind by a bellows and worked by means of keys), though Augustine (约 400 年) knew this 作为 specific 语义 拉丁语 organa. entries.etymology: 1660s, "organic structure, organization," from organize + -ism. Sense of "living animal or plant" first recorded 1842. Related: Organismic.
entries.etymologyZh: 1660 年代, "organic structure, organization," 源自 organize + -ism. 义为 "living animal or plant" 首见于 1842 年. 同源词：Organismic.

example.en: A single-celled organism can survive in extreme temperatures that would kill most living things.
example.zh: 单细胞生物能够在会杀死大多数生物的极端温度下存活。

definitionLines: n. 组织，体制；团体，机构
entries.definition: n. 组织，体制；团体，机构
entries.etymology: mid-15c., "act of organizing," from Middle French organisation and directly from Medieval Latin organizationem (nominative organizatio), noun of action from past participle stem of organizare, from Latin organum "instrument, organ" (see organ). Meaning "system, establishment" is from 1873. Organization man is from title of 1956 book by American sociologist William H. Whyte (1917-1999). Related: Organizational.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "act of organizing," 源自 中古法语 organisation and 直接源自 中古拉丁语 organizationem (主格 organizatio), 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of organizare, 源自 拉丁语 organum "instrument, organ" （参见 organ). 义为 "system, establishment" 始于 1873 年. Organization man 始于 title of 1956 年 book by American sociologist William H. Whyte (1917 年-1999 年). 同源词：Organizational.

example.en: The organization raised funds to help victims of the flood.
example.zh: 该组织筹集资金帮助洪水受难者。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "construct, establish," from Middle French organiser and directly from Medieval Latin organizare, from Latin organum "instrument, organ" (see organ). Related: Organized; organizing.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "construct, establish," 源自 中古法语 organiser and 直接源自 中古拉丁语 organizare, 源自 拉丁语 organum "instrument, organ" （参见 organ). 同源词：Organized; organizing.

example.en: They hired a manager to organize the annual charity event.

entries.etymology: c. 1400, "ancestry, race," from Old French origine "origin, race," and directly from Latin originem (nominative origo) "a rise, commencement, beginning, source; descent, lineage, birth," from stem of oriri "arise, rise, get up; become visible, appear; be born, be descended, receive life;" figuratively "come forth, take origin, proceed, start" (of rivers, rumors, etc.), from PIE root *ergh- "to mount" (see orchestra).

entries.definition: a.最初的，原始的，原文的；新 颖的，有独创性的

entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "first in time, earliest," 源自 古法语 original "first" (13 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 originalis, 源自 originem (主格 origo) "beginning, source, birth," 源自 oriri "to rise" （参见 orchestra). entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Late Latin orphanus "parentless child" (source of Old French orfeno, Italian orfano), from Greek orphanos "orphaned, without parents, fatherless," literally "deprived," from orphos "bereft," from PIE *orbho- "bereft of father," also "deprived of free status," from root *orbh- "to change allegiance, to pass from one status to another" (source also of Hittite harb- "change allegiance," Latin orbus "bereft," Sanskrit arbhah "weak, child," Armenian orb "orphan," Old Irish orbe "heir," Old Church Slavonic rabu "slave," rabota "servitude" (see robot), Gothic arbja, German erbe, Old English ierfa "heir," Old High German arabeit, German Arbeit "work," Old Frisian arbed, Old English earfoð "hardship, suffering, trouble"). As an adjective from late 15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 晚期拉丁语 orphanus "parentless child" (source of 古法语 orfeno, 意大利语 orfano), 源自 希腊语 orphanos "orphaned, without parents, fatherless," 字面义为 "deprived," 源自 orphos "bereft," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *orbho- "bereft of father," also "deprived of free status," 源自 root *orbh- "to change allegiance, to pass from one status to another" (source also of Hittite harb- "change allegiance," 拉丁语 orbus "bereft," 梵语 arbhah "weak, child," Armenian orb "orphan," Old 爱尔兰语 orbe "heir," Old Church Slavonic rabu "slave," rabota "servitude" （参见 robot), Gothic arbja, 德语 erbe, 古英语 ierfa "heir," 古高地德语 arabeit, 德语 Arbeit "work," 古弗里西语 arbed, 古英语 earfoð "hardship, suffering, trouble"). 作形容词时 源自 15 世纪晚期

definitionLines: a. 另外的，别的；另一，其他的
entries.definition: a. 另外的，别的；另一，其他的 pron. 别的东西，别人
entries.etymology:
Old English oþer "the second" (adj.), also as a pronoun, "one of the two, other," from Proto-Germanic *antharaz (source also of Old Saxon athar, Old Frisian other, Old Norse annarr, Middle Dutch and Dutch ander, Old High German andar, German ander, Gothic anþar "other").

These are from PIE *an-tero-, variant of *al-tero- "the other of two" (source of Lithuanian antras, Sanskrit antarah "other, foreign," Latin alter), from root *al- (1) "beyond" (see alias (adv.)) + adjectival comparative suffix *-tero-. The Old English, Old Saxon, and Old Frisian forms show "a normal loss of n before fricatives" [Barnhart]. Meaning "different" is mid-13c.

Sense of "second" was detached from this word in English (which uses second, from Latin) and German (zweiter, from zwei "two") to avoid ambiguity. In Scandinavian, however, the second floor is still the "other" floor (Swedish andra, Danish anden). Also compare Old English oþergeara "next year."

The other woman "a woman with whom a man begins a love affair while he is already committed" is from 1855. The other day originally (mid-12c.) was "the next day;" later (c. 1300) "yesterday;" and now, loosely, "a day or two ago" (early 15c.). Phrase other half in reference to either the poor or the rich, is recorded from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 oþer "the second" （形）, also 作为 pronoun, "one of the two, other," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *antharaz (source also of 古撒克逊语 athar, 古弗里西语 other, 古北欧语 annarr, Middle 荷兰语 and 荷兰语 ander, 古高地德语 andar, 德语 ander, Gothic anþar "other"). These 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *an-tero-, 为 … 的变体 *al-tero- "the other of two" (source of Lithuanian antras, 梵语 antarah "other, foreign," 拉丁语 alter), 源自 root *al- (1) "beyond" （参见 alias （副）) + adjectival comparative suffix *-tero-. The 古英语, 古撒克逊语, and 古弗里西语 forms show "a normal loss of n before fricatives" [Barnhart]. 义为 "different" is 13 世纪中期 义为 "second" was detached 源自 this word in English (which uses second, 源自 拉丁语) and 德语 (zweiter, 源自 zwei "two") to avoid ambiguity. In Scandinavian, however, the second floor is still the "other" floor (Swedish andra, Danish anden). Also 对比 古英语 oþergeara "next year." The other woman "a woman with whom a man begins a love affair while he is already committed" 始于 1855 年. The other day 原义为 (12 世纪中期) was "the next day;" later (约 1300 年) "yesterday;" and 现在, loosely, "a day or two ago" (15 世纪初). Phrase other half in reference to either the poor or the rich, 见于 约 1600 年.

definitionLines: ad. 在外，向外，出外，不在家； 熄灭，完结；出现，问世
entries.definition: ad. 在外，向外，出外，不在家； 熄灭，完结；出现，问世
entries.etymology:
Old English ut "out, without, outside," common Germanic (Old Norse, Old Frisian, Old Saxon, Gothic ut, Middle Dutch uut, Dutch uit, Old High German uz, German aus), from PIE root *ud- "up, out, up away" (source also of Sanskrit ut "up, out," uttarah "higher, upper, later, northern;" Avestan uz- "up, out," Old Irish ud- "out," Latin usque "all the way to, without interruption," Greek hysteros "the latter," Russian vy- "out"). Meaning "into public notice" is from 1540s. As an adjective from c. 1200. Meaning "unconscious" is attested from 1898, originally in boxing. Sense of "not popular or modern" is from 1966. As a preposition from mid-13c.

Sense in baseball (1860) was earlier in cricket (1746). Adverbial phrase out-and-out "thoroughly" is attested from early 14c.; adjective usage is attested from 1813; out-of-the-way (adj.) "remote, secluded" is attested from late 15c. Out-of-towner "one not from a certain place" is from 1911. Shakespeare's It out-herods Herod ("Hamlet") reflects Herod as stock braggart and bully in old religious drama and was widely imitated 19c. Out to lunch "insane" is student slang from 1955; out of this world "excellent" is from 1938; out of sight "excellent, superior" is from 1891.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ut "out, without, outside," common 日耳曼语 (古北欧语, 古弗里西语, 古撒克逊语, Gothic ut, Middle 荷兰语 uut, 荷兰语 uit, 古高地德语 uz, 德语 aus), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ud- "up, out, up away" (source also of 梵语 ut "up, out," uttarah "higher, upper, later, northern;" Avestan uz- "up, out," Old 爱尔兰语 ud- "out," 拉丁语 usque "all the way to, without interruption," 希腊语 hysteros "the latter," 俄语 vy- "out"). 义为 "into public notice" 始于 1540 年代. 作形容词时 源自 约 1200 年. 义为 "unconscious" 见于 1898 年, 原义为 in boxing. 义为 "not popular or modern" 始于 1966 年. 作为 preposition 源自 13 世纪中期 Sense in baseball (1860 年) was earlier in cricket (1746 年). Adverbial phrase out-and-out "thoroughly" 见于 14 世纪初; 形容词 usage 见于 1813 年; out-of-the-way （形） "remote, secluded" 见于 15 世纪晚期 Out-of-towner "one not from a certain place" 始于 1911 年. Shakespeare's It out-herods Herod ("Hamlet") reflects Herod as stock braggart and bully in old religious drama and was widely imitated 19 世纪 Out to lunch "insane" is student 俚语 自 1955 年起; out of this world "excellent" 始于 1938 年; out of sight "excellent, superior" 始于 1891 年.

entries.etymologyZh: 1660 年代, "lines by which a figure is delineated," 源自 out + line （动）. 义为 "rough draft in words" 始于 1759 年.

example.en: The teacher asked students to write an outline before drafting their essays.
example.zh: 老师要求学生在起草文章之前先写好提纲。

definitionLines: n. 展望，远景；眼界，观点
entries.definition: n. 展望，远景；眼界，观点
entries.etymology: "mental view or survey," 1742, from out (adv.) + look (v.). The meaning "prospect for the future" is attested from 1851. Earliest sense was "a look-out" (1660s). The literal sense of "vigilant watch, act or practice of looking out" (1815) is rare; look-out being used instead for this.
entries.etymologyZh: "mental view or survey," 1742 年, 源自 out （副） + look （动）. The 意为 "prospect for the future" 见于 1851 年. Earliest sense was "a look-out" (1660 年代). The literal 语义 "vigilant watch, act or practice of looking out" (1815 年) is rare; look-out being used instead for this.

example.en: The economic outlook for next year looks more optimistic than expected.
example.zh: 明年的经济前景看起来比预期更为乐观。

entries.etymology: 1839, from out + put (v.). Till c. 1880, a technical term in the iron and coal trade [OED]. The verb is attested from mid-14c., originally "to expel;" meaning "to produce" is from 1858.
entries.etymologyZh: 1839 年, 源自 out + put （动）. Till 约 1880 年, a technical term in the iron and coal trade [OED]. The 动词 见于 14 世纪中期, 原义为 "to expel;" 意为 "to produce" 始于 1858 年.

example.en: The factory increased its output by twenty percent this year.
example.zh: 这家工厂今年将产量提高了百分之二十。

definitionLines: n. 暴行；侮辱；愤怒，愤慨
entries.definition: n. 暴行；侮辱；愤怒，愤慨 vt.凌辱；激起愤怒
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "evil deed, offense, crime; affront, indignity," from Old French outrage "harm, damage; insult; criminal behavior; presumption, insolence, overweening" (12c.), earlier oltrage (11c.), from Vulgar Latin *ultraticum "excess," from Latin ultra "beyond" (see ultra-). Etymologically, "the passing beyond reasonable bounds" in any sense; meaning narrowed in English toward violent excesses because of folk etymology from out + rage. Of injuries to feelings, principles, etc., from 1769.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "evil deed, offense, crime; affront, indignity," 源自 古法语 outrage "harm, damage; insult; criminal behavior; presumption, insolence, overweening" (12 世纪), earlier oltrage (11 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *ultraticum "excess," 源自 拉丁语 ultra "beyond" （参见 ultra-). Etymologically, "the passing beyond reasonable bounds" in any sense; 意为 narrowed in English toward violent excesses because of folk etymology 源自 out + rage. Of injuries to feelings, principles, etc., 自 1769 年起.

entries.etymology: "act of setting out on a journey, business, etc." 1759, from out + set (v.). The earlier word for this was outsetting (1670s).
entries.etymologyZh: "act of setting out on a journey, business, etc." 1759 年, 源自 out + set （动）. The earlier word for this was outsetting (1670 年代).

entries.definition: a./n. 外面，外部 ad. 向外，在外 prep.在…•外
entries.etymology: c. 1500, "outer side," from out + side (n.). The adjective is attested from 1630s; the preposition from 1826; the adverb from 1813. Phrase outside of "with exception of" is from 1859.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年, "outer side," 源自 out + side （名）. The 形容词 见于 1630 年代; the preposition 自 1826 年起; the 副词 自 1813 年起. Phrase outside of "with exception of" 始于 1859 年.

definitionLines: n. 局外人，外人；第三者
entries.definition: n. 局外人，外人；第三者
entries.etymology: 1800, from outside; figurative sense of "a person isolated from conventional society" is first recorded 1907. The sense of race horses "outside" the favorites is from 1836; hence outside chance (1909).
entries.etymologyZh: 1800 年, 源自 outside; figurative 语义 "a person isolated from conventional society" is 首见于 1907 年. The 语义 race horses "outside" the favorites 始于 1836 年; hence outside chance (1909 年).

example.en: As an outsider, he struggled to understand the group's inside jokes.
example.zh: 作为局外人，他很难理解这个群体的内部笑话。

entries.definition: a.突出的，显著的 outward（s） a. 向外的 ad. 向外，在外
entries.etymology: 1610s, "projecting, prominent, detached," present participle adjective from outstand (v.) "endure successfully, hold out against," from out (adv.) + stand (v.). Figurative sense of "conspicuous, striking" is first recorded 1830. Meaning "unpaid, unsettled" is from 1797. Related: Outstandingly.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "projecting, prominent, detached," present participle 形容词 源自 outstand （动） "endure successfully, hold out against," 源自 out （副） + stand （动）. Figurative 语义 "conspicuous, striking" is 首见于 1830 年. 义为 "unpaid, unsettled" 始于 1797 年. 同源词：Outstandingly.

example.en: Her outstanding contribution to the project earned her a promotion.
example.zh: 她对项目的杰出贡献使她获得了晋升。

entries.definition: a.卵形的，椭圆的 n.卵形，椭圆形
entries.etymology: 1570s, from Modern Latin ovalis "egg-shaped" (source of French oval, 1540s), literally "of or pertaining to an egg," from Latin ovum "egg" (see ovary). The classical Latin word was ovatus.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, 源自 现代 拉丁语 ovalis "egg-shaped" (source of 法语 oval, 1540 年代), 字面义为 "of or pertaining to an egg," 源自 拉丁语 ovum "egg" （参见 ovary). The classical 拉丁语 word was ovatus.

example.en: The mirror had an oval outline, shaped like an egg rather than a perfect circle.
example.zh: 镜子的轮廓是椭圆形的，像鸡蛋，而非正圆形。

entries.etymology: Old English ofen "furnace, oven," from Proto-Germanic *ukhnaz (source also of Old Frisian, Dutch oven, Old High German ovan, German Ofen, Old Norse ofn, Old Swedish oghn, Gothic auhns), from PIE *aukw- "cooking pot" (source also of Sanskrit ukhah "pot, cooking pot," Latin aulla "pot," Greek ipnos), originally, perhaps, "something hollowed out." The oven-bird (1825) so called because of the shape of its nest. In slang, of a woman, to have (something) in the oven "to be pregnant" is attested from 1962.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ofen "furnace, oven," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *ukhnaz (source also of 古弗里西语, 荷兰语 oven, 古高地德语 ovan, 德语 Ofen, 古北欧语 ofn, Old Swedish oghn, Gothic auhns), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *aukw- "cooking pot" (source also of 梵语 ukhah "pot, cooking pot," 拉丁语 aulla "pot," 希腊语 ipnos), 原义为, 或许, "something hollowed out." The oven-bird (1825 年) so called because of the shape of its nest. In 俚语, of a woman, to have (something) in the oven "to be pregnant" 见于 1962 年.

example.en: Preheat the oven to 180 degrees before placing the cake inside.
example.zh: 把蛋糕放进去之前，先将烤箱预热到180度。

definitionLines: prep. 在……上方；高于，超 过；在（做）…•…时候；越 过，横跨；关于，在…… 方面；到处，遍及
ad.翻过来；以上，超过；越过； 在/向那边
entries.definition: prep. 在……上方；高于，超 过；在（做）…•…时候；越 过，横跨；关于，在…… 方面；到处，遍及 ad.翻过来；以上，超过；越过； 在/向那边 a.完了，结束；太，过度
entries.etymology: Old English ofer "beyond, above, upon, in, across, past; on high," from Proto-Germanic *uberi (source also of Old Saxon obar, Old Frisian over, Old Norse yfir, Old High German ubar, German über, Gothic ufar "over, above"), from PIE *uper (see super-). As an adjective from Old English uffera. As an adverb from late Old English. Sense of "finished" is attested from late 14c. Meaning "recovered from" is from 1929. In radio communication, used to indicate the speaker has finished speaking (1926). Adjective phrase over-the-counter is attested from 1875, originally of stocks and shares.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ofer "beyond, above, upon, in, across, past; on high," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *uberi (source also of 古撒克逊语 obar, 古弗里西语 over, 古北欧语 yfir, 古高地德语 ubar, 德语 über, Gothic ufar "over, above"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *uper （参见 super-). 作形容词时 源自 古英语 uffera. 作为 副词 源自 late 古英语. 义为 "finished" 见于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "recovered from" 始于 1929 年. In radio communication, used to indicate the speaker has finished speaking (1926 年). Adjective phrase over-the-counter 见于 1875 年, 原义为 of stocks and shares.

entries.etymology: "everywhere," Old English ofer eall, from ofer "over" (see over) + eall (see all). Sense of "including everything" is from 1894. The noun in the clothing sense (usually plural) of "loose trousers of a strong material worn by cowboys, etc." is from 1782. Specific sense "loose fitting canvas trousers with a bib and strap top" (originally worn by workmen over other clothes to protect them from wet, dirt, etc.) is attested from 1897.
entries.etymologyZh: "everywhere," 古英语 ofer eall, 源自 ofer "over" （参见 over) + eall （参见 all). 义为 "including everything" 始于 1894 年. The 名词 in the clothing sense (通常 plural) of "loose trousers of a strong material worn by cowboys, etc." 始于 1782 年. Specific sense "loose fitting canvas trousers with a bib and strap top" (原义为 worn by workmen over other clothes to protect them 源自 wet, dirt, etc.) 见于 1897 年.

example.en: The overall performance of the team improved after the new coach arrived.
example.zh: 新教练到来后，球队的整体表现有所提升。

entries.etymology: "large coat worn over ordinary clothing," 1802, from over- + coat (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: "large coat worn over ordinary clothing," 1802 年, 源自 over- + coat （名）.

entries.etymology: Old English ofercuman "to reach, overtake," also "to conquer, prevail over," from ofer (see over) + cuman "to come" (see come (v.)). A common Germanic compound (Middle Dutch overkomen, Old High German ubarqueman, German überkommen). In reference to mental or chemical force, "to overwhelm, render helpless," it is in late Old English. Meaning "to surmount" (a difficulty or obstacle) is from c. 1200. The Civil Rights anthem "We Shall Overcome" was put together c. 1950s from lyrics from Charles Tindley's spiritual "I'll Overcome Some Day" (1901), and melody from pre-Civil War spiritual "No More Auction Block for Me." Related: Overcame; overcoming.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ofercuman "to reach, overtake," also "to conquer, prevail over," 源自 ofer （参见 over) + cuman "to come" （参见 come （动）). A common 日耳曼语 复合词 (Middle 荷兰语 overkomen, 古高地德语 ubarqueman, 德语 überkommen). In reference to mental or chemical force, "to overwhelm, render helpless," it is in late 古英语. 义为 "to surmount" (a difficulty or obstacle) 始于 约 1200 年. The Civil Rights anthem "We Shall Overcome" was put together c. 1950 年代 源自 lyrics 源自 Charles Tindley's spiritual "I'll Overcome Some Day" (1901), and melody from pre-Civil War spiritual "No More Auction Block for Me." 同源词：Overcame; overcoming.

example.en: She trained hard to overcome her fear of public speaking.
example.zh: 她刻苦训练以克服对公开演讲的恐惧。

definitionLines: n. 泛滥；超值；溢值；充满，洋溢
entries.definition: n. 泛滥；超值；溢值；充满，洋溢
entries.etymology: Old English oferfleow "to flow across, flood, inundate," also "to flow over (a brim or bank);" see over- + flow (v.). Related: Overflowed; overflowing.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 oferfleow "to flow across, flood, inundate," also "to flow over (a brim or bank);" 参见 over- + flow （动）. 同源词：Overflowed; overflowing.

definitionLines: ad. 在头顶上，在空中，在高处
entries.definition: ad. 在头顶上，在空中，在高处
entries.etymology: 1530s, "above one's head" (adv.), from over- + head. The adjective is attested from 1874. As a noun, short for overhead costs, etc., it is attested from 1914.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "above one's head" （副）, 源自 over- + head. The 形容词 见于 1874 年. 作名词时, short for overhead costs, etc., it 见于 1914 年.

example.en: A flock of birds flew overhead as we walked through the open field.
example.zh: 当我们走过开阔的田野时，一群鸟从头顶飞过。

entries.etymology: "to hear what one is not meant to hear," 1540s, from over- + hear. The notion is perhaps "to hear beyond the intended range of the voice." Old English oferhieran also meant "to not listen, to disregard, disobey" (compare overlook for negative force of over; also Middle High German überhaeren, Middle Dutch overhoren in same sense). Related: Overheard; overhearing.
entries.etymologyZh: "to hear what one is not meant to hear," 1540 年代, 源自 over- + hear. The notion is 或许 "to hear beyond the intended range of the voice." 古英语 oferhieran also meant "to not listen, to disregard, disobey" (对比 overlook for negative force of over; also Middle High 德语 überhaeren, Middle 荷兰语 overhoren in same sense). 同源词：Overheard; overhearing.

entries.definition: n. 重叠；重复 vi. 部分重叠 vt. 与……重叠
entries.etymology: "to partially extend over," 1726; see over- + lap (v.2). Verbal phrase lap over "extend beyond" is recorded from 1630s. Related: Overlapped; overlapping.
entries.etymologyZh: "to partially extend over," 1726 年; 参见 over- + lap (v.2). Verbal phrase lap over "extend beyond" 见于 1630 年代. 同源词：Overlapped; overlapping.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "to examine, scrutinize, inspect," from over- + look (v.). Another Middle English sense was "to peer over the top of." These two literal senses have given rise to the two main modern meanings. Meaning "to look over or beyond and thus not see," via notion of "to choose to not notice" is first recorded 1520s. Seemingly contradictory sense of "to watch over officially, keep an eye on, superintend" is from 1530s. Related: Overlooked; overlooking. In Shekaspeare's day, overlooking also was a common term for "inflicting the evil eye on" (someone or something).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "to examine, scrutinize, inspect," 源自 over- + look （动）. Another 中古英语 sense was "to peer over the top of." These two literal senses have given rise to the two main modern meanings. 义为 "to look over or beyond and thus not see," 经由 概念 "to choose to not notice" is 首见于 1520 年代. Seemingly contradictory 语义 "to watch over officially, keep an eye on, superintend" 始于 1530 年代. 同源词：Overlooked; overlooking. In Shekaspeare's day, overlooking also was a common term for "inflicting the evil eye on" (someone or something).

example.en: The manager tended to overlook minor errors in the team's reports.
example.zh: 经理倾向于忽视团队报告中的小错误。

definitionLines: a. /ad. 晚上，一夜间；一下子
entries.definition: a. /ad. 晚上，一夜间；一下子

entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, 源自 over- + night （名）. Originally "on the preceding evening;" 语义 "during the night" 见于 1530 年代. 义为 "in the course of a single night, hence seemingly instantaneously" 见于 1939 年.

example.en: The startup became famous almost overnight.
example.zh: 这家初创公司几乎在一夜之间出了名。

entries.etymologyZh: "stretch of road that passes over another," 1929 年, American English, 源自 over- + pass （动）. + Overpass has been a 动词 自 13 世纪晚期

entries.etymology: early 14c., "open to view," from Old French overt (Modern French ouvert), past participle of ovrir "to open," from Latin aperire "to open, uncover," from PIE compound *ap-wer-yo- from *ap- "off, away" (see abo-) + base *wer- (5) "to cover" (see weir). Compare Latin operire "to cover," from the same root with PIE prefix *op- "over;" and Lithuanian atveriu "open," uzveriu "shut."
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "open to view," 源自 古法语 overt (现代法语 ouvert), 为 … 的过去分词 ovrir "to open," 源自 拉丁语 aperire "to open, uncover," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) 复合词 *ap-wer-yo- 源自 *ap- "off, away" （参见 abo-) + base *wer- (5) "to cover" （参见 weir). 对比 拉丁语 operire "to cover," 源自 same root with 原始印欧语 (PIE) prefix *op- "over;" and Lithuanian atveriu "open," uzveriu "shut."

entries.etymology: "to come up to, to catch in pursuit," early 13c., from over- + take (v.). Old English had oferniman "to take away, carry off, seize, ravish."
entries.etymologyZh: "to come up to, to catch in pursuit," 13 世纪初, 源自 over- + take （动）. According to OED, 原义为 "the running down and catching of a fugitive or beast of chase"; it finds the 语义 over- in this word "not so clear." 同源词：Overtaken; overtaking. 古英语 had oferniman "to take away, carry off, seize, ravish."

entries.etymology: early 14c., "to knock down," from over- + throw (v.). Figurative sense of "to cast down from power, defeat" is attested from late 14c. Related: Overthrown; overthrowing. Earlier in same senses was overwerpen "to overturn (something), overthrow; destroy," from Old English oferweorpan (see warp (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "to knock down," 源自 over- + throw （动）. Figurative 语义 "to cast down from power, defeat" 见于 14 世纪晚期 同源词：Overthrown; overthrowing. Earlier in same senses was overwerpen "to overturn (something), overthrow; destroy," 源自 古英语 oferweorpan （参见 warp （动）).

entries.etymologyZh: "time above the regular hours of work," 1846 年, 源自 over- + time （名）. Sporting sense 最早见于 1921 年, in an ice hockey context.

entries.etymology: early 13c., of a wheel, "to rotate, roll over," from over- + turn (v.). Attested from c. 1300 in general transitive sense "to throw over violently;" figurative meaning "to ruin, destroy" is from late 14c. Of judicial decisions, "to reverse," it is attested from 1826. Related: Overturned; overturning.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, of a wheel, "to rotate, roll over," 源自 over- + turn （动）. Attested 源自 约 1300 年 in general transitive sense "to throw over violently;" figurative 意为 "to ruin, destroy" 始于 14 世纪晚期 Of judicial decisions, "to reverse," it 见于 1826 年. 同源词：Overturned; overturning.

example.en: The appeals court voted to overturn the lower court's original ruling.
example.zh: 上诉法院投票推翻了下级法院的原判决。

definitionLines: vt. 淹没，覆没；受打击；制服， 压倒
entries.definition: vt. 淹没，覆没；受打击；制服， 压倒
entries.etymology: early 14c., "to turn upside down, to overthrow," from over- + Middle English whelmen "to turn upside down" (see whelm). Meaning "to submerge completely" is mid-15c. Perhaps the connecting notion is a boat, etc., washed over, and overset, by a big wave. Figurative sense of "to bring to ruin" is attested from 1520s. Related: Overwhelmed; overwhelming; overwhelmingly.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "to turn upside down, to overthrow," 源自 over- + 中古英语 whelmen "to turn upside down" （参见 whelm). 义为 "to submerge completely" is 15 世纪中期 Perhaps the connecting notion is a boat, etc., washed over, and overset, by a big wave. Figurative 语义 "to bring to ruin" 见于 1520 年代. 同源词：Overwhelmed; overwhelming; overwhelmingly.

example.en: The scale of the disaster began to overwhelm the rescue workers.
example.zh: 灾难的规模开始压垮救援人员。

definitionLines: vt.欠，应向……付出；得感谢， 应归功于……
entries.definition: vt.欠，应向……付出；得感谢， 应归功于……
entries.etymology:
Old English agan (past tense ahte) "to have, own," from Proto-Germanic *aigan "to possess" (source also of Old Frisian aga, Old Norse eiga, Old High German eigan, Gothic aigan "to possess, have"), from PIE *aik- "to be master of, possess" (source also of Sanskrit ise "he owns," isah "owner, lord, ruler;" Avestan is- "riches," isvan- "well-off, rich").

Sense of "to have to repay" began in late Old English with the phrase agan to geldanne literally "to own to yield," which was used to translate Latin debere (earlier in Old English this would have been sceal "shall"); by late 12c. the phrase had been shortened to simply agan, and own (v.) took over this word's original sense.

An original Germanic preterite-present verb (along with can (v.1), dare, may, etc.). New past tense form owed arose 15c. to replace oughte, which developed into ought (v.).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 agan (past tense ahte) "to have, own," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *aigan "to possess" (source also of 古弗里西语 aga, 古北欧语 eiga, 古高地德语 eigan, Gothic aigan "to possess, have"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *aik- "to be master of, possess" (source also of 梵语 ise "he owns," isah "owner, lord, ruler;" Avestan is- "riches," isvan- "well-off, rich"). 义为 "to have to repay" began in late 古英语 with the phrase agan to geldanne 字面义为 "to own to yield," which was used to translate 拉丁语 debere (earlier in 古英语 this would have been sceal "shall"); by 12 世纪晚期 the phrase had been shortened to simply agan, and own （动） took over this word's original sense. An original 日耳曼语 preterite-present 动词 (along with can (v.1), dare, may, etc.). New past tense form owed arose 15 世纪 to replace oughte, which developed into ought （动）.

example.en: He has long since spent the money, but he still owes his colleague fifty dollars and feels guilty about it.
example.zh: 那笔钱他早就花掉了，但他仍欠同事五十美元，并为此感到愧疚。

entries.etymology: "compound of oxygen with another element," 1790, from French oxide (1787), coined by G. de Morveau and A. Lavoisier from ox(ygène) (see oxygen) + (ac)ide "acid" (see acid).

entries.etymology:
gaseous chemical element, 1790, from French oxygène, coined in 1777 by French chemist Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier (1743-1794), from Greek oxys "sharp, acid" (see acrid) + French -gène "something that produces" (from Greek -genes "formation, creation;" see -gen).

Intended to mean "acidifying (principle)," it was a Greeking of French principe acidifiant. So called because oxygen was then considered essential in the formation of acids (it is now known not to be). The element was isolated by Priestley (1774), who, using the old model of chemistry, called it dephlogisticated air. The downfall of the phlogiston theory required a new name, which Lavoisier provided.
entries.etymologyZh: gaseous chemical element, 1790 年, 源自 法语 oxygène, coined 于 1777 年 by 法语 chemist Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier (1743 年-1794 年), 源自 希腊语 oxys "sharp, acid" （参见 acrid) + 法语 -gène "something that produces" (源自 希腊语 -genes "formation, creation;" 参见 -gen). Intended to mean "acidifying (principle)," it was a Greeking of 法语 principe acidifiant. So called because oxygen was 之后 considered essential in the formation of acids (it is 现在 known not to be). The element was isolated by Priestley (1774 年), who, using the old model of chemistry, called it dephlogisticated air. The downfall of the phlogiston theory required a new name, which Lavoisier provided.

example.en: Plants release oxygen during the process of photosynthesis.

entries.etymology: late 13c., "a step in walking; rate of motion," from Old French pas "a step, pace, trace," and directly from Latin passus, passum "a step, pace, stride," noun use of past participle of pandere "to stretch (the leg), spread out," probably from PIE *pat-no-, a nasalized variant of root *pete- "to spread" (source also of Greek petannynai "to spread out," petalon "a leaf," patane "plate, dish;" Old Norse faðmr "embrace, bosom," Old English fæðm "embrace, bosom, fathom," Old Saxon fathmos "the outstretched arms"). Also, "a measure of five feet" [Johnson]. Pace-setter in fashion is from 1895.

definitionLines: vt. 包装，打包；塞满，挤满
entries.definition: vt. 包装，打包；塞满，挤满 n. （一）包，（一）群，（一）幅
entries.etymology:
"bundle," early 13c., probably from a Low German word (compare Middle Dutch pac, pack "bundle," Middle Low German pak, Middle Flemish pac, attested from late 12c.), originally a term of wool traders in Flanders; or possibly from Old Norse pakki. All are of unknown origin.

Italian pacco is a Dutch loan word; French pacque probably is from Flemish. Meaning "set of persons" (usually of a low character) is c. 1300, older than sense of "group of hunting animals" (early 15c.). Extended to collective sets of playing cards (1590s), floating ice (1791), cigarettes (1924), and submarines (1943). Meaning "knapsack on a frame" is attested from 1916. Pack of lies first attested 1763.
entries.etymologyZh: "bundle," 13 世纪初, 可能 源自 a Low 德语 word (对比 Middle 荷兰语 pac, pack "bundle," Middle Low 德语 pak, Middle Flemish pac, attested 源自 12 世纪晚期), 原义为 a term of wool traders in Flanders; or possibly 源自 古北欧语 pakki. All are 来源不详. 意大利语 pacco is a 荷兰语 loan word; 法语 pacque 可能 始于 Flemish. 义为 "set of persons" (通常 of a low character) is 约 1300 年, older than 语义 "group of hunting animals" (15 世纪初). Extended to collective sets of playing cards (1590 年代), floating ice (1791 年), cigarettes (1924 年), and submarines (1943 年). 义为 "knapsack on a frame" 见于 1916 年. Pack of lies 最早见于 1763 年.

definitionLines: n. 垫，衬垫；便笺本，拍纸簿
entries.definition: n. 垫，衬垫；便笺本，拍纸簿
entries.etymology:
1550s, "bundle of straw to lie on," possibly from or related to Low German or obsolete Flemish pad "sole of the foot," which is perhaps from PIE *pent- "to tread, go" (see find (v.)), but see path (n.). Meaning "cushion-like part of an animal foot" is from 1790 in English. Generalized sense of "something soft" is from c. 1700; the sense of "a number of sheets fastened together" (in writing pad, drawing pad, etc.) is from 1865.

Sense of "takeoff or landing place for a helicopter" is from 1960. The word persisted in underworld slang from early 18c. in the sense "sleeping place," and was popularized again c. 1959, originally in beatnik speech (later hippie slang) in its original English sense of "place to sleep temporarily."
entries.etymologyZh: 1550 年代, "bundle of straw to lie on," possibly 源自 or related to Low 德语 or 已废 Flemish pad "sole of the foot," which is 或源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *pent- "to tread, go" （参见 find （动）), but 参见 path （名）. 义为 "cushion-like part of an animal foot" 始于 1790 年 in English. Generalized 语义 "something soft" 始于 约 1700 年; the 语义 "a number of sheets fastened together" (in writing pad, drawing pad, etc.) 始于 1865 年. 义为 "takeoff or landing place for a helicopter" 始于 1960 年. The word persisted in underworld 俚语 源自 18 世纪初 in the sense "sleeping place," and was popularized again 约 1959 年, 原义为 in beatnik speech (later hippie 俚语) in its original English 语义 "place to sleep temporarily."

example.en: He jotted down the phone number on a small pad by the desk.

definitionLines: n. 痛苦，疼痛；（p.）努力， 劳苦
entries.definition: n. 痛苦，疼痛；（p.）努力， 劳苦
entries.etymology:
late 13c., "punishment," especially for a crime; also "condition one feels when hurt, opposite of pleasure," from Old French peine "difficulty, woe, suffering, punishment, Hell's torments" (11c.), from Latin poena "punishment, penalty, retribution, indemnification" (in Late Latin also "torment, hardship, suffering"), from Greek poine "retribution, penalty, quit-money for spilled blood," from PIE *kwei- "to pay, atone, compensate" (see penal). The earliest sense in English survives in phrase on pain of death.

Phrase to give (someone) a pain "be annoying and irritating" is from 1908; localized as pain in the neck (1924) and pain in the ass (1934), though this last might have gone long unrecorded and be the original sense and the others euphemisms. Pains "great care taken (for some purpose)" is first recorded 1520s (in the singular in this sense, it is attested from c. 1300). First record of pain-killer is from 1853.

The earliest sense in English survives in phrase on pain of death. Phrase to give (someone) a pain "be annoying and irritating" 始于 1908 年; localized as pain in the neck (1924 年) and pain in the ass (1934 年), though this last might have gone long unrecorded and be the original sense and the others euphemisms. Pains "great care taken (for some purpose)" is 首见于 1520 年代 (in the singular in this sense, it 见于 约 1300 年). First record of pain-killer 始于 1853 年.

entries.definition: v. 涂，漆；画；绘，描述 n. 油漆，颜料
entries.etymology:
early 13c., "represent in painting or drawing, portray;" early 14c., "paint the surface of, color, stain;" from Old French peintier "to paint," from peint, past participle of peindre "to paint," from Latin pingere "to paint, represent in a picture, stain; embroider, tattoo," from PIE root *peig- (1), also *peik- "to cut" (source also of Sanskrit pimsati "hews out, cuts, carves, adorns," Old Church Slavonic pila "file, saw," Lithuanian pela "file").

Sense evolution between PIE and Latin was, presumably, from "decorate with cut marks" to "decorate" to "decorate with color." Compare Sanskrit pingah "reddish," pesalah "adorned, decorated, lovely," Old Church Slavonic pegu "variegated;" Greek poikilos "variegated;" Old High German fehjan "to adorn;" Old Church Slavonic pisati, Lithuanian piesiu "to write." Probably also representing the "cutting" branch of the family is Old English feol (see file (n.2)).

To paint the town (red) "go on a spree" first recorded 1884; to paint (someone or something) black "represent it as wicked or evil" is from 1590s. Adjective paint-by-numbers "simple" is attested by 1970; the art-for-beginners kits themselves date to c. 1953.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "represent in painting or drawing, portray;" 14 世纪初, "paint the surface of, color, stain;" 源自 古法语 peintier "to paint," 源自 peint, 为 … 的过去分词 peindre "to paint," 源自 拉丁语 pingere "to paint, represent in a picture, stain; embroider, tattoo," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *peig- (1), also *peik- "to cut" (source also of 梵语 pimsati "hews out, cuts, carves, adorns," Old Church Slavonic pila "file, saw," Lithuanian pela "file"). Sense evolution between 原始印欧语 (PIE) and 拉丁语 was, presumably, 源自 "decorate with cut marks" to "decorate" to "decorate with color." 对比 梵语 pingah "reddish," pesalah "adorned, decorated, lovely," Old Church Slavonic pegu "variegated;" 希腊语 poikilos "variegated;" 古高地德语 fehjan "to adorn;" Old Church Slavonic pisati, Lithuanian piesiu "to write." Probably also representing the "cutting" branch of the family is 古英语 feol （参见 file (n.2)). To paint the town (red) "go on a spree" 首见于 1884 年; to paint (someone or something) black "represent it as wicked or evil" 始于 1590 年代. Adjective paint-by-numbers "simple" is attested 截至 1970 年; the art-for-beginners kits themselves date to 约 1953 年.

entries.etymology: mid-13c., "two of a kind coupled in use," from Old French paire "pair, couple," and directly from Medieval Latin paria "equals," neuter plural of Latin par (genitive paris) "a pair, counterpart, equal," noun use of par (adj.) "equal, equal-sized, well-matched" (see par (n.)). Originally of things. Of persons from late 14c. Meaning "a woman's breasts" is attested from 1922. Pair bond (v.) is first attested 1940, in reference to birds mating.

example.en: She bought a pair of gloves to keep her hands warm in winter.

entries.etymology:
early 13c., "official residence of an emperor, king, archbishop, etc.," from Old French palais "palace, court," from Medieval Latin palacium "a palace" (source of Spanish palacio, Italian palazzo), from Latin palatium "the Palatine hill," in plural, "a palace," from Mons Palatinus "the Palatine Hill," one of the seven hills of ancient Rome, where Augustus Caesar's house stood (the original "palace"), later the site of the splendid residence built by Nero. In English, the general sense of "splendid dwelling place" is from late 14c.

The hill name probably is ultimately from palus "stake," on the notion of "enclosure." Another guess is that it is from Etruscan and connected with Pales, supposed name of an Italic goddess of shepherds and cattle.

Pale-face, supposed North American Indian word for "European," is attested from 1822.

entries.etymology: "small, unbound treatise," late 14c., from Anglo-Latin panfletus, popular short form of "Pamphilus, seu de Amore" ("Pamphilus, or about Love"), a short 12c. Latin love poem popular and widely copied in Middle Ages; the name from Greek pamphilos "loved by all," from pan- "all" + philos "loving, dear" see -phile). Meaning "brief work dealing with questions of current interest" is late 16c.
entries.etymologyZh: "small, unbound treatise," 14 世纪晚期, 源自 Anglo-拉丁语 panfletus, popular short form of "Pamphilus, seu de Amore" ("Pamphilus, or about Love"), a short 12 世纪 拉丁语 love poem popular and widely copied in Middle Ages; the name 源自 希腊语 pamphilos "loved by all," 源自 pan- "all" + philos "loving, dear" 参见 -phile). 义为 "brief work dealing with questions of current interest" is 16 世纪晚期

entries.etymology: Arcadian shepherd god with upper body of a man and horns and lower part like a goat, late 14c., a god of the woods and fields, from Latin, from Greek Pan. Klein says perhaps cognate with Sanskrit pusan, a Vedic god, guardian and multiplier of cattle and other human possessions, literally "nourisher." Similarity to pan "all" (see pan-) led to his being regarded as a personification of nature. Pan-pipe, upon which he supposedly played, is attested from 1820.
entries.etymologyZh: Arcadian shepherd god with upper body of a man and horns and lower part like a goat, 14 世纪晚期, a god of the woods and fields, 源自 拉丁语, 源自 希腊语 Pan. Klein says 或许 与 … 同源 梵语 pusan, a Vedic god, guardian and multiplier of cattle and other human possessions, 字面义为 "nourisher." Similarity to pan "all" （参见 pan-) led to his being regarded 作为 personification of nature. Pan-pipe, upon which he supposedly played, 见于 1820 年.

example.en: She heated the sauce in a small pan over a low flame.
example.zh: 她用小火在一口小平底锅里加热酱汁。

entries.etymology: 1835, from French, apparently from the Nepalese name of a raccoon-like mammal (lesser panda) found there. First reference to the Giant Panda is from 1901; since its discovery in 1869 by French missionary Armand David (1826-1900) it had been known as parti-colored bear, but the name was changed after the zoological relationship to the red panda was established.
entries.etymologyZh: 1835 年, 源自 法语, 似乎 源自 Nepalese name of a raccoon-like mammal (lesser panda) found there. First reference to the Giant Panda 始于 1901 年; 自 its discovery 于 1869 年 by 法语 missionary Armand David (1826 年-1900 年) it had been known as parti-colored bear, but the name was changed after the zoological relationship to the red panda was established.

definitionLines: n. 专门小组；面板；控制板， 仪表盘
entries.definition: n. 专门小组；面板；控制板， 仪表盘
entries.etymology: early 14c., from Old French panel "piece of cloth, piece, saddle cushion" (Modern French panneau), from Vulgar Latin *pannellus, diminutive of Latin pannus "piece of cloth" (see pane). Anglo-French legalese sense of "piece of parchment (cloth) listing jurors" led by late 14c. to meaning "jury." General sense of "persons called on to advise, judge, discuss," etc. is from 1570s. Sense of "distinct part of surface of a wall, door, etc." is first recorded c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, 源自 古法语 panel "piece of cloth, piece, saddle cushion" (现代法语 panneau), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *pannellus, 为 … 的指小形式 拉丁语 pannus "piece of cloth" （参见 pane). 盎格鲁-法语 legalese 语义 "piece of parchment (cloth) listing jurors" led by 14 世纪晚期 to 意为 "jury." General 语义 "persons called on to advise, judge, discuss," etc. 始于 1570 年代. 义为 "distinct part of surface of a wall, door, etc." is 首见于 约 1600 年.

example.en: A panel of experts was assembled to review the new safety regulations.
example.zh: 一个专家小组被召集来审查新的安全法规。

entries.definition: n. 惊慌，恐慌 a.恐慌的，惊慌的
entries.etymology: 1827, "to afflict with panic," from panic (n.). Intransitive sense of "to lose one's head, get into a panic" is from 1902. Related: Panicked; panicking.
entries.etymologyZh: 1827 年, "to afflict with panic," 源自 panic （名）. Intransitive 语义 "to lose one's head, get into a panic" 始于 1902 年. 同源词：Panicked; panicking.

example.en: A sudden loud noise caused panic among the crowd at the event.
example.zh: 一声突然的巨响在活动现场引起了人群恐慌。

entries.etymology: trousers, 1840, see pantaloons. Colloquial singular pant is attested from 1893. To wear the pants "be the dominant member of a household" is first attested 1931. To do something by the seat of (one's) pants "by human instinct" is from 1942, originally of pilots, perhaps with some notion of being able to sense the condition and situation of the plane by engine vibrations, etc. To be caught with (one's) pants down "discovered in an embarrassing condition" is from 1932.
entries.etymologyZh: trousers, 1840 年, 参见 pantaloons. Colloquial singular pant 见于 1893 年. To wear the pants "be the dominant member of a household" is 最早见于 1931 年. To do something by the seat of (one's) pants "by human instinct" is from 1942, originally of pilots, perhaps with some notion of being able to sense the condition and situation of the plane by engine vibrations, etc. To be caught with (one's) pants down "discovered in an embarrassing condition" 始于 1932 年.

definitionLines: n. 纸；报纸；（pL.）文件；论文， 文章；试卷
entries.definition: n. 纸；报纸；（pL.）文件；论文， 文章；试卷
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., from Anglo-French paper, Old French papier "paper, document," from Latin papyrus "paper, paper made of papyrus stalks" (see papyrus).

Meaning "paper money" attested from 1722. As shortened form of newspaper, first attested 1640s. In plural, "collection of papers to establish one's identity, credentials, etc.," it is attested from 1680s. Paper chase is British slang from 1932.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 paper, 古法语 papier "paper, document," 源自 拉丁语 papyrus "paper, paper made of papyrus stalks" （参见 papyrus). 义为 "paper money" attested 自 1722 年起. As shortened form of newspaper, 最早见于 1640 年代. In plural, "collection of papers to establish one's identity, credentials, etc.," it 见于 1680 年代. Paper chase is British 俚语 自 1932 年起.

example.en: Please submit your research paper before the end of the month.
example.zh: 请在月底前提交你的研究论文。

entries.etymology: 1899, from paper (n.) + back (n.). Adjective paper-backed attested from 1888.
entries.etymologyZh: 1899 年, 源自 paper （名） + back （名）. Adjective paper-backed attested 自 1888 年起.

entries.etymology: 1580s, "things made of paper," from paper (n.) + work (n.). Meaning "work done on paper" is from 1889.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "things made of paper," 源自 paper （名） + work （名）. 义为 "work done on paper" 始于 1889 年.

entries.etymology: 1784 (the year the use of one first was attempted, in Paris), from French parachute, literally "that which protects against a fall," hybrid coined by French aeronaut François Blanchard (1753-1809) from para- "defense against" (see para- (2)) + chute "a fall" (see chute).
entries.etymologyZh: 1784 年 (the year the use of one first was attempted, in Paris), 源自 法语 parachute, 字面义为 "that which protects against a fall," hybrid coined by 法语 aeronaut François Blanchard (1753 年-1809 年) 源自 para- "defense against" （参见 para- (2)) + chute "a fall" （参见 chute).

entries.definition: n. 游行，检阅 v.游行
entries.etymology: 1650s, "a show of bravado," also "an assembly of troops for inspections," from French parade "display, show, military parade," from Middle French parade (15c.), or from Italian parate "a warding or defending, a garish setting forth," or Spanish parada "a staying or stopping," all from Vulgar Latin *parata, from Latin parere "arrange, prepare, adorn" (see pare), which developed widespread senses in Romanic derivatives. Non-military sense of "march, procession" is first recorded 1670s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, "a show of bravado," also "an assembly of troops for inspections," 源自 法语 parade "display, show, military parade," 源自 中古法语 parade (15 世纪)，或源自 意大利语 parate "a warding or defending, a garish setting forth," or 西班牙语 parada "a staying or stopping," all 源自 通俗拉丁语 *parata, 源自 拉丁语 parere "arrange, prepare, adorn" （参见 pare), which developed widespread senses in Romanic derivatives. Non-military 语义 "march, procession" is 首见于 1670 年代.

example.en: Thousands of people lined the streets to watch the victory parade.
example.zh: 数千人站在街道两旁观看胜利游行。

entries.etymology:
late 12c., "Garden of Eden," from Old French paradis "paradise, Garden of Eden" (11c.), from Late Latin paradisus, from Greek paradeisos "park, paradise, Garden of Eden," from an Iranian source similar to Avestan pairidaeza "enclosure, park" (Modern Persian and Arabic firdaus "garden, paradise"), compound of pairi- "around" + diz "to make, form (a wall)."

The first element is cognate with Greek peri- "around, about" (see per), the second is from PIE root *dheigh- "to form, build" (see dough).

The Greek word, originally used for an orchard or hunting park in Persia, was used in Septuagint to mean "Garden of Eden," and in New Testament translations of Luke xxiii:43 to mean "heaven" (a sense attested in English from c. 1200). Meaning "place like or compared to Paradise" is from c. 1300.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪晚期, "Garden of Eden," 源自 古法语 paradis "paradise, Garden of Eden" (11 世纪), 源自 晚期拉丁语 paradisus, 源自 希腊语 paradeisos "park, paradise, Garden of Eden," 源自 an Iranian source similar to Avestan pairidaeza "enclosure, park" (现代 波斯语 and 阿拉伯语 firdaus "garden, paradise"), 由 … 复合而成 pairi- "around" + diz "to make, form (a wall)." The first element is 与 … 同源 希腊语 peri- "around, about" （参见 per), the second 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *dheigh- "to form, build" （参见 dough). The 希腊语 word, 原义为 used for an orchard or hunting park in Persia, was used in Septuagint to mean "Garden of Eden," and in New Testament translations of Luke xxiii:43 to mean "heaven" (a sense 见于 English 源自 约 1200 年). 义为 "place like or compared to Paradise" 始于 约 1300 年.

definitionLines: n.似非而是的论点；悖论， 反论；自相矛盾的人或事
entries.definition: n.似非而是的论点；悖论， 反论；自相矛盾的人或事
entries.etymology: 1530s, "statement contrary to common belief or expectation," from Middle French paradoxe (14c.) and directly from Latin paradoxum "paradox, statement seemingly absurd yet really true," from Greek paradoxon, noun use of neuter of adjective paradoxos "contrary to expectation, incredible," from para- "contrary to" (see para- (1)) + doxa "opinion," from dokein "to appear, seem, think" (see decent). Meaning "statement that is seemingly self-contradictory yet not illogical or obviously untrue" is from 1560s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "statement contrary to common belief or expectation," 源自 中古法语 paradoxe (14 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 paradoxum "paradox, statement seemingly absurd yet really true," 源自 希腊语 paradoxon, 为 … 的名词用法 neuter of 形容词 paradoxos "contrary to expectation, incredible," 源自 para- "contrary to" （参见 para- (1)) + doxa "opinion," 源自 dokein "to appear, seem, think" （参见 decent). 义为 "statement that is seemingly self-contradictory yet not illogical or obviously untrue" 始于 1560 年代.

entries.etymology: late 15c., from Middle French paragraphe "division of text" (13c., Old French paragrafe), from Medieval Latin paragraphus "sign for start of a new section of discourse" (the sign looked something like a stylized letter -P-), from Greek paragraphos "short stroke in the margin marking a break in sense," also "a passage so marked," literally "anything written beside," from paragraphein "write by the side," from para- "beside" (see para- (1)) + graphein "to write" (see -graphy).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, 源自 中古法语 paragraphe "division of text" (13 世纪, 古法语 paragrafe), 源自 中古拉丁语 paragraphus "sign for start of a new section of discourse" (the sign looked something like a stylized letter -P-), 源自 希腊语 paragraphos "short stroke in the margin marking a break in sense," also "a passage so marked," 字面义为 "anything written beside," 源自 paragraphein "write by the side," 源自 para- "beside" （参见 para- (1)) + graphein "to write" （参见 -graphy).

example.en: The editor asked her to add a new paragraph explaining the background.
example.zh: 编辑让她另加一段来解释背景情况。

definitionLines: a. 与……平行的；并列的；类 似的
n.平行线；纬线；可相比拟的事 物；相似处
entries.definition: a. 与……平行的；并列的；类 似的 n.平行线；纬线；可相比拟的事 物；相似处
entries.etymology: 1540s, from Middle French parallèle (16c.) and directly from Latin parallelus, from Greek parallelos "parallel," from para allelois "beside one another," from para- "beside" (see para- (1)) + allelois "each other," from allos "other" (see alias (adv.)). As a noun from 1550s. Parallel bars as gymnastics apparatus are recorded from 1868.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, 源自 中古法语 parallèle (16 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 parallelus, 源自 希腊语 parallelos "parallel," 源自 para allelois "beside one another," 源自 para- "beside" （参见 para- (1)) + allelois "each other," 源自 allos "other" （参见 alias （副）). 作名词时 源自 1550 年代. Parallel bars as gymnastics apparatus are recorded 自 1868 年起.

example.en: The two countries developed parallel education systems during the same era.
example.zh: 这两个国家在同一时期发展出了相似的教育体系。

entries.etymology:
1650s in geometry, from Modern Latin parameter (1630s), from Greek para- "beside, subsidiary" (see para- (1)) + metron "measure" (see meter (n.2)).

A geometry term until 1920s when it yielded sense of "measurable factor which helps to define a particular system" (1927). Common modern meaning (influenced by perimeter) of "boundary, limit, characteristic factor" is from 1950s. Related: Parametric.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代 in geometry, 源自 现代 拉丁语 parameter (1630 年代), 源自 希腊语 para- "beside, subsidiary" （参见 para- (1)) + metron "measure" （参见 meter (n.2)). A geometry term until 1920 年代 when it yielded 语义 "measurable factor which helps to define a particular system" (1927 年). Common modern 意为 (influenced by perimeter) of "boundary, limit, characteristic factor" 始于 1950 年代. 同源词：Parametric.

example.en: Engineers must adjust the parameter settings before running the simulation.
example.zh: 工程师在运行模拟之前必须调整参数设置。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "a hanger-on, a toady, person who lives on others," from Middle French parasite (16c.) or directly from Latin parasitus "toady, sponger," and directly from Greek parasitos "one who lives at another's expense, person who eats at the table of another," from noun use of an adjective meaning "feeding beside," from para- "beside" (see para- (1)) + sitos "food," of unknown origin. Scientific meaning "animal or plant that lives on others" is first recorded 1640s (implied in parasitical).
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "a hanger-on, a toady, person who lives on others," 源自 中古法语 parasite (16 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 parasitus "toady, sponger," and 直接源自 希腊语 parasitos "one who lives at another's expense, person who eats at the table of another," 源自 为 … 的名词用法 an 形容词 意为 "feeding beside," 源自 para- "beside" （参见 para- (1)) + sitos "food," 来源不详. Scientific 意为 "animal or plant that lives on others" is 首见于 1640 年代 (implied in parasitical).

entries.definition: n. 包裹，邮包 vt. 打包
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "a portion of something, a part" (sense preserved in phrase parcel of land, c. 1400), from Old French parcele "small piece, particle, parcel," from Vulgar Latin *particella, extended form (via diminutive suffix, but not necessarily implying smallness) of Latin particula "small part, little bit," itself a diminutive of pars (genitive partis) "part" (see part (n.)).

Meaning "package" is first recorded 1640s, earlier "a quantity of goods in a package" (mid-15c.), from late 14c. sense of "an amount or quantity of anything." The expression part and parcel (early 15c.) also preserves the older sense; both words mean the same, the multiplicity is for emphasis.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "a portion of something, a part" (sense preserved in phrase parcel of land, 约 1400 年), 源自 古法语 parcele "small piece, particle, parcel," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *particella, extended form (经由 diminutive suffix, but not necessarily implying smallness) of 拉丁语 particula "small part, little bit," itself a 为 … 的指小形式 pars (属格 partis) "part" （参见 part （名）). 义为 "package" is 首见于 1640 年代, earlier "a quantity of goods in a package" (15 世纪中期), 源自 14 世纪晚期 语义 "an amount or quantity of anything." The expression part and parcel (15 世纪初) also preserves the older sense; both words mean the same, the multiplicity is for emphasis.

entries.definition: n. 原谅，请再说一遍 vt. 原谅，饶恕，豁免
entries.etymology:
late 13c., "papal indulgence," from Old French pardon, from pardoner "to grant; forgive" (11c., Modern French pardonner), "to grant, forgive," from Vulgar Latin *perdonare "to give wholeheartedly, to remit," from Latin per- "through, thoroughly" (see per) + donare "give, present" (see donation).

Meaning "passing over an offense without punishment" is from c. 1300, also in the strictly ecclesiastical sense; sense of "pardon for a civil or criminal offense; release from penalty or obligation" is from late 14c. earlier in Anglo-French. Weaker sense of "excuse for a minor fault" is attested from 1540s.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "papal indulgence," 源自 古法语 pardon, 源自 pardoner "to grant; forgive" (11 世纪, 现代法语 pardonner), "to grant, forgive," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *perdonare "to give wholeheartedly, to remit," 源自 拉丁语 per- "through, thoroughly" （参见 per) + donare "give, present" （参见 donation). 义为 "passing over an offense without punishment" 始于 约 1300 年, also in the strictly ecclesiastical sense; 语义 "pardon for a civil or criminal offense; release from penalty or obligation" 始于 14 世纪晚期 earlier in 盎格鲁-法语. Weaker 语义 "excuse for a minor fault" 见于 1540 年代.

entries.etymology: early 15c. (late 12c. as a surname), from Old French parent "father, parent, relative, kin" (11c.), from Latin parentem (nominative parens) "father or mother, ancestor," noun use of present participle of parere "bring forth, give birth to, produce," from PIE root *pere- (1) "to bring forth" (see pare). Began to replace native elder after c. 1500.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初 (12 世纪晚期 作为 surname), 源自 古法语 parent "father, parent, relative, kin" (11 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 parentem (主格 parens) "father or mother, ancestor," 为 … 的名词用法 为 … 的现在分词 parere "bring forth, give birth to, produce," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *pere- (1) "to bring forth" （参见 pare). Began to replace 本族 elder after 约 1500 年.

example.en: Her parent encouraged her to pursue a career in medicine.
example.zh: 她的父母鼓励她从事医学事业。

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "consultation; formal conference, assembly," from Old French parlement (11c.), originally "a speaking, talk," from parler "to speak" (see parley (n.)); spelling altered c. 1400 to conform with Medieval Latin parliamentum.

Anglo-Latin parliamentum is attested from early 13c. Specific sense "representative assembly of England or Ireland" emerged by mid-14c. from general meaning "a conference of the secular and/or ecclesiastical aristocracy summoned by a monarch."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "consultation; formal conference, assembly," 源自 古法语 parlement (11 世纪), 原义为 "a speaking, talk," 源自 parler "to speak" （参见 parley （名）); spelling altered 约 1400 年 to conform with 中古拉丁语 parliamentum. Anglo-拉丁语 parliamentum 见于 13 世纪初 Specific sense "representative assembly of England or Ireland" emerged by 14 世纪中期 源自 general 意为 "a conference of the secular and/or ecclesiastical aristocracy summoned by a monarch."

example.en: The bill was passed by parliament after months of heated debate.
example.zh: 该法案经过数月激烈辩论后在议会获得通过。

definitionLines: n. 部分，份儿；角色，作用； 一方；零件
entries.definition: n. 部分，份儿；角色，作用； 一方；零件 v.（使）分开，分离，分别
entries.etymology:
mid-13c., "division, portion of a whole," from Old French part "share, portion; character; power, dominion; side, way, path," from Latin partem (nominative pars) "a part, piece, a share, a division; a party or faction; a part of the body; a fraction; a function, office," related to portio "share, portion," from PIE root *pere- (2) "to assign, grant, allot" (reciprocally, "to get in return;" source also of Greek peprotai "it has been granted," Sanskrit purtam "reward," Hittite parshiya- "fraction, part").

It has replaced native deal (n.) in most senses. Theatrical sense (late 15c.) is from an actor's "share" in a performance (The Latin plural partis was used in the same sense). Meaning "the parting of the hair" is 1890, American English.

As an adjective from 1590s. Late Old English part "part of speech" did not survive and the modern word is considered a separate borrowing. Phrase for the most part is from late 14c. To take part "participate" is from late 14c.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, "division, portion of a whole," 源自 古法语 part "share, portion; character; power, dominion; side, way, path," 源自 拉丁语 partem (主格 pars) "a part, piece, a share, a division; a party or faction; a part of the body; a fraction; a function, office," related to portio "share, portion," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *pere- (2) "to assign, grant, allot" (reciprocally, "to get in return;" source also of 希腊语 peprotai "it has been granted," 梵语 purtam "reward," Hittite parshiya- "fraction, part"). It has replaced 本族 deal （名） in most senses. Theatrical sense (15 世纪晚期) 始于 an actor's "share" in a performance (The 拉丁语 plural partis was used in the same sense). 义为 "the parting of the hair" is 1890 年, American English. 作形容词时 源自 1590 年代. Late 古英语 part "part of speech" did not survive and the modern word is considered a separate borrowing. Phrase for the most part 始于 14 世纪晚期 To take part "participate" 始于 14 世纪晚期

example.en: The director gave her the part of the lead character in the new film.
example.zh: 导演把新电影中主角的角色给了她。

definitionLines: a.部分的，局部的；偏爱的， 不公平的
entries.definition: a.部分的，局部的；偏爱的， 不公平的
entries.etymology: early 15c., "one-sided, biased," from Old French parcial (14c., Modern French partial), from Medieval Latin partialis "divisible, solitary, partial," from Latin pars (genitive partis) "part" (see part (n.)). Sense of "not whole, incomplete" is attested from late 14c. Related: Partially (mid-15c. as "incompletely").
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "one-sided, biased," 源自 古法语 parcial (14 世纪, 现代法语 partial), 源自 中古拉丁语 partialis "divisible, solitary, partial," 源自 拉丁语 pars (属格 partis) "part" （参见 part （名）). 义为 "not whole, incomplete" 见于 14 世纪晚期 同源词：Partially (15 世纪中期 as "incompletely").

example.en: The report gave only a partial account of what actually happened.
example.zh: 这份报告只对实际发生的事情作了局部性的描述。

entries.etymology: 1540s, from Latin participantem (nominative participans), present participle of participare "to share in, partake of," from particeps "sharing, partaking" (see participation).
