entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "a supplication or prayer, especially to a deity," 源自 古法语 peticion "request, petition" (12 世纪, 现代法语 pétition) and 直接源自 拉丁语 petitionem (主格 petitio) "a blow, thrust, attack, aim; a seeking, searching," in law "a claim, suit," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of petere "to make for, go to; attack, assail; seek, strive after; ask for, beg, beseech, request; fetch; derive; demand, require," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *pet-, also *pete- "to rush; to fly" (source also of 梵语 pattram "wing, feather, leaf," patara- "flying, fleeting;" Hittite pittar "wing;" 希腊语 piptein "to fall," potamos "rushing water," pteryx "wing;" 古英语 feðer "feather;" 拉丁语 penna "feather, wing;" Old Church Slavonic pero "feather;" Old Welsh eterin "bird"). 义为 "formal written request to a superior (earthly)" 见于 15 世纪初

example.en: Residents submitted a petition to city hall demanding better street lighting.
example.zh: 居民们向市政厅提交请愿书，要求改善街道照明。

entries.etymology: early 15c. "petroleum, rock oil" (mid-14c. in Anglo-French), from Medieval Latin petroleum, from Latin petra "rock" (see petrous) + oleum "oil" (see oil (n.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初 "petroleum, rock oil" (14 世纪中期 in 盎格鲁-法语), 源自 中古拉丁语 petroleum, 源自 拉丁语 petra "rock" （参见 petrous) + oleum "oil" （参见 oil （名）).

definitionLines: a. 不重要的，次要的；渺小的， 褊狭的
entries.definition: a. 不重要的，次要的；渺小的， 褊狭的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "small," from phonemic spelling of Old French petit "small" (see petit). In English, not originally disparaging (as still in petty cash, 1834; petty officer, 1570s). Meaning "of small importance" is recorded from 1520s; that of "small-minded" is from 1580s. Related: Pettily; pettiness. An old name for "Northern Lights" was petty dancers.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "small," 源自 phonemic spelling of 古法语 petit "small" （参见 petit). In English, not 原义为 disparaging (as still in petty cash, 1834 年; petty officer, 1570 年代). 义为 "of small importance" 见于 1520 年代; that of "small-minded" 始于 1580 年代. 同源词：Pettily; pettiness. An old name for "Northern Lights" was petty dancers.

example.en: It is petty to argue over such a small amount of money.
example.zh: 为这么小一笔钱争吵是很小气的。

definitionLines: n. 药房，药剂学，配药业， 制药业
entries.definition: n. 药房，药剂学，配药业， 制药业
entries.etymology: late 14c., "a medicine," from Old French farmacie "a purgative" (13c.), from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Greek pharmakeia "use of drugs, medicines, potions, or spells; poisoning, witchcraft; remedy, cure," from pharmakeus (fem. pharmakis) "preparer of drugs, poisoner, sorcerer" from pharmakon "drug, poison, philter, charm, spell, enchantment." Meaning "use or administration of drugs" is attested from c. 1400; that of "place where drugs are prepared and dispensed" is first recorded 1833. The ph- was restored 16c. in French, 17c. in English (see ph).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "a medicine," 源自 古法语 farmacie "a purgative" (13 世纪), 源自 中古拉丁语 pharmacia, 源自 希腊语 pharmakeia "use of drugs, medicines, potions, or spells; poisoning, witchcraft; remedy, cure," 源自 pharmakeus (fem. pharmakis) "preparer of drugs, poisoner, sorcerer" 源自 pharmakon "drug, poison, philter, charm, spell, enchantment." 义为 "use or administration of drugs" 见于 约 1400 年; that of "place where drugs are prepared and dispensed" is 首见于 1833 年. The ph- was restored 16 世纪 in 法语, 17 世纪 in English （参见 ph).

entries.etymology: 1705, "phase of the moon," back-formed as a singular from Modern Latin phases, plural of phasis, from Greek phasis "appearance" (of a star), "phase" (of the moon), from stem of phainein "to show, to make appear" (see phantasm). Latin singular phasis was used in English from 1660. Non-lunar application is first attested 1841. Meaning "temporary difficult period" (especially of adolescents) is attested from 1913.
entries.etymologyZh: 1705 年, "phase of the moon," back-formed 作为 singular 源自 现代 拉丁语 phases, 为 … 的复数 phasis, 源自 希腊语 phasis "appearance" (of a star), "phase" (of the moon), 源自 stem of phainein "to show, to make appear" （参见 phantasm). 拉丁语 singular phasis was used in English 自 1660 年起. Non-lunar application is 最早见于 1841 年. 义为 "temporary difficult period" (尤指 of adolescents) 见于 1913 年.

example.en: The project is currently in its initial phase and will take months to complete.
example.zh: 该项目目前处于初始阶段，还需数月才能完成。

definitionLines: a. 现象的；能知觉的；异常的； 杰出的，惊人的
entries.definition: a. 现象的；能知觉的；异常的； 杰出的，惊人的
entries.etymology:
1803, "of the nature of a phenomenon," a hybrid from phenomenon + -al (1). Meaning "remarkable, exceptional" is from 1850.

Related: Phenomenally.
entries.etymologyZh: 1803 年, "of the nature of a phenomenon," a hybrid 源自 phenomenon + -al (1). 义为 "remarkable, exceptional" 始于 1850 年. 同源词：Phenomenally.

entries.etymology: 1570s, "fact, occurrence," from Late Latin phænomenon, from Greek phainomenon "that which appears or is seen," noun use of neuter present participle of phainesthai "to appear," passive of phainein (see phantasm). Meaning "extraordinary occurrence" first recorded 1771. Plural is phenomena.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "fact, occurrence," 源自 晚期拉丁语 phænomenon, 源自 希腊语 phainomenon "that which appears or is seen," 为 … 的名词用法 neuter 为 … 的现在分词 phainesthai "to appear," passive of phainein （参见 phantasm). 义为 "extraordinary occurrence" 首见于 1771 年. Plural is phenomena.

example.en: Researchers are still trying to explain this unusual natural phenomenon.
example.zh: 研究人员仍在努力解释这一不寻常的自然现象。

entries.etymology:
from Old English philosophe, from Latin philosophus "philosopher," from Greek philosophos "philosopher, sage, one who speculates on the nature of things and truth," literally "lover of wisdom," from philos "loving" (see -phile) + sophos "wise, a sage" (see sophist). Modern form with -r appears early 14c., from an Anglo-French or Old French variant of philosophe, with an agent-noun ending.
 
Philosophy also was used of alchemy in Middle Ages, hence Philosophers' stone (late 14c., translating Medieval Latin lapis philosophorum, early 12c.), a reputed solid substance supposed by alchemists to change baser metals into gold or silver; also identified with the elixir and thus given the attribute of prolonging life indefinitely and curing wounds and disease. (French pierre philosophale, German der Stein der Weisen).
entries.etymologyZh: 源自 古英语 philosophe, 源自 拉丁语 philosophus "philosopher," 源自 希腊语 philosophos "philosopher, sage, one who speculates on the nature of things and truth," 字面义为 "lover of wisdom," 源自 philos "loving" （参见 -phile) + sophos "wise, a sage" （参见 sophist). 现代 form with -r appears 14 世纪初, 源自 an 盎格鲁-法语 or 古法语 为 … 的变体 philosophe, with an agent-名词 ending. Philosophy also was used of alchemy in Middle Ages, hence Philosophers' stone (14 世纪晚期, translating 中古拉丁语 lapis philosophorum, 12 世纪初), a reputed solid substance supposed by alchemists to change baser metals into gold or silver; also identified with the elixir and thus given the attribute of prolonging life indefinitely and curing wounds and disease. (法语 pierre philosophale, 德语 der Stein der Weisen).

example.en: The ancient philosopher argued that virtue is the highest form of happiness.
example.zh: 这位古代哲学家认为，美德是幸福的最高形式。

definitionLines: n. 哲学；人生哲学，见解，观点
entries.definition: n. 哲学；人生哲学，见解，观点
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "knowledge, body of knowledge," from Old French filosofie "philosophy, knowledge" (12c., Modern French philosophie) and directly from Latin philosophia and from Greek philosophia "love of knowledge, pursuit of wisdom; systematic investigation," from philo- "loving" (see philo-) + sophia "knowledge, wisdom," from sophis "wise, learned;" of unknown origin.Meaning "system a person forms for conduct of life" is attested from 1771.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "knowledge, body of knowledge," 源自 古法语 filosofie "philosophy, knowledge" (12 世纪, 现代法语 philosophie) and 直接源自 拉丁语 philosophia and 源自 希腊语 philosophia "love of knowledge, pursuit of wisdom; systematic investigation," 源自 philo- "loving" （参见 philo-) + sophia "knowledge, wisdom," 源自 sophis "wise, learned;" 来源不详.义为 "system a person forms for conduct of life" 见于 1771 年.

example.en: His philosophy of life centers on the belief that kindness is its own reward.
example.zh: 他的人生哲学以善良本身就是回报这一信念为核心。

entries.etymology: Old English and Old French fenix, from Medieval Latin phenix, from Latin phoenix, from Greek phoinix, the mythical bird of Arabia which flew to Egypt every 500 years to be reborn; it also meant "the date" (fruit and tree), and "Phoenician," literally "purple-red," perhaps a foreign word (Egyptian has been suggested), or from phoinos "blood-red." The exact relation and order of the senses in Greek is unclear.Spelling assimilated to Greek 16c. (see ph). Figurative sense of "that which rises from the ashes of what was destroyed" is attested from 1590s. The city in Arizona, U.S., so called because it was founded in 1867 on the site of an ancient Native American settlement.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 and 古法语 fenix, 源自 中古拉丁语 phenix, 源自 拉丁语 phoenix, 源自 希腊语 phoinix, the mythical bird of Arabia which flew to Egypt every 500 years to be reborn; it also meant "the date" (fruit and tree), and "Phoenician," 字面义为 "purple-red," 或许 a foreign word (Egyptian has been suggested)，或源自 phoinos "blood-red." The exact relation and order of the senses in 希腊语 is unclear.Spelling assimilated to 希腊语 16 世纪 （参见 ph). Figurative 语义 "that which rises from the ashes of what was destroyed" 见于 1590 年代. The city in Arizona, U.S., so called because it was founded 于 1867 年 on the site of an ancient Native American settlement.

entries.definition: n. 电话 vt. 打电话 photo=photograph
entries.etymology: 1884, from phone (n.). Related: Phoned; phoning.
entries.etymologyZh: 1884 年, 源自 phone （名）. 同源词：Phoned; phoning.

example.en: He forgot his wallet but luckily had his phone to call for help.
example.zh: 他忘记带钱包，但幸好有手机可以打电话求助。

entries.etymology: 1924 in the sense of "make a photographic reproduction," from photo- "photographic" + copy (v.). The usual modern meaning arose 1942 with the advent of xerography. The noun is recorded from 1934. Related: Photocopied; photocopying.
entries.etymologyZh: 1924 年 in the 语义 "make a photographic reproduction," 源自 photo- "photographic" + copy （动）. The usual modern 意为 arose 1942 年 with the advent of xerography. The 名词 见于 1934 年. 同源词：Photocopied; photocopying.

entries.etymology: 1839, "picture obtained by photography," coined by Sir John Herschel from photo- + -graph "instrument for recording; something written." It won out over other suggestions, such as photogene and heliograph. Neo-Anglo-Saxonists prefer sunprint; and sun-picture (1846) was an early Englishing of the word. The verb, as well as photography, are first found in a paper read before the Royal Society on March 14, 1839. Related: Photographed; photographing.
entries.etymologyZh: 1839 年, "picture obtained by photography," coined by Sir John Herschel 源自 photo- + -graph "instrument for recording; something written." It won out over other suggestions, such as photogene and heliograph. Neo-Anglo-Saxonists prefer sunprint; and sun-picture (1846 年) was an early Englishing of the word. The 动词, as well as photography, are first found in a paper read before the Royal Society on March 14, 1839 年. 同源词：Photographed; photographing.

example.en: The journalist captured a stunning photograph of the rare bird in flight using a telephoto lens.
example.zh: 记者用长焦镜头拍下了这只罕见鸟儿飞翔中的一张精彩照片。

entries.etymology: 1898, loan-translation of German Photosynthese, from photo- "light" (see photo-) + synthese "synthesis" (see synthesis). Another early word for it was photosyntax.
entries.etymologyZh: 1898 年, loan-translation of 德语 Photosynthese, 源自 photo- "light" （参见 photo-) + synthese "synthesis" （参见 synthesis). Another early word for it was photosyntax.

entries.etymology: 1520s, "manner or style of expression," also "group of words with some unity," from Late Latin phrasis "diction," from Greek phrasis "speech, way of speaking, enunciation, phraseology," from phrazein "to express, tell," from phrazesthai "to consider," from PIE *gwhren- "to think" (see frenetic). The musical sense of "short passage" is from 1789.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "manner or style of expression," also "group of words with some unity," 源自 晚期拉丁语 phrasis "diction," 源自 希腊语 phrasis "speech, way of speaking, enunciation, phraseology," 源自 phrazein "to express, tell," 源自 phrazesthai "to consider," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *gwhren- "to think" （参见 frenetic). The musical 语义 "short passage" 始于 1789 年.

example.en: The teacher asked students to identify the key phrase in each sentence.
example.zh: 老师要求学生找出每个句子中的关键短语。

definitionLines: a，物质的，有形的；身体的； 自然科学的，物理的
entries.definition: a，物质的，有形的；身体的； 自然科学的，物理的
entries.etymology: early 15c., "of or pertaining to material nature" (in medicine, opposed to surgical), from Medieval Latin physicalis "of nature, natural," from Latin physica "study of nature" (see physic). Meaning "pertaining to matter" is from 1590s; meaning "having to do with the body, corporeal" is attested from 1780. Meaning "characterized by bodily attributes or activities" is attested from 1970. Physical education first recorded 1838; abbreviated form phys ed is from 1955. Physical therapy is from 1922. Related: Physically.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "of or pertaining to material nature" (in medicine, opposed to surgical), 源自 中古拉丁语 physicalis "of nature, natural," 源自 拉丁语 physica "study of nature" （参见 physic). 义为 "pertaining to matter" 始于 1590 年代; 意为 "having to do with the body, corporeal" 见于 1780 年. 义为 "characterized by bodily attributes or activities" 见于 1970 年. Physical education 首见于 1838 年; abbreviated form phys ed 始于 1955 年. Physical therapy 始于 1922 年. 同源词：Physically.

example.en: Regular physical exercise helps reduce the risk of heart disease.
example.zh: 规律的体育锻炼有助于降低心脏病风险。

entries.etymology: early 13c., fisicien "a healer, a medical practitioner," from Old French fisiciien "physician, doctor, sage" (12c., Modern French physicien means "physicist"), from fisique "art of healing," from Latin physica "natural science" (see physic). Distinguished from surgeon from c. 1400. The ph- spelling attested from late 14c. (see ph).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, fisicien "a healer, a medical practitioner," 源自 古法语 fisiciien "physician, doctor, sage" (12 世纪, 现代法语 physicien means "physicist"), 源自 fisique "art of healing," 源自 拉丁语 physica "natural science" （参见 physic). Distinguished 源自 surgeon 源自 约 1400 年. The ph- spelling attested 源自 14 世纪晚期 （参见 ph).

example.en: The physician examined the patient and prescribed medication.
example.zh: 内科医生检查了病人并开了药方。

entries.etymology: 1836, from physics + -ist. Coined by the Rev. William Whewell (1794-1866), English polymath, to denote a "cultivator of physics" as opposed to a physician.
entries.etymologyZh: 1836 年, 源自 physics + -ist. Coined by the Rev. William Whewell (1794 年-1866 年), English polymath, to denote a "cultivator of physics" as opposed to a physician.

example.en: The physicist spent decades studying the behavior of subatomic particles.
example.zh: 这位物理学家花了数十年研究亚原子粒子的行为。

entries.etymology: 1580s, "natural science," from physic in sense of "natural science." Also see -ics. Based on Latin physica (neuter plural), from Greek ta physika, literally "the natural things," name of Aristotle's treatise on nature. Specific sense of "science treating of properties of matter and energy" is from 1715.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "natural science," 源自 physic in 语义 "natural science." Also 参见 -ics. Based on 拉丁语 physica (neuter plural), 源自 希腊语 ta physika, 字面义为 "the natural things," name of Aristotle's treatise on nature. Specific 语义 "science treating of properties of matter and energy" 始于 1715 年.

example.en: She developed a passion for physics after winning her school's science fair.
example.zh: 在赢得学校科学展览会后，她对物理学产生了浓厚的兴趣。

entries.etymology: 1560s, "study and description of natural objects," from Middle French physiologie or directly from Latin physiologia "natural science, study of nature," from Greek physiologia "natural science, inquiry into nature," from physio- "nature" (see physio-) + logia "study" (see -logy). Meaning "science of the normal function of living things" is attested from 1610s. Related: Physiologic; physiologist.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, "study and description of natural objects," 源自 中古法语 physiologie or 直接源自 拉丁语 physiologia "natural science, study of nature," 源自 希腊语 physiologia "natural science, inquiry into nature," 源自 physio- "nature" （参见 physio-) + logia "study" （参见 -logy). 义为 "science of the normal function of living things" 见于 1610 年代. 同源词：Physiologic; physiologist.

definitionLines: n. 钢琴家；钢琴演奏者
entries.definition: n. 钢琴家；钢琴演奏者
entries.etymology: 1822, from French pianiste, from Italian pianista; see piano + -ist. Earlier in English in the French form, pianiste (1816).
entries.etymologyZh: 1822 年, 源自 法语 pianiste, 源自 意大利语 pianista; 参见 piano + -ist. Earlier in English in the 法语 form, pianiste (1816 年).

entries.etymology: 1803, from French piano (18c.), Italian piano, shortened forms of pianoforte (q.v.). As an adverb, "softly," in musical directions (superlative pianissimo), attested from 1680s. Piano wire attested from 1831.
entries.etymologyZh: 1803 年, 源自 法语 piano (18 世纪), 意大利语 piano, shortened forms of pianoforte (q.v.). 作为 副词, "softly," in musical directions (superlative pianissimo), attested 源自 1680 年代. Piano wire attested 自 1831 年起.

example.en: She has been practicing piano for three hours every day since she was six.
example.zh: 她从六岁起每天练习钢琴三个小时。

entries.definition: n. 郊游，野餐 vi.（去）野餐
entries.etymology: 1748 (in Chesterfield's "Letters"), but rare before c. 1800 as an English institution; originally a fashionable pot-luck social affair, not necessarily out of doors; from French piquenique (1690s), perhaps a reduplication of piquer "to pick, peck," from Old French (see pike (n.2)), or the second element may be nique "worthless thing," from a Germanic source. Figurative sense of "something easy" is from 1886. Picnic table recorded from 1926, originally a folding table.
entries.etymologyZh: 1748 年 (in Chesterfield's "Letters"), but rare before 约 1800 年 作为 English institution; 原义为 a fashionable pot-luck social affair, not necessarily out of doors; 源自 法语 piquenique (1690 年代), 或许 a reduplication of piquer "to pick, peck," 源自 古法语 （参见 pike (n.2))，或the second element may be nique "worthless thing," 源自 a 日耳曼语 source. Figurative 语义 "something easy" 始于 1886 年. Picnic table recorded 自 1926 年起, 原义为 a folding table.

example.en: The family decided to have a picnic by the lake on Sunday afternoon.
example.zh: 这家人决定周日下午在湖边野餐。

example.en: She baked a delicious apple pie for the family gathering.
example.zh: 她为家庭聚会烤了一个美味的苹果馅饼。

definitionLines: n. （一）件，（一）片，（一）篇； 碎块，片断
entries.definition: n. （一）件，（一）片，（一）篇； 碎块，片断 vt. 拼合，修补
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "fixed amount, measure, portion," from Old French piece "piece, bit portion; item; coin" (12c.), from Vulgar Latin *pettia, probably from Gaulish *pettsi (compare Welsh peth "thing," Breton pez "piece, a little"), perhaps from an Old Celtic base *kwezd-i-, from PIE root *kwezd- "a part, piece" (source also of Russian chast' "part"). Related: Pieces.

Sense of "portable firearm" first recorded 1580s; that of "chessman" is from 1560s. Meaning "person regarded as a sex object" is first recorded 1785 (compare piece of ass, human beings colloquially called piece of flesh from 1590s; also compare Latin scortum "bimbo, anyone available for a price," literally "skin"). Meaning "a portion of a distance" is from 1610s; that of "literary composition" dates from 1530s. Piece of (one's) mind is from 1570s. Piece of work "remarkable person" echoes Hamlet. Piece as "a coin" is attested in English from 1570s, hence Piece of eight, old name for the Spanish dollar (c. 1600) of the value of 8 reals.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "fixed amount, measure, portion," 源自 古法语 piece "piece, bit portion; item; coin" (12 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *pettia, 可能 源自 Gaulish *pettsi (对比 Welsh peth "thing," Breton pez "piece, a little"), 或源自 an Old Celtic base *kwezd-i-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *kwezd- "a part, piece" (source also of 俄语 chast' "part"). Related: Pieces. Sense of "portable firearm" first recorded 1580s; that of "chessman" is from 1560s. Meaning "person regarded as a sex object" is first recorded 1785 (compare piece of ass, human beings colloquially called piece of flesh from 1590s; also compare Latin scortum "bimbo, anyone available for a price," literally "skin"). Meaning "a portion of a distance" is from 1610s; that of "literary composition" dates from 1530s. Piece of (one's) mind 始于 1570 年代. Piece of work "remarkable person" echoes Hamlet. Piece as "a coin" is 见于 English 源自 1570 年代, hence Piece of eight, old name for the 西班牙语 dollar (约 1600 年) of the value of 8 reals.

example.en: She played a piece of classical music on the piano.
example.zh: 她在钢琴上演奏了一首古典音乐作品。

definitionLines: vt. 刺穿，刺破，穿透；突破， 深深感动
entries.definition: vt. 刺穿，刺破，穿透；突破， 深深感动
entries.etymology: late 13c. "make a hole in; force one's way through," from Anglo-French perser, Old French percier "pierce, transfix, drive through" (12c., Modern French percer), probably from Vulgar Latin *pertusiare, frequentative of Latin pertusus, past participle of pertundere "to thrust or bore through," from per- "through" (see per) + tundere "to beat, pound," from PIE *tund-, from root *(s)teu- "to push, strike, knock, beat, thrust" (see obtuse). Related: Pierced; piercing.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期 "make a hole in; force one's way through," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 perser, 古法语 percier "pierce, transfix, drive through" (12 世纪, 现代法语 percer), 可能 源自 通俗拉丁语 *pertusiare, 为 … 的反复体 拉丁语 pertusus, 为 … 的过去分词 pertundere "to thrust or bore through," 源自 per- "through" （参见 per) + tundere "to beat, pound," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *tund-, 源自 root *(s)teu- "to push, strike, knock, beat, thrust" （参见 obtuse). 同源词：Pierced; piercing.

entries.etymology:
probably from Old English *picg, found in compounds, further etymology unknown. Originally "young pig" (the word for adults was swine). Apparently related to Low German bigge, Dutch big ("but the phonology is difficult" -- OED). The meaning "oblong piece of metal" is first attested 1580s, on the notion of "large mass." Applied to persons, usually in contempt, since 1540s; the derogatory slang meaning "police officer" has been in underworld slang since at least 1811.

Another Old English word for "pig" was fearh, related to furh "furrow," from PIE *perk- "dig, furrow" (source also of Latin porc-us "pig," see pork). "This reflects a widespread IE tendency to name animals from typical attributes or activities" [Lass]. Synonyms grunter, porker are from sailors' and fishermen's euphemistic avoidance of uttering the word pig at sea, a superstition perhaps based on the fate of the Gadarene swine, who drowned. The image of a pig in a poke is attested from 1520s (see poke (n.3)). Flying pigs as a type of something unreal is from 1610s.
entries.etymologyZh: 可能 源自 古英语 *picg, found in compounds, further etymology unknown. Originally "young pig" (the word for adults was swine). Apparently related to Low 德语 bigge, 荷兰语 big ("but the phonology is difficult" -- OED). The 意为 "oblong piece of metal" is 最早见于 1580 年代, on the 概念 "large mass." Applied to persons, 通常 in contempt, 自 1540 年代; the derogatory 俚语 意为 "police officer" has been in underworld 俚语 自 at least 1811 年. Another 古英语 word for "pig" was fearh, related to furh "furrow," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *perk- "dig, furrow" (source also of 拉丁语 porc-us "pig," 参见 pork). "This reflects a widespread IE tendency to name animals from typical attributes or activities" [Lass]. Synonyms grunter, porker 始于 sailors' and fishermen's euphemistic avoidance of uttering the word pig at sea, a superstition 或许 based on the fate of the Gadarene swine, who drowned. The image of a pig in a poke 见于 1520 年代 （参见 poke (n.3)). Flying pigs 作为 type of something unreal 始于 1610 年代.

entries.etymology: late 14c. (early 13c. as a surname), from Old French pigeon "young dove" (13c.), probably from Vulgar Latin *pibionem, dissimilation from Late Latin pipionem (nominative pipio) "squab, young chirping bird" (3c.), from pipire "to peep, chirp," of imitative origin. Meaning "one easily duped" is from 1590s. Replaced culver (Old English culufre, from Vulgar Latin *columbra, from Latin columbula) and native dove.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期 (13 世纪初 作为 surname), 源自 古法语 pigeon "young dove" (13 世纪), 可能 源自 通俗拉丁语 *pibionem, dissimilation 源自 晚期拉丁语 pipionem (主格 pipio) "squab, young chirping bird" (3 世纪), 源自 pipire "to peep, chirp," of imitative origin. 义为 "one easily duped" 始于 1590 年代. Replaced culver (古英语 culufre, 源自 通俗拉丁语 *columbra, 源自 拉丁语 columbula) and 本族 dove.

entries.etymology: "to heap up," mid-14c.; see pile (n.1). Related: Piled; piling. Figurative verbal expression pile on "attack vigorously, attack en masse," is from 1894, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: "to heap up," 14 世纪中期; 参见 pile (n.1). 同源词：Piled; piling. Figurative verbal expression pile on "attack vigorously, attack en masse," 始于 1894 年, American English.

example.en: Books and papers piled up on his desk over the weeks.
example.zh: 几周下来，书籍和文件在他的桌上越堆越高。

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, pilegrim, from Old French pelerin, peregrin "pilgrim, crusader; foreigner, stranger" (11c., Modern French pèlerin), from Late Latin pelegrinus, dissimilated from Latin peregrinus "foreigner" (source of Italian pellegrino, Spanish peregrino), from peregre (adv.) "from abroad," from per- "beyond" + agri, locative case of ager "country" (see acre).

Change of first -r- to -l- in most Romance languages by dissimilation; the -m appears to be a Germanic modification. Pilgrim Fathers "English Puritans who founded Plymouth colony" is first found 1799 (they called themselves Pilgrims from c. 1630, in reference to Hebrew xi:13).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, pilegrim, 源自 古法语 pelerin, peregrin "pilgrim, crusader; foreigner, stranger" (11 世纪, 现代法语 pèlerin), 源自 晚期拉丁语 pelegrinus, dissimilated 源自 拉丁语 peregrinus "foreigner" (source of 意大利语 pellegrino, 西班牙语 peregrino), 源自 peregre （副） "from abroad," 源自 per- "beyond" + agri, locative case of ager "country" （参见 acre). Change of first -r- to -l- in most Romance languages by dissimilation; the -m appears to be a 日耳曼语 modification. Pilgrim Fathers "English Puritans who founded Plymouth colony" is first found 1799 年 (they called themselves Pilgrims 源自 约 1630 年, in reference to 希伯来语 xi:13).

entries.etymology: "small ball or round mass of medicine," c. 1400, from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German pille and Middle French pile, all from Latin pilula "pill," literally "little ball," diminutive of pila "a ball, playing ball," said to be related to pilus "hair" if the original notion was "hairball." Figurative sense "something disagreeable that must be swallowed" is from 1540s; slang meaning "boring person" is recorded from 1871. The pill "contraceptive pill" is from 1957.
entries.etymologyZh: "small ball or round mass of medicine," 约 1400 年, 源自 Middle 荷兰语 or Middle Low 德语 pille and 中古法语 pile, all 源自 拉丁语 pilula "pill," 字面义为 "little ball," 为 … 的指小形式 pila "a ball, playing ball," said to be related to pilus "hair" if the original notion was "hairball." Figurative sense "something disagreeable that must be swallowed" 始于 1540 年代; 俚语 意为 "boring person" 见于 1871 年. The pill "contraceptive pill" 始于 1957 年.

example.en: The doctor advised her to take one pill three times a day before meals.
example.zh: 医生建议她每天饭前服用一粒药丸，共三次。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French piler "pillar, column, pier" (12c., Modern French pilier) and directly from Medieval Latin pilare, from Latin pila "pillar, stone barrier." Figurative sense of "prop or support of an institution or community" is first recorded early 14c. Phrase pillar to post is c. 1600, originally of tennis, exact meaning obscure.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 piler "pillar, column, pier" (12 世纪, 现代法语 pilier) and 直接源自 中古拉丁语 pilare, 源自 拉丁语 pila "pillar, stone barrier." Figurative 语义 "prop or support of an institution or community" is 首见于 14 世纪初 Phrase pillar to post is 约 1600 年, 原义为 of tennis, exact 意为 obscure.

example.en: He was considered a pillar of the local community for decades.
example.zh: 几十年来，他被视为当地社区的支柱。

entries.etymology: Middle English pilwe, from Old English pyle "pillow," from West Germanic *pulwi(n) (source also of Old Saxon puli, Middle Dutch polu, Dutch peluw, Old High German pfuliwi, German Pfühl), an early borrowing (2c. or 3c.) from Latin pulvinus "little cushion, small pillow," of uncertain origin. Modern spelling is from mid-15c. Pillow fight (n.) attested from 1837; slang pillow talk (n.) first recorded 1939.
entries.etymologyZh: 中古英语 pilwe, 源自 古英语 pyle "pillow," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *pulwi(n) (source also of 古撒克逊语 puli, Middle 荷兰语 polu, 荷兰语 peluw, 古高地德语 pfuliwi, 德语 Pfühl), an early borrowing (2 世纪 or 3 世纪) 源自 拉丁语 pulvinus "little cushion, small pillow," 来源存疑. 现代 spelling 始于 15 世纪中期 Pillow fight （名） attested 自 1837 年起; 俚语 pillow talk （名） 首见于 1939 年.

definitionLines: n. 驾驶员，飞行员；领航员
entries.definition: n. 驾驶员，飞行员；领航员 v. 驾驶（飞机等）；领航
entries.etymology:
1510s, "one who steers a ship," from Middle French pillote (16c.), from Italian piloto, supposed to be an alteration of Old Italian pedoto, which usually is said to be from Medieval Greek *pedotes "rudder, helmsman," from Greek pedon "steering oar," related to pous (genitive podos) "foot," from PIE root *ped- (1) "a foot" (see foot (n.)). Change of -d- to -l- in Latin ("Sabine -l-") parallels that in odor/olfactory; see lachrymose.

Sense extended 1848 to "one who controls a balloon," and 1907 to "one who flies an airplane." As an adjective, 1788 as "pertaining to a pilot;" from 1928 as "serving as a prototype." Thus the noun pilot meaning "pilot episode" (etc.), attested from 1962. Pilot light is from 1890.
entries.etymologyZh: 1510 年代, "one who steers a ship," 源自 中古法语 pillote (16 世纪), 源自 意大利语 piloto, supposed to be an alteration of Old 意大利语 pedoto, which 通常 is said to be 源自 Medieval 希腊语 *pedotes "rudder, helmsman," 源自 希腊语 pedon "steering oar," related to pous (属格 podos) "foot," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ped- (1) "a foot" （参见 foot （名）). Change of -d- to -l- in 拉丁语 ("Sabine -l-") parallels that in odor/olfactory; 参见 lachrymose. Sense extended 1848 年 to "one who controls a balloon," and 1907 年 to "one who flies an airplane." 作形容词时, 1788 年 as "pertaining to a pilot;" 自 1928 年起 as "serving as a prototype." Thus the 名词 pilot 意为 "pilot episode" (etc.), attested 自 1962 年起. Pilot light 始于 1890 年.

example.en: The experienced pilot landed the plane safely despite strong crosswinds.
example.zh: 经验丰富的飞行员尽管顶着强劲的侧风，仍安全降落了飞机。

entries.etymology: early 13c., from Old North French *pinchier "to pinch, squeeze, nip; steal" (Old French pincier, Modern French pincer), of uncertain origin, possibly from Vulgar Latin *punctiare "to pierce," which might be a blend of Latin punctum "point" + *piccare "to pierce." Meaning "to steal" in English is from 1650s. Sense of "to be stingy" is recorded from early 14c. Related: Pinched; pinching.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 Old North 法语 *pinchier "to pinch, squeeze, nip; steal" (古法语 pincier, 现代法语 pincer), 来源存疑, possibly 源自 通俗拉丁语 *punctiare "to pierce," which might be a blend of 拉丁语 punctum "point" + *piccare "to pierce." 义为 "to steal" in English 始于 1650 年代. 义为 "to be stingy" 见于 14 世纪初 同源词：Pinched; pinching.

entries.etymology: "coniferous tree," Old English pin (in compounds), from Old French pin and directly from Latin pinus "pine, pine-tree, fir-tree," which is perhaps from a PIE *pi-nu-, from root *peie- "to be fat, swell" (see fat (adj.)). If so, the tree's name would be a reference to its sap or pitch. Compare Sanskrit pituh "juice, sap, resin," pitudaruh "pine tree," Greek pitys "pine tree." Also see pitch (n.1). Pine-top "cheap illicit whiskey," first recorded 1858, Southern U.S. slang. Pine-needle (n.) attested from 1866.
entries.etymologyZh: "coniferous tree," 古英语 pin (in compounds), 源自 古法语 pin and 直接源自 拉丁语 pinus "pine, pine-tree, fir-tree," which is 或源自 a 原始印欧语 (PIE) *pi-nu-, 源自 root *peie- "to be fat, swell" （参见 fat （形）). If so, the tree's name would be a reference to its sap or pitch. 对比 梵语 pituh "juice, sap, resin," pitudaruh "pine tree," 希腊语 pitys "pine tree." Also 参见 pitch (n.1). Pine-top "cheap illicit whiskey," 首见于 1858 年, Southern U.S. 俚语. Pine-needle （名） attested 自 1866 年起.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, pungde "pierce, stab," later (early 14c.) "make holes in; spur a horse," of uncertain origin; perhaps from a Romanic stem that also yielded French piquer, Spanish picar (see pike (n.2)). Or perhaps from Old English pyngan and directly from Latin pungere "to prick, pierce," related to pugnus "a fist" (see pugnacious). Surviving mainly in pinking shears.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, pungde "pierce, stab," later (14 世纪初) "make holes in; spur a horse," 来源存疑; 或源自 a Romanic stem that also yielded 法语 piquer, 西班牙语 picar （参见 pike (n.2)). Or 或源自 古英语 pyngan and 直接源自 拉丁语 pungere "to prick, pierce," related to pugnus "a fist" （参见 pugnacious). Surviving mainly in pinking shears.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., from Old French pinte "liquid measure, pint" (13c.), probably from Vulgar Latin *pincta (source of Old Provençal, Spanish, Italian pinta), altered from Latin picta "painted," fem. past participle of pingere "to paint" (see paint (v.)), on notion of a painted mark on a vessel indicating this measure. Used elliptically for "pint of ale" (or beer) from 1742. Pint-sized "small" (especially in reference to children) is recorded from 1938.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 pinte "liquid measure, pint" (13 世纪), 可能 源自 通俗拉丁语 *pincta (source of Old Provençal, 西班牙语, 意大利语 pinta), altered 源自 拉丁语 picta "painted," fem. 为 … 的过去分词 pingere "to paint" （参见 paint （动）), on 概念 a painted mark on a vessel indicating this measure. Used elliptically for "pint of ale" (or beer) 自 1742 年起. Pint-sized "small" (尤指 in reference to children) 见于 1938 年.

entries.definition: n. 先驱，先锋，开拓者 vt. 开拓，开创
entries.etymology: 1520s, "foot soldier who prepares the way for the army," from Middle French pionnier "foot-soldier, pioneer," from Old French paonier "foot-soldier" (11c.), from peon (see pawn (n.2)). Figurative sense of "person who goes first or does something first" is from c. 1600. Related: Pioneers.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "foot soldier who prepares the way for the army," 源自 中古法语 pionnier "foot-soldier, pioneer," 源自 古法语 paonier "foot-soldier" (11 世纪), 源自 peon （参见 pawn (n.2)). Figurative 语义 "person who goes first or does something first" 始于 约 1600 年. 同源词：Pioneers.

example.en: Marie Curie was a true pioneer in the field of radioactivity research.
example.zh: 玛丽·居里是放射性研究领域真正的先驱。

entries.etymology: Old English pipian "to play on a pipe," from Latin pipare "to peep, chirp"  (see pipe (n.1)). Compare Dutch pijpen, German pfeifen. Meaning "convey through pipes" is first recorded 1887. Related: Piped; piping. Piping hot is in Chaucer, a reference to hissing of food in a frying pan; to pipe up (early 15c.) originally meant "to begin to play" (on a musical instrument); sense of "to speak out" is from 1856. Pipe down "be quiet" is from 1900, probably a reversal of this, but earlier (and concurrently) in nautical jargon it was a bo'sun's whistle signal to dismiss the men from duty (1833).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 pipian "to play on a pipe," 源自 拉丁语 pipare "to peep, chirp" （参见 pipe (n.1)). 对比 荷兰语 pijpen, 德语 pfeifen. 义为 "convey through pipes" is 首见于 1887 年. 同源词：Piped; piping. Piping hot is in Chaucer, a reference to hissing of food in a frying pan; to pipe up (15 世纪初) 原义为 meant "to begin to play" (on a musical instrument); 语义 "to speak out" 始于 1856 年. Pipe down "be quiet" 始于 1900 年, 可能 a reversal of this, but earlier (and concurrently) in nautical jargon it was a bo'sun's whistle signal to dismiss the men 源自 duty (1833 年).

example.en: A burst pipe under the street caused flooding in the neighborhood.
example.zh: 街道下方一根破裂的管道导致附近发生水涝。

entries.etymology:
"small hand-held firearm," 1570s, from Middle French pistole "short firearm" (1566), of uncertain origin, sometimes said to be from German Pistole, from Czech pis'tala "firearm," literally "tube, pipe," from pisteti "to whistle," of imitative origin, related to Russian pischal "shepherd's pipe."

But earlier English form pistolet (1550) is said to be from Middle French pistolet "a small firearm," also "a small dagger," which may be the literal sense; though some connect this word with Italian pistolese, in reference to Pistoia, town in Tuscany noted for gunsmithing. Pistol-whip (v.) is first recorded 1942.
entries.etymologyZh: "small hand-held firearm," 1570 年代, 源自 中古法语 pistole "short firearm" (1566 年), 来源存疑, 有时 said to be 源自 德语 Pistole, 源自 Czech pis'tala "firearm," literally "tube, pipe," from pisteti "to whistle," of imitative origin, related to Russian pischal "shepherd's pipe." But earlier English form pistolet (1550) is said to be from Middle French pistolet "a small firearm," also "a small dagger," which may be the literal sense; though some connect this word with 意大利语 pistolese, in reference to Pistoia, town in Tuscany noted for gunsmithing. Pistol-whip （动） is 首见于 1942 年.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "to put into a pit," from pit (n.1); especially for purposes of fighting (of cocks, dogs, pugilists) from 1760. Figurative sense of "to set in rivalry" is from 1754. Meaning "to make pits in" is from late 15c. Related: Pitted; pitting. Compare Pit-bull as a dog breed attested from 1922, short for pit-bull terrier (by 1912). This also is the notion behind the meaning "the part of a theater on the floor of the house" (1640s).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "to put into a pit," 源自 pit (n.1); 尤指 for purposes of fighting (of cocks, dogs, pugilists) 自 1760 年起. Figurative 语义 "to set in rivalry" 始于 1754 年. 义为 "to make pits in" 始于 15 世纪晚期 同源词：Pitted; pitting. 对比 Pit-bull 作为 dog breed attested 自 1922 年起, short for pit-bull terrier (截至 1912 年). This also is the notion behind the 意为 "the part of a theater on the floor of the house" (1640 年代).

example.en: The pitcher pitch the ball straight across the center of the plate.
example.zh: 投手将球直接投过本垒板中央。

entries.definition: vt./n. 怜悯，惋惜 n. 可惜的事，憾事
entries.etymology: early 13c., from Old French pite, pitet "pity, mercy, compassion, care, tenderness; pitiful state, wretched condition" (11c., Modern French pitié), from Latin pietatem (nominative pietas) "piety, loyalty, duty" (see piety). Replaced Old English mildheortness, literally "mild-heartness," itself a loan-translation of Latin misericordia. English pity and piety were not fully distinguished until 17c. Transferred sense of "grounds or cause for pity" is from late 14c.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 古法语 pite, pitet "pity, mercy, compassion, care, tenderness; pitiful state, wretched condition" (11 世纪, 现代法语 pitié), 源自 拉丁语 pietatem (主格 pietas) "piety, loyalty, duty" （参见 piety). Replaced 古英语 mildheortness, 字面义为 "mild-heartness," itself a loan-translation of 拉丁语 misericordia. English pity and piety were not fully distinguished until 17 世纪 Transferred 语义 "grounds or cause for pity" 始于 14 世纪晚期

entries.etymology: 1935, from Italian pizza, originally "cake, tart, pie," of uncertain origin. The 1907 "Vocabolario Etimologico della Lingua Italiana" reports it is said to be from dialectal pinza "clamp" (from Latin pinsere "to pound, stamp"). Klein suggests a connection via loan-translation with Medieval Greek pitta "cake, pie," from Greek pitta "pitch" (cognate with Latin adjective piceus "of pitch"). See also pita.

The 1907 年 "Vocabolario Etimologico della Lingua Italiana" reports it is said to be 源自 方言 pinza "clamp" (源自 拉丁语 pinsere "to pound, stamp"). Klein suggests a connection 经由 loan-translation with Medieval 希腊语 pitta "cake, pie," 源自 希腊语 pitta "pitch" (与 … 同源 拉丁语 形容词 piceus "of pitch"). See also pita.

definitionLines: n. 地方，地点，位置；职位，职 责；住所，寓所；地位，等级， 名次
vt. 放，置；安排，任命；发出（订 单等）
entries.definition: n. 地方，地点，位置；职位，职 责；住所，寓所；地位，等级， 名次 vt. 放，置；安排，任命；发出（订 单等）
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "space, dimensional extent, room, area," from Old French place "place, spot" (12c.) and directly from Medieval Latin placea "place, spot," from Latin platea "courtyard, open space; broad way, avenue," from Greek plateia (hodos) "broad (way)," fem. of platys "broad" (see plaice (n.)).

Replaced Old English stow and stede. From mid-13c. as "particular part of space, extent, definite location, spot, site;" from early 14c. as "position or place occupied by custom, etc.; position on some social scale;" from late 14c. as "inhabited place, town, country," also "place on the surface of something, portion of something, part," also, "office, post." Meaning "group of houses in a town" is from 1580s.

Also from the same Latin source are Italian piazza, Catalan plassa, Spanish plaza, Middle Dutch plaetse, Dutch plaats, German Platz, Danish plads, Norwegian plass. Wide application in English covers meanings that in French require three words: place, lieu, and endroit. Cognate Italian piazza and Spanish plaza retain more of the etymological sense.

To take place "happen" is from mid-15c. To know (one's) place is from c. 1600; hence figurative expression put (someone) in his or her place (1855). Place of worship attested from 1689, originally in official papers and in reference to assemblies of dissenters from the Church of England. All over the place "in disorder" is attested from 1923.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "space, dimensional extent, room, area," 源自 古法语 place "place, spot" (12 世纪) and 直接源自 中古拉丁语 placea "place, spot," 源自 拉丁语 platea "courtyard, open space; broad way, avenue," 源自 希腊语 plateia (hodos) "broad (way)," fem. of platys "broad" （参见 plaice （名）). Replaced 古英语 stow and stede. From 13 世纪中期 as "particular part of space, extent, definite location, spot, site;" 源自 14 世纪初 as "position or place occupied by custom, etc.; position on some social scale;" 源自 14 世纪晚期 as "inhabited place, town, country," also "place on the surface of something, portion of something, part," also, "office, post." 义为 "group of houses in a town" 始于 1580 年代. Also 源自 same 拉丁语 source are 意大利语 piazza, Catalan plassa, 西班牙语 plaza, Middle 荷兰语 plaetse, 荷兰语 plaats, 德语 Platz, Danish plads, Norwegian plass. Wide application in English covers meanings that in 法语 require three words: place, lieu, and endroit. Cognate 意大利语 piazza and 西班牙语 plaza retain more of the etymological sense. To take place "happen" 始于 15 世纪中期 To know (one's) place 始于 约 1600 年; hence figurative expression put (someone) in his or her place (1855 年). Place of worship attested 自 1689 年起, 原义为 in official papers and in reference to assemblies of dissenters 源自 Church of England. All over the place "in disorder" 见于 1923 年.

example.en: The park bench by the fountain is my favorite place to read books.
example.zh: 喷泉旁边的公园长椅是我最喜欢读书的地方。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., plage, "affliction, calamity, evil, scourge;" early 15c., "malignant disease," from Old French plage (14c.), from Late Latin plaga, used in Vulgate for "pestilence," from Latin plaga "stroke, wound," probably from root of plangere "to strike, lament (by beating the breast)," from or cognate with Greek (Doric) plaga "blow," from PIE *plak- (2) "to strike, to hit" (source also of Greek plazein "to drive away," plessein "to beat, strike;" Old English flocan "to strike, beat;" Gothic flokan "to bewail;" German fluchen, Old Frisian floka "to curse").

The Latin word also is the source of Old Irish plag (genitive plaige) "plague, pestilence," German Plage, Dutch plaage. Meaning "epidemic that causes many deaths" is from 1540s; specifically in reference to bubonic plague from c. 1600. Modern spelling follows French, which had plague from 15c. Weakened sense of "anything annoying" is from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, plage, "affliction, calamity, evil, scourge;" 15 世纪初, "malignant disease," 源自 古法语 plage (14 世纪), 源自 晚期拉丁语 plaga, used in Vulgate for "pestilence," 源自 拉丁语 plaga "stroke, wound," 可能 源自 root of plangere "to strike, lament (by beating the breast)," 源自 or 与 … 同源 希腊语 (Doric) plaga "blow," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *plak- (2) "to strike, to hit" (source also of 希腊语 plazein "to drive away," plessein "to beat, strike;" 古英语 flocan "to strike, beat;" Gothic flokan "to bewail;" 德语 fluchen, 古弗里西语 floka "to curse"). The 拉丁语 word also is the source of Old 爱尔兰语 plag (属格 plaige) "plague, pestilence," 德语 Plage, 荷兰语 plaage. 义为 "epidemic that causes many deaths" 始于 1540 年代; specifically in reference to bubonic plague 源自 约 1600 年. 现代 spelling follows 法语, which had plague 源自 15 世纪 Weakened 语义 "anything annoying" 始于 约 1600 年.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "flat, smooth," from Old French plain "flat, smooth, even" (12c.), from Latin planus "flat, even, level" (see plane (n.1)). Sense of "evident" is from, c. 1300; that of "free from obstruction" is early 14c.; meaning "simple, sincere, ordinary" is recorded from late 14c., especially of dress, "unembellished, without decoration."

In reference to the dress and speech of Quakers, it is recorded from 1824; of Amish and Mennonites, from 1894 (in the Dutch regions of Pennsylvania Plain with the capital is shorthand adjective for "Amish and Old Order Mennonite"). Of appearance, as a euphemism for "ill-favored, ugly" it dates from 1749. Of envelopes from 1913. As an adverb from early 14c. Plain English is from c. 1500. Plain dealer "one who deals plainly or speaks candidly" is from 1570s, marked "Now rare" in OED 2nd edition. To be as plain as the nose on (one's) face is from 1690s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "flat, smooth," 源自 古法语 plain "flat, smooth, even" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 planus "flat, even, level" （参见 plane (n.1)). 义为 "evident" 始于, 约 1300 年; that of "free from obstruction" is 14 世纪初; 意为 "simple, sincere, ordinary" 见于 14 世纪晚期, 尤指 of dress, "unembellished, without decoration." In reference to the dress and speech of Quakers, it 见于 1824 年; of Amish and Mennonites, 自 1894 年起 (in the 荷兰语 regions of Pennsylvania Plain with the capital is shorthand 形容词 for "Amish and Old Order Mennonite"). Of appearance, 作为 euphemism for "ill-favored, ugly" it dates 自 1749 年起. Of envelopes 自 1913 年起. 作为 副词 源自 14 世纪初 Plain English 始于 约 1500 年. Plain dealer "one who deals plainly or speaks candidly" 始于 1570 年代, marked "Now rare" in OED 2nd edition. To be as plain as the nose on (one's) face 始于 1690 年代.

example.en: The vast plain stretched for hundreds of miles with no hills or trees in sight.
example.zh: 广阔的平原绵延数百英里，看不到任何丘陵或树木。

entries.definition: n. 计划，打算；平面图 vt. 计划，制订计划 vi. 计划
entries.etymology: 1670s as a technical term in perspective drawing; 1706 as "drawing, sketch, or diagram of any object," from French plan "ground plan, map," literally "plane surface" (mid-16c.), from Latin planum "level or flat surface," noun use of adjective planus "level, flat" (see plane (n.1)). The notion is of "a drawing on a flat surface." Meaning "scheme of action, design" is first recorded 1706, possibly influenced by French planter "to plant," from Italian planta "ground plan."
entries.etymologyZh: 1670 年代 作为 technical term in perspective drawing; 1706 年 as "drawing, sketch, or diagram of any object," 源自 法语 plan "ground plan, map," 字面义为 "plane surface" (16 世纪中期), 源自 拉丁语 planum "level or flat surface," 为 … 的名词用法 形容词 planus "level, flat" （参见 plane (n.1)). The notion is of "a drawing on a flat surface." 义为 "scheme of action, design" is 首见于 1706 年, possibly influenced by 法语 planter "to plant," 源自 意大利语 planta "ground plan."

example.en: The team presented a detailed plan for the new urban development project.
example.zh: 团队就新的城市发展项目提交了一份详细的计划。

entries.etymology: late Old English planete, from Old French planete (Modern French planète), from Late Latin planeta, from Greek planetes, from (asteres) planetai "wandering (stars)," from planasthai "to wander," of unknown origin, possibly from PIE *pele- (2) "flat, to spread" on notion of "spread out." So called because they have apparent motion, unlike the "fixed" stars. Originally including also the moon and sun; modern scientific sense of "world that orbits a star" is from 1630s.

example.en: Mars is the planet most likely to support some form of microbial life.
example.zh: 火星是最有可能支持某种微生物生命的行星。

entries.definition: n. 植物；工厂 vt. 种，植，播
entries.etymology:
Old English plante "young tree or shrub, herb newly planted," from Latin planta "sprout, shoot, cutting" (source of Spanish planta, French plante), perhaps from *plantare "to drive in with the feet, push into the ground with the feet," from planta "sole of the foot," from nasalized form of PIE *plat- "to spread, flat" (see place (n.)).

Broader sense of "any vegetable life, vegetation generally" is first recorded 1550s. Most extended usages are from the verb, on the notion of "something planted;" such as "construction for an industrial process," 1789, at first with reference to the set-up of machinery, later also the building; also slang meaning "a spy" (1812). Many of these follow similar developments in the French form of the word. German Pflanz, Irish cland, Welsh plant are from Latin.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 plante "young tree or shrub, herb newly planted," 源自 拉丁语 planta "sprout, shoot, cutting" (source of 西班牙语 planta, 法语 plante), 或源自 *plantare "to drive in with the feet, push into the ground with the feet," 源自 planta "sole of the foot," 源自 nasalized form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) *plat- "to spread, flat" （参见 place （名）). Broader 语义 "any vegetable life, vegetation generally" is 首见于 1550 年代. Most extended usages 始于 the 动词, on the 概念 "something planted;" such as "construction for an industrial process," 1789 年, at first with reference to the set-up of machinery, later also the building; also 俚语 意为 "a spy" (1812 年). Many of these follow similar developments in the 法语 form of the word. 德语 Pflanz, 爱尔兰语 cland, Welsh plant 始于 拉丁语.

example.en: She hired a gardener to plant tulip bulbs along the front fence.
example.zh: 她雇了一位园丁沿前围栏种植郁金香球茎。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "action of planting," from Middle French plantation, from Latin plantationem (nominative plantatio) "a planting," noun of action from past participle stem of plantare "to plant" (see plant). Historically used for "colony, settlement in a new land" (1610s); meaning "large farm on which tobacco or cotton is grown" is first recorded 1706.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "action of planting," 源自 中古法语 plantation, 源自 拉丁语 plantationem (主格 plantatio) "a planting," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of plantare "to plant" （参见 plant). definitionLines: a. 塑料的，塑性的；可塑的
entries.definition: n. （pl.）塑料 a. 塑料的，塑性的；可塑的
entries.etymology: 1630s, "capable of shaping or molding," from Latin plasticus, from Greek plastikos "able to be molded, pertaining to molding, fit for molding," also in reference to the arts, from plastos "molded, formed," verbal adjective from plassein "to mold" (see plasma). Surgical sense of "remedying a deficiency of structure" is first recorded 1839 (in plastic surgery). Meaning "made of plastic" is from 1909. Picked up in counterculture slang with meaning "false, superficial" (1963). Plastic explosive (n.) attested from 1894.

Plastic explosive （名） attested 自 1894 年起.

example.en: Many countries are trying to reduce their use of single-use plastic products.

entries.definition: n. 盘子，盆子；板，钢板 vt. 镀，电镀
entries.etymology: mid-13c., "flat sheet of gold or silver," also "flat, round coin," from Old French plate "thin piece of metal" (late 12c.), from Medieval Latin plata "plate, piece of metal," perhaps via Vulgar Latin *plattus, formed on model of Greek platys "flat, broad" (see plaice (n.)). The cognate in Spanish (plata) and Portuguese (prata) has become the usual word for "silver," superseding argento via shortening of *plata d'argento "plate of silver, coin." Meaning "table utensils" (originally of silver or gold only) is from Middle English. Meaning "shallow dish for food," now usually of china or earthenware, originally of metal or wood, is from mid-15c. Baseball sense is from 1857. Geological sense is first attested 1904; plate tectonics first recorded 1969. Plate-glass first recorded 1727.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, "flat sheet of gold or silver," also "flat, round coin," 源自 古法语 plate "thin piece of metal" (12 世纪晚期), 源自 中古拉丁语 plata "plate, piece of metal," 或许 经由 通俗拉丁语 *plattus, formed on model of 希腊语 platys "flat, broad" （参见 plaice （名）). The 同源 in 西班牙语 (plata) and 葡萄牙语 (prata) has become the usual word for "silver," superseding argento 经由 shortening of *plata d'argento "plate of silver, coin." 义为 "table utensils" (原义为 of silver or gold only) 始于 中古英语. 义为 "shallow dish for food," 现在 通常 of china or earthenware, 原义为 of metal or wood, 始于 15 世纪中期 Baseball sense 始于 1857 年. Geological sense is 最早见于 1904 年; plate tectonics 首见于 1969 年. Plate-glass 首见于 1727 年.

entries.etymology: 1796, "elevated tract of relatively level land," from French plateau "table-land," from Old French platel (12c.) "flat piece of metal, wood, etc.," diminutive of plat "flat surface or thing," noun use of adjective plat "flat, stretched out" (12c.), perhaps from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Greek platys "flat, wide, broad" (see plaice). Meaning "stage at which no progress is apparent" is attested from 1897, originally in psychology of learning. In reference to sexual stimulation from 1960.
entries.etymologyZh: 1796 年, "elevated tract of relatively level land," 源自 法语 plateau "table-land," 源自 古法语 platel (12 世纪) "flat piece of metal, wood, etc.," 为 … 的指小形式 plat "flat surface or thing," 为 … 的名词用法 形容词 plat "flat, stretched out" (12 世纪), 或源自 通俗拉丁语 *plattus, 源自 希腊语 platys "flat, wide, broad" （参见 plaice). 义为 "stage at which no progress is apparent" 见于 1897 年, 原义为 in psychology of learning. definitionLines: n. 台，讲台；站台，月台；平台
entries.definition: n. 台，讲台；站台，月台；平台
entries.etymology: 1540s, "plan of action, scheme, design," from Middle French plateforme, platte fourme, literally "flat form," from Old French plat "flat" (see plateau (n.)) + forme "form" (see form (n.)). The literal sense of "raised, level surface" in English is first recorded 1550s. Political meaning, "statement of party policies," is from 1803, probably originally an image of a literal platform on which politicians gather, stand, and make their appeals, perhaps influenced by earlier sense of "set of rules governing church doctrine" (first attested 1570s). Railroad station sense is from 1838.

The literal 语义 "raised, level surface" in English is 首见于 1550 年代. Political 意为, "statement of party policies," 始于 1803 年, 可能 原义为 an image of a literal platform on which politicians gather, stand, and make their appeals, 或许 influenced by earlier 语义 "set of rules governing church doctrine" (最早见于 1570 年代). definitionLines: n. 游戏，娱乐；剧本，戏剧； 比赛，运动
entries.definition: v.玩，游玩；演奏，表演；比赛 n. 游戏，娱乐；剧本，戏剧； 比赛，运动
entries.etymology:
Old English plegan, plegian "move rapidly, occupy or busy oneself, exercise; frolic; make sport of, mock; perform music," from West Germanic *plegan "occupy oneself about"  (source also of Old Saxon plegan "vouch for, take charge of," Old Frisian plega "tend to," Middle Dutch pleyen "to rejoice, be glad," German pflegen "take care of, cultivate"), from PIE root *dlegh- "to engage oneself," forming words in Celtic, Germanic, Slavic, and possibly Latin.

Meaning "to take part in a game" is from c. 1200. Opposed to work (v.) since late 14c. Related: Played; playing. To play up "emphasize" is from 1909; to play down "minimize" is from 1930; to play along "cooperate" is from 1929. To play with oneself "masturbate" is from 1896; play for keeps is from 1861, originally of marbles or other children's games with tokens. To play second fiddle in the figurative sense is from 1809 ("Gil Blas"). To play into the hands (of someone) is from 1705. To play the _______ card is attested from 1886; to play fair is from mid-15c. To play (something) safe is from 1911; to play favorites is attested from 1902. For play the field see field (n.).

To play with oneself "masturbate" 始于 1896 年; play for keeps 始于 1861 年, 原义为 of marbles or other children's games with tokens. To play second fiddle in the figurative sense 始于 1809 年 ("Gil Blas"). To play into the hands (of someone) 始于 1705 年. To play the _______ card 见于 1886 年; to play fair 始于 15 世纪中期 To play (something) safe 始于 1911 年; to play favorites 见于 1902 年. For play the field 参见 field （名）.

definitionLines: n. 恳求，请求；辩解，辩护
entries.definition: n. 恳求，请求；辩解，辩护
entries.etymology: early 13c., "lawsuit," from Anglo-French plai (late 12c.), Old French plait "lawsuit, decision, decree" (9c.), from Medieval Latin placitum "lawsuit," in classical Latin, "opinion, decree," literally "that which pleases, thing which is agreed upon," properly neuter past participle of placere (see please). Sense development seems to be from "something pleasant," to "something that pleases both sides," to "something that has been decided." Meaning "a pleading, an agreement in a suit" is attested from late 14c. Plea-bargaining is first attested 1963. Common pleas (early 13c.) originally were legal proceedings over which the Crown did not claim exclusive jurisdiction (as distinct from pleas of the Crown); later "actions brought by one subject against another."
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "lawsuit," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 plai (12 世纪晚期), 古法语 plait "lawsuit, decision, decree" (9 世纪), 源自 中古拉丁语 placitum "lawsuit," in classical 拉丁语, "opinion, decree," 字面义为 "that which pleases, thing which is agreed upon," properly neuter 为 … 的过去分词 placere （参见 please). Sense development seems to be 源自 "something pleasant," to "something that pleases both sides," to "something that has been decided." 义为 "a pleading, an agreement in a suit" 见于 14 世纪晚期 Plea-bargaining is 最早见于 1963 年. Common pleas (13 世纪初) 原义为 were legal proceedings over which the Crown did not claim exclusive jurisdiction (as distinct 源自 pleas of the Crown); later "actions brought by one subject against another."

definitionLines: vt.使愉快，使满意；喜欢，愿意
entries.definition: int.请 vt.使愉快，使满意；喜欢，愿意
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "to be agreeable," from Old French plaisir "to please, give pleasure to, satisfy" (11c., Modern French plaire, the form of which is perhaps due to analogy of faire), from Latin placere "to be acceptable, be liked, be approved," related to placare "to soothe, quiet" (source of Spanish placer, Italian piacere), possibly from PIE *plak-e- "to be calm," via notion of still water, etc., from root *plak- (1) "to be flat" (see placenta).

Meaning "to delight" in English is from late 14c. Inverted use for "to be pleased" is from c. 1500, first in Scottish, and paralleling the evolution of synonymous like (v.). Intransitive sense (do as you please) first recorded c. 1500; imperative use (please do this), first recorded 1620s, was probably a shortening of if it please (you) (late 14c.). Related: Pleased; pleasing; pleasingly.

Verbs for "please" supply the stereotype polite word ("Please come in," short for may it please you to ...) in many languages (French, Italian), "But more widespread is the use of the first singular of a verb for 'ask, request' " [Buck, who cites German bitte, Polish proszę, etc.]. Spanish favor is short for hace el favor "do the favor." Danish has in this sense vær saa god, literally "be so good."

Intransitive sense (do as you please) 首见于 约 1500 年; imperative use (please do this), 首见于 1620 年代, was 可能 a shortening of if it please (you) (14 世纪晚期). 同源词：Pleased; pleasing; pleasingly. Verbs for "please" supply the stereotype polite word ("Please come in," short for may it please you to ...) in many languages (法语, 意大利语), "But more widespread is the use of the first singular of a verb for 'ask, request' " [Buck, who cites 德语 bitte, Polish proszę, etc.]. 西班牙语 favor is short for hace el favor "do the favor." Danish has in this sense vær saa god, 字面义为 "be so good."

definitionLines: a. 高兴的；喜欢的；乐意做某事
entries.definition: a. 高兴的；喜欢的；乐意做某事
entries.etymology: "satisfied, contented," late 14c., past participle adjective from please (v.).

definitionLines: n. 愉快，欢乐；乐事，乐趣
entries.definition: n. 愉快，欢乐；乐事，乐趣
entries.etymology: late 14c., "condition of enjoyment," from Old French plesir, also plaisir "enjoyment, delight, desire, will" (12c.), from noun use of infinitive plaisir (v.) "to please," from Latin placere "to please, give pleasure, be approved" (see please (v.)). Ending altered in English 14c. by influence of words in -ure (measure, etc.). Meaning "sensual enjoyment as the chief object of life" is attested from 1520s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "condition of enjoyment," 源自 古法语 plesir, also plaisir "enjoyment, delight, desire, will" (12 世纪), 源自 为 … 的名词用法 infinitive plaisir （动） "to please," 源自 拉丁语 placere "to please, give pleasure, be approved" （参见 please （动）). Ending altered in English 14 世纪 by influence of words in -ure (measure, etc.). 义为 "sensual enjoyment as the chief object of life" 见于 1520 年代.

entries.definition: n. 誓约，保证 vt. 发誓，保证
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "surety, bail," from Old French plege (Modern French pleige) "hostage, security, bail," probably from Frankish *plegan "to guarantee," from *pleg-, a West Germanic root meaning "have responsibility for" (source also of Old Saxon plegan "vouch for," Middle Dutch plien "to answer for, guarantee," Old High German pflegan "to care for, be accustomed to," Old English pleon "to risk the loss of, expose to danger;" see plight (v.)).

Meaning "allegiance vow attested by drinking with another" is from 1630s. Sense of "solemn promise" first recorded 1814, though this notion is from 16c. in the verb. Weekley notes the "curious contradiction" in pledge (v.) "to toast with a drink" (1540s) and pledge (n.) "the vow to abstain from drinking" (1833). Meaning "student who has agreed to join a fraternity or sorority" dates from 1901.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "surety, bail," 源自 古法语 plege (现代法语 pleige) "hostage, security, bail," 可能 源自 Frankish *plegan "to guarantee," 源自 *pleg-, a West 日耳曼语 root 意为 "have responsibility for" (source also of 古撒克逊语 plegan "vouch for," Middle 荷兰语 plien "to answer for, guarantee," 古高地德语 pflegan "to care for, be accustomed to," 古英语 pleon "to risk the loss of, expose to danger;" 参见 plight （动）). 义为 "allegiance vow attested by drinking with another" 始于 1630 年代. 义为 "solemn promise" 首见于 1814 年, though this notion 始于 16 世纪 in the 动词. Weekley notes the "curious contradiction" in pledge （动） "to toast with a drink" (1540 年代) and pledge （名） "the vow to abstain from drinking" (1833 年). 义为 "student who has agreed to join a fraternity or sorority" dates 自 1901 年起.

example.en: The candidate made a public pledge to lower taxes if elected.

entries.etymology: mid-13c., "as much as one could desire," from Old French plentee, earlier plentet "abundance, profusion" (12c., Modern French dialectal plenté), from Latin plenitatem (nominative plenitas) "fullness," from plenus "complete, full" (see plenary). Meaning "condition of general abundance" is from late 14c. The colloquial adverb meaning "very much" is first attested 1842. Middle English had parallel formation plenteth, from the older Old French form of the word.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, "as much as one could desire," 源自 古法语 plentee, earlier plentet "abundance, profusion" (12 世纪, 现代法语 方言 plenté), 源自 拉丁语 plenitatem (主格 plenitas) "fullness," 源自 plenus "complete, full" （参见 plenary). 义为 "condition of general abundance" 始于 14 世纪晚期 The 口语 副词 意为 "very much" is 最早见于 1842 年. 中古英语 had parallel formation plenteth, 源自 older 古法语 form of the word.

entries.etymology: "to pledge" (obsolete except in archaic plight one's troth), from Old English pligtan, plihtan "to endanger, imperil, compromise," verb form of pliht (n.) "danger, risk," from PIE root *dlegh- "to engage oneself," forming words in Celtic, Germanic, Slavic, and possibly Latin (see play (v.)). Related: Plighted; plighting.

entries.definition: n.一块地；计策，阴谋；情节 v.策划
entries.etymology: Old English plot "small piece of ground," of unknown origin. Sense of "ground plan," and thus "map, chart" is 1550s; that of "a secret, plan, scheme" is 1580s, probably by accidental similarity to complot, from Old French complot "combined plan," of unknown origin, perhaps a back-formation from compeloter "to roll into a ball," from pelote "ball." Meaning "set of events in a story" is from 1640s. Plot-line (n.) attested from 1957.

Plot-line （名） attested 自 1957 年起.

entries.definition: n. 插头；塞子 n. 堵，插
entries.etymology: 1620s, originally a seamen's term, probably from Dutch plug, Middle Dutch plugge "bung, stopper," related to Norwegian plugg, Danish pløg, North Frisian plaak, Middle Low German pluck, German Pflock; further etymology uncertain. Irish and Gaelic words are from English. Sense of "wad or stick of tobacco" is attested from 1728, based on resemblance. Electrical sense is from 1883, based on being inserted; meaning "sparking device in an internal combustion engine" is from 1886. Meaning "advertisement" first recorded 1902, American English, perhaps from verb sense "work energetically at" (c. 1865).

entries.etymology: late 14c., "to put or thrust violently into," also intransitive, from Old French plongier "plunge, sink into; plunge into, dive in" (mid-12c., Modern French plonger), from Vulgar Latin *plumbicare "to heave the lead," from Latin plumbum "lead" (see plumb (n.)). entries.definition: prep.加 n.加号，正号 a.正的，加的
entries.etymology:
1570s, the oral rendering of the arithmetical sign +, from Latin plus "more, in greater number, more often" (comparative of multus "much"), altered (by influence of minus) from *pleos, from PIE *pele- (1) "to fill" (see poly-).

As a preposition, between two numbers to indicate addition, from 1660s. [Barnhart writes that this sense "did not exist in Latin and probably originated in commercial language of the Middle Ages."] Placed after a whole number to indicate "and a little more," it is attested from 1902. As a conjunction, "and," it is American English colloquial, attested from 1968. As a noun meaning "an advantage" from 1791. Plus fours (1921) were four inches longer in the leg than standard knickerbockers, to produce an overhang, originally a style associated with golfers. The plus sign itself has been well-known since at least late 15c. and is perhaps an abbreviation of Latin et (see et cetera).

[Barnhart writes that this sense "did not exist in Latin and probably originated in commercial language of the Middle Ages."] Placed after a whole number to indicate "and a little more," it 见于 1902 年. 作为 conjunction, "and," it is American English 口语, attested 自 1968 年起. 作名词时 意为 "an advantage" 自 1791 年起. Plus fours (1921 年) were four inches longer in the leg than standard knickerbockers, to produce an overhang, 原义为 a style associated with golfers. The plus sign itself has been well-known 自 at least 15 世纪晚期 and is 或许 an abbreviation of 拉丁语 et （参见 et cetera).

entries.etymology: Roman god of the underworld, from Latin Pluto, Pluton, from Greek Plouton "god of wealth," literally "wealth, riches," probably originally "overflowing," from PIE *pleu- "to flow" (see pluvial). The alternative Greek name of Hades in his function as the god of wealth (precious metals and gems, coming from beneath the earth, form part of his realm). The planet (since downgraded) was discovered 1930 by C.W. Tombaugh; Minerva also was suggested as a name for it. The cartoon dog first appeared in Walt Disney's "Moose Hunt," released April 1931.

entries.definition: n. 衣袋 a. 袖珍的
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., pokete, "bag, pouch, small sack," from Anglo-French pokete (13c.), diminutive of Old North French poque "bag" (Old French pouche), from a Germanic source akin to Frankish *pokka "bag," from Proto-Germanic *puk- (see poke (n.)).

Meaning "small bag worn on the person, especially one sewn into a garment" is from early 15c. Sense in billiards is from 1754. Mining sense is attested from 1850; military sense of "area held by troops surrounded by the enemy" is from 1918; the general sense of "small area different than its surroundings" (1926) apparently was extended from the military use. Figuratively, "one's money" (conceived as being kept in a pocket) is from 1717. Pope Pokett (late 15c.) was figurative of the greedy and corrupt Church.

Figuratively, "one's money" (conceived as being kept in a pocket) 始于 1717 年. Pope Pokett (15 世纪晚期) was figurative of the greedy and corrupt Church.

entries.etymology:
early 14c., "a poet, a singer" (c. 1200 as a surname), from Old French poete (12c., Modern French poète) and directly from Latin poeta "a poet," from Greek poetes "maker, author, poet," variant of poietes, from poein, poiein "to make, create, compose," from PIE *kwoiwo- "making," from root *kwei- "to pile up, build, make" (source also of Sanskrit cinoti "heaping up, piling up," Old Church Slavonic činu "act, deed, order").

Replaced Old English scop (which survives in scoff). Used in 14c., as in classical languages, for all sorts of writers or composers of works of literature. Poète maudit, "a poet insufficiently appreciated by his contemporaries," literally "cursed poet," attested by 1930, from French (1884, Verlaine). For poet laureate see laureate.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "poetry; a poem; ancient literature; poetical works, fables, or tales," from Old French poetrie (13c.), and perhaps directly from Medieval Latin poetria (c.650), from Latin poeta (see poet). In classical Latin, poetria meant "poetess."

Figurative use from 1660s. Old English had metergeweorc "verse," metercræft "art of versification." Modern English lacks a true verb form in this group of words, though poeticize (1804), poetize (1580s, from French poétiser), and poetrize (c. 1600) have been tried. Poetry in motion (1826) perhaps is from poetry of motion (1813) "dance" (also poetry of the foot, 1660s).

In classical 拉丁语, poetria meant "poetess." Figurative use 源自 1660 年代. 古英语 had metergeweorc "verse," metercræft "art of versification." 现代英语 lacks a true 动词 form in this group of words, though poeticize (1804 年), poetize (1580 年代, 源自 法语 poétiser), and poetrize (约 1600 年) have been tried. Poetry in motion (1826 年) 或许 始于 poetry of motion (1813 年) "dance" (also poetry of the foot, 1660 年代).

definitionLines: n. 尖端，头；点，小数点；论点， 观点，要点；分数，得分
entries.definition: v.指 n. 尖端，头；点，小数点；论点， 观点，要点；分数，得分
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "minute amount, single item in a whole; sharp end of a sword, etc.," a merger of two words, both ultimately from Latin pungere "to prick, pierce," related to pugnus "a fist" (see pugnacious). The Latin neuter past participle punctum was used as a noun, meaning "small hole made by pricking," subsequently extended to anything that looked like one, hence, "dot, particle," etc. This yielded Old French point "dot; smallest amount," which was borrowed in Middle English by c. 1300.

Meanwhile the Latin fem. past participle of pungere was puncta, which was used in Medieval Latin to mean "sharp tip," and became Old French pointe "point of a weapon, vanguard of an army," which also passed into English, early 14c.

The senses have merged in English, but remain distinct in French. Extended senses are from the notion of "minute, single, or separate items in an extended whole." Meaning "small mark, dot" in English is mid-14c. Meaning "distinguishing feature" is recorded from late 15c. Meaning "a unit of score in a game" is first recorded 1746. As a typeface unit (in Britain and U.S., one twelfth of a pica), it went into use in U.S. 1883. As a measure of weight for precious stones (one one-hundredth of a carat) it is recorded from 1931.

The point "the matter being discussed" is attested from late 14c.; meaning "sense, purpose, advantage" (usually in the negative, as in what's the point?) is first recorded 1903. Point of honor (1610s) translates French point d'honneur. Point of no return (1941) is originally aviators' term for the point in a flight "before which any engine failure requires an immediate turn around and return to the point of departure, and beyond which such return is no longer practical."

The 拉丁语 neuter past participle punctum was used 作名词时, 意为 "small hole made by pricking," subsequently extended to anything that looked like one, hence, "dot, particle," etc. This yielded 古法语 point "dot; smallest amount," which was borrowed in 中古英语 by 约 1300 年. Meanwhile the 拉丁语 fem. 为 … 的过去分词 pungere was puncta, which was used in 中古拉丁语 to mean "sharp tip," and became 古法语 pointe "point of a weapon, vanguard of an army," which also passed into English, 14 世纪初 The senses have merged in English, but remain distinct in 法语. Extended senses 始于 the 概念 "minute, single, or separate items in an extended whole." 义为 "small mark, dot" in English is 14 世纪中期 义为 "distinguishing feature" 见于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "a unit of score in a game" is 首见于 1746 年. 作为 typeface unit (in Britain and U.S., one twelfth of a pica), it went into use in U.S. 1883 年. 作为 measure of weight for precious stones (one one-hundredth of a carat) it 见于 1931 年. entries.definition: n. 毒物，毒药 v. 放毒，毒害
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "a deadly potion or substance," also figuratively, from Old French poison, puison (12c., Modern French poison) "a drink," especially a medical drink, later "a (magic) potion, poisonous drink" (14c.), from Latin potionem (nominative potio) "a drinking, a drink," also "poisonous drink" (Cicero), from potare "to drink" (see potion).

For form evolution from Latin to French, compare raison from rationem. The Latin word also is the source of Old Spanish pozon, Italian pozione, Spanish pocion. The more usual Indo-European word for this is represented in English by virus. The Old English word was ator (see attercop) or lybb. Slang sense of "alcoholic drink" first attested 1805, American English.

For sense evolution, compare Old French enerber, enherber "to kill with poisonous plants." In many Germanic languages "poison" is named by a word equivalent to English gift (such as Old High German gift, German Gift, Danish and Swedish gift; Dutch gift, vergift). This shift might have been partly euphemistic, partly by influence of Greek dosis "a portion prescribed," literally "a giving," used by Galen and other Greek physicians to mean an amount of medicine (see dose (n.)).

Figuratively from late 15c.; of persons by 1910. As an adjective from 1520s; with plant names from 18c. Poison ivy first recorded 1784; poison oak is from 1743. Poison gas first recorded 1915. Poison-pen (letter) popularized 1913 by a notorious criminal case in Pennsylvania, U.S.; the phrase dates to 1898.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "a deadly potion or substance," also figuratively, 源自 古法语 poison, puison (12 世纪, 现代法语 poison) "a drink," 尤指 a medical drink, later "a (magic) potion, poisonous drink" (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 potionem (主格 potio) "a drinking, a drink," also "poisonous drink" (Cicero), 源自 potare "to drink" （参见 potion). For form evolution 源自 拉丁语 to 法语, 对比 raison 源自 rationem. The 拉丁语 word also is the source of Old 西班牙语 pozon, 意大利语 pozione, 西班牙语 pocion. The more usual Indo-European word for this is represented in English by virus. The 古英语 word was ator （参见 attercop) or lybb. Slang 语义 "alcoholic drink" 最早见于 1805 年, American English. For sense evolution, 对比 古法语 enerber, enherber "to kill with poisonous plants." In many 日耳曼语 languages "poison" is named by a word equivalent to English gift (such as 古高地德语 gift, 德语 Gift, Danish and Swedish gift; 荷兰语 gift, vergift). This shift might have been partly euphemistic, partly by influence of 希腊语 dosis "a portion prescribed," 字面义为 "a giving," used by Galen and other 希腊语 physicians to mean an amount of medicine （参见 dose （名）). Figuratively 源自 15 世纪晚期; of persons 截至 1910 年. 作形容词时 源自 1520 年代; with plant names 源自 18 世纪 Poison ivy 首见于 1784 年; poison oak 始于 1743 年. Poison gas 首见于 1915 年. Poison-pen (letter) popularized 1913 年 by a notorious criminal case in Pennsylvania, U.S.; the phrase dates to 1898 年.

entries.etymology:
c. 1530, at first essentially the same word as policy (n.1); from Middle French police (late 15c.), from Latin politia "civil administration," from Greek polis "city" (see polis).

Until mid-19c. used in England for "civil administration;" application to "administration of public order" (1716) is from French (late 17c.), and originally in English referred to France or other foreign nations. The first force so-named in England was the Marine Police, set up 1798 to protect merchandise at the Port of London. Police state "state regulated by means of national police" first recorded 1865, with reference to Austria. Police action in the international sense of "military intervention short of war, ostensibly to correct lawlessness" is from 1933. Police officer is attested from 1800. Police station is from 1817.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1530 年, at first essentially the same word as policy (n.1); 源自 中古法语 police (15 世纪晚期), 源自 拉丁语 politia "civil administration," 源自 希腊语 polis "city" （参见 polis). Until 19 世纪中期 used in England for "civil administration;" application to "administration of public order" (1716 年) 始于 法语 (17 世纪晚期), and 原义为 in English referred to France or other foreign nations. The first force so-named in England was the Marine Police, set up 1798 年 to protect merchandise at the Port of London. Police state "state regulated by means of national police" 首见于 1865 年, with reference to Austria. Police action in the international 语义 "military intervention short of war, ostensibly to correct lawlessness" 始于 1933 年. Police officer 见于 1800 年. Police station 始于 1817 年.
