U.S. slang phrase up the river "in prison" (1891) is originally in reference to Sing Sing prison, which was literally "up the (Hudson) river" from New York City. Phrase down the river "done for, finished" perhaps echoes sense in sell down the river (1851), originally of troublesome slaves, to sell from the Upper South to the harsher cotton plantations of the Deep South.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 rivere, 古法语 riviere "river, riverside, river bank" (12 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *riparia "riverbank, seashore, river" (source also of 西班牙语 ribera, 意大利语 riviera), 为 … 的名词用法 fem. of 拉丁语 riparius "of a riverbank" （参见 riparian). Generalized 语义 "a copious flow" of anything 始于 14 世纪晚期 The 古英语 word was ea "river," 与 … 同源 Gothic ahwa, 拉丁语 aqua （参见 aqua-). Romanic 同源 words tend to retain the sense "river bank" as the main one，或else the secondary 拉丁语 sense "coast of the sea" (对比 Riviera). U.S. 俚语 phrase up the river "in prison" (1891 年) is 原义为 in reference to Sing Sing prison, which was 字面义为 "up the (Hudson) river" 源自 New York City. Phrase down the river "done for, finished" 或许 echoes sense in sell down the river (1851 年), 原义为 of troublesome slaves, to sell 源自 Upper South to the harsher cotton plantations of the Deep South.

entries.etymology:
Old English rad "riding expedition, journey, hostile incursion," from Proto-Germanic *raido (source also of Old Frisian red "ride," Old Saxon reda, Middle Dutch rede, Old High German reita "foray, raid"), from PIE *reidh- "to ride" (see ride (v.)). Also related to raid (n.). In Middle English, "a riding, a journey;" sense of "open way for traveling between two places" is first recorded 1590s. Meaning "narrow stretch of sheltered water" is from early 14c. (as in Hampton Roads in Virginia).

Modern spelling established 18c. In 19c. U.S. use, often meaning "railroad." On the road "travelling" is from 1640s. Road test (n.) is from 1906; as a verb from 1937. Road hog is attested from 1886; road rage is from 1988. Road map is from 1786; road trip is by 1950, originally of baseball teams. Old English had radwerig "weary of travelling."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 rad "riding expedition, journey, hostile incursion," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *raido (source also of 古弗里西语 red "ride," 古撒克逊语 reda, Middle 荷兰语 rede, 古高地德语 reita "foray, raid"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *reidh- "to ride" （参见 ride （动）). Also related to raid （名）. In 中古英语, "a riding, a journey;" 语义 "open way for traveling between two places" is 首见于 1590 年代. 义为 "narrow stretch of sheltered water" 始于 14 世纪初 (as in Hampton Roads in Virginia). 现代 spelling established 18 世纪 In 19 世纪 U.S. use, 常 意为 "railroad." On the road "travelling" 始于 1640 年代. Road test （名） 始于 1906 年; 作动词时 自 1937 年起. Road hog 见于 1886 年; road rage 始于 1988 年. Road map 始于 1786 年; road trip is 截至 1950 年, 原义为 of baseball teams. 古英语 had radwerig "weary of travelling."

example.en: The road between the two cities was closed due to heavy snowfall.
example.zh: 由于大雪，两个城市之间的道路被封闭了。

entries.etymology: Old English rarian "roar, wail, lament, bellow, cry," probably of imitative origin (compare Middle Dutch reeren, German röhren "to roar;" Sanskrit ragati "barks;" Lithuanian reju "to scold;" Old Church Slavonic revo "I roar;" Latin raucus "hoarse"). Related: Roared; roaring.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 rarian "roar, wail, lament, bellow, cry," 可能 of imitative origin (对比 Middle 荷兰语 reeren, 德语 röhren "to roar;" 梵语 ragati "barks;" Lithuanian reju "to scold;" Old Church Slavonic revo "I roar;" 拉丁语 raucus "hoarse"). 同源词：Roared; roaring.

example.en: The crowd let out a roar of approval when the goal was scored.
example.zh: 进球时，人群发出一阵欢呼的咆哮声。

entries.etymology:
late 13c., "to cook by dry heat," from Old French rostir "to roast, burn" (Modern French rôtir), from Frankish *hraustjan (cognate with Old High German rosten, German rösten, Middle Dutch roosten "to roast"), originally "cook on a grate or gridiron," related to Germanic words meaning "gridiron, grate;" such as German Rost, Middle Dutch roost.

Intransitive sense "be very hot, be exposed to great heat" is from c. 1300. The meaning "make fun of in an affectionate way" is from 1710. From the same source as roster. Related: Roasted; roasting. Roast beef first recorded 1630s (French rosbif is from English).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "to cook by dry heat," 源自 古法语 rostir "to roast, burn" (现代法语 rôtir), 源自 Frankish *hraustjan (与 … 同源 古高地德语 rosten, 德语 rösten, Middle 荷兰语 roosten "to roast"), 原义为 "cook on a grate or gridiron," related to 日耳曼语 words 意为 "gridiron, grate;" such as 德语 Rost, Middle 荷兰语 roost. Intransitive sense "be very hot, be exposed to great heat" 始于 约 1300 年. The 意为 "make fun of in an affectionate way" 始于 1710 年. From the same source as roster. 同源词：Roasted; roasting. Roast beef 首见于 1630 年代 (法语 rosbif 始于 English).

entries.etymology: late 12c., from Old French rober "rob, steal, pillage, ransack, rape," from West Germanic *rauba "booty" (source also of Old High German roubon "to rob," roub "spoil, plunder;" Old English reafian, source of the reave in bereave), from Proto-Germanic *raubon "to rob," from PIE *reup-, *reub- "to snatch" (see rip (v.)).To rob the cradle is attested from 1864 in reference to drafting young men in the American Civil War; by 1949 in reference to seductions or romantic relationships with younger persons. Related: Robbed; robbing.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 rober "rob, steal, pillage, ransack, rape," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *rauba "booty" (source also of 古高地德语 roubon "to rob," roub "spoil, plunder;" 古英语 reafian, source of the reave in bereave), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *raubon "to rob," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *reup-, *reub- "to snatch" （参见 rip （动）).To rob the cradle 见于 1864 年 in reference to drafting young men in the American Civil War; 截至 1949 年 in reference to seductions or romantic relationships with younger persons. 同源词：Robbed; robbing.

example.en: Two masked men tried to rob the bank in broad daylight.
example.zh: 两名蒙面男子企图在光天化日之下抢劫这家银行。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French roberie "robbery, theft," from rober "to rob" (see rob).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 roberie "robbery, theft," 源自 rober "to rob" （参见 rob).

example.en: The bank robbery was caught on camera and the suspect was arrested within hours.
example.zh: 银行抢劫案被摄像头拍下，嫌疑人在数小时内被逮捕。

entries.etymology: 1923, from English translation of 1920 play "R.U.R." ("Rossum's Universal Robots"), by Karel Capek (1890-1938), from Czech robotnik "slave," from robota "forced labor, compulsory service, drudgery," from robotiti "to work, drudge," from an Old Czech source akin to Old Church Slavonic rabota "servitude," from rabu "slave," from Old Slavic *orbu-, from PIE *orbh- "pass from one status to another" (see orphan). The Slavic word thus is a cousin to German Arbeit "work" (Old High German arabeit). According to Rawson the word was popularized by Karel Capek's play, "but was coined by his brother Josef (the two often collaborated), who used it initially in a short story."
entries.etymologyZh: 1923 年, 源自 English translation of 1920 年 play "R.U.R." ("Rossum's Universal Robots"), by Karel Capek (1890 年-1938 年), 源自 Czech robotnik "slave," 源自 robota "forced labor, compulsory service, drudgery," 源自 robotiti "to work, drudge," 源自 an Old Czech source akin to Old Church Slavonic rabota "servitude," 源自 rabu "slave," 源自 Old Slavic *orbu-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *orbh- "pass from one status to another" （参见 orphan). The Slavic word thus is a cousin to 德语 Arbeit "work" (古高地德语 arabeit). According to Rawson the word was popularized by Karel Capek's play, "but was coined by his brother Josef (the two often collaborated), who used it initially in a short story."

entries.etymology: 1540s, from Middle French robuste (14c.) and directly from Latin robustus "strong and hardy," literally "as strong as oak," originally "oaken," from robur, robus "hard timber, strength," also "a special kind of oak," named for its reddish heartwood, from Latin ruber "red" (related to robigo "rust"), from PIE *reudh- (see red (adj.1)). Related: Robustly; robustness. Robustious (1540s) was a common form in 17c. (see "Hamlet" iii.2); it fell from use by mid-18c., but was somewhat revived by mid-19c. antiquarian writers.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, 源自 中古法语 robuste (14 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 robustus "strong and hardy," 字面义为 "as strong as oak," 原义为 "oaken," 源自 robur, robus "hard timber, strength," also "a special kind of oak," named for its reddish heartwood, 源自 拉丁语 ruber "red" (related to robigo "rust"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *reudh- （参见 red (adj.1)). 同源词：Robustly; robustness. Robustious (1540 年代) was a common form in 17 世纪 （参见 "Hamlet" iii.2); it fell 源自 use by 18 世纪中期, but was somewhat revived by 19 世纪中期 antiquarian writers.

example.en: The athlete maintained a robust physique through daily training.
example.zh: 这名运动员通过每日训练保持着强健的体魄。

entries.etymology: "to spring like a rocket," 1860, from rocket (n.2). Earlier "to attack with rockets" (1799). Related: Rocketed; rocketing.
entries.etymologyZh: "to spring like a rocket," 1860 年, 源自 rocket (n.2). Earlier "to attack with rockets" (1799 年). 同源词：Rocketed; rocketing.

example.en: The space agency launched a rocket carrying supplies to the station.
example.zh: 航天局发射了一枚运送补给品到空间站的火箭。

entries.etymology:
Old English rodd "a rod, pole," which is probably cognate with Old Norse rudda "club," from Proto-Germanic *rudd- "stick, club," from PIE *reudh- "to clear land."

As a long, tapering elastic pole for fishing, from mid-15c. Figurative sense of "offshoot" (mid-15c.) led to Biblical meaning "scion, tribe." As an instrument of punishment, attested from mid-12c.; also used figuratively for "any sort of correction or punishment," but the basic notion is of beating someone with a stick.

As a unit of measure (5½ yards or 16½ feet, also called perch or pole) first attested mid-15c., from the stick used to measure it off. As a measure of area, "a square perch," from late 15c., the usual measure in brickwork. Meaning "light-sensitive cell in a retina" is from 1866, so-called for its shape. Slang meaning "penis" is recorded from 1902; that of "gun, revolver" is from 1903.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 rodd "a rod, pole," which is 可能 与 … 同源 古北欧语 rudda "club," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *rudd- "stick, club," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *reudh- "to clear land." 作为 long, tapering elastic pole for fishing, 源自 15 世纪中期 Figurative 语义 "offshoot" (15 世纪中期) led to Biblical 意为 "scion, tribe." 作为 instrument of punishment, attested 源自 12 世纪中期; also used figuratively for "any sort of correction or punishment," but the basic notion is of beating someone with a stick. 作为 unit of measure (5½ yards or 16½ feet, also called perch or pole) 最早见于 15 世纪中期, 源自 stick used to measure it off. 作为 measure of area, "a square perch," 源自 15 世纪晚期, the usual measure in brickwork. 义为 "light-sensitive cell in a retina" 始于 1866 年, so-called for its shape. Slang 意为 "penis" 见于 1902 年; that of "gun, revolver" 始于 1903 年.

entries.etymology: "part or character one takes," c. 1600, from French rôle "part played by a person in life," literally "roll (of paper) on which an actor's part is written," from Old French rolle (see roll (n.)). Meaning "function performed characteristically by someone" is from 1875. In the social psychology sense from 1913. Role model first attested 1957.
entries.etymologyZh: "part or character one takes," 约 1600 年, 源自 法语 rôle "part played by a person in life," 字面义为 "roll (of paper) on which an actor's part is written," 源自 古法语 rolle （参见 roll （名）). 义为 "function performed characteristically by someone" 始于 1875 年. example.en: Teachers play a vital role in shaping the critical thinking skills of young students.
example.zh: 教师在培养年轻学生的批判性思维能力方面扮演着至关重要的角色。

entries.definition: v.滚动，转动；卷，绕 n. 卷，卷状物，面包卷；名册， 名单
entries.etymology:
c. 1300 "turn over and over, move by rotating" (intransitive); late 14c. as "to move (something) by turning it over and over;" from Old French roeller "roll, wheel round" (Modern French rouler), from Medieval Latin rotulare, from Latin rotula, diminutive of rota "wheel" (see rotary). Related: Rolled; rolling.

Of sounds (such as thunder) somehow suggestive of a rolling ball, 1590s; of a drum from 1680s. Of eyes, from late 14c. Of a movie camera, "to start filming," from 1938. Sense of "rob a stuporous drunk" is from 1873, from the action required to get to his pockets. To roll up "gather, congregate" is from 1861, originally Australian. To be on a roll is from 1976. To roll with the punches is a metaphor from boxing (1940). Heads will roll is a Hitlerism:

To roll up "gather, congregate" 始于 1861 年, 原义为 Australian. To be on a roll 始于 1976 年. To roll with the punches is a metaphor 源自 boxing (1940 年). Heads will roll is a Hitlerism:

example.en: The children watched the ball roll slowly down the hill.
example.zh: 孩子们看着球慢慢地滚下山坡。

entries.definition: a.罗马的，罗马数字的 n. 罗马人
entries.etymology:
Old English, from Latin Romanus "of Rome, Roman," from Roma "Rome" (see Rome). The adjective is c. 1300, from Old French Romain. The Old English adjective was romanisc, which yielded Middle English Romanisshe.

As a type of numeral (usually contrasted to Arabic) it is attested from 1728; as a type of lettering (based on the upright style typical of Roman inscriptions, contrasted to Gothic, or black letter, and italic) it is recorded from 1510s. Roman nose is from 1620s. Roman candle as a type of fireworks is recorded from 1834. Roman Catholic is attested from c. 1600, a conciliatory formation from the time of the Spanish Match, replacing Romanist, Romish which by that time had the taint of insult in Protestant England.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语, 源自 拉丁语 Romanus "of Rome, Roman," 源自 Roma "Rome" （参见 Rome). The 形容词 is 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 Romain. The 古英语 形容词 was romanisc, which yielded 中古英语 Romanisshe. 作为 type of numeral (通常 contrasted to 阿拉伯语) it 见于 1728 年; 作为 type of lettering (based on the upright style typical of Roman inscriptions, contrasted to Gothic，或black letter, and italic) it 见于 1510 年代. Roman nose 始于 1620 年代. Roman candle 作为 type of fireworks 见于 1834 年. Roman Catholic 见于 约 1600 年, a conciliatory formation 源自 time of the 西班牙语 Match, replacing Romanist, Romish which by that time had the taint of insult in Protestant England.

definitionLines: n. 浪漫史；冒险故事；传奇
entries.definition: n. 浪漫史；冒险故事；传奇
entries.etymology: mid-14c., "French; in the vernacular language of France" (contrasted to Latin), from Old French romanz "French; vernacular," from Late Latin Romanice, from Latin Romanicus (see Roman). Extended 1610s to other modern tongues derived from Latin (Spanish, Italian, etc.); thus "pertaining to the languages which arose out of the Latin language of the provinces of Rome." Compare romance (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "French; in the vernacular language of France" (contrasted to 拉丁语), 源自 古法语 romanz "French; vernacular," 源自 晚期拉丁语 Romanice, 源自 拉丁语 Romanicus （参见 Roman). Extended 1610 年代 to other modern tongues derived 源自 拉丁语 (西班牙语, 意大利语, etc.); thus "pertaining to the languages which arose out of the Latin language of the provinces of Rome." 对比 romance （名）.

example.en: Their romance began with a chance meeting on a train.
example.zh: 他们的浪漫恋情始于一次在火车上的偶遇。

definitionLines: a. 浪漫的，传奇式的；不切实际 的，好幻想的
entries.definition: a. 浪漫的，传奇式的；不切实际 的，好幻想的
entries.etymology:
1650s, "of the nature of a literary romance," from French romantique, from Middle French romant "a romance," oblique case of Old French romanz "verse narrative" (see romance (n.)).

As a literary style, opposed to classical since before 1812; in music, from 1885. Meaning "characteristic of an ideal love affair" (such as usually formed the subject of literary romances) is from 1660s. Meaning "having a love affair as a theme" is from 1960. Related: Romantical (1670s); romantically. Compare romanticism.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, "of the nature of a literary romance," 源自 法语 romantique, 源自 中古法语 romant "a romance," oblique case of 古法语 romanz "verse narrative" （参见 romance （名）). 作为 literary style, opposed to classical 自 1812 年之前; in music, 自 1885 年起. 义为 "characteristic of an ideal love affair" (such as 通常 formed the subject of literary romances) 始于 1660 年代. 义为 "having a love affair as a theme" 始于 1960 年. 同源词：Romantical (1670 年代); romantically. 对比 romanticism.

example.en: They shared a romantic candlelit dinner by the sea.
example.zh: 他们在海边共享了一顿浪漫的烛光晚餐。

entries.etymology:
Old English hrof "roof, ceiling, top, summit; heaven, sky," also figuratively, "highest point of something," from Proto-Germanic *khrofam (source also of Old Frisian rhoof "roof," Middle Dutch roof, rouf "cover, roof," Dutch roef "deckhouse, cabin, coffin-lid," Middle High German rof "penthouse," Old Norse hrof "boat shed").

No apparent connections outside Germanic. "English alone has retained the word in a general sense, for which the other languages use forms corresponding to OE. þæc thatch" [OED]. Roof of the mouth is from late Old English. Raise the roof "create an uproar" is attested from 1860, originally in U.S. Southern dialect.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 hrof "roof, ceiling, top, summit; heaven, sky," also figuratively, "highest point of something," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *khrofam (source also of 古弗里西语 rhoof "roof," Middle 荷兰语 roof, rouf "cover, roof," 荷兰语 roef "deckhouse, cabin, coffin-lid," Middle High 德语 rof "penthouse," 古北欧语 hrof "boat shed"). No apparent connections outside 日耳曼语. "English alone has retained the word in a general sense, for which the other languages use forms corresponding to OE. þæc thatch" [OED]. Roof of the mouth 始于 late 古英语. Raise the roof "create an uproar" 见于 1860 年, 原义为 in U.S. Southern dialect.

example.en: Heavy snow had damaged the roof of the old barn.

entries.etymology:
Old English rum "space" (extent or time); "scope, opportunity," from Proto-Germanic *ruman (source also of Old Norse, Old Saxon, Old High German, Gothic rum, German Raum "space," Dutch ruim "hold of a ship, nave"), nouns formed from Germanic adjective *ruma- "roomy, spacious," from PIE root *reue- (1) "to open; space" (source also of Avestan ravah- "space," Latin rus "open country," Old Irish roi, roe "plain field," Old Church Slavonic ravinu "level," Russian ravnina "a plain"). Old English also had a frequent adjective rum "roomy, wide, long, spacious."

Original sense preserved in make room "clear space for oneself" (late 14c.); meaning "chamber, cabin" first recorded early 14c. as a nautical term, and first applied mid-15c. to chambers within houses. The Old English word for this was cofa, ancestor of cove. Room-service is attested from 1913; room-temperature from 1879. Roomth "sufficient space" (1530s) now is obsolete.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 rum "space" (extent or time); "scope, opportunity," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *ruman (source also of 古北欧语, 古撒克逊语, 古高地德语, Gothic rum, 德语 Raum "space," 荷兰语 ruim "hold of a ship, nave"), nouns formed 源自 日耳曼语 形容词 *ruma- "roomy, spacious," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *reue- (1) "to open; space" (source also of Avestan ravah- "space," 拉丁语 rus "open country," Old 爱尔兰语 roi, roe "plain field," Old Church Slavonic ravinu "level," 俄语 ravnina "a plain"). 古英语 also had a frequent 形容词 rum "roomy, wide, long, spacious." Original sense preserved in make room "clear space for oneself" (14 世纪晚期); 意为 "chamber, cabin" 首见于 14 世纪初 作为 nautical term, and first applied 15 世纪中期 to chambers within houses. The 古英语 word for this was cofa, ancestor of cove. Room-service 见于 1913 年; room-temperature 自 1879 年起. Roomth "sufficient space" (1530 年代) 现在 is 已废.

entries.etymology:
"underground part of a plant," late Old English rot, from a Scandinavian source akin to Old Norse rot "root," figuratively "cause, origin," from Proto-Germanic *wrot (source also of Old English wyrt "root, herb, plant," Old High German wurz, German Wurz "a plant," Gothic waurts "a root," with characteristic Scandinavian loss of -w- before -r-), from PIE *wrad- (see radish (n.), and compare wort). The usual Old English words for "root" were wyrttruma and wyrtwala.

Figurative use is from c. 1200. Of teeth, hair, etc., from early 13c. Mathematical sense is from 1550s. Philological sense from 1520s. Slang meaning "penis" is recorded from 1846. In African-American vernacular use, "a spell effected by magical properties of roots," 1935. To take root is from 1530s. Root beer, made from the extracts of various roots, first recorded 1841, American English; root doctor is from 1821. Root cap is from 1875.

entries.etymology:
Old English rap "rope, cord, cable," from Proto-Germanic *raipaz (source also of Old Norse reip, West Frisian reap, Middle Dutch, Dutch reep "rope," Old Frisian silrap "shoe-thong," Gothic skauda-raip "shoe-lace," Old High German, German reif "ring, hoop"). Technically, only cordage above one inch in circumference and below 10 (bigger-around than that is a cable). Nautical use varies. Finnish raippa "hoop, rope, twig" is a Germanic loan-word.

To know the ropes (1840, Dana) originally is a seaman's term. Phrase on the ropes "defeated" is attested from 1924, a figurative extension from the fight ring, where ropes figure from 1829. To be at the end of (one's) rope "out of resources and options" is first attested 1680s. Formerly also in many slang and extended uses related to punishment by hanging, such as John Roper's window "a noose," rope-ripe "deserving to be hanged," both 16c. To give someone (enough) rope (to hang himself) is from 1650s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 rap "rope, cord, cable," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *raipaz (source also of 古北欧语 reip, West Frisian reap, Middle 荷兰语, 荷兰语 reep "rope," 古弗里西语 silrap "shoe-thong," Gothic skauda-raip "shoe-lace," 古高地德语, 德语 reif "ring, hoop"). Technically, only cordage above one inch in circumference and below 10 (bigger-around than that is a cable). Nautical use varies. Finnish raippa "hoop, rope, twig" is a 日耳曼语 loan-word. To know the ropes (1840 年, Dana) 原义为 is a seaman's term. Phrase on the ropes "defeated" is attested from 1924, a figurative extension from the fight ring, where ropes figure from 1829. To be at the end of (one's) rope "out of resources and options" is 最早见于 1680 年代. Formerly also in many 俚语 and extended uses related to punishment by hanging, such as John Roper's window "a noose," rope-ripe "deserving to be hanged," both 16 世纪 To give someone (enough) rope (to hang himself) 始于 1650 年代.

entries.etymology:
Old English ruh "rough, coarse (of cloth); hairy, shaggy; untrimmed, uncultivated," from West Germanic *rukhwaz "shaggy, hairy, rough" (source also of Middle Dutch ruuch, Dutch ruig, Old High German ruher, German rauh), from Proto-Germanic *rukhaz, from PIE *reue- (2) "to smash, knock down, tear out, dig up" (source also of Sanskrit ruksah "rough;" Latin ruga "wrinkle," ruere "to rush, fall violently, collapse," ruina "a collapse;" Lithuanian raukas "wrinkle," rukti "to shrink").

The original -gh- sound was guttural, as in Scottish loch. Sense of "approximate" is first recorded c. 1600. Of places, "riotous, disorderly, characterized by violent action," 1863. Rough draft is from 1690s. Rough-and-ready is from 1810, originally military; rough-and-tumble (1810) is from a style of free-fighting.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 ruh "rough, coarse (of cloth); hairy, shaggy; untrimmed, uncultivated," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *rukhwaz "shaggy, hairy, rough" (source also of Middle 荷兰语 ruuch, 荷兰语 ruig, 古高地德语 ruher, 德语 rauh), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *rukhaz, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *reue- (2) "to smash, knock down, tear out, dig up" (source also of 梵语 ruksah "rough;" 拉丁语 ruga "wrinkle," ruere "to rush, fall violently, collapse," ruina "a collapse;" Lithuanian raukas "wrinkle," rukti "to shrink"). The original -gh- sound was guttural, as in 苏格兰语 loch. 义为 "approximate" is 首见于 约 1600 年. Of places, "riotous, disorderly, characterized by violent action," 1863 年. Rough draft 始于 1690 年代. Rough-and-ready 始于 1810 年, 原义为 military; rough-and-tumble (1810 年) 始于 a style of free-fighting.

entries.etymology:
late 13c., from Anglo-French rounde, Old French roont (12c., Modern French rond), probably originally *redond, from Vulgar Latin *retundus (source also of Provençal redon, Spanish redondo, Old Italian ritondo), from Latin rotundus "like a wheel, circular, round," related to rota "wheel" (see rotary).

As an adverb from c. 1300; as a preposition from c. 1600. In many uses it is a shortened form of around. The French word is the source of Middle Dutch ront (Dutch rond), Middle High German runt (German rund) and similar Germanic words.

Of numbers from mid-14c., from earlier sense "full, complete, brought to completion" (mid-14c., notion of symmetry extended to that of completeness). First record of round trip is from 1844, originally of railways. Round heels attested from 1926, in reference to incompetent boxers, 1927 in reference to loose women, in either case implying an inability to avoid ending up flat on one's back.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 rounde, 古法语 roont (12 世纪, 现代法语 rond), 可能 原义为 *redond, 源自 通俗拉丁语 *retundus (source also of Provençal redon, 西班牙语 redondo, Old 意大利语 ritondo), 源自 拉丁语 rotundus "like a wheel, circular, round," related to rota "wheel" （参见 rotary). 作为 副词 源自 约 1300 年; 作为 preposition 源自 约 1600 年. In many uses it is a shortened form of around. The 法语 word is the source of Middle 荷兰语 ront (荷兰语 rond), Middle High 德语 runt (德语 rund) and similar 日耳曼语 words. Of numbers 源自 14 世纪中期, 源自 earlier sense "full, complete, brought to completion" (14 世纪中期, 概念 symmetry extended to that of completeness). First record of round trip 始于 1844 年, 原义为 of railways. Round heels attested 自 1926 年起, in reference to incompetent boxers, 1927 年 in reference to loose women, in either case implying an inability to avoid ending up flat on one's back.

entries.etymology: early 13c., from Old French rute "road, way, path" (12c.), from Latin rupta (via) "(a road) opened by force," from rupta, fem. past participle of rumpere "to break" (see rupture (n.)). Sense of "fixed or regular course for carrying things" (as in mail route) is 1792, an extension of the meaning "customary path of animals" (early 15c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, 源自 古法语 rute "road, way, path" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 rupta (经由) "(a road) opened by force," 源自 rupta, fem. 为 … 的过去分词 rumpere "to break" （参见 rupture （名）). 义为 "fixed or regular course for carrying things" (as in mail route) is 1792 年, an extension of the 意为 "customary path of animals" (15 世纪初).

entries.etymology:
mid-13c., "fit for a king;" late 14c., "pertaining to a king," from Old French roial "royal, regal; splendid, magnificent" (12c., Modern French royal), from Latin regalis "of a king, kingly, royal, regal," from rex (genitive regis) "king" (see rex). Meaning "thorough, total" attested from 1940s; that of "splendid, first-rate" from 1853. 

Battle royal (1670s) preserves the French custom of putting the adjective after the noun (as in attorney general); the sense of the adjective here is "on a grand scale" (compare pair-royal "three of a kind in cards or dice," c. 1600). The Royal Oak was a tree in Boscobel in Shropshire in which Charles II hid himself during flight after the Battle of Worcester in 1651. Sprigs of oak were worn to commemorate his restoration in 1660.

Battle royal (1670 年代) preserves the 法语 custom of putting the 形容词 after the 名词 (as in attorney general); the 语义 the 形容词 here is "on a grand scale" (对比 pair-royal "three of a kind in cards or dice," 约 1600 年). entries.etymology:
early 14c., transitive and intransitive, of uncertain origin, perhaps related to East Frisian rubben "to scratch, rub," and Low German rubbeling "rough, uneven," or similar words in Scandinavian (compare Danish rubbe "to rub, scrub," Norwegian rubba), of uncertain origin. Related: Rubbed; rubbing.

To rub (someone) the wrong way is from 1853; probably the notion is of cats' fur. To rub noses in greeting as a sign of friendship (attested from 1822) formerly was common among Eskimos, Maoris, and some other Pacific Islanders. Rub out "obliterate" is from 1560s; underworld slang sense of "kill" is recorded from 1848, American English. Rub off "remove by rubbing" is from 1590s; meaning "have an influence" is recorded from 1959.

To rub (someone) the wrong way 始于 1853 年; 可能 the notion is of cats' fur. To rub noses in greeting 作为 sign of friendship (attested 自 1822 年起) formerly was common among Eskimos, Maoris, and some other Pacific Islanders. Rub out "obliterate" 始于 1560 年代; underworld 俚语 语义 "kill" 见于 1848 年, American English. Rub off "remove by rubbing" 始于 1590 年代; 意为 "have an influence" 见于 1959 年.

entries.etymology: "thing that rubs" (a brush, cloth, etc.), 1530s, agent noun from rub (v.). The meaning "elastic substance from tropical plants" (short for India rubber) first recorded 1788, introduced to Europe 1744 by Charles Marie de la Condamine, so called because it originally was used as an eraser.Meaning "overshoe made of rubber" is 1842, American English; slang sense of "condom" is by 1930s. Sense of "deciding match" in a game or contest is 1590s, of unknown signification, and perhaps an entirely separate word. Rubber stamp (n.) is from 1881; figurative sense of "institution whose power is formal but not real" is from 1919; the verb in this sense is from 1934. Rubber cement is attested from 1856 (from 1823 as India-rubber cement). Rubber check (one that "bounces") is from 1927.

entries.etymology: c. 1400, robous, from Anglo-French rubouses (late 14c.), of unknown origin. No apparent cognates in Old French; apparently somehow related to rubble (see OED). Spelling with -ish is from late 15c. The verb sense of "disparage, criticize harshly" is first attested 1953 in Australian and New Zealand slang. Related: Rubbished; rubbishing.

entries.etymology: 1550s, "coarse fabric," of Scandinavian origin; compare Norwegian dialectal rugga "coarse coverlet," from Old Norse rogg "shaggy tuft," from Proto-Germanic *rawwa-, perhaps related to rag (n.) and rough (adj.). Sense evolved to "coverlet, wrap" (1590s), then "mat for the floor" (1808). Meaning "toupee" is theater slang from 1940. Cut a rug "dance" is slang first attested 1942. To sweep (something) under the rug in the figurative sense is from 1954. Figurative expression pull the rug out from under (someone) "suddenly deprive of important support" is from 1936, American English. Earlier in same sense was cut the grass under (one's) feet (1580s).

Sense evolved to "coverlet, wrap" (1590 年代), 之后 "mat for the floor" (1808 年). 义为 "toupee" is theater 俚语 自 1940 年起. Cut a rug "dance" is 俚语 最早见于 1942 年. To sweep (something) under the rug in the figurative sense 始于 1954 年. Figurative expression pull the rug out 源自 under (someone) "suddenly deprive of important support" 始于 1936 年, American English. Earlier in same sense was cut the grass under (one's) feet (1580 年代).

entries.etymology: late 14c., "act of giving way and falling down," from Old French ruine "a collapse" (14c.), and directly from Latin ruina "a collapse, a rushing down, a tumbling down" (source also of Spanish ruina, Italian rovina), related to ruere "to rush, fall violently, collapse," from PIE *reue- (2) "to smash, knock down, tear out, dig up" (see rough (adj.)). Meaning "complete destruction of anything" is from 1670s. Ruins "remains of a decayed building or town" is from mid-15c.; the same sense was in the Latin plural noun.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "act of giving way and falling down," 源自 古法语 ruine "a collapse" (14 世纪), and 直接源自 拉丁语 ruina "a collapse, a rushing down, a tumbling down" (source also of 西班牙语 ruina, 意大利语 rovina), related to ruere "to rush, fall violently, collapse," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *reue- (2) "to smash, knock down, tear out, dig up" （参见 rough （形）). 义为 "complete destruction of anything" 始于 1670 年代. Ruins "remains of a decayed building or town" 始于 15 世纪中期; the same sense was in the 拉丁语 plural 名词.

definitionLines: n. 规则，规章，规律；惯例，常规
entries.definition: n./v.统治，支配 n. 规则，规章，规律；惯例，常规 v. 裁决，裁定
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "principle or maxim governing conduct, formula to which conduct must be conformed" from Old French riule, Norman reule "rule, custom, (religious) order" (in Modern French partially re-Latinized as règle), from Vulgar Latin *regula, from Latin regula "straight stick, bar, ruler;" figuratively "a pattern, a model," related to regere "to rule, straighten, guide" (see regal). Replaced Old English wealdan.

Meaning "regulation governing play of a game, etc." is from 1690s. Phrase rule of thumb first attested 1690s. Rule of law "supremacy of impartial and well-defined laws to any individual's power" is from 1883. Meaning "strip used for making straight lines or measuring" is recorded from mid-14c. Typography sense is attested from 1680s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "principle or maxim governing conduct, formula to which conduct must be conformed" 源自 古法语 riule, Norman reule "rule, custom, (religious) order" (in 现代法语 partially re-Latinized as règle), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *regula, 源自 拉丁语 regula "straight stick, bar, ruler;" figuratively "a pattern, a model," related to regere "to rule, straighten, guide" （参见 regal). Replaced 古英语 wealdan. 义为 "regulation governing play of a game, etc." 始于 1690 年代. Phrase rule of thumb 最早见于 1690 年代. Rule of law "supremacy of impartial and well-defined laws to any individual's power" 始于 1883 年. 义为 "strip used for making straight lines or measuring" 见于 14 世纪中期 Typography sense 见于 1680 年代.

entries.etymology:
the modern verb is a merger of two related Old English words, in both of which the first letters sometimes switched places. The first is intransitive rinnan, irnan "to run, flow, run together" (past tense ran, past participle runnen), cognate with Middle Dutch runnen, Old Saxon, Old High German, Gothic rinnan, German rinnen "to flow, run."

The second is Old English transitive weak verb ærnan, earnan "ride, run to, reach, gain by running" (probably a metathesis of *rennan), from Proto-Germanic *rannjanan, causative of the root *ren- "to run." This is cognate with Old Saxon renian, Old High German rennen, German rennen, Gothic rannjan.

Both are from PIE *ri-ne-a-, nasalized form of root *reie- "to flow, run"  (see Rhine).

Of streams, etc., from c. 1200; of machinery, from 1560s. Meaning "be in charge of" is first attested 1861, originally American English. Meaning "seek office in an election" is from 1826, American English. Phrase run for it "take flight" is attested from 1640s. Many figurative uses are from horseracing or hunting (such as to run (something) into the ground, 1836, American English).

To run across "meet" is attested from 1855, American English. To run short "exhaust one's supply" is from 1752; to run out of in the same sense is from 1713. To run around with "consort with" is from 1887. Run away "flee in the face of danger" is from late 14c. To run late is from 1954.
entries.etymologyZh: the modern 动词 is a merger of two related 古英语 words, in both of which the first letters 有时 switched places. The first is intransitive rinnan, irnan "to run, flow, run together" (past tense ran, past participle runnen), 与 … 同源 Middle 荷兰语 runnen, 古撒克逊语, 古高地德语, Gothic rinnan, 德语 rinnen "to flow, run." The second is 古英语 transitive weak 动词 ærnan, earnan "ride, run to, reach, gain by running" (可能 a metathesis of *rennan), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *rannjanan, 为 … 的使役形式 the root *ren- "to run." This is 与 … 同源 古撒克逊语 renian, 古高地德语 rennen, 德语 rennen, Gothic rannjan. Both 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *ri-ne-a-, nasalized form of root *reie- "to flow, run" （参见 Rhine). Of streams, etc., 源自 约 1200 年; of machinery, 源自 1560 年代. 义为 "be in charge of" is 最早见于 1861 年, 原义为 American English. 义为 "seek office in an election" 始于 1826 年, American English. Phrase run for it "take flight" 见于 1640 年代. Many figurative uses 始于 horseracing or hunting (such as to run (something) into the ground, 1836 年, American English). Run away "flee in the face of danger" 始于 14 世纪晚期 To run late 始于 1954 年.

entries.etymology:
mid-14c. (implied in rushing), "to drive back or down," from Anglo-French russher, from Old French ruser "to dodge, repel" (see ruse). Meaning "to do something quickly" is from 1650s; transitive sense of "to hurry up (someone or something)" is from 1850. U.S. Football sense originally was in rugby (1857).

Fraternity/sorority sense is from 1896 (originally it was what the fraternity did to the student); from 1899 as a noun in this sense. Earlier it was a name on U.S. campuses for various tests of strength or athletic skill between freshmen and sophomores as classes (1860).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期 (implied in rushing), "to drive back or down," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 russher, 源自 古法语 ruser "to dodge, repel" （参见 ruse). 义为 "to do something quickly" 始于 1650 年代; transitive 语义 "to hurry up (someone or something)" 始于 1850 年. U.S. Football sense 原义为 was in rugby (1857 年). Fraternity/sorority sense 始于 1896 年 (原义为 it was what the fraternity did to the student); 自 1899 年起 作名词时 in this sense. Earlier it was a name on U.S. campuses for various tests of strength or athletic skill between freshmen and sophomores as classes (1860 年).

entries.etymology:
"red oxide of iron," Old English rust "rust; moral canker," related to rudu "redness," from Proto-Germanic *rusta- (source also of Frisian rust, Old High German and German rost, Middle Dutch ro(e)st), from PIE *reudh-s-to- (source also of Lithuanian rustas "brownish," rudeti "to rust;" Latin robigo, Old Church Slavonic ruzda "rust"), from root *reudh- "red" (see red (adj.1)).

As a plant disease, attested from mid-14c. Rust Belt "decayed urban industrial areas of mid-central U.S." (1984) was popularized, if not coined, by Walter Mondale's presidential campaign.

definitionLines: a.神圣的；庄严的；宗教的； 神的
entries.definition: a.神圣的；庄严的；宗教的； 神的
entries.etymology:
late 14c., past participle adjective from obsolete verb sacren "to make holy" (c. 1200), from Old French sacrer "consecrate, anoint, dedicate" (12c.) or directly from Latin sacrare "to make sacred, consecrate; hold sacred; immortalize; set apart, dedicate," from sacer (genitive sacri) "sacred, dedicated, holy, accursed," from Old Latin saceres, from PIE root *sak- "to sanctify." Buck groups it with Oscan sakrim, Umbrian sacra and calls it "a distinctive Italic group, without any clear outside connections." Related: Sacredness.

Nasalized form is sancire "make sacred, confirm, ratify, ordain." An Old English word for "sacred" was godcund. Sacred cow "object of Hindu veneration," is from 1891; figurative sense of "one who must not be criticized" is first recorded 1910, reflecting Western views of Hinduism. Sacred Heart "the heart of Jesus as an object of religious veneration" is from 1765.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, past participle 形容词 源自 已废 动词 sacren "to make holy" (约 1200 年), 源自 古法语 sacrer "consecrate, anoint, dedicate" (12 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 sacrare "to make sacred, consecrate; hold sacred; immortalize; set apart, dedicate," 源自 sacer (属格 sacri) "sacred, dedicated, holy, accursed," 源自 Old 拉丁语 saceres, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sak- "to sanctify." Buck groups it with Oscan sakrim, Umbrian sacra and calls it "a distinctive Italic group, without any clear outside connections." 同源词：Sacredness. Nasalized form is sancire "make sacred, confirm, ratify, ordain." An 古英语 word for "sacred" was godcund. Sacred cow "object of Hindu veneration," 始于 1891 年; figurative 语义 "one who must not be criticized" is 首见于 1910 年, reflecting Western views of Hinduism. Sacred Heart "the heart of Jesus as an object of religious veneration" 始于 1765 年.

definitionLines: n. 牺牲，牺牲品；祭品，供物
entries.definition: n. 牺牲，牺牲品；祭品，供物 v. 献祭，牺牲
entries.etymology:
late 13c., "offering of something (especially a life) to a deity as an act of propitiation or homage;" mid-14c., "that which is offered in sacrifice," from Old French sacrifise "sacrifice, offering" (12c.), from Latin sacrificium, from sacrificus "performing priestly functions or sacrifices," from sacra "sacred rites" (properly neuter plural of sacer "sacred;" see sacred) + root of facere "to do, perform" (see factitious).

Latin sacrificium is glossed in Old English by ansegdniss. Sense of "act of giving up one thing for another; something given up for the sake of another" is first recorded 1590s. Baseball sense first attested 1880.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "offering of something (especially a life) to a deity as an act of propitiation or homage;" 14 世纪中期, "that which is offered in sacrifice," 源自 古法语 sacrifise "sacrifice, offering" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 sacrificium, 源自 sacrificus "performing priestly functions or sacrifices," 源自 sacra "sacred rites" (properly neuter 为 … 的复数 sacer "sacred;" 参见 sacred) + root of facere "to do, perform" （参见 factitious). 拉丁语 sacrificium is glossed in 古英语 by ansegdniss. 义为 "act of giving up one thing for another; something given up for the sake of another" is 首见于 1590 年代. entries.etymology:
Old English sæd "sated, full, having had one's fill (of food, drink, fighting, etc.), weary of," from Proto-Germanic *sathaz (source also of Old Norse saðr, Middle Dutch sat, Dutch zad, Old High German sat, German satt, Gothic saþs "satiated, sated, full"), from PIE *seto- (source also of Latin satis "enough, sufficient," Greek hadros "thick, bulky," Old Church Slavonic sytu, Lithuanian sotus "satiated," Old Irish saith "satiety," sathach "sated"), from root *sa- "to satisfy" (source also of Sanskrit a-sinvan "insatiable").

Sense development passed through the meaning "heavy, ponderous" (i.e. "full" mentally or physically), and "weary, tired of" before emerging c. 1300 as "unhappy." An alternative course would be through the common Middle English sense of "steadfast, firmly established, fixed" (as in sad-ware "tough pewter vessels") and "serious" to "grave." In the main modern sense, it replaced Old English unrot, negative of rot "cheerful, glad."

Meaning "very bad" is from 1690s. Slang sense of "inferior, pathetic" is from 1899; sad sack is 1920s, popularized by World War II armed forces (specifically by cartoon character invented by Sgt. George Baker, 1942, and published in U.S. Armed Forces magazine "Yank"), probably a euphemistic shortening of common military slang phrase sad sack of shit.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sæd "sated, full, having had one's fill (of food, drink, fighting, etc.), weary of," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sathaz (source also of 古北欧语 saðr, Middle 荷兰语 sat, 荷兰语 zad, 古高地德语 sat, 德语 satt, Gothic saþs "satiated, sated, full"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *seto- (source also of 拉丁语 satis "enough, sufficient," 希腊语 hadros "thick, bulky," Old Church Slavonic sytu, Lithuanian sotus "satiated," Old 爱尔兰语 saith "satiety," sathach "sated"), 源自 root *sa- "to satisfy" (source also of 梵语 a-sinvan "insatiable"). Sense development passed through the 意为 "heavy, ponderous" (i.e. "full" mentally or physically), and "weary, tired of" before emerging 约 1300 年 as "unhappy." An alternative course would be through the common 中古英语 语义 "steadfast, firmly established, fixed" (as in sad-ware "tough pewter vessels") and "serious" to "grave." In the main modern sense, it replaced 古英语 unrot, negative of rot "cheerful, glad." 义为 "very bad" 始于 1690 年代. Slang 语义 "inferior, pathetic" 始于 1899 年; sad sack is 1920 年代, popularized by World War II armed forces (specifically by cartoon character invented by Sgt. George Baker, 1942 年, and published in U.S. Armed Forces magazine "Yank"), 可能 a euphemistic shortening of common military 俚语 phrase sad sack of shit.

entries.definition: a. 安全的，牢靠的 n. 保险箱
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "unscathed, unhurt, uninjured; free from danger or molestation, in safety, secure; saved spiritually, redeemed, not damned;" from Old French sauf "protected, watched-over; assured of salvation," from Latin salvus "uninjured, in good health, safe," related to salus "good health," saluber "healthful," all from PIE *solwos from root *sol- "whole" (source also of Latin solidus "solid," Sanskrit sarvah "uninjured, intact, whole," Avestan haurva- "uninjured, intact," Old Persian haruva-, Greek holos "whole").

As a quasi-preposition from c. 1300, on model of French and Latin cognates. From late 14c. as "rescued, delivered; protected; left alive, unkilled." Meaning "not exposed to danger" (of places) is attested from late 14c.; of actions, etc., "free from risk," first recorded 1580s. Meaning "sure, reliable, not a danger" is from c. 1600. Sense of "conservative, cautious" is from 1823. Paired alliteratively with sound (adj.) from late 14c. The noun safe-conduct (late 13c.) is from Old French sauf-conduit (13c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "unscathed, unhurt, uninjured; free from danger or molestation, in safety, secure; saved spiritually, redeemed, not damned;" 源自 古法语 sauf "protected, watched-over; assured of salvation," 源自 拉丁语 salvus "uninjured, in good health, safe," related to salus "good health," saluber "healthful," all 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *solwos 源自 root *sol- "whole" (source also of 拉丁语 solidus "solid," 梵语 sarvah "uninjured, intact, whole," Avestan haurva- "uninjured, intact," Old 波斯语 haruva-, 希腊语 holos "whole"). 作为 quasi-preposition 源自 约 1300 年, on model of 法语 and 拉丁语 cognates. From 14 世纪晚期 as "rescued, delivered; protected; left alive, unkilled." 义为 "not exposed to danger" (of places) 见于 14 世纪晚期; of actions, etc., "free from risk," 首见于 1580 年代. 义为 "sure, reliable, not a danger" 始于 约 1600 年. 义为 "conservative, cautious" 始于 1823 年. Paired alliteratively with sound （形） 源自 14 世纪晚期 The 名词 safe-conduct (13 世纪晚期) 始于 古法语 sauf-conduit (13 世纪).

example.en: Always wear a helmet to keep yourself safe while cycling.
example.zh: 骑自行车时一定要戴头盔以保证自身安全。

definitionLines: n. 保护；保卫；保护措施
entries.definition: n. 保护；保卫；保护措施 vt.保护，护卫
entries.etymology: late 14c., "protection, safety," from Middle French sauvegarde "safekeeping, safeguard" (13c.), from Old French salve, sauve (fem. of sauf; see safe (adj.)) + garde "a keeping" (see guard (n.)). Meaning "something that offers security from danger" is recorded from late 15c.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "protection, safety," 源自 中古法语 sauvegarde "safekeeping, safeguard" (13 世纪), 源自 古法语 salve, sauve (fem. of sauf; 参见 safe （形）) + garde "a keeping" （参见 guard （名）). 义为 "something that offers security from danger" 见于 15 世纪晚期

entries.etymology:
early 14c., from Old French sauvete "safety, safeguard; salvation; security, surety," earlier salvetet (11c., Modern French sauveté), from Medieval Latin salvitatem (nominative salvitas) "safety," from Latin salvus (see safe (adj.)). Meaning "trigger-lock on a gun" is attested from 1881.

As a North American football position, first recorded 1931. As a type of score against one's own team, 1881. Safety-valve, which diminishes the risk of explosion, is from 1797; figurative sense recorded from 1818. Safety-net in literal sense (in machinery) by 1916, later of aerial circus performances (1920s); figurative use by 1950. Safety-first as an accident-prevention slogan first recorded 1873.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, 源自 古法语 sauvete "safety, safeguard; salvation; security, surety," earlier salvetet (11 世纪, 现代法语 sauveté), 源自 中古拉丁语 salvitatem (主格 salvitas) "safety," 源自 拉丁语 salvus （参见 safe （形）). 义为 "trigger-lock on a gun" 见于 1881 年. 作为 North American football position, 首见于 1931 年. 作为 type of score against one's own team, 1881 年. Safety-valve, which diminishes the risk of explosion, 始于 1797 年; figurative sense recorded 自 1818 年起. Safety-net in literal sense (in machinery) 截至 1916 年, later of aerial circus performances (1920 年代); figurative use 截至 1950 年. Safety-first 作为 accident-prevention slogan 首见于 1873 年.

example.en: Wearing a helmet is essential for your safety while cycling on busy roads.
example.zh: 在繁忙道路上骑自行车时，戴头盔对人身安全至关重要。

entries.definition: n. 帆，航行 v. 航行，开航
entries.etymology: Old English segl "sail, veil, curtain," from Proto-Germanic *seglom (source also of Old Saxon, Swedish segel, Old Norse segl, Old Frisian seil, Dutch zeil, Old High German segal, German Segel), of obscure origin with no known cognates outside Germanic (Irish seol, Welsh hwyl "sail" are Germanic loan-words). In some sources (Klein, OED) referred to PIE root *sek- "to cut," as if meaning "a cut piece of cloth." To take the wind out of (someone's) sails (1888) is to deprive (someone) of the means of progress, especially by sudden and unexpected action, "as by one vessel sailing between the wind and another vessel," ["The Encyclopaedic Dictionary," 1888].
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 segl "sail, veil, curtain," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *seglom (source also of 古撒克逊语, Swedish segel, 古北欧语 segl, 古弗里西语 seil, 荷兰语 zeil, 古高地德语 segal, 德语 Segel), of obscure origin with no known cognates outside 日耳曼语 (爱尔兰语 seol, Welsh hwyl "sail" are 日耳曼语 loan-words). In some sources (Klein, OED) referred to 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sek- "to cut," as if 意为 "a cut piece of cloth." To take the wind out of (someone's) sails (1888 年) is to deprive (someone) of the means of progress, 尤指 by sudden and unexpected action, "as by one vessel sailing between the wind and another vessel," ["The Encyclopaedic Dictionary," 1888 年].

example.en: The ship will sail to the port at dawn tomorrow.

entries.etymology: c. 1400, sailer, agent noun from sail (v.). Spelling with -o- arose 16c., probably by influence of tailor, etc., and to distinguish the meaning "seaman, mariner" from "thing that sails." It replaced much older seaman and mariner (q.q.v.). Old English also had merefara "sailor." Applied as an adjective from 1870s to clothing styles and items based on a sailor's characteristic attire.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, sailer, agent 名词 源自 sail （动）. Spelling with -o- arose 16 世纪, 可能 by influence of tailor, etc., and to distinguish the 意为 "seaman, mariner" 源自 "thing that sails." It replaced much older seaman and mariner (q.q.v.). 古英语 also had merefara "sailor." Applied 作形容词时 源自 1870 年代 to clothing styles and items based on a sailor's characteristic attire.

entries.etymology:
early 12c., from Old French saint, seinte "a saint; a holy relic," displacing or altering Old English sanct, both from Latin sanctus "holy, consecrated" (used as a noun in Late Latin; also source of Spanish santo, santa, Italian san, etc.), properly past participle of sancire "consecrate" (see sacred). Adopted into most Germanic languages (Old Frisian sankt, Dutch sint, German Sanct).

Originally an adjective prefixed to the name of a canonized person; by c. 1300 it came to be regarded as a noun. Meaning "person of extraordinary holiness" is recorded from 1560s.

Saint Bernard, the breed of mastiff dogs (1839), so called because the monks of the hospice of the pass of St. Bernard (between Italy and Switzerland) sent them to rescue snowbound travelers; St. Elmo's Fire "corposant" (1560s) is from Italian fuoco di Sant'Elmo, named for the patron saint of Mediterranean sailors, a corruption of the name of St. Erasmus, an Italian bishop martyred in 303.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪初, 源自 古法语 saint, seinte "a saint; a holy relic," displacing or altering 古英语 sanct, both 源自 拉丁语 sanctus "holy, consecrated" (used 作名词时 in 晚期拉丁语; also source of 西班牙语 santo, santa, 意大利语 san, etc.), properly 为 … 的过去分词 sancire "consecrate" （参见 sacred). Adopted into most 日耳曼语 languages (古弗里西语 sankt, 荷兰语 sint, 德语 Sanct). Originally an 形容词 prefixed to the name of a canonized person; by 约 1300 年 it came to be regarded 作名词时. 义为 "person of extraordinary holiness" 见于 1560 年代. Saint Bernard, the breed of mastiff dogs (1839 年), so called because the monks of the hospice of the pass of St. Bernard (between Italy and Switzerland) sent them to rescue snowbound travelers; St. Elmo's Fire "corposant" (1560s) is from Italian fuoco di Sant'Elmo, named for the patron saint of Mediterranean sailors, a corruption of the name of St. Erasmus, an 意大利语 bishop martyred in 303.

example.en: He quit his job for the sake of his family's wellbeing.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Old French salade (14c.), from Vulgar Latin *salata, literally "salted," short for herba salata "salted vegetables" (vegetables seasoned with brine, a popular Roman dish), from fem. past participle of *salare "to salt," from Latin sal (genitive salis) "salt" (see salt (n.)).

Dutch salade, German Salat, Swedish salat, Russian salat are from Romanic languages. Salad days "time of youthful inexperience" (perhaps on notion of "green") is first recorded 1606 in Shakespeare and probably owes its survival, if not its existence, to him. Salad bar first attested 1940, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 salade (14 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *salata, 字面义为 "salted," short for herba salata "salted vegetables" (vegetables seasoned with brine, a popular Roman dish), 源自 fem. 为 … 的过去分词 *salare "to salt," 源自 拉丁语 sal (属格 salis) "salt" （参见 salt （名）). 荷兰语 salade, 德语 Salat, Swedish salat, 俄语 salat 始于 Romanic languages. Salad days "time of youthful inexperience" (或许 on 概念 "green") is 首见于 1606 年 in Shakespeare and 可能 owes its survival, if not its existence, to him. Salad bar 最早见于 1940 年, American English.

entries.etymology: late 13c., "compensation, payment," whether periodical, for regular service or for a specific service; from Anglo-French salarie, Old French salaire "wages, pay, reward," from Latin salarium "salary, stipend, pension," originally "salt-money, soldier's allowance for the purchase of salt," noun use of neuter of adjective salarius "pertaining to salt," from sal (genitive salis) "salt" (see salt (n.)). Japanese sarariman "male salaried worker," literally "salary-man," is from English.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "compensation, payment," whether periodical, for regular service or for a specific service; 源自 盎格鲁-法语 salarie, 古法语 salaire "wages, pay, reward," 源自 拉丁语 salarium "salary, stipend, pension," 原义为 "salt-money, soldier's allowance for the purchase of salt," 为 … 的名词用法 neuter of 形容词 salarius "pertaining to salt," 源自 sal (属格 salis) "salt" （参见 salt （名）). 日语 sarariman "male salaried worker," 字面义为 "salary-man," 始于 English.

entries.etymology: late Old English sala "a sale, act of selling," from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse sala "sale," from Proto-Germanic *salo (source also of Old High German sala, Swedish salu, Danish salg), from PIE root *sal- (3) "to grasp, take." Sense of "a selling of shop goods at lower prices than usual" first appeared 1866. Sales tax attested by 1886. Sales associate by 1946. Sales representative is from 1910.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "to greet courteously and respectfully," earlier salue (c. 1300), from Latin salutare "to greet, pay respects," literally "wish health to," from salus (genitive salutis) "greeting, good health," related to salvus "safe" (see safe (adj.)). The military and nautical sense of "display flags, fire cannons, etc., as a mark of respect" is recorded from 1580s; specific sense of "raise the hand to the cap in the presence of a superior officer" is from 1844.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, originally in the Christian sense, "the saving of the soul," from Old French salvaciun and directly from Late Latin salvationem (nominative salvatio, a Church Latin translation of Greek soteria), noun of action from past participle stem of salvare "to save" (see save (v.)). In general (non-religious) sense, attested from late 14c. Meaning "source of salvation" is from late 14c. Salvation Army is from 1878, founded by the Rev. William Booth.

entries.etymology:
perhaps abstracted from Old English swa same "the same as," but more likely from Old Norse same, samr "same," both from Proto-Germanic *sama- "same" (source also of Old Saxon, Old High German, Gothic sama, Old High German samant, German samt "together, with," Gothic samana "together," Dutch zamelen "to collect," German zusammen "together"), from PIE *samos "same," from root *sem- (1) "one," also "as one" (adv.), "together with" (source also of Sanskrit samah "even, level, similar, identical;" Avestan hama "similar, the same;" Greek hama "together with, at the same time," homos "one and the same," homios "like, resembling," homalos "even;" Latin similis "like;" Old Irish samail "likeness;" Old Church Slavonic samu "himself").

Old English had lost the pure form of the word; the modern word replaced synonymous ilk. As a pronoun from c. 1300. Colloquial phrase same here as an exclamation of agreement is from 1895. Same difference curious way to say "equal," is attested from 1945.
entries.etymologyZh: 或许 abstracted 源自 古英语 swa same "the same as," but more likely 源自 古北欧语 same, samr "same," both 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sama- "same" (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古高地德语, Gothic sama, 古高地德语 samant, 德语 samt "together, with," Gothic samana "together," 荷兰语 zamelen "to collect," 德语 zusammen "together"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *samos "same," 源自 root *sem- (1) "one," also "as one" （副）, "together with" (source also of 梵语 samah "even, level, similar, identical;" Avestan hama "similar, the same;" 希腊语 hama "together with, at the same time," homos "one and the same," homios "like, resembling," homalos "even;" 拉丁语 similis "like;" Old 爱尔兰语 samail "likeness;" Old Church Slavonic samu "himself"). 古英语 had lost the pure form of the word; the modern word replaced synonymous ilk. 作为 pronoun 源自 约 1300 年. Colloquial phrase same here 作为 exclamation of agreement 始于 1895 年. Same difference curious way to say "equal," 见于 1945 年.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "something which confirms a proposition or statement," from Anglo-French saumple, a shortening of Old French essample, from Latin exemplum "a sample" (see example). Meaning "small quantity (of something) from which the general quality (of the whole) may be inferred" (usually in a commercial sense) is recorded from early 15c.; sense of "specimen for scientific sampling" is from 1878. As an adjective from 1820.

entries.etymology:
Old English sand, from Proto-Germanic *sandam (source also of Old Norse sandr, Old Frisian sond, Middle Dutch sant, Dutch zand, German Sand), from PIE *bhs-amadho- (source also of Greek psammos "sand;" Latin sabulum "coarse sand," source of Italian sabbia, French sable), suffixed form of root *bhes- "to rub."

Historically, the line between sand and gravel cannot be distinctly drawn. Used figuratively in Old English in reference to innumerability and instability. General Germanic, but not attested in Gothic, which used in this sense malma, related to Old High German melm "dust," the first element of the Swedish city name Malmö (the second element meaning "island"), and to Latin molere "to grind." Metaphoric for "innumerability" since Old English. Sand dollar, type of flat sea-urchin, so called from 1884, so called for its shape; sand dune attested from 1830.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sand, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sandam (source also of 古北欧语 sandr, 古弗里西语 sond, Middle 荷兰语 sant, 荷兰语 zand, 德语 Sand), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *bhs-amadho- (source also of 希腊语 psammos "sand;" 拉丁语 sabulum "coarse sand," source of 意大利语 sabbia, 法语 sable), suffixed form of root *bhes- "to rub." Historically, the line between sand and gravel cannot be distinctly drawn. Used figuratively in 古英语 in reference to innumerability and instability. General 日耳曼语, but not 见于 Gothic, which used in this sense malma, related to 古高地德语 melm "dust," the first element of the Swedish city name Malmö (the second element 意为 "island"), and to 拉丁语 molere "to grind." Metaphoric for "innumerability" 自 古英语. Sand dollar, type of flat sea-urchin, so called 自 1884 年起, so called for its shape; sand dune attested 自 1830 年起.

entries.etymology: 1762, said to be a reference to John Montagu (1718-1792), Fourth Earl Sandwich, who was said to be an inveterate gambler who ate slices of cold meat between bread at the gaming table during marathon sessions rather than get up for a proper meal (this account dates to 1770). It was in his honor that Cook named the Hawaiian islands (1778) when Montagu was first lord of the Admiralty. The family name is from the place in Kent, Old English Sandwicæ, literally "sandy harbor (or trading center)." For pronunciation, see cabbage. Sandwich board, one carried before and one behind, is from 1864.

entries.etymology:
1540s, "follower or attendant of a superior person," from Middle French satellite (14c.), from Latin satellitem (nominative satelles) "attendant, companion, courtier, accomplice, assistant," perhaps from Etruscan satnal (Klein), or a compound of roots *satro- "full, enough" + *leit- (1) "to go" (Tucker); compare English follow, which is constructed of similar roots.

Meaning "planet that revolves about a larger one" first attested 1660s, in reference to the moons of Jupiter, from Latin satellites, which was used in this sense 1610s by German astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571-1630). Galileo, who had discovered them, called them Sidera Medicæa in honor of the Medici family. Meaning "man-made machinery orbiting the Earth" first recorded 1936 as theory, 1957 as fact. Meaning "country dependent and subservient to another" is recorded from 1800.

Galileo, who had discovered them, called them Sidera Medicæa in honor of the Medici family. 义为 "man-made machinery orbiting the Earth" 首见于 1936 年 as theory, 1957 年 as fact. 义为 "country dependent and subservient to another" 见于 1800 年.

entries.etymology: early 14c., "performance of an act set forth by a priest or other Church authority to atone for sin," from Old French satisfaction (12c.), from Latin satisfactionem (nominative satisfactio) "a satisfying of a creditor," noun of action from past participle stem of satisfacere (see satisfy). entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "capable of atoning for sin," 源自 中古法语 satisfactoire (14 世纪) and 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 satisfactorius, 源自 拉丁语 satisfactus, 为 … 的过去分词 satisfacere （参见 satisfy). 义为 "adequate" 始于 1630 年代. 同源词：Satisfactorily; satisfactoriness.

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Middle French satisfier, from Old French satisfaire "pay, repay, make reparation" (14c., Modern French satisfaire), from Latin satisfacere "discharge fully, comply with, make amends," literally "do enough," from satis "enough" (from PIE root *sa- "to satisfy;" see sad) + facere "to make, do, perform" (see factitious). Related: Satisfied; satisfying.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 中古法语 satisfier, 源自 古法语 satisfaire "pay, repay, make reparation" (14 世纪, 现代法语 satisfaire), 源自 拉丁语 satisfacere "discharge fully, comply with, make amends," 字面义为 "do enough," 源自 satis "enough" (源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sa- "to satisfy;" 参见 sad) + facere "to make, do, perform" （参见 factitious). 同源词：Satisfied; satisfying.

entries.etymology: 1530s, "to satisfy, satiate," from Latin saturatus, past participle of saturare "to fill full, sate, drench," from satur "sated, full," from PIE root *sa- "to satisfy" (see sad). Meaning "soak thoroughly" first recorded 1756. Marketing sense first recorded 1958. Related: Saturated; saturating.

entries.etymology:
seventh day of the week, Old English sæterdæg, sæternesdæg, literally "day of the planet Saturn," from Sæternes (genitive of Sætern; see Saturn) + Old English dæg (see day). Partial loan-translation of Latin Saturni dies "Saturn's day" (compare Dutch Zaterdag, Old Frisian Saterdi, Middle Low German Satersdach; Irish dia Sathuirn, Welsh dydd Sadwrn). The Latin word itself is a loan-translation of Greek kronou hemera, literally "the day of Cronus."

Unlike other English day names, no god substitution seems to have been attempted, perhaps because the northern European pantheon lacks a clear corresponding figure to Roman Saturn. A homely ancient Nordic custom, however, seems to be preserved in Old Norse laugardagr, Danish lørdag, Swedish lördag "Saturday," literally "bath day" (Old Norse laug "bath").

German Samstag (Old High German sambaztag) appears to be from a Greek *sambaton, a nasalized colloquial form of sabbaton "sabbath," also attested in Old Church Slavonic sabota, Polish sobota, Russian subbota, Hungarian szombat, French samedi.

Saturday night has been used figuratively to suggest "drunkenness and looseness in relations between the young men and young women" since at least mid-19c. Saturday-night special "cheap, low-caliber handgun" is American English, attested from 1976 (earlier Saturday-night pistol, 1929).
entries.etymologyZh: seventh day of the week, 古英语 sæterdæg, sæternesdæg, 字面义为 "day of the planet Saturn," 源自 Sæternes (属格 of Sætern; 参见 Saturn) + 古英语 dæg （参见 day). Partial loan-translation of 拉丁语 Saturni dies "Saturn's day" (对比 荷兰语 Zaterdag, 古弗里西语 Saterdi, Middle Low 德语 Satersdach; 爱尔兰语 dia Sathuirn, Welsh dydd Sadwrn). The 拉丁语 word itself is a loan-translation of 希腊语 kronou hemera, 字面义为 "the day of Cronus." Unlike other English day names, no god substitution seems to have been attempted, 或许 because the northern European pantheon lacks a clear corresponding figure to Roman Saturn. A homely ancient Nordic custom, however, seems to be preserved in 古北欧语 laugardagr, Danish lørdag, Swedish lördag "Saturday," 字面义为 "bath day" (古北欧语 laug "bath"). 德语 Samstag (古高地德语 sambaztag) appears to be 源自 a 希腊语 *sambaton, a nasalized 口语 form of sabbaton "sabbath," also 见于 Old Church Slavonic sabota, Polish sobota, 俄语 subbota, Hungarian szombat, 法语 samedi. Saturday night has been used figuratively to suggest "drunkenness and looseness in relations between the young men and young women" 自 at least 19 世纪中期 Saturday-night special "cheap, low-caliber handgun" is American English, attested 自 1976 年起 (earlier Saturday-night pistol, 1929 年).

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., from Old French sauce, sausse, from Latin salsa "things salted, salt food," noun use of fem. singular or neuter plural of adjective salsus "salted," from past participle of Old Latin sallere "to salt," from sal (genitive salis) "salt" (see salt (n.)).

Meaning "something which adds piquancy to words or actions" is recorded from c. 1500; sense of "impertinence" first recorded 1835 (see saucy, and compare sass). Slang meaning "liquor" first attested 1940.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 sauce, sausse, 源自 拉丁语 salsa "things salted, salt food," 为 … 的名词用法 fem. singular or neuter 为 … 的复数 形容词 salsus "salted," 源自 为 … 的过去分词 Old 拉丁语 sallere "to salt," 源自 sal (属格 salis) "salt" （参见 salt （名）). 义为 "something which adds piquancy to words or actions" 见于 约 1500 年; 语义 "impertinence" 首见于 1835 年 （参见 saucy, and 对比 sass). definitionLines: vt.救，拯救；储存，贮存；节省， 节约
entries.definition: vt.救，拯救；储存，贮存；节省， 节约
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "to deliver from some danger; rescue from peril, bring to safety," also "prevent the death of;" also theological, "to deliver from sin or its consequences; admit to eternal life; gain salvation," from Old French sauver "keep (safe), protect, redeem," from Late Latin salvare "make safe, secure," from Latin salvus "safe" (see safe (adj.)). From c. 1300 as "reserve for future use, hold back, store up instead of spending;" hence "keep possession of" (late 14c.).

Save face (1898) first was used among the British community in China and is said to be from Chinese; it has not been found in Chinese, but tiu lien "to lose face" does occur. To not (do something) to save one's life is recorded from 1848. To save (one's) breath "cease talking or arguing" is from 1926.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "to deliver from some danger; rescue from peril, bring to safety," also "prevent the death of;" also theological, "to deliver from sin or its consequences; admit to eternal life; gain salvation," 源自 古法语 sauver "keep (safe), protect, redeem," 源自 晚期拉丁语 salvare "make safe, secure," 源自 拉丁语 salvus "safe" （参见 safe （形）). From 约 1300 年 as "reserve for future use, hold back, store up instead of spending;" hence "keep possession of" (14 世纪晚期). Save face (1898 年) first was used among the British community in China and is said to be 源自 汉语; it has not been found in 汉语, but tiu lien "to lose face" does occur. To not (do something) to save one's life is recorded from 1848. To save (one's) breath "cease talking or arguing" 始于 1926 年.

definitionLines: vt.说，讲；说明，表明；比方说， 大约
entries.definition: vt.说，讲；说明，表明；比方说， 大约 vi.说，发表意见
entries.etymology:
Old English secgan "to utter, inform, speak, tell, relate," from Proto-Germanic *sagjanan (source also of Old Saxon seggian, Old Norse segja, Danish sige, Old Frisian sedsa, Middle Dutch segghen, Dutch zeggen, Old High German sagen, German sagen "to say"), from PIE *sokwyo-, from root *sekw- (3) "to say, utter" (source also of Hittite shakiya- "to declare," Lithuanian sakyti "to say," Old Church Slavonic sociti "to vindicate, show," Old Irish insce "speech," Old Latin inseque "to tell say").

Past tense said developed from Old English segde. Not attested in use with inanimate objects (clocks, signs, etc.) as subjects before 1930. You said it "you're right" first recorded 1919; you can say that again as a phrase expressing agreement is recorded from 1942, American English. You don't say (so) as an expression of astonishment (often ironic) is first recorded 1779, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 secgan "to utter, inform, speak, tell, relate," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sagjanan (source also of 古撒克逊语 seggian, 古北欧语 segja, Danish sige, 古弗里西语 sedsa, Middle 荷兰语 segghen, 荷兰语 zeggen, 古高地德语 sagen, 德语 sagen "to say"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sokwyo-, 源自 root *sekw- (3) "to say, utter" (source also of Hittite shakiya- "to declare," Lithuanian sakyti "to say," Old Church Slavonic sociti "to vindicate, show," Old 爱尔兰语 insce "speech," Old 拉丁语 inseque "to tell say"). Past tense said developed 源自 古英语 segde. Not 见于 use with inanimate objects (clocks, signs, etc.) as subjects 1930 年之前. You said it "you're right" 首见于 1919 年; you can say that again 作为 phrase expressing agreement 见于 1942 年, American English. You don't say (so) 作为 expression of astonishment (常 ironic) is 首见于 1779 年, American English.

entries.definition: n. 浏览；扫描 v. 浏览；扫描
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "mark off verse in metric feet," from Late Latin scandere "to scan verse," originally, in classical Latin, "to climb, rise, mount" (the connecting notion is of the rising and falling rhythm of poetry), from PIE *skand- "to spring, leap, climb" (source also of Sanskrit skandati "hastens, leaps, jumps;" Greek skandalon "stumbling block;" Middle Irish sescaind "he sprang, jumped," sceinm "a bound, jump").

Missing -d in English is probably from confusion with suffix -ed (see lawn (n.1)). Sense of "look at closely, examine minutely (as one does when counting metrical feet in poetry)" first recorded 1540s. The (opposite) sense of "look over quickly, skim" is first attested 1926. Related: Scanned; scanning.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "mark off verse in metric feet," 源自 晚期拉丁语 scandere "to scan verse," 原义为, in classical 拉丁语, "to climb, rise, mount" (the connecting notion is of the rising and falling rhythm of poetry), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *skand- "to spring, leap, climb" (source also of 梵语 skandati "hastens, leaps, jumps;" 希腊语 skandalon "stumbling block;" Middle 爱尔兰语 sescaind "he sprang, jumped," sceinm "a bound, jump"). Missing -d in English is 可能 源自 confusion with suffix -ed （参见 lawn (n.1)). 义为 "look at closely, examine minutely (as one does when counting metrical feet in poetry)" 首见于 1540 年代. The (opposite) 语义 "look over quickly, skim" is 最早见于 1926 年. 同源词：Scanned; scanning.

definitionLines: n. 丑行，丑闻；诽谤，流言蜚语
entries.definition: n. 丑行，丑闻；诽谤，流言蜚语
entries.etymology:
1580s, "discredit caused by irreligious conduct," from Middle French scandale (12c.), from Late Latin scandalum "cause for offense, stumbling block, temptation," from Greek skandalon "a trap or snare laid for an enemy," in New Testament, metaphorically as "a stumbling block, offense;" originally "trap with a springing device," from PIE *skand- "to leap, climb" (see scan (v.); also see slander (n.), which is another form of the same word).

Attested from early 13c., but the modern word likely is a reborrowing. Meaning "malicious gossip," also "shameful action or event" is from 1590s; sense of "person whose conduct is a disgrace" is from 1630s. Scandal sheet "sensational newspaper" is from 1939. Scandal-monger is from 1702.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "discredit caused by irreligious conduct," 源自 中古法语 scandale (12 世纪), 源自 晚期拉丁语 scandalum "cause for offense, stumbling block, temptation," 源自 希腊语 skandalon "a trap or snare laid for an enemy," in New Testament, metaphorically as "a stumbling block, offense;" 原义为 "trap with a springing device," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *skand- "to leap, climb" （参见 scan （动）; also 参见 slander （名）, which is another form of the same word). Attested 源自 13 世纪初, but the modern word likely is a reborrowing. 义为 "malicious gossip," also "shameful action or event" 始于 1590 年代; 语义 "person whose conduct is a disgrace" 始于 1630 年代. Scandal sheet "sensational newspaper" 始于 1939 年. Scandal-monger 始于 1702 年.

As an adverb early 14c. from the adjective. Phrase to make oneself scarce "go away" first attested 1771, noted as a current "cant phrase." Related: Scarcely.

entries.definition: vt. 惊吓，受惊 n. 惊慌，惊恐
entries.etymology: 1590s, alteration of Middle English skerren (c. 1200), from Old Norse skirra "to frighten; to shrink from, shun; to prevent, avert," related to skjarr "timid, shy, afraid of," of unknown origin. In Scottish also skair, skar, and in dialectal English skeer, skear, which seems to preserve the older pronunciation. To scare up "procure, obtain" is first recorded 1846, American English, from notion of rousing game from cover. Related: Scared; scaring.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, alteration of 中古英语 skerren (约 1200 年), 源自 古北欧语 skirra "to frighten; to shrink from, shun; to prevent, avert," related to skjarr "timid, shy, afraid of," 来源不详. definitionLines: n. 景色，景象；（戏）一场； 布景；镜头
entries.definition: n. 景色，景象；（戏）一场； 布景；镜头
entries.etymology:
1530s, "subdivision of an act of a play," also "stage-setting," from Middle French scène (14c.), from Latin scaena, scena "scene, stage of a theater," from Greek skene "wooden stage for actors," also "that which is represented on stage," originally "tent or booth," related to skia "shadow, shade," via notion of "something that gives shade," from PIE root *skai- "to shine, flicker, glimmer" (see shine (v.)).

Meaning "material apparatus of a theatrical stage" is from 1540s. Meaning "place in which the action of a literary work occurs" is attested from 1590s; general (non-literary) sense of "place where anything is done or takes place" is recorded from 1590s. Hence U.S. slang sense of "setting or milieu for a specific group or activity," attested from 1951 in Beat jargon. Meaning "stormy encounter between two or more persons" is attested from 1761. Behind the scenes "having knowledge of affairs not apparent to the public" (1660s) is an image from the theater, "amid actors and stage machinery" (out of sight of the audience). Scene of the crime (1923) first attested in Agatha Christie.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "subdivision of an act of a play," also "stage-setting," 源自 中古法语 scène (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 scaena, scena "scene, stage of a theater," 源自 希腊语 skene "wooden stage for actors," also "that which is represented on stage," 原义为 "tent or booth," related to skia "shadow, shade," 经由 概念 "something that gives shade," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *skai- "to shine, flicker, glimmer" （参见 shine （动）). 义为 "material apparatus of a theatrical stage" 始于 1540 年代. 义为 "place in which the action of a literary work occurs" 见于 1590 年代; general (non-literary) 语义 "place where anything is done or takes place" 见于 1590 年代. Hence U.S. 俚语 语义 "setting or milieu for a specific group or activity," attested 自 1951 年起 in Beat jargon. 义为 "stormy encounter between two or more persons" 见于 1761 年. Behind the scenes "having knowledge of affairs not apparent to the public" (1660 年代) is an image 源自 theater, "amid actors and stage machinery" (out of sight of the audience). Scene of the crime (1923 年) 最早见于 in Agatha Christie.

example.en: The opening scene of the play takes place in a small village.
example.zh: 这部话剧的开场场景发生在一个小村庄里。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., sent "to find the scent of," from Old French sentir "to feel, smell, touch, taste; realize, perceive; make love to," from Latin sentire " to feel, perceive, sense, discern, hear, see" (see sense (n.)).

Originally a hunting term. The -c- appeared 17c., perhaps by influence of ascent, descent, etc., or by influence of science. This was a tendency in early Modern English, also in scythe and for a time threatening to make scite and scituate. Figurative use from 1550s. Transitive sense "impregnate with an odor, perfume" is from 1690s. Related: Scented; scenting.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, sent "to find the scent of," 源自 古法语 sentir "to feel, smell, touch, taste; realize, perceive; make love to," 源自 拉丁语 sentire " to feel, perceive, sense, discern, hear, see" （参见 sense （名）). Originally a hunting term. The -c- appeared 17 世纪, 或许 by influence of ascent, descent, etc.，或by influence of science. This was a tendency in early 现代英语, also in scythe and for a time threatening to make scite and scituate. Figurative use 源自 1550 年代. Transitive sense "impregnate with an odor, perfume" 始于 1690 年代. 同源词：Scented; scenting.

example.en: The dog followed the scent of the missing child through the forest.
example.zh: 那只狗穿越森林追踪失踪孩子留下的气味。

definitionLines: n. 时间表；进度表；一览表
entries.definition: n. 时间表；进度表；一览表 vt. 安排；排定，预定
entries.etymology:
late 14c., sedule, cedule "ticket, label, slip of paper with writing on it," from Old French cedule (Modern French cédule), from Late Latin schedula "strip of paper" (in Medieval Latin also "a note, schedule"), diminutive of Latin scheda, scida "one of the strips forming a papyrus sheet," from Greek skhida "splinter," from stem of skhizein "to cleave, split" (see shed (v.)). Also from the Latin word are Spanish cédula, German Zettel.

The notion is of slips of paper attached to a document as an appendix (a sense maintained in U.S. tax forms). The specific meaning "printed timetable" is first recorded 1863 in railway use. Modern spelling is a 15c. imitation of Latin, but pronunciation remained "sed-yul" for centuries afterward; the modern British pronunciation ("shed-yul") is from French influence, while the U.S. pronunciation ("sked-yul") is from the practice of Webster, based on the Greek original.

entries.etymology: Old English scolere "student," from Medieval Latin scholaris, noun use of Late Latin scholaris "of a school," from Latin schola (see school (n.1)). entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "what is known, knowledge (of something) acquired by study; information;" also "assurance of knowledge, certitude, certainty," from Old French science "knowledge, learning, application; corpus of human knowledge" (12c.), from Latin scientia "knowledge, a knowing; expertness," from sciens (genitive scientis) "intelligent, skilled," present participle of scire "to know," probably originally "to separate one thing from another, to distinguish," related to scindere "to cut, divide," from PIE root *skei- "to cut, to split" (source also of Greek skhizein "to split, rend, cleave," Gothic skaidan, Old English sceadan "to divide, separate;" see shed (v.)).

From late 14c. in English as "book-learning," also "a particular branch of knowledge or of learning;" also "skillfulness, cleverness; craftiness." From c. 1400 as "experiential knowledge;" also "a skill, handicraft; a trade." From late 14c. as "collective human knowledge" (especially "that gained by systematic observation, experiment, and reasoning). Modern (restricted) sense of "body of regular or methodical observations or propositions concerning a particular subject or speculation" is attested from 1725; in 17c.-18c. this concept commonly was called philosophy. Sense of "non-arts studies" is attested from 1670s.

The distinction is commonly understood as between theoretical truth (Greek episteme) and methods for effecting practical results (tekhne), but science sometimes is used for practical applications and art for applications of skill. To blind (someone) with science "confuse by the use of big words or complex explanations" is attested from 1937, originally noted as a phrase from Australia and New Zealand.
