entries.etymology:
1580s, from Middle French scientifique, from Medieval Latin scientificus "pertaining to science," from Latin scientia "knowledge" (see science) + -ficus "making" + facere "to make" (see factitious). Originally used to translate Greek epistemonikos "making knowledge" in Aristotle's "Ethics."

Sciential (mid-15c., "based on knowledge," from Latin scientialis) is the classical purists' choice for an adjective based on science. Scientic (1540s) and scient (late 15c.) also have been used. First record of scientific revolution is from 1803; scientific method is from 1854; scientific notation is from 1961. Related: Scientifical; scientifically.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., sisoures, from Old French cisoires (plural) "shears," from Vulgar Latin *cisoria (plural) "cutting instrument," from *cisus (in compounds such as Latin excisus, past participle of excidere "to cut out"), ultimately from Latin caedere "to cut" (see -cide). Spelling with sc- is 16c., from influence of Medieval Latin scissor "tailor," in classical Latin "carver, cutter," from past participle stem of scindere "to split."

Usually with pair of (attested from c. 1400) when indication of just one is required, but a singular form without the -s occasionally was used (cysowre, mid-15c.). In Scotland, shears answers for all sizes, according to OED; but in England generally that word is used only for those too large to be worked by one hand. Sense in wrestling is from 1904. Oh scissors! was a 19c. exclamation of impatience or disgust (1843). In reference to a type of swimming kick, from 1902 (the image itself is from 1880s).

entries.etymology:
late Old English scoru "twenty," from Old Norse skor "mark, notch, incision; a rift in rock," also, in Icelandic, "twenty," from Proto-Germanic *skura-, from PIE root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear).

The connecting notion probably is counting large numbers (of sheep, etc.) with a notch in a stick for each 20. That way of counting, called vigesimalism, also exists in French: In Old French, "twenty" (vint) or a multiple of it could be used as a base, as in vint et doze ("32"), dous vinz et diz ("50"). Vigesimalism was or is a feature of Welsh, Irish, Gaelic and Breton (as well as non-IE Basque), and it is speculated that the English and the French picked it up from the Celts. Compare tally (n.).

The prehistoric sense of the Germanic word, then, likely was "straight mark like a scratch, line drawn by a sharp instrument," but in English this is attested only from c. 1400, along with the sense "mark made (on a chalkboard, etc.) to keep count of a customer's drinks in a tavern." This sense was extended by 1670s to "mark made for purpose of recording a point in a game or match," and thus "aggregate of points made by contestants in certain games and matches" (1742, originally in whist).

From the tavern-keeping sense comes the meaning "amount on an innkeeper's bill" (c. 1600) and thus the figurative verbal expression settle scores (1775).  Meaning "printed piece of music" first recorded 1701, said to be from the practice of connecting related staves by scores of lines. Especially "music composed for a film" (1927). Meaning "act of obtaining narcotic drugs" is by 1951.

Scoreboard is from 1826; 
score-keeping- from 1905; newspaper sports section score line is from 1965; baseball score-card is from 1877.

c. 1200, a shortening of Old French escarn "mockery, derision, contempt," a common Romanic word (Spanish escarnio, Italian scherno) of Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *skarnjan "mock, deride" (source also of Old High German skern "mockery, jest, sport," Middle High German scherzen "to jump with joy").

Probably influenced by Old French escorne "affront, disgrace," which is a back-formation from escorner, literally "to break off (someone's) horns," from Vulgar Latin *excornare (source of Italian scornare "treat with contempt"), from Latin ex- "without" (see ex-) + cornu "horn" (see horn (n.)).

mid-14c., "upright piece of furniture providing protection from heat of a fire, drafts, etc.," probably from a shortened (Anglo-French? compare Anglo-Latin screna) variant of Old North French escren, Old French escran "fire-screen" (early 14c.), perhaps from Middle Dutch scherm "screen, cover, shield," or Frankish *skrank "barrier," from Proto-Germanic *skerm- (source also of Old High German skirm, skerm "protection," from PIE *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)).

Meaning "net-wire frame used in windows and doors" is recorded from 1859. Meaning "flat vertical surface for reception of projected images" is from 1810, originally in reference to magic lantern shows; later of movies. Transferred sense of "cinema world collectively" is attested from 1914; hence screen test (1918), etc. Screen saver first attested 1990. Screen printing recorded from 1918.

Transferred 语义 "cinema world collectively" 见于 1914 年; hence screen test (1918 年), etc. Screen saver 最早见于 1990 年. Screen printing recorded 自 1918 年起.

entries.definition: n1. 螺钉，螺丝 vt. 拧，拧紧
entries.etymology:
"cylinder of wood or metal with a spiral ridge round it; hole in which a screw turns," c. 1400, from Middle French escroue "nut, cylindrical socket, screwhole," of uncertain etymology; not found in other Romanic languages. Perhaps via Gallo-Roman *scroba or West Germanic *scruva from Vulgar Latin scrobis "screw-head groove," in classical Latin "ditch, trench," also "vagina" (Diez, though OED finds this "phonologically impossible").

Kluge, Watkins and others trace it to Latin scrofa "breeding sow," perhaps based on the shape of a pig's penis (compare Portuguese porca, Spanish perca "a female screw," from Latin porca "sow"). Latin scrofa is literally "digger, rooter," from PIE root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)). A group of apparently cognate Germanic words (Middle Low German, Middle Dutch schruve, Dutch schroef, German Schraube, Swedish skrufva "screw") are said to be French loan-words.

Sense of "means of pressure or coercion" is from 1640s, probably in reference to instruments of torture (such as thumbscrews). Meaning "prison guard, warden" is 1812 in underworld slang, originally in reference to the key they carried (screw as slang for "key" attested from 1795). Slang meaning "an act of copulation" is recorded from 1929 (meaning "a prostitute" is attested from 1725). To have a screw loose "have a dangerous (usually mental) weakness" is recorded from 1810.
entries.etymologyZh: "cylinder of wood or metal with a spiral ridge round it; hole in which a screw turns," 约 1400 年, 源自 中古法语 escroue "nut, cylindrical socket, screwhole," of uncertain etymology; not found in other Romanic languages. Perhaps 经由 Gallo-Roman *scroba or West 日耳曼语 *scruva 源自 通俗拉丁语 scrobis "screw-head groove," in classical 拉丁语 "ditch, trench," also "vagina" (Diez, though OED finds this "phonologically impossible"). Kluge, Watkins and others trace it to 拉丁语 scrofa "breeding sow," 或许 based on the shape of a pig's penis (对比 葡萄牙语 porca, 西班牙语 perca "a female screw," 源自 拉丁语 porca "sow"). 拉丁语 scrofa is 字面义为 "digger, rooter," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" （参见 shear （动）). A group of 似乎 同源 日耳曼语 words (Middle Low 德语, Middle 荷兰语 schruve, 荷兰语 schroef, 德语 Schraube, Swedish skrufva "screw") are said to be 法语 loan-words. 义为 "means of pressure or coercion" 始于 1640 年代, 可能 in reference to instruments of torture (such as thumbscrews). 义为 "prison guard, warden" is 1812 年 in underworld 俚语, 原义为 in reference to the key they carried (screw as 俚语 for "key" attested 自 1795 年起). Slang 意为 "an act of copulation" 见于 1929 年 (意为 "a prostitute" 见于 1725 年). To have a screw loose "have a dangerous (usually mental) weakness" 见于 1810 年.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "something written," earlier scrite (c. 1300), from Old French escrit "piece of writing, written paper; credit note, IOU; deed, bond" (Modern French écrit) from Latin scriptum "a writing, book; law; line, mark," noun use of neuter past participle of scribere "to write," from PIE *skribh- "to cut, separate, sift" (source also of Greek skariphasthai "to scratch an outline, sketch," Lettish skripat "scratch, write," Old Norse hrifa "scratch"), from root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)) on the notion of carving marks in stone, wood, etc.

Meaning "handwriting" is recorded from 1860. Theatrical use, short for manuscript, is attested from 1884. The importance of Rome to the spread of civilization in Europe is attested by the fact that the word for "write" in Celtic and Germanic (as well as Romanic) languages derives from scribere (French écrire, Irish scriobhaim, Welsh ysgrifennu, German schreiben). The cognate Old English scrifan means "to allot, assign, decree" (see shrive; also compare Old Norse skript "penance") and Modern English uses write (v.) to express this action.

Theatrical use, short for manuscript, 见于 1884 年. The importance of Rome to the spread of civilization in Europe is attested by the fact that the word for "write" in Celtic and 日耳曼语 (as well as Romanic) languages derives 源自 scribere (法语 écrire, 爱尔兰语 scriobhaim, Welsh ysgrifennu, 德语 schreiben). The 同源 古英语 scrifan means "to allot, assign, decree" （参见 shrive; also 对比 古北欧语 skript "penance") and 现代英语 uses write （动） to express this action.

entries.etymology:
"rub hard," early 15c., earlier shrubben (c. 1300), perhaps from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German schrubben "to scrub," or from an unrecorded Old English cognate, or from a Scandinavian source (such as Danish skrubbe "to scrub"), probably ultimately from the Proto-Germanic root of shrub, used as a cleaning tool (compare the evolution of broom, brush (n.1)).

Meaning "to cancel" is attested from 1828 (popularized during World War II with reference to flights), probably from notion of "to rub out, erase" an entry on a listing. Related: Scrubbed; scrubbing.

entries.etymology:
Old English sæ "sheet of water, sea, lake, pool," from Proto-Germanic *saiwaz (source also of Old Saxon seo, Old Frisian se, Middle Dutch see, Swedish sjö), of unknown origin, outside connections "wholly doubtful" [Buck]. Meaning "large quantity" (of anything) is from c. 1200.  Meaning "dark area of the moon's surface" is attested from 1660s (see mare (n.2)).

Germanic languages also use the general Indo-European word (represented by English mere (n.)), but have no firm distinction between "sea" and "lake," either by size, by inland or open, or by salt vs. fresh. This may reflect the Baltic geography where the languages are thought to have originated. The two words are used more or less interchangeably in Germanic, and exist in opposite senses (such as Gothic saiws "lake," marei "sea;" but Dutch zee "sea," meer "lake"). Compare also Old Norse sær "sea," but Danish sø, usually "lake" but "sea" in phrases. German See is "sea" (fem.) or "lake" (masc.). The single Old English word sæ glosses Latin mare, aequor, pontus, pelagus, and marmor.

Phrase sea change "transformation" is attested from 1610, first in Shakespeare ("The Tempest," I.ii). Sea anemone is from 1742; sea legs is from 1712; sea level from 1806; sea urchin from 1590s. At sea in the figurative sense of "perplexed" is attested from 1768, from literal sense of "out of sight of land" (c. 1300).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sæ "sheet of water, sea, lake, pool," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *saiwaz (source also of 古撒克逊语 seo, 古弗里西语 se, Middle 荷兰语 参见, Swedish sjö), 来源不详, outside connections "wholly doubtful" [Buck]. 义为 "large quantity" (of anything) 始于 约 1200 年. 义为 "dark area of the moon's surface" 见于 1660 年代 （参见 mare (n.2)). 日耳曼语 languages also use the general Indo-European word (represented by English mere （名）), but have no firm distinction between "sea" and "lake," either by size, by inland or open，或by salt vs. fresh. This may reflect the Baltic geography where the languages are thought to have originated. The two words are used more or less interchangeably in 日耳曼语, and exist in opposite senses (such as Gothic saiws "lake," marei "sea;" but 荷兰语 zee "sea," meer "lake"). 对比 also 古北欧语 sær "sea," but Danish sø, 通常 "lake" but "sea" in phrases. 德语 See is "sea" (fem.) or "lake" (masc.). The single 古英语 word sæ glosses 拉丁语 mare, aequor, pontus, pelagus, and marmor. Phrase sea change "transformation" 见于 1610 年, first in Shakespeare ("The Tempest," I.ii). Sea anemone 始于 1742 年; sea legs 始于 1712 年; sea level 自 1806 年起; sea urchin 源自 1590 年代. At sea in the figurative 语义 "perplexed" 见于 1768 年, 源自 literal 语义 "out of sight of land" (约 1300 年).

entries.etymology: "to fasten with (or as with) a seal," c. 1200, from seal (n.1). Meaning "to place a seal on (a document)" is recorded from mid-14c.; hence "to conclude, ratify, render official" (late 15c.). Sense of "to close up with wax, lead, cement, etc." is attested from 1660s, from the notion of wax seals on envelopes. In reference to the actions of wood-coatings, 1940. Related: Sealed; sealing. Sealing-wax is attested from c. 1300. To seal (one's) fate (1799) probably reflects the notion of a seal on an execution warrant.
entries.etymologyZh: "to fasten with (or as with) a seal," 约 1200 年, 源自 seal (n.1). 义为 "to place a seal on (a document)" 见于 14 世纪中期; hence "to conclude, ratify, render official" (15 世纪晚期). 义为 "to close up with wax, lead, cement, etc." 见于 1660 年代, 源自 概念 wax seals on envelopes. In reference to the actions of wood-coatings, 1940 年. 同源词：Sealed; sealing. Sealing-wax 见于 约 1300 年. To seal (one's) fate (1799 年) 可能 reflects the 概念 a seal on an execution warrant.

example.en: Please seal the envelope before dropping it in the mailbox.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "a period of the year," with reference to weather or work, also "proper time, suitable occasion," from Old French seison, also saison "season, date; right moment, appropriate time" (Modern French saison) "a sowing, planting," from Latin sationem (nominative satio) "a sowing, planting," noun of action from past participle stem of serere "to sow" (see sow (v.)).

Sense shifted in Vulgar Latin from "act of sowing" to "time of sowing," especially "spring, regarded as the chief sowing season." In Old Provençal and Old French (and thus in English), this was extended to "season" in general. In other Indo-European languages, generic "season" (of the year) words typically are from words for "time," sometimes with a word for "year" (as in Latin tempus (anni), German Jahreszeit). Of game (as in out of season) from late 14c. Spanish estacion, Italian stagione are unrelated, being from Latin statio "station."

Meaning "time of year during which a place is most frequented" is from 1705. Season ticket is attested from 1820.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "a period of the year," with reference to weather or work, also "proper time, suitable occasion," 源自 古法语 seison, also saison "season, date; right moment, appropriate time" (现代法语 saison) "a sowing, planting," 源自 拉丁语 sationem (主格 satio) "a sowing, planting," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of serere "to sow" （参见 sow （动）). Sense shifted in 通俗拉丁语 源自 "act of sowing" to "time of sowing," 尤指 "spring, regarded as the chief sowing season." In Old Provençal and 古法语 (and thus in English), this was extended to "season" in general. In other Indo-European languages, generic "season" (of the year) words typically 始于 words for "time," 有时 with a word for "year" (as in 拉丁语 tempus (anni), 德语 Jahreszeit). Of game (as in out of season) 源自 14 世纪晚期 西班牙语 estacion, 意大利语 stagione are unrelated, being 源自 拉丁语 statio "station." 义为 "time of year during which a place is most frequented" 始于 1705 年. Season ticket 见于 1820 年.

example.en: Spring is the most beautiful season in this mountain village.

entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, 源自 sea + weed （名）. An 古英语 word for it was sæwar; also fleotwyrt ('float-wort').

Second sight is from 1610s; an etymologically perverse term, because it means in reality the sight of events before, not after, they occur. Second fiddle first attested 1809:
entries.etymologyZh: "next after first," 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 second, secont, and 直接源自 拉丁语 secundus "following, next in time or order," also "secondary, subordinate, inferior," 源自 root of sequi "follow" （参见 sequel). entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Latin secretus "set apart, withdrawn; hidden, concealed, private," past participle of secernere "to set apart, part, divide; exclude," from se- "without, apart," properly "on one's own" (see se-) + cernere "separate" (see crisis).

As an adjective from late 14c., from French secret, adjective use of noun. Open secret is from 1828. Secret agent first recorded 1715; secret service is from 1737; secret weapon is from 1936.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 拉丁语 secretus "set apart, withdrawn; hidden, concealed, private," 为 … 的过去分词 secernere "to set apart, part, divide; exclude," 源自 se- "without, apart," properly "on one's own" （参见 se-) + cernere "separate" （参见 crisis). 作形容词时 源自 14 世纪晚期, 源自 法语 secret, 为 … 的形容词用法 名词. Open secret 始于 1828 年. Secret agent 首见于 1715 年; secret service 始于 1737 年; secret weapon 始于 1936 年.

example.en: He kept the surprise party a secret until the very last moment.

definitionLines: n. 书记；秘书；部长，大臣
entries.definition: n. 书记；秘书；部长，大臣
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "person entrusted with secrets," from Medieval Latin secretarius "clerk, notary, confidential officer, confidant," a title applied to various confidential officers, noun use of adjective meaning "private, secret, pertaining to private or secret matters" (compare Latin secretarium "a council-chamber, conclave, consistory"), from Latin secretum "a secret, a hidden thing" (see secret (n.)).

Meaning "person who keeps records, write letters, etc.," originally for a king, first recorded c. 1400. As title of ministers presiding over executive departments of state, it is from 1590s. The word also is used in both French and English to mean "a private desk," sometimes in French form secretaire. The South African secretary bird so called (1786) in reference to its crest, which, when smooth, resembles a pen stuck over the ear. Compare Late Latin silentiarius "privy councilor, 'silentiary," from Latin silentium "a being silent."
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "person entrusted with secrets," 源自 中古拉丁语 secretarius "clerk, notary, confidential officer, confidant," a title applied to various confidential officers, 为 … 的名词用法 形容词 意为 "private, secret, pertaining to private or secret matters" (对比 拉丁语 secretarium "a council-chamber, conclave, consistory"), 源自 拉丁语 secretum "a secret, a hidden thing" （参见 secret （名）). 义为 "person who keeps records, write letters, etc.," 原义为 for a king, 首见于 约 1400 年. As title of ministers presiding over executive departments of state, it 始于 1590 年代. The word also is used in both 法语 and English to mean "a private desk," 有时 in 法语 form secretaire. The South African secretary bird so called (1786 年) in reference to its crest, which, when smooth, resembles a pen stuck over the ear. 对比 晚期拉丁语 silentiarius "privy councilor, 'silentiary," 源自 拉丁语 silentium "a being silent."

example.en: The secretary typed up the meeting notes and sent them to all staff.
example.zh: 秘书整理好会议记录后发给了所有员工。

definitionLines: n. 章节；部分；地区；截面，剖 视图
entries.definition: n. 章节；部分；地区；截面，剖 视图
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "intersection of two straight lines; division of a scale;" from Old French section or directly from Latin sectionem (nominative sectio) "a cutting, cutting off, division," noun of action from past participle stem of secare "to cut," from PIE root *sek- "to cut" (source also of Old Church Slavonic seko, sešti "to cut," se čivo "ax, hatchet;" Lithuanian isekti "to engrave, carve;" Albanian šate "mattock;" Old Saxon segasna, Old English sigðe "scythe;" Old English secg "sword," seax "knife, short sword;" Old Irish doescim "I cut;" Latin saxum "rock, stone").

From 1550s as "act of cutting or dividing." Meaning "subdivision of a written work, statute, etc." is from 1570s. Meaning "a part cut off from the rest" is from early 15c.

entries.etymology: 1560s, "section of a circle between two radii," from Late Latin sector "section of a circle," in classical Latin "a cutter, one who cuts," from sectus, past participle of secare "to cut" (see section (n.)). Translated Greek tomeus in Latin editions of Archimedes. Meaning "area, division" appeared 1920, generalized from military sense (1916) of "part of a front," based on a circle centered on a headquarters. As a verb from 1884. Related: Sectoral; sectorial.

example.en: The technology sector has seen rapid growth over the past decade.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "living in the world, not belonging to a religious order," also "belonging to the state," from Old French seculer (Modern French séculier), from Late Latin saecularis "worldly, secular, pertaining to a generation or age," from Latin saecularis "of an age, occurring once in an age," from saeculum "age, span of time, generation."

According to Watkins, this is probably from PIE *sai-tlo-, with instrumental element *-tlo- + *sai- "to bind, tie" (see sinew), extended metaphorically to successive human generations as links in the chain of life. Another theory connects it with words for "seed," from PIE root *se- "to sow" (see sow (v.), and compare Gothic mana-seþs "mankind, world," literally "seed of men").

Used in ecclesiastical writing like Greek aion "of this world" (see cosmos). It is source of French siècle. Ancient Roman ludi saeculares was a three-day, day-and-night celebration coming once in an "age" (120 years). In English, in reference to humanism and the exclusion of belief in God from matters of ethics and morality, from 1850s.

example.en: The course covers both secular and religious influences on medieval European art.
example.zh: 该课程涵盖了世俗和宗教对中世纪欧洲艺术的双重影响。

definitionLines: vt. 得到，获得；防护，保卫
entries.definition: a. 安全的，可靠的 vt. 得到，获得；防护，保卫
entries.etymology:
1530s, "without care, dreading no evil," from Latin securus, of persons, "free from care, quiet, easy," also in a bad sense, "careless, reckless;" of things, "tranquil; free from danger, safe," from *se cura, from se "free from" (see secret (n.1)) + cura "care" (see cure (n.)).

In English, of places, "free from danger, unexposed," from 1580s. Meaning "firmly fixed" (of material things) is from 1841, on notion of "affording grounds for confidence." Of telephones, "not wiretapped," from 1961. Replaced Middle English siker, from Old English sicor, from the Latin word. Related: Securely.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "without care, dreading no evil," 源自 拉丁语 securus, of persons, "free from care, quiet, easy," also in a bad sense, "careless, reckless;" of things, "tranquil; free from danger, safe," 源自 *se cura, 源自 se "free from" （参见 secret (n.1)) + cura "care" （参见 cure （名）). In English, of places, "free from danger, unexposed," 源自 1580 年代. 义为 "firmly fixed" (of material things) 始于 1841 年, on 概念 "affording grounds for confidence." Of telephones, "not wiretapped," 自 1961 年起. Replaced 中古英语 siker, 源自 古英语 sicor, 源自 拉丁语 word. 同源词：Securely.

example.en: The vault is secure against unauthorized access with biometric locks.
example.zh: 这个保险库通过生物识别锁防止未授权访问，安全有保障。

definitionLines: n. 安全，治安防卫；（pl.）证 券，债券
entries.definition: n. 安全，治安防卫；（pl.）证 券，债券
entries.etymology:
mid-15c., "condition of being secure," from Latin securitas, from securus "free from care" (see secure). Replacing sikerte (early 15c.), from an earlier borrowing from Latin; earlier in the sense "security" was sikerhede (early 13c.); sikernesse (c. 1200).

Meaning "something which secures" is from 1580s; "safety of a state, person, etc." is from 1941. Legal sense of "property in bonds" is from mid-15c.; that of "document held by a creditor" is from 1680s. Phrase security blanket in figurative sense is attested from 1966, in reference to the crib blanket carried by the character Linus in the "Peanuts" comic strip (1956).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "condition of being secure," 源自 拉丁语 securitas, 源自 securus "free from care" （参见 secure). example.en: The airport upgraded its security systems after the incident.

definitionLines: vt. 看见；理解，明白；会见，见 面；获悉，知道；送行，陪；经 历，目睹

entries.etymology:
1630s, "covered chair on poles," possibly from a southern Italian dialect derivative of Italian sede "chair" (compare Italian seggietta, 1590s; the thing itself was said to have been introduced from Naples), from Latin sedes, related to sedere "sit" (see sedentary). Since Johnson's conjecture, often derived from the town of Sedan in France, where it was said to have been made or first used, but historical evidence for this is lacking.

Introduced in England by Sir Sanders Duncombe in 1634 and first called a covered chair. "In Paris the sedan-chair man was usually an Auvergnat, in London an Irishman" ["Encyclopaedia Britannica," 1929]. Meaning "closed automobile seating four or more" first recorded 1912, American English.

entries.etymology: Old English sed, sæd "that which may be sown; an individual grain of seed; offspring, posterity," from Proto-Germanic *sediz "seed" (source also of Old Norse sað, Old Saxon sad, Old Frisian sed, Middle Dutch saet, Old High German sat, German Saat), from PIE *se-ti- "sowing," from root *se- (1) "to sow" (see sow (v.)). Figurative use in Old English. Meaning "offspring, progeny" rare now except in biblical use. Meaning "semen" is from c. 1300. For sporting sense, see seed (v.).

Figurative use in 古英语. 义为 "offspring, progeny" rare 现在 except in biblical use. 义为 "semen" 始于 约 1300 年. For sporting sense, 参见 seed （动）.

definitionLines: U. （for/after） 寻找，探求；试 图，企图

entries.etymology: Old English secan "inquire, search for; pursue; long for, wish for, desire; look for, expect from," influenced by Old Norse soekja, both from Proto-Germanic *sokjan (source also of Old Saxon sokian, Old Frisian seka, Middle Dutch soekan, Old High German suohhan, German suchen, Gothic sokjan), from PIE *sag-yo-, from root *sag- "to track down, seek out" (source also of Latin sagire "to perceive quickly or keenly," sagus "presaging, predicting," Old Irish saigim "seek"). The natural modern form of the Anglo-Saxon word as uninfluenced by Norse is in beseech. Related: Sought; seeking.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "to appear to be;" c. 1300, "to be fitting, be appropriate, be suitable," though the more recent sense in English is the etymological one; from Old Norse soema "to honor; to put up with; to conform to (the world, etc.)," verb derived from adjective soemr "fitting," from Proto-Germanic *somi- (source also of Old English som "agreement, reconciliation," seman "to conciliate," source of Middle English semen "to settle a dispute," literally "to make one;" Old Danish some "to be proper or seemly"), from PIE *som-i-, from root *sem- "one, as one" (see same). Related: Seemed; seeming.

definitionLines: vt. 抓住，捉住；夺取，占领
entries.definition: vt. 抓住，捉住；夺取，占领 vi. （on/upon） 利用，采用
entries.etymology:
mid-13c., from Old French seisir "to take possession of, take by force; put in possession of, bestow upon" (Modern French saisir), from Late Latin sacire, which is generally held to be from a Germanic source, but the exact origin is uncertain. Perhaps from Frankish *sakjan "lay claim to" (compare Gothic sokjan, Old English secan "to seek;" see seek). Or perhaps from Proto-Germanic *satjan "to place" (see set (v.)).

Originally a legal term in reference to feudal property holdings or offices. Meaning "to grip with the hands or teeth" is from c. 1300; that of "to take possession by force or capture" (of a city, etc.) is from mid-14c. Figurative use, with reference to death, disease, fear, etc. is from late 14c. Meaning "to grasp with the mind" is attested from 1855. Of engines or other mechanisms, attested from 1878. Related: Seized; seizing.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 seisir "to take possession of, take by force; put in possession of, bestow upon" (现代法语 saisir), 源自 晚期拉丁语 sacire, which is generally held to be 源自 a 日耳曼语 source, but the exact origin is uncertain. example.en: The police managed to seize the suspect before he could escape.

entries.etymology:
late Old English seldum, alteration of seldan "seldom, rarely,"  from Proto-Germanic *selda- "strange, rare" (source also of Old Norse sjaldan, Old Frisian selden, Dutch zelden, Old High German seltan, German selten), perhaps ultimately from the base of self (q.v.).

Form shifted on analogy of adverbial dative plurals in -um (such as whilom "at one time," from while). The same development also created litlum from little, miclum from mickle. German seltsam "strange, odd," Dutch zeldzaam are related, but with the second element conformed to their versions of -some.

Seldom-times is from mid-15c. (Old English had seldhwanne "seldwhen"). Seldom-seen is from mid-15c. (Old English had seldsiene, "seld-seen").

Some compounds using the old form survived through Middle English, such as selcouth"rarely or little-known, unusual, strange, wonderful," from Old English selcuð, seld-cuð, from seldan + cuð  (see couth). Old English seldan had comparative seldor, superlative seldost; in early Middle English, as seldan changed form and lost its connection with these, selde was formed as a positive. Shakespeare uses seld-shown.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 seldum, alteration of seldan "seldom, rarely," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *selda- "strange, rare" (source also of 古北欧语 sjaldan, 古弗里西语 selden, 荷兰语 zelden, 古高地德语 seltan, 德语 selten), 或许 最终源自 the base of self (q.v.). Shakespeare uses seld-shown.

example.en: She seldom goes to the cinema since she prefers watching films at home.
example.zh: 她很少去电影院，因为她更喜欢在家看电影。

entries.definition: vt.选择，挑选 a. 精选的，选择的
entries.etymology: 1560s, from Latin selectus, past participle of seligere "choose out, single out, select; separate, cull," from se- "apart" (see secret (n.)) + legere "to gather, select" (see lecture (n.)). The noun meaning "a selected person or thing, that which is choice" is recorded from c. 1600. New England selectman first recorded 1640s.

The 名词 意为 "a selected person or thing, that which is choice" 见于 约 1600 年. New England selectman 首见于 1640 年代.

entries.definition: n. 选择，挑选；被挑选出来的 人，精选品
entries.etymology: 1620s, "act of selecting," from Latin selectionem (nominative selectio) "a choosing out, choice, selection," noun of action from past participle stem of seligere (see select (adj.)). Meaning "thing selected" is from 1805. Biological sense is from 1837; applied to actions of breeders (methodical selection), hence its use by Darwin (natural selection; 1857). French sélection is a 19c. borrowing from English.

example.en: The store offers a carefully curated selection of organic foods.
example.zh: 这家店提供经过精心筛选的有机食品系列。

entries.etymology:
Old English self, seolf, sylf "one's own person, -self; own, same," from Proto-Germanic *selbaz (source also of Old Norse sjalfr, Old Frisian self, Dutch zelf, Old High German selb, German selb, selbst, Gothic silba), Proto-Germanic *selbaz "self," from PIE *sel-bho-, suffixed form of root *s(w)e-, pronoun of the third person and reflexive (referring back to the subject of a sentence), also used in forms denoting the speaker's social group, "(we our-)selves" (see idiom).

Its use in compounds to form reflexive pronouns grew out of independent use in Old English. As a noun from early 14c.

example.en: She worked hard to build a positive self after years of self-doubt.

entries.etymology:
1630s, from self- + -ish. Said in Hacket's life of Archbishop Williams (1693) to have been coined by Presbyterians. In the 17c., synonyms included self-seeking (1620s), self-ended and self-ful.
Related: Selfishly; selfishness.
Similar formations in German selbstisch, Swedish sjelfvisk, Danish selvisk.
entries.etymologyZh: 1630 年代, 源自 self- + -ish. Said in Hacket's life of Archbishop Williams (1693 年) to have been coined by Presbyterians. In the 17 世纪, synonyms included self-seeking (1620 年代), self-ended and self-ful. 同源词：Selfishly; selfishness. Similar formations in 德语 selbstisch, Swedish sjelfvisk, Danish selvisk.

entries.etymology:
Old English sellan "to give, furnish, supply, lend; surrender, give up; deliver to; promise," from Proto-Germanic *saljan "offer up, deliver" (source also of Old Norse selja "to hand over, deliver, sell;" Old Frisian sella, Old High German sellen "to give, hand over, sell;" Gothic saljan "to offer a sacrifice"), ultimately from PIE root *sel- (3) "to take, grasp."

Meaning "to give up for money" had emerged by c. 1000, but in Chaucer selle still can mean "to give." Students of Old English learn early that the word that looks like sell usually means "give." An Old English word for "to sell" was bebycgan, from bycgan "to buy."

Slang meaning "to swindle" is from 1590s. The noun phrase hard sell is recorded from 1952. To sell one's soul is from c. 1570. Sell-by date is from 1972. To sell like hot cakes is from 1839. Selling-point attested from 1959.

To sell (someone) down the river figuratively is by 1927, probably from or with recollection of slavery days, on notion of sale from the Upper South to the cotton plantations of the Deep South (attested in this literal sense since 1851).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sellan "to give, furnish, supply, lend; surrender, give up; deliver to; promise," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *saljan "offer up, deliver" (source also of 古北欧语 selja "to hand over, deliver, sell;" 古弗里西语 sella, 古高地德语 sellen "to give, hand over, sell;" Gothic saljan "to offer a sacrifice"), 最终源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sel- (3) "to take, grasp." 义为 "to give up for money" had emerged by 约 1000 年, but in Chaucer selle still can mean "to give." Students of 古英语 learn early that the word that looks like sell 通常 means "give." An 古英语 word for "to sell" was bebycgan, 源自 bycgan "to buy." Slang 意为 "to swindle" 始于 1590 年代. The 名词 phrase hard sell 见于 1952 年. To sell one's soul 始于 约 1570 年. Sell-by date 始于 1972 年. To sell like hot cakes 始于 1839 年. Selling-point attested 自 1959 年起. To sell (someone) down the river figuratively is 截至 1927 年, 可能 源自 or with recollection of slavery days, on 概念 sale 源自 Upper South to the cotton plantations of the Deep South (见于 this literal sense 自 1851 年).

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "member of an (ancient) senate," from Old French senator (Modern French sénateur), from Latin senator "member of the senate," from senex "old; old man" (see senate). entries.etymology:
Old English sendan "send, send forth; throw, impel," from Proto-Germanic *sandijan (source also of Old Saxon sendian, Old Norse and Old Frisian senda, Middle Low German and Middle Dutch senden, Dutch zenden, German senden, Gothic sandjan), causative form of base *sinþan, denoting "go, journey" (source of Old English sið "way, journey," Old Norse sinn, Gothic sinþs "going, walk, time"), from PIE root *sent- "to head for, go" (source also of Lithuanian siusti "send;" see sense (n.)).

Also used in Old English of divine ordinance (as in godsend, from Old English sand "messenger, message," from Proto-Germanic *sandaz "that which is sent"). Slang sense of "to transport with emotion, delight" is recorded from 1932, in American English jazz slang.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sendan "send, send forth; throw, impel," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sandijan (source also of 古撒克逊语 sendian, 古北欧语 and 古弗里西语 senda, Middle Low 德语 and Middle 荷兰语 senden, 荷兰语 zenden, 德语 senden, Gothic sandjan), causative form of base *sinþan, denoting "go, journey" (source of 古英语 sið "way, journey," 古北欧语 sinn, Gothic sinþs "going, walk, time"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sent- "to head for, go" (source also of Lithuanian siusti "send;" 参见 sense （名）). Also used in 古英语 of divine ordinance (as in godsend, 源自 古英语 sand "messenger, message," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sandaz "that which is sent"). Slang 语义 "to transport with emotion, delight" 见于 1932 年, in American English jazz 俚语.

entries.etymology:
late 13c., from Latin senior "older," comparative of senex (genitive senis) "old," from PIE root *sen- "old" (see senile). Original use in English was as an addition to a personal name indicating "the father" when father and son had the same name; meaning "higher in rank, longer in service" first recorded 1510s.

The Latin word yielded titles of respect in many languages, such as French sire, Spanish señor, Portuguese senhor, Italian signor. Senior citizen first recorded 1938, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, 源自 拉丁语 senior "older," comparative of senex (属格 senis) "old," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sen- "old" （参见 senile). Original use in English was 作为 addition to a personal name indicating "the father" when father and son had the same name; 意为 "higher in rank, longer in service" 首见于 1510 年代. The 拉丁语 word yielded titles of respect in many languages, such as 法语 sire, 西班牙语 señor, 葡萄牙语 senhor, 意大利语 signor. Senior citizen 首见于 1938 年, American English.

entries.etymology:
c. 1400, "faculty of perception," also "meaning, import, interpretation" (especially of Holy Scripture), from Old French sens "one of the five senses; meaning; wit, understanding" (12c.) and directly from Latin sensus "perception, feeling, undertaking, meaning," from sentire "perceive, feel, know," probably a figurative use of a literally meaning "to find one's way," or "to go mentally," from PIE root *sent- "to go" (source also of Old High German sinnan "to go, travel, strive after, have in mind, perceive," German Sinn "sense, mind," Old English sið "way, journey," Old Irish set, Welsh hynt "way"). Application to any one of the external or outward senses (touch, sight, hearing, etc.) in English first recorded 1520s.

Meaning "that which is wise" is from c. 1600. Meaning "capacity for perception and appreciation" is from c. 1600 (as in sense of humor, attested by 1783, sense of shame, 1640s).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "faculty of perception," also "meaning, import, interpretation" (尤指 of Holy Scripture), 源自 古法语 sens "one of the five senses; meaning; wit, understanding" (12 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 sensus "perception, feeling, undertaking, meaning," 源自 sentire "perceive, feel, know," 可能 a figurative use of a 字面义为 意为 "to find one's way," or "to go mentally," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sent- "to go" (source also of 古高地德语 sinnan "to go, travel, strive after, have in mind, perceive," 德语 Sinn "sense, mind," 古英语 sið "way, journey," Old 爱尔兰语 set, Welsh hynt "way"). Application to any one of the external or outward senses (touch, sight, hearing, etc.) in English 首见于 1520 年代. 义为 "that which is wise" 始于 约 1600 年. 义为 "capacity for perception and appreciation" 始于 约 1600 年 (as in 语义 humor, attested 截至 1783 年, 语义 shame, 1640 年代).

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "capable of sensation or feeling;" also "capable of being sensed or felt, perceptible to the senses," hence "easily understood; logical, reasonable," from Late Latin sensibilis "having feeling: perceptible by the senses," from sensus, past participle of sentire "perceive, feel" (see sense (n.)). Of persons, "aware, cognizant (of something)" early 15c.; "having good sense, capable of reasoning, discerning, clever," mid-15c. Of clothes, shoes, etc., "practical rather than fashionable" it is attested from 1855.

Other Middle English senses included "susceptible to injury or pain" (early 15c., now gone with sensitive); "worldly, temporal, outward" (c. 1400); "carnal, unspiritual" (early 15c., now gone with sensual). Related: Sensibleness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "capable of sensation or feeling;" also "capable of being sensed or felt, perceptible to the senses," hence "easily understood; logical, reasonable," 源自 晚期拉丁语 sensibilis "having feeling: perceptible by the senses," 源自 sensus, 为 … 的过去分词 sentire "perceive, feel" （参见 sense （名）). Of persons, "aware, cognizant (of something)" 15 世纪初; "having good sense, capable of reasoning, discerning, clever," 15 世纪中期 Of clothes, shoes, etc., "practical rather than fashionable" it 见于 1855 年. Other 中古英语 senses included "susceptible to injury or pain" (15 世纪初, 现在 gone with sensitive); "worldly, temporal, outward" (约 1400 年); "carnal, unspiritual" (15 世纪初, 现在 gone with sensual). 同源词：Sensibleness.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., in reference to the body or its parts, "having the function of sensation;" also (early 15c.) "pertaining to the faculty of the soul that receives and analyzes sensory information;" from Old French sensitif "capable of feeling" (13c.) and directly from Medieval Latin sensitivus "capable of sensation," from Latin sensus, past participle of sentire "feel perceive" (see sense (n.)).

Meaning "easily affected" (with reference to mental feelings) first recorded 1816; meaning "having intense physical sensation" is from 1849. Original meaning is preserved in sensitive plant (1630s), which is "mechanically irritable in a higher degree than almost any other plant" [Century Dictionary]. Meaning "involving national security" is recorded from 1953. Related: Sensitively; sensitiveness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, in reference to the body or its parts, "having the function of sensation;" also (15 世纪初) "pertaining to the faculty of the soul that receives and analyzes sensory information;" 源自 古法语 sensitif "capable of feeling" (13 世纪) and 直接源自 中古拉丁语 sensitivus "capable of sensation," 源自 拉丁语 sensus, 为 … 的过去分词 sentire "feel perceive" （参见 sense （名）). 义为 "easily affected" (with reference to mental feelings) 首见于 1816 年; 意为 "having intense physical sensation" 始于 1849 年. Original 意为 is preserved in sensitive plant (1630 年代), which is "mechanically irritable in a higher degree than almost any other plant" [Century Dictionary]. 义为 "involving national security" 见于 1953 年. 同源词：Sensitively; sensitiveness.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "carnal, unspiritual;" mid-15c., "of or pertaining to the senses," from Middle French sensuel (15c.) and directly from Late Latin sensualis "endowed with feeling" (see sensuality). entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "carnal, unspiritual;" 15 世纪中期, "of or pertaining to the senses," 源自 中古法语 sensuel (15 世纪) and 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 sensualis "endowed with feeling" （参见 sensuality). 义为 "connected with gratification of the senses," 尤指 "lewd, unchaste" 见于 15 世纪晚期

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "doctrine, authoritative teaching; an authoritative pronouncement," from Old French sentence "judgment, decision; meaning; aphorism, maxim; statement of authority" (12c.) and directly from Latin sententia "thought, way of thinking, opinion; judgment, decision," also "a thought expressed; aphorism, saying," from sentientem, present participle of sentire "be of opinion, feel, perceive" (see sense (n.)). Loss of first -i- in Latin by dissimilation.

From early 14c. as "judgment rendered by God, or by one in authority; a verdict, decision in court;" from late 14c. as "understanding, wisdom; edifying subject matter." From late 14c. as "subject matter or content of a letter, book, speech, etc.," also in reference to a passage in a written work. Sense of "grammatically complete statement" is attested from mid-15c. "Meaning," then "meaning expressed in words." Related: Sentential.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "doctrine, authoritative teaching; an authoritative pronouncement," 源自 古法语 sentence "judgment, decision; meaning; aphorism, maxim; statement of authority" (12 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 sententia "thought, way of thinking, opinion; judgment, decision," also "a thought expressed; aphorism, saying," 源自 sentientem, 为 … 的现在分词 sentire "be of opinion, feel, perceive" （参见 sense （名）). Loss of first -i- in 拉丁语 by dissimilation. From 14 世纪初 as "judgment rendered by God, or by one in authority; a verdict, decision in court;" 源自 14 世纪晚期 as "understanding, wisdom; edifying subject matter." From 14 世纪晚期 as "subject matter or content of a letter, book, speech, etc.," also in reference to a passage in a written work. 义为 "grammatically complete statement" 见于 15 世纪中期 "Meaning," 之后 "meaning expressed in words." 同源词：Sentential.

definitionLines: n. 多愁善感；感情，情绪
entries.definition: n. 多愁善感；感情，情绪
entries.etymology:
late 14c., sentement, "personal experience, one's own feeling," from Old French sentement (12c.), from Medieval Latin sentimentum "feeling, affection, opinion," from Latin sentire "to feel" (see sense (n.)).

Meaning "what one feels about something" (1630s) and modern spelling seem to be a re-introduction from French (where it was spelled sentiment by 17c.). A vogue word mid-18c. with wide application, commonly "a thought colored by or proceeding from emotion" (1762), especially as expressed in literature or art. The 17c. sense is preserved in phrases such as my sentiments exactly.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, sentement, "personal experience, one's own feeling," 源自 古法语 sentement (12 世纪), 源自 中古拉丁语 sentimentum "feeling, affection, opinion," 源自 拉丁语 sentire "to feel" （参见 sense （名）). 义为 "what one feels about something" (1630 年代) and modern spelling seem to be a re-introduction 源自 法语 (where it was spelled sentiment by 17 世纪). A vogue word 18 世纪中期 with wide application, commonly "a thought colored by or proceeding from emotion" (1762 年), 尤指 as expressed in literature or art. The 17 世纪 sense is preserved in phrases such as my sentiments exactly.

entries.etymology: late Old English, from Latin September (also source of Old French Septembre, Spanish Setiembre, Italian Settembre, German September), from septem "seven" (see seven). So called because it was the seventh month of the old Roman calendar, which began the year in March; Julian calendar reform (46 B.C.E.) shifted the new year back two months. For -ber suffix, see December. Replaced Old English hærfestmonað, haligmonað. Related: Septembral.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语, 源自 拉丁语 September (also source of 古法语 Septembre, 西班牙语 Setiembre, 意大利语 Settembre, 德语 September), 源自 septem "seven" （参见 seven). So called because it was the seventh month of the old Roman calendar, which began the year in March; Julian calendar reform (46 B.C.E.) shifted the new year back two months. For -ber suffix, 参见 December. Replaced 古英语 hærfestmonað, haligmonað. 同源词：Septembral.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "servant," from Old French sergent, serjant "(domestic) servant, valet; court official; soldier," from Medieval Latin servientum (nominative serviens) "servant, vassal, soldier" (in Late Latin "public official"), from Latin servientem "serving," present participle of servire "to serve" (see serve (v.)); cognate with Spanish sirviente, Italian servente; a twin of servant, and 16c. writers sometimes use the two words interchangeably.

Specific sense of "military servant" is attested from late 13c.; that of "officer whose duty is to enforce judgments of a tribunal or legislative body" is from c. 1300 (sergeant at arms is attested from late 14c.). Meaning "non-commissioned military officer" first recorded 1540s. Originally a much more important rank than presently. As a police rank, in Great Britain from 1839.

Middle English alternative spelling serjeant (from Old French) was retained in Britain in special use as title of a superior order of barristers (c. 1300, from legal Latin serviens ad legem, "one who serves (the king) in matters of law"), from which Common Law judges were chosen; also used of certain other officers of the royal household. sergeant-major is from 1570s. The sergeant-fish (1871) so-called for lateral markings resembling a sergeant's stripes. Related: Sergeancy.

Specific 语义 "military servant" 见于 13 世纪晚期; that of "officer whose duty is to enforce judgments of a tribunal or legislative body" 始于 约 1300 年 (sergeant at arms 见于 14 世纪晚期). 义为 "non-commissioned military officer" 首见于 1540 年代. Originally a much more important rank than presently. 作为 police rank, in Great Britain 自 1839 年起. 中古英语 alternative spelling serjeant (源自 古法语) was retained in Britain in special use as title of a superior order of barristers (约 1300 年, 源自 legal 拉丁语 serviens ad legem, "one who serves (the king) in matters of law"), 源自 which Common Law judges were chosen; also used of certain other officers of the royal household. sergeant-major 始于 1570 年代. The sergeant-fish (1871 年) so-called for lateral markings resembling a sergeant's stripes. 同源词：Sergeancy.

entries.etymology: "coming in regular succession," 1840, from series + -al (1); popularized in reference to Dickens' novels, published one part at a time in periodicals (as opposed to all at once in a book). Found to be a useful word and given wide application. Serial number, indicating position in a series, first recorded 1866, originally of papers, packages, etc.; of soldiers from 1918. Serial killer is first attested 1981 (in relation to John Wayne Gacy and Ted Bundy), though serial had been used in connection with murders since the early 1960s. Related: Serially.

definitionLines: n. 一系列，一连串，序列；丛书
entries.definition: n. 一系列，一连串，序列；丛书
entries.etymology:
1610s, "a number or set of things of one kind arranged in a line," from Latin series "row, chain, series, sequence, succession," from serere "to join, link, bind together, arrange, attach, put; join in speech, discuss," from PIE root *ser- (3) "to line up, join" (source also of Sanskrit sarat- "thread," Greek eirein "to fasten together in rows," Gothic sarwa (plural) "armor, arms," Old Norse sörve "necklace of stringed pearls," Old Irish sernaid "he joins together," Welsh ystret "row").

Meaning "set of printed works published consecutively" is from 1711. Meaning "set of radio or television programs with the same characters and themes" is attested from 1949. Baseball sense "set of games on consecutive days between the same teams" is from 1862.

Meaning "professed lover, one devoted to the service of a lady" is from mid-14c. In North American colonies and U.S., the usual designation for "slave" 17c.-18c. (in 14c.-15c. and later in Biblical translations the word often was used to render Latin servus, Greek doulos "slave"). Public servant is attested from 1670s.

entries.etymology:
late 12c., "to render habitual obedience to," also "minister, give aid, give help," from Old French servir "to do duty toward, show devotion to; set table, serve at table; offer, provide with," from Latin servire "be a servant, be in service, be enslaved;" figuratively "be devoted; be governed by; comply with; conform; flatter," originally "be a slave," related to servus "slave," perhaps from Etruscan (compare Etruscan proper names Servi, Serve, Latinized as Servius).

By c. 1200 also as "to be in the service of, perform a service for; attend upon, be personal servant to; be a slave; owe allegiance to; officiate at Mass or other religious rites;" from early 13c. as "set food at table;" mid-14c. as "to wait on (customers)." From late 14c. as "treat (someone or something) in some fashion." To serve (someone) right "to treat as he deserves" is recorded from 1580s.

Sense of "be useful, be beneficial, be suitable for a purpose or function" is from early 14c.; that of "take the place or meet the needs of, be equal to the task" is from late 14c.; that of "suffice" is from mid-15c. Meaning "render active military service" is from 1510s. Sporting sense, in tennis, badminton, etc., first recorded 1580s. Legal sense "present" (a writ, warrant,etc.), "give legal notice of" is from early 15c.

From 14 世纪晚期 as "treat (someone or something) in some fashion." To serve (someone) right "to treat as he deserves" 见于 1580 年代. 义为 "be useful, be beneficial, be suitable for a purpose or function" 始于 14 世纪初; that of "take the place or meet the needs of, be equal to the task" 始于 14 世纪晚期; that of "suffice" 始于 15 世纪中期 义为 "render active military service" 始于 1510 年代. entries.etymology:
"come to rest," Old English setlan "cause to sit, place, put," from setl "a seat" (see settle (n.)). Related: Settling. Compare German siedeln "to settle, colonize." 

From c. 1300 of birds, etc., "to alight." From early 14c. as "sink down, descend; cave in." Early 15c. in reference to suspended particles in a liquid. Sense of "establish a permanent residence" first recorded 1620s; that of "decide" is 1620s. Meaning "secure title to by deed" is from 1660s.

Meaning "reconcile" (a quarrel, differences, etc.) perhaps is influenced by Middle English sahtlen "to reconcile," from Old English saht "reconciliation," from Old Norse satt "reconciliation." To settle down "become content" is from 1853; transitive sense from 1520s; as what married couples do in establishing domesticity, from 1718. To settle for "content oneself with" is from 1943.

From 约 1300 年 of birds, etc., "to alight." From 14 世纪初 as "sink down, descend; cave in." Early 15 世纪 in reference to suspended particles in a liquid. 义为 "establish a permanent residence" 首见于 1620 年代; that of "decide" is 1620 年代. 义为 "secure title to by deed" 始于 1660 年代. 义为 "reconcile" (a quarrel, differences, etc.) 或许 is influenced by 中古英语 sahtlen "to reconcile," 源自 古英语 saht "reconciliation," 源自 古北欧语 satt "reconciliation." To settle down "become content" 始于 1853 年; transitive sense 源自 1520 年代; as what married couples do in establishing domesticity, 自 1718 年起. To settle for "content oneself with" 始于 1943 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English seofon, from Proto-Germanic *sebun (source also of Old Saxon sibun, Old Norse sjau, Swedish sju, Danish syv, Old Frisian sowen, siugun, Middle Dutch seven, Dutch zeven, Old High German sibun, German sieben, Gothic sibun), from PIE *septm "seven" (source also of Sanskrit sapta, Avestan hapta, Hittite shipta, Greek hepta, Latin septem, Old Church Slavonic sedmi, Lithuanian septyni, Old Irish secht, Welsh saith).

Long regarded as a number of perfection (seven wonders; seven sleepers, the latter translating Latin septem dormientes; seven against Thebes, etc.), but that notion is late in Old English and in German a nasty, troublesome woman could be eine böse Sieben "an evil seven" (1662).

Magical power or healing skill associated since 16c. with the seventh son ["The seuenth Male Chyld by iust order (neuer a Gyrle or Wench being borne betweene)," Thomas Lupton, "A Thousand Notable Things," 1579]. The typical number for "very great, strong," as in seven-league boots in the fairy story of Hop o'my Thumb. The Seven Years' War (1756-63) is also the Third Silesian War.

The Seven Stars (Old English sibunsterri), usually refers to the Pleiades, though in 15c. and after this name occasionally was given to the Big Dipper (which also has seven stars), or the seven planets of classical astronomy. Popular as a tavern sign, it might also (with six in a circle, one in the center) be a Masonic symbol.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 seofon, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sebun (source also of 古撒克逊语 sibun, 古北欧语 sjau, Swedish sju, Danish syv, 古弗里西语 sowen, siugun, Middle 荷兰语 seven, 荷兰语 zeven, 古高地德语 sibun, 德语 sieben, Gothic sibun), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *septm "seven" (source also of 梵语 sapta, Avestan hapta, Hittite shipta, 希腊语 hepta, 拉丁语 septem, Old Church Slavonic sedmi, Lithuanian septyni, Old 爱尔兰语 secht, Welsh saith). Long regarded 作为 number of perfection (seven wonders; seven sleepers, the latter translating 拉丁语 septem dormientes; seven against Thebes, etc.), but that notion is late in 古英语 and in 德语 a nasty, troublesome woman could be eine böse Sieben "an evil seven" (1662 年). Magical power or healing skill associated 自 16 世纪 with the seventh son ["The seuenth Male Chyld by iust order (neuer a Gyrle or Wench being borne betweene)," Thomas Lupton, "A Thousand Notable Things," 1579 年]. The typical number for "very great, strong," as in seven-league boots in the fairy story of Hop o'my Thumb. The Seven Years' War (1756 年-63) is also the Third Silesian War. The Seven Stars (古英语 sibunsterri), 通常 refers to the Pleiades, though in 15 世纪 and after this name occasionally was given to the Big Dipper (which also has seven stars)，或the seven planets of classical astronomy. Popular 作为 tavern sign, it might also (with six in a circle, one in the center) be a Masonic symbol.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from seven + -th (1); earlier sevende, seveth, from Old English seofunda (Anglian, Northumbrian), seofoþa (West Saxon), from Proto-Germanic *sebundon (source also of Old Norse sjaundi, Old Saxon sivondo, Old High German sibunto, German siebente, siebte). The music note sense is from 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 seven + -th (1); earlier sevende, seveth, 源自 古英语 seofunda (Anglian, Northumbrian), seofoþa (West Saxon), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sebundon (source also of 古北欧语 sjaundi, 古撒克逊语 sivondo, 古高地德语 sibunto, 德语 siebente, siebte). The music note sense 始于 1590 年代.

entries.etymology:
early 15c., "existing apart," from Anglo-French several, from Middle French seperalis "separate," from Medieval Latin separalis, from Latin separ "separate, different," back-formation from separare "to separate" (see separate (v.)). Meaning "various, diverse, different" is attested from c. 1500; that of "more than one" is from 1530s, originally in legal use.

Related: Severalty. Jocular ordinal form severalth attested from 1902 in American English dialect (see -th (2)).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "existing apart," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 several, 源自 中古法语 seperalis "separate," 源自 中古拉丁语 separalis, 源自 拉丁语 separ "separate, different," back-formation 源自 separare "to separate" （参见 separate （动）). 义为 "various, diverse, different" 见于 约 1500 年; that of "more than one" 始于 1530 年代, 原义为 in legal use. 同源词：Severalty. Jocular ordinal form severalth attested 自 1902 年起 in American English dialect （参见 -th (2)).

entries.etymology: Old English siwian "to stitch, sew, mend, patch, knit together," earlier siowian, from Proto-Germanic *siwjanan (source also of Old Norse syja, Swedish sy, Danish sye, Old Frisian sia, Old High German siuwan, Gothic siujan "to sew"), from PIE root *syu- "to bind, sew" (source also of Sanskrit sivyati "sews," sutram "thread, string;" Greek hymen "thin skin, membrane," hymnos "song;" Latin suere "to sew, sew together;" Old Church Slavonic šijo "to sew," šivu "seam;" Lettish siuviu, siuti "to sew," siuvikis "tailor;" Russian švec "tailor"). Related: Sewed; sewing. To sew (something) up "bring it to a conclusion" is a figurative use attested by 1904.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 siwian "to stitch, sew, mend, patch, knit together," earlier siowian, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *siwjanan (source also of 古北欧语 syja, Swedish sy, Danish sye, 古弗里西语 sia, 古高地德语 siuwan, Gothic siujan "to sew"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *syu- "to bind, sew" (source also of 梵语 sivyati "sews," sutram "thread, string;" 希腊语 hymen "thin skin, membrane," hymnos "song;" 拉丁语 suere "to sew, sew together;" Old Church Slavonic šijo "to sew," šivu "seam;" Lettish siuviu, siuti "to sew," siuvikis "tailor;" 俄语 švec "tailor"). 同源词：Sewed; sewing. To sew (something) up "bring it to a conclusion" is a figurative use attested 截至 1904 年.

example.en: My grandmother taught me how to sew buttons onto a shirt.
example.zh: 我祖母教我如何将纽扣缝在衬衫上。

entries.etymology: 1884, "to determine the sex of," from sex (n.); to sex (something) up "increase the sex appeal of" is recorded from 1942. Related: Sexed; sexing.
entries.etymologyZh: 1884 年, "to determine the sex of," 源自 sex （名）; to sex (something) up "increase the sex appeal of" 见于 1942 年. 同源词：Sexed; sexing.

entries.etymology: 1650s, "of or pertaining to the fact of being male or female," from Late Latin sexualis "relating to sex," from Latin sexus (see sex (n.)). Meaning "pertaining to copulation or generation" is from 1766; sexual intercourse attested by 1771; sexual orientation by 1967; sexual harassment by 1975. Sexual revolution attested by 1962. Sexual politics is from 1970. Related: Sexually.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, "of or pertaining to the fact of being male or female," 源自 晚期拉丁语 sexualis "relating to sex," 源自 拉丁语 sexus （参见 sex （名）). 义为 "pertaining to copulation or generation" 始于 1766 年; sexual intercourse attested 截至 1771 年; sexual orientation 截至 1967 年; sexual harassment 截至 1975 年. Sexual revolution attested 截至 1962 年. Sexual politics 始于 1970 年. 同源词：Sexually.

entries.etymology:
Middle English schade, Kentish ssed, from late Old English scead "partial darkness; shelter, protection," also partly from sceadu "shade, shadow, darkness; shady place, arbor, protection from glare or heat," both from Proto-Germanic *skadwaz (source also of Old Saxon skado, Middle Dutch scade, Dutch schaduw, Old High German scato, German Schatten, Gothic skadus), from PIE *skot-wo-, from root *skot- "dark, shade" (source also of Greek skotos "darkness, gloom," Albanian kot "darkness," Old Irish scath, Old Welsh scod, Breton squeut "darkness," Gaelic sgath "shade, shadow, shelter").

Figurative use in reference to comparative obscurity is from 1640s. Meaning "a ghost" is from 1610s; dramatic (or mock-dramatic) expression "shades of _____" to invoke or acknowledge a memory is from 1818, from the "ghost" sense. Meaning "lamp cover" is from 1780. Sense of "window blind" first recorded 1845. Meaning "cover to protect the eyes" is from 1801. Meaning "grade of color" first recorded 1680s; that of "degree or gradiation of darkness in a color" is from 1680s (compare nuance, from French nue "cloud"). Meaning "small amount or degree" is from 1782.
entries.etymologyZh: 中古英语 schade, Kentish ssed, 源自 late 古英语 scead "partial darkness; shelter, protection," also partly 源自 sceadu "shade, shadow, darkness; shady place, arbor, protection from glare or heat," both 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skadwaz (source also of 古撒克逊语 skado, Middle 荷兰语 scade, 荷兰语 schaduw, 古高地德语 scato, 德语 Schatten, Gothic skadus), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *skot-wo-, 源自 root *skot- "dark, shade" (source also of 希腊语 skotos "darkness, gloom," Albanian kot "darkness," Old 爱尔兰语 scath, Old Welsh scod, Breton squeut "darkness," Gaelic sgath "shade, shadow, shelter"). Figurative use in reference to comparative obscurity 始于 1640 年代. 义为 "a ghost" 始于 1610 年代; dramatic (or mock-dramatic) expression "shades of _____" to invoke or acknowledge a memory 始于 1818 年, 源自 "ghost" sense. 义为 "lamp cover" 始于 1780 年. 义为 "window blind" 首见于 1845 年. 义为 "cover to protect the eyes" 始于 1801 年. 义为 "grade of color" 首见于 1680 年代; that of "degree or gradiation of darkness in a color" 始于 1680 年代 (对比 nuance, 源自 法语 nue "cloud"). 义为 "small amount or degree" 始于 1782 年.

example.en: The tree cast a cool shade over the garden bench.
example.zh: 那棵树在花园长椅上投下一片凉爽的阴影。

definitionLines: n. 影子，阴影；暗处，阴暗
entries.definition: n. 影子，阴影；暗处，阴暗
entries.etymology: Middle English schadowen, Kentish ssedwi, from late Old English sceadwian "to protect as with covering wings" (also see overshadow), from the root of shadow (n.). Similar formation in Old Saxon skadoian, Dutch schaduwen, Old High German scatewen, German (über)schatten. From mid-14c. as "provide shade;" late 14c. as "cast a shadow over" (literal and figurative), from early 15c. as "darken" (in illustration, etc.). Meaning "to follow like a shadow" is from c. 1600 in an isolated instance; not attested again until 1872. Related: Shadowed; shadowing.
entries.etymologyZh: 中古英语 schadowen, Kentish ssedwi, 源自 late 古英语 sceadwian "to protect as with covering wings" (also 参见 overshadow), 源自 root of shadow （名）. Similar formation in 古撒克逊语 skadoian, 荷兰语 schaduwen, 古高地德语 scatewen, 德语 (über)schatten. From 14 世纪中期 as "provide shade;" 14 世纪晚期 as "cast a shadow over" (literal and figurative), 源自 15 世纪初 as "darken" (in illustration, etc.). 义为 "to follow like a shadow" 始于 约 1600 年 in an isolated instance; not attested again until 1872 年. 同源词：Shadowed; shadowing.

example.en: The tree cast a long shadow on the garden path.
example.zh: 那棵树在花园小径上投下了长长的影子。

definitionLines: v. 摇，摇动；震动，颤抖；握手
entries.definition: v. 摇，摇动；震动，颤抖；握手 n. 摇动，震动，抖动
entries.etymology: late 14c., "charge, onrush," from shake (v.). Meaning "a hard shock" is from 1560s. From 1580s as "act of shaking;" 1660s as "irregular vibration." The hand-grip salutation so called by 1712. As a figure of instantaneous action, it is recorded from 1816. Phrase fair shake "honest deal" is attested from 1830, American English (Bartlett calls it "A New England vulgarism"). The shakes "nervous agitation" is from 1620s. Short for milk shake from 1911. Dismissive phrase no great shakes (1816, Byron) perhaps is from dicing.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "charge, onrush," 源自 shake （动）. 义为 "a hard shock" 始于 1560 年代. From 1580 年代 as "act of shaking;" 1660 年代 as "irregular vibration." The hand-grip salutation so called 截至 1712 年. 作为 figure of instantaneous action, it 见于 1816 年. Phrase fair shake "honest deal" 见于 1830 年, American English (Bartlett calls it "A New England vulgarism"). The shakes "nervous agitation" 始于 1620 年代. Short for milk shake 自 1911 年起. Dismissive phrase no great shakes (1816 年, Byron) 或许 始于 dicing.

example.en: The explosion caused the ground to shake for several seconds.
example.zh: 爆炸使地面震动了好几秒钟。

definitionLines: a.摇晃的；不可靠的；不坚定的
entries.definition: a.摇晃的；不可靠的；不坚定的
entries.etymology: 1840, of handwriting; 1841 of persons, horses, and credit; 1850 of structures; from shake (v.) + -y (2). General sense of "uncertain, of questionable integrity" is from 1834. Earliest of trees or logs, "split, having fissures" (1808). Related: Shakily; shakiness.
entries.etymologyZh: 1840 年, of handwriting; 1841 年 of persons, horses, and credit; 1850 年 of structures; 源自 shake （动） + -y (2). General 语义 "uncertain, of questionable integrity" 始于 1834 年. Earliest of trees or logs, "split, having fissures" (1808 年). 同源词：Shakily; shakiness.

definitionLines: auz. v. 将，将要；必须，应该
entries.definition: auz. v. 将，将要；必须，应该
entries.etymology:
Old English sceal, Northumbrian scule "I owe/he owes, will have to, ought to, must" (infinitive sculan, past tense sceolde), a common Germanic preterite-present verb (along with can, may, will), from Proto-Germanic *skal- (source also of Old Saxon sculan, Old Frisian skil, Old Norse and Swedish skola, Middle Dutch sullen, Old High German solan, German sollen, Gothic skulan "to owe, be under obligation;" related via past tense form to Old English scyld "guilt," German Schuld "guilt, debt;" also Old Norse Skuld, name of one of the Norns), from PIE root *skel- (2) "to be under an obligation."

Ground sense of the Germanic word probably is "I owe," hence "I ought." The sense shifted in Middle English from a notion of "obligation" to include "futurity." Its past tense form has become should (q.v.). Cognates outside Germanic are Lithuanian skeleti "to be guilty," skilti "to get into debt;" Old Prussian skallisnan "duty," skellants "guilty."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sceal, Northumbrian scule "I owe/he owes, will have to, ought to, must" (infinitive sculan, past tense sceolde), a common 日耳曼语 preterite-present 动词 (along with can, may, will), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skal- (source also of 古撒克逊语 sculan, 古弗里西语 skil, 古北欧语 and Swedish skola, Middle 荷兰语 sullen, 古高地德语 solan, 德语 sollen, Gothic skulan "to owe, be under obligation;" related 经由 past tense form to 古英语 scyld "guilt," 德语 Schuld "guilt, debt;" also 古北欧语 Skuld, name of one of the Norns), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *skel- (2) "to be under an obligation." Ground 语义 the 日耳曼语 word 可能 is "I owe," hence "I ought." The sense shifted in 中古英语 源自 a 概念 "obligation" to include "futurity." Its past tense form has become should (q.v.). Cognates outside 日耳曼语 are Lithuanian skeleti "to be guilty," skilti "to get into debt;" Old Prussian skallisnan "duty," skellants "guilty."

entries.definition: a. 浅；浅薄，肤浅的 n. （pl.）浅滩，浅处
entries.etymology: c. 1400, schalowe "not deep," probably from or related to Old English sceald (see shoal (n.)). Of breathing, attested from 1875; of thought or feeling, "superficial," first recorded 1580s. The noun, usually shallows, is first recorded 1570s, from the adjective.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, schalowe "not deep," 可能 源自 or related to 古英语 sceald （参见 shoal （名）). Of breathing, attested 自 1875 年起; of thought or feeling, "superficial," 首见于 1580 年代. The 名词, 通常 shallows, is 首见于 1570 年代, 源自 形容词.

example.en: Children played safely in the shallow end of the pool.
example.zh: 孩子们在泳池的浅水区安全地玩耍。

definitionLines: n. 羞愧，耻辱；可耻的人/物
entries.definition: n. 羞愧，耻辱；可耻的人/物 vt. 使羞愧，玷辱
entries.etymology:
Old English scamu, sceomu "feeling of guilt or disgrace; confusion caused by shame; disgrace, dishonor, insult, loss of esteem or reputation; shameful circumstance, what brings disgrace; modesty; private parts," from Proto-Germanic *skamo (source also of Old Saxon skama, Old Norse skömm, Swedish skam, Old Frisian scome, Dutch schaamte, Old High German scama, German Scham). The best guess is that this is from PIE *skem-, from *kem- "to cover" (covering oneself being a common expression of shame).

Until modern times English had a productive duplicate form in shand. An Old Norse word for it was kinnroði, literally "cheek-redness," hence, "blush of shame." Greek distinguished shame in the bad sense of "disgrace, dishonor" (aiskhyne) from shame in the good sense of "modesty, bashfulness" (aidos). To put (someone or something) to shame is mid-13c. Shame culture attested by 1947.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scamu, sceomu "feeling of guilt or disgrace; confusion caused by shame; disgrace, dishonor, insult, loss of esteem or reputation; shameful circumstance, what brings disgrace; modesty; private parts," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skamo (source also of 古撒克逊语 skama, 古北欧语 skömm, Swedish skam, 古弗里西语 scome, 荷兰语 schaamte, 古高地德语 scama, 德语 Scham). The best guess is that this 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *skem-, 源自 *kem- "to cover" (covering oneself being a common expression of shame). Until modern times English had a productive duplicate form in shand. An 古北欧语 word for it was kinnroði, 字面义为 "cheek-redness," hence, "blush of shame." 希腊语 distinguished shame in the bad 语义 "disgrace, dishonor" (aiskhyne) 源自 shame in the good 语义 "modesty, bashfulness" (aidos). To put (someone or something) to shame is 13 世纪中期 Shame culture attested 截至 1947 年.

example.en: The politician felt deep shame after the corruption scandal was exposed.
example.zh: 腐败丑闻曝光后，这位政客感到深深的羞耻。

definitionLines: n. 形状，外形；状况，状态
entries.definition: n. 形状，外形；状况，状态 vt.形成，成形
entries.etymology: Old English sceap, gesceap "form; created being, creature; creation; condition; sex, genitalia," from root of shape (v.)). Meaning "contours of the body" is attested from late 14c. Meaning "condition, state" is first recorded 1865, American English. In Middle English, the word in plural also had a sense of "a woman's private parts." Shape-shifter attested from 1820. Out of shape "not in proper shape" is from 1690s. Shapesmith "one who undertakes to improve the form of the body" was used in 1715.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sceap, gesceap "form; created being, creature; creation; condition; sex, genitalia," 源自 root of shape （动）). 义为 "contours of the body" 见于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "condition, state" is 首见于 1865 年, American English. In 中古英语, the word in plural also had a 语义 "a woman's private parts." Shape-shifter attested 自 1820 年起. Out of shape "not in proper shape" 始于 1690 年代. Shapesmith "one who undertakes to improve the form of the body" was used 于 1715 年.

example.en: Early childhood experiences often shape a person's values and outlook on life.
example.zh: 童年早期经历往往会塑造一个人的价值观和人生观。

definitionLines: vt. 分享，分担；均分，分配
n. 部分，一份；分担；份子，份 额，股份
entries.definition: vt. 分享，分担；均分，分配 vi. （in）分担 n. 部分，一份；分担；份子，份 额，股份
entries.etymology: 1580s, "to apportion to someone as his share; to apportion out to others; to enjoy or suffer (something) with others," from share (n.1). Meaning "to divide one's own and give part to others" is recorded from 1590s. Meaning "confess one's sins openly" (1932, implied in sharing) is from "the language of Moral Rearmament" [OED]. Related: Shared; sharer; sharing.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "to apportion to someone as his share; to apportion out to others; to enjoy or suffer (something) with others," 源自 share (n.1). 义为 "to divide one's own and give part to others" 见于 1590 年代. 义为 "confess one's sins openly" (1932 年, implied in sharing) 始于 "the language of Moral Rearmament" [OED]. 同源词：Shared; sharer; sharing.

example.en: He was happy to share his class notes with anyone who had missed the lecture.
example.zh: 他很乐意把课堂笔记分享给任何缺课的同学。

entries.etymology: c. 1830, from share (n.1) in the financial sense + agent noun from hold (v.).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1830 年, 源自 share (n.1) in the financial sense + agent 名词 源自 hold （动）.

example.en: Each shareholder received a detailed report on the company's annual performance.
example.zh: 每位股东都收到了一份关于公司年度业绩的详细报告。

entries.etymology:
1560s, of uncertain origin; apparently the word and the first specimen were brought to London by Capt. John Hawkins's second expedition (landed 1565; see Hakluyt).

The meaning "dishonest person who preys on others," though attested only from 1599 (sharker "artful swindler" in this sense is from 1594), may be the original sense, later transferred to the large, voracious marine fish. If so, it is possibly from German Schorck, a variant of Schurke "scoundrel, villain," agent noun of Middle High German schürgen (German schüren) "to poke, stir."

But on another theory, the English word is from a Mayan word, xoc, which might have meant "shark." Northern Europeans seem not to have been familiar with sharks before voyages to the tropics began. A slightly earlier name for it in English was tiburon, via Spanish (where it is attested by 1520s), from the Carib name for the fish.

The English word was applied (or re-applied) to voracious or predatory persons, on the image of the fish, from 1707 (originally of pick-pockets); loan shark is attested from 1905. Sharkskin (1851) was used for binding books, etc. As the name of a type of fabric held to resemble it, it is recorded from 1932.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, 来源存疑; 似乎 the word and the first specimen were brought to London by Capt. John Hawkins's second expedition (landed 1565 年; 参见 Hakluyt). If so, it is possibly 源自 德语 Schorck, a 为 … 的变体 Schurke "scoundrel, villain," agent 名词 of Middle High 德语 schürgen (德语 schüren) "to poke, stir." But on another theory, the English word 始于 a Mayan word, xoc, which might have meant "shark." Northern Europeans seem not to have been familiar with sharks before voyages to the tropics began. A slightly earlier name for it in English was tiburon, 经由 西班牙语 (where it is attested by 1520 年代), 源自 Carib name for the fish. The English word was applied (or re-applied) to voracious or predatory persons, on the image of the fish, 自 1707 年起 (原义为 of pick-pockets); loan shark 见于 1905 年. example.en: Divers spotted a shark circling near the reef just below the surface.
example.zh: 潜水员发现一条鲨鱼在礁石附近的水面下盘旋。

definitionLines: a. 锋利的；强烈的；尖刻的；敏 锐的，灵敏的；线条分明的， 鲜明的；急转的，突然的；尖 声的，刺耳的
entries.definition: a. 锋利的；强烈的；尖刻的；敏 锐的，灵敏的；线条分明的， 鲜明的；急转的，突然的；尖 声的，刺耳的 ad.（时间）整，准（时）
entries.etymology: "a cheat at games," 1797, short for sharper (1680s) in this sense. Meaning "expert, connoisseur" is attested from 1840, and likely is from sharp (adj.). Music sense is from 1570s. The noun was used 14c. as "a sharp weapon, edge of a sword."
entries.etymologyZh: "a cheat at games," 1797 年, short for sharper (1680 年代) in this sense. 义为 "expert, connoisseur" 见于 1840 年, and likely 始于 sharp （形）. Music sense 始于 1570 年代. The 名词 was used 14 世纪 as "a sharp weapon, edge of a sword."

example.en: She has a sharp eye for typographical errors in manuscripts.
example.zh: 她对手稿中的排版错误有敏锐的眼光。

entries.definition: vt. 削尖；使敏捷 vi.变锋利
entries.etymology: 1520s, "bring to an edge or point," from sharp (adj.) + -en (1). Related: Sharpened; sharpening. Old English verb scearpian meant "to score, scarify;" also compare scearpung "scarifying." To sharpen (one's) pencil "prepare to get to work" is from 1957, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "bring to an edge or point," 源自 sharp （形） + -en (1). 同源词：Sharpened; sharpening. 古英语 动词 scearpian meant "to score, scarify;" also 对比 scearpung "scarifying." To sharpen (one's) pencil "prepare to get to work" 始于 1957 年, American English.

entries.etymology: Old English scearplice "acutely, keenly; painfully, severely; attentively, quickly;" see sharp (adj.) + -ly (2). Old English also had adverbial form scearpe "sharply."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scearplice "acutely, keenly; painfully, severely; attentively, quickly;" 参见 sharp （形） + -ly (2). 古英语 also had adverbial form scearpe "sharply."

example.en: Temperatures dropped sharply overnight, catching many people off guard.
example.zh: 气温在一夜之间急剧下降，让许多人措手不及。

definitionLines: vt. 打碎；破掉；粉碎；破坏
entries.definition: vt. 打碎；破掉；粉碎；破坏 vi. 粉碎；损坏
entries.etymology: early 14c., transitive, probably a variant of Middle English scateren (see scatter (v.)). Compare Old Dutch schetteren Low German schateren. Formations such as scatter-brained had parallel forms in shatter-brained, etc. Intransitive sense from 1560s. Related: Shattered; shattering. Carlyle (1841) used shatterment. Shatters "fragments" is from 1630s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, transitive, 可能 a 为 … 的变体 中古英语 scateren （参见 scatter （动）). 对比 古荷兰语 schetteren Low 德语 schateren. Formations such as scatter-brained had parallel forms in shatter-brained, etc. Intransitive sense 源自 1560 年代. 同源词：Shattered; shattering. Carlyle (1841 年) used shatterment. Shatters "fragments" 始于 1630 年代.

example.en: The vase fell off the shelf and shattered into a hundred pieces on the floor.
example.zh: 花瓶从架子上掉落，在地板上摔成了无数碎片。

entries.definition: vt. 剃，刮，削 vi. 修面，刮脸 n.刮脸
entries.etymology: c. 1600, "something shaved off;" from shave (v.); Old English sceafa meant "tool for shaving." Meaning "operation of shaving" is from 1838. Meaning "a grazing touch" is recorded from 1834. Phrase a close shave is from 1856, on notion of "a slight, grazing touch."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1600 年, "something shaved off;" 源自 shave （动）; 古英语 sceafa meant "tool for shaving." 义为 "operation of shaving" 始于 1838 年. 义为 "a grazing touch" 见于 1834 年. Phrase a close shave 始于 1856 年, on 概念 "a slight, grazing touch."

example.en: He forgot to shave before the job interview and looked quite scruffy.

entries.etymology: mid-12c., probably evolving from Old English seo, sio (accusative sie), fem. of demonstrative pronoun (masc. se) "the," from PIE root *so- "this, that" (see the). The Old English word for "she" was heo, hio, however by 13c. the pronunciation of this had converged by phonetic evolution with he "he," which apparently led to the fem. demonstrative pronoun being used in place of the pronoun (compare similar development in Dutch zij, German sie, Greek he, etc.). The original h- survives in her. A relic of the Old English pronoun is in Manchester-area dialectal oo "she." As a noun meaning "a female," she is attested from 1530s.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪中期, 可能 evolving 源自 古英语 seo, sio (宾格 sie), fem. of demonstrative pronoun (masc. se) "the," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *so- "this, that" （参见 the). The 古英语 word for "she" was heo, hio, however by 13 世纪 the pronunciation of this had converged by phonetic evolution with he "he," which 似乎 led to the fem. demonstrative pronoun being used in place of the pronoun (对比 similar development in 荷兰语 zij, 德语 sie, 希腊语 he, etc.). The original h- survives in her. A relic of the 古英语 pronoun is in Manchester-area 方言 oo "she." 作名词时 意为 "a female," she 见于 1530 年代.
