entries.etymology:
ruminant mammal, Old English sceap, scep, from West Germanic *skæpan (source also of Old Saxon scap, Old Frisian skep, Middle Low German schap, Middle Dutch scaep, Dutch schaap, Old High German scaf, German Schaf), of unknown origin. Not found in Scandinavian (Danish has faar for "sheep") or Gothic (which uses lamb), and with no known cognates outside Germanic. The more usual Indo-European word for the animal is represented in English by ewe.

The plural form was leveled with the singular in Old English, but Old Northumbrian had a plural scipo. Used since Old English as a type of timidity and figuratively of those under the guidance of God. The meaning "stupid, timid person" is attested from 1540s. The image of the wolf in sheep's clothing was in Old English (from Matt. vii:15); that of separating the sheep from the goats is from Matt. xxv:33. To count sheep in a bid to induce sleep is recorded from 1854 but seems not to have been commonly written about until 1870s. It might simply be a type of a tedious activity, but an account of shepherd life from Australia from 1849 ["Sidney's Emigrant's Journal"] describes the night-shepherd ("hut-keeper") taking a count of the sheep regularly at the end of his shift to protect against being answerable for any animals later lost or killed. 

Sheep's eyes "loving looks" is attested from 1520s (compare West Frisian skiepseach, Dutch schaapsoog, German Schafsauge). A sheep-biter was "a dog that worries sheep" (1540s); "a mutton-monger" (1590s); and "a whore-monger" (1610s, i.e. one who "chases mutton"); hence Shakespeare's sheep-biting "thieving, sneaky."

Sheep's eyes "loving looks" 见于 1520 年代 (对比 West Frisian skiepseach, 荷兰语 schaapsoog, 德语 Schafsauge). entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "exempt, free from guilt" (as in Sheer Thursday, the Thursday of Holy Week); later schiere "thin, sparse" (c. 1400), from Old English scir "bright, clear, gleaming; translucent; pure, unmixed," and influenced by Old Norse cognate scær "bright, clean, pure," both from Proto-Germanic *skeran- (source also of Old Saxon skiri, Old Frisian skire, German schier, Gothic skeirs "clean, pure"), from PIE root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)). 

Sense of "absolute, utter" (sheer nonsense) developed 1580s, probably from the notion of "unmixed;" that of "very steep" (a sheer cliff) is first recorded 1800, probably from notion of "continued without halting." Meaning "diaphanous" is from 1560s. As an adverb from c. 1600.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., from Middle Low German schelf "shelf, set of shelves," or from Old English cognate scylfe, which perhaps meant "shelf, ledge, floor," and scylf "peak, pinnacle," from Proto-Germanic *skelf- "split," possibly from the notion of a split piece of wood (compare Old Norse skjölf "bench"), from PIE root *(s)kel- (1) "to cut, cleave" (see scale (n.1)).

Shelf life first recorded 1927. Phrase on the shelf "out of the way, inactive" is attested from 1570s; of unmarried women with no prospects from 1839. Off the shelf "ready-made" is from 1936. Meaning "ledge of rock" is from 1809, perhaps from or influenced by shelf (n.2). Related: Shelves.

Off the shelf "ready-made" 始于 1936 年. 义为 "ledge of rock" 始于 1809 年, 或源自 or influenced by shelf (n.2). 同源词：Shelves.

entries.etymology: 1560s, "to remove (a nut, etc.) from a shell," from shell (n.). The meaning "to bombard with shells" is first attested 1856. To shell out "disburse" (1801) is a figurative use from the image of extracting nuts. Related: Shelled; shelling.

entries.definition: n.躲避处，掩蔽部 v./n.掩蔽，庇护
entries.etymology:
1580s, "structure affording protection," possibly an alteration of Middle English sheltron, sheldtrume "roof or wall formed by locked shields," from Old English scyldtruma, from scield "shield" (see shield (n.)) + truma "troop," related to Old English trum "firm, strong" (see trim).

If so, the original notion is of a compact body of men protected by interlocking shields. OED finds this "untenable" and proposed derivation from shield + -ture. Figurative sense is recorded from 1580s; meaning "temporary lodging for homeless poor" is first recorded 1890 in Salvation Army jargon; sense of "temporary home for animals" is from 1971. Related: Shelterless.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "structure affording protection," possibly an alteration of 中古英语 sheltron, sheldtrume "roof or wall formed by locked shields," 源自 古英语 scyldtruma, 源自 scield "shield" （参见 shield （名）) + truma "troop," related to 古英语 trum "firm, strong" （参见 trim). example.en: The refugees sought shelter in the abandoned warehouse during the blizzard.

entries.etymology: Old English sceaphierde, from sceap "sheep" (see sheep) + hierde "herder," from heord "a herd" (see herd (n.)). Similar formation in Middle Low German, Middle Dutch schaphirde, Middle High German schafhirte, German dialectal Schafhirt. Shepherds customarily were buried with a tuft of wool in hand, to prove on Doomsday their occupation and be excused for often missing Sunday church. Shepherd's pie is recorded from 1877.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sceaphierde, 源自 sceap "sheep" （参见 sheep) + hierde "herder," 源自 heord "a herd" （参见 herd （名）). entries.definition: n. 盾，屏障 vt. 防护，保护
entries.etymology: Old English scield, scild "shield; protector, defense," literally "board," from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (source also of Old Norse skjöldr, Old Saxon skild, Middle Dutch scilt, Dutch schild, German Schild, Gothic skildus), from *skel- "divide, split, separate," from PIE root *(s)kel- (1) "to cut" (see scale (n.1)). Perhaps the notion is of a flat piece of wood made by splitting a log. Shield volcano (1911) translates German Schildvulkan (1910). Plate tectonics sense is from 1906, translating Suess (1888).

entries.etymology:
Old English sciftan, scyftan "arrange, place, order," also "divide, partition; distribute, allot, share," from Proto-Germanic *skiftan (source also of Old Norse skipta "to divide, change, separate," Old Frisian skifta "to decide, determine, test," Dutch schiften "to divide, turn," German schichten "to classify," Schicht "shift"). This is said to be related to the source of Old English sceadan "divide, separate," (see shed (v.)).

c. 1200 as "to dispose; make ready; set in order, control," also intransitive, "take care of oneself." From c. 1300 as "to go, move, depart; move (someone or something), transport." Sense of "to alter, to change" appeared mid-13c. (compare shiftless). Meaning "change the gear setting of an engine" is from 1910; to shift gears in the figurative sense is from 1961. Related: Shifted; shifting.

entries.definition: v.（使）发光，照耀，擦亮 n. 光，光泽
entries.etymology: 1520s, "brightness," from shine (v.). Meaning "polish given to a pair of boots" is from 1871. Derogatory meaning "black person" is from 1908 (perhaps from glossiness of skin or, on another guess, from frequent employment as shoeshines). Phrase to take a shine to "fancy" is American English slang from 1839, perhaps from shine up to "attempt to please as a suitor." Shiner is from late 14c. as "something that shines;" sense of "black eye" first recorded 1903, American English, in East Side immigrant dialect.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to send or transport (merchandise, people) by ship; to board a ship; to travel by ship, sail, set sail," also figurative, from ship (n.). Old English scipian is attested only in the senses "take ship, embark; be furnished with a ship." Transferred to other means of conveyance (railroad, etc.) from 1857, originally American English. Related: Shipped; shipping.

entries.etymology:
Old English scyrte "skirt, tunic," from Proto-Germanic *skurtjon "a short garment" (source also of Old Norse skyrta, Swedish skjorta "skirt, kirtle;" Middle Dutch scorte, Dutch schort "apron;" Middle High German schurz, German Schurz "apron"), related to Old English  scort, sceort "short," from PIE *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)).

Formerly of the chief garment worn by both sexes, but in modern use long only of that for men; in reference to women's tops, reintroduced 1896. Bloody shirt, exposed as a symbol of outrage, is attested from 1580s. To give (someone) the shirt off one's back is from 1771. To lose one's shirt "suffer total financial loss" is from 1935. To keep one's shirt on "be patient" (1904) is from the notion of (not) stripping down for a fight.

entries.etymology:
Old English sceotan "to hurl missiles, cast; strike, hit, push; run, rush; send forth swiftly; wound with missiles" (class II strong verb; past tense sceat, past participle scoten), from Proto-Germanic *skeutanan (source also of Old Saxon skiotan, Old Norse skjota "to shoot with (a weapon); shoot, launch, push, shove quickly," Old Frisian skiata, Middle Dutch skieten, Dutch schieten, Old High German skiozan, German schießen), from PIE root *skeud- "to shoot, to chase, to throw, to project" (source also of Sanskrit skundate "hastens, makes haste," Old Church Slavonic iskydati "to throw out," Lithuanian skudrus "quick, nimble").

In reference to pool playing, from 1926. Meaning "to strive (for)" is from 1967, American English. Sense of "descend (a river) quickly" is from 1610s. Meaning "to inject by means of a hypodermic needle" is attested from 1914. Meaning "photograph" (especially a movie) is from 1890. As an interjection, an arbitrary euphemistic alteration of shit, it is recorded from 1934. Shoot the breeze "chat" first recorded 1941. Shoot-'em-up (adj.) in reference to violent entertainment (Western movies, etc.) is from 1942. Shoot to kill first attested 1867. Shoot the cat "to vomit" is from 1785. To shoot the moon originally meant "depart by night with ones goods to escape back rent" (1829).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sceotan "to hurl missiles, cast; strike, hit, push; run, rush; send forth swiftly; wound with missiles" (class II strong 动词; past tense sceat, past participle scoten), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skeutanan (source also of 古撒克逊语 skiotan, 古北欧语 skjota "to shoot with (a weapon); shoot, launch, push, shove quickly," 古弗里西语 skiata, Middle 荷兰语 skieten, 荷兰语 schieten, 古高地德语 skiozan, 德语 schießen), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *skeud- "to shoot, to chase, to throw, to project" (source also of 梵语 skundate "hastens, makes haste," Old Church Slavonic iskydati "to throw out," Lithuanian skudrus "quick, nimble"). In reference to pool playing, 自 1926 年起. 义为 "to strive (for)" 始于 1967 年, American English. 义为 "descend (a river) quickly" 始于 1610 年代. 义为 "to inject by means of a hypodermic needle" 见于 1914 年. 义为 "photograph" (尤指 a movie) 始于 1890 年. 作为 interjection, an arbitrary euphemistic alteration of shit, it 见于 1934 年. Shoot the breeze "chat" 首见于 1941 年. Shoot-'em-up （形） in reference to violent entertainment (Western movies, etc.) 始于 1942 年. Shoot to kill 最早见于 1867 年. Shoot the cat "to vomit" 始于 1785 年. To shoot the moon 原义为 meant "depart by night with ones goods to escape back rent" (1829 年).

example.en: The director asked the crew to shoot the final scene before sunset.
example.zh: 导演要求摄制组在日落前拍摄最后一个场景。

entries.definition: 商店，店铺；工场，车间 vi. 购物
entries.etymology: 1680s, "to bring something to a shop, to expose for sale," from shop (n.). The meaning "to visit shops for the purpose of examining or purchasing goods" is first attested 1764. Related: Shopped; shopping. Shop around is from 1922. Shopping cart is recorded from 1956; shopping list first attested 1913; transferred and figurative use is from 1959.
entries.etymologyZh: 1680 年代, "to bring something to a shop, to expose for sale," 源自 shop （名）. The 意为 "to visit shops for the purpose of examining or purchasing goods" is 最早见于 1764 年. 同源词：Shopped; shopping. Shop around 始于 1922 年. Shopping cart 见于 1956 年; shopping list 最早见于 1913 年; transferred and figurative use 始于 1959 年.

entries.etymology: 1764, "act or practice of visiting shops," verbal noun from shop (v.). Meaning "goods that have been purchased" is from 1934. Shopping bag attested from 1886; shopping list from 1913.
entries.etymologyZh: 1764 年, "act or practice of visiting shops," verbal 名词 源自 shop （动）. 义为 "goods that have been purchased" 始于 1934 年. Shopping bag attested 自 1886 年起; shopping list 自 1913 年起.

example.en: She spent the entire afternoon shopping for a birthday gift in the mall.
example.zh: 她花了整个下午在商场里购物，寻找生日礼物。

entries.etymology:
"land bordering a large body of water," c. 1300, from an Old English word or from Middle Low German schor "shore, coast, headland," or Middle Dutch scorre "land washed by the sea," all probably from Proto-Germanic *skur-o- "cut," from PIE *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)).

According to etymologists originally with a sense of "division" between land and water. But if the word began on the North Sea coast of the continent, it might as well have meant originally "land 'cut off' from the mainland by tidal marshes" (compare Old Norse skerg "an isolated rock in the sea," related to sker "to cut, shear"). Old English words for "coast, shore" were strand (n.), waroþ, ofer. Few Indo-European languages have such a single comprehensive word for "land bordering water" (Homer uses one word for sandy beaches, another for rocky headlands). General application to "country near a seacoast" is attested from 1610s.
entries.etymologyZh: "land bordering a large body of water," 约 1300 年, 源自 an 古英语 word or 源自 Middle Low 德语 schor "shore, coast, headland," or Middle 荷兰语 scorre "land washed by the sea," all 可能 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skur-o- "cut," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" （参见 shear （动）). According to etymologists 原义为 with a 语义 "division" between land and water. But if the word began on the North Sea coast of the continent, it might as well have meant 原义为 "land 'cut off' from the mainland by tidal marshes" (对比 古北欧语 skerg "an isolated rock in the sea," related to sker "to cut, shear"). 古英语 words for "coast, shore" were strand （名）, waroþ, ofer. Few Indo-European languages have such a single comprehensive word for "land bordering water" (Homer uses one word for sandy beaches, another for rocky headlands). General application to "country near a seacoast" 见于 1610 年代.

example.en: The children played on the sandy shore all afternoon.
example.zh: 孩子们整个下午都在沙岸上玩耍。

definitionLines: a. 短，矮；（of）缺乏的，不足的
entries.definition: a. 短，矮；（of）缺乏的，不足的 n.. （pl.）短裤
entries.etymology: 1580s, the short "the result, the total," from short (adj.). Meaning "electrical short circuit" first recorded 1906 (see short circuit). Meaning "contraction of a name or phrase" is from 1873 (as in for short). Slang meaning "car" is attested from 1897; originally "street car," so called because street cars (or the rides taken in them) were "shorter" than railroad cars.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, the short "the result, the total," 源自 short （形）. 义为 "electrical short circuit" 首见于 1906 年 （参见 short circuit). 义为 "contraction of a name or phrase" 始于 1873 年 (as in for short). Slang 意为 "car" 见于 1897 年; 原义为 "street car," so called because street cars (or the rides taken in them) were "shorter" than railroad cars.

entries.etymologyZh: 1862 年, American English, 源自 short + -age.

example.en: The region faces a severe shortage of clean drinking water.

entries.etymology: 1670s, from the phrase to come short "be inadequate" (1570s); see short (adj.). Related: Shortcomings.
entries.etymologyZh: 1670 年代, 源自 phrase to come short "be inadequate" (1570 年代); 参见 short （形）. 同源词：Shortcomings.

entries.etymology: Old English scortlice "briefly," also, in late Old English, "in short time;" from short (adj.) + -ly (2).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scortlice "briefly," also, in late 古英语, "in short time;" 源自 short （形） + -ly (2).

example.en: The bus will depart shortly after the last passenger boards.
example.zh: 最后一名乘客上车后，巴士将很快出发。

entries.etymology: "short pants," 1826, from short (adj.). Short-shorts is attested from 1946, originally men's briefs.
entries.etymologyZh: "short pants," 1826 年, 源自 short （形）. Short-shorts 见于 1946 年, 原义为 men's briefs.

example.en: He changed into shorts and a T-shirt before heading to the gym.
example.zh: 他换上短裤和T恤后前往健身房。

definitionLines: n. 射击，枪声；射门，投篮；弹 丸，炮弹
entries.definition: n. 射击，枪声；射门，投篮；弹 丸，炮弹
entries.etymology:
Old English scot, sceot "a shot, a shooting, an act of shooting; that which is discharged in shooting, what is shot forth; darting, rapid motion," from Proto-Germanic *skutan (source also of Old Norse skutr, Old Frisian skete, Middle Dutch scote, German Schuß "a shot"), related to sceotan "to shoot" (see shoot (v.)).

Meaning "discharge of a bow, missile," also is from related Old English gesceot. Extended to other projectiles in Middle English, and to sports (hockey, basketball, etc.) 1868. Another original meaning, "payment" (perhaps literally "money thrown down") is preserved in scot-free. "Throwing down" might also have led to the meaning "a drink," first attested 1670s, the more precise meaning "small drink of straight liquor" by 1928 (shot glass by 1955). Camera view sense is from 1958. Sense of "hypodermic injection" first attested 1904; figurative phrase shot in the arm "stimulant" first recorded 1922. Meaning "try, attempt" is from 1756; sense of "remark meant to wound" is recorded from 1841. Meaning "an expert in shooting" is from 1780. To call the shots "control events, make decisions" is American English, 1922, perhaps from sport shooting. Shot in the dark "uninformed guess" is from 1885. Big shot "important person" is from 1861.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scot, sceot "a shot, a shooting, an act of shooting; that which is discharged in shooting, what is shot forth; darting, rapid motion," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skutan (source also of 古北欧语 skutr, 古弗里西语 skete, Middle 荷兰语 scote, 德语 Schuß "a shot"), related to sceotan "to shoot" （参见 shoot （动）). 义为 "discharge of a bow, missile," also 始于 related 古英语 gesceot. Extended to other projectiles in 中古英语, and to sports (hockey, basketball, etc.) 1868 年. Another original 意为, "payment" (或许 字面义为 "money thrown down") is preserved in scot-free. "Throwing down" might also have led to the 意为 "a drink," 最早见于 1670 年代, the more precise 意为 "small drink of straight liquor" 截至 1928 年 (shot glass 截至 1955 年). Camera view sense 始于 1958 年. 义为 "hypodermic injection" 最早见于 1904 年; figurative phrase shot in the arm "stimulant" 首见于 1922 年. 义为 "try, attempt" 始于 1756 年; 语义 "remark meant to wound" 见于 1841 年. 义为 "an expert in shooting" 始于 1780 年. To call the shots "control events, make decisions" is American English, 1922 年, 或源自 sport shooting. Shot in the dark "uninformed guess" 始于 1885 年. Big shot "important person" 始于 1861 年.

example.en: The photographer captured a perfect shot of the winning goal.
example.zh: 摄影师抓拍到了致胜进球的完美瞬间。

definitionLines: auz. v. ［shall的过去式］；［假 设 万一；［义务、责任］ 应当，应该；［说话者意 愿］就，该；［可能、推 测］可能，该；［惊奇、遗 憾］竟然会
entries.definition: auz. v. ［shall的过去式］；［假 设 万一；［义务、责任］ 应当，应该；［说话者意 愿］就，该；［可能、推 测］可能，该；［惊奇、遗 憾］竟然会
entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old English sceolde, past tense of sceal (see shall). Preserves the original notion of "obligation" that has all but dropped from shall.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古英语 sceolde, 为 … 的过去时 sceal （参见 shall). Preserves the original 概念 "obligation" that has all but dropped 源自 shall.

entries.etymology: Old English sculdor "shoulder," from West Germanic *skuldro (source also of Middle Dutch scouder, Dutch schouder, Old Frisian skoldere, Middle Low German scholder, Old High German scultra, German Schulter), of unknown origin, perhaps related to shield (n.). Meaning "edge of the road" is attested from 1933. Cold shoulder (Neh. ix:29) translates Latin humerum recedentum dare in Vulgate (but see cold shoulder). Shoulder-length, of hair, is from 1951.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sculdor "shoulder," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *skuldro (source also of Middle 荷兰语 scouder, 荷兰语 schouder, 古弗里西语 skoldere, Middle Low 德语 scholder, 古高地德语 scultra, 德语 Schulter), 来源不详, 或许 related to shield （名）. 义为 "edge of the road" 见于 1933 年. Cold shoulder (Neh. ix:29) translates 拉丁语 humerum recedentum dare in Vulgate (but 参见 cold shoulder). Shoulder-length, of hair, 始于 1951 年.

entries.definition: n. 呼喊，呼叫 n. 呼喊，叫声
entries.etymology: c. 1300, schowten "to call or cry out loudly," of unknown origin; perhaps from the root of shoot (v.) on the notion of "throw the voice out loudly," or related to Old Norse skuta "a taunt" (compare scout (v.2)). Related: Shouted; shouting.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, schowten "to call or cry out loudly," 来源不详; 或源自 the root of shoot （动） on the 概念 "throw the voice out loudly," or related to 古北欧语 skuta "a taunt" (对比 scout (v.2)). 同源词：Shouted; shouting.

example.en: He let out a loud shout when he saw the spider.
example.zh: 看到蜘蛛时，他大叫了一声。

definitionLines: n. 表演，节目；展出，陈列；展览 会/物
vt.给（人）看，出示；带领；说 明，示范；表明，证明；指示， 指出
entries.definition: n. 表演，节目；展出，陈列；展览 会/物 vt.给（人）看，出示；带领；说 明，示范；表明，证明；指示， 指出 vi. 显示，露面；演出
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "act of exhibiting to view," from show (v.). Sense of "appearance put on with intention to deceive" is recorded from 1520s. Meaning "display, spectacle" is first recorded 1560s; that of "ostentatious display" is from 1713 (showy is from 1712). Sense of "entertainment program on radio or TV" is first recorded 1932. Meaning "third place in a horse race" is from 1925, American English (see the verb).

Show of hands is attested from 1789; Phrase for show "for appearance's sake" is from c. 1700. Show business is attested from 1850; shortened form show biz used in "Billboard" from 1942. Actor's creed the show must go on is attested from 1890. Show-stopper is from 1926; show trial first recorded 1937.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "act of exhibiting to view," 源自 show （动）. 义为 "appearance put on with intention to deceive" 见于 1520 年代. 义为 "display, spectacle" is 首见于 1560 年代; that of "ostentatious display" 始于 1713 年 (showy 始于 1712 年). 义为 "entertainment program on radio or TV" is 首见于 1932 年. 义为 "third place in a horse race" 始于 1925 年, American English （参见 the 动词). Show of hands 见于 1789 年; Phrase for show "for appearance's sake" 始于 约 1700 年. Show business 见于 1850 年; shortened form show biz used in "Billboard" 自 1942 年起. Actor's creed the show must go on 见于 1890 年. Show-stopper 始于 1926 年; show trial 首见于 1937 年.

example.en: The evening show at the theater sold out within two hours of opening.
example.zh: 剧院的晚间演出在开票两小时内售罄。

definitionLines: n. /vi. （下）阵雨；（冲）淋浴； 似阵雨般降落
entries.definition: n. /vi. （下）阵雨；（冲）淋浴； 似阵雨般降落 vt.倾注
entries.etymology: 1570s, "come down in showers;" 1580s, "to discharge a shower," from shower (n.1). Intransitive sense from 1930. Related: Showered; showering.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "come down in showers;" 1580 年代, "to discharge a shower," 源自 shower (n.1). Intransitive sense 自 1930 年起. 同源词：Showered; showering.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "wicked, evil," from shrewe "wicked man" (see shrew). Compare crabbed from crab (n.), dogged from dog (n.), wicked from witch (n.). The sense of "cunning" is first recorded 1510s. Related: Shrewdly; shrewdness. Strutt's "Sports and Pastimes of the People of England" (1801) has a shrewdness of apes for a company or group of them. Shrewdie "cunning person" is from 1916.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "wicked, evil," 源自 shrewe "wicked man" （参见 shrew). 对比 crabbed 源自 crab （名）, dogged 源自 dog （名）, wicked 源自 witch （名）. The 语义 "cunning" is 首见于 1510 年代. 同源词：Shrewdly; shrewdness. Strutt's "Sports and Pastimes of the People of England" (1801 年) has a shrewdness of apes for a company or group of them. Shrewdie "cunning person" 始于 1916 年.

definitionLines: vi. 起皱，收缩；退缩，畏缩
entries.definition: vi. 起皱，收缩；退缩，畏缩
entries.etymology:
Old English scrincan "to draw in the limbs, contract, shrivel up; wither, pine away" (class III strong verb; past tense scranc, past participle scruncen), from Proto-Germanic *skrink- (source also of Middle Dutch schrinken), probably from PIE root *(s)ker- (3) "to turn, bend" (see ring (n.1)).

Originally with causal shrench (compare drink/drench). Sense of "become reduced in size" recorded from late 13c. The meaning "draw back, recoil" (early 14c.) perhaps was suggested by the behavior of snails. Transitive sense, "cause to shrink" is from late 14c. Shrink-wrap is attested from 1961 (shrinking-wrap from 1959). Shrinking violet "shy person" attested from 1882.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scrincan "to draw in the limbs, contract, shrivel up; wither, pine away" (class III strong 动词; past tense scranc, past participle scruncen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skrink- (source also of Middle 荷兰语 schrinken), 可能 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *(s)ker- (3) "to turn, bend" （参见 ring (n.1)). Originally with causal shrench (对比 drink/drench). 义为 "become reduced in size" recorded 源自 13 世纪晚期 The 意为 "draw back, recoil" (14 世纪初) 或许 was suggested by the behavior of snails. Transitive sense, "cause to shrink" 始于 14 世纪晚期 Shrink-wrap 见于 1961 年 (shrinking-wrap 自 1959 年起). Shrinking violet "shy person" attested 自 1882 年起.

example.en: Wool garments tend to shrink when washed in hot water.
example.zh: 羊毛衣物用热水洗涤时往往会缩水。

entries.etymology: Old English scrybb "brushwood, shrubbery," a rare and late word (but preserved also, perhaps, in Shrewsbury), possibly from a Scandinavian source (compare dialectal Danish skrub "brushwood," Norwegian skrubba "dwarf tree"). Presumably related to North Frisian skrobb "broom plant, brushwood;" West Flemish schrobbe "climbing wild pea," with a base notion of "rough plant," from PIE *(s)kerb-, extended form of root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" (see shear (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scrybb "brushwood, shrubbery," a rare and late word (but preserved also, 或许, in Shrewsbury), possibly 源自 a Scandinavian source (对比 方言 Danish skrub "brushwood," Norwegian skrubba "dwarf tree"). Presumably related to North Frisian skrobb "broom plant, brushwood;" West Flemish schrobbe "climbing wild pea," with a base 概念 "rough plant," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *(s)kerb-, extended form of root *(s)ker- (1) "to cut" （参见 shear （动）).

entries.etymology: c. 1400, schurgyng, of uncertain origin. Perhaps connected to Danish skrugge "to stoop, crouch." Related: Shrugged; shrugging. To shrug (something) off "dismiss" is recorded from 1909.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, schurgyng, 来源存疑. Perhaps connected to Danish skrugge "to stoop, crouch." 同源词：Shrugged; shrugging. To shrug (something) off "dismiss" 见于 1909 年.

example.en: He just gave a shrug when asked if he agreed.
example.zh: 当被问及是否同意时，他只是耸了耸肩。

definitionLines: vt. 关，关闭；停止营业；禁闭
entries.definition: vt. 关，关闭；停止营业；禁闭 vi.关上
entries.etymology:
Old English scyttan "to put (a bolt) in place so as to fasten a door or gate, bolt, shut to; discharge, pay off," from West Germanic *skutjan (source also of Old Frisian schetta, Middle Dutch schutten "to shut, shut up, obstruct"), from PIE *skeud- "to shoot, chase, throw" (see shoot (v.)). Related: Shutting.

Meaning "to close by folding or bringing together" is from mid-14c. Meaning "prevent ingress and egress" is from mid-14c. Sense of "to set (someone) free (from)" (c. 1500) is obsolete except in dialectal phrases such as to get shut of. To shut (one's) mouth "desist from speaking" is recorded from mid-14c.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 scyttan "to put (a bolt) in place so as to fasten a door or gate, bolt, shut to; discharge, pay off," 源自 West 日耳曼语 *skutjan (source also of 古弗里西语 schetta, Middle 荷兰语 schutten "to shut, shut up, obstruct"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *skeud- "to shoot, chase, throw" （参见 shoot （动）). 同源词：Shutting. 义为 "to close by folding or bringing together" 始于 14 世纪中期 义为 "prevent ingress and egress" 始于 14 世纪中期 义为 "to set (someone) free (from)" (约 1500 年) is 已废 except in 方言 phrases such as to get shut of. To shut (one's) mouth "desist from speaking" 见于 14 世纪中期

example.en: Please shut the window before you leave; it looks like rain.
example.zh: 你离开之前请把窗户关上，看起来要下雨了。

definitionLines: n. 关闭物；百叶窗；快门
entries.definition: n. 关闭物；百叶窗；快门
entries.etymology: 1540s, "one who shuts" (see shut (v.)); meaning "movable wooden or iron screen for a window" is from 1680s. Photographic sense of "device for opening and closing the aperture of a lens" is from 1862.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "one who shuts" （参见 shut （动）); 意为 "movable wooden or iron screen for a window" 始于 1680 年代. Photographic 语义 "device for opening and closing the aperture of a lens" 始于 1862 年.

definitionLines: n. 往返汽车/列车/飞机；航天 飞机；梭子；穿梭
entries.definition: n. 往返汽车/列车/飞机；航天 飞机；梭子；穿梭 v. 穿梭往返
entries.etymology: 1550s, "move rapidly to and fro," from shuttle (n.); sense of "transport via a shuttle service" is recorded from 1930. Related: Shuttled; shuttling.
entries.etymologyZh: 1550 年代, "move rapidly to and fro," 源自 shuttle （名）; 语义 "transport via a shuttle service" 见于 1930 年. 同源词：Shuttled; shuttling.

example.en: A free shuttle bus runs between the hotel and the airport every hour.
example.zh: 酒店和机场之间每小时有一班免费穿梭巴士。

definitionLines: a.害羞的，腼腆的；易受惊的， 胆怯的
entries.definition: a.害羞的，腼腆的；易受惊的， 胆怯的
entries.etymology: late Old English sceoh "timid, easily startled," from Proto-Germanic *skeukh(w)az "afraid" (source also of Middle Low German schüwe, Dutch schuw, German scheu "shy;" Old High German sciuhen, German scheuchen "to scare away"). Uncertain cognates outside Germanic, unless in Old Church Slavonic shchuti "to hunt, incite." Italian schivare "to avoid," Old French eschiver "to shun" are Germanic loan-words. Meaning "lacking, short of" is from 1895, American English gambling slang. Related: Shyly; shyness.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 sceoh "timid, easily startled," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skeukh(w)az "afraid" (source also of Middle Low 德语 schüwe, 荷兰语 schuw, 德语 scheu "shy;" 古高地德语 sciuhen, 德语 scheuchen "to scare away"). Uncertain cognates outside 日耳曼语, unless in Old Church Slavonic shchuti "to hunt, incite." 意大利语 schivare "to avoid," 古法语 eschiver "to shun" are 日耳曼语 loan-words. 义为 "lacking, short of" 始于 1895 年, American English gambling 俚语. 同源词：Shyly; shyness.

example.en: He was too shy to speak up during the meeting.
example.zh: 他太害羞了，在会议上不敢发言。

entries.etymology: "to chase, set upon" (as in command sick him!), 1845, dialectal variant of seek. Used as an imperative to incite a dog to attack a person or animal; hence "cause to pursue." Related: Sicked; sicking.
entries.etymologyZh: "to chase, set upon" (as in command sick him!), 1845 年, 方言 为 … 的变体 seek. Used 作为 imperative to incite a dog to attack a person or animal; hence "cause to pursue." 同源词：Sicked; sicking.

example.en: He called in sick and spent the whole day resting at home.
example.zh: 他请了病假，整天在家休息。

definitionLines: 旁边，侧面；坡，岸；一边， 一侧，一方
entries.definition: 旁边，侧面；坡，岸；一边， 一侧，一方 vi.（with）支持
entries.etymology: late 15c., "to cut into sides" (of meat), from side (n.). Meaning "to support one of the parties in a discussion, dispute, etc.," is first attested 1590s, from side (n.) in the figurative sense; earlier to hold sides (late 15c.). Related: Sided; siding.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "to cut into sides" (of meat), 源自 side （名）. 义为 "to support one of the parties in a discussion, dispute, etc.," is 最早见于 1590 年代, 源自 side （名） in the figurative sense; earlier to hold sides (15 世纪晚期). 同源词：Sided; siding.

example.en: In the debate, most students took the side of environmental protection.
example.zh: 在辩论中，大多数学生站在环境保护这一边。

entries.etymology: "path for pedestrians on the side of a street," 1739, from side (adj.) + walk (n.). The use of sidewalk for pavement as one of the characteristic differences between American and British English has been noted since at least 1902.
entries.etymologyZh: "path for pedestrians on the side of a street," 1739 年, 源自 side （形） + walk （名）. The use of sidewalk for pavement as one of the characteristic differences between American and British English has been noted 自 at least 1902 年.

example.en: Cyclists must not ride on the sidewalk as it is reserved for pedestrians.
example.zh: 骑行者不得在人行道上骑行，因为那是专为行人保留的。

entries.definition: ad. 向侧面地；向一旁 a.向侧面的；一旁的
entries.etymology: 1570s, from side (n.) + way (n.), with adverbial genitive. To look sideways "cast scornful glances" is recorded from 1844.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, 源自 side （名） + way （名）, with adverbial 属格. To look sideways "cast scornful glances" 见于 1844 年.

entries.etymology: early 13c., "a seat" (as in Siege Perilous, early 13c., the vacant seat at Arthur's Round Table, according to prophecy to be occupied safely only by the knight destined to find the Holy Grail), from Old French sege "seat, throne," from Vulgar Latin *sedicum "seat," from Latin sedere "sit" (see sedentary). The military sense is attested from c. 1300; the notion is of an army "sitting down" before a fortress.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "a seat" (as in Siege Perilous, 13 世纪初, the vacant seat at Arthur's Round Table, according to prophecy to be occupied safely only by the knight destined to find the Holy Grail), 源自 古法语 sege "seat, throne," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *sedicum "seat," 源自 拉丁语 sedere "sit" （参见 sedentary). The military sense 见于 约 1300 年; the notion is of an army "sitting down" before a fortress.

entries.etymology: mid-13c., probably a Middle English back-formation from sighte, past tense of Old English sican "to sigh," perhaps echoic of the sound of sighing. Related: Sighed; sighing.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, 可能 a 中古英语 back-formation 源自 sighte, 为 … 的过去时 古英语 sican "to sigh," 或许 echoic of the sound of sighing. 同源词：Sighed; sighing.

example.en: She let out a deep sigh and turned away from the window.
example.zh: 她深深地叹了口气，转身离开窗边。

definitionLines: n. 视力，视觉；望见，瞥见； 情景，奇观；（pl.）风景， 名胜
entries.definition: n. 视力，视觉；望见，瞥见； 情景，奇观；（pl.）风景， 名胜
entries.etymology:
Old English sihð, gesiht, gesihð "thing seen; faculty of sight; aspect; vision; apparition," from Proto-Germanic *sekh(w)- (source also of Danish sigte, Swedish sigt, Middle Dutch sicht, Dutch zicht, Old High German siht, German Sicht, Gesicht), stem that also yielded Old English seon (see see (v.)), with noun suffix -th (2), later -t.

Meaning "perception or apprehension by means of the eyes" is from early 13c. Meaning "device on a firearm to assist in aiming" is from 1580s. A "show" of something, hence, colloquially, "a great many; a lot" (late 14c.). Sight for sore eyes "welcome visitor" is attested from 1738; sight unseen "without previous inspection" is from 1892. Sight gag first attested 1944. Middle English had sighty (late 14c.) "visible, conspicuous; bright, shining; attractive, handsome;" c. 1400 as "keen-sighted;" mid-15c. as "discerning" (compare German sichtig "visible").
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sihð, gesiht, gesihð "thing seen; faculty of sight; aspect; vision; apparition," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sekh(w)- (source also of Danish sigte, Swedish sigt, Middle 荷兰语 sicht, 荷兰语 zicht, 古高地德语 siht, 德语 Sicht, Gesicht), stem that also yielded 古英语 seon （参见 参见 （动）), with 名词 suffix -th (2), later -t. 义为 "perception or apprehension by means of the eyes" 始于 13 世纪初 义为 "device on a firearm to assist in aiming" 始于 1580 年代. A "show" of something, hence, colloquially, "a great many; a lot" (14 世纪晚期). Sight for sore eyes "welcome visitor" 见于 1738 年; sight unseen "without previous inspection" 始于 1892 年. Sight gag 最早见于 1944 年. 中古英语 had sighty (14 世纪晚期) "visible, conspicuous; bright, shining; attractive, handsome;" 约 1400 年 as "keen-sighted;" 15 世纪中期 as "discerning" (对比 德语 sichtig "visible").

example.en: The waterfall was the most breathtaking sight on their entire hiking trip.
example.zh: 瀑布是他们整个徒步旅行中最令人叹为观止的景色。

entries.etymology: also sight-seeing, 1821, from sight (see sights) + present participle of see (v.). Sight-see (v.) is from 1824. Sight-seer first recorded 1821.
entries.etymologyZh: also sight-seeing, 1821 年, 源自 sight （参见 sights) + 为 … 的现在分词 参见 （动）. Sight-参见 （动） 始于 1824 年. Sight-seer 首见于 1821 年.

definitionLines: n. 符号，标记，招牌；征兆，迹象
entries.definition: n. 符号，标记，招牌；征兆，迹象 v. 签（名），签署
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to make the sign of the cross," from Old French signier "to make a sign (to someone); to mark," from Latin signare "to set a mark upon, mark out, designate; mark with a stamp; distinguish, adorn;" figuratively "to point out, signify, indicate," from signum (see sign (n.)). Sense of "to mark, stamp" is attested from mid-14c.; that of "to affix one's name" is from late 15c. Meaning "to communicate by hand signs" is recorded from 1700. Related: Signed; signing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to make the sign of the cross," 源自 古法语 signier "to make a sign (to someone); to mark," 源自 拉丁语 signare "to set a mark upon, mark out, designate; mark with a stamp; distinguish, adorn;" figuratively "to point out, signify, indicate," 源自 signum （参见 sign （名）). 义为 "to mark, stamp" 见于 14 世纪中期; that of "to affix one's name" 始于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "to communicate by hand signs" 见于 1700 年. 同源词：Signed; signing.

example.en: Both companies agreed to sign the contract by the end of the week.
example.zh: 两家公司同意在本周末前签署合同。

entries.definition: n. 信号，暗号 v.发信号，打暗号
entries.etymology: "remarkable, striking, notable" ("serving as a sign"), 1640s, from French signalé, past participle of signaler "to distinguish, signal" (see signal (n.)).
entries.etymologyZh: "remarkable, striking, notable" ("serving as a sign"), 1640 年代, 源自 法语 signalé, 为 … 的过去分词 signaler "to distinguish, signal" （参见 signal （名）).

example.en: A red light is a signal for drivers to stop.
example.zh: 红灯是司机停车的信号。

entries.etymology:
1530s, a kind of document in Scottish law, from Middle French signature (16c.) or directly from Medieval Latin signatura "signature, a rescript," in classical Latin "the matrix of a seal," from signatus, past participle of signare "to mark with a stamp, sign" (see sign (v.)).

Meaning "one's own name written in one's own hand" is from 1570s, replacing sign-manual (early 15c.) in this sense. Musical sense of "signs placed it the beginning of a staff to indicate the key and rhythm" is from 1806. Meaning "a distinguishing mark of any kind" is from 1620s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, a kind of document in 苏格兰语 law, 源自 中古法语 signature (16 世纪) or 直接源自 中古拉丁语 signatura "signature, a rescript," in classical 拉丁语 "the matrix of a seal," 源自 signatus, 为 … 的过去分词 signare "to mark with a stamp, sign" （参见 sign （动）). 义为 "one's own name written in one's own hand" 始于 1570 年代, replacing sign-manual (15 世纪初) in this sense. Musical 语义 "signs placed it the beginning of a staff to indicate the key and rhythm" 始于 1806 年. 义为 "a distinguishing mark of any kind" 始于 1620 年代.

example.en: Please add your signature at the bottom of the contract.
example.zh: 请在合同底部签上您的名字。

entries.etymology: c. 1400, "meaning," from Old French significance or directly from Latin significantia "meaning, force, energy," from significans, present participle of significare "to mean, import, signify" (see signify). The earlier word was signifiance (mid-13c.). Meaning "importance" is from 1725. Related: Significancy.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "meaning," 源自 古法语 significance or 直接源自 拉丁语 significantia "meaning, force, energy," 源自 significans, 为 … 的现在分词 significare "to mean, import, signify" （参见 signify). The earlier word was signifiance (13 世纪中期). 义为 "importance" 始于 1725 年. 同源词：Significancy.

example.en: The discovery holds great significance for the treatment of rare diseases.
example.zh: 这一发现对罕见病的治疗具有重大意义。

definitionLines: a.重大的；重要的；意味深长的
entries.definition: a.重大的；重要的；意味深长的
entries.etymology: 1570s, "having a meaning," from Latin significantem (nominative significans, present participle of significare "make known, indicate" (see signify). Earlier in the same sense was significative (c. 1400). Often "having a special or secret meaning," hence "important" (1761). Related: Significantly. Significant figure is from 1680s. Significant other (n.) attested by 1961, in psychology, "the most influential other person in the patient's world."
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "having a meaning," 源自 拉丁语 significantem (主格 significans, 为 … 的现在分词 significare "make known, indicate" （参见 signify). Earlier in the same sense was significative (约 1400 年). Often "having a special or secret meaning," hence "important" (1761 年). 同源词：Significantly. Significant figure 始于 1680 年代. Significant other （名） attested 截至 1961 年, in psychology, "the most influential other person in the patient's world."

example.en: The survey revealed a significant rise in unemployment over the past year.
example.zh: 这项调查显示，过去一年里失业率出现了显著的上升。

entries.definition: vt. 表示；意味 vi. 有重要性
entries.etymology: late 13c., "be a sign of, indicate, mean," from Old French signifier (12c.), from Latin significare "to make signs, show by signs, point out, express; mean, signify; foreshadow, portend," from significus (adj.), from signum "sign" (see sign (n.)) + root of facere "to make" (see factitious). Intransitive sense of "to be of importance" is attested from 1660s. Meaning "engage in mock-hostile banter" is African-American vernacular, by 1932.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "be a sign of, indicate, mean," 源自 古法语 signifier (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 significare "to make signs, show by signs, point out, express; mean, signify; foreshadow, portend," 源自 significus （形）, 源自 signum "sign" （参见 sign （名）) + root of facere "to make" （参见 factitious). Intransitive 语义 "to be of importance" 见于 1660 年代. 义为 "engage in mock-hostile banter" is African-American vernacular, 截至 1932 年.

entries.definition: n. 寂静，沉默 vt. 使寂静，使沉默
entries.etymology: c. 1200, "muteness, state of being silent," from Old French silence "state of being silent; absence of sound," from Latin silentium "a being silent," from silens, present participle of silere "be quiet or still," of unknown origin. Meaning "absence of sound" in English is from late 14c.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "muteness, state of being silent," 源自 古法语 silence "state of being silent; absence of sound," 源自 拉丁语 silentium "a being silent," 源自 silens, 为 … 的现在分词 silere "be quiet or still," 来源不详. 义为 "absence of sound" in English 始于 14 世纪晚期

example.en: A brief silence fell over the room when the teacher announced the exam date.
example.zh: 当老师宣布考试日期时，房间里短暂地陷入了沉默。

entries.etymology:
c. 1500, "without speech, silent, not speaking," from Latin silentem (nominative silens) "still, calm, quiet," present participle of silere "be quiet or still" (see silence (n.)). Meaning "free from noise or sound" is from 1580s.

Of letters, c. 1600; of films, 1914. In the looser sense "of few words," from 1840. Phrase strong, silent (type) is attested from 1905. Silent majority in the political sense of "mass of people whose moderate views are not publicly expressed and thus overlooked" is first attested 1955 in a British context and was used by John F. Kennedy but is most associated in U.S. with the rhetoric of the Nixon administration (1969-74).

In Victorian use, the phrase meant "the dead" (1874; compare Roman use of the noun plural of "silent" to mean "the dead"). Silence is golden (1831) is Carlyle's translation ["Sartor Resartus"] of part of the "Swiss Inscription" Sprechen ist silbern, Schweigen ist golden. In one 14c. text Latin "one who is silent" is translated by a beere stille.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年, "without speech, silent, not speaking," 源自 拉丁语 silentem (主格 silens) "still, calm, quiet," 为 … 的现在分词 silere "be quiet or still" （参见 silence （名）). 义为 "free from noise or sound" 始于 1580 年代. Of letters, 约 1600 年; of films, 1914 年. In the looser sense "of few words," 自 1840 年起. Phrase strong, silent (type) 见于 1905 年. Silent majority in the political 语义 "mass of people whose moderate views are not publicly expressed and thus overlooked" is 最早见于 1955 年 in a British context and was used by John F. Kennedy but is most associated in U.S. with the rhetoric of the Nixon administration (1969 年-74). In Victorian use, the phrase meant "the dead" (1874 年; 对比 Roman use of the 名词 为 … 的复数 "silent" to mean "the dead"). Silence is golden (1831 年) is Carlyle's translation ["Sartor Resartus"] of part of the "Swiss Inscription" Sprechen ist silbern, Schweigen ist golden. In one 14 世纪 text 拉丁语 "one who is silent" is translated by a beere stille.

example.en: The library was completely silent during the exam period.
example.zh: 考试期间图书馆完全安静。

entries.etymology: nonmetallic element, 1817, coined by British chemist Thomas Thomson from silica (silicon dioxide), from which it was isolated. The name is patterned on carbon, etc. Silicon chip first attested 1965; Silicon Valley for the Santa Clara Valley south of San Francisco, U.S., first attested 1974, from the concentration of manufacturers of silicon chips used in computers, watches, etc.
entries.etymologyZh: nonmetallic element, 1817 年, coined by British chemist Thomas Thomson 源自 silica (silicon dioxide), 源自 which it was isolated. The name is patterned on carbon, etc. Silicon chip 最早见于 1965 年; Silicon Valley for the Santa Clara Valley south of San Francisco, U.S., 最早见于 1974 年, 源自 concentration of manufacturers of silicon chips used in computers, watches, etc.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, from Old English seoloc, sioloc "silk, silken cloth," from Latin sericum "silk," plural serica "silken garments, silks," literally "Seric stuff," neuter of Sericus, from Greek Serikos "silken; pertaining to the Seres," an oriental people of Asia from whom the Greeks got silks. Western cultivation began 552 C.E., when agents from Byzantium impersonating monks smuggled silkworms and mulberry leaves out of China. Chinese si "silk," Manchurian sirghe, Mongolian sirkek have been compared to this and the people name in Greek might be a rendering via Mongolian of the Chinese word for "silk," but this is uncertain.

Also found in Old Norse as silki but not elsewhere in Germanic. The more common Germanic form is represented by Middle English say, from Old French seie, with Spanish seda, Italian seta, Dutch zijde, German Seide  is from Medieval Latin seta  "silk," perhaps elliptical for seta serica, or else a particular use of seta "bristle, hair" (see seta (n.)).

According to some sources [Buck, OED], the use of -l- instead of -r- in the Balto-Slavic form of the word (Old Church Slavonic šelku, Lithuanian šilkai) passed into English via the Baltic trade and may reflect a Chinese dialectal form, or a Slavic alteration of the Greek word. But the Slavic linguist Vasmer dismisses that, based on the initial sh- in the Slavic words, and suggests the Slavic words are from Scandinavian rather than the reverse.

As an adjective from mid-14c. In reference to the "hair" of corn, 1660s, American English. Figurative use of silk-stocking (n.) is from 1590s; as an adjective meaning "wealthy" it is attested from 1798, American English (silk stockings, especially worn by men, being regarded as extravagant and reprehensible, indicative of luxurious habits). Silk-screen (n.) is first attested 1930; as a verb from 1961. Silk road so called in English from 1931.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 源自 古英语 seoloc, sioloc "silk, silken cloth," 源自 拉丁语 sericum "silk," plural serica "silken garments, silks," 字面义为 "Seric stuff," neuter of Sericus, 源自 希腊语 Serikos "silken; pertaining to the Seres," an oriental people of Asia 源自 whom the Greeks got silks. Western cultivation began 552 C.E., when agents 源自 Byzantium impersonating monks smuggled silkworms and mulberry leaves out of China. 汉语 si "silk," Manchurian sirghe, Mongolian sirkek have been compared to this and the people name in 希腊语 might be a rendering 经由 Mongolian of the 汉语 word for "silk," but this is uncertain. Also found in 古北欧语 as silki but not elsewhere in 日耳曼语. The more common 日耳曼语 form is represented by 中古英语 say, 源自 古法语 seie, with 西班牙语 seda, 意大利语 seta, 荷兰语 zijde, 德语 Seide 始于 中古拉丁语 seta "silk," 或许 elliptical for seta serica，或else a particular use of seta "bristle, hair" （参见 seta （名）). According to some sources [Buck, OED], the use of -l- instead of -r- in the Balto-Slavic form of the word (Old Church Slavonic šelku, Lithuanian šilkai) passed into English 经由 the Baltic trade and may reflect a 汉语 方言 form，或a Slavic alteration of the 希腊语 word. But the Slavic linguist Vasmer dismisses that, based on the initial sh- in the Slavic words, and suggests the Slavic words 始于 Scandinavian rather than the reverse. 作形容词时 源自 14 世纪中期 In reference to the "hair" of corn, 1660 年代, American English. Figurative use of silk-stocking （名） 始于 1590 年代; 作形容词时 意为 "wealthy" it 见于 1798 年, American English (silk stockings, 尤指 worn by men, being regarded as extravagant and reprehensible, indicative of luxurious habits). Silk-screen （名） is 最早见于 1930 年; 作动词时 自 1961 年起. Silk road so called in English 自 1931 年起.

example.en: The dress was made of pure silk and felt incredibly soft.
example.zh: 这条裙子由纯丝绸制成，手感无比柔滑。

entries.etymology:
Old English gesælig "happy, fortuitous, prosperous" (related to sæl "happiness"), from Proto-Germanic *sæligas (source also of Old Norse sæll "happy," Old Saxon salig, Middle Dutch salich, Old High German salig, German selig "blessed, happy, blissful," Gothic sels "good, kindhearted"), from PIE *sele- "of good mood; to favor," from root *sel- (2) "happy, of good mood; to favor" (source also of Latin solari "to comfort," Greek hilaros "cheerful, gay, merry, joyous").

The word's considerable sense development moved from "happy" to "blessed" to "pious," to "innocent" (c. 1200), to "harmless," to "pitiable" (late 13c.), "weak" (c. 1300), to "feeble in mind, lacking in reason, foolish" (1570s). Further tendency toward "stunned, dazed as by a blow" (1886) in knocked silly, etc. Silly season in journalism slang is from 1861 (August and September, when newspapers compensate for a lack of hard news by filling up with trivial stories). Silly Putty trademark claims use from July 1949.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 gesælig "happy, fortuitous, prosperous" (related to sæl "happiness"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sæligas (source also of 古北欧语 sæll "happy," 古撒克逊语 salig, Middle 荷兰语 salich, 古高地德语 salig, 德语 selig "blessed, happy, blissful," Gothic sels "good, kindhearted"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sele- "of good mood; to favor," 源自 root *sel- (2) "happy, of good mood; to favor" (source also of 拉丁语 solari "to comfort," 希腊语 hilaros "cheerful, gay, merry, joyous"). The word's considerable sense development moved 源自 "happy" to "blessed" to "pious," to "innocent" (约 1200 年), to "harmless," to "pitiable" (13 世纪晚期), "weak" (约 1300 年), to "feeble in mind, lacking in reason, foolish" (1570 年代). Further tendency toward "stunned, dazed as by a blow" (1886 年) in knocked silly, etc. Silly season in journalism 俚语 始于 1861 年 (August and September, when newspapers compensate for a lack of hard news by filling up with trivial stories). Silly Putty trademark claims use 源自 July 1949 年.

example.en: It was silly of him to leave his wallet on the park bench.
example.zh: 他把钱包留在公园长椅上真是太蠢了。

entries.etymology:
Old English seolfor, Mercian sylfur "silver; money," from Proto-Germanic *silubra- (source also of Old Saxon silvbar, Old Frisian selover, Old Norse silfr, Middle Dutch silver, Dutch zilver, Old High German silabar, German silber "silver; money," Gothic silubr "silver"), from a common Germanic/Balto-Slavic word (source also of Old Church Slavonic s(u)rebo, Russian serebro, Polish srebro, Lithuanian sidabras "silver") of uncertain relationship and origin. According to Klein's sources, possibly from a language of Asia Minor, perhaps from Akkadian sarpu "silver," literally "refined silver," related to sarapu "to refine, smelt."

As an adjective from late Old English (also silvern). As a color name from late 15c. Of voices, words, etc., from 1520s in reference to the metal's pleasing resonance; silver-tongued is from 1590s. The silver age (1560s) was a phrase used by Greek and Roman poets. Chemical abbreviation Ag is from Latin argentum "silver," from the usual PIE word for the metal (see argent), which is missing in Germanic.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 seolfor, Mercian sylfur "silver; money," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *silubra- (source also of 古撒克逊语 silvbar, 古弗里西语 selover, 古北欧语 silfr, Middle 荷兰语 silver, 荷兰语 zilver, 古高地德语 silabar, 德语 silber "silver; money," Gothic silubr "silver"), 源自 a common 日耳曼语/Balto-Slavic word (source also of Old Church Slavonic s(u)rebo, 俄语 serebro, Polish srebro, Lithuanian sidabras "silver") of uncertain relationship and origin. According to Klein's sources, possibly from a language of Asia Minor, perhaps from Akkadian sarpu "silver," literally "refined silver," related to sarapu "to refine, smelt." As an adjective from late Old English (also silvern). As a color name from late 15c. Of voices, words, etc., from 1520s in reference to the metal's pleasing resonance; silver-tongued 始于 1590 年代. The silver age (1560 年代) was a phrase used by 希腊语 and Roman poets. Chemical abbreviation Ag 始于 拉丁语 argentum "silver," 源自 usual 原始印欧语 (PIE) word for the metal （参见 argent), which is missing in 日耳曼语.

entries.etymology: "having characteristics in common," 1610s (earlier similary, 1560s), from French similaire, from a Medieval Latin extended form of Latin similis "like, resembling," from Old Latin semol "together," from PIE root *sem- (1) "one, as one, together with" (see same). The noun meaning "that which is similar" is from 1650s. Related: Similarly.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "free from duplicity, upright, guileless; blameless, innocently harmless," also "ignorant, uneducated; unsophisticated; simple-minded, foolish," from Old French simple (12c.) "plain, decent; friendly, sweet; naive, foolish, stupid," hence "wretched, miserable," from Latin simplus, variant of simplex "simple, uncompounded," literally "onefold" (see simplex). Sense of "free from pride, humble, meek" is mid-13c. As "consisting of only one substance or ingredient" (opposite of composite or compounded) it dates from late 14c.; as "easily done" (opposite of complicated) it dates from late 15c.

From mid-14c. as "unqualified; mere; sheer;" also "clear, straightforward; easily understood." From late 14c. as "single, individual; whole." From late 14c. of clothing, etc., "modest, plain, unadorned," and of food, "plain, not sumptuous." In medicine, of fractures, etc., "lacking complications," late 14c. As a law term, "lacking additional legal stipulations, unlimited," from mid-14c.

In Middle English with wider senses than recently, such as "inadequate, insufficient; weak, feeble; mere; few; sad, downcast; mournful; of little value; low in price; impoverished, destitute;" of hair, "straight, not curly." As noun, "an innocent or a guileless person; a humble or modest person" (late 14c.), also "an uncompounded substance." From c. 1500 as "ignorant people."

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "singleness of nature, unity, indivisibility; immutability," from Old French simplicite (12c., Modern French simplicité), from Latin simplicitatem (nominative simplicitas) "state of being simple, frankness, openness, artlessness, candor, directness," from simplex (genitive simplicis) "simple" (see simplex). Sense of "ignorance" is from c. 1400; that of "simplicity of expression, plainness of style" is early 15c.

Middle English also had simplesse, from French, attested in English from mid-14c. in sense "humility, lack of pride," late 14c. as "wholeness, unity;" c. 1400 as "ignorance."

entries.etymology:
early 15c., synnes, from sithenes "since," from sithen (plus adverbial genitive -es), from Old English siððan "afterward, from now on, hereafter, further, later, as soon as, after that," originally sið ðan "after that," from sið "after" (see sith) + ðan, weakened form of ðam, dative of ðæt (see that).

As a conjunction from late 14c.; as a preposition from 1510s; "from the time when," hence "as a consequence of the fact that." Modern spelling replaced syns, synnes 16c. to indicate voiceless final -s- sound. Since when? often expressing incredulity, is from 1907.

entries.etymology:
1530s, "pure, unmixed," from Middle French sincere (16c.), from Latin sincerus, of things, "whole, clean, pure, uninjured, unmixed," figuratively "sound, genuine, pure, true, candid, truthful," of uncertain origin. The ground sense seems to be "that which is not falsified." Meaning "free from pretense or falsehood" in English is from 1530s.

There has been a temptation to see the first element as Latin sine "without." But there is no etymological justification for the common story that the word means "without wax" (*sin cerae), which is dismissed out of hand by OED and others, and the stories invented to justify that folk etymology are even less plausible. Watkins has it as originally "of one growth" (i.e. "not hybrid, unmixed"), from PIE *sm-ke-ro-, from *sem- "one" (see same) + root of crescere "to grow" (see crescent). De Vaan finds plausible a source in a lost adjective *caerus "whole, intact," from a PIE root meaning "whole."

entries.etymology:
Old English singan "to chant, sing, celebrate, or tell in song," also used of birds (class III strong verb; past tense sang, past participle sungen), from Proto-Germanic *sengwan (source also of Old Saxon singan, Old Frisian sionga, Middle Dutch singhen, Dutch zingen, Old High German singan, German singen, Gothic siggwan, Old Norse syngva, Swedish sjunga), from PIE root *sengwh- "to sing, make an incantation." The criminal slang sense of "to confess to authorities" is attested from 1610s.

No related forms in other languages, unless perhaps it is connected to Greek omphe "voice" (especially of a god), "oracle;" and Welsh dehongli "explain, interpret." The typical Indo-European root is represented by Latin canere (see chant (v.)). Other words meaning "sing" derive from roots meaning "cry, shout," but Irish gaibim is literally "take, seize," with sense evolution via "take up" a song or melody.

The criminal 俚语 语义 "to confess to authorities" 见于 1610 年代. No related forms in other languages, unless 或许 it is connected to 希腊语 omphe "voice" (尤指 of a god), "oracle;" and Welsh dehongli "explain, interpret." The typical Indo-European root is represented by 拉丁语 canere （参见 chant （动）). Other words 意为 "sing" derive 源自 roots 意为 "cry, shout," but 爱尔兰语 gaibim is 字面义为 "take, seize," with sense evolution 经由 "take up" a song or melody.

definitionLines: a.单人的；单身的；单一的， 单个的
entries.definition: a.单人的；单身的；单一的， 单个的
entries.etymology: c. 1400, "unmarried person," mid-15c., "a person alone, an individual," from single (adj.). Given various technical meanings from 16c. Sports sense is attested from 1851 (cricket), 1858 (baseball). Of single things from 1640s. Meaning "one-dollar bill" is from 1936. Meaning "phonograph record with one song on each side" is from 1949. Meaning "unmarried swinger" is from 1964; singles bar attested from 1969. An earlier modern word for "unmarried or unattached person" is singleton (1937).

Meaning "remarkably good, unusual, rare, separated from others (by excellence), uncommon" is from c. 1400 in English; this also was a common meaning of Latin singularis.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "cesspool, pit for reception of wastewater or sewage," from sink (v.). Figurative sense of "place where corruption and vice abound" is from 1520s. Meaning "drain for carrying water to a sink" is from late 15c. Sense of "shallow basin (especially in a kitchen) with a drainpipe for carrying off dirty water" first recorded 1560s. In science and technical use, "place where heat or other energy is removed from a system" (opposite of source), from 1855.

entries.etymology:
mid-13c., from Old English sweostor, swuster "sister," or a Scandinavian cognate (Old Norse systir, Swedish syster, Danish søster), in either case from Proto-Germanic *swestr- (source also of Old Saxon swestar, Old Frisian swester, Middle Dutch suster, Dutch zuster, Old High German swester, German Schwester, Gothic swistar).

These are from PIE *swesor, one of the most persistent and unchanging PIE root words, recognizable in almost every modern Indo-European language (Sanskrit svasar-, Avestan shanhar-, Latin soror, Old Church Slavonic, Russian sestra, Lithuanian sesuo, Old Irish siur, Welsh chwaer, Greek eor). French soeur "a sister" (11c., instead of *sereur) is directly from Latin soror, a rare case of a borrowing from the nominative case.

According to Klein's sources, probably from PIE roots *swe- "one's own" + *ser- "woman." For vowel evolution, see bury. Used of nuns in Old English; of a woman in general from 1906; of a black woman from 1926; and in the sense of "fellow feminist" from 1912. Meaning "female fellow-Christian" is from mid-15c. Sister act "variety act by two or more sisters" is from vaudeville (1908).

entries.etymology:
Old English sittan "to occupy a seat, be seated, sit down, seat oneself; remain, continue; settle, encamp, occupy; lie in wait; besiege" (class V strong verb; past tense sæt, past participle seten), from Proto-Germanic *setjan (source also of Old Saxon sittian, Old Norse sitja, Danish sidde, Old Frisian sitta, Middle Dutch sitten, Dutch zitten, Old High German sizzan, German sitzen, Gothic sitan), from PIE root *sed- (1) "to sit" (see sedentary).

With past tense sat, formerly also set, now restricted to dialect, and sate, now archaic; and past participle sat, formerly sitten. In reference to a legislative assembly, from 1510s. Meaning "to baby-sit" is recorded from 1966.

To sit back "be inactive" is from 1943. To sit on one's hands was originally "to withhold applause" (1926); later, "to do nothing" (1959). To sit around "be idle, do nothing" is 1915, American English. To sit out "not take part" is from 1650s. Sitting pretty is from 1916.

entries.etymology: early 13c., verbal noun from sit (v.). Meaning "a meeting of a body" is from c. 1400. Meaning "interval during which one sits" (for some purpose, especially to have one's portrait taken) is from 1706. Sitting-room first recorded 1771. Slang sitting duck "easy target" first recorded 1944; literal sense is from 1867 (it is considered not sporting to shoot at one).
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, verbal 名词 源自 sit （动）. 义为 "a meeting of a body" 始于 约 1400 年. 义为 "interval during which one sits" (for some purpose, 尤指 to have one's portrait taken) 始于 1706 年. Sitting-room 首见于 1771 年. Slang sitting duck "easy target" 首见于 1944 年; literal sense 始于 1867 年 (it is considered not sporting to shoot at one).

definitionLines: n.形势，局面；环境，状况； 位置，地点
entries.definition: n.形势，局面；环境，状况； 位置，地点
entries.etymology: early 15c., "place, position, or location," from Middle French situation or directly from Medieval Latin situationem (nominative situatio) "a position, situation," noun of action from past participle stem of situare "to place, locate" (see situate). Meaning "state of affairs" is from 1710; meaning "employment post" is from 1803.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "place, position, or location," 源自 中古法语 situation or 直接源自 中古拉丁语 situationem (主格 situatio) "a position, situation," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of situare "to place, locate" （参见 situate). 义为 "state of affairs" 始于 1710 年; 意为 "employment post" 始于 1803 年.

example.en: The rescue team had to assess the situation before entering the building.
example.zh: 救援队在进入大楼前必须评估当前形势。

entries.etymology:
Old English siex, six, sex, from Proto-Germanic *sekhs (source also of Old Saxon and Danish seks, Old Norse, Swedish, and Old Frisian sex, Middle Dutch sesse, Dutch zes, Old High German sehs, German sechs, Gothic saihs), from PIE *s(w)eks (source also of Sanskrit sas, Avestan kshvash, Persian shash, Greek hex, Latin sex, Old Church Slavonic sesti, Polish sześć, Russian shesti, Lithuanian szeszi, Old Irish se, Welsh chwech).

Six-shooter, usually a revolver with six chambers, is first attested 1844; six-pack of beverage containers is from 1952, of abdominal muscles by 1995. Six of one and half-a-dozen of the other "little difference" is recorded from 1833. Six-figure in reference to hundreds of thousands (of dollars, etc.) is from 1840. Six feet under "dead" is from 1942.

Phrase at sixes and sevens originally was "hazarding all one's chances," first in Chaucer, perhaps from dicing (the original form was on six and seven); it could be a corruption of on cinque and sice, using the French names (which were common in Middle English) for the highest numbers on the dice. Meaning "at odds, in disagreement or confusion" is from 1785, perhaps via a notion of "left unsettled."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 siex, six, sex, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sekhs (source also of 古撒克逊语 and Danish seks, 古北欧语, Swedish, and 古弗里西语 sex, Middle 荷兰语 sesse, 荷兰语 zes, 古高地德语 sehs, 德语 sechs, Gothic saihs), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *s(w)eks (source also of 梵语 sas, Avestan kshvash, 波斯语 shash, 希腊语 hex, 拉丁语 sex, Old Church Slavonic sesti, Polish sześć, 俄语 shesti, Lithuanian szeszi, Old 爱尔兰语 se, Welsh chwech). Six-shooter, 通常 a revolver with six chambers, is 最早见于 1844 年; six-pack of beverage containers 始于 1952 年, of abdominal muscles 截至 1995 年. Six of one and half-a-dozen of the other "little difference" 见于 1833 年. Six-figure in reference to hundreds of thousands (of dollars, etc.) 始于 1840 年. Six feet under "dead" 始于 1942 年. Phrase at sixes and sevens 原义为 was "hazarding all one's chances," first in Chaucer, 或源自 dicing (the original form was on six and seven); it could be a corruption of on cinque and sice, using the 法语 names (which were common in 中古英语) for the highest numbers on the dice. 义为 "at odds, in disagreement or confusion" 始于 1785 年, 或许 经由 a 概念 "left unsettled."

entries.etymology:
Old English sixtyne, from siex (see six) + -teen. Similar formation in Old Frisian sextine, Middle Dutch sestien, Dutch zestien, German sechzehn, Old Norse sextan.

From Latin contracted form sexdecim, sedecim come Italian sedici, French seize.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sixtyne, 源自 siex （参见 six) + -teen. Similar formation in 古弗里西语 sextine, Middle 荷兰语 sestien, 荷兰语 zestien, 德语 sechzehn, 古北欧语 sextan. From 拉丁语 contracted form sexdecim, sedecim come 意大利语 sedici, 法语 seize.

entries.definition: num.第六 n. 六分之一
entries.etymology: 1520s, replacing Middle English sixte (c. 1200), from Old English syxte, from siex (see six). Compare Old Frisian sexta, Middle Dutch seste, Old High German sehsto, German sechste, Gothic saihsta. With ending conformed to -th (1). Related: Sixthly. The noun meaning "a sixth part" is from 1550s. As a music tone, from 1590s. Sixth sense "supernatural perception of objects" is attested from 1712; earlier it meant "titillation, the sense that apprehends sexual pleasure" (1690s, from Scaliger).
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, replacing 中古英语 sixte (约 1200 年), 源自 古英语 syxte, 源自 siex （参见 six). 对比 古弗里西语 sexta, Middle 荷兰语 seste, 古高地德语 sehsto, 德语 sechste, Gothic saihsta. With ending conformed to -th (1). 同源词：Sixthly. The 名词 意为 "a sixth part" 始于 1550 年代. 作为 music tone, 源自 1590 年代. Sixth sense "supernatural perception of objects" 见于 1712 年; earlier it meant "titillation, the sense that apprehends sexual pleasure" (1690 年代, 源自 Scaliger).

entries.etymology: Old English sixtig, from siex (see six) + -tig (see -ty (1)). Similar formation in Old Norse sextugr, sextögr, sextigir, Old Frisian sextich, Middle Dutch sestig, Dutch zestig, Old High German sehszug, German sechzig. Phrase sixty-four dollar question is 1942, from radio quiz show where that was the top prize.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sixtig, 源自 siex （参见 six) + -tig （参见 -ty (1)). Similar formation in 古北欧语 sextugr, sextögr, sextigir, 古弗里西语 sextich, Middle 荷兰语 sestig, 荷兰语 zestig, 古高地德语 sehszug, 德语 sechzig. Phrase sixty-four dollar question is 1942 年, 源自 radio quiz show where that was the top prize.

definitionLines: n. 大小，尺寸；号码，尺码
entries.definition: n. 大小，尺寸；号码，尺码
entries.etymology: c. 1400, "to regulate," from size (n.). Meaning "to make of a certain size" is from c. 1600; that of "to classify according to size" is first attested 1630s. Verbal phrase size up "estimate, assess" is from 1847 and retains the root sense of size (n.). Related: Sized; sizing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "to regulate," 源自 size （名）. 义为 "to make of a certain size" 始于 约 1600 年; that of "to classify according to size" is 最早见于 1630 年代. Verbal phrase size up "estimate, assess" 始于 1847 年 and retains the root 语义 size （名）. 同源词：Sized; sizing.

example.en: Please check the size of the box before ordering the packaging.
example.zh: 在订购包装之前，请检查箱子的尺寸。

entries.definition: vi. 溜冰，滑冰 n. 冰鞋
entries.etymology: 1690s, "to ice-skate," from skate (n.2). U.S. slang sense of "to get away with something" is attested from 1945. Related: Skated; skating. A modern Latinate word for an ice-skating rink is glaciarium (1876).
entries.etymologyZh: 1690 年代, "to ice-skate," 源自 skate (n.2). U.S. 俚语 语义 "to get away with something" 见于 1945 年. 同源词：Skated; skating. A modern Latinate word for an ice-skating rink is glaciarium (1876 年).

example.en: Every winter, the kids love to skate on the frozen lake.
example.zh: 每年冬天，孩子们都喜欢在结冰的湖面上溜冰。

definitionLines: n. （动物之）骨架，骨骼；基干， 纲要
entries.definition: n. （动物之）骨架，骨骼；基干， 纲要
entries.etymology:
1570s, from Modern Latin sceleton "bones, bony framework of the body," from Greek skeleton soma "dried-up body, mummy, skeleton," from neuter of skeletos "dried-up" (also, as a noun, "dried body, mummy"), from skellein "dry up, make dry, parch," from PIE root *skele- "to parch, wither" (see sclero-).

Skelton was an early variant form. The noun use of Greek skeletos passed into Late Latin (sceletus), hence French squelette and rare English skelet (1560s), Spanish esqueleto, Italian scheletro. The meaning "bare outline" is first recorded c. 1600; hence skeleton crew (1778), skeleton key, etc. Phrase skeleton in the closet "source of secret shame to a person or family" is from 1812 (the image is perhaps from the Bluebeard fable).
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, 源自 现代 拉丁语 sceleton "bones, bony framework of the body," 源自 希腊语 skeleton soma "dried-up body, mummy, skeleton," 源自 neuter of skeletos "dried-up" (also, 作名词时, "dried body, mummy"), 源自 skellein "dry up, make dry, parch," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *skele- "to parch, wither" （参见 sclero-). Skelton was an early variant form. The 为 … 的名词用法 希腊语 skeletos passed into 晚期拉丁语 (sceletus), hence 法语 squelette and rare English skelet (1560 年代), 西班牙语 esqueleto, 意大利语 scheletro. The 意为 "bare outline" is 首见于 约 1600 年; hence skeleton crew (1778 年), skeleton key, etc. Phrase skeleton in the closet "source of secret shame to a person or family" 始于 1812 年 (the image is 或源自 the Bluebeard fable).

example.en: The museum displayed a complete skeleton of a prehistoric whale.
example.zh: 博物馆展示了一具完整的史前鲸鱼骨骼。

definitionLines: 一 1. 素描，速写；略图；梗概，大意
vt. 速写，写生；概述，简述
entries.definition: 一 1. 素描，速写；略图；梗概，大意 vt. 速写，写生；概述，简述
entries.etymology:
"rough drawing intended to serve as the basis for a finished picture," 1660s, from Dutch schets or Low German skizze, both apparently 17c. artists' borrowings from Italian schizzo "sketch, drawing," which is commonly said to be from Latin *schedius (OED compares schedia "raft," schedium "an extemporaneous poem"), from or related to Greek skhedios "temporary, extemporaneous, done or made off-hand," related to skhema "form, shape, appearance" (see scheme (n.)). But according to Barnhart Italian schizzo is a special use of schizzo "a splash, squirt," from schizzare "to splash or squirt," of uncertain origin.

Extended sense of "brief account" is from 1660s; meaning "short play or performance, usually comic" is from 1789. Sketch-book recorded from 1820. German Skizze, French esquisse, Spanish esquicio are likewise from Italian schizzo.
entries.etymologyZh: "rough drawing intended to serve as the basis for a finished picture," 1660 年代, 源自 荷兰语 schets or Low 德语 skizze, both 似乎 17 世纪 artists' borrowings 源自 意大利语 schizzo "sketch, drawing," which is commonly said to be 源自 拉丁语 *schedius (OED compares schedia "raft," schedium "an extemporaneous poem"), 源自 or related to 希腊语 skhedios "temporary, extemporaneous, done or made off-hand," related to skhema "form, shape, appearance" （参见 scheme （名）). But according to Barnhart 意大利语 schizzo is a special use of schizzo "a splash, squirt," 源自 schizzare "to splash or squirt," 来源存疑. Extended 语义 "brief account" 始于 1660 年代; 意为 "short play or performance, usually comic" 始于 1789 年. Sketch-book recorded 自 1820 年起. 德语 Skizze, 法语 esquisse, 西班牙语 esquicio are likewise 源自 意大利语 schizzo.

example.en: The artist made a quick sketch of the landscape before the sun set.
example.zh: 艺术家在日落前迅速画了一幅风景素描。

entries.definition: n. 雪橇 vi.滑雪 skill）ful a. 灵巧的，娴熟的
entries.etymology: 1883 (there is an isolated instance from 1755; in early use often spelled skee), from Norwegian ski, related to Old Norse skið "long snowshoe," literally "stick of wood, firewood," cognate with Old English scid "stick of wood," obsolete English shide "piece of wood split off from timber;" Old High German skit, German Scheit "log," from Proto-Germanic *skid- "to divide, split," from PIE root *skei- "to cut, split" (see shed (v.)). Ski-jumper is from 1894; ski bum first attested 1960; ski-mask is from 1963; noted as part of criminal disguises from 1968.
entries.etymologyZh: 1883 年 (there is an isolated instance 自 1755 年起; in early use 常 spelled skee), 源自 Norwegian ski, related to 古北欧语 skið "long snowshoe," 字面义为 "stick of wood, firewood," 与 … 同源 古英语 scid "stick of wood," 已废 English shide "piece of wood split off from timber;" 古高地德语 skit, 德语 Scheit "log," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skid- "to divide, split," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *skei- "to cut, split" （参见 shed （动）). Ski-jumper 始于 1894 年; ski bum 最早见于 1960 年; ski-mask 始于 1963 年; noted as part of criminal disguises 自 1968 年起.

example.en: She learned to ski on the snowy slopes during winter vacation.
example.zh: 寒假期间，她在雪坡上学会了滑雪。

definitionLines: n. 技巧，技能，手艺；熟练
entries.definition: n. 技巧，技能，手艺；熟练
entries.etymology: late 12c., "power of discernment," from Old Norse skil "distinction, ability to make out, discernment, adjustment," related to skilja (v.) "to separate; discern, understand," from Proto-Germanic *skaljo- "divide, separate" (source also of Swedish skäl "reason," Danish skjel "a separation, boundary, limit," Middle Low German schillen "to differ," Middle Low German, Middle Dutch schele "separation, discrimination;" see shell (n.)). Sense of "ability, cleverness" first recorded early 13c.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪晚期, "power of discernment," 源自 古北欧语 skil "distinction, ability to make out, discernment, adjustment," related to skilja （动） "to separate; discern, understand," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skaljo- "divide, separate" (source also of Swedish skäl "reason," Danish skjel "a separation, boundary, limit," Middle Low 德语 schillen "to differ," Middle Low 德语, Middle 荷兰语 schele "separation, discrimination;" 参见 shell （名）). 义为 "ability, cleverness" 首见于 13 世纪初

example.en: Good communication skills are essential for any leadership role.

definitionLines: a. 有技能的，熟练的；需要技 能的
entries.definition: a. 有技能的，熟练的；需要技 能的
entries.etymology: 1550s, past participle adjective from skill (v.) "to have personal and practical knowledge" (c. 1200), from Old Norse skilja "separate, part, divide; break off, break up; part company, take leave; discern, distinguish; understand, find out; decide, settle," from the source of skill (n.).

example.en: The factory needed skilled workers to operate the equipment.
example.zh: 工厂需要有技术的工人来操作设备。

entries.etymology: early 15c. (skimmer, the utensil, is attested from late 14c.), "to clear (a liquid) from matter floating on the surface, lift the scum from," from Old French escumer "remove scum," from escume (Modern French écume) "scum," from a Germanic source (compare Old High German scum "scum," German Schaum; see scum). Meaning "to throw (a stone) so as to skip across the surface of (water) is from 1610s. Meaning "to move lightly and rapidly over the surface of" is from 1650s, from the motion involved in skimming liquid; that of "to glance over carelessly" (in reference to printed matter) recorded by 1799. Related: Skimmed; skimming.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初 (skimmer, the utensil, 见于 14 世纪晚期), "to clear (a liquid) from matter floating on the surface, lift the scum from," 源自 古法语 escumer "remove scum," 源自 escume (现代法语 écume) "scum," 源自 a 日耳曼语 source (对比 古高地德语 scum "scum," 德语 Schaum; 参见 scum). 义为 "to throw (a stone) so as to skip across the surface of (water) is from 1610s. Meaning "to move lightly and rapidly over the surface of" is from 1650s, from the motion involved in skimming liquid; that of "to glance over carelessly" (in reference to printed matter) recorded 截至 1799 年. 同源词：Skimmed; skimming.

entries.definition: n. 皮，皮肤 vt. 剥皮
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "animal hide" (usually dressed and tanned), from Old Norse skinn "animal hide, fur," from Proto-Germanic *skintha- (source also of Old English scinn (rare), Old High German scinten, German schinden "to flay, skin;" German dialectal schind "skin of a fruit," Flemish schinde "bark"), from PIE *sken- "to cut off" (source also of Breton scant "scale of a fish," Irish scainim "I tear, I burst"), from root *sek- "to cut" (see section (n.)).

The usual Anglo-Saxon word is hide (n.1). Meaning "epidermis of a living animal or person" is attested from early 14c.; extended to fruits, vegetables, etc. late 14c. Jazz slang sense of "drum" is from 1927. Meaning "a skinhead" is from 1970. As an adjective, it formerly had a slang sense of "cheating" (1868); sense of "pornographic" is attested from 1968. Skin deep is first attested in this:

The skin of one's teeth as the narrowest of margins is attested from 1550s in the Geneva Bible literal translation of the Hebrew text in Job xix:20. To get under (someone's) skin "annoy" is from 1896. Skin-graft is from 1871. Skin merchant "recruiting officer" is from 1792.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "animal hide" (通常 dressed and tanned), 源自 古北欧语 skinn "animal hide, fur," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skintha- (source also of 古英语 scinn (rare), 古高地德语 scinten, 德语 schinden "to flay, skin;" 德语 方言 schind "skin of a fruit," Flemish schinde "bark"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sken- "to cut off" (source also of Breton scant "scale of a fish," 爱尔兰语 scainim "I tear, I burst"), 源自 root *sek- "to cut" （参见 section （名）). The usual 盎格鲁-撒克逊语 word is hide (n.1). 义为 "epidermis of a living animal or person" 见于 14 世纪初; extended to fruits, vegetables, etc. 14 世纪晚期 Jazz 俚语 语义 "drum" 始于 1927 年. 义为 "a skinhead" 始于 1970 年. 作形容词时, it formerly had a 俚语 语义 "cheating" (1868 年); 语义 "pornographic" 见于 1968 年. Skin deep is 最早见于 in this: The skin of one's teeth as the narrowest of margins is attested from 1550s in the Geneva Bible literal translation of the Hebrew text in Job xix:20. To get under (someone's) skin "annoy" 始于 1896 年. Skin-graft 始于 1871 年. Skin merchant "recruiting officer" 始于 1792 年.

example.en: Apply sunscreen daily to protect your skin from UV damage.
example.zh: 每天涂抹防晒霜，保护你的皮肤免受紫外线伤害。

entries.etymology: early 14c., "lower part of a woman's dress," from Old Norse skyrta "shirt, a kind of kirtle;" see shirt. Sense development from "shirt" to "skirt" is possibly related to the long shirts of peasant garb (compare Low German cognate Schört, in some dialects "woman's gown"). Sense of "border, edge" (in outskirts, etc.) first recorded late 15c. Metonymic use for "women collectively" is from 1550s; slang sense of "young woman" is from 1906; skirt-chaser first attested 1942.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "lower part of a woman's dress," 源自 古北欧语 skyrta "shirt, a kind of kirtle;" 参见 shirt.
