example.en: She wore a floral skirt that reached just below her knees.
example.zh: 她穿着一条刚到膝盖以下的碎花裙子。

entries.etymology: "bony framework of the head," c. 1200, probably from Old Norse skalli "a bald head, skull," a general Scandinavian word (compare Swedish skulle, Norwegian skult), probably related to Old English scealu "husk" (see shell (n.)). But early prominence in southwestern texts suggests rather origin from a Dutch or Low German cognate (such as Dutch schol "turf, piece of ice," but the sense of "head bone framework" is wanting). Derivation from Old French escuelle seems unlikely on grounds of sound and sense. Old English words for skull include heafod-bolla.
entries.etymologyZh: "bony framework of the head," 约 1200 年, 可能 源自 古北欧语 skalli "a bald head, skull," a general Scandinavian word (对比 Swedish skulle, Norwegian skult), 可能 related to 古英语 scealu "husk" （参见 shell （名）). But early prominence in southwestern texts suggests rather origin 源自 a 荷兰语 or Low 德语 同源 (such as 荷兰语 schol "turf, piece of ice," but the 语义 "head bone framework" is wanting). Derivation 源自 古法语 escuelle seems unlikely on grounds of sound and sense. 古英语 words for skull include heafod-bolla.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "a cloud," from Old Norse sky "cloud," from Proto-Germanic *skeujam "cloud, cloud cover" (source also of Old English sceo, Old Saxon scio "cloud, region of the clouds, sky;" Old High German scuwo, Old English scua, Old Norse skuggi "shadow;" Gothic skuggwa "mirror"), from PIE root *(s)keu- "to cover, conceal" (see hide (n.1)).

Meaning "upper regions of the air" is attested from c. 1300; replaced native heofon in this sense (see heaven). In Middle English, the word can still mean both "cloud" and "heaven," as still in the skies, originally "the clouds." Sky-high is from 1812; phrase the sky's the limit is attested from 1908. Sky-dive first recorded 1965; sky-writing is from 1922.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "a cloud," 源自 古北欧语 sky "cloud," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *skeujam "cloud, cloud cover" (source also of 古英语 sceo, 古撒克逊语 scio "cloud, region of the clouds, sky;" 古高地德语 scuwo, 古英语 scua, 古北欧语 skuggi "shadow;" Gothic skuggwa "mirror"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *(s)keu- "to cover, conceal" （参见 hide (n.1)). 义为 "upper regions of the air" 见于 约 1300 年; replaced 本族 heofon in this sense （参见 heaven). In 中古英语, the word can still mean both "cloud" and "heaven," as still in the skies, 原义为 "the clouds." Sky-high 始于 1812 年; phrase the sky's the limit 见于 1908 年. Sky-dive 首见于 1965 年; sky-writing 始于 1922 年.

definitionLines: n. 地平线；空中轮廓线
entries.definition: n. 地平线；空中轮廓线
entries.etymology: "horizon," 1824, from sky (n.) + line (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: "horizon," 1824 年, 源自 sky （名） + line （名）.

entries.etymology:
Old English slæc "remiss, lax, characterized by lack of energy, sluggish, indolent, languid; slow, gentle, easy," from Proto-Germanic *slakas (source also of Old Saxon slak, Old Norse slakr, Old High German slah "slack," Middle Dutch lac "fault, lack"), from PIE root *(s)leg- "to be slack" (see lax).

Sense of "not tight" (in reference to things) is first recorded c. 1300. As an adverb from late 14c. Slack-key (1975) translates Hawaiian ki ho'alu. Slack water (n.) "time when tide is not flowing" is from 1769. Slack-handed "remiss" is from 1670s. Slack-baked "baked imperfectly, half-baked" is from 1823; figuratively from 1840.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 slæc "remiss, lax, characterized by lack of energy, sluggish, indolent, languid; slow, gentle, easy," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slakas (source also of 古撒克逊语 slak, 古北欧语 slakr, 古高地德语 slah "slack," Middle 荷兰语 lac "fault, lack"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *(s)leg- "to be slack" （参见 lax). 义为 "not tight" (in reference to things) is 首见于 约 1300 年. 作为 副词 源自 14 世纪晚期 Slack-key (1975 年) translates Hawaiian ki ho'alu. Slack water （名） "time when tide is not flowing" 始于 1769 年. Slack-handed "remiss" 始于 1670 年代. Slack-baked "baked imperfectly, half-baked" 始于 1823 年; figuratively 自 1840 年起.

definitionLines: v. 砰地关上，砰地放下，猛力 抨击
entries.definition: v. 砰地关上，砰地放下，猛力 抨击 n. 砰，猛击，撞击
entries.etymology: 1690s, "to beat, slap;" 1775 as "to shut with force," from slam (n.1). Meaning "throw or push with force" is from 1870. Meaning "say uncomplimentary things about" is from 1916. Related: Slammed; slamming.
entries.etymologyZh: 1690 年代, "to beat, slap;" 1775 年 as "to shut with force," 源自 slam (n.1). 义为 "throw or push with force" 始于 1870 年. 义为 "say uncomplimentary things about" 始于 1916 年. 同源词：Slammed; slamming.

example.en: She slammed the door so hard that the windows rattled.
example.zh: 她用力将门砰地关上，窗户都颤动了。

entries.etymology: very tall urban building, 1888, in a Chicago context, from sky (n.) + agent noun of scrape (v.). Used earlier for "ornament atop a building" (1883), "very tall man" (1857), "high-flying bird" (1840), "light sail at the top of a mast" (1794), and the name of a racehorse (1789). Compare cognate French gratte-ciel, from gratter "to scrape" + ciel "sky;" German Wolkenkratzer, from Wolke "cloud" + Kratzer "scraper."
entries.etymologyZh: very tall urban building, 1888 年, in a Chicago context, 源自 sky （名） + agent 名词 of scrape （动）. Used earlier for "ornament atop a building" (1883 年), "very tall man" (1857 年), "high-flying bird" (1840 年), "light sail at the top of a mast" (1794 年), and the name of a racehorse (1789 年). 对比 同源 法语 gratte-ciel, 源自 gratter "to scrape" + ciel "sky;" 德语 Wolkenkratzer, 源自 Wolke "cloud" + Kratzer "scraper."

entries.etymology: late 15c., "strike with the open hand," from slap (n.). As an adverb, 1670s, "suddenly;" 1829, "directly." Related: Slapped; slapping.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "strike with the open hand," 源自 slap （名）. 作为 副词, 1670 年代, "suddenly;" 1829 年, "directly." 同源词：Slapped; slapping.

example.en: She slapped her knee against the table in frustration.
example.zh: 她沮丧地用手拍打膝盖撞到了桌子。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "killing of a cattle or sheep for food, killing of a person," from a Scandinavian *slahtr, akin to Old Norse slatr "a butchering, butcher meat," slatra "to slaughter," slattr "a mowing" from Proto-Germanic *slukhtis, related to Old Norse sla "to strike" (see slay (v.)) + formative suffix (as in laugh/laughter). Meaning "killing of a large number of persons in battle" is attested from mid-14c. Old English had slieht "stroke, slaughter, murder, death; animals for slaughter;" as in sliehtswyn "pig for killing."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "killing of a cattle or sheep for food, killing of a person," 源自 a Scandinavian *slahtr, akin to 古北欧语 slatr "a butchering, butcher meat," slatra "to slaughter," slattr "a mowing" 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slukhtis, related to 古北欧语 sla "to strike" （参见 slay （动）) + formative suffix (as in laugh/laughter). 义为 "killing of a large number of persons in battle" 见于 14 世纪中期 古英语 had slieht "stroke, slaughter, murder, death; animals for slaughter;" as in sliehtswyn "pig for killing."

entries.etymology: Indian tribe of northwestern Canada, 1789, from slave (n.), translating Cree (Algonquian) awahkan "captive, slave."
entries.etymologyZh: Indian tribe of northwestern Canada, 1789 年, 源自 slave （名）, translating Cree (Algonquian) awahkan "captive, slave."

example.en: Thousands of slaves were forced to work on the plantation without pay.
example.zh: 数千名奴隶被迫在种植园里无偿劳作。

entries.etymology: 1550s, "severe toil, hard work, drudgery;" from slave (v.) + -ery. Meaning "state of servitude" is from 1570s; meaning "keeping or holding of slaves" is from 1728.
entries.etymologyZh: 1550 年代, "severe toil, hard work, drudgery;" 源自 slave （动） + -ery. 义为 "state of servitude" 始于 1570 年代; 意为 "keeping or holding of slaves" 始于 1728 年.

example.en: The movement sought to abolish slavery and grant freedom to all people.
example.zh: 该运动致力于废除奴隶制，给予所有人自由。

entries.etymology:
Old English slæp "sleep, sleepiness, inactivity," from Proto-Germanic *slepaz, from the root of sleep (v.); compare cognate Old Saxon slap, Old Frisian slep, Middle Dutch slæp, Dutch slaap, Old High German slaf, German Schlaf, Gothic sleps.

Personified in English from late 14c., on model of Latin Somnus), Greek Hypnos. Figurative use for "repose of death" was in Old English; to put (an animal) to sleep "kill painlessly" is recorded from 1923 (a similar imagery is in cemetery). Sleep deprivation attested from 1906. Sleep-walker "somnambulist" is attested from 1747; sleep-walking is from 1840. To be able to do something in (one's) sleep "easily" is recorded from 1953.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 slæp "sleep, sleepiness, inactivity," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slepaz, 源自 root of sleep （动）; 对比 同源 古撒克逊语 slap, 古弗里西语 slep, Middle 荷兰语 slæp, 荷兰语 slaap, 古高地德语 slaf, 德语 Schlaf, Gothic sleps. Personified in English 源自 14 世纪晚期, on model of 拉丁语 Somnus), 希腊语 Hypnos. Figurative use for "repose of death" was in 古英语; to put (an animal) to sleep "kill painlessly" 见于 1923 年 (a similar imagery is in cemetery). Sleep deprivation attested 自 1906 年起. Sleep-walker "somnambulist" 见于 1747 年; sleep-walking 始于 1840 年. To be able to do something in (one's) sleep "easily" 见于 1953 年.

entries.etymology: early 13c. from sleep (n.) + -y (2). Perhaps in Old English but not recorded. Old English had slæpor, slæpwerig in the sense "sleepy;" slæpnes "sleepiness." Similar formation in Old High German slafag. Of places, from 1851 (Irving's Sleepy Hollow is from 1820). Sleepy-head is from 1570s. Related: Sleepily; sleepiness.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初 源自 sleep （名） + -y (2). Perhaps in 古英语 but not recorded. 古英语 had slæpor, slæpwerig in the sense "sleepy;" slæpnes "sleepiness." Similar formation in 古高地德语 slafag. Of places, 自 1851 年起 (Irving's Sleepy Hollow 始于 1820 年). Sleepy-head 始于 1570 年代. 同源词：Sleepily; sleepiness.

entries.etymology:
Old English sliefe (West Saxon), slefe (Mercian) "arm-covering part of a garment," probably literally "that into which the arm slips," from Proto-Germanic *slaubjon (source also of Middle Low German sloven "to dress carelessly," Old High German sloufen "to put on or off"). Related to Old English slefan, sliefan "to slip on (clothes)" and slupan "to slip, glide," from PIE root *sleubh- "to slide, slip."

Compare slipper, Old English slefescoh "slipper," slip (n.2) "woman's garment," and expression slip into "dress in." Mechanical sense is attested from 1864. Meaning "the English Channel" translates French La Manche. To have something up one's sleeve is recorded from c. 1500 (large sleeves formerly doubled as pockets). To wear one's heart on (one's) sleeve is from "Othello" (1604).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sliefe (West Saxon), slefe (Mercian) "arm-covering part of a garment," 可能 字面义为 "that into which the arm slips," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slaubjon (source also of Middle Low 德语 sloven "to dress carelessly," 古高地德语 sloufen "to put on or off"). Related to 古英语 slefan, sliefan "to slip on (clothes)" and slupan "to slip, glide," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sleubh- "to slide, slip." 对比 slipper, 古英语 slefescoh "slipper," slip (n.2) "woman's garment," and expression slip into "dress in." Mechanical sense 见于 1864 年. 义为 "the English Channel" translates 法语 La Manche. To have something up one's sleeve is recorded from c. 1500 (large sleeves formerly doubled as pockets). To wear one's heart on (one's) sleeve 始于 "Othello" (1604 年).

example.en: She rolled up her sleeves before washing the dishes.
example.zh: 她在洗碗前把袖子卷了起来。

entries.etymology: c. 1400, earlier sclendre (late 14c.), probably from a French source, often said to be from Old French esclendre "thin, slender," which could be from Old Dutch slinder, but the connections, and even the existence of these words, is doubtful. Related: Slenderly; slenderness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, earlier sclendre (14 世纪晚期), 可能 源自 a 法语 source, 常 said to be 源自 古法语 esclendre "thin, slender," which could be 源自 古荷兰语 slinder, but the connections, and even the existence of these words, is doubtful. 同源词：Slenderly; slenderness.

example.en: In her sketch, the fingers were slender: long, thin, and graceful rather than thick.
example.zh: 在她的素描中，手指显得修长纤细：又长又细、姿态优美，并不粗厚。

entries.etymology: late 15c., from Middle French esclicier, from Old French escliz (see slice (n.)). Golfing sense is from 1890. Related: Sliced; slicing. Sliced bread is attested from 1929 and was touted in advertisements; greatest thing since ... first attested 1969.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, 源自 中古法语 esclicier, 源自 古法语 escliz （参见 slice （名）). Golfing sense 始于 1890 年. 同源词：Sliced; slicing. Sliced bread 见于 1929 年 and was touted in advertisements; greatest thing 自 ... 最早见于 1969 年.

example.en: He cut a thin slice of bread and spread butter on it.
example.zh: 他切了一片薄薄的面包，涂上黄油。

entries.etymology:
Old English slidan (intransitive, past tense slad, past participle sliden) "to glide, slip, fall, fall down;" figuratively "fail, lapse morally, err; be transitory or unstable," from Proto-Germanic *slidan "to slip, slide" (source also of Old High German slito, German Schlitten "sleigh, sled"), from PIE root *sleidh- "to slide, slip" (source also of Lithuanian slystu "to glide, slide," Old Church Slavonic sledu "track," Greek olisthos "slipperiness," olisthanein "to slip," Middle Irish sloet "slide").

Meaning "slip, lose one's footing" is from early 13c. Transitive sense from 1530s. Phrase let (something) slide "let it take its own course" is in Chaucer (late 14c.). Sliding scale in reference to payments, etc., is from 1842.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 slidan (intransitive, past tense slad, past participle sliden) "to glide, slip, fall, fall down;" figuratively "fail, lapse morally, err; be transitory or unstable," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slidan "to slip, slide" (source also of 古高地德语 slito, 德语 Schlitten "sleigh, sled"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sleidh- "to slide, slip" (source also of Lithuanian slystu "to glide, slide," Old Church Slavonic sledu "track," 希腊语 olisthos "slipperiness," olisthanein "to slip," Middle 爱尔兰语 sloet "slide"). 义为 "slip, lose one's footing" 始于 13 世纪初 Transitive sense 源自 1530 年代. Phrase let (something) slide "let it take its own course" is in Chaucer (14 世纪晚期). Sliding scale in reference to payments, etc., 始于 1842 年.

example.en: The child watched the toy car slide down the ramp.
example.zh: 孩子看着玩具车沿斜面滑下去。

definitionLines: a. 轻微的，细微的；纤细的， 瘦弱的
entries.definition: a. 轻微的，细微的；纤细的， 瘦弱的
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "flat, smooth; hairless," probably from a Scandinavian source akin to Old Norse slettr "smooth, sleek," from Proto-Germanic *slikhtaz (source also of Old Saxon slicht; Low German slicht "smooth, plain common;" Old English -sliht "level," attested in eorðslihtes "level with the ground;" Old Frisian sliucht "smooth, slight," Middle Dutch sleht "even, plain," Old High German sleht, Gothic slaihts "smooth"), probably from a collateral form of PIE *sleig- "to smooth, glide, be muddy," from root *(s)lei- "slimy" (see slime (n.)).

Sense evolution probably is from "smooth" (c. 1300), to "slim, slender; of light texture," hence "not good or strong; insubstantial, trifling, inferior, insignificant" (early 14c.). Meaning "small in amount" is from 1520s. Sense of German cognate schlecht developed from "smooth, plain, simple" to "bad, mean, base," and as it did it was replaced in the original senses by schlicht, a back-formation from schlichten "to smooth, to plane," a derivative of schlecht in the old sense [Klein].
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "flat, smooth; hairless," 可能 源自 a Scandinavian source akin to 古北欧语 slettr "smooth, sleek," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slikhtaz (source also of 古撒克逊语 slicht; Low 德语 slicht "smooth, plain common;" 古英语 -sliht "level," 见于 eorðslihtes "level with the ground;" 古弗里西语 sliucht "smooth, slight," Middle 荷兰语 sleht "even, plain," 古高地德语 sleht, Gothic slaihts "smooth"), 可能 源自 a collateral form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sleig- "to smooth, glide, be muddy," 源自 root *(s)lei- "slimy" （参见 slime （名）). Sense evolution 可能 始于 "smooth" (约 1300 年), to "slim, slender; of light texture," hence "not good or strong; insubstantial, trifling, inferior, insignificant" (14 世纪初). 义为 "small in amount" 始于 1520 年代. 义为 德语 同源 schlecht developed 源自 "smooth, plain, simple" to "bad, mean, base," and as it did it was replaced in the original senses by schlicht, a back-formation 源自 schlichten "to smooth, to plane," a 为 … 的派生形式 schlecht in the old sense [Klein].

example.en: She felt a slight headache after staring at the screen for hours.
example.zh: 长时间盯着屏幕后，她感到轻微头痛。

definitionLines: a.苗条的，纤细的；不足取的， 无价值的；细长的
entries.definition: a.苗条的，纤细的；不足取的， 无价值的；细长的 v.变细，减肥
entries.etymology: 1650s, "thin, slight, slender," from Dutch slim "bad, sly, clever," from Middle Dutch slim "bad, crooked," from Proto-Germanic *slembaz "oblique, crooked" (source also of Middle High German slimp "slanting, awry," German schlimm "bad, cunning, unwell"). In English 17c. also sometimes with a sense "sly, cunning, crafty." Related: Slimly; slimness. With obsolete extended adjectival forms Slimsy "flimsy, unsubstantial" (1845); slimikin "small and slender" (1745). Slim Jim attested from 1887 in sense of "very thin person;" from 1902 as a type of slender cigar; from 1975 as a brand of meat snack.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, "thin, slight, slender," 源自 荷兰语 slim "bad, sly, clever," 源自 Middle 荷兰语 slim "bad, crooked," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slembaz "oblique, crooked" (source also of Middle High 德语 slimp "slanting, awry," 德语 schlimm "bad, cunning, unwell"). In English 17 世纪 also 有时 with a sense "sly, cunning, crafty." 同源词：Slimly; slimness. With 已废 extended adjectival forms Slimsy "flimsy, unsubstantial" (1845 年); slimikin "small and slender" (1745 年). Slim Jim attested 自 1887 年起 in 语义 "very thin person;" 自 1902 年起 作为 type of slender cigar; 自 1975 年起 作为 brand of meat snack.

example.en: She followed a strict diet to maintain her slim figure.
example.zh: 她严格节食以保持苗条的身材。

definitionLines: vi. 滑，滑倒；溜走；犯错误
entries.definition: vi. 滑，滑倒；溜走；犯错误 n. 疏忽，笔误，口误
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "to escape, to move softly and quickly," from an unrecorded Old English word or cognate Middle Low German slippen "to glide, slide," from Proto-Germanic *slipan (source also of Old High German slifan, Middle Dutch slippen, German schleifen "to glide, slide"), from PIE *sleib-, from root *(s)lei- "slimy, sticky, slippery" (see slime (n.)).

From mid-14c. with senses "lose one's footing," "slide out of place," "fall into error or fault." Sense of "pass unguarded or untaken" is from mid-15c. That of "slide, glide" is from 1520s. Transitive sense from 1510s; meaning "insert surreptitiously" is from 1680s. Related: Slipped; slipping. To slip up "make a mistake" is from 1855; to slip through the net "evade detection" is from 1902.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "to escape, to move softly and quickly," 源自 an unrecorded 古英语 word or 同源 Middle Low 德语 slippen "to glide, slide," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slipan (source also of 古高地德语 slifan, Middle 荷兰语 slippen, 德语 schleifen "to glide, slide"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sleib-, 源自 root *(s)lei- "slimy, sticky, slippery" （参见 slime （名）). From 14 世纪中期 with senses "lose one's footing," "slide out of place," "fall into error or fault." 义为 "pass unguarded or untaken" 始于 15 世纪中期 That of "slide, glide" 始于 1520 年代. Transitive sense 源自 1510 年代; 意为 "insert surreptitiously" 始于 1680 年代. 同源词：Slipped; slipping. To slip up "make a mistake" 始于 1855 年; to slip through the net "evade detection" 始于 1902 年.

example.en: He slip on the icy sidewalk and twisted his ankle badly.
example.zh: 他在结冰的人行道上滑倒，脚踝严重扭伤。

entries.etymology: type of loose, light indoor footwear, late 15c., agent noun from slip (v.), the notion being of a shoe that is "slipped" onto the foot. Old English had slypescoh "slipper," literally "slip-shoe."
entries.etymologyZh: type of loose, light indoor footwear, 15 世纪晚期, agent 名词 源自 slip （动）, the notion being of a shoe that is "slipped" onto the foot. 古英语 had slypescoh "slipper," 字面义为 "slip-shoe."

definitionLines: a. 滑的，滑溜的；狡猾的
entries.definition: a. 滑的，滑溜的；狡猾的
entries.etymology: "having a slippery surface," c. 1500, from Middle English sliper (adj.) "readily slipping," from Old English slipor "slippery, having a smooth surface" (see slip (v.)) + -y (2). Metaphoric sense of "deceitful, untrustworthy" is first recorded 1550s. Related: Slipperiness. In a figurative sense, slippery slope is first attested 1844. Slippery elm (1748) so called for its mucilaginous inner bark.
entries.etymologyZh: "having a slippery surface," 约 1500 年, 源自 中古英语 sliper （形） "readily slipping," 源自 古英语 slipor "slippery, having a smooth surface" （参见 slip （动）) + -y (2). Metaphoric 语义 "deceitful, untrustworthy" is 首见于 1550 年代. 同源词：Slipperiness. In a figurative sense, slippery slope is 最早见于 1844 年. Slippery elm (1748 年) so called for its mucilaginous inner bark.

entries.etymology: 1670s, earlier slogorne (1510s), "battle cry," from Gaelic sluagh-ghairm "battle cry used by Scottish Highland or Irish clans," from sluagh "army, host, slew," from Celtic and Balto-Slavic *slough- "help, service." Second element is gairm "a cry" (see garrulous). Metaphoric sense of "distinctive word or phrase used by a political or other group" is first attested 1704.
entries.etymologyZh: 1670 年代, earlier slogorne (1510 年代), "battle cry," 源自 Gaelic sluagh-ghairm "battle cry used by Scottish Highland or Irish clans," 源自 sluagh "army, host, slew," 源自 Celtic and Balto-Slavic *slough- "help, service." Second element is gairm "a cry" （参见 garrulous). Metaphoric 语义 "distinctive word or phrase used by a political or other group" is 最早见于 1704 年.

example.en: The campaign's slogan was catchy enough to be remembered by millions of people.
example.zh: 这次活动的标语朗朗上口，让数百万人记住了它。

entries.etymology: 1590s, "go in an oblique direction," from earlier adjective meaning "slanting" (c. 1500), probably from Middle English aslope (adv.) "on the incline" (late 15c.), from Old English *aslopen, past participle of aslupan "to slip away," from a- "away" + slupan "to slip" (see sleeve). From 1709 as "to be in a slanting position;" transitive sense "place in a slanting position" is from c. 1600. Related: Sloped; sloping.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "go in an oblique direction," 源自 earlier 形容词 意为 "slanting" (约 1500 年), 可能 源自 中古英语 aslope （副） "on the incline" (15 世纪晚期), 源自 古英语 *aslopen, 为 … 的过去分词 aslupan "to slip away," 源自 a- "away" + slupan "to slip" （参见 sleeve). From 1709 年 as "to be in a slanting position;" transitive sense "place in a slanting position" 始于 约 1600 年. 同源词：Sloped; sloping.

example.en: The hikers carefully made their way down the steep slope after the rain.
example.zh: 徒步者在雨后小心翼翼地沿着陡坡下行。

example.en: There is only one open slot left in the doctor's schedule this week.
example.zh: 这周医生的日程表里只剩下一个空档。

entries.definition: a. 慢，缓慢；迟钝 n. 放慢，减速
entries.etymology: Old English slaw "inactive, sluggish, torpid, lazy," also "not clever," from Proto-Germanic *slæwaz (source also of Old Saxon sleu "blunt, dull," Middle Dutch slee, Dutch sleeuw "sour, tart, blunt," Old High German sleo "blunt, dull," Old Norse sljor, Danish sløv, Swedish slö "blunt, dull"). Meaning "taking a long time" is attested from early 13c. Meaning "dull, tedious" is from 1841. As an adverb c. 1500. The slows "imaginary disease to account for lethargy" is from 1843.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 slaw "inactive, sluggish, torpid, lazy," also "not clever," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *slæwaz (source also of 古撒克逊语 sleu "blunt, dull," Middle 荷兰语 slee, 荷兰语 sleeuw "sour, tart, blunt," 古高地德语 sleo "blunt, dull," 古北欧语 sljor, Danish sløv, Swedish slö "blunt, dull"). 义为 "taking a long time" 见于 13 世纪初 义为 "dull, tedious" 始于 1841 年. 作为 副词 约 1500 年. example.en: The driver had to slow down when approaching the school zone.

entries.etymology: 1845, from back slum "dirty back alley of a city, street of poor or low people" (1825), originally a slang or cant word meaning "room," especially "back room" (1812), of unknown origin, pastime popularized by East End novels. Related: slums. Slumscape is from 1947.

entries.etymology:
1670s, "fall or sink into a muddy place," probably from a Scandinavian source such as Norwegian and Danish slumpe "fall upon," Swedish slumpa; perhaps ultimately of imitative origin. Related: Slumped; slumping.

Economic sense from 1888.
entries.etymologyZh: 1670 年代, "fall or sink into a muddy place," 可能 源自 a Scandinavian source such as Norwegian and Danish slumpe "fall upon," Swedish slumpa; 或许 ultimately of imitative origin. 同源词：Slumped; slumping. Economic sense 自 1888 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English smæl "thin, slender, narrow; fine," from Proto-Germanic *smal- "small animal; small" (source also of Old Saxon, Danish, Swedish, Middle Dutch, Dutch, Old High German smal, Old Frisian smel, German schmal "narrow, slender," Gothic smalista "smallest," Old Norse smali "small cattle, sheep"), perhaps from a PIE root *(s)melo- "smaller animal" (source also of Greek melon, Old Irish mil "a small animal;" Old Church Slavonic malu "bad"). Original sense of "narrow" now almost obsolete, except in reference to waistline and intestines.

Sense of "not large, of little size" developed in Old English. Of children, "young," from mid-13c. Meaning "inferior in degree or amount" is from late 13c. Meaning "trivial, unimportant" is from mid-14c. Sense of "having little property or trade" is from 1746. That of "characterized by littleness of mind or spirit, base, low, mean" is from 1824. As an adverb by late 14c.
Small fry, first recorded 1690s of little fish, 1885 of insignificant people. Small potatoes "no great matter" first attested 1924; small change "something of little value" is from 1902; small talk "chit-chat, trifling conversation" (1751) first recorded in Chesterfield's "Letters." Small world as a comment upon an unexpected meeting of acquaintances is recorded from 1895. Small-arms, indicating those capable of being carried in the hand (contrasted to ordnance) is recorded from 1710.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 smæl "thin, slender, narrow; fine," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *smal- "small animal; small" (source also of 古撒克逊语, Danish, Swedish, Middle 荷兰语, 荷兰语, 古高地德语 smal, 古弗里西语 smel, 德语 schmal "narrow, slender," Gothic smalista "smallest," 古北欧语 smali "small cattle, sheep"), 或源自 a 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *(s)melo- "smaller animal" (source also of 希腊语 melon, Old 爱尔兰语 mil "a small animal;" Old Church Slavonic malu "bad"). Original 语义 "narrow" 现在 almost 已废, except in reference to waistline and intestines. 义为 "not large, of little size" developed in 古英语. Of children, "young," 源自 13 世纪中期 义为 "inferior in degree or amount" 始于 13 世纪晚期 义为 "trivial, unimportant" 始于 14 世纪中期 义为 "having little property or trade" 始于 1746 年. That of "characterized by littleness of mind or spirit, base, low, mean" 始于 1824 年. 作为 副词 by 14 世纪晚期 Small fry, 首见于 1690 年代 of little fish, 1885 年 of insignificant people. Small potatoes "no great matter" 最早见于 1924 年; small change "something of little value" 始于 1902 年; small talk "chit-chat, trifling conversation" (1751 年) 首见于 in Chesterfield's "Letters." Small world 作为 comment upon an unexpected meeting of acquaintances 见于 1895 年. Small-arms, indicating those capable of being carried in the hand (contrasted to ordnance) 见于 1710 年.

definitionLines: a. 漂亮，时髦；聪明，机智；敏捷
entries.definition: a. 漂亮，时髦；聪明，机智；敏捷
entries.etymology:
late Old English smeart "painful, severe, stinging; causing a sharp pain," related to smeortan (see smart (v.)). Meaning "executed with force and vigor" is from c. 1300. Meaning "quick, active, clever" is attested from c. 1300, from the notion of "cutting" wit, words, etc., or else "keen in bargaining." Meaning "trim in attire" first attested 1718, "ascending from the kitchen to the drawing-room c. 1880" [Weekley]. For sense evolution, compare sharp (adj.).

In reference to devices, the sense of "behaving as though guided by intelligence" (as in smart bomb) first attested 1972. Smarts "good sense, intelligence," is first recorded 1968 (Middle English had ingeny "intellectual capacity, cleverness" (early 15c.)). Smart cookie is from 1948.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 smeart "painful, severe, stinging; causing a sharp pain," related to smeortan （参见 smart （动）). 义为 "executed with force and vigor" 始于 约 1300 年. 义为 "quick, active, clever" 见于 约 1300 年, 源自 概念 "cutting" wit, words, etc.，或else "keen in bargaining." 义为 "trim in attire" 最早见于 1718 年, "ascending from the kitchen to the drawing-room c. 1880" [Weekley]. For sense evolution, 对比 sharp （形）. In reference to devices, the 语义 "behaving as though guided by intelligence" (as in smart bomb) 最早见于 1972 年. Smarts "good sense, intelligence," is 首见于 1968 年 (中古英语 had ingeny "intellectual capacity, cleverness" (15 世纪初)). Smart cookie 始于 1948 年.

example.en: The smart boy quickly memorized all the vocabulary words in one evening.
example.zh: 这个聪明的男孩在一个晚上就快速记住了所有单词。

entries.etymology: 1759, "break to pieces," earlier "kick downstairs" (c. 1700), probably of imitative origin (compare smack (v.), mash (v.), crush (v.)). Meaning "act with crushing force" is from 1813; that of "strike violently" is from 1835. Tennis sense is from 1882. Smash-and-grab (adj.) is first attested 1927.

example.en: He accidentally smashed the glass when he knocked it off the table.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, perhaps from Middle Low German *smilen or a Scandinavian source (such as Danish smile "smile," Swedish smila "smile, smirk, simper, fawn"), from Proto-Germanic *smil-, extended form of PIE root *smei- "to laugh, smile" (source also of Old English smerian "to laugh at, scorn," Old High German smieron "to smile," Latin mirus "wonderful," mirari "to wonder"). Related: Smiled; smiling. 

Gradually pushed the usual Old English word, smearcian (modern smirk), into a specific, unpleasant sense. Of the eyes, from 1759. Figuratively, as indicating favor or encouragement, from c. 1400. Romance, Celtic, and Slavic languages tend to use a diminutive of the word for "laugh" to mean "smile" (such as Latin ridere "laugh;" subridere "smile"), perhaps literally "small laugh" or "low laugh."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, 或源自 Middle Low 德语 *smilen or a Scandinavian source (such as Danish smile "smile," Swedish smila "smile, smirk, simper, fawn"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *smil-, extended form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *smei- "to laugh, smile" (source also of 古英语 smerian "to laugh at, scorn," 古高地德语 smieron "to smile," 拉丁语 mirus "wonderful," mirari "to wonder"). 同源词：Smiled; smiling. Gradually pushed the usual 古英语 word, smearcian (modern smirk), into a specific, unpleasant sense. Of the eyes, 自 1759 年起. Figuratively, as indicating favor or encouragement, 源自 约 1400 年. Romance, Celtic, and Slavic languages tend to use a 为 … 的指小形式 the word for "laugh" to mean "smile" (such as 拉丁语 ridere "laugh;" subridere "smile"), 或许 字面义为 "small laugh" or "low laugh."

example.en: The shy girl smiled nervously when the teacher called her name.
example.zh: 当老师叫到她名字时，那个害羞的女孩紧张地微笑了。

entries.definition: n. 烟，烟尘 v./n.吸烟，抽烟 v. 冒烟，冒气
entries.etymology: Old English smocian "to produce smoke, emit smoke," especially as a result of burning, from smoke (n.1). Meaning "to drive out or away or into the open by means of smoke" is attested from 1590s. Meaning "to apply smoke to, to cure (bacon, fish, etc.) by exposure to smoke" is first attested 1590s. In connection with tobacco, "draw fumes from burning into the mouth," first recorded 1604 in James I's "Counterblast to Tobacco." Related: Smoked; smoking. Smoking gun in figurative sense of "incontestable evidence" is from 1974.

In connection with tobacco, "draw fumes from burning into the mouth," 首见于 1604 年 in James I's "Counterblast to Tobacco." 同源词：Smoked; smoking. Smoking gun in figurative 语义 "incontestable evidence" 始于 1974 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English smoð "smooth, serene, calm," variant of smeðe "free from roughness, not harsh, polished; soft; suave; agreeable," of unknown origin and with no known cognates. Of words, looks, "pleasant, polite, sincere" late 14c., but later "flattering, insinuating" (mid-15c.). Slang meaning "superior, classy, clever" is attested from 1893. Sense of "stylish" is from 1922.

Smooth-bore in reference to guns is from 1812. smooth talk (v.) is recorded from 1950. A 1599 dictionary has smoothboots "a flatterer, a faire spoken man, a cunning tongued fellow." The usual Old English form was smeðe, and there is a dialectal smeeth found in places names, such as Smithfield, Smedley.

The usual 古英语 form was smeðe, and there is a 方言 smeeth found in places names, such as Smithfield, Smedley.

example.en: Thanks to careful planning, the event proceeded smooth.
example.zh: 得益于精心筹划，活动进行得非常顺利。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to bite or snap" (of a dog), probably from Middle Dutch or Flemish snacken "to snatch, snap; chatter," which Watkins traces to a hypothetical Germanic imitative root *snu- forming words having to do with the nose (see snout). The meaning "have a mere bite or morsel, eat a light meal" is first attested 1807. Related: Snacked; snacking.

The 意为 "have a mere bite or morsel, eat a light meal" is 最早见于 1807 年. 同源词：Snacked; snacking.

example.en: She grabbed a quick snack between classes to keep her energy up.
example.zh: 她在课间抓紧吃了点零食来保持精力。

entries.etymology:
Old English snaca, from Proto-Germanic *snakon (source also of Old Norse snakr "snake," Swedish snok, German Schnake "ring snake"), from PIE root *sneg- "to crawl, creeping thing" (source also of Old Irish snaighim "to creep," Lithuanian snake "snail," Old High German snahhan "to creep"). In Modern English, gradually replacing serpent in popular use.

Traditionally applied to the British serpent, as distinguished from the poisonous adder. Meaning "treacherous person" first recorded 1580s (compare Old Church Slavonic gadu "reptile," gadinu "foul, hateful"). Applied from 17c. to various snake-like devices and appliances. Snakes! as an exclamation is from 1839.

Snake eyes in crap-shooting sense is from 1919. Snake-bitten "unlucky" is sports slang from 1957, from a literal sense, perhaps suggesting one doomed by being poisoned. The game of Snakes and Ladders is attested from 1907. Snake charmer is from 1813. Snake pit is from 1883, as a supposed primitive test of truth or courage; figurative sense is from 1941. Phrase snake in the grass is from Virgil's Latet anguis in herba [Ecl. III:93].
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 snaca, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *snakon (source also of 古北欧语 snakr "snake," Swedish snok, 德语 Schnake "ring snake"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sneg- "to crawl, creeping thing" (source also of Old 爱尔兰语 snaighim "to creep," Lithuanian snake "snail," 古高地德语 snahhan "to creep"). In 现代英语, gradually replacing serpent in popular use. Traditionally applied to the British serpent, as distinguished 源自 poisonous adder. 义为 "treacherous person" 首见于 1580 年代 (对比 Old Church Slavonic gadu "reptile," gadinu "foul, hateful"). Applied 源自 17 世纪 to various snake-like devices and appliances. Snakes! 作为 exclamation 始于 1839 年. Snake eyes in crap-shooting sense 始于 1919 年. Snake-bitten "unlucky" is sports 俚语 自 1957 年起, 源自 a literal sense, 或许 suggesting one doomed by being poisoned. The game of Snakes and Ladders 见于 1907 年. Snake charmer 始于 1813 年. Snake pit 始于 1883 年, 作为 supposed primitive test of truth or courage; figurative sense 始于 1941 年. Phrase snake in the grass 始于 Virgil's Latet anguis in herba [Ecl. III:93].

definitionLines: v. 猛地吸住，突然折断；使劈啪 地响；猛咬
entries.definition: v. 猛地吸住，突然折断；使劈啪 地响；猛咬 n.猛咬，突然折断，劈啪声 a.突然的
entries.etymology:
late 15c., "quick, sudden bite or cut," from Dutch or Low German snappen "to snap," probably related to Middle Low German or Middle Dutch snavel "bill, beak," from West Germanic *snu-, an imitative root forming words having to do with the nose (see snout).

As an adjective from 1790. Commonly used to indicate instantaneous action, as in snap judgment (1841). Sense of "quick movement" is first recorded 1630s; that of "something easily done" is 1877. Meaning "brief or sudden spell" of weather (usually cold) is from 1740. Meaning "catch or fastener that closes with a snapping sound" is from 1815. The card game name is attested from 1881, from a call used in the game. Meaning "a snap-shot" is from 1894. U.S. football sense is from 1912, earlier snap-back (1880), which also was a name for the center position. Snap, Crackle and Pop, cartoon characters associated with Kellogg breakfast cereal Rice Krispies, are from 1940.

Commonly used to indicate instantaneous action, as in snap judgment (1841 年). 义为 "quick movement" is 首见于 1630 年代; that of "something easily done" is 1877 年. 义为 "brief or sudden spell" of weather (通常 cold) 始于 1740 年. 义为 "catch or fastener that closes with a snapping sound" 始于 1815 年. The card game name 见于 1881 年, 源自 a call used in the game. 义为 "a snap-shot" 始于 1894 年. U.S. football sense 始于 1912 年, earlier snap-back (1880 年), which also was a name for the center position. Snap, Crackle and Pop, cartoon characters associated with Kellogg breakfast cereal Rice Krispies, 始于 1940 年.

example.en: The dry branch will snap under pressure with a sharp crack.
example.zh: 这根干树枝在压力下会突然脆断，发出清脆的声响。

entries.etymology: also snap-shot, 1808, "a quick shot with a gun, without aim, at a fast-moving target," from snap + shot (n.). Photographic sense is attested from 1890. Figuratively, of something captured at a moment in time, from 1897.
entries.etymologyZh: also snap-shot, 1808 年, "a quick shot with a gun, without aim, at a fast-moving target," 源自 snap + shot （名）. Photographic sense 见于 1890 年. Figuratively, of something captured at a moment in time, 自 1897 年起.

entries.etymology: early 13c., "make a sudden snap or bite" (at something), of uncertain origin; perhaps from an unrecorded Old English *snæccan or Middle Dutch snacken "to snatch, chatter." Compare snack (n.). Meaning "lay hold of suddenly" is from early 14c.; especially "take from someone's hands" (1580s). Weight-lifting sense is attested from 1928. Related: Snatched; snatching.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪初, "make a sudden snap or bite" (at something), 来源存疑; 或源自 an unrecorded 古英语 *snæccan or Middle 荷兰语 snacken "to snatch, chatter." 对比 snack （名）. 义为 "lay hold of suddenly" 始于 14 世纪初; 尤指 "take from someone's hands" (1580 年代). Weight-lifting sense 见于 1928 年. 同源词：Snatched; snatching.

example.en: The thief managed to snatch her purse and run into the crowd.
example.zh: 那个小偷抢走了她的钱包，随即跑进人群。

entries.etymology: Old English snaw "snow, that which falls as snow; a fall of snow; a snowstorm," from Proto-Germanic *snaiwaz (source also of Old Saxon and Old High German sneo, Old Frisian and Middle Low German sne, Middle Dutch snee, Dutch sneeuw, German Schnee, Old Norse snjor, Gothic snaiws "snow"), from PIE root *sniegwh- "snow; to snow" (source also of Greek nipha, Latin nix (genitive nivis), Old Irish snechta, Irish sneachd, Welsh nyf, Lithuanian sniegas, Old Prussian snaygis, Old Church Slavonic snegu, Russian snieg', Slovak sneh "snow"). The cognate in Sanskrit, snihyati, came to mean "he gets wet." As slang for "cocaine" it is attested from 1914.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 snaw "snow, that which falls as snow; a fall of snow; a snowstorm," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *snaiwaz (source also of 古撒克逊语 and 古高地德语 sneo, 古弗里西语 and Middle Low 德语 sne, Middle 荷兰语 snee, 荷兰语 sneeuw, 德语 Schnee, 古北欧语 snjor, Gothic snaiws "snow"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sniegwh- "snow; to snow" (source also of 希腊语 nipha, 拉丁语 nix (属格 nivis), Old 爱尔兰语 snechta, 爱尔兰语 sneachd, Welsh nyf, Lithuanian sniegas, Old Prussian snaygis, Old Church Slavonic snegu, 俄语 snieg', Slovak sneh "snow"). entries.etymology:
Old English sape "soap, salve" (originally a reddish hair dye used by Germanic warriors to give a frightening appearance), from Proto-Germanic *saipon "dripping thing, resin" (source also of Middle Low German sepe, West Frisian sjippe, Dutch zeep, Old High German seiffa, German seife "soap," Old High German seifar "foam," Old English sipian "to drip"), from PIE *soi-bon-, from root *seib- "to pour out, drip, trickle" (source also of Latin sebum "tallow, suet, grease").

Romans and Greeks used oil to clean skin; the Romance words for "soap" (Italian sapone, French savon, Spanish jabon) are from Late Latin sapo "pomade for coloring the hair" (first mentioned in Pliny), which is a Germanic loan-word, as is Finnish saippua. The meaning "flattery" is recorded from 1853.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sape "soap, salve" (原义为 a reddish hair dye used by 日耳曼语 warriors to give a frightening appearance), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *saipon "dripping thing, resin" (source also of Middle Low 德语 sepe, West Frisian sjippe, 荷兰语 zeep, 古高地德语 seiffa, 德语 seife "soap," 古高地德语 seifar "foam," 古英语 sipian "to drip"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *soi-bon-, 源自 root *seib- "to pour out, drip, trickle" (source also of 拉丁语 sebum "tallow, suet, grease"). Romans and Greeks used oil to clean skin; the Romance words for "soap" (意大利语 sapone, 法语 savon, 西班牙语 jabon) 始于 晚期拉丁语 sapo "pomade for coloring the hair" (first mentioned in Pliny), which is a 日耳曼语 loan-word, as is Finnish saippua. The 意为 "flattery" 见于 1853 年.

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French essorer "fly up, soar," from Vulgar Latin *exaurare "rise into the air," from Latin ex- "out" (see ex-) + aura "breeze, air" (see aura). Of mountains, buildings, etc., by 1812; of prices, emotions, etc. from 1929. Related: Soared; soaring.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 essorer "fly up, soar," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *exaurare "rise into the air," 源自 拉丁语 ex- "out" （参见 ex-) + aura "breeze, air" （参见 aura). Of mountains, buildings, etc., 截至 1812 年; of prices, emotions, etc. 自 1929 年起. 同源词：Soared; soaring.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "moderate in desires or actions, temperate, restrained," especially "abstaining from strong drink," also "calm, quiet, not overcome by emotion," from Old French sobre "decent; sober" (12c.), from Latin sobrius "not drunk, temperate, moderate, sensible," from a variant of se- "without" (see se-) + ebrius "drunk," of unknown origin. Meaning "not drunk at the moment" is from late 14c.; also "appropriately solemn, serious, not giddy." Related: Soberly; soberness. Sobersides "sedate, serious-minded person" is recorded from 1705.

definitionLines: a. 社会的；社交的，交际的
entries.definition: a. 社会的；社交的，交际的
entries.etymology:
late 15c., "devoted to or relating to home life;" 1560s as "living with others," from Middle French social (14c.) and directly from Latin socialis "of companionship, of allies; united, living with others; of marriage, conjugal," from socius "companion, ally," probably originally "follower," from PIE *sokw-yo-, suffixed form of root *sekw- (1) "to follow," and thus related to sequi "to follow" (see sequel). Compare Old English secg, Old Norse seggr "companion," which seem to have been formed on the same notion). Related: Socially.

Sense of "characterized by friendliness or geniality" is from 1660s. Meaning "living or liking to live with others; companionable, disposed to friendly intercourse" is from 1720s. Meaning "of or pertaining to society as a natural condition of human life" first attested 1695, in Locke. Sense of "pertaining to fashionable society" is from 1873.
Social climber is from 1893; social work is 1890; social worker 1886. Social drinking first attested 1807. Social studies as an inclusive term for history, geography, economics, etc., is attested from 1916. Social security "system of state support for needy citizens" is attested from 1907 (the Social Security Act was passed by U.S. Congress in 1935). Social butterfly is from 1867, in figurative reference to "flitting."

Social contract (1763) is from translations of Rousseau. Social Darwinism attested from 1887. Social engineering attested from 1899. Social science is from 1785.
In late 19c. newspapers, social evil is "prostitution." Social justice is attested by 1718; social network by 1971; social networking by 1984; social media by 2008.

The word begins to be used in French in the modern sense c. 1835.

entries.etymology:
"one who advocates socialism," 1827, from French socialiste, or else a native formation based on it, in reference to the teachings of Comte de Saint-Simon, founder of French socialism. The word begins to be used in French in the modern sense c. 1835. Socialista, with a different sense, was applied 18c. to followers and pupils of Dutch jurist Grotius (1583-1645), from his use of socialistus. Socialist realism attested from 1934.

Compare socialism.

entries.definition: n. 社会；协会，会；社交界，上流 社会
entries.etymology:
1530s, "companionship, friendly association with others," from Old French societe "company" (12c., Modern French société), from Latin societatem (nominative societas) "fellowship, association, alliance, union, community," from socius "companion" (see social (adj.)).

Meaning "group, club" is from 1540s, originally of associations of persons for some specific purpose. Meaning "people bound by neighborhood and intercourse aware of living together in an ordered community" is from 1630s. Sense of "the more cultivated part of any community" first recorded 1823, hence "fashionable people and their doings." The Society Islands were named 1769 by Cook on his third Pacific voyage in honor of the Royal Society, which financed his travels across the world to observe the transit of Venus.

entries.etymology:
late 15c., "sodium carbonate," an alkaline substance extracted from certain ashes (now made artificially), from Italian sida (or Medieval Latin soda) "a kind of saltwort," from which soda was obtained, of uncertain origin. Perhaps it is from a Catalan sosa, attested from late 13c., of uncertain origin. Proposed Arabic sources in a name of a variety of saltwort have not been attested and that theory is no longer considered valid. Another theory, considered far-fetched in some quarters, traces it to Medieval Latin sodanum "a headache remedy," ultimately from Arabic suda "splitting headache."

Soda is found naturally in alkaline lakes, in deposits where such lakes have dried, and from ash produced by burning various seaside plants. A major trading commodity in the medieval Mediterranean, since commercial manufacture of it began in France in late 18c., these other sources have been abandoned. Washing soda (sodium carbonate) is commonly distinguished from baking soda (sodium bicarbonate). A soda-cracker (1863) has baking soda as an ingredient. 

The meaning "carbonated water" is first recorded 1834, a shortening of soda water (1802) "water into which carbonic acid has been forced under pressure." "It rarely contains soda in any form; but the name originally applied when sodium carbonate was contained in it has been retained" [Century Dictionary, 1902]. Since 19c. typically flavored and sweetened with syrups.  First record of soda pop is from 1863, and the most frequent modern use of the word is as a shortening of this or other terms for "flavored, sweetened soda water." Compare pop (n.1). Soda fountain is from 1824; soda jerk first attested 1915 (soda-jerker is from 1883). Colloquial pronunciation "sody" is represented in print from 1900 (U.S. Midwestern).

entries.etymology:
Old English softe, earlier sefte, "gentle, mild-natured; easeful, comfortable, calm, undisturbed; luxurious," from West Germanic *samfti, from Proto-Germanic *samftijaz "level, even, smooth, gentle, soft" (source also of Old Saxon safti, Old High German semfti, German sanft; and from a variant form with -ch- for -f-, Middle Dutch sachte, Dutch zacht, German sacht), from root *som- "fitting, agreeable."

From c. 1200 of material things, "not stiff, not coarse, fine; yielding to weight." From late 14c. of wind, rain, etc. Of sounds, "quiet, not loud," from early 13c. Of words, "mild, restrained; courteous" mid-14c. From late 14c. as "indulgent," also "physically feeble; easily overcome, lacking manly courage." From 1755 of water ("relatively free from mineral salts"), from 1789 of coal. Meaning "foolish, simple, silly" is attested from 1620s; earlier "easily moved or swayed; soft-hearted, sympathetic; docile" (early 13c.). In reference to drinks, "non-alcoholic" from 1880. As an adverb, Old English softe "gently;" late 13c. as "quietly." As an interjection from 1540s.

Soft landing is from 1958 and the U.S. space program. Adjective soft-core (in reference to pornography) is from 1966 (see hardcore). Soft rock as a music style is attested from 1969. Soft sell is from 1955. Soft-shoe as a dancing style is attested from 1927. Soft-boiled is from 1757 of eggs; of persons, ideas, etc., 1930 (compare half-baked). Soft-focus (adj.) of camera shots is from 1917. The softer sex "women collectively" is from 1640s.

entries.etymology: early 13c., "to defile or pollute with sin," from Old French soillier "to splatter with mud, to foul or make dirty," originally "to wallow" (12c., Modern French souillier), from souil "tub, wild boar's wallow, pigsty," which is from either Latin solium "tub for bathing; seat," or Latin suculus "little pig," from sus "pig." Literal meaning "to make dirty, begrime" is attested from c. 1300 in English. Related: Soiled; soiling.

entries.etymology:
mid-15c., "pertaining to the sun," from Latin solaris "of the sun," from sol "sun" (see sol). Meaning "living room on an upper story" is from Old English, from Latin solarium (see solarium). Old English had sunlic "solar."

Astrological sense from 1620s. Meaning "operated by means of the sun" is from 1740; solar power is attested from 1915, solar cell from 1955, solar panel from 1964. Solar system is attested from c. 1704; solar wind is from 1958. Solar plexus (1771) "complex of nerves in the pit of the stomach," apparently so called from its central position in the body (see plexus).

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, souder, from Old French soudier, soldier "one who serves in the army for pay," from Medieval Latin soldarius "a soldier" (source also of Spanish soldado, Italian soldato), literally "one having pay," from Late Latin soldum, extended sense of accusative of Latin solidus, name of a Roman gold coin (see solidus).

The -l- has been regular in English since mid-14c., in imitation of Latin. Willie and Joe always say sojer in the Bill Mauldin cartoons, and this seems to mirror 16c.-17c. spellings sojar, soger, sojour. Modern French soldat is borrowed from Italian and displaced the older French word; one of many military (and other) terms picked up during the Italian Wars in early 16c.; such as alert, arsenal, colonel, infantrie, sentinel.

Old slang names for military men circa early 19c. include mud-crusher "infantryman," cat-shooter "volunteer," fly-slicer "cavalryman," jolly gravel-grinder "marine."

entries.etymology: "single, alone, having no husband or wife; one and only, singular, unique," late 14c., from Old French soul "only, alone, just," from Latin solus "alone, only, single, sole; forsaken; extraordinary," of unknown origin, perhaps related to se "oneself," from PIE reflexive root *swo- (see so).

example.en: She was the sole survivor of the plane crash.

definitionLines: a. 庄严的，严肃的；隆重的
entries.definition: a. 庄严的，严肃的；隆重的
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "performed with due religious ceremony or reverence, sacred, devoted to religious observances," also, of a vow, etc., "made under religious sanction, binding," from Old French solempne (12c., Modern French solennel) and directly from Latin sollemnis "annual, established, religiously fixed, formal, ceremonial, traditional," perhaps related to sollus "whole" (see safe (adj.)).

"The explanation that Latin sollemnis was formed from sollus whole + annus year is not considered valid" [Barnhart], but some assimilation via folk-etymology is possible. In Middle English also "famous, important; imposing, grand," hence Chaucer's friar, a ful solempne man. Meaning "marked by seriousness or earnestness" is from late 14c.; sense of "fitted to inspire devout reflection" is from c. 1400. Related: Solemnly.

"The explanation that Latin sollemnis was formed from sollus whole + annus year is not considered valid" [Barnhart], but some assimilation 经由 folk-etymology is possible. In 中古英语 also "famous, important; imposing, grand," hence Chaucer's friar, a ful solempne man. 义为 "marked by seriousness or earnestness" 始于 14 世纪晚期; 语义 "fitted to inspire devout reflection" 始于 约 1400 年. 同源词：Solemnly.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "one who urges," from Middle French soliciteur, from soliciter (see solicit). Meaning "one who conducts matters on behalf of another" is from early 15c. As a name for a specific class of legal practitioners in Britain, it is attested from 1570s. Both the fem. forms, solicitress (1630s) and solicitrix (1610s), have been in the sexual sense, but the latter seems more common in non-pejorative use.

definitionLines: a.固体的；实心的；结实的，稳 固的，可靠的
entries.definition: n./a.固体 a.固体的；实心的；结实的，稳 固的，可靠的
entries.etymology:
late 14c., "not empty or hollow," from Old French solide "firm, dense, compact," from Latin solidus "firm, whole, undivided, entire," figuratively "sound, trustworthy, genuine," from PIE *sol-ido-, suffixed form of root *sol- "whole" (source also of Greek holos "whole," Latin salus "health," salvus "safe;" see safe (adj.)).

Meaning "firm, hard, compact" is from 1530s. Meaning "entirely of the same stuff" is from 1710. Of qualities, "well-established, considerable" c. 1600. As a mere intensifier, 1830. Slang sense of "wonderful, remarkable" first attested 1920 among jazz musicians. As an adverb, "solidly, completely," 1650s. Solid South in U.S. political history is attested from 1858. Solid state as a term in physics is recorded from 1953; meaning "employing printed circuits and solid transistors" (as opposed to wires and vacuum tubes) is from 1959. Related: Solidly.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "not empty or hollow," 源自 古法语 solide "firm, dense, compact," 源自 拉丁语 solidus "firm, whole, undivided, entire," figuratively "sound, trustworthy, genuine," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sol-ido-, suffixed form of root *sol- "whole" (source also of 希腊语 holos "whole," 拉丁语 salus "health," salvus "safe;" 参见 safe （形）). 义为 "firm, hard, compact" 始于 1530 年代. 义为 "entirely of the same stuff" 始于 1710 年. Of qualities, "well-established, considerable" 约 1600 年. 作为 mere intensifier, 1830 年. Slang 语义 "wonderful, remarkable" 最早见于 1920 年 among jazz musicians. 作为 副词, "solidly, completely," 1650 年代. Solid South in U.S. political history 见于 1858 年. Solid state 作为 term in physics 见于 1953 年; 意为 "employing printed circuits and solid transistors" (as opposed to wires and vacuum tubes) 始于 1959 年. 同源词：Solidly.

example.en: The old stone wall remained solid despite decades of bad weather.
example.zh: 尽管经历了数十年的恶劣天气，这堵石墙依然坚固。

entries.etymology: 1829, from French solidarité "communion of interests and responsibilities, mutual responsibility," a coinage of the "Encyclopédie" (1765), from solidaire "interdependent, complete, entire," from solide (see solid (adj.)). With a capital S-, the name of an independent trade union movement in Poland, formed September 1980, from Polish Solidarność.

entries.etymology: 1690s, "piece of music for one voice or instrument," from Italian solo, literally "alone," from Latin solus "alone" (see sole (adj.)). As an adjective in English from 1712, originally in the non-musical sense of "alone, unassisted;" in reference to aircraft flying from 1909. The verb is first attested 1858 in the musical sense, 1886 in a non-musical sense. Related: Soloed; soloing.

entries.definition: a. 可溶的，可溶解的；可解决的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "capable of being dissolved," from Old French soluble "expungable, eradicable" (13c.), from Late Latin solubilis "that may be loosened or dissolved," from stem of Latin solvere "loosen, dissolve" (see solve). Meaning "capable of being solved" is attested from 1705. Substances are soluble, not solvable; problems can be either.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "to disperse, dissipate, loosen," from Latin solvere "to loosen, dissolve; untie, release, detach; depart; unlock; scatter; dismiss; accomplish, fulfill; explain; remove," from PIE *se-lu-, from reflexive pronoun *s(w)e- (see idiom) + root *leu- "to loosen, divide, cut apart" (see lose). entries.etymology:
Old English sum "some, a, a certain one, something, a certain quantity; a certain number;" with numerals "out of" (as in sum feowra "one of four"); from Proto-Germanic *suma- (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Old High German sum, Old Norse sumr, Gothic sums), from PIE *smm-o-, suffixed form of root *sem- (1) "one," also "as one" (adv.), "together with" (see same). For substitution of -o- for -u-, see come.

As a pronoun from c. 1100; as an adverb from late 13c. Meaning "remarkable" is attested from 1808, American English colloquial. A possessive form is attested from 1560s, but always was rare. Many combination forms (somewhat, sometime, somewhere) were in Middle English but often written as two words till 17-19c. Somewhen is rare and since 19c. used almost exclusively in combination with the more common compounds; somewho "someone" is attested from late 14c. but did not endure. Scott (1816) has somegate "somewhere, in some way, somehow," and somekins "some kind of a" is recorded from c. 1200. Get some "have sexual intercourse" is attested 1899 in a quote attributed to Abe Lincoln from c. 1840.

For substitution of -o- for -u-, 参见 come. 作为 pronoun 源自 约 1100 年; 作为 副词 源自 13 世纪晚期 义为 "remarkable" 见于 1808 年, American English 口语. A possessive form 见于 1560 年代, but always was rare. Many combination forms (somewhat, sometime, somewhere) were in 中古英语 but 常 written as two words till 17-19 世纪 Somewhen is rare and 自 19 世纪 used almost exclusively in combination with the more common compounds; somewho "someone" 见于 14 世纪晚期 but did not endure. entries.etymology:
Old English sunu "son, descendant," from Proto-Germanic *sunuz (source also of Old Saxon and Old Frisian sunu, Old Norse sonr, Danish søn, Swedish son, Middle Dutch sone, Dutch zoon, Old High German sunu, German Sohn, Gothic sunus "son"). The Germanic words are from PIE *su(e)-nu- "son" (source also of Sanskrit sunus, Greek huios, Avestan hunush, Armenian ustr, Lithuanian sunus, Old Church Slavonic synu, Russian and Polish syn "son"), a derived noun from root *seue- (1) "to give birth" (source also of Sanskrit sauti "gives birth," Old Irish suth "birth, offspring").

Son of _____ as the title of a sequel to a book or movie is recorded from 1917 ("Son of Tarzan"). Most explanations for son of a gun (1708) are more than a century after its appearance. Henley (1903) describes it as meaning originally "a soldier's bastard;" Smyth's "Sailor's Word-Book" (1867) describes it as "An epithet conveying contempt in a slight degree, and originally applied to boys born afloat, when women were permitted to accompany their husbands to sea ...."

The 日耳曼语 words 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *su(e)-nu- "son" (source also of 梵语 sunus, 希腊语 huios, Avestan hunush, Armenian ustr, Lithuanian sunus, Old Church Slavonic synu, 俄语 and Polish syn "son"), a derived 名词 源自 root *seue- (1) "to give birth" (source also of 梵语 sauti "gives birth," Old 爱尔兰语 suth "birth, offspring"). Son of _____ as the title of a sequel to a book or movie 见于 1917 年 ("Son of Tarzan"). Most explanations for son of a gun (1708 年) are more than a century after its appearance. entries.etymology:
Old English sang "voice, song, art of singing; metrical composition adapted for singing, psalm, poem," from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz (source also of Old Norse söngr, Norwegian song, Swedish sång, Old Saxon, Danish, Old Frisian, Old High German, German sang, Middle Dutch sanc, Dutch zang, Gothic saggws), from PIE *songwh-o- "singing, song," from *sengwh- "to sing, make an incantation" (see sing (v.)).

Phrase for a song "for a trifle, for little or nothing" is from "All's Well" III.ii.9 (the identical image, por du son, is in Old French. With a song in (one's) heart "feeling joy" is first attested 1930 in Lorenz Hart's lyric. Song and dance as a form of vaudeville act is attested from 1872; figurative sense of "rigmarole" is from 1895.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sang "voice, song, art of singing; metrical composition adapted for singing, psalm, poem," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sangwaz (source also of 古北欧语 söngr, Norwegian song, Swedish sång, 古撒克逊语, Danish, 古弗里西语, 古高地德语, 德语 sang, Middle 荷兰语 sanc, 荷兰语 zang, Gothic saggws), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *songwh-o- "singing, song," 源自 *sengwh- "to sing, make an incantation" （参见 sing （动）). Phrase for a song "for a trifle, for little or nothing" 始于 "All's Well" III.ii.9 (the identical image, por du son, is in 古法语. With a song in (one's) heart "feeling joy" is first attested 1930 in Lorenz Hart's lyric. Song and dance 作为 form of vaudeville act 见于 1872 年; figurative 语义 "rigmarole" 始于 1895 年.

entries.etymology: Old English sona "at once, immediately, directly, forthwith," from Proto-Germanic *sæno (source also of Old Frisian son, Old Saxon sana, Old High German san, Gothic suns "soon"). Sense softened early Middle English to "within a short time" (compare anon, just (adv.)). American English. Sooner for "Oklahoma native" is 1930 (earlier "one who acts prematurely," 1889), from the 1889 opening to whites of what was then part of Indian Territory, when many would-be settlers sneaked onto public land and staked their claims "sooner" than the legal date and time.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sona "at once, immediately, directly, forthwith," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sæno (source also of 古弗里西语 son, 古撒克逊语 sana, 古高地德语 san, Gothic suns "soon"). entries.etymology:
Old English sar "painful, grievous, aching, sad, wounding," influenced in meaning by Old Norse sarr "sore, wounded," from Proto-Germanic *saira- "suffering, sick, ill" (source also of Old Frisian sar "painful," Middle Dutch seer, Dutch zeer "sore, ache," Old High German ser "painful," Gothic sair "pain, sorrow, travail"), from PIE root *sai- (1) "suffering" (source also of Old Irish saeth "pain, sickness").

Adverbial use (as in sore afraid) is from Old English sare but has mostly died out (replaced by sorely), but remains the main meaning of German cognate sehr "very." Slang meaning "angry, irritated" is first recorded 1738.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sar "painful, grievous, aching, sad, wounding," influenced in 意为 by 古北欧语 sarr "sore, wounded," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *saira- "suffering, sick, ill" (source also of 古弗里西语 sar "painful," Middle 荷兰语 seer, 荷兰语 zeer "sore, ache," 古高地德语 ser "painful," Gothic sair "pain, sorrow, travail"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sai- (1) "suffering" (source also of Old 爱尔兰语 saeth "pain, sickness"). Adverbial use (as in sore afraid) 始于 古英语 sare but has mostly died out (replaced by sorely), but remains the main 意为 of 德语 同源 sehr "very." Slang 意为 "angry, irritated" is 首见于 1738 年.

example.en: My throat is sore after talking all day at the conference.

entries.etymology: Old English sorg "grief, regret, trouble, care, pain, anxiety," from Proto-Germanic *sorg- (source also of Old Saxon sorga, Old Norse sorg, Middle Dutch sorghe, Dutch zorg, Old High German soraga, German sorge, Gothic saurga), perhaps from PIE *swergh- "to worry, be sick" (source also of Sanskrit surksati "cares for," Lithuanian sergu "to be sick," Old Church Slavonic sraga "sickness," Old Irish serg "sickness"). entries.etymology: Old English sarig "distressed, grieved, full of sorrow" (not found in the physical sense of "sore"), from Proto-Germanic *sairiga- "painful" (source also of Old Saxon serag, Middle Dutch seerigh "sore; sad, sorry," Dutch zeerig "sore, full of sores," Old High German serag, Swedish sårig "sore, full of sores"), from *sairaz "pain" (physical and mental); related to *saira- "suffering, sick, ill" (see sore (adj.)). Meaning "wretched, worthless, poor" first recorded mid-13c. Spelling shift from -a- to -o- by influence of sorrow. Apologetic sense (short for I'm sorry) is attested from 1834; phrase sorry about that popularized 1960s by U.S. TV show "Get Smart." Related: Sorrily; sorriness.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "group of people, animals, etc.; kind or variety of person or animal," from Old French sorte "class, kind," from Latin sortem (nominative sors) "lot; fate, destiny; share, portion; rank, category; sex, class, oracular response, prophecy," from PIE root *ser- (3) "to line up" (source also of Latin serere "to arrange, attach, join;" see series). The sense evolution in Vulgar Latin is from "what is allotted to one by fate," to "fortune, condition," to "rank, class, order." Later (mid-15c.) "group, class, or category of items; kind or variety of thing; pattern, design." Out of sorts "not in usual good condition" is attested from 1620s, with literal sense of "out of stock."

entries.etymology: "free from special defect or injury," c. 1200, from Old English gesund "sound, safe, having the organs and faculties complete and in perfect action," from Proto-Germanic *sunda-, from Germanic root *swen-to- "healthy, strong" (source also of Old Saxon gisund, Old Frisian sund, Dutch gezond, Old High German gisunt, German gesund "healthy," as in the post-sneezing interjection gesundheit; also Old English swið "strong," Gothic swinþs "strong," German geschwind "fast, quick"), with connections in Indo-Iranian and Balto-Slavic. Meaning "right, correct, free from error" is from mid-15c. Meaning "financially solid or safe" is attested from c. 1600; of sleep, "undisturbed," from 1540s. Sense of "holding accepted opinions" is from 1520s.

entries.etymology:
"liquid food," 1650s, from French soupe "soup, broth" (13c.), from Late Latin suppa "bread soaked in broth," from a Germanic source (compare Middle Dutch sop "sop, broth"), from Proto-Germanic *sup-, from PIE *sub-, from root *seue- (2) "to take liquid" (see sup (v.2)).

Primordial soup is from a concept first expressed 1929 by J.B.S. Haldane. Soup to nuts "everything" is from 1910. Soup-kitchen, "public establishment supported by voluntary contributions, for preparing and serving soup to the poor at no cost" is attested from 1839. In Ireland, souper meant "Protestant clergyman seeking to make proselytes by dispensing soup in charity" (1854).

Old English sur "sour, tart, acid, fermented," from Proto-Germanic *sura- "sour" (source also of Old Norse surr, Middle Dutch suur, Dutch zuur, Old High German sur, German Sauer), from PIE root *suro- "sour, salty, bitter" (source also of Old Church Slavonic syru, Russian syroi "moist, raw;" Lithuanian suras "salty," suris "cheese").

Meaning "having a peevish disposition" is from early 13c. Sense in whisky sour (1885) is "with lemon added" (1862). Sour cream is attested from 1855. French sur "sour, tart" (12c.) is a Germanic loan-word.

entries.etymology:
Old English suð "southward, to the south, southern, in the south," from Proto-Germanic *sunthaz, perhaps literally "sun-side" (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian suth "southward, in the south," Middle Dutch suut, Dutch zuid, German Süden), and related to base of *sunnon "sun" (see sun (v.)). Old French sur, sud (French sud), Spanish sur, sud are loan-words from Germanic, perhaps from Old Norse suðr.

As an adjective from c. 1300; as a noun, "one of the four cardinal points," also "southern region of a country," both late 13c. The Southern states of the U.S. have been collectively called The South since 1779 (in early use this often referred only to Georgia and South Carolina). South country in Britain means the part below the Tweed, in England the part below the Wash, and in Scotland the part below the Forth. South Sea meant "the Mediterranean" (late 14c.) and "the English Channel" (early 15c.) before it came to mean (in plural) "the South Pacific Ocean" (1520s). The nautical coat called a sou'wester (1836) protects the wearer against severe weather, such as a gale out of the southwest.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "extent or area; room" (to do something), a shortening of Old French espace "period of time, distance, interval" (12c.), from Latin spatium "room, area, distance, stretch of time," of unknown origin (also source of Spanish espacio, Italian spazio).

From early 14c. as "a place," also "amount or extent of time." From mid-14c. as "distance, interval of space;" from late 14c. as "ground, land, territory; extension in three dimensions; distance between two or more points." From early 15c. as "size, bulk," also "an assigned position." Typographical sense is attested from 1670s (typewriter space-bar is from 1876, earlier space-key, 1860).

Astronomical sense of "stellar depths, immense emptiness between the worlds" is by 1723, perhaps as early as "Paradise Lost" (1667), common from 1890s. Space age is attested from 1946. Many compounds first appeared in science fiction and speculative writing, such as spaceship (1894, "A Journey in Other Worlds," John Jacob Astor); spacecraft (1928, "Popular Science"); space travel (1931); space station (1936, "Rockets Through Space"); spaceman (1942, "Thrilling Wonder Stories"). Space race attested from 1959. Space shuttle attested by 1970.

From 14 世纪初 as "a place," also "amount or extent of time." From 14 世纪中期 as "distance, interval of space;" 源自 14 世纪晚期 as "ground, land, territory; extension in three dimensions; distance between two or more points." Astronomical 语义 "stellar depths, immense emptiness between the worlds" is 截至 1723 年, 或许 as early as "Paradise Lost" (1667 年), common 源自 1890 年代. Space age 见于 1946 年. Space race attested 自 1959 年起. Space shuttle attested 截至 1970 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English spannan "to join, link, clasp, fasten, bind, connect; stretch, span," from Proto-Germanic *spannan (source also of Old Norse spenna, Old Frisian spanna, Middle Dutch spannen, Dutch spannan "stretch, bend, hoist, hitch," Old High German spannan, German spannen "to join, fasten, extend, connect"), from PIE root *(s)pen- "to draw, stretch, spin" (source also of Latin pendere "to hang, to cause to hang," pondus "weight" (perhaps the notion is the weight of a thing measured by how much it stretches a cord), pensare "to weigh, consider;" Greek ponos "toil," ponein "to toil;" Lithuanian spendziu "lay a snare;" Old Church Slavonic peti "stretch, strain," pato "fetter," pina "I span;" Old English spinnan "to spin;" for other cognates, see spin (v.)).

The meaning "to encircle with the hand(s)" is from 1781; in the sense of "to form an arch over (something)" it is first recorded 1630s. Related: Spanned; spanning.

entries.definition: a.西班牙（人/语）的 n. 西班牙人/语
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, Spainisc, from Spaine "Spain," from Old French Espaigne (see Spaniard) + -ish. Replaced Old English Speonisc. Altered 16c. by influence of Latin. As a noun, "the Spanish language," from late 15c.

For Spanish Main see main. Spanish moss is attested from 1823. Spanish fly, the fabled aphrodisiac (ground-up cantharis blister-beetles), is attested from c. 1600. Spanish-American War was so called in British press speculations early 1898, even before it began in April. For Spanish Inquisition (by c. 1600), see Inquisition.
