entries.definition: vi. 站立；坐落，位于；经受， 忍受 n. 台，座；货摊；置物架；看台， 观众席；立场，看法
entries.etymology:
Old English standan "occupy a place; stand firm; congeal; stay, continue, abide; be valid, be, exist, take place; oppose, resist attack; stand up, be on one's feet; consist, amount to" (class VI strong verb; past tense stod, past participle standen), from Proto-Germanic *sta-n-d- (source also of Old Norse standa, Old Saxon and Gothic standan, Old High German stantan, parallel with simpler forms, such as Swedish stå, Dutch staan, German stehen [see discussion in OED]), from PIE root *sta- "to stand" (see stet).

Sense of "to exist, be present" is attested from c. 1300. Meaning "encounter without flinching" is from 1590s; weaker sense of "put up with" is from 1620s. Meaning "to submit" (to chances, etc.) is from c. 1700. Meaning "to pay for as a treat" is from 1821. Meaning "become a candidate for office" is from 1550s. Nautical sense of "hold a course at sea" is from 1620s. Meaning "to be so high when standing" is from 1831.

Stand back "keep (one's) distance" is from c. 1400. Phrase stand pat is from poker (1882), earlier simply stand (1824 in other card games). To stand down is from 1680s, originally of witnesses in court; in the military sense of "come off duty" it is first recorded 1916. To let (something) stand is from c. 1200. To stand for is c. 1300 as "count for;" early 14c. as "be considered in lieu of;" late 14c. as "represent by way of sign;" sense of "tolerate" first recorded 1620s. Phrase stands to reason (1620) is from earlier stands (is constant) with reason.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 standan "occupy a place; stand firm; congeal; stay, continue, abide; be valid, be, exist, take place; oppose, resist attack; stand up, be on one's feet; consist, amount to" (class VI strong 动词; past tense stod, past participle standen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sta-n-d- (source also of 古北欧语 standa, 古撒克逊语 and Gothic standan, 古高地德语 stantan, parallel with simpler forms, such as Swedish stå, 荷兰语 staan, 德语 stehen [参见 discussion in OED]), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *sta- "to stand" （参见 stet). 义为 "to exist, be present" 见于 约 1300 年. 义为 "encounter without flinching" 始于 1590 年代; weaker 语义 "put up with" 始于 1620 年代. 义为 "to submit" (to chances, etc.) 始于 约 1700 年. 义为 "to pay for as a treat" 始于 1821 年. 义为 "become a candidate for office" 始于 1550 年代. Nautical 语义 "hold a course at sea" 始于 1620 年代. 义为 "to be so high when standing" 始于 1831 年. Stand back "keep (one's) distance" 始于 约 1400 年. Phrase stand pat 始于 poker (1882 年), earlier simply stand (1824 年 in other card games). To stand down 始于 1680 年代, 原义为 of witnesses in court; in the military 语义 "come off duty" it is 首见于 1916 年. To let (something) stand 始于 约 1200 年. To stand for is 约 1300 年 as "count for;" 14 世纪初 as "be considered in lieu of;" 14 世纪晚期 as "represent by way of sign;" 语义 "tolerate" 首见于 1620 年代. Phrase stands to reason (1620 年) 始于 earlier stands (is constant) with reason.

example.en: He could barely stand after running a marathon in the scorching heat.
example.zh: 在酷暑中跑完马拉松后，他几乎站不住了。

entries.etymology: 1620s, "serving as a standard," from standard (adj.). Earlier it meant "upright" (1530s). Standard-bred "bred up to some agreed-upon standard of excellence" is from 1888.
entries.etymologyZh: 1620 年代, "serving as a standard," 源自 standard （形）. Earlier it meant "upright" (1530 年代). Standard-bred "bred up to some agreed-upon standard of excellence" 始于 1888 年.

example.en: The product did not meet the safety standard required by law.
example.zh: 该产品未达到法律要求的安全标准。

entries.definition: a.备用的 ad. 待命地；备用地

entries.etymology: 1829, from stand (v.) + point (n.). A loan-translation of German Standpunkt. Century Dictionary calls it "a word objected to by purists."
entries.etymologyZh: 1829 年, 源自 stand （动） + point （名）. A loan-translation of 德语 Standpunkt. Century Dictionary calls it "a word objected to by purists."

entries.definition: n. 星，恒星；明星，名人 vi.主演
entries.etymology: 1590s, "to affix a star or asterisk to," from star (n.). From 1718 as "to set with stars." Meaning "perform the lead part" (of actors, singers, etc.) is from 1824. Sporting sense is from 1916. Related: Starred; starring.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "to affix a star or asterisk to," 源自 star （名）. From 1718 年 as "to set with stars." 义为 "perform the lead part" (of actors, singers, etc.) 始于 1824 年. Sporting sense 始于 1916 年. 同源词：Starred; starring.

example.en: The young actress is set to star in the studio's biggest film of the year.
example.zh: 这位年轻女演员将主演该制片公司年度最大制作的影片。

entries.etymology:
Old English starian "to stare, gaze, look fixedly at," from Proto-Germanic *staren "be rigid" (source also of Old Norse stara, Middle Low German and Middle Dutch staren, Old High German staren, German starren "to stare at;" German starren "to stiffen," starr "stiff;" Old Norse storr "proud;" Old High German storren "to stand out, project;" Gothic andstaurran "to be obstinate"), from PIE root *ster- (1) "strong, firm, stiff, rigid" (see stereo- and compare torpor).

Not originally implying rudeness. To stare (someone) down is from 1848. Related: Stared; staring.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 starian "to stare, gaze, look fixedly at," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *staren "be rigid" (source also of 古北欧语 stara, Middle Low 德语 and Middle 荷兰语 staren, 古高地德语 staren, 德语 starren "to stare at;" 德语 starren "to stiffen," starr "stiff;" 古北欧语 storr "proud;" 古高地德语 storren "to stand out, project;" Gothic andstaurran "to be obstinate"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ster- (1) "strong, firm, stiff, rigid" （参见 stereo- and 对比 torpor). Not 原义为 implying rudeness. To stare (someone) down 始于 1848 年. 同源词：Stared; staring.

example.en: The child stared at the colorful fish in the aquarium for minutes.
example.zh: 那个孩子在水族馆里盯着五颜六色的鱼看了好几分钟。

definitionLines: vt.开始，着手；启动，开动； 使发生，引起；开设，创办
vi. 启动，开动；动身，出发
n. 开端，起点；动身，出发；吃惊
entries.definition: vt.开始，着手；启动，开动； 使发生，引起；开设，创办 vi. 启动，开动；动身，出发 n. 开端，起点；动身，出发；吃惊
entries.etymology: late 14c., "an involuntary movement of the body, a sudden jump," from start (v.). Meaning "act of beginning to move or act" is from 1560s. Meaning "act of beginning to build a house" is from 1946. That of "opportunity at the beginning of a career or course of action" is from 1849. Paired with finish (n.) at least from 1839. False start first attested 1850.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "an involuntary movement of the body, a sudden jump," 源自 start （动）. 义为 "act of beginning to move or act" 始于 1560 年代. 义为 "act of beginning to build a house" 始于 1946 年. That of "opportunity at the beginning of a career or course of action" 始于 1849 年. Paired with finish （名） at least 自 1839 年起. False start 最早见于 1850 年.

example.en: The engine took a few seconds to start on that cold morning.
example.zh: 那个寒冷的早晨，引擎花了几秒钟才启动。

entries.definition: vt. 使吓一跳；使惊奇 vi. 惊吓；惊跳；惊奇 n. 惊愕；惊恐
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "run to and fro" (intransitive), frequentative of sterten (see start (v.)). Sense of "move suddenly in surprise or fear" first recorded 1520s. Transitive meaning "frighten suddenly" is from 1590s. The word retains more of the original meaning of start (v.). Related: Startled; startling; startlingly. As a noun from 1714.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "run to and fro" (intransitive), 为 … 的反复体 sterten （参见 start （动）). 义为 "move suddenly in surprise or fear" 首见于 1520 年代. Transitive 意为 "frighten suddenly" 始于 1590 年代. The word retains more of the original 意为 of start （动）. 同源词：Startled; startling; startlingly. 作名词时 自 1714 年起.

example.en: The loud thunder startled the baby and made her burst into tears.
example.zh: 巨大的雷声吓了婴儿一跳，让她放声大哭。

entries.etymology:
Old English steorfan "to die" (past tense stearf, past participle storfen), literally "become stiff," from Proto-Germanic *sterban "be stiff" (source also of Old Frisian sterva, Old Saxon sterban, Dutch sterven, Old High German sterban "to die," Old Norse stjarfi "tetanus"), from PIE root *ster- (1) "stiff, rigid" (see stereo-).

The conjugation became weak in English by 16c. The sense narrowed to "die of cold" (14c.); transitive meaning "to kill with hunger" is first recorded 1520s (earlier to starve of hunger, early 12c.). Intransitive sense of "to die of hunger" dates from 1570s. German cognate sterben retains the original sense of the word, but the English has come so far from its origins that starve to death (1910) is now common.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 steorfan "to die" (past tense stearf, past participle storfen), 字面义为 "become stiff," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sterban "be stiff" (source also of 古弗里西语 sterva, 古撒克逊语 sterban, 荷兰语 sterven, 古高地德语 sterban "to die," 古北欧语 stjarfi "tetanus"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ster- (1) "stiff, rigid" （参见 stereo-). The conjugation became weak in English by 16 世纪 The sense narrowed to "die of cold" (14 世纪); transitive 意为 "to kill with hunger" is 首见于 1520 年代 (earlier to starve of hunger, 12 世纪初). Intransitive 语义 "to die of hunger" dates 源自 1570 年代. 德语 同源 sterben retains the original 语义 the word, but the English has come so far 源自 its origins that starve to death (1910 年) is 现在 common.

entries.definition: n. 国家，州；情况，状态 vt. 声明，陈述
entries.etymology: 1590s, "to set in a position," from state (n.1); the sense of "declare in words" is first attested 1640s, from the notion of "placing" something on the record. Related: Stated; stating.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "to set in a position," 源自 state (n.1); the 语义 "declare in words" is 最早见于 1640 年代, 源自 概念 "placing" something on the record. 同源词：Stated; stating.

example.en: At the press conference, the minister refused to state his views on the scandal.
example.zh: 在新闻发布会上，那位部长拒绝就这桩丑闻陈述自己的观点。

entries.etymology: 1775, "what is stated," from state (v.) + -ment. From 1789 as "action of stating;" 1885 in the commercial sense "document displaying debits and credits."
entries.etymologyZh: 1775 年, "what is stated," 源自 state （动） + -ment. From 1789 年 as "action of stating;" 1885 年 in the commercial sense "document displaying debits and credits."

example.en: The minister issued an official statement denying any involvement in the scandal.
example.zh: 部长发表了一份官方声明，否认与丑闻有任何关联。

entries.etymology: 1590s, after French homme d'état; see state (n.1) + man (n.). Related: Statesmanly; statesmanship. Stateswoman attested from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, after 法语 homme d'état; 参见 state (n.1) + man （名）. 同源词：Statesmanly; statesmanship. Stateswoman attested 源自 约 1600 年.

entries.etymology: 1630s, "pertaining to the science of weight and its mechanical effects," from Modern Latin statica, from Greek statikos "causing to stand, skilled in weighing," from stem of histanai "to make to stand, set; to place in the balance, weigh," from PIE root *stā- "to stand" (see stet). Earlier statical (1560s). The sense of "having to do with bodies at rest or with forces that balance each other" is first recorded 1802. Applied to frictional electricity from 1839.
entries.etymologyZh: 1630 年代, "pertaining to the science of weight and its mechanical effects," 源自 现代 拉丁语 statica, 源自 希腊语 statikos "causing to stand, skilled in weighing," 源自 stem of histanai "to make to stand, set; to place in the balance, weigh," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). Earlier statical (1560 年代). The 语义 "having to do with bodies at rest or with forces that balance each other" is 首见于 1802 年. Applied to frictional electricity 自 1839 年起.

example.en: The economy has remained static for several years without significant growth.
example.zh: 这个经济体已经停滞了好几年，没有明显增长。

definitionLines: n. 车站；站，局，所；身份，地位； 岗位，位置
entries.definition: n. 车站；站，局，所；身份，地位； 岗位，位置
entries.etymology:
late 13c., "place which one normally occupies," from Old French stacion, estacion "site, location; station of the Cross; stop, standstill," from Latin stationem (nominative statio) "a standing, standing firm; a post, job, position; military post; a watch, guard, sentinel; anchorage, port" (related to stare "to stand"), from PIE *ste-ti-, suffixed form of root *stā- "to stand" (see stet).

 Meaning "each of a number of holy places visited in succession by pilgrims" is from late 14c., as in Station of the Cross (1550s). Meaning "fixed uniform distance in surveying" is from 1570s. Sense of "status, rank" is from c. 1600. Meaning "military post" in English is from c. 1600. The meaning "place where people are stationed for some special purpose" (as in polling station) is first recorded 1823. Radio station is from 1912; station break, pause in broadcasting to give the local station a chance to identify itself, is from 1942.

The meaning "regular stopping place" is first recorded 1797, in reference to coach routes; applied to railroads 1830. Station-master is from 1836. Station wagon in the automobile sense is first recorded 1929, from earlier use for a horse-drawn conveyance that took passengers to and from railroad stations (1894). Station house "police station" is attested from 1836.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "place which one normally occupies," 源自 古法语 stacion, estacion "site, location; station of the Cross; stop, standstill," 源自 拉丁语 stationem (主格 statio) "a standing, standing firm; a post, job, position; military post; a watch, guard, sentinel; anchorage, port" (related to stare "to stand"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *ste-ti-, suffixed form of root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). 义为 "each of a number of holy places visited in succession by pilgrims" 始于 14 世纪晚期, as in Station of the Cross (1550 年代). 义为 "fixed uniform distance in surveying" 始于 1570 年代. 义为 "status, rank" 始于 约 1600 年. 义为 "military post" in English 始于 约 1600 年. The 意为 "place where people are stationed for some special purpose" (as in polling station) is 首见于 1823 年. Radio station 始于 1912 年; station break, pause in broadcasting to give the local station a chance to identify itself, 始于 1942 年. The 意为 "regular stopping place" is 首见于 1797 年, in reference to coach routes; applied to railroads 1830 年. Station-master 始于 1836 年. Station wagon in the automobile sense is 首见于 1929 年, 源自 earlier use for a horse-drawn conveyance that took passengers to and 源自 railroad stations (1894 年). Station house "police station" 见于 1836 年.

example.en: The bus station is only a five-minute walk from the hotel entrance.
example.zh: 公交车站离酒店入口只有五分钟步行路程。

definitionLines: a.静止的；固定的；定居的； 常备军的
entries.definition: a.静止的；固定的；定居的； 常备军的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "having no apparent motion" (in reference to planets), from Middle French stationnaire "motionless" and directly from Latin stationarius, from the stem of statio "a standing, post, job, position" (see station (n.)). Meaning "unmovable" is from 1620s. In classical Latin, stationarius is recorded only in the sense "of a military station;" the word for "stationary, steady" being statarius.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "having no apparent motion" (in reference to planets), 源自 中古法语 stationnaire "motionless" and 直接源自 拉丁语 stationarius, 源自 stem of statio "a standing, post, job, position" （参见 station （名）). 义为 "unmovable" 始于 1620 年代. In classical 拉丁语, stationarius is recorded only in the sense "of a military station;" the word for "stationary, steady" being statarius.

entries.etymology: 1852, "one numerical statistic," see statistics. From 1939 in reference to a person (considered as nothing more than an example of some measured quantity).
entries.etymologyZh: 1852 年, "one numerical statistic," 参见 statistics. From 1939 年 in reference to a person (considered as nothing more than an example of some measured quantity).

entries.etymology: 1770, "science dealing with data about the condition of a state or community" [Barnhart], from German Statistik, popularized and perhaps coined by German political scientist Gottfried Aschenwall (1719-1772) in his "Vorbereitung zur Staatswissenschaft" (1748), from Modern Latin statisticum (collegium) "(lecture course on) state affairs," from Italian statista "one skilled in statecraft," from Latin status (see state (n.2)). OED points out that "the context shows that [Aschenwall] did not regard the term as novel," but current use of it seems to trace to him. Sir John Sinclair is credited with introducing it in English use. Meaning "numerical data collected and classified" is from 1829; hence the study of any subject by means of extensive enumeration. Abbreviated form stats first recorded 1961.
entries.etymologyZh: 1770 年, "science dealing with data about the condition of a state or community" [Barnhart], 源自 德语 Statistik, popularized and 或许 coined by 德语 political scientist Gottfried Aschenwall (1719 年-1772 年) in his "Vorbereitung zur Staatswissenschaft" (1748 年), 源自 现代 拉丁语 statisticum (collegium) "(lecture course on) state affairs," 源自 意大利语 statista "one skilled in statecraft," 源自 拉丁语 status （参见 state (n.2)). OED points out that "the context shows that [Aschenwall] did not regard the term as novel," but current use of it seems to trace to him. Sir John Sinclair is credited with introducing it in English use. 义为 "numerical data collected and classified" 始于 1829 年; hence the study of any subject by means of extensive enumeration. Abbreviated form stats 首见于 1961 年.

example.en: According to the latest government statistics, unemployment has dropped to five percent.
example.zh: 根据政府最新统计数据，失业率已降至5%。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French statue, estatue "(pagan) statue, graven image" (12c.), from Latin statua "image, statue, monumental figure, representation in metal," properly "that which is set up," back-formation from statuere "to cause to stand, set up," from status "a standing, position" (see status). The children's game of statues is attested from 1906.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 statue, estatue "(pagan) statue, graven image" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 statua "image, statue, monumental figure, representation in metal," properly "that which is set up," back-formation 源自 statuere "to cause to stand, set up," 源自 status "a standing, position" （参见 status). The children's game of statues 见于 1906 年.

example.en: Tourists came from around the world to see the ancient statue.
example.zh: 来自世界各地的游客专程前来参观这座古老的雕像。

entries.etymology: 1670s, "height" of a situation or condition, later "legal standing of a person" (1791), from Latin status "condition, position, state, manner, attitude" from past participle stem of stare "to stand," from PIE *ste-tu-, from root *stā- "to stand" (see stet). Sense of "standing in one's society or profession" is from 1820. Status symbol first recorded 1955; status-seeker from 1956. Status-anxiety is from 1959.
entries.etymologyZh: 1670 年代, "height" of a situation or condition, later "legal standing of a person" (1791 年), 源自 拉丁语 status "condition, position, state, manner, attitude" 源自 past participle stem of stare "to stand," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *ste-tu-, 源自 root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). 义为 "standing in one's society or profession" 始于 1820 年. Status symbol 首见于 1955 年; status-seeker 自 1956 年起. Status-anxiety 始于 1959 年.

example.en: Her status as a Nobel laureate brought immediate recognition in academic circles.
example.zh: 她诺贝尔奖得主的身份在学术界立即赢得了广泛认可。

example.en: They plan to stay at a beachside hotel during the three-day holiday.
example.zh: 他们计划在三天假期里住在海边酒店。

definitionLines: a. 稳定，不变；稳固，平稳； 坚定，扎实
entries.definition: a. 稳定，不变；稳固，平稳； 坚定，扎实 v.（使）稳定
entries.etymology:
1520s, "firmly fixed in place or station" (replacing earlier steadfast), from stead + adjectival suffix -y (2), perhaps on model of Middle Dutch, Middle Low German stadig. Old English had stæððig "grave, serious," and stedig "barren," but neither seems to be the direct source of the modern word. Old Norse cognate stoðugr "steady, stable" was closer in sense. As an adverb from c. 1600.

Originally of things; of persons or minds from c. 1600. Meaning "working at an even rate" is first recorded in 1540s. Steady progress is etymologically a contradiction in terms. Steady state first attested 1885; as a cosmological theory (propounded by Bondi, Gold, and Hoyle), it is attested from 1948. Related: Steadily.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "firmly fixed in place or station" (replacing earlier steadfast), 源自 stead + adjectival suffix -y (2), 或许 on model of Middle 荷兰语, Middle Low 德语 stadig. 古英语 had stæððig "grave, serious," and stedig "barren," but neither seems to be the direct source of the modern word. 古北欧语 同源 stoðugr "steady, stable" was closer in sense. 作为 副词 源自 约 1600 年. Originally of things; of persons or minds 源自 约 1600 年. 义为 "working at an even rate" is 首见于 in 1540 年代. Steady progress is etymologically a contradiction in terms. Steady state 最早见于 1885 年; 作为 cosmological theory (propounded by Bondi, Gold, and Hoyle), it 见于 1948 年. 同源词：Steadily.

example.en: She took a deep breath to steady her nerves before the speech.
example.zh: 她在演讲前深吸一口气，让自己的情绪平静下来。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "thick slice of meat cut for roasting," probably from a Scandinavian source such as Old Norse steik "roast meat," related to steikja "to roast on a spit," and ultimately meaning "something stuck" (on a spit), from Proto-Germanic *staiko-, from PIE *steig- "to stick; pointed" (see stick (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "thick slice of meat cut for roasting," 可能 源自 a Scandinavian source such as 古北欧语 steik "roast meat," related to steikja "to roast on a spit," and ultimately 意为 "something stuck" (on a spit), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *staiko-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *steig- "to stick; pointed" （参见 stick （动）).

entries.etymology:
Old English stelan "to commit a theft, to take and carry off clandestinely and without right or leave" (class IV strong verb; past tense stæl, past participle stolen), from Proto-Germanic *stelan (source also of Old Saxon stelan, Old Norse, Old Frisian stela "to steal, to rob one of," Dutch stelen, Old High German stelan, German stehlen, Gothic stilan "to steal"), from PIE *stel-, possibly a variant of *ster- (3) "to rob, steal."

"The notion of secrecy ... seems to be part of the original meaning of the vb." [OED]. Intransitive meaning "to depart or withdraw stealthily and secretly" is from late Old English. Most IE words for steal have roots in notions of "hide," "carry off," or "collect, heap up." Attested as a verb of stealthy motion from c. 1300 (as in to steal away, late 14c.); of kisses from late 14c.; of glances, sighs, etc., from 1580s. The various sports senses begin 1836. To steal (someone) blind first recorded 1974.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 stelan "to commit a theft, to take and carry off clandestinely and without right or leave" (class IV strong 动词; past tense stæl, past participle stolen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *stelan (source also of 古撒克逊语 stelan, 古北欧语, 古弗里西语 stela "to steal, to rob one of," 荷兰语 stelen, 古高地德语 stelan, 德语 stehlen, Gothic stilan "to steal"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *stel-, possibly a 为 … 的变体 *ster- (3) "to rob, steal." "The notion of secrecy ... seems to be part of the original meaning of the vb." [OED]. Intransitive 意为 "to depart or withdraw stealthily and secretly" 始于 late 古英语. Most IE words for steal have roots in notions of "hide," "carry off," or "collect, heap up." Attested 作动词时 of stealthy motion 源自 约 1300 年 (as in to steal away, 14 世纪晚期); of kisses 源自 14 世纪晚期; of glances, sighs, etc., 源自 1580 年代. The various sports senses begin 1836 年. To steal (someone) blind 首见于 1974 年.

example.en: Someone tried to steal the wallet from his back pocket on the subway.
example.zh: 有人试图在地铁上从他的后兜里偷走钱包。

entries.definition: n. （蒸）汽 vi. 发出蒸汽；行驶 vt.蒸煮
entries.etymology: Old English steam "vapor, fume, water in a gaseous state," from Proto-Germanic *staumaz (source also of Dutch stoom "steam"), of unknown origin. Meaning "vapor of boiling water used to drive an engine" is from 1690s, hence steam age (1828) and many figurative uses, such as let off steam (1831, literal), blow off steam (1857, figurative), full-steam (1878), get up steam (1887, figurative). Steam heat is from 1820s in thermodynamics; as a method of temperature control from 1904.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 steam "vapor, fume, water in a gaseous state," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *staumaz (source also of 荷兰语 stoom "steam"), 来源不详. 义为 "vapor of boiling water used to drive an engine" 始于 1690 年代, hence steam age (1828 年) and many figurative uses, such as let off steam (1831 年, literal), blow off steam (1857 年, figurative), full-steam (1878 年), get up steam (1887 年, figurative). Steam heat 始于 1820 年代 in thermodynamics; 作为 method of temperature control 自 1904 年起.

example.en: The old engine ran on steam generated from burning coal.
example.zh: 这台旧发动机靠燃烧煤炭产生的蒸汽驱动。

entries.etymology: 1814 in the cookery sense, agent noun from steam (v.). From 1825 as "a vessel propelled by steam," hence steamer trunk (1885), one that carries the essentials for a voyage.
entries.etymologyZh: 1814 年 in the cookery sense, agent 名词 源自 steam （动）. From 1825 年 as "a vessel propelled by steam," hence steamer trunk (1885 年), one that carries the essentials for a voyage.

entries.etymology:
modified form of iron with a small portion of carbon, not found in nature but known in ancient times, Old English style "steel," from noun use of Proto-Germanic adjective *stakhlijan "made of steel" (source also of Old Saxon stehli, Old Norse, Middle Low German stal, Danish staal, Swedish stål, Middle Dutch stael, Dutch staal, Old High German stahal, German Stahl), related to *stakhla "standing fast," from PIE *stek-lo-, from root *stak- "to stand, place, be firm" (see stay (n.1)). The notion is perhaps "that which stands firm." No corresponding word exists outside Germanic except those likely borrowed from Germanic languages.

As an adjective from c. 1200 (Old English used stylen "*steel-en." Steel wool is attested from 1896. Steel drum is from 1952.
entries.etymologyZh: modified form of iron with a small portion of carbon, not found in nature but known in ancient times, 古英语 style "steel," 源自 为 … 的名词用法 原始日耳曼语 形容词 *stakhlijan "made of steel" (source also of 古撒克逊语 stehli, 古北欧语, Middle Low 德语 stal, Danish staal, Swedish stål, Middle 荷兰语 stael, 荷兰语 staal, 古高地德语 stahal, 德语 Stahl), related to *stakhla "standing fast," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *stek-lo-, 源自 root *stak- "to stand, place, be firm" （参见 stay (n.1)). The notion is 或许 "that which stands firm." No corresponding word exists outside 日耳曼语 except those likely 借自 日耳曼语 languages. 作形容词时 源自 约 1200 年 (古英语 used stylen "*steel-en." Steel wool 见于 1896 年. Steel drum 始于 1952 年.

example.en: The bridge was constructed with reinforced steel beams to withstand heavy loads.
example.zh: 这座桥使用钢筋钢梁建造，以承受重载。

entries.etymology: "having a sharp slope," Old English steap "high, lofty; deep; prominent, projecting," from Proto-Germanic *staupaz (source also of Old Frisian stap "high, lofty," Middle High German *stouf), from PIE *steup-, extended form of root *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat," with derivations referring to projecting objects (source also of Greek typtein "to strike," typos "a blow, mold, die;" Sanskrit tup- "harm," tundate "pushes, stabs;" Gothic stautan "push;" Old Norse stuttr "short"). The sense of "precipitous" is from c. 1200. The slang sense "at a high price" is a U.S. coinage first attested 1856. Related: Steeply; steepness. The noun meaning "steep place" is from 1550s.
entries.etymologyZh: "having a sharp slope," 古英语 steap "high, lofty; deep; prominent, projecting," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *staupaz (source also of 古弗里西语 stap "high, lofty," Middle High 德语 *stouf), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *steup-, extended form of root *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat," with derivations referring to projecting objects (source also of 希腊语 typtein "to strike," typos "a blow, mold, die;" 梵语 tup- "harm," tundate "pushes, stabs;" Gothic stautan "push;" 古北欧语 stuttr "short"). The 语义 "precipitous" 始于 约 1200 年. The 俚语 sense "at a high price" is a U.S. coinage 最早见于 1856 年. 同源词：Steeply; steepness. The 名词 意为 "steep place" 始于 1550 年代.

example.en: The hikers struggled to climb the steep mountain path.
example.zh: 登山者费力地攀爬那条陡峭的山路。

entries.etymology:
"guide the course of a vehicle," originally by a rudder or something like it, Old English steran (Mercian), stieran (West Saxon) "steer, guide, direct; govern, rule; restrain, correct, punish," from Proto-Germanic *steurjan (source also of Old Norse styra, Old Frisian stiora, Dutch sturen, Old High German stiuren, German steuern "to steer," Gothic stiurjan "to establish, assert"), related to *steuro "a rudder, a steering," from PIE *steu-ro- (source also of Greek stauros "stake, pole"), extended form of root *stā- "to stand" (see stet).

The notion is of a stiff, upright pillar or post used in steering, or else perhaps "establish," hence "direct, steer." Intransitive sense also was in Old English. To steer clear of in the figurative sense of "to avoid completely" is recorded from 1723. Related: Steered; steering.
entries.etymologyZh: "guide the course of a vehicle," 原义为 by a rudder or something like it, 古英语 steran (Mercian), stieran (West Saxon) "steer, guide, direct; govern, rule; restrain, correct, punish," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *steurjan (source also of 古北欧语 styra, 古弗里西语 stiora, 荷兰语 sturen, 古高地德语 stiuren, 德语 steuern "to steer," Gothic stiurjan "to establish, assert"), related to *steuro "a rudder, a steering," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *steu-ro- (source also of 希腊语 stauros "stake, pole"), extended form of root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). The notion is of a stiff, upright pillar or post used in steering，或else 或许 "establish," hence "direct, steer." Intransitive sense also was in 古英语. To steer clear of in the figurative 语义 "to avoid completely" 见于 1723 年. 同源词：Steered; steering.

example.en: He carefully steered the boat through the narrow channel.
example.zh: 他小心地驾驶船只穿过狭窄的水道。

entries.definition: n. 茎，干 vt. 堵住，挡住 vi. 起源于，由……造成
entries.etymology:
Old English stemn, stefn "stem of a plant, trunk of a tree," also "either end-post of a ship," from Proto-Germanic *stamniz (source also of Old Saxon stamm, Old Norse stafn "stem of a ship;" Danish stamme, Swedish stam "trunk of a tree;" Old High German stam, German Stamm), from suffixed form of PIE root *stā- "to stand" (see stet).

Meaning "support of a wineglass" is from 1835. Meaning "unchanging part of a word" is from 1830. Stems slang for "legs" is from 1860. The nautical sense is preserved in the phrase stem to stern "along the full length" (of a ship), attested from 1620s. Stem cell attested by 1885.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 stemn, stefn "stem of a plant, trunk of a tree," also "either end-post of a ship," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *stamniz (source also of 古撒克逊语 stamm, 古北欧语 stafn "stem of a ship;" Danish stamme, Swedish stam "trunk of a tree;" 古高地德语 stam, 德语 Stamm), 源自 suffixed form of 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *stā- "to stand" （参见 stet). 义为 "support of a wineglass" 始于 1835 年. 义为 "unchanging part of a word" 始于 1830 年. Stems 俚语 for "legs" 始于 1860 年. The nautical sense is preserved in the phrase stem to stern "along the full length" (of a ship), attested 源自 1620 年代. Stem cell attested 截至 1885 年.

example.en: The stem of the rose bush was covered in sharp thorns.
example.zh: 玫瑰丛的茎干上布满了尖刺。

definitionLines: n. 脚步，脚步声；台阶，梯级；步 骤，措施

entries.etymology: Old English steppa (Mercian), stæpe, stepe (West Saxon) "stair, act of stepping," from the source of step (v.). Compare Old Frisian, Middle Dutch, Dutch stap, Old High German stapfo, German Stapfe "footstep"). From late Old English as "degree on a scale." Figurative meaning "action which leads toward a result" is recorded from 1540s. In dancing, from 1670s. Meaning "type of military pace" is from 1798. Warning phrase watch your step is attested from 1911 (Wyclif (late 14c.) has keep thy foot in essentially the same sense). Step by step indicating steady progression is from 1580s. To follow in (someone's) steps is from mid-13c.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 steppa (Mercian), stæpe, stepe (West Saxon) "stair, act of stepping," 源自 source of step （动）. 对比 古弗里西语, Middle 荷兰语, 荷兰语 stap, 古高地德语 stapfo, 德语 Stapfe "footstep"). From late 古英语 as "degree on a scale." Figurative 意为 "action which leads toward a result" 见于 1540 年代. In dancing, 源自 1670 年代. 义为 "type of military pace" 始于 1798 年. Warning phrase watch your step 见于 1911 年 (Wyclif (14 世纪晚期) has keep thy foot in essentially the same sense). Step by step indicating steady progression 始于 1580 年代. To follow in (someone's) steps 始于 13 世纪中期

example.en: Taking the first step toward recovery requires both courage and a clear plan.

entries.etymology: 1798, "method of printing from a plate," from French stéréotype (adj.) "printed by means of a solid plate of type," from Greek stereos "solid" (see stereo-) + French type "type" (see type (n.)). Meaning "a stereotype plate" is from 1817. Meaning "image perpetuated without change" is first recorded 1850, from the verb in this sense. Meaning "preconceived and oversimplified notion of characteristics typical of a person or group" is recorded from 1922.
entries.etymologyZh: 1798 年, "method of printing from a plate," 源自 法语 stéréotype （形） "printed by means of a solid plate of type," 源自 希腊语 stereos "solid" （参见 stereo-) + 法语 type "type" （参见 type （名）). 义为 "a stereotype plate" 始于 1817 年. 义为 "image perpetuated without change" is 首见于 1850 年, 源自 动词 in this sense. 义为 "preconceived and oversimplified notion of characteristics typical of a person or group" 见于 1922 年.

entries.etymology: Old English styrne "severe, strict, grave, hard, cruel," from Proto-Germanic *sternijaz (source also of Middle High German sterre, German starr "stiff," störrig "obstinate;" Gothic andstaurran "to be stiff;" Old Norse stara; Old English starian "to look or gaze upon"), from PIE root *ster- (1) "rigid, stiff" (see stereo-). Related: Sternly; sternness.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 styrne "severe, strict, grave, hard, cruel," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sternijaz (source also of Middle High 德语 sterre, 德语 starr "stiff," störrig "obstinate;" Gothic andstaurran "to be stiff;" 古北欧语 stara; 古英语 starian "to look or gaze upon"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ster- (1) "rigid, stiff" （参见 stereo-). 同源词：Sternly; sternness.

entries.etymology: Old English sticca "rod, twig, peg; spoon," from Proto-Germanic *stikkon- "pierce, prick" (source also of Old Norse stik, Middle Dutch stecke, stec, Old High German stehho, German Stecken "stick, staff"), from PIE *steig- "to stick; pointed" (see stick (v.)). Meaning "staff used in a game" is from 1670s (originally billiards); meaning "manual gearshift lever" first recorded 1914. Alliterative connection of sticks and stones is recorded from mid-15c.; originally "every part of a building." Stick-bug is from 1870, American English; stick-figure is from 1949.

entries.etymology: plural stimuli, 1680s, originally as a medical term, "something that goads a lazy organ" (often the male member), from a modern use of Latin stimulus "a goad, a pointed stick," figuratively "a sting, a pang; incitement, spur," from PIE *sti- "point, prick, pierce" (see stick (v.)). General sense of "something that excites or arouses the mind or spirit" is from 1791. Psychological sense is first recorded 1894.

Old English stingan "to stab, pierce, or prick with a point" (of weapons, insects, plants, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *stingan (source also of Old Norse stinga, Old High German stungen "to prick," Gothic us-stagg "to prick out," Old High German stanga, German stange "pole, perch," German stengel "stalk, stem"), perhaps from PIE *stengh-, nasalized form of root *stegh- "to prick, sting" (source also of Old English stagga "stag," Greek stokhos "pointed stake").

Specialized to insects late 15c. Intransitive sense "be sharply painful" is from 1848. Slang meaning "to cheat, swindle" is from 1812. Old English past tense stang, past participle stungen; the past tense later leveled to stung.

entries.etymology: "to supply (a store) with stock," 1620s, from stock (n.2). Meaning "to lay up in store" is from c. 1700. Earliest sense is "to imprison in stocks" (early 14c.). Related: Stocked; stocking.

entries.etymology: "close-fitting garment covering the foot and lower leg," 1580s, from stock "leg covering, stocking" (late 15c.), from Old English stocu "sleeve," related to Old English stocc "trunk, log" (see stock (n.1)). Probably so called because of a fancied resemblance of legs to tree trunks, or a reference to the punishing stocks. Cognates include Old Norse stuka, Old High German stuhha, from the same Proto-Germanic source. Restriction to women's hose is 20c. As a receptacle for Christmas presents, attested from 1853; hence stocking stuffer first recorded 1945. Stocking-feet "without shoes" is from 1802.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., earlier stomak (early 14c.), "internal pouch into which food is digested," from Old French stomaque, estomac "stomach," from Latin stomachus "throat, gullet; stomach," also "taste, inclination, liking; distaste, dislike;" also "pride, indignation," which were thought to have their origin in that organ (source also of Spanish estómago, Italian stomaco), from Greek stomachos "throat, gullet, esophagus," literally "mouth, opening," from stoma "mouth" (see stoma).

Applied anciently to the openings of various internal organs, especially that of the stomach, then by the later Greek physicians to the stomach itself. The native word is maw. Some 16c. anatomists tried to correct the sense back to "esophagus" and introduce ventricle for what we call the stomach. Meaning "belly, midriff, part of the body that contains the stomach" is from late 14c.

The spelling of the ending of the word was conformed to Latin, but the pronunciation remains as in Middle English. Related: stomachial (1580s); stomachical (c. 1600); stomachic (1650s). Pugilistic stomacher "punch in the stomach" is from 1814; from mid-15c. as "vest or other garment which covers the belly." The Latin figurative senses also were in Middle English (such as "relish, inclination, desire," mid-15c.) or early Modern English. Also sometimes regarded in Middle Ages as the seat of sexual desire.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, earlier stomak (14 世纪初), "internal pouch into which food is digested," 源自 古法语 stomaque, estomac "stomach," 源自 拉丁语 stomachus "throat, gullet; stomach," also "taste, inclination, liking; distaste, dislike;" also "pride, indignation," which were thought to have their origin in that organ (source also of 西班牙语 estómago, 意大利语 stomaco), 源自 希腊语 stomachos "throat, gullet, esophagus," 字面义为 "mouth, opening," 源自 stoma "mouth" （参见 stoma). Applied anciently to the openings of various internal organs, 尤指 that of the stomach, 之后 by the later 希腊语 physicians to the stomach itself. The 本族 word is maw. Some 16 世纪 anatomists tried to correct the sense back to "esophagus" and introduce ventricle for what we call the stomach. 义为 "belly, midriff, part of the body that contains the stomach" 始于 14 世纪晚期 The spelling of the ending of the word was conformed to 拉丁语, but the pronunciation remains as in 中古英语. 同源词：stomachial (1580 年代); stomachical (约 1600 年); stomachic (1650 年代). Pugilistic stomacher "punch in the stomach" 始于 1814 年; 源自 15 世纪中期 as "vest or other garment which covers the belly." The 拉丁语 figurative senses also were in 中古英语 (such as "relish, inclination, desire," 15 世纪中期) or early 现代英语. Also 有时 regarded in Middle Ages as the seat of sexual desire.

example.en: He felt a sharp pain in his stomach after eating too quickly.

entries.etymology:
Old English stol "seat for one person," from Proto-Germanic *stolaz (source also of Old Frisian stol, Old Norse stoll, Old High German stuol, German Stuhl "seat," Gothic stols "high seat, throne"), from PIE *sta-lo-, locative of root *stā- "to stand" (source also of Lithuanian pa-stolas "stand," Old Church Slavonic stolu "stool;" see stet).

Originally used of thrones (as in cynestol "royal seat, throne"); decline in sense began with adoption of chair (n.) from French, which relegated stool to small seats without arms or backs, then to "privy" (early 15c.) and thence to "bowel movement" (1530s).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 stol "seat for one person," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *stolaz (source also of 古弗里西语 stol, 古北欧语 stoll, 古高地德语 stuol, 德语 Stuhl "seat," Gothic stols "high seat, throne"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sta-lo-, locative of root *stā- "to stand" (source also of Lithuanian pa-stolas "stand," Old Church Slavonic stolu "stool;" 参见 stet). Originally used of thrones (as in cynestol "royal seat, throne"); decline in sense began with adoption of chair （名） 源自 法语, which relegated stool to small seats without arms or backs, 之后 to "privy" (15 世纪初) and thence to "bowel movement" (1530 年代).

example.en: He sat on a wooden stool at the kitchen counter and ate breakfast.
example.zh: 他坐在厨房吧台边的一张木凳上吃早餐。

entries.etymology: "bend forward," Old English stupian "to bow, bend," from Proto-Germanic *stup- (source also of Middle Dutch stupen "to bow, bend," Norwegian stupa "fall, drop"), from PIE *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" (see steep (adj.)). Figurative sense of "condescend," especially expressing a lowering of the moral self, is from 1570s. Sense of "swoop" is first recorded 1570s in falconry. Related: Stooped; stooping. The noun meaning "an act of stooping" is from c. 1300. Stoop-shouldered attested from 1773.
entries.etymologyZh: "bend forward," 古英语 stupian "to bow, bend," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *stup- (source also of Middle 荷兰语 stupen "to bow, bend," Norwegian stupa "fall, drop"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" （参见 steep （形）). Figurative 语义 "condescend," 尤指 expressing a lowering of the moral self, 始于 1570 年代. 义为 "swoop" is 首见于 1570 年代 in falconry. 同源词：Stooped; stooping. The 名词 意为 "an act of stooping" 始于 约 1300 年. Stoop-shouldered attested 自 1773 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English -stoppian (in forstoppian "to stop up, stifle"), a general West Germanic word, cognate with Old Saxon stuppon, West Frisian stopje, Middle Low German stoppen, Old High German stopfon, German stopfen "to plug, stop up," Old Low Frankish (be)stuppon "to stop (the ears)."

These words are said by many sources to be a Germanic borrowing of Vulgar Latin *stuppare "to stop or stuff with tow or oakum" (source of Italian stoppare, French étouper "to stop with tow"), from Latin stuppa "coarse part of flax, tow." In support of this theory, it is said that plugs made of tow were used from ancient times in Rhine valley. Century Dictionary says this "suits phonetically," but "is on grounds of meaning somewhat doubtful." Barnhart, for one, proposes the whole Germanic group might be native, from a base *stoppon. 

Sense of "bring or come to a halt, discontinue" (mid-15c.) is from notion of preventing a flow by blocking a hole, and the word's development in this sense is unique to English, though it since has been widely adopted in other languages; perhaps influenced by Latin stupere "be stunned, be stupefied." Intransitive meaning "check oneself" is from 1680s. Meaning "make a halt or stay, tarry" is from 1711. Stop-light is from 1922; stop-sign is from 1918. Stop-motion is from 1851, originally of looms. Related: Stopped; stopping.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 -stoppian (in forstoppian "to stop up, stifle"), a general West 日耳曼语 word, 与 … 同源 古撒克逊语 stuppon, West Frisian stopje, Middle Low 德语 stoppen, 古高地德语 stopfon, 德语 stopfen "to plug, stop up," Old Low Frankish (be)stuppon "to stop (the ears)." These words are said by many sources to be a 日耳曼语 borrowing of 通俗拉丁语 *stuppare "to stop or stuff with tow or oakum" (source of 意大利语 stoppare, 法语 étouper "to stop with tow"), 源自 拉丁语 stuppa "coarse part of flax, tow." In support of this theory, it is said that plugs made of tow were used 源自 ancient times in Rhine valley. Century Dictionary says this "suits phonetically," but "is on grounds of meaning somewhat doubtful." Barnhart, for one, proposes the whole 日耳曼语 group might be 本族, 源自 a base *stoppon. 义为 "bring or come to a halt, discontinue" (15 世纪中期) 始于 概念 preventing a flow by blocking a hole, and the word's development in this sense is unique to English, though it 自 has been widely adopted in other languages; 或许 influenced by 拉丁语 stupere "be stunned, be stupefied." Intransitive 意为 "check oneself" 始于 1680 年代. 义为 "make a halt or stay, tarry" 始于 1711 年. Stop-light 始于 1922 年; stop-sign 始于 1918 年. Stop-motion 始于 1851 年, 原义为 of looms. 同源词：Stopped; stopping.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "supplies or provisions for a household, camp, etc.," from store (v.) or else from Old French estore "provisions; a fleet, navy, army," from estorer or from Medieval Latin staurum, instaurum "store." General sense of "sufficient supply" is attested from late 15c. The meaning "place where goods are kept for sale" is first recorded 1721 in American English (British English prefers shop (n.)), from the sense "place where supplies and provisions are kept" (1660s).

Stores "articles and equipment for an army" is from 1630s. In store "laid up for future use" (also of events, etc.) is recorded from late 14c. Store-bought is attested from 1912, American English; earlier store-boughten (1872).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "supplies or provisions for a household, camp, etc.," 源自 store （动） or else 源自 古法语 estore "provisions; a fleet, navy, army," 源自 estorer or 源自 中古拉丁语 staurum, instaurum "store." General 语义 "sufficient supply" 见于 15 世纪晚期 The 意为 "place where goods are kept for sale" is 首见于 1721 年 in American English (British English prefers shop （名）), 源自 sense "place where supplies and provisions are kept" (1660 年代). Stores "articles and equipment for an army" 始于 1630 年代. In store "laid up for future use" (also of events, etc.) 见于 14 世纪晚期 Store-bought 见于 1912 年, American English; earlier store-boughten (1872 年).

example.en: The cold warehouse can store up to ten thousand boxes of frozen goods.

entries.etymology:
Old English storm "violent disturbance of the atmosphere, tempest; onrush, attack, tumult; disturbance," from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz "storm" (source also of Old Norse stormr, Old Saxon, Middle Low German, Middle Dutch, Dutch storm, Old High German sturm, German Sturm), from PIE *stur-mo-, from root *(s)twer- (1) "to turn, whirl." Old French estour "onset, tumult," Italian stormo "a fight" are Germanic loan-words. Figurative (non-meteorological) sense was in late Old English.

Storm-wind is from 1798. Storm-door first recorded 1872; storm-water is from 1847; storm-window is attested from 1824. Storm surge attested from 1872. Adverbial phrase _______ up a storm is from 1946.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 storm "violent disturbance of the atmosphere, tempest; onrush, attack, tumult; disturbance," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *sturmaz "storm" (source also of 古北欧语 stormr, 古撒克逊语, Middle Low 德语, Middle 荷兰语, 荷兰语 storm, 古高地德语 sturm, 德语 Sturm), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *stur-mo-, 源自 root *(s)twer- (1) "to turn, whirl." 古法语 estour "onset, tumult," 意大利语 stormo "a fight" are 日耳曼语 loan-words. Figurative (non-meteorological) sense was in late 古英语. Storm-wind 始于 1798 年. Storm-door 首见于 1872 年; storm-water 始于 1847 年; storm-window 见于 1824 年. Storm surge attested 自 1872 年起. Adverbial phrase _______ up a storm 始于 1946 年.

example.en: The coastal village was destroyed by a violent storm.

entries.etymology:
mid-15c., "heated room, bath-room," from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch stove, both meaning "heated room," which was the original sense in English; a general West Germanic word (Old English stofa "bath-room," Old High German stuba, German Stube "sitting room").

Of uncertain relationship to similar words in Romance languages (Italian stufa, French étuve "sweating-room;" see stew (v.)). One theory traces them all to Vulgar Latin *extufare "take a steam bath." The meaning "device for heating or cooking" is first recorded 1610s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "heated room, bath-room," 源自 Middle Low 德语 or Middle 荷兰语 stove, both 意为 "heated room," which was the original sense in English; a general West 日耳曼语 word (古英语 stofa "bath-room," 古高地德语 stuba, 德语 Stube "sitting room"). Of uncertain relationship to similar words in Romance languages (意大利语 stufa, 法语 étuve "sweating-room;" 参见 stew （动）). One theory traces them all to 通俗拉丁语 *extufare "take a steam bath." The 意为 "device for heating or cooking" is 首见于 1610 年代.

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "tie, bind, fasten, gird," from present participle stem of Old French estreindre "bind tightly, clasp, squeeze," from Latin stringere (2) "draw tight, bind tight, compress, press together," from PIE root *streig- "to stroke, rub, press" (source also of Lithuanian stregti "congeal, freeze, become stiff;" Greek strangein "twist;" Old High German strician "mends nets;" Old English streccian "to stretch;" German stramm, Dutch stram "stiff").

From late 14c. as "tighten; make taut," also "exert oneself; overexert (a body part)," Sense of "press through a filter, put (a liquid) through a strainer" is from early 14c. (implied in strainer); that of "to stress beyond measure, carry too far, make a forced interpretation of" is from mid-15c. Related: Strained; straining.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "tie, bind, fasten, gird," 源自 present participle stem of 古法语 estreindre "bind tightly, clasp, squeeze," 源自 拉丁语 stringere (2) "draw tight, bind tight, compress, press together," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *streig- "to stroke, rub, press" (source also of Lithuanian stregti "congeal, freeze, become stiff;" 希腊语 strangein "twist;" 古高地德语 strician "mends nets;" 古英语 streccian "to stretch;" 德语 stramm, 荷兰语 stram "stiff"). From 14 世纪晚期 as "tighten; make taut," also "exert oneself; overexert (a body part)," 义为 "press through a filter, put (a liquid) through a strainer" 始于 14 世纪初 (implied in strainer); that of "to stress beyond measure, carry too far, make a forced interpretation of" 始于 15 世纪中期 同源词：Strained; straining.

In early use also strounge, straunge. Sense of "queer, surprising" is attested from late 14c. In nuclear physics, from 1956.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "unknown person, foreigner," from strange + -er (1) or else from Old French estrangier "foreigner" (Modern French étranger), from estrange. Latin used the adjective extraneus as a noun to mean "stranger." The English noun never picked up the secondary sense of the adjective. As a form of address to an unknown person, it is recorded from 1817, American English rural colloquial. Meaning "one who has stopped visiting" is recorded from 1520s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "unknown person, foreigner," 源自 strange + -er (1) or else 源自 古法语 estrangier "foreigner" (现代法语 étranger), 源自 estrange. 拉丁语 used the 形容词 extraneus 作名词时 to mean "stranger." The English 名词 never picked up the secondary 语义 the 形容词. 作为 form of address to an unknown person, it 见于 1817 年, American English rural 口语. 义为 "one who has stopped visiting" 见于 1520 年代.

Old English stropp, Dutch strop "halter" also are borrowed from Latin, and the Old English word might be the source of the modern one. Slang meaning "credit" is from 1828.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "band of leather," 源自 苏格兰语 and/or nautical 为 … 的变体 strope "loop or strap on a harness" (14 世纪中期), 可能 源自 古法语 estrop "strap," 源自 拉丁语 stroppus "strap, band," 或许 经由 Etruscan, 最终源自 希腊语 strophos "twisted band; a cord, rope," 源自 strephein "to turn" （参见 strophe). 古英语 stropp, 荷兰语 strop "halter" also are 借自 拉丁语, and the 古英语 word might be the source of the modern one. Slang 意为 "credit" 始于 1828 年.

example.en: He used a leather strap to secure the bag to his bicycle.

entries.etymology: "pertaining to strategy, characterized by strategy," 1807, from French stratégique and directly from Greek strategikos in classical use "of or for a general; fitted for command," from strategos (see strategy). Related: Strategical; strategically (1810).
entries.etymologyZh: "pertaining to strategy, characterized by strategy," 1807 年, 源自 法语 stratégique and 直接源自 希腊语 strategikos in classical use "of or for a general; fitted for command," 源自 strategos （参见 strategy). 同源词：Strategical; strategically (1810 年).

entries.etymology: 1810, "art of a general," from French stratégie (18c.) and directly from Greek strategia "office or command of a general," from strategos "general, commander of an army," also the title of various civil officials and magistrates, from stratos "multitude, army, expedition, encamped army," literally "that which is spread out" (see structure (n.)) + agos "leader," from agein "to lead" (see act (n.)). In non-military use from 1887.
entries.etymologyZh: 1810 年, "art of a general," 源自 法语 stratégie (18 世纪) and 直接源自 希腊语 strategia "office or command of a general," 源自 strategos "general, commander of an army," also the title of various civil officials and magistrates, 源自 stratos "multitude, army, expedition, encamped army," 字面义为 "that which is spread out" （参见 structure （名）) + agos "leader," 源自 agein "to lead" （参见 act （名）). In non-military use 自 1887 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English streaw (rare) "stems or stalks of certain species of grains," apparently literally "that which is scattered or strewn," related to streowian (see strew), from Proto-Germanic *strawam "that which is scattered" (source also of Old Norse stra, Danish straa, Swedish strå, Old Saxon stro, Old Frisian stre, Old Dutch, Old High German stro, Dutch stroo, German Stroh "straw"), from PIE *stere- "to spread" (see structure (n.)). The notion perhaps is of dried grain stalks strewn on a floor as carpeting or bedding.

As a type of what is trifling or unimportant, attested from late 13c. Meaning "hollow tube through which a drink is sucked" is recorded from 1851. To draw straws as a means of deciding something is recorded from 1779 (the custom probably is older). As an adjective, "made of straw," mid-15c.; hence "false, sham." Straw poll is from 1932; earlier straw vote (1866). Straw hat first attested mid-15c. To clutch (or grasp or catch) at straws (1748) is what a drowning man proverbially would do. The last straw (1836 apart from the full phrase) is from the proverbial image: "it is the last straw that breaks the camel's back" (or, less often, the mare's, the horse's, or the elephant's), an image in use in English by 1755.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 streaw (rare) "stems or stalks of certain species of grains," 似乎 字面义为 "that which is scattered or strewn," related to streowian （参见 strew), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *strawam "that which is scattered" (source also of 古北欧语 stra, Danish straa, Swedish strå, 古撒克逊语 stro, 古弗里西语 stre, 古荷兰语, 古高地德语 stro, 荷兰语 stroo, 德语 Stroh "straw"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *stere- "to spread" （参见 structure （名）). The notion 或许 is of dried grain stalks strewn on a floor as carpeting or bedding. 作为 type of what is trifling or unimportant, attested 源自 13 世纪晚期 义为 "hollow tube through which a drink is sucked" 见于 1851 年. To draw straws 作为 means of deciding something 见于 1779 年 (the custom 可能 is older). 作形容词时, "made of straw," 15 世纪中期; hence "false, sham." Straw poll 始于 1932 年; earlier straw vote (1866 年). Straw hat 最早见于 15 世纪中期 To clutch (or grasp or catch) at straws (1748 年) is what a drowning man proverbially would do. The last straw (1836 年 apart 源自 full phrase) 始于 the proverbial image: "it is the last straw that breaks the camel's back" (or, less 常, the mare's, the horse's，或the elephant's), an image in use in English 截至 1755 年.

entries.definition: vi.迷路；偏离 a. 迷路的；离群的
entries.etymology: c. 1300, a shortening of Old French estraier "wander about, roam, drift, run loose," said of animals, especially a horse without a master, also of persons, perhaps literally "go about the streets," from estree "route, highway," from Late Latin via strata "paved road" (see street). On another theory, the Old French word is from Vulgar Latin *estragare, a contraction of *estravagare, representing Latin extra vagari "to wander outside" (see extravagant). Figurative sense of "to wander from the path of rectitude" is attested from early 14c. Related: Strayed; straying.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, a shortening of 古法语 estraier "wander about, roam, drift, run loose," said of animals, 尤指 a horse without a master, also of persons, 或许 字面义为 "go about the streets," 源自 estree "route, highway," 源自 晚期拉丁语 经由 strata "paved road" （参见 street). entries.definition: n.小河，溪流 一 vi.流，流出
entries.etymology:
Old English stream "a course of water," from Proto-Germanic *straumaz (source also of Old Saxon strom, Old Norse straumr, Danish strøm, Swedish ström, Norwegian straum, Old Frisian stram, Dutch stroom, Old High German stroum, German Strom "current, river"), from PIE root *sreu- "to flow" (see rheum).

From early 12c. as "anything issuing from a source and flowing continuously." Meaning "current in the sea" (as in Gulf Stream) is recorded from late 14c., as is the sense of "steady current in a river." Stream of consciousness in lit crit first recorded 1930, originally in psychology (1855). Stream of thought is from 1890.

example.en: A clear mountain stream ran through the middle of the village.

entries.etymology: 1868, "line drawn from point to point, so that its direction is everywhere that of the motion of the fluid" [Lamb, "Hydrodynamics," 1906], from stream (n.) + line (n.). entries.etymology:
Old English stret (Mercian, Kentish), stræt (West Saxon) "street, high road," from Late Latin strata, used elliptically for via strata "paved road," from fem. past participle of Latin sternere "lay down, spread out, pave," from PIE *stre-to- "to stretch, extend," from root *stere- "to spread, extend, stretch out" (see structure (n.)).

One of the few words in use in England continuously from Roman times. An early and widespread Germanic borrowing (Old Frisian strete, Old Saxon strata, Middle Dutch strate, Dutch straat, Old High German straza, German Strasse, Swedish stråt, Danish sträde "street"). The Latin is also the source of Spanish estrada, Old French estrée, Italian strada.

"The normal term in OE for a paved way or Roman road, later extended to other roads, urban streets, and in SE dialects to a street of dwellings, a straggling village or hamlet" [Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names]. Originally of Roman roads (Watling Street, Icknield Street). "In the Middle Ages, a road or way was merely a direction in which people rode or went, the name street being reserved for the made road" [Weekley].

Used since c. 1400 to mean "the people in the street;" modern sense of "the realm of the people as the source of political support" dates from 1931. The street for an especially important street is from 1560s (originally of London's Lombard-street). Man in the street "ordinary person, non-expert" is attested from 1831. Street people "the homeless" is from 1967; expression on the street "homeless" is from 1852. Street smarts is from 1971; street-credibility is from 1979. Street-sweeper as an occupation is from 1848.

The 拉丁语 is also the source of 西班牙语 estrada, 古法语 estrée, 意大利语 strada. "The normal term in OE for a paved way or Roman road, later extended to other roads, urban streets, and in SE dialects to a street of dwellings, a straggling village or hamlet" [Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names]. Street people "the homeless" 始于 1967 年; expression on the street "homeless" 始于 1852 年. Street smarts 始于 1971 年; street-credibility 始于 1979 年. Street-sweeper 作为 occupation 始于 1848 年.

Compare length/long. From the same root as strong,

example.en: Regular exercise can build up your physical strength over time.

entries.etymology: late 14c., from strength + -en (1). Related: Strengthened; strengthening; strengthener. Earlier verb was simply strength (12c.).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 strength + -en (1). 同源词：Strengthened; strengthening; strengthener. Earlier 动词 was simply strength (12 世纪).

example.en: Regular exercise can strengthen the muscles and improve overall health.
example.zh: 规律锻炼可以增强肌肉、改善整体健康。

entries.definition: n. 压力；紧迫；强调 vt. 强调，着重
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to subject (someone) to force or compulsion," from Middle French estrecier, from Vulgar Latin *strictiare, from Latin stringere "draw tight," which also is the source of stress (n.). The figurative meaning "put emphasis on" is first recorded 1896, from notion of laying pressure on something by relying on it. Related: Stressed; stressing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to subject (someone) to force or compulsion," 源自 中古法语 estrecier, 源自 通俗拉丁语 *strictiare, 源自 拉丁语 stringere "draw tight," which also is the source of stress （名）. The figurative 意为 "put emphasis on" is 首见于 1896 年, 源自 概念 laying pressure on something by relying on it. 同源词：Stressed; stressing.

example.en: Meditation helps lower blood pressure and reduce chronic stress in busy professionals.
example.zh: 冥想有助于降低血压，减轻繁忙职场人士的慢性压力。

definitionLines: n. 连续的一段时间；一大片
entries.definition: v./n. 拉长，延，伸 n. 连续的一段时间；一大片
entries.etymology: late 12c., "expanse of land;" 1540s, "act of stretching," from stretch (v.); meaning "unbroken continuance of some activity" is first recorded 1660s; meaning "straightaway of a race course" (as in home stretch) is recorded from 1839.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪晚期, "expanse of land;" 1540 年代, "act of stretching," 源自 stretch （动）; 意为 "unbroken continuance of some activity" is 首见于 1660 年代; 意为 "straightaway of a race course" (as in home stretch) 见于 1839 年.

example.en: Before the race, the athlete paused to stretch her leg muscles thoroughly.
example.zh: 赛前，运动员停下来彻底伸展了腿部肌肉。

entries.etymology: 1510s, "wounded, affected (by disease, trouble, etc.)," adjective use of archaic past participle of strike (v.). Figurative meaning "overwhelmed with terror, grief, etc." is from 1530s. An earlier development is reflected in 13c. phrase striken in elde "advanced in years," from strike in the sense of "to move, go," hence "far advanced."
entries.etymologyZh: 1510 年代, "wounded, affected (by disease, trouble, etc.)," 为 … 的形容词用法 古旧 为 … 的过去分词 strike （动）. Figurative 意为 "overwhelmed with terror, grief, etc." 始于 1530 年代. definitionLines: a. 严格的；严谨的，精确的
entries.definition: a. 严格的；严谨的，精确的
entries.etymology: early 15c., "narrow, drawn in, small," from Latin strictus "drawn together, close, tight," past participle of stringere (2) "to draw or bind tight" (see strain (v.)). The sense of "stringent and rigorous" (of law) is first found in 1570s; of qualities or conditions generally, 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "narrow, drawn in, small," 源自 拉丁语 strictus "drawn together, close, tight," 为 … 的过去分词 stringere (2) "to draw or bind tight" （参见 strain （动）). The 语义 "stringent and rigorous" (of law) is first found in 1570 年代; of qualities or conditions generally, 1590 年代.

example.en: The military academy has strict rules that cadets must follow at all times.
example.zh: 军校有严格的规定，学员必须随时遵守。

definitionLines: vt. 打，击；攻击，冲击；给…•• 深刻印象
entries.definition: vi./n. 罢工；敲响，报点 vt. 打，击；攻击，冲击；给…•• 深刻印象
entries.etymology: 1580s, "act of striking," from strike (v.). Meaning "concentrated cessation of work by a body of employees" is from 1810. Baseball sense is first recorded 1841, originally meaning any contact with the ball; modern sense developed by 1890s, apparently from foul strike, which counted against the batter, and as hit came to be used for "contact with the ball" this word was left for "a swing and a miss" that counts against the batter; figurative sense of have two strikes against (of a possible three) is from 1938. Bowling sense attested from 1859. Meaning "sudden military attack" is attested from 1942.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "act of striking," 源自 strike （动）. 义为 "concentrated cessation of work by a body of employees" 始于 1810 年. Baseball sense is 首见于 1841 年, 原义为 意为 any contact with the ball; modern sense developed by 1890 年代, 似乎 源自 foul strike, which counted against the batter, and as hit came to be used for "contact with the ball" this word was left for "a swing and a miss" that counts against the batter; figurative 语义 have two strikes against (of a possible three) 始于 1938 年. Bowling sense attested 自 1859 年起. 义为 "sudden military attack" 见于 1942 年.

example.en: Workers voted to strike after the company refused to raise wages.
example.zh: 工人在公司拒绝加薪后投票决定罢工。

entries.etymology: 1610s, "that strikes," present participle adjective from strike (v.). Meaning "producing a vivid impression" id from 1752, from the verb in the sense of "to catch the fancy of" (1590s). Related: Strikingly.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "that strikes," present participle 形容词 源自 strike （动）. 义为 "producing a vivid impression" id 自 1752 年起, 源自 动词 in the 语义 "to catch the fancy of" (1590 年代). 同源词：Strikingly.

example.en: The striking difference in performance between the two groups surprised researchers.
example.zh: 两组之间显著的表现差异令研究人员感到惊讶。

entries.etymology: c. 1400, "to fit a bow with a string," from string (n.). Meaning "to thread (beads, etc.) on a string" is from 1610s. Of musical instruments from 1520s (stringed instrument is from c. 1600). To string (someone) along is slang from 1902; string (v.) in the sense "deceive" is attested in British dialect from c. 1812; perhaps ultimately from the musical instrument sense and with a notion of "to 'tune' someone (for some purpose)." Related: Stringed (later strung); stringing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "to fit a bow with a string," 源自 string （名）. 义为 "to thread (beads, etc.) on a string" 始于 1610 年代. Of musical instruments 源自 1520 年代 (stringed instrument 始于 约 1600 年). example.en: She plucked the string of her guitar gently to test the tuning.
example.zh: 她轻轻拨动吉他弦来测试音调。

entries.etymology:
"make bare," early 13c., from Old English -striepan, -strypan "to plunder, despoil" (as in West Saxon bestrypan "to plunder"), from Proto-Germanic *straupijan (source also of Middle Dutch stropen "to strip off, to ramble about plundering," Old High German stroufen "to strip off, plunder," German streifen "strip off, touch upon, to ramble, roam, rove"). Meaning "to unclothe" is recorded from early 13c. Intransitive sense from late 14c. Of screw threads, from 1839; of gear wheels, from 1873. Meaning "perform a strip-tease" is from 1929. Related: Stripped; stripping. Strip poker is attested from 1916, in a joke in "The Technology Monthly and Harvard Engineering Journal":

strip search is from 1947, in reference to World War II prison camps.

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "quarrel, contend," from Old French estriver "to quarrel, dispute, resist, struggle, put up a fight, compete," from estrif, estrit "quarrel" (see strife). It became a strong verb (past tense strove) by rhyming association with drive, dive, etc. Meaning "try hard" is from early 14c. Related: Striving.

example.en: Athletes must strive for excellence if they want to reach the top.

entries.definition: n. 击，敲；（报时）钟声；抚摸； 一划，一笔，一击；突然发作， 中风；抚摸，抚爱
entries.etymology:
"act of striking," c. 1300, probably from Old English *strac "stroke," from Proto-Germanic *straik- (source also of Middle Low German strek, German streich, Gothic striks "stroke"); see stroke (v.).

The meaning "mark of a pen" is from 1560s; that of "a striking of a clock" is from mid-15c. Sense of "feat, achievement" (as in stroke of luck, 1853) first found 1670s; the meaning "single pull of an oar or single movement of machinery" is from 1731. example.en: He suffered a severe stroke that left him unable to move his left arm.

example.en: After dinner, they took a leisurely stroll along the riverside.

definitionLines: a. 强壮，强大；强硬；强烈
entries.definition: a. 强壮，强大；强硬；强烈
entries.etymology: Old English strange "strongly, violently, severely, furiously" (alongside strongly), from the same source as strong (adj.). Going strong (1898) is from racing. To come on strong was originally come it strong (1812).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 strange "strongly, violently, severely, furiously" (alongside strongly), 源自 same source as strong （形）. Going strong (1898 年) 始于 racing. To come on strong was 原义为 come it strong (1812 年).

example.en: The union took a strong stance against any reduction in workers' benefits.
example.zh: 工会对任何削减工人福利的举措采取了强硬立场。

entries.etymology:
mid-15c., "action or process of building or construction;" 1610s, "that which is constructed, a building or edifice;" from Latin structura "a fitting together, adjustment; a building, mode of building;" figuratively, "arrangement, order," from structus, past participle of struere "to pile, place together, heap up; build, assemble, arrange, make by joining together," related to strues "heap," from PIE *stere- "to spread, extend, stretch out."

The widespread descendants of this ancient root are believed to include: Sanskrit strnoti "strews, throws down;" Avestan star- "to spread out, stretch out;" Greek stronymi "strew," stroma "bedding, mattress," sternon "breast, breastbone;" Latin sternere "to stretch, extend;" Old Church Slavonic stira, streti "spread," strama "district;" Russian stroji "order;" Gothic straujan, Old High German strouwen, Old English streowian "to sprinkle, strew;" Old English streon "strain," streaw "straw, that which is scattered;" Old High German stirna "forehead," strala "arrow, lightning bolt;" Old Irish fo-sernaim "spread out," srath "a wide river valley;" Welsh srat "plain."
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "action or process of building or construction;" 1610 年代, "that which is constructed, a building or edifice;" 源自 拉丁语 structura "a fitting together, adjustment; a building, mode of building;" figuratively, "arrangement, order," 源自 structus, 为 … 的过去分词 struere "to pile, place together, heap up; build, assemble, arrange, make by joining together," related to strues "heap," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *stere- "to spread, extend, stretch out." The widespread descendants of this ancient root are believed to include: 梵语 strnoti "strews, throws down;" Avestan star- "to spread out, stretch out;" 希腊语 stronymi "strew," stroma "bedding, mattress," sternon "breast, breastbone;" 拉丁语 sternere "to stretch, extend;" Old Church Slavonic stira, streti "spread," strama "district;" 俄语 stroji "order;" Gothic straujan, 古高地德语 strouwen, 古英语 streowian "to sprinkle, strew;" 古英语 streon "strain," streaw "straw, that which is scattered;" 古高地德语 stirna "forehead," strala "arrow, lightning bolt;" Old 爱尔兰语 fo-sernaim "spread out," srath "a wide river valley;" Welsh srat "plain."

example.en: Engineers inspected the bridge's structure after the earthquake.
example.zh: 地震过后，工程师检查了桥梁的结构。

entries.etymology: late 14c., of uncertain origin, probably a frequentative form with -el (3) (compare trample, wrestle), but the first element is of uncertain origin. Skeat suggests Old Norse strugr "ill will;" others suggest a connection to Dutch struikelen, German straucheln "to stumble." Related: Struggled; struggling.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 来源存疑, 可能 a frequentative form with -el (3) (对比 trample, wrestle), but the first element is 来源存疑. Skeat suggests 古北欧语 strugr "ill will;" others suggest a connection to 荷兰语 struikelen, 德语 straucheln "to stumble." 同源词：Struggled; struggling.

example.en: She had to struggle to balance work and family life.
example.zh: 她不得不努力在工作和家庭生活之间取得平衡。

definitionLines: a. 顽固的；难处理的；顽强的
entries.definition: a. 顽固的；难处理的；顽强的
entries.etymology: late 14c., of uncertain origin. Earliest form is stiborn. OED, Liberman doubt any connection with stub (n.). Related: Stubbornly; stubbornness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 来源存疑. Earliest form is stiborn. OED, Liberman doubt any connection with stub （名）. 同源词：Stubbornly; stubbornness.

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French estudiant "student, scholar, one who is studying" (Modern French étudiant), noun use of past participle of estudiier, from Medieval Latin studiare "to study," from Latin studium (see study (v.)). An Old English word for it was leorningcild "student, disciple." Student-teacher of a teacher in training working in a classroom is from 1851, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 estudiant "student, scholar, one who is studying" (现代法语 étudiant), 为 … 的名词用法 为 … 的过去分词 estudiier, 源自 中古拉丁语 studiare "to study," 源自 拉丁语 studium （参见 study （动）). An 古英语 word for it was leorningcild "student, disciple." Student-teacher of a teacher in training working in a classroom 始于 1851 年, American English.

example.en: Every student in the class was expected to give a short presentation.
example.zh: 班上每位学生都被要求做一个简短的演讲。

definitionLines: n. 画室，工作室，播音室
entries.definition: n. 画室，工作室，播音室
entries.etymology: 1819, "work-room of a sculptor or painter," usually one with windows to admit light from the sky, from Italian studio "room for study," from Latin studium (see study (v.)). Motion picture sense first recorded 1911; radio broadcasting sense 1922; television sense 1938. Studio apartment first recorded 1903.
entries.etymologyZh: 1819 年, "work-room of a sculptor or painter," 通常 one with windows to admit light 源自 sky, 源自 意大利语 studio "room for study," 源自 拉丁语 studium （参见 study （动）). Motion picture sense 首见于 1911 年; radio broadcasting sense 1922 年; television sense 1938 年. Studio apartment 首见于 1903 年.

example.en: The artist spent long hours in her studio perfecting each painting.
example.zh: 这位艺术家在她的工作室里花了很长时间来完善每一幅画。

definitionLines: vt. 学习，读书；研究，探讨； 细看
entries.definition: vt. 学习，读书；研究，探讨； 细看
entries.etymology:
early 12c., "to strive toward, devote oneself to, cultivate" (translating Latin occupatur), from Old French estudiier "to study, apply oneself, show zeal for; examine" (13c., Modern French étudier), from Medieval Latin studiare, from Latin studium "study, application," originally "eagerness," from studere "to be diligent," from PIE *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" (see steep (adj.)). The notion appears to be "pressing forward, thrusting toward," hence "strive after."

From c. 1300 as "apply oneself to the acquisition of learning, pursue a formal course of study," also "read a book or writings intently or meditatively." From mid-14c. as "reflect, muse, think, ponder." Meaning "regard attentively" is from 1660s. Related: Studied; studying.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪初, "to strive toward, devote oneself to, cultivate" (translating 拉丁语 occupatur), 源自 古法语 estudiier "to study, apply oneself, show zeal for; examine" (13 世纪, 现代法语 étudier), 源自 中古拉丁语 studiare, 源自 拉丁语 studium "study, application," 原义为 "eagerness," 源自 studere "to be diligent," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" （参见 steep （形）). The notion appears to be "pressing forward, thrusting toward," hence "strive after." From 约 1300 年 as "apply oneself to the acquisition of learning, pursue a formal course of study," also "read a book or writings intently or meditatively." From 14 世纪中期 as "reflect, muse, think, ponder." 义为 "regard attentively" 始于 1660 年代. 同源词：Studied; studying.

example.en: Scientists spent a decade to study the long-term effects of this medication on the brain.
example.zh: 科学家花了十年时间研究这种药物对大脑的长期影响。

definitionLines: n. 物品，物质；个人所有物； 材料，原料；东西
entries.definition: n. 物品，物质；个人所有物； 材料，原料；东西 vt. 填满，塞满
entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "furnish with" (goods, provisions, etc.), also "reinforce" (troops), from Old French estofer "pad, upholster, fit out" (Modern French étoffer), from estoffe, and probably also in part from stuff (n.).

From c. 1400 as "fill, cram full; fill (the belly) with food or drink, gorge;" from early 15c. as "to clog" (the sinuses, etc.); from late 14c. as "fill (a mattress, etc.) with padding, line with padding;" also in the cookery sense, in reference to filing the interior of a pastry or the cavity of a fowl or beast. The ballot-box sense is attested from 1854, American English; in expressions of contempt and suggestive of bodily orifices, it dates from 1952.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "furnish with" (goods, provisions, etc.), also "reinforce" (troops), 源自 古法语 estofer "pad, upholster, fit out" (现代法语 étoffer), 源自 estoffe, and 可能 also in part 源自 stuff （名）. From 约 1400 年 as "fill, cram full; fill (the belly) with food or drink, gorge;" 源自 15 世纪初 as "to clog" (the sinuses, etc.); 源自 14 世纪晚期 as "fill (a mattress, etc.) with padding, line with padding;" also in the cookery sense, in reference to filing the interior of a pastry or the cavity of a fowl or beast. The ballot-box sense 见于 1854 年, American English; in expressions of contempt and suggestive of bodily orifices, it dates 自 1952 年起.

example.en: She packed all her stuff into one large suitcase before the flight.
example.zh: 飞行前她把所有的东西都塞进了一个大手提箱。

entries.definition: vi. 踌躇，蹒跚 n. 绊倒；蹒跚而行
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to trip or miss one's footing" (physically or morally), probably from a Scandinavian source (compare dialectal Norwegian stumla, Swedish stambla "to stumble"), probably from a variant of the Proto-Germanic base *stam-, source of Old English stamerian "to stammer," German stumm, Dutch stom "dumb, silent." Possibly influenced in form by stumpen "to stumble," but the -b- may be purely euphonious. Meaning "to come (upon) by chance" is attested from 1550s. Related: Stumbled; stumbling. Stumbling-block first recorded 1526 (Tindale), used in Rom. xiv:13, where usually it translates Greek skandalon.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to trip or miss one's footing" (physically or morally), 可能 源自 a Scandinavian source (对比 方言 Norwegian stumla, Swedish stambla "to stumble"), 可能 源自 a 为 … 的变体 the 原始日耳曼语 base *stam-, source of 古英语 stamerian "to stammer," 德语 stumm, 荷兰语 stom "dumb, silent." Possibly influenced in form by stumpen "to stumble," but the -b- may be purely euphonious. 义为 "to come (upon) by chance" 见于 1550 年代. 同源词：Stumbled; stumbling. Stumbling-block 首见于 1526 年 (Tindale), used in Rom. xiv:13, where 通常 it translates 希腊语 skandalon.

example.en: He stumble over a rock and nearly fell into the river.
example.zh: 他被一块石头绊了一下，差点掉进河里。

entries.definition: vt. 打昏；使震惊 n. 打昏；昏迷；惊倒
entries.etymology: early 14c., "to daze or render unconscious" (from a blow, powerful emotion, etc.), probably a shortening of Old French estoner "to stun" (see astonish). Related: Stunned; stunning.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "to daze or render unconscious" (源自 a blow, powerful emotion, etc.), 可能 a shortening of 古法语 estoner "to stun" （参见 astonish). 同源词：Stunned; stunning.

example.en: The audience was stunned by the magician's final, breathtaking trick.
example.zh: 观众被魔术师最后那个令人叹为观止的表演惊呆了。

entries.etymology:
1540s, "mentally slow, lacking ordinary activity of mind, dull, inane," from Middle French stupide (16c.) and directly from Latin stupidus "amazed, confounded; dull, foolish," literally "struck senseless," from stupere "be stunned, amazed, confounded," from PIE *stupe- "hit," from root *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" (see steep (adj.)). Related: Stupidly; stupidness.

Native words for this idea include negative compounds with words for "wise" (Old English unwis, unsnotor, ungleaw), also dol (see dull (adj.)), and dysig (see dizzy (adj.)). Stupid retained its association with stupor and its overtones of "stunned by surprise, grief, etc." into mid-18c. The difference between stupid and the less opprobrious foolish roughly parallels that of German töricht vs. dumm but does not exist in most European languages.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "mentally slow, lacking ordinary activity of mind, dull, inane," 源自 中古法语 stupide (16 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 stupidus "amazed, confounded; dull, foolish," 字面义为 "struck senseless," 源自 stupere "be stunned, amazed, confounded," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *stupe- "hit," 源自 root *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" （参见 steep （形）). 同源词：Stupidly; stupidness. Native words for this idea include negative compounds with words for "wise" (古英语 unwis, unsnotor, ungleaw), also dol （参见 dull （形）), and dysig （参见 dizzy （形）). Stupid retained its association with stupor and its overtones of "stunned by surprise, grief, etc." into 18 世纪中期 The difference between stupid and the less opprobrious foolish roughly parallels that of 德语 töricht vs. dumm but does not exist in most European languages.

example.en: It was stupid of him to sign the contract without reading it first.
example.zh: 他没有先阅读就签合同，真是太愚蠢了。

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "hard to manage, reckless, violent," from Old French estordi (11c., Modern French étourdi) "violent," originally "dazed," past participle of estordiir "to daze, stun, stupefy," from Vulgar Latin *exturdire, which some presume to be from Latin intensive prefix ex- + turdus "thrush." Barnhart suggests the notion is of thrushes eating grape remnants at wineries and behaving as if drunk (Italian tordo "thrush" also means "simpleton," and French has the expression soûl comme une grive "drunk as a thrush"). OED, however, regards all this as "open to grave objection." Century Dictionary compares Latin torpidus "dull."
