Spelling in English influenced 14c. by learned Old French forms closer to Latin suspicionem. Used as a verb meaning "to suspect," it figures in literary representations of U.S. Western (Kentucky) slang from 1830s.

"Suspicion" words in other Indo-European languages also tend to be words for "think" or "look" with prefixes meaning "under, behind;" such as Greek hypopsia (hypo "under," opsis "sight"), hyponoia (noein "to think"); Lettish aizduomas (aiz "behind," duomat "think"); Russian podozrenie (Slavic podu "under," Old Church Slavonic zireti "see, look"); Dutch achterdocht (achter "behind," denken "to think").
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "act of suspecting; unverified conjecture of wrongdoing; mistrust, distrust," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 suspecioun, corresponding to 古法语 suspicion, sospeçon "mistrust, suspicion" (现代法语 soupçon), 源自 晚期拉丁语 suspectionem (主格 suspectio) "mistrust, suspicion, fear, awe," 名词 of state 源自 past participle stem of 拉丁语 suspicere "look up at" （参见 suspect （形）). Spelling in English influenced 14 世纪 by learned 古法语 forms closer to 拉丁语 suspicionem. Used 作动词时 意为 "to suspect," it figures in literary representations of U.S. Western (Kentucky) 俚语 源自 1830 年代. "Suspicion" words in other Indo-European languages also tend to be words for "think" or "look" with prefixes 意为 "under, behind;" such as 希腊语 hypopsia (hypo "under," opsis "sight"), hyponoia (noein "to think"); Lettish aizduomas (aiz "behind," duomat "think"); 俄语 podozrenie (Slavic podu "under," Old Church Slavonic zireti "see, look"); 荷兰语 achterdocht (achter "behind," denken "to think").

example.en: His sudden change of behavior aroused suspicion among his colleagues.
example.zh: 他突然改变的行为在同事中引起了怀疑。

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "deserving of or exciting suspicion," from Old French sospecious, from Latin suspiciosus, suspitiosus "exciting suspicion, causing mistrust," also "full of suspicion, ready to suspect," from stem of suspicere (see suspicion). Meaning "full of suspicion, inclined to suspect" in English is attested from c. 1400. Poe (c. 1845) proposed suspectful to take one of the two conflicting senses. Related: suspiciously; suspiciousness.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "deserving of or exciting suspicion," 源自 古法语 sospecious, 源自 拉丁语 suspiciosus, suspitiosus "exciting suspicion, causing mistrust," also "full of suspicion, ready to suspect," 源自 stem of suspicere （参见 suspicion). 义为 "full of suspicion, inclined to suspect" in English 见于 约 1400 年. Poe (约 1845 年) proposed suspectful to take one of the two conflicting senses. 同源词：suspiciously; suspiciousness.

example.en: The detective grew suspicious when the witness changed his story twice.
example.zh: 当证人两次改变陈述时，侦探开始起疑心。

definitionLines: vt. 支撑，承担；维持；忍受； 供养
entries.definition: vt. 支撑，承担；维持；忍受； 供养
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "give support to," from stem of Old French sostenir "hold up, bear; suffer, endure" (13c.), from Latin sustinere "hold up, hold upright; furnish with means of support; bear, undergo, endure," from sub "up from below" (see sub-) + tenere "to hold" (see tenet). Meaning "continue, keep up" (an action, etc.) is from early 14c. Sense of "endure without failing or yielding" is from c. 1400. Related: Sustained; sustaining.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "give support to," 源自 stem of 古法语 sostenir "hold up, bear; suffer, endure" (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 sustinere "hold up, hold upright; furnish with means of support; bear, undergo, endure," 源自 sub "up from below" （参见 sub-) + tenere "to hold" （参见 tenet). 义为 "continue, keep up" (an action, etc.) 始于 14 世纪初 义为 "endure without failing or yielding" 始于 约 1400 年. 同源词：Sustained; sustaining.

example.en: The charity could barely sustain its food programs without extra funding.
example.zh: 没有额外资金，该慈善机构几乎无法维持其食品项目。

entries.etymology: 1610s, "bearable," from sustain + -able. Attested from 1845 in the sense "defensible;" from 1965 with the meaning "capable of being continued at a certain level."  Sustainable growth is recorded from 1965. Related: Sustainably.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "bearable," 源自 sustain + -able. Attested 自 1845 年起 in the sense "defensible;" 自 1965 年起 with the 意为 "capable of being continued at a certain level." Sustainable growth 见于 1965 年. 同源词：Sustainably.

example.en: The company committed to sustainable energy practices.
example.zh: 这家公司承诺采用可持续的能源做法。

entries.definition: n. 燕子；吞咽 vt. 咽；淹没，吞没 vi. 吞下，咽下
entries.etymology:
"ingest through the throat" (transitive), Old English swelgan "swallow, imbibe, absorb" (class III strong verb; past tense swealg, past participle swolgen), from Proto-Germanic *swelgan/*swelhan (source also of Old Saxon farswelgan, Old Norse svelgja "to swallow," Middle Dutch swelghen, Dutch zwelgen "to gulp, swallow," Old High German swelahan "to swallow," German schwelgen "to revel"), probably from PIE root *swel- (1) "to eat, drink" (source also of Iranian *khvara- "eating").

Intransitive sense "perform the act of swallowing" is from c. 1700. Sense of "consume, destroy" is attested from mid-14c. Meaning "to accept without question" is from 1590s. Related: Swallowed; swallowing.
entries.etymologyZh: "ingest through the throat" (transitive), 古英语 swelgan "swallow, imbibe, absorb" (class III strong 动词; past tense swealg, past participle swolgen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swelgan/*swelhan (source also of 古撒克逊语 farswelgan, 古北欧语 svelgja "to swallow," Middle 荷兰语 swelghen, 荷兰语 zwelgen "to gulp, swallow," 古高地德语 swelahan "to swallow," 德语 schwelgen "to revel"), 可能 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *swel- (1) "to eat, drink" (source also of Iranian *khvara- "eating"). Intransitive sense "perform the act of swallowing" 始于 约 1700 年. 义为 "consume, destroy" 见于 14 世纪中期 义为 "to accept without question" 始于 1590 年代. 同源词：Swallowed; swallowing.

example.en: He took a sip of water to help him swallow the large pill.
example.zh: 他喝了一口水，帮助自己把大药片咽下去。

entries.etymology:
c. 1500 (implied in swampwatyr "swamp-water"), of uncertain origin, perhaps [Barnhart] a dialectal survival from an Old English cognate of Old Norse svöppr "sponge, fungus," from Proto-Germanic *swampuz; but traditionally connected with Middle English sompe "morass, swamp," which probably is from Middle Dutch somp or Middle Low German sump "swamp" (see sump). All of these likely are ultimately related to each other, from PIE *swombho- "spongy; mushroom," via the notion of "spongy ground."

More popular in U.S. (swamp (n.) by itself is first attested 1624 in Capt. John Smith's description of Virginia). Swamp-oak is from 1680s, American English. Swamp Yankee "rural, rustic New Englander" is attested from 1941. Thornton's "American Glossary" (1912) has swamp-angel "dweller in a swamp," swamp-law "might makes right."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年 (implied in swampwatyr "swamp-water"), 来源存疑, 或许 [Barnhart] a 方言 survival 源自 an 古英语 同源 of 古北欧语 svöppr "sponge, fungus," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swampuz; but traditionally connected with 中古英语 sompe "morass, swamp," which 可能 始于 Middle 荷兰语 somp or Middle Low 德语 sump "swamp" （参见 sump). All of these likely are ultimately related to each other, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *swombho- "spongy; mushroom," 经由 the 概念 "spongy ground." More popular in U.S. (swamp （名） by itself is 最早见于 1624 年 in Capt. John Smith's description of Virginia). Swamp-oak is from 1680s, American English. Swamp Yankee "rural, rustic New Englander" is attested from 1941. Thornton's "American Glossary" (1912 年) has swamp-angel "dweller in a swamp," swamp-law "might makes right."

example.en: The hiking trail ended abruptly at the edge of a vast swamp.
example.zh: 那条徒步小径在一片广阔的沼泽边缘突然中断。

entries.etymology:
Old English swan "swan," from Proto-Germanic *swanaz "singer" (source also of Old Saxon swan, Old Norse svanr, Danish svane, Swedish svan, Middle Dutch swane, Dutch zwaan, Old High German swan, German Schwan), probably literally "the singing bird," from PIE root *swen- "to sing, make sound" (see sound (n.1)); thus related to Old English geswin "melody, song" and swinsian "to make melody."

In classical mythology, sacred to Apollo and to Venus. The singing of swans before death was alluded to by Chaucer (late 14c.), but swan-song (1831) is a translation of German Schwanengesang. The ancient Indo-European mythical swan-maiden so called by mythographers from 1829. Swan dive is recorded from 1898. A black swan was proverbial for "something extremely rare or non-existent" (late 14c.), after Juvenal ["Sat." vi. 164], but later they turned up in Australia (Chenopsis atratus).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 swan "swan," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swanaz "singer" (source also of 古撒克逊语 swan, 古北欧语 svanr, Danish svane, Swedish svan, Middle 荷兰语 swane, 荷兰语 zwaan, 古高地德语 swan, 德语 Schwan), 可能 字面义为 "the singing bird," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *swen- "to sing, make sound" （参见 sound (n.1)); thus related to 古英语 geswin "melody, song" and swinsian "to make melody." In classical mythology, sacred to Apollo and to Venus. The singing of swans before death was alluded to by Chaucer (14 世纪晚期), but swan-song (1831 年) is a translation of 德语 Schwanengesang. The ancient Indo-European mythical swan-maiden so called by mythographers 自 1829 年起. Swan dive 见于 1898 年. A black swan was proverbial for "something extremely rare or non-existent" (14 世纪晚期), after Juvenal ["Sat." vi. 164], but later they turned up in Australia (Chenopsis atratus).

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "to strike, strike the hands together," of uncertain origin, possibly imitative of the sound of hitting or slapping. The sense of "to exchange, barter, trade" is first recorded 1590s, possibly from the notion of slapping hands together as a sign of agreement in bargaining (as in strike a bargain). Related: Swapped; swapping. The noun in this sense is attested from 1620s; earlier "a striking, an act of striking" (mid-13c.). Swap-meet attested from 1968, American English.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "to strike, strike the hands together," 来源存疑, possibly imitative of the sound of hitting or slapping. The 语义 "to exchange, barter, trade" is 首见于 1590 年代, possibly 源自 概念 slapping hands together 作为 sign of agreement in bargaining (as in strike a bargain). 同源词：Swapped; swapping. The 名词 in this sense 见于 1620 年代; earlier "a striking, an act of striking" (13 世纪中期). Swap-meet attested 自 1968 年起, American English.

entries.etymology:
early 14c., "move, go, go quickly; move (something) along, carry," probably from a Scandinavian source akin to Old Norse sveigja "to bend, swing, give way," Old Danish svegja, perhaps merged with an unrecorded Old English cognate. The whole group might be related to swag (v.) and swing (v.).

The sense of "swing, waver, move in a swaying or sweeping motion" is from late 14c. Meaning "move from side to side" is from c. 1500; transitive sense "cause to move from side to side" is from 1550s (according to OED, not common before 19c.). Figurative sense "cause to be directed toward one side, prejudice" is from 1590s. Related: Swayed; swaying.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "move, go, go quickly; move (something) along, carry," 可能 源自 a Scandinavian source akin to 古北欧语 sveigja "to bend, swing, give way," Old Danish svegja, 或许 merged with an unrecorded 古英语 同源. The whole group might be related to swag （动） and swing （动）. The 语义 "swing, waver, move in a swaying or sweeping motion" 始于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "move from side to side" 始于 约 1500 年; transitive sense "cause to move from side to side" 始于 1550 年代 (according to OED, not common before 19 世纪). Figurative sense "cause to be directed toward one side, prejudice" 始于 1590 年代. 同源词：Swayed; swaying.

example.en: The tall trees swayed gently in the evening breeze.
example.zh: 高大的树木在晚风中轻轻摇曳。

entries.etymology:
Old English swerian "take an oath" (class VI strong verb; past tense swor, past participle sworen), from Proto-Germanic *swarjan-, (source also of Old Saxon swerian, Old Frisian swera, Old Norse sverja, Danish sverge, Middle Dutch swaren, Old High German swerien, German schwören, Gothic swaren "to swear"), from PIE root *swer- (1) "to speak, talk, say" (source also of Old Church Slavonic svara "quarrel," Oscan sverrunei "to the speaker").

Also related to the second element in answer. The secondary sense of "use bad language" (early 15c.) developed from the notion of "invoke sacred names." Swear off "desist as with a vow" is from 1898. Swear in "install in office by administration of an oath" is from 1700 in modern use, echoing Old English.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 swerian "take an oath" (class VI strong 动词; past tense swor, past participle sworen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swarjan-, (source also of 古撒克逊语 swerian, 古弗里西语 swera, 古北欧语 sverja, Danish sverge, Middle 荷兰语 swaren, 古高地德语 swerien, 德语 schwören, Gothic swaren "to swear"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *swer- (1) "to speak, talk, say" (source also of Old Church Slavonic svara "quarrel," Oscan sverrunei "to the speaker"). Also related to the second element in answer. The secondary 语义 "use bad language" (15 世纪初) developed 源自 概念 "invoke sacred names." Swear off "desist as with a vow" 始于 1898 年. Swear in "install in office by administration of an oath" 始于 1700 年 in modern use, echoing 古英语.

example.en: He raised his hand and began to swear an oath before the court.
example.zh: 他举起手，开始在法庭前宣誓。

entries.etymology: Old English swætan "perspire," also "work hard," from Proto-Germanic *swaitjan "to sweat," from the source of sweat (n.). Compare Frisian swette, Dutch zweeten, Danish svede, German schwitzen. Meaning "to be worried, vexed" is recorded from c. 1400. Transitive sense is from late 14c. Related: Sweated; sweating. Sweating sickness was a sudden, often-fatal fever, accompanied by intense sweating, that struck England 1485 and returned periodically through mid-16c., described in the original citation (a chronicle from 1502) as "a grete deth and hasty."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 swætan "perspire," also "work hard," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swaitjan "to sweat," 源自 source of sweat （名）. 对比 Frisian swette, 荷兰语 zweeten, Danish svede, 德语 schwitzen. 义为 "to be worried, vexed" 见于 约 1400 年. Transitive sense 始于 14 世纪晚期 同源词：Sweated; sweating. Sweating sickness was a sudden, 常-fatal fever, accompanied by intense sweating, that struck England 1485 年 and returned periodically through 16 世纪中期, described in the original citation (a chronicle 自 1502 年起) as "a grete deth and hasty."

example.en: Workers were dripping with sweat after hours of clearing debris under the hot sun.
example.zh: 在烈日下清理废墟数小时后，工人们汗流浃背。

entries.etymology: "woolen vest or jersey, originally worn in rowing," 1882, from earlier sweaters "clothing worn to produce sweating and reduce weight" (1828), plural agent noun from sweat (v.). As a fashion garment, attested from 1925. Earlier it meant "one who works hard" (1520s). Sweater girl is attested from 1940; Lana Turner (1920-1995) was the first, from her appearance in the film "They Won't Forget" (1937).
entries.etymologyZh: "woolen vest or jersey, originally worn in rowing," 1882 年, 源自 earlier sweaters "clothing worn to produce sweating and reduce weight" (1828 年), plural agent 名词 源自 sweat （动）. 作为 fashion garment, attested 自 1925 年起. Earlier it meant "one who works hard" (1520 年代). Sweater girl 见于 1940 年; Lana Turner (1920 年-1995 年) was the first, 源自 her appearance in the film "They Won't Forget" (1937 年).

definitionLines: vt.扫，打扫；冲走，席卷；掠过， 扫过
entries.definition: vt.扫，打扫；冲走，席卷；掠过， 扫过 vi.快速移动，扫描
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "make clean by sweeping with a broom;" mid-14c., "perform the act of sweeping," of uncertain origin, perhaps from a past tense form of Middle English swope "sweep," from Old English swapan "to sweep" (transitive & intransitive); see swoop (v.), or perhaps from a Scandinavian source. Related: Swept; sweeping.

From late 14c. as "hasten, rush, move swiftly and strongly;" also "collect by sweeping." From c. 1400 in transitive sense "drive quickly, impel, move or carry forward by force;" mid-15c. as "clear (something) away." Meaning "win all the events" is 1960, American English. Sense of "pass systematically over in search of something" is from 1966. To sweep (someone) off (his or her) feet "affect with infatuation" is from 1913.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "make clean by sweeping with a broom;" 14 世纪中期, "perform the act of sweeping," 来源存疑, 或源自 a past tense form of 中古英语 swope "sweep," 源自 古英语 swapan "to sweep" (transitive & intransitive); 参见 swoop （动），或或源自 a Scandinavian source. 同源词：Swept; sweeping. From 14 世纪晚期 as "hasten, rush, move swiftly and strongly;" also "collect by sweeping." From 约 1400 年 in transitive sense "drive quickly, impel, move or carry forward by force;" 15 世纪中期 as "clear (something) away." 义为 "win all the events" is 1960 年, American English. 义为 "pass systematically over in search of something" 始于 1966 年. To sweep (someone) off (his or her) feet "affect with infatuation" 始于 1913 年.

example.en: She used a broom to sweep the fallen leaves off the porch.
example.zh: 她用扫帚把门廊上的落叶扫掉。

definitionLines: a. 甜，香；悦耳/目；可爱的；亲 切的；温柔的；舒服的
entries.definition: a. 甜，香；悦耳/目；可爱的；亲 切的；温柔的；舒服的 n. （p.）糖果，甜食
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "something sweet to the taste," also "beloved one," from sweet (adj.); the specific meaning "candy drop" is 1851 (earlier sweetie, 1721). Meaning "one who is dear to another" is from 14c. Old English swete (n.) meant "sweetness."
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "something sweet to the taste," also "beloved one," 源自 sweet （形）; the specific 意为 "candy drop" is 1851 年 (earlier sweetie, 1721 年). 义为 "one who is dear to another" 始于 14 世纪 古英语 swete （名） meant "sweetness."

example.en: She added a little honey to make the tea taste sweet.
example.zh: 她加了一点蜂蜜，让茶喝起来更甜。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "a morbid swelling," from swell (v.). In reference to a rise of the sea, it is attested from c. 1600; of music, by 1803. The meaning "wealthy, elegant person" is first recorded 1786, connected to the now-obsolete sense "pompousness, arrogance" (1724), both from the notion of "puffed-up" demeanor or behavior.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "a morbid swelling," 源自 swell （动）. In reference to a rise of the sea, it 见于 约 1600 年; of music, 截至 1803 年. The 意为 "wealthy, elegant person" is 首见于 1786 年, connected to the 现在-已废 sense "pompousness, arrogance" (1724 年), both 源自 概念 "puffed-up" demeanor or behavior.

example.en: His ankle began to swell after he twisted it during the race.
example.zh: 在比赛中扭伤脚踝后，他的脚踝开始肿胀。

entries.etymology: Old English swift "moving quickly," perhaps originally "turning quickly," from Proto-Germanic swip- (see swivel (n.)). Related: Swiftly; swiftness.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 swift "moving quickly," 或许 原义为 "turning quickly," 源自 原始日耳曼语 swip- （参见 swivel （名）). 同源词：Swiftly; swiftness.

entries.etymology: 1540s, "the clear part of any liquid" (above the sediment), from swim (v.). Meaning "part of a river or stream frequented by fish" (and hence fishermen) is from 1828, and is probably the source of the figurative meaning "the current of the latest affairs or events" (as in in the swim "on the inside, involved with current events," 1869). Meaning "act of swimming" is from 1764.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "the clear part of any liquid" (above the sediment), 源自 swim （动）. 义为 "part of a river or stream frequented by fish" (and hence fishermen) 始于 1828 年, and is 可能 the source of the figurative 意为 "the current of the latest affairs or events" (as in in the swim "on the inside, involved with current events," 1869 年). 义为 "act of swimming" 始于 1764 年.

example.en: She learned to swim before she started school.
example.zh: 她在上学之前就学会了游泳。

definitionLines: vi. 摇摆，摇荡；回转，转向
entries.definition: vi. 摇摆，摇荡；回转，转向 n. 秋千
entries.etymology:
Old English swingan "beat, strike; scourge, flog; to rush, fling oneself" (strong verb, past tense swang, past participle swungen), from Proto-Germanic *swingan (source also of Old Saxon, Old High German swingan, Old Frisian swinga, German schwingen "to swing, swingle, oscillate"), from PIE *sweng(w)- "to swing, turn, toss" (perhaps Germanic only).

The meaning "move freely back and forth" is first recorded 1540s. Transitive sense "cause to oscillate" is from 1550s. Sense of "bring about, make happen" is from 1934. Sense of "engage in promiscuous sex" is from 1964; earlier, more generally, "enjoy oneself unconventionally" (1957). Related: Swung; swinging. Swing-voter "independent who often determines the outcome of an election" is from 1966.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 swingan "beat, strike; scourge, flog; to rush, fling oneself" (strong 动词, past tense swang, past participle swungen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swingan (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古高地德语 swingan, 古弗里西语 swinga, 德语 schwingen "to swing, swingle, oscillate"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *sweng(w)- "to swing, turn, toss" (或许 日耳曼语 only). The 意为 "move freely back and forth" is 首见于 1540 年代. Transitive sense "cause to oscillate" 始于 1550 年代. 义为 "bring about, make happen" 始于 1934 年. 义为 "engage in promiscuous sex" 始于 1964 年; earlier, more generally, "enjoy oneself unconventionally" (1957 年). 同源词：Swung; swinging. Swing-voter "independent who often determines the outcome of an election" 始于 1966 年.

example.en: The child laughed as she began to swing on the playground swing.
example.zh: 孩子开心地笑着，开始在操场的秋千上荡起来。

entries.etymology: 1510s, from Middle French Suisse, from Middle High German Suizer, from Suiz "Switzerland" (see Switzerland and compare Switzer (1570s), archaic word for "a Swiss," and German Schweiz). As an adjective from 1520s. Swiss banks were notable for assuring anonymity and security by 1949. Swiss cheese is attested from 1808; as a type of something full of holes, from 1924.
entries.etymologyZh: 1510 年代, 源自 中古法语 Suisse, 源自 Middle High 德语 Suizer, 源自 Suiz "Switzerland" （参见 Switzerland and 对比 Switzer (1570 年代), 古旧 word for "a Swiss," and 德语 Schweiz). 作形容词时 源自 1520 年代. Swiss banks were notable for assuring anonymity and security 截至 1949 年. Swiss cheese 见于 1808 年; 作为 type of something full of holes, 自 1924 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English sweord, swyrd (West Saxon), sword (Northumbrian) "sword," from Proto-Germanic *swerdam (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian swerd, Old Norse sverð, Swedish svärd, Middle Dutch swaert, Dutch zwaard, Old High German swert, German Schwert "a sword"), related to Old High German sweran "to hurt," from *swertha-, literally "the cutting weapon," from PIE root *swer- (3) "to cut, pierce."

Contrast with plowshare is from the Old Testament (Isaiah ii:4, Micah iv:3). Phrase put (originally do) to the sword "kill, slaughter" is recorded from mid-14c. An older Germanic word for it is in Old Saxon heoru, Gothic hairus "a sword."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 sweord, swyrd (West Saxon), sword (Northumbrian) "sword," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *swerdam (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古弗里西语 swerd, 古北欧语 sverð, Swedish svärd, Middle 荷兰语 swaert, 荷兰语 zwaard, 古高地德语 swert, 德语 Schwert "a sword"), related to 古高地德语 sweran "to hurt," 源自 *swertha-, 字面义为 "the cutting weapon," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *swer- (3) "to cut, pierce." Contrast with plowshare 始于 the Old Testament (Isaiah ii:4, Micah iv:3). Phrase put (原义为 do) to the sword "kill, slaughter" 见于 14 世纪中期 An older 日耳曼语 word for it is in 古撒克逊语 heoru, Gothic hairus "a sword."

entries.etymology:
early 15c., "creed, summary, religious belief," from Late Latin symbolum "creed, token, mark," from Greek symbolon "token, watchword, sign by which one infers; ticket, a permit, license" (the word was applied c.250 by Cyprian of Carthage to the Apostles' Creed, on the notion of the "mark" that distinguishes Christians from pagans), literally "that which is thrown or cast together," from assimilated form of syn- "together" (see syn-) + bole "a throwing, a casting, the stroke of a missile, bolt, beam," from bol-, nominative stem of ballein "to throw" (see ballistics).

The sense evolution in Greek is from "throwing things together" to "contrasting" to "comparing" to "token used in comparisons to determine if something is genuine." Hence, "outward sign" of something. The meaning "something which stands for something else" first recorded 1590 (in "Faerie Queene"). As a written character, 1610s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "creed, summary, religious belief," 源自 晚期拉丁语 symbolum "creed, token, mark," 源自 希腊语 symbolon "token, watchword, sign by which one infers; ticket, a permit, license" (the word was applied 约 250 年 by Cyprian of Carthage to the Apostles' Creed, on the 概念 the "mark" that distinguishes Christians 源自 pagans), 字面义为 "that which is thrown or cast together," 源自 为 … 的同化形式 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + bole "a throwing, a casting, the stroke of a missile, bolt, beam," 源自 bol-, 主格 stem of ballein "to throw" （参见 ballistics). The sense evolution in 希腊语 始于 "throwing things together" to "contrasting" to "comparing" to "token used in comparisons to determine if something is genuine." Hence, "outward sign" of something. The 意为 "something which stands for something else" 首见于 1590 年 (in "Faerie Queene"). 作为 written character, 1610 年代.

example.en: The olive branch has long been used as a symbol of peace in Western culture.
example.zh: 橄榄枝在西方文化中长期被用作和平的象征。

definitionLines: a. 象征的，象征性的；符号的， 记号的；象征主义的
entries.definition: a. 象征的，象征性的；符号的， 记号的；象征主义的
entries.etymology: 1650s, from symbol + -ic, or from Greek symbolikos. Related: Symbolical (c. 1600); symbolically.
entries.etymologyZh: 1650 年代, 源自 symbol + -ic，或源自 希腊语 symbolikos. 同源词：Symbolical (约 1600 年); symbolically.

example.en: The white dove is symbolic of peace in many cultures around the world.
example.zh: 在世界许多文化中，白鸽象征着和平。

entries.etymology: 1560s, "relation of parts, proportion," from Middle French symmétrie (16c.) and directly from Latin symmetria, from Greek symmetria "agreement in dimensions, due proportion, arrangement," from symmetros "having a common measure, even, proportionate," from assimilated form of syn- "together" (see syn-) + metron "meter" (see meter (n.2)). Meaning "harmonic arrangement of parts" first recorded 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, "relation of parts, proportion," 源自 中古法语 symmétrie (16 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 symmetria, 源自 希腊语 symmetria "agreement in dimensions, due proportion, arrangement," 源自 symmetros "having a common measure, even, proportionate," 源自 为 … 的同化形式 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + metron "meter" （参见 meter (n.2)). 义为 "harmonic arrangement of parts" 首见于 1590 年代.

entries.etymology:
1640s, "pertaining to sympathy," from Modern Latin sympatheticus, from late Greek sympathetikos "having sympathy," from sympathein, from sympathes "having a fellow feeling, affected by like feelings" (see sympathy). In English, the meaning "having fellow feeling, susceptible to altruistic feelings" is recorded from 1718.

In the anatomical sense, "subject to a common nervous influence," the word is attested from 1769, from Modern Latin (nervus) sympathicus, coined by Jacques-Benigne Winslow (1669-1760), Danish anatomist living in Paris. Related: Sympathetical (1630s); Sympathetically (1620s).
entries.etymologyZh: 1640 年代, "pertaining to sympathy," 源自 现代 拉丁语 sympatheticus, 源自 late 希腊语 sympathetikos "having sympathy," 源自 sympathein, 源自 sympathes "having a fellow feeling, affected by like feelings" （参见 sympathy). In English, the 意为 "having fellow feeling, susceptible to altruistic feelings" 见于 1718 年. In the anatomical sense, "subject to a common nervous influence," the word 见于 1769 年, 源自 现代 拉丁语 (nervus) sympathicus, coined by Jacques-Benigne Winslow (1669 年-1760 年), Danish anatomist living in Paris. 同源词：Sympathetical (1630 年代); Sympathetically (1620 年代).

example.en: The counselor was warm and sympathetic toward students in distress.
example.zh: 这位辅导员对处于困境中的学生态度温暖、富有同情心。

definitionLines: vt. 同情，怜悯；共鸣，同感
entries.definition: vt. 同情，怜悯；共鸣，同感
entries.etymology: "have fellow-feeling," c. 1600, from Middle French sympathiser, from sympathie (see sympathy). Earlier in a physiological sense (1590s). As "express sympathy," from 1748. Related: Sympathized; sympathizing.
entries.etymologyZh: "have fellow-feeling," 约 1600 年, 源自 中古法语 sympathiser, 源自 sympathie （参见 sympathy). Earlier in a physiological sense (1590 年代). As "express sympathy," 自 1748 年起. 同源词：Sympathized; sympathizing.

definitionLines: n. 同情，同情心；赞同，同感
entries.definition: n. 同情，同情心；赞同，同感
entries.etymology:
1570s, "affinity between certain things," from Middle French sympathie (16c.) and directly from Late Latin sympathia "community of feeling, sympathy," from Greek sympatheia "fellow-feeling, community of feeling," from sympathes "having a fellow feeling, affected by like feelings," from assimilated form of syn- "together" (see syn-) + pathos "feeling" (see pathos).

In English, almost a magical notion at first; used in reference to medicines that heal wounds when applied to a cloth stained with blood from the wound. Meaning "conformity of feelings" is from 1590s; sense of "fellow feeling, compassion" is first attested c. 1600. An Old English loan-translation of sympathy was efensargung.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, "affinity between certain things," 源自 中古法语 sympathie (16 世纪) and 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 sympathia "community of feeling, sympathy," 源自 希腊语 sympatheia "fellow-feeling, community of feeling," 源自 sympathes "having a fellow feeling, affected by like feelings," 源自 为 … 的同化形式 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + pathos "feeling" （参见 pathos). In English, almost a magical notion at first; used in reference to medicines that heal wounds when applied to a cloth stained with blood 源自 wound. 义为 "conformity of feelings" 始于 1590 年代; 语义 "fellow feeling, compassion" is 最早见于 约 1600 年. An 古英语 loan-translation of sympathy was efensargung.

example.en: She expressed deep sympathy for the victims of the disaster.
example.zh: 她对灾难受害者表达了深切的同情。

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, a name given to various types of musical instruments, from Old French simphonie, sifonie, simfone "musical harmony; stringed instrument" (12c., Modern French symphonie) and directly from Latin symphonia "a unison of sounds, harmony," from Greek symphonia "harmony, concord of sounds," from symphonos "harmonious, agreeing in sound," from assimilated form of syn- "together" (see syn-) + phone "voice, sound," from PIE root *bha- (2) "to speak, tell, say" (see fame (n.)).

Meaning "harmony of sounds" in English is attested from late 14c.; sense of "music in parts" is from 1590s. "It was only after the advent of Haydn that this word began to mean a sonata for full orchestra. Before that time it meant a prelude, postlude, or interlude, or any short instrumental work." ["Elson's Music Dictionary"] Meaning "elaborate orchestral composition" first attested 1789. Elliptical for "symphony orchestra" from 1926. Diminutive symphonette is recorded from 1947.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, a name given to various types of musical instruments, 源自 古法语 simphonie, sifonie, simfone "musical harmony; stringed instrument" (12 世纪, 现代法语 symphonie) and 直接源自 拉丁语 symphonia "a unison of sounds, harmony," 源自 希腊语 symphonia "harmony, concord of sounds," 源自 symphonos "harmonious, agreeing in sound," 源自 为 … 的同化形式 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + phone "voice, sound," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *bha- (2) "to speak, tell, say" （参见 fame （名）). 义为 "harmony of sounds" in English 见于 14 世纪晚期; 语义 "music in parts" 始于 1590 年代. "It was only after the advent of Haydn that this word began to mean a sonata for full orchestra. Before that time it meant a prelude, postlude, or interlude, or any short instrumental work." ["Elson's Music Dictionary"] 义为 "elaborate orchestral composition" 最早见于 1789 年. Elliptical for "symphony orchestra" 自 1926 年起. Diminutive symphonette 见于 1947 年.

entries.etymology:
1580s, "account of a gathering or party," from Latin symposium "drinking party, symposium," from Greek symposion "drinking party, convivial gathering of the educated" (related to sympotes "drinking companion"), from assimilated form of syn- "together" (see syn-) + posis "a drinking," from a stem of Aeolic ponen "to drink," cognate with Latin potare "to drink" (see potion).
The sense of "a meeting on some subject" is from 1784. Reflecting the Greek fondness for mixing wine and intellectual discussion, the modern sense is especially from the word being used as a title for one of Plato's dialogues. Greek plural is symposia, and the leader of one is a symposiarch (c. 1600 in English). Related: Symposiac (adj.); symposial.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, "account of a gathering or party," 源自 拉丁语 symposium "drinking party, symposium," 源自 希腊语 symposion "drinking party, convivial gathering of the educated" (related to sympotes "drinking companion"), 源自 为 … 的同化形式 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + posis "a drinking," 源自 a stem of Aeolic ponen "to drink," 与 … 同源 拉丁语 potare "to drink" （参见 potion). The 语义 "a meeting on some subject" 始于 1784 年. Reflecting the 希腊语 fondness for mixing wine and intellectual discussion, the modern sense is 尤指 源自 word being used 作为 title for one of Plato's dialogues. 希腊语 plural is symposia, and the leader of one is a symposiarch (约 1600 年 in English). 同源词：Symposiac （形）; symposial.

entries.etymology:
1540s, re-Latinized from sinthoma (late 14c.), from Medieval Latin sinthoma "symptom of a disease," altered from Late Latin symptoma, from Greek symptoma "a happening, accident, disease," from stem of sympiptein "to befall, happen; coincide, fall together," from assimilated form of syn- "together" (see syn-) + piptein "to fall," from PIE *pi-pt-, reduplicated form of root *pet- "to rush; to fly" (see petition (n.)).

Spelling restored in early Modern English in part by influence of Middle French symptome (16c.). General (non-medical) use is from 1610s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, re-Latinized 源自 sinthoma (14 世纪晚期), 源自 中古拉丁语 sinthoma "symptom of a disease," altered 源自 晚期拉丁语 symptoma, 源自 希腊语 symptoma "a happening, accident, disease," 源自 stem of sympiptein "to befall, happen; coincide, fall together," 源自 为 … 的同化形式 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + piptein "to fall," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *pi-pt-, reduplicated form of root *pet- "to rush; to fly" （参见 petition （名）). Spelling restored in early 现代英语 in part by influence of 中古法语 symptome (16 世纪). General (non-medical) use 始于 1610 年代.

example.en: Fever and fatigue are common symptom of the flu.
example.zh: 发烧和疲劳是流感的常见症状。

entries.etymology: "a number of symptoms occurring together," 1540s, from medical Latin, from Greek syndrome "concurrence of symptoms, concourse of people," from syndromos "place where several roads meet," literally "a running together," from syn- "with" (see syn-) + dromos "a running, course" (see dromedary). Psychological sense is from 1955.
entries.etymologyZh: "a number of symptoms occurring together," 1540 年代, 源自 medical 拉丁语, 源自 希腊语 syndrome "concurrence of symptoms, concourse of people," 源自 syndromos "place where several roads meet," 字面义为 "a running together," 源自 syn- "with" （参见 syn-) + dromos "a running, course" （参见 dromedary). Psychological sense 始于 1955 年.

example.en: Burnout syndrome affects many workers who face constant pressure at their jobs.
example.zh: 倦怠综合征影响着许多在工作中持续面临压力的员工。

entries.etymology: 1610s, "deductive reasoning," from Latin synthesis "collection, set, suit of clothes, composition (of a medication)," from Greek synthesis "composition, a putting together," from syntithenai "put together, combine," from syn- "together" (see syn-) + tithenai "put, place" (see theme). From 1733 as "a combination of parts into a whole." Earlier borrowed in Middle English as sintecis (mid-15c.). Plural syntheses.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "deductive reasoning," 源自 拉丁语 synthesis "collection, set, suit of clothes, composition (of a medication)," 源自 希腊语 synthesis "composition, a putting together," 源自 syntithenai "put together, combine," 源自 syn- "together" （参见 syn-) + tithenai "put, place" （参见 theme). From 1733 年 as "a combination of parts into a whole." Earlier borrowed in 中古英语 as sintecis (15 世纪中期). Plural syntheses.

entries.etymology: 1690s, as a term in logic, "deductive," from French synthétique (17c.) and directly from Modern Latin syntheticus, from Greek synthetikos "skilled in putting together, constructive," from synthetos "put together, constructed, compounded," past participle of syntithenai "to put together" (see synthesis). From 1874 in reference to products or materials made artificially by chemical synthesis; hence "artificial" (1930). As a noun, "synthetic material," from 1934. Related: Synthetical (1620s in logic).
entries.etymologyZh: 1690 年代, 作为 term in logic, "deductive," 源自 法语 synthétique (17 世纪) and 直接源自 现代 拉丁语 syntheticus, 源自 希腊语 synthetikos "skilled in putting together, constructive," 源自 synthetos "put together, constructed, compounded," 为 … 的过去分词 syntithenai "to put together" （参见 synthesis). From 1874 年 in reference to products or materials made artificially by chemical synthesis; hence "artificial" (1930 年). 作名词时, "synthetic material," 自 1934 年起. 同源词：Synthetical (1620 年代 in logic).

definitionLines: n. 系统，体系；制度，体制
a. 系统的；有计划的，有步骤 的；有秩序的，有规则的
entries.definition: n. 系统，体系；制度，体制 systematic（al） a. 系统的；有计划的，有步骤 的；有秩序的，有规则的
entries.etymology:
1610s, "the whole creation, the universe," from Late Latin systema "an arrangement, system," from Greek systema "organized whole, a whole compounded of parts," from stem of synistanai "to place together, organize, form in order," from syn- "together" (see syn-) + root of histanai "cause to stand" from PIE root *stā- "to stand" (see stet).

Meaning "set of correlated principles, facts, ideas, etc." first recorded 1630s. Meaning "animal body as an organized whole, sum of the vital processes in an organism" is recorded from 1680s; hence figurative phrase to get (something) out of one's system (1900). Computer sense of "group of related programs" is recorded from 1963. All systems go (1962) is from U.S. space program. The system "prevailing social order" is from 1806.

entries.etymology:
late 12c., "board, slab, plate," from Old French table "board, square panel, plank; writing table; picture; food, fare" (11c.), and late Old English tabele "writing tablet, gaming table," from Germanic *tabal (source also of Dutch tafel, Danish tavle, Old High German zabel "board, plank," German Tafel). Both the French and Germanic words are from Latin tabula "a board, plank; writing table; list, schedule; picture, painted panel," originally "small flat slab or piece" usually for inscriptions or for games (source also of Spanish tabla, Italian tavola), of uncertain origin, related to Umbrian tafle "on the board."

The sense of "piece of furniture with the flat top and legs" first recorded c. 1300 (the usual Latin word for this was mensa (see mensa); Old English writers used bord (see board (n.1)). Especially the table at which people eat, hence "food placed upon a table" (c. 1400 in English). The meaning "arrangement of numbers or other figures on a tabular surface for convenience" is recorded from late 14c. (as in table of contents, mid-15c.).

Figurative phrase turn the tables (1630s) is from backgammon (in Old and Middle English the game was called tables). Table talk "familiar conversation around a table" is attested from 1560s, translating Latin colloquia mensalis. Table-manners is from 1824. Table-hopping is first recorded 1943. The adjectival phrase under-the-table "hidden from view" is recorded from 1949; to be under the table "passed out from excess drinking" is recorded from 1913. Table tennis "ping-pong" is recorded from 1887. Table-rapping in spiritualism, supposedly an effect of supernatural powers, is from 1853.

entries.etymology: also tabu, 1777 (in Cook's "A Voyage to the Pacific Ocean"), "consecrated, inviolable, forbidden, unclean or cursed," explained in some English sources as being from Tongan (Polynesian language of the island of Tonga) ta-bu "sacred," from ta "mark" + bu "especially." But this may be folk etymology, as linguists in the Pacific have reconstructed an irreducable Proto-Polynesian *tapu, from Proto-Oceanic *tabu "sacred, forbidden" (compare Hawaiian kapu "taboo, prohibition, sacred, holy, consecrated;" Tahitian tapu "restriction, sacred;" Maori tapu "be under ritual restriction, prohibited"). The noun and verb are English innovations first recorded in Cook's book.

entries.etymology: mid-13c., "apparatus, gear," especially the rigging of a ship, from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German takel "the rigging of a ship," perhaps related to Middle Dutch taken "grasp, seize" (see take (v.)), or perhaps from root of tack (n.1), which, if not the origin, has influenced the sense. Meaning "apparatus for fishing" is recorded from late 14c. Meaning "device for grasping and shifting or moving" is from 1530s. Meaning "act of tackling" in the sporting sense is recorded from 1876 (see tackle (v.)); as the name of a position in North American football, it is recorded from 1884. Welsh tacl is fro English.

entries.definition: vt. 缝制，剪裁 n. 裁缝
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, from Anglo-French tailour, Old French tailleor "tailor," also "stone-mason" (13c., Modern French tailleur), literally "a cutter," from tailler "to cut," from Late Latin or old Medieval Latin taliare "to split" (compare Medieval Latin taliator vestium "a cutter of clothes"), from Latin talea "a slender stick, rod, staff; a cutting, twig."

The post-Latin sense development would be "piece of a plant cut for grafting," hence a verb, "cut a shoot," then, generally, "to cut." Possible cognates include Sanskrit talah "wine palm," Old Lithuanian talokas "a young girl," Greek talis "a marriageable girl" (for sense, compare slip of a girl, twiggy), Etruscan Tholna, name of the goddess of youth.

One who makes outer garments to order, as opposed to a clothier, who makes them for sale ready-made. Tailor-made first recorded 1832 (in a figurative sense); literal sense was "heavy and plain, with attention to exact fit and with little ornamentation," as of women's garments made by a tailor rather than a dress-maker.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, talken, probably a diminutive or frequentative form related to Middle English tale "story," and ultimately from the same source as tale, with rare English formative -k (compare hark from hear, stalk from steal, smirk from smile) and replacing that word as a verb. East Frisian has talken "to talk, chatter, whisper." Related: Talked; talking.

To talk (something) up "discuss in order to promote" is from 1722. To talk shop is from 1854. To talk turkey is from 1824, supposedly from an elaborate joke about a swindled Indian. To talk back "answer impudently or rudely" is from 1869. Phrase talking head is by 1966 in the jargon of television production, "an in-tight closeup of a human head talking on television." In reference to a person who habitually appears on television in talking-head shots (usually a news anchor), by 1970. The phrase is used earlier, in reference to the well-known magic trick (such as Señor Wences's talking head-in-the-box "Pedro" on the "Ed Sullivan Show"), and to actual talking heads in mythology around the world (Orpheus, Bran).

entries.etymology:
Old English talu "series, calculation," also "story, tale, statement, deposition, narrative, fable, accusation, action of telling," from Proto-Germanic *talo (source also of Dutch taal "speech, language," Danish tale "speech, talk, discourse," German Erzählung "story," Gothic talzjan "to teach"), from PIE root *del- (2) "to recount, count." The secondary Modern English sense of "number, numerical reckoning" (c. 1200) probably was the primary one in Germanic; see tell (v.), teller and Old Frisian tale, Middle Dutch tal, Old Saxon tala, Danish tal, Old High German zala, German Zahl "number."

The ground sense of the Modern English word in its main meaning, then, might have been "an account of things in their due order." Related to talk (v.) and tell (v.). Meaning "things divulged that were given secretly, gossip" is from mid-14c.; first record of talebearer "tattletale" is late 15c.

entries.etymology:
late 13c., "inclination, disposition, will, desire," from Old French talent (12c.), from Medieval Latin talenta, plural of talentum "inclination, leaning, will, desire" (11c.), in classical Latin "balance, weight; sum of money," from Greek talanton "a balance, pair of scales," hence "weight, definite weight, anything weighed," and in later times sum of money," from PIE *tele- "to lift, support, weigh," "with derivatives referring to measured weights and thence money and payment" [Watkins]; see extol.

According to Liddell & Scott, as a monetary sum, considered to consist of 6,000 drachmae, or, in Attica, 57.75 lbs. of silver. Also borrowed in other Germanic languages and Celtic. Attested in Old English as talente). The Medieval Latin and common Romanic sense developed from figurative use of the word in the sense of "money." Meaning "special natural ability, aptitude, gift committed to one for use and improvement" developed by mid-15c., in part perhaps from figurative sense "wealth," but mostly from the parable of the talents in Matt. xxv:14-30. Meaning "persons of ability collectively" is from 1856.

entries.etymology:
early Middle English tame "in a state of subjection, physically subdued, restrained in behavior" (c. 1200); of animals "domesticated, reclaimed from wildness," also, of persons, "meek, gentle-natured, compliant, intent on homely or domestic activities" (mid-13c.), from oblique forms of Old English tom, tam "domesticated, docile," from Proto-Germanic *tamaz (source also of Old Norse tamr, Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Middle Low German, Middle Dutch tam, Old High German zam, German zahm "tame," Gothic tamjan "to tame"), from PIE *deme- "to constrain, to force, to break (horses)" (source also of Sanskrit damayati "tames;" Persian dam "a tame animal;" Greek daman "to tame, subdue," dmetos "tame;" Latin domare "to tame, subdue;" Old Irish damnaim "I tie up, fasten, I tame, subdue").

A possible ulterior connection is with PIE *dem- "house, household" (see domestic (adj.)). Meaning "spiritless, weak, dull, uninspiring, insipid" is recorded from c. 1600. Related: Tamely; tameness.

entries.etymology:
1610s, "pool or lake for irrigation or drinking water," a word originally brought by the Portuguese from India, from a Hindi source, such as Gujarati tankh "cistern, underground reservoir for water," Marathi tanken, or tanka "reservoir of water, tank." Perhaps ultimately from Sanskrit tadaga-m "pond, lake pool," and reinforced in later sense of "large artificial container for liquid" (1680s) by Portuguese tanque "reservoir," from estancar "hold back a current of water," from Vulgar Latin *stanticare (see stanch). But other sources say the Portuguese word is the source of the Indian ones. Meaning "fuel container" is recorded from 1902. Slang meaning "detention cell" is from 1912. Railroad tank-car is from 1874.

In military use, "armored, gun-mounted vehicle moving on continuous articulated tracks," the word originated late 1915. In "Tanks in the Great War" [1920], Brevet Col. J.F.C. Fuller quotes a memorandum of the Committee of Imperial Defence dated Dec. 24, 1915, recommending the proposed "caterpillar machine-gun destroyer" machines be entrusted to an organization "which, for secrecy, shall be called the 'Tank Supply Committee,' ..." In a footnote, Fuller writes, "This is the first appearance of the word 'tank' in the history of the machine." He writes that "cistern" and "reservoir" also were put forth as possible cover names, "all of which were applicable to the steel-like structure of the machines in the early stages of manufacture. Because it was less clumsy and monosyllabic, the name 'tank' was decided on." They were first used in action at Pozieres ridge, on the Western Front, Sept. 15, 1916, and the name was quickly picked up by the soldiers. Tank-trap attested from 1920.

entries.etymology: 1590s, with -ize + Latin Tantalus, from Greek Tantalos, king of Phrygia, son of Zeus, father of Pelops and Niobe, punished in the afterlife (for an offense variously given) by being made to stand in a river up to his chin, under branches laden with fruit, all of which withdrew from his reach whenever he tried to eat or drink. His story was known to Chaucer (c. 1369). Related: Tantalized; tantalizing; tantalizingly; tantalization.

entries.etymology:
Old English tæppe "narrow strip of cloth used for tying, measuring, etc.," of uncertain origin; perhaps [Klein] a back-formation from Latin tapete "cloth, carpet," compare also Old Frisian tapia, Middle Low German tapen "to pull, pluck, tear." The original short vowel became long in Middle English.

Adhesive tape is from 1885; also in early use sometimes friction tape. Tape recorder "device for recording sound on magnetic tape" first attested 1932; from earlier meaning "device for recording data on ticker tape" (1892), from tape in the sense of "paper strip of a printer" (1884). Tape-record (v.) is from 1950. Tape-measure is attested from 1873; tape-delay is from 1968.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 tæppe "narrow strip of cloth used for tying, measuring, etc.," 来源存疑; 或许 [Klein] a back-formation 源自 拉丁语 tapete "cloth, carpet," 对比 also 古弗里西语 tapia, Middle Low 德语 tapen "to pull, pluck, tear." The original short vowel became long in 中古英语. Adhesive tape 始于 1885 年; also in early use 有时 friction tape. Tape recorder "device for recording sound on magnetic tape" 最早见于 1932 年; 源自 earlier 意为 "device for recording data on ticker tape" (1892 年), 源自 tape in the 语义 "paper strip of a printer" (1884 年). Tape-record （动） 始于 1950 年. Tape-measure 见于 1873 年; tape-delay 始于 1968 年.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "shield," diminutive of late Old English targe, from Old French targe "light shield" (12c.), from Frankish *targa "shield," from Proto-Germanic *targ- (source also of Old High German zarga "edging, border," German zarge "border, edge, frame," Old English targe, Old Norse targa "shield, buckler"), perhaps originally "edge of a shield." Meaning "round object to be aimed at in shooting" first recorded 1757, originally in archery, perhaps suggested by the concentric circles in both. Target-practice is from 1801. Target audience is by 1951; early reference is to Cold War psychological warfare.

entries.etymology: 1590s, "arithmetical table," also "official list of customs duties on imports or exports; law regulating import duties," from Italian tariffa "tariff, price, assessment," Medieval Latin tarifa "list of prices, book of rates," from Arabic ta'rif "information, notification, a making known; inventory of fees to be paid," verbal noun from arafa "he made known, he taught." Sense of "classified list of charges made in a business" is recorded from 1757. The U.S. Tariff of Abominations was passed in 1828.

entries.etymology:
early 14c., "a quantity of labor imposed as a duty," from Old North French tasque (12c., Old French tasche, Modern French tâche) "duty, tax," from Vulgar Latin *tasca "a duty, assessment," metathesis of Medieval Latin taxa, a back-formation of Latin taxare "to evaluate, estimate, assess" (see tax (v.)). General sense of "any piece of work that has to be done" is first recorded 1590s. Phrase take one to task (1680s) preserves the sense that is closer to tax.

German tasche "pocket" is from the same Vulgar Latin source (via Old High German tasca), with presumable sense evolution from "amount of work imposed by some authority," to "payment for that work," to "wages," to "pocket into which money is put," to "any pocket."
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "a quantity of labor imposed as a duty," 源自 Old North 法语 tasque (12 世纪, 古法语 tasche, 现代法语 tâche) "duty, tax," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *tasca "a duty, assessment," metathesis of 中古拉丁语 taxa, a back-formation of 拉丁语 taxare "to evaluate, estimate, assess" （参见 tax （动）). General 语义 "any piece of work that has to be done" is 首见于 1590 年代. Phrase take one to task (1680 年代) preserves the sense that is closer to tax. 德语 tasche "pocket" 始于 the same 通俗拉丁语 source (经由 古高地德语 tasca), with presumable sense evolution 源自 "amount of work imposed by some authority," to "payment for that work," to "wages," to "pocket into which money is put," to "any pocket."

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "to touch, to handle," from Old French taster "to taste, sample by mouth; enjoy" (13c.), earlier "to feel, touch, pat, stroke" (12c., Modern French tâter), from Vulgar Latin *tastare, apparently an alteration (perhaps by influence of gustare) of taxtare, a frequentative form of Latin taxare "evaluate, handle" (see tax (v.)). Meaning "to take a little food or drink" is from c. 1300; that of "to perceive by sense of taste" is recorded from mid-14c. Of substances, "to have a certain taste or flavor," it is attested from 1550s (replaced native smack (v.3) in this sense). For another PIE root in this sense, see gusto.

Sense of "to know by experience" is from 1520s. Related: Tasted; tasting. Taste buds is from 1879; also taste goblets.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "to touch, to handle," 源自 古法语 taster "to taste, sample by mouth; enjoy" (13 世纪), earlier "to feel, touch, pat, stroke" (12 世纪, 现代法语 tâter), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *tastare, 似乎 an alteration (或许 by influence of gustare) of taxtare, a 为 … 的反复体 拉丁语 taxare "evaluate, handle" （参见 tax （动）). 义为 "to take a little food or drink" 始于 约 1300 年; that of "to perceive by sense of taste" 见于 14 世纪中期 Of substances, "to have a certain taste or flavor," it 见于 1550 年代 (replaced 本族 smack (v.3) in this sense). For another 原始印欧语 (PIE) root in this sense, 参见 gusto. 义为 "to know by experience" 始于 1520 年代. 同源词：Tasted; tasting. Taste buds 始于 1879 年; also taste goblets.

example.en: He loves to taste different foods when he travels abroad.
example.zh: 他喜欢在出国旅行时品尝不同的食物。

entries.etymology: 1610s, "having agreeable flavor, palatable," from taste (n.) + -y (2); in late 18c. it also could mean "tasteful, elegant" (from the secondary sense of taste (n.)). Related: Tastiness.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "having agreeable flavor, palatable," 源自 taste （名） + -y (2); in 18 世纪晚期 it also could mean "tasteful, elegant" (源自 secondary 语义 taste （名）). 同源词：Tastiness.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "impose a tax on," from Old French taxer "impose a tax" (13c.) and directly from Latin taxare "evaluate, estimate, assess, handle," also "censure, charge," probably a frequentative form of tangere "to touch" (see tangent (adj.)). Sense of "to burden, put a strain on" first recorded early 14c.; that of "censure, reprove" is from 1560s. Its use in Luke ii for Greek apographein "to enter on a list, enroll" is due to Tyndale. Related: Taxed; taxing.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "impose a tax on," 源自 古法语 taxer "impose a tax" (13 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 taxare "evaluate, estimate, assess, handle," also "censure, charge," 可能 a 为 … 的反复体 tangere "to touch" （参见 tangent （形）). 义为 "to burden, put a strain on" 首见于 14 世纪初; that of "censure, reprove" 始于 1560 年代. Its use in Luke ii for 希腊语 apographein "to enter on a list, enroll" is due to Tyndale. 同源词：Taxed; taxing.

example.en: The government plans to raise tax on luxury goods next year.
example.zh: 政府计划明年对奢侈品提高税率。

entries.etymology:
1907, shortening of taximeter cab (introduced in London in March 1907), from taximeter "automatic meter to record the distance and fare" (1898), from French taximètre, from German Taxameter (1890), coined from Medieval Latin taxa "tax, charge."

An earlier English form was taxameter (1894), used in horse-drawn cabs. Taxi dancer "woman whose services may be hired at a dance hall" is recorded from 1930. Taxi squad in U.S. football is 1966, said to be from a former Cleveland Browns owner who gave his reserves jobs with his taxicab company to keep them paid and available ["Dictionary of American Slang"], but other explanations ("short-term hire" or "shuttling back and forth" from the main team) seem possible.
entries.etymologyZh: 1907 年, shortening of taximeter cab (introduced in London in March 1907 年), 源自 taximeter "automatic meter to record the distance and fare" (1898 年), 源自 法语 taximètre, 源自 德语 Taxameter (1890 年), coined 源自 中古拉丁语 taxa "tax, charge." An earlier English form was taxameter (1894 年), used in horse-drawn cabs. Taxi dancer "woman whose services may be hired at a dance hall" 见于 1930 年. Taxi squad in U.S. football is 1966 年, said to be 源自 a former Cleveland Browns owner who gave his reserves jobs with his taxicab company to keep them paid and available ["Dictionary of American Slang"], but other explanations ("short-term hire" or "shuttling back and forth" 源自 main team) seem possible.

entries.etymology:
Old English tæcan (past tense tæhte, past participle tæht) "to show, point out, declare, demonstrate," also "to give instruction, train, assign, direct; warn; persuade," from Proto-Germanic *taikijan "to show" (source also of Old High German zihan, German zeihen "to accuse," Gothic ga-teihan "to announce"), from PIE *deik- "to show, point out" (see diction). Related to Old English tacen, tacn "sign, mark" (see token). Related: Taught; teaching.

The usual sense of Old English tæcan was "show, declare, warn, persuade" (compare German zeigen "to show," from the same root); while the Old English word for "to teach, instruct, guide" was more commonly læran, source of modern learn and lore.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 tæcan (past tense tæhte, past participle tæht) "to show, point out, declare, demonstrate," also "to give instruction, train, assign, direct; warn; persuade," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *taikijan "to show" (source also of 古高地德语 zihan, 德语 zeihen "to accuse," Gothic ga-teihan "to announce"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *deik- "to show, point out" （参见 diction). Related to 古英语 tacen, tacn "sign, mark" （参见 token). 同源词：Taught; teaching. The usual 语义 古英语 tæcan was "show, declare, warn, persuade" (对比 德语 zeigen "to show," 源自 same root); while the 古英语 word for "to teach, instruct, guide" was more commonly læran, source of modern learn and lore.

entries.etymologyZh: "one who teaches," 约 1300 年; agent 名词 源自 teach （动）. It was used earlier in a 语义 "index finger" (13 世纪晚期). Teacher's pet attested 自 1856 年起.

entries.etymology:
Old English team "descendant, family, race, line; child-bearing, brood; company, band; set of draft animals yoked together," from Proto-Germanic *tau(h)maz (source also of Old Norse taumr, Old Frisian tam "bridle; progeny, line of descent," Dutch toom, Old High German zoum, German Zaum "bridle"), probably literally "that which draws," from PIE *douk-mo-, from root *deuk- "to pull" (see duke (n.)).

Applied in Old English to groups of persons working together for some purpose, especially "group of people acting together to bring suit;" modern sense of "persons associated in some joint action" is from 1520s. Team spirit is recorded from 1928. Team player attested from 1886, originally in baseball.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 team "descendant, family, race, line; child-bearing, brood; company, band; set of draft animals yoked together," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *tau(h)maz (source also of 古北欧语 taumr, 古弗里西语 tam "bridle; progeny, line of descent," 荷兰语 toom, 古高地德语 zoum, 德语 Zaum "bridle"), 可能 字面义为 "that which draws," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *douk-mo-, 源自 root *deuk- "to pull" （参见 duke （名）). Applied in 古英语 to groups of persons working together for some purpose, 尤指 "group of people acting together to bring suit;" modern 语义 "persons associated in some joint action" 始于 1520 年代. Team spirit 见于 1928 年. Team player attested 自 1886 年起, 原义为 in baseball.

example.en: A tear rolled down her cheek as she read the letter.

entries.etymology:
formerly also teaze, Old English tæsan "pluck, pull, tear; pull apart, comb" (fibers of wool, flax, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *taisijan (source also of Danish tæse, Middle Dutch tesen, Dutch tezen "to draw, pull, scratch," Old High German zeisan "to tease, pick wool").

The original sense is of running thorns through wool or flax to separate, shred, or card the fibers. The figurative sense of "vex, worry, annoy" (sometimes done in good humor) emerged 1610s. For similar sense development, compare heckle. Hairdressing sense is recorded from 1957. Related: Teased; teasing; teasingly.
entries.etymologyZh: formerly also teaze, 古英语 tæsan "pluck, pull, tear; pull apart, comb" (fibers of wool, flax, etc.), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *taisijan (source also of Danish tæse, Middle 荷兰语 tesen, 荷兰语 tezen "to draw, pull, scratch," 古高地德语 zeisan "to tease, pick wool"). entries.etymology:
1610s, "skilled in a particular art or subject," formed in English from technic + -al (1), or in part from Greek tekhnikos "of art; systematic," in reference to persons "skillful, artistic," from tekhne "art, skill, craft" (see techno-).

The sense narrowed to "having to do with the mechanical arts" (1727). Basketball technical foul (one which does not involve contact between opponents) is recorded from 1934. Boxing technical knock-out (one in which the loser is not knocked out) is recorded from 1921; abbreviation TKO is from 1940s. Technical difficulty is from 1805.
entries.etymologyZh: 1610 年代, "skilled in a particular art or subject," formed in English 源自 technic + -al (1)，或in part 源自 希腊语 tekhnikos "of art; systematic," in reference to persons "skillful, artistic," 源自 tekhne "art, skill, craft" （参见 techno-). The sense narrowed to "having to do with the mechanical arts" (1727 年). Basketball technical foul (one which does not involve contact between opponents) 见于 1934 年. Boxing technical knock-out (one in which the loser is not knocked out) 见于 1921 年; abbreviation TKO 始于 1940 年代. Technical difficulty 始于 1805 年.

"of art, technical," from Greek tekhnikos "pertaining to art," from tekhne "art, skill, craft in work" (see techno-).

entries.etymology: 1610s, "a discourse or treatise on an art or the arts," from Greek tekhnologia "systematic treatment of an art, craft, or technique," originally referring to grammar, from tekhno- (see techno-) + -logy. High technology attested from 1964; short form high-tech is from 1972.

entries.etymology:
"telegraphic dispatch," according to Bartlett's 1859 edition a coinage of E. Peshine Smith of Rochester, N.Y., from tele-, as in telegraph + -gram, and introduced in the Albany "Evening Journal" of April 6, 1852. Damned in the cradle by purists who pointed out that the correct formation would be telegrapheme (which is close to the Modern Greek word).

Related: Telegrammic.

entries.etymology: 1794, "semaphor apparatus" (hence the Telegraph Hill in many cities), literally "that which writes at a distance," from French télégraphe, from télé- "far" (from Greek tele-; see tele-) + -graphe (see -graphy). The signaling device had been invented in France in 1791 by the brothers Chappe, who had called it tachygraphe, literally "that which writes fast," but the better name was suggested to them by French diplomat Comte André-François Miot de Mélito (1762-1841). First applied 1797 to an experimental electric telegraph (designed by Dr. Don Francisco Salva at Barcelona); the practical version was developed 1830s by U.S. inventor Samuel F.B. Morse (1791-1872). Meaning "telegraphic message" is from 1821. Related: Telegraphy.
entries.etymologyZh: 1794 年, "semaphor apparatus" (hence the Telegraph Hill in many cities), 字面义为 "that which writes at a distance," 源自 法语 télégraphe, 源自 télé- "far" (源自 希腊语 tele-; 参见 tele-) + -graphe （参见 -graphy). The signaling device had been invented in France 于 1791 年 by the brothers Chappe, who had called it tachygraphe, 字面义为 "that which writes fast," but the better name was suggested to them by 法语 diplomat Comte André-François Miot de Mélito (1762 年-1841 年). First applied 1797 年 to an experimental electric telegraph (designed by Dr. Don Francisco Salva at Barcelona); the practical version was developed 1830 年代 by U.S. inventor Samuel F.B. Morse (1791 年-1872 年). 义为 "telegraphic message" 始于 1821 年. 同源词：Telegraphy.

entries.etymology: 1640s, from Italian telescopio (Galileo, 1611), and Modern Latin telescopium (Kepler, 1613), both from Greek teleskopos "far-seeing," from tele- "far" (see tele-) + -skopos "watcher" (see scope (n.1)). Said to have been coined by Prince Cesi, founder and head of the Roman Academy of the Lincei (Galileo was a member). Used in English in Latin form from 1619.
entries.etymologyZh: 1640 年代, 源自 意大利语 telescopio (Galileo, 1611 年), and 现代 拉丁语 telescopium (Kepler, 1613 年), both 源自 希腊语 teleskopos "far-seeing," 源自 tele- "far" （参见 tele-) + -skopos "watcher" （参见 scope (n.1)). Said to have been coined by Prince Cesi, founder and head of the Roman Academy of the Lincei (Galileo was a member). Used in English in 拉丁语 form 自 1619 年起.

example.en: Astronomers used a powerful telescope to observe distant galaxies.
example.zh: 天文学家用一架强大的望远镜观测遥远的星系。

entries.etymology:
1907, as a theoretical system to transmit moving images over telegraph or telephone wires; formed in English or borrowed from French télévision, from tele- + vision.

Other proposals for the name of a then-hypothetical technology for sending pictures over distance were telephote (1880) and televista (1904). The technology was developed in the 1920s and '30s. Nativized in German as Fernsehen. Shortened form TV is from 1948. Meaning "a television set" is from 1941. Meaning "television as a medium" is from 1927.
entries.etymologyZh: 1907 年, 作为 theoretical system to transmit moving images over telegraph or telephone wires; formed in English or 借自 法语 télévision, 源自 tele- + vision. Other proposals for the name of a 之后-hypothetical technology for sending pictures over distance were telephote (1880 年) and televista (1904 年). The technology was developed in the 1920 年代 and '30s. Nativized in 德语 as Fernsehen. Shortened form TV 始于 1948 年. 义为 "a television set" 始于 1941 年. 义为 "television as a medium" 始于 1927 年.

definitionLines: vt.告诉，讲述；告诫，劝告；吩 咐，命令；辨别，区别
entries.definition: vt.告诉，讲述；告诫，劝告；吩 咐，命令；辨别，区别
entries.etymology:
Old English tellan "to reckon, calculate, number, compute; consider, think, esteem, account" (past tense tealde, past participle teald), from Proto-Germanic *taljan "to mention in order" (source also of Old Saxon tellian "tell," Old Norse telja "to count, number; to tell, say," Old Frisian tella "to count; to tell," Middle Dutch and Dutch tellen, Old Saxon talon "to count, reckon," Danish tale "to speak," Old High German zalon, German zählen "to count, reckon"), from PIE root *del- (2) "to count, reckon" (see tale).

Meaning "to narrate, announce, relate" in English is from c. 1000; that of "to make known by speech or writing, announce" is from early 12c. Sense of "to reveal or disclose" is from c. 1400; that of "to act as an informer, to 'peach' " is recorded from 1901. Meaning "to order (someone to do something)" is from 1590s. To tell (someone) off "reprimand" is from 1919.

Original sense in teller and phrase to tell time. For sense evolution, compare French conter "to count," raconter "to recount;" Italian contare, Spanish contar "to count, recount, narrate;" German zählen "to count," erzählen "to recount, narrate." Klein also compares Hebrew saphar "he counted," sipper "he told."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 tellan "to reckon, calculate, number, compute; consider, think, esteem, account" (past tense tealde, past participle teald), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *taljan "to mention in order" (source also of 古撒克逊语 tellian "tell," 古北欧语 telja "to count, number; to tell, say," 古弗里西语 tella "to count; to tell," Middle 荷兰语 and 荷兰语 tellen, 古撒克逊语 talon "to count, reckon," Danish tale "to speak," 古高地德语 zalon, 德语 zählen "to count, reckon"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *del- (2) "to count, reckon" （参见 tale). 义为 "to narrate, announce, relate" in English 始于 约 1000 年; that of "to make known by speech or writing, announce" 始于 12 世纪初 义为 "to reveal or disclose" 始于 约 1400 年; that of "to act as an informer, to 'peach' " 见于 1901 年. 义为 "to order (someone to do something)" 始于 1590 年代. To tell (someone) off "reprimand" 始于 1919 年. Original sense in teller and phrase to tell time. For sense evolution, 对比 法语 conter "to count," raconter "to recount;" 意大利语 contare, 西班牙语 contar "to count, recount, narrate;" 德语 zählen "to count," erzählen "to recount, narrate." Klein also compares 希伯来语 saphar "he counted," sipper "he told."

example.en: Could you tell me how to get to the nearest subway station from here?
example.zh: 你能告诉我从这里怎么去最近的地铁站吗？

entries.etymology: late Old English temprian "to moderate, bring to a proper or suitable state, to modify some excessive quality, to restrain within due limits," from Latin temperare "observe proper measure, be moderate, restrain oneself," also transitive, "mix correctly, mix in due proportion; regulate, rule, govern, manage." This is often described as from Latin tempus "time, season" (see temporal), with a sense of "proper time or season." But as the root sense of tempus seems to be "stretch," the words in the "restrain, modify" sense might be from a semantic shift from "stretching" to "measuring" (compare temple (n.1)). Meaning "to make (steel) hard and elastic" is from late 14c. Sense of "tune the pitch of a musical instrument" is recorded from c. 1300. Related: Tempered; tempering.
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 temprian "to moderate, bring to a proper or suitable state, to modify some excessive quality, to restrain within due limits," 源自 拉丁语 temperare "observe proper measure, be moderate, restrain oneself," also transitive, "mix correctly, mix in due proportion; regulate, rule, govern, manage." This is 常 described as 源自 拉丁语 tempus "time, season" （参见 temporal), with a 语义 "proper time or season." But as the root 语义 tempus seems to be "stretch," the words in the "restrain, modify" sense might be 源自 a semantic shift 源自 "stretching" to "measuring" (对比 temple (n.1)). 义为 "to make (steel) hard and elastic" 始于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "tune the pitch of a musical instrument" 见于 约 1300 年. 同源词：Tempered; tempering.

example.en: He has a short temper and often loses his patience in traffic.
example.zh: 他脾气急躁，在堵车时经常失去耐心。

definitionLines: n. 气质，性情，性格；急躁
entries.definition: n. 气质，性情，性格；急躁
entries.etymology: late 14c., "proportioned mixture of elements," from Latin temperamentum "proper mixture, a mixing in due proportion," from temperare "to mix in due proportion, modify, blend; restrain oneself" (see temper (v.)). In medieval theory, it meant a combination of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determined the nature of an organism; thus also "a combination of the four humors (sanguine, choleric, phlegmatic, and melancholic) that made up a person's characteristic disposition." General sense of "habit of mind, natural disposition" is from 1821.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "proportioned mixture of elements," 源自 拉丁语 temperamentum "proper mixture, a mixing in due proportion," 源自 temperare "to mix in due proportion, modify, blend; restrain oneself" （参见 temper （动）). In medieval theory, it meant a combination of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determined the nature of an organism; thus also "a combination of the four humors (sanguine, choleric, phlegmatic, and melancholic) that made up a person's characteristic disposition." General 语义 "habit of mind, natural disposition" 始于 1821 年.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "fact of being tempered, proper proportion;" 1530s, "character or nature of a substance," from Latin temperatura "a tempering, moderation," from temperatus, past participle of temperare "to mix in due proportion, modify, blend; restrain oneself" (see temper (v.)). Sense of "degree of heat or cold" first recorded 1670 (Boyle), from Latin temperatura, used in this sense by Galileo. Meaning "fever, high temperature" is attested from 1898.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "fact of being tempered, proper proportion;" 1530 年代, "character or nature of a substance," 源自 拉丁语 temperatura "a tempering, moderation," 源自 temperatus, 为 … 的过去分词 temperare "to mix in due proportion, modify, blend; restrain oneself" （参见 temper （动）). 义为 "degree of heat or cold" 首见于 1670 年 (Boyle), 源自 拉丁语 temperatura, used in this sense by Galileo. 义为 "fever, high temperature" 见于 1898 年.

example.en: The temperature in the room dropped sharply after the window was left open overnight.
example.zh: 窗户开了一夜之后，房间里的温度急剧下降。

example.en: Visitors removed their shoes before entering the ancient temple.
example.zh: 参观者在进入古老的寺庙前脱掉了鞋子。

entries.etymology: "lasting only for a time," 1540s, from Latin temporarius "of seasonal character, lasting a short time," from tempus (genitive temporis) "time, season" (see temporal, late 14c., which was the earlier word for "lasting but for a time"). The noun meaning "person employed only for a time" is recorded from 1848. Related: Temporarily; temporariness.
entries.etymologyZh: "lasting only for a time," 1540 年代, 源自 拉丁语 temporarius "of seasonal character, lasting a short time," 源自 tempus (属格 temporis) "time, season" （参见 temporal, 14 世纪晚期, which was the earlier word for "lasting but for a time"). The 名词 意为 "person employed only for a time" 见于 1848 年. 同源词：Temporarily; temporariness.

example.en: The repair is only temporary and will need to be replaced soon.
example.zh: 这次修缮只是临时性的，很快就需要更换。

definitionLines: vt. 诱惑；吸引，使感兴趣
entries.definition: vt. 诱惑；吸引，使感兴趣
entries.etymology: c. 1200, of the devil, flesh, etc., "draw or entice to evil or sin, lure (someone) from God's law; be alluring or seductive," from Old French tempter (12c.), from Latin temptare "to feel, try out, attempt to influence, test," a variant of tentare "handle, touch, try, test." The Latin alteration is "explainable only as an ancient error due to some confusion" [Century Dictionary]. From late 14c. as "to provoke, defy" (God, fate, etc.). Related: Tempted; tempting.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, of the devil, flesh, etc., "draw or entice to evil or sin, lure (someone) from God's law; be alluring or seductive," 源自 古法语 tempter (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 temptare "to feel, try out, attempt to influence, test," a 为 … 的变体 tentare "handle, touch, try, test." The 拉丁语 alteration is "explainable only as an ancient error due to some confusion" [Century Dictionary]. From 14 世纪晚期 as "to provoke, defy" (God, fate, etc.). 同源词：Tempted; tempting.

example.en: The smell of fresh bread from the bakery tempted her to go inside and buy a loaf.
example.zh: 面包店里新鲜面包的香味诱使她走进去买了一条面包。

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "act of enticing someone to sin," also "an experience or state of being tempted," from Old French temptacion (12c., Modern French tentation), from Latin temptationem (nominative temptatio), noun of action from past participle stem of temptare "to feel, try out" (see tempt). Meaning "that which tempts a person (to sin)" is from c. 1500.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "act of enticing someone to sin," also "an experience or state of being tempted," 源自 古法语 temptacion (12 世纪, 现代法语 tentation), 源自 拉丁语 temptationem (主格 temptatio), 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of temptare "to feel, try out" （参见 tempt). 义为 "that which tempts a person (to sin)" 始于 约 1500 年.

example.en: She resisted the temptation to check her phone during the lecture.
example.zh: 她在讲课期间抵制住了看手机的诱惑。

example.zh: 年龄较大的选民倾向于支持更保守的政策。

entries.etymology: 1620s, from Medieval Latin tendentia "inclination, leaning," from Latin tendens, present participle of tendere "to stretch, extend, aim" (see tenet). Earlier in same sense was tendaunce (mid-15c.), from Old French tendance.
entries.etymologyZh: 1620 年代, 源自 中古拉丁语 tendentia "inclination, leaning," 源自 拉丁语 tendens, 为 … 的现在分词 tendere "to stretch, extend, aim" （参见 tenet). Earlier in same sense was tendaunce (15 世纪中期), 源自 古法语 tendance.

example.en: There is a growing tendency among young people to avoid social media before bedtime.

entries.etymology:
"soft, easily injured," early 13c., from Old French tendre "soft, delicate; young" (11c.), from Latin tenerem (nominative tener) "soft, delicate; of tender age, youthful," from a derivative of PIE root *ten- "stretch" (see tenet), on the notion of "stretched," hence "thin," hence "weak" or "young." Compare Sanskrit tarunah "young, tender," Greek teren "tender, delicate," Armenian t'arm "young, fresh, green." 

Meaning "kind, affectionate, loving" first recorded early 14c. Meaning "having the delicacy of youth, immature" is attested in English from early 14c. Related: Tenderly; tenderness. Tender-hearted first recorded 1530s.
entries.etymologyZh: "soft, easily injured," 13 世纪初, 源自 古法语 tendre "soft, delicate; young" (11 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 tenerem (主格 tener) "soft, delicate; of tender age, youthful," 源自 a 为 … 的派生形式 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ten- "stretch" （参见 tenet), on the 概念 "stretched," hence "thin," hence "weak" or "young." 对比 梵语 tarunah "young, tender," 希腊语 teren "tender, delicate," Armenian t'arm "young, fresh, green." 义为 "kind, affectionate, loving" 首见于 14 世纪初 义为 "having the delicacy of youth, immature" is 见于 English 源自 14 世纪初 同源词：Tenderly; tenderness. Tender-hearted 首见于 1530 年代.

example.en: She spoke to the child in a tender and reassuring voice.
example.zh: 她用温柔而令人安心的声音跟孩子说话。

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., most likely from Anglo-French tenetz "hold! receive! take!," from Old French tenez, imperative of tenir "to hold, receive, take" (see tenet), which was used as a call from the server to his opponent. The original version of the game (a favorite sport of medieval French knights) was played by striking the ball with the palm of the hand, and in Old French was called la paulme, literally "the palm," but to an onlooker the service cry would naturally seem to identify the game. Century Dictionary says all of this is "purely imaginary."

The use of the word for the modern game is from 1874, short for lawn tennis, which originally was called sphairistike (1873), from Greek sphairistike (tekhne) "(skill) in playing at ball," from the root of sphere. It was invented, and named, by Maj. Walter C. Wingfield and first played at a garden party in Wales, inspired by the popularity of badminton.

Tennis-ball attested from mid-15c.; tennis-court from 1560s; tennis-elbow from 1883; tennis-shoes from 1887.

It was invented, and named, by Maj. Walter C. Wingfield and first played at a garden party in Wales, inspired by the popularity of badminton. example.en: She has been playing tennis since she was six years old.
example.zh: 她从六岁起就开始打网球了。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "a stretched condition," from Middle French tension (16c.) or directly from Latin tensionem (nominative tensio) "a stretching" (in Medieval Latin "a struggle, contest"), noun of state from tensus, past participle of tendere "to stretch," from PIE root *ten- "stretch" (see tenet). The sense of "nervous strain" is first recorded 1763. The meaning "stress along lines of electromotive force" (as in high-tension wires) is recorded from 1785.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "a stretched condition," 源自 中古法语 tension (16 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 tensionem (主格 tensio) "a stretching" (in 中古拉丁语 "a struggle, contest"), 名词 of state 源自 tensus, 为 … 的过去分词 tendere "to stretch," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *ten- "stretch" （参见 tenet). example.en: There was visible tension between the two team leaders during the budget meeting.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "portable shelter of skins or coarse cloth stretched over poles," from Old French tente "tent, hanging, tapestry" (12c.), from Medieval Latin tenta "a tent," literally "something stretched out," noun use of fem. singular of Latin tentus "stretched," variant past participle of tendere "to stretch" (see tenet). The notion is of "stretching" hides over a framework. Tent caterpillar first recorded 1854, so called from the tent-like silken webs in which they live gregariously.

example.en: We set up our tent near the river before it got dark.
example.zh: 天黑之前我们在河边搭好了帐篷。

entries.etymology: 1580s, from Medieval Latin tentativus "trying, testing," from Latin tentatus, past participle of tentare "to feel, try." Related: Tentatively; tentativeness.
entries.etymologyZh: 1580 年代, 源自 中古拉丁语 tentativus "trying, testing," 源自 拉丁语 tentatus, 为 … 的过去分词 tentare "to feel, try." 同源词：Tentatively; tentativeness.

entries.etymology: mid-12c., tenðe; see ten + -th (1). Replacing Old English teoða (West Saxon), teiða (Northumbrian), which is preserved in tithe. Compare Old Saxon tehando, Old Frisian tegotha, Dutch tiende, Old High German zehanto, German zehnte, Gothic taihunda. As a noun from c. 1200.
