entries.etymology:
c. 1500, "trade, commerce," from Middle French trafique (15c.), from Italian traffico (14c.), from trafficare "carry on trade," of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *transfricare "to rub across," from Latin trans- "across" (see trans-) + fricare "to rub" (see friction), with the original sense of the Italian verb being "touch repeatedly, handle."

Or the second element may be an unexplained alteration of Latin facere "to make, do." Klein suggests ultimate derivation of the Italian word from Arabic tafriq "distribution." Meaning "people and vehicles coming and going" first recorded 1825. Traffic jam is 1917, ousting earlier traffic block (1895). Traffic circle is from 1938.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1500 年, "trade, commerce," 源自 中古法语 trafique (15 世纪), 源自 意大利语 traffico (14 世纪), 源自 trafficare "carry on trade," 来源存疑, 或源自 a 通俗拉丁语 *transfricare "to rub across," 源自 拉丁语 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + fricare "to rub" （参见 friction), with the original 语义 the 意大利语 动词 being "touch repeatedly, handle." Or the second element may be an unexplained alteration of 拉丁语 facere "to make, do." Klein suggests ultimate derivation of the 意大利语 word 源自 阿拉伯语 tafriq "distribution." 义为 "people and vehicles coming and going" 首见于 1825 年. Traffic jam is 1917 年, ousting earlier traffic block (1895 年). Traffic circle 始于 1938 年.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "play or other serious literary work with an unhappy ending," from Old French tragedie (14c.), from Latin tragedia "a tragedy," from Greek tragodia "a dramatic poem or play in formal language and having an unhappy resolution," apparently literally "goat song," from tragos "goat" + oide "song" (see ode).

The connection may be via satyric drama, from which tragedy later developed, in which actors or singers were dressed in goatskins to represent satyrs. But many other theories have been made (including "singer who competes for a goat as a prize"), and even the "goat" connection is at times questioned. Meaning "any unhappy event, disaster" is from c. 1500.

entries.definition: n. 痕迹，足迹 vt. 跟踪，追踪
entries.etymology: c. 1300, "to hang down loosely and flow behind" (of a gown, sleeve, etc.), from Old French trailler "to tow; pick up the scent of a quarry," ultimately from Vulgar Latin *tragulare "to drag," from Latin tragula "dragnet, javelin thrown by a strap," probably related to trahere "to pull" (see tract (n.1)). Transitive sense of "to tow or pull along the ground" is from c. 1400. The meaning "follow the trail of" (an animal, etc.) is first recorded late 14c. Meaning "to lag behind" is from 1957. Related: Trailed; trailing.

entries.definition: vt.培训，训练 n. 列车；一连串
entries.etymology:
early 14c., "a drawing out, delay;" late 14c., "trailing part of a skirt, gown, or cloak;" also "retinue, procession," from Old French train "tracks, path, trail (of a rome or gown); act of dragging," from trainer "to pull, drag, draw," from Vulgar Latin *traginare, extended from *tragere "to pull," back-formation from tractus, past participle of Latin trahere "to pull, draw" (see tract (n.1)).,

General sense of "series, progression, succession, continuous course" is from late 15c. Train of thought first attested 1650s. The railroad sense "locomotive and the cars coupled to it" is recorded from 1820 (publication year, dated 1816), from notion of a "train" of wagons or carriages pulled by a mechanical engine.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "a drawing out, delay;" 14 世纪晚期, "trailing part of a skirt, gown, or cloak;" also "retinue, procession," 源自 古法语 train "tracks, path, trail (of a rome or gown); act of dragging," 源自 trainer "to pull, drag, draw," 源自 通俗拉丁语 *traginare, extended 源自 *tragere "to pull," back-formation 源自 tractus, 为 … 的过去分词 拉丁语 trahere "to pull, draw" （参见 tract (n.1))., General 语义 "series, progression, succession, continuous course" 始于 15 世纪晚期 Train of thought 最早见于 1650 年代. The railroad sense "locomotive and the cars coupled to it" 见于 1820 年 (publication year, dated 1816 年), 源自 概念 a "train" of wagons or carriages pulled by a mechanical engine.

example.en: The company will train new employees on safety procedures before they start work.
example.zh: 公司将在新员工开始工作前对其进行安全规程培训。

entries.etymology: 1841, from train (v.) in the "instruct" sense + -ee.
entries.etymologyZh: 1841 年, 源自 train （动） in the "instruct" sense + -ee.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "protraction, delay," verbal noun from train (v.). From 1540s as "discipline and instruction to develop powers or skills;" 1786 as "exercise to improve bodily vigor." Training wheels as an attachment to a bicycle is from 1953.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "protraction, delay," verbal 名词 源自 train （动）. From 1540 年代 as "discipline and instruction to develop powers or skills;" 1786 年 as "exercise to improve bodily vigor." Training wheels 作为 attachment to a bicycle 始于 1953 年.

example.en: New employees must complete a week of safety training before starting.
example.zh: 新员工在上岗前必须完成一周的安全培训。

entries.etymology: late 15c., "shot, missiles;" later "a stroke in drawing, a short line" (1580s), from Middle French trait "line, stroke, feature, tract," from Latin tractus "drawing, drawing out, dragging, pulling," later "line drawn, feature," from past participle stem of trahere "to pull, draw" (see tract (n.1)). Sense of "particular feature, distinguishing quality" in English is first recorded 1752.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "shot, missiles;" later "a stroke in drawing, a short line" (1580 年代), 源自 中古法语 trait "line, stroke, feature, tract," 源自 拉丁语 tractus "drawing, drawing out, dragging, pulling," later "line drawn, feature," 源自 past participle stem of trahere "to pull, draw" （参见 tract (n.1)). 义为 "particular feature, distinguishing quality" in English is 首见于 1752 年.

example.en: Honesty is a trait that employers value highly in job candidates.
example.zh: 诚实是雇主在求职者身上高度重视的一种品质。

definitionLines: n. 交易，事务，处理事务
entries.definition: n. 交易，事务，处理事务
entries.etymology: mid-15c., "the adjustment of a dispute, a negotiated agreement, management or settlement of an affair," from Old French transaccion "exchange, transaction," from Late Latin transactionem (nominative transactio) "an agreement, accomplishment," noun of action from past participle stem of transigere "stab through; accomplish, perform, drive or carry through, come to a settlement," from trans- "through" (see trans-) + agere "to drive" (see act (n.)). Meaning "a piece of business" is attested from 1640s. Related: Transactions; transactional.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "the adjustment of a dispute, a negotiated agreement, management or settlement of an affair," 源自 古法语 transaccion "exchange, transaction," 源自 晚期拉丁语 transactionem (主格 transactio) "an agreement, accomplishment," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of transigere "stab through; accomplish, perform, drive or carry through, come to a settlement," 源自 trans- "through" （参见 trans-) + agere "to drive" （参见 act （名）). 义为 "a piece of business" 见于 1640 年代. 同源词：Transactions; transactional.

example.en: All online transaction must be verified with a one-time password.
example.zh: 所有网上交易都必须通过一次性密码进行验证。

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "escape inclusion in; lie beyond the scope of," from Old French transcendre "transcend, surpass," and directly from Latin transcendere "climb over or beyond, surmount, overstep," from trans- "beyond" (see trans-) + scandere "to climb" (see scan (v.)). Meanings "be surpassing, outdo, excel; surmount, move beyond" are from early 15c. Related: Transcended; transcending.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "escape inclusion in; lie beyond the scope of," 源自 古法语 transcendre "transcend, surpass," and 直接源自 拉丁语 transcendere "climb over or beyond, surmount, overstep," 源自 trans- "beyond" （参见 trans-) + scandere "to climb" （参见 scan （动）). Meanings "be surpassing, outdo, excel; surmount, move beyond" 始于 15 世纪初 同源词：Transcended; transcending.

entries.etymology: 1660s, from Medieval Latin transcendentalis, from Latin transcendentem (see transcendent). Related: Transcendentally. Transcendental meditation attested by 1966.
entries.etymologyZh: 1660 年代, 源自 中古拉丁语 transcendentalis, 源自 拉丁语 transcendentem （参见 transcendent). 同源词：Transcendentally. Transcendental meditation attested 截至 1966 年.

definitionLines: vt.迁移，调动；换车；转让， 过户
n.迁移，调动；换车；转让，过户
entries.definition: vt.迁移，调动；换车；转让， 过户 n.迁移，调动；换车；转让，过户
entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French transferer or directly from Latin transferre "bear across, carry over, bring through; transfer, copy, translate," from trans- "across" (see trans-) + ferre "to carry" (see infer). Related: Transferred; transferring.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 transferer or 直接源自 拉丁语 transferre "bear across, carry over, bring through; transfer, copy, translate," 源自 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + ferre "to carry" （参见 infer). 同源词：Transferred; transferring.

example.en: Please transfer the full payment to the bank account listed at the bottom of the invoice.
example.zh: 请将全额款项转账至发票底部所列的银行账户。

definitionLines: vt.转换，变形，变革；变化， 变压
entries.definition: vt.转换，变形，变革；变化， 变压
entries.etymology: mid-14c., "change the form of" (transitive), from Old French transformer (14c.), from Latin transformare "change in shape, metamorphose," from trans- "across" (see trans-) + formare "to form" (see form (v.)). Intransitive sense "undergo a change of form" is from 1590s. Related: Transformed; transforming.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "change the form of" (transitive), 源自 古法语 transformer (14 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 transformare "change in shape, metamorphose," 源自 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + formare "to form" （参见 form （动）). Intransitive sense "undergo a change of form" 始于 1590 年代. 同源词：Transformed; transforming.

example.en: Education can transform an entire community, lifting it out of poverty within a single generation.
example.zh: 教育能够彻底改变整个社区，使其在一代人的时间内摆脱贫困。

entries.etymology: small electronic device, 1948, from transfer + resistor, so called because it transfers an electrical current across a resistor. Said to have been coined by U.S. electrical engineer John Robinson Pierce (1910-2002) of Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, N.J., where the device was invented in 1947. It took over many functions of the vacuum tube. Transistor radio is first recorded 1958.
entries.etymologyZh: small electronic device, 1948 年, 源自 transfer + resistor, so called because it transfers an electrical current across a resistor. Said to have been coined by U.S. electrical engineer John Robinson Pierce (1910 年-2002 年) of Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, N.J., where the device was invented 于 1947 年. It took over many functions of the vacuum tube. Transistor radio is 首见于 1958 年.

entries.etymology: mid-15c., from Latin transitionem (nominative transitio) "a going across or over," noun of action from past participle stem of transire "go or cross over" (see transient).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 拉丁语 transitionem (主格 transitio) "a going across or over," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of transire "go or cross over" （参见 transient).

example.en: The country is going through a difficult transition from a planned to a market economy.
example.zh: 这个国家正经历从计划经济向市场经济的艰难转型。

entries.etymology: early 14c., "to remove from one place to another," also "to turn from one language to another," from Old French translater and directly from Latin translatus "carried over," serving as past participle of transferre "to bring over, carry over" (see transfer), from trans- (see trans-) + latus "borne, carried" (see oblate (n.)). Related: Translated; translating. A similar notion is behind the Old English word it replaced, awendan, from wendan "to turn, direct" (see wend).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, "to remove from one place to another," also "to turn from one language to another," 源自 古法语 translater and 直接源自 拉丁语 translatus "carried over," serving as 为 … 的过去分词 transferre "to bring over, carry over" （参见 transfer), 源自 trans- （参见 trans-) + latus "borne, carried" （参见 oblate （名）). 同源词：Translated; translating. A similar notion is behind the 古英语 word it replaced, awendan, 源自 wendan "to turn, direct" （参见 wend).

example.en: It took her two hours to translate the document from French into English.
example.zh: 她花了两个小时把这份文件从法语翻译成英语。

entries.etymology: mid-14c., "removal of a saint's body or relics to a new place," also "rendering of a text from one language to another," from Old French translacion "translation" of text, also of the bones of a saint, etc. (12c.) or directly from Latin translationem (nominative translatio) "a carrying across, removal, transporting; transfer of meaning," noun of action from past participle stem of transferre (see transfer (v.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, "removal of a saint's body or relics to a new place," also "rendering of a text from one language to another," 源自 古法语 translacion "translation" of text, also of the bones of a saint, etc. (12 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 translationem (主格 translatio) "a carrying across, removal, transporting; transfer of meaning," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of transferre （参见 transfer （动）).

example.en: The translation of the novel from Spanish to English took nearly two years.
example.zh: 这部小说从西班牙语到英语的翻译工作花了将近两年时间。

definitionLines: vt. 传输，转送，传达，传导，发射
entries.definition: vt. 传输，转送，传达，传导，发射 vi. 发射信号，发报
entries.etymology: c. 1400, from Latin transmittere "send across, cause to go across, transfer, pass on," from trans- "across" (see trans-) + mittere "to send" (see mission). Related: Transmitted; transmitting.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, 源自 拉丁语 transmittere "send across, cause to go across, transfer, pass on," 源自 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + mittere "to send" （参见 mission). 同源词：Transmitted; transmitting.

example.en: Satellites transmit television signals to millions of homes around the world.
example.zh: 卫星将电视信号传输到全球数百万个家庭。

entries.etymology: early 15c., from Medieval Latin transparentem (nominative transparens), present participle of transparere "show light through," from Latin trans- "through" (see trans-) + parere "come in sight, appear" (see appear). Figurative sense of "easily seen through" is first attested 1590s. The attempt to back-form a verb transpare (c. 1600) died with the 17c. Related: Transparently.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, 源自 中古拉丁语 transparentem (主格 transparens), 为 … 的现在分词 transparere "show light through," 源自 拉丁语 trans- "through" （参见 trans-) + parere "come in sight, appear" （参见 appear). Figurative 语义 "easily seen through" is 最早见于 1590 年代. The attempt to back-form a 动词 transpare (约 1600 年) died with the 17 世纪 同源词：Transparently.

example.en: The company promised to be transparent about its financial operations.
example.zh: 该公司承诺在财务运营方面保持透明。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., from Late Latin transplantare "plant again in a different place," from Latin trans- "across" (see trans-) + plantare "to plant" (see plant (v.)). Extended to people (1550s) and then to organs or tissue (1786). Related: Transplanted; transplanting.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 源自 晚期拉丁语 transplantare "plant again in a different place," 源自 拉丁语 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + plantare "to plant" （参见 plant （动）). Extended to people (1550 年代) and 之后 to organs or tissue (1786 年). 同源词：Transplanted; transplanting.

example.en: Surgeons successfully managed to transplant a kidney from the donor to the patient.
example.zh: 外科医生成功地将肾脏从捐献者移植到患者体内。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "convey from one place to another," from Old French transporter "carry or convey across; overwhelm (emotionally)" (14c.) or directly from Latin transportare "carry over, take across, convey, remove," from trans- "across" (see trans-) + portare "to carry" (see port (n.1)). Sense of "carry away with strong feelings" is first recorded c. 1500. Meaning "to carry away into banishment" is recorded from 1660s.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "convey from one place to another," 源自 古法语 transporter "carry or convey across; overwhelm (emotionally)" (14 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 transportare "carry over, take across, convey, remove," 源自 trans- "across" （参见 trans-) + portare "to carry" （参见 port (n.1)). 义为 "carry away with strong feelings" is 首见于 约 1500 年. 义为 "to carry away into banishment" 见于 1660 年代.

example.en: The company uses refrigerated trucks to transport fresh produce across the country.
example.zh: 该公司使用冷藏卡车将新鲜农产品运送到全国各地。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "act of transporting," noun of action from transport (v.). Middle English used verbal noun transporting (early 15c.). In the sense of "means of conveyance" it is first recorded 1853.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "act of transporting," 名词 of action 源自 transport （动）. 中古英语 used verbal 名词 transporting (15 世纪初). In the 语义 "means of conveyance" it is 首见于 1853 年.

example.en: The city invested heavily in public transportation to reduce traffic congestion.
example.zh: 该市大力投资公共交通以缓解交通拥堵。

entries.definition: n. 陷阱，圈套 vt. 诱捕，使中圈套 trash n. 垃圾，废物
entries.etymology:
"contrivance for catching unawares," late Old English træppe, treppe "snare, trap," from Proto-Germanic *trep- (source also of Middle Dutch trappe "trap, snare"), related to Germanic words for "stair, step, tread" (Middle Dutch, Middle Low German trappe, treppe, German Treppe "step, stair," English tread (v.)), and probably literally "that on or into which one steps," from PIE *dreb-, extended form of root *der- (1), an assumed base of words meaning "to run, walk, step." Probably akin to Old French trape, Spanish trampa "trap, pit, snare," but the exact relationship is uncertain.

Sense of "deceitful practice, device or contrivance to betray one" is first recorded c. 1400. Meaning "U-shaped section of a drain pipe" is from 1833. Slang meaning "mouth" is from 1776. Speed trap recorded from 1908. Trap door "door in a floor or ceiling" (often hidden and leading to a passageway or secret place) is first attested late 14c.
entries.etymologyZh: "contrivance for catching unawares," late 古英语 træppe, treppe "snare, trap," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *trep- (source also of Middle 荷兰语 trappe "trap, snare"), related to 日耳曼语 words for "stair, step, tread" (Middle 荷兰语, Middle Low 德语 trappe, treppe, 德语 Treppe "step, stair," English tread （动）), and 可能 字面义为 "that on or into which one steps," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *dreb-, extended form of root *der- (1), an assumed base of words 意为 "to run, walk, step." Probably akin to 古法语 trape, 西班牙语 trampa "trap, pit, snare," but the exact relationship is uncertain. 义为 "deceitful practice, device or contrivance to betray one" is 首见于 约 1400 年. 义为 "U-shaped section of a drain pipe" 始于 1833 年. Slang 意为 "mouth" 始于 1776 年. Speed trap recorded 自 1908 年起. Trap door "door in a floor or ceiling" (常 hidden and leading to a passageway or secret place) is 最早见于 14 世纪晚期

example.en: The undercover officer was nearly caught in the criminal's own trap.
example.zh: 那名卧底警察差点落入罪犯自己设下的陷阱。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "to journey," from travailen (1300) "to make a journey," originally "to toil, labor" (see travail). The semantic development may have been via the notion of "go on a difficult journey," but it also may reflect the difficulty of any journey in the Middle Ages. Replaced Old English faran. Related: Traveled; traveling. Traveled (adj.) "having made journeys, experienced in travel" is from early 15c. Traveling salesman is attested from 1885.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "to journey," 源自 travailen (1300 年) "to make a journey," 原义为 "to toil, labor" （参见 travail). The semantic development may have been 经由 the 概念 "go on a difficult journey," but it also may reflect the difficulty of any journey in the Middle Ages. Replaced 古英语 faran. 同源词：Traveled; traveling. Traveled （形） "having made journeys, experienced in travel" 始于 15 世纪初 Traveling salesman 见于 1885 年.

example.en: He plans to travel across Southeast Asia by train during his summer vacation.
example.zh: 他计划暑假期间乘火车游历东南亚。

entries.etymology: Old English treg, trig "flat wooden board with a low rim," from Proto-Germanic *traujam (source also of Old Swedish tro, a corn measure), from PIE *drou-, variant of *deru-, forming words refering to objects made of wood (see tree (n.)). The primary sense may have been "wooden vessel."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 treg, trig "flat wooden board with a low rim," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *traujam (source also of Old Swedish tro, a corn measure), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *drou-, 为 … 的变体 *deru-, forming words refering to objects made of wood （参见 tree （名）). The primary sense may have been "wooden vessel."

definitionLines: n. 财宝，财富；宝贝，珍宝
entries.definition: n. 财宝，财富；宝贝，珍宝 vt. 珍视，珍爱
entries.etymology: mid-12c., tresor, from Old French tresor "treasury, hoard, treasure" (11c., Modern French trésor), from Gallo-Roman *tresaurus, from Latin thesaurus "treasury, treasure" (source also of Spanish, Italian tesoro), from Greek thesauros "store, treasure, treasure house" (see thesaurus). In Middle English also thresur, etc.; modern spelling is from 16c. Replaced Old English goldhord. General sense of "anything valued" is recorded from c. 1200. Treasure hunt is first recorded 1913. For treasure trove, see trove.
entries.etymologyZh: 12 世纪中期, tresor, 源自 古法语 tresor "treasury, hoard, treasure" (11 世纪, 现代法语 trésor), 源自 Gallo-Roman *tresaurus, 源自 拉丁语 thesaurus "treasury, treasure" (source also of 西班牙语, 意大利语 tesoro), 源自 希腊语 thesauros "store, treasure, treasure house" （参见 thesaurus). In 中古英语 also thresur, etc.; modern spelling 始于 16 世纪 Replaced 古英语 goldhord. General 语义 "anything valued" 见于 约 1200 年. Treasure hunt is 首见于 1913 年. For treasure trove, 参见 trove.

example.en: He will always treasure the memories of his childhood.
example.zh: 他将永远珍视童年的记忆。

entries.definition: v. 对待，处理；治疗 n. /n.款待，请客
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "negotiate, bargain, deal with," from Old French traitier "deal with, act toward; set forth (in speech or writing)" (12c.), from Latin tractare "manage, handle, deal with, conduct oneself toward," originally "drag about, tug, haul, pull violently," frequentative of trahere (past participle tractus) "to pull, draw" (see tract (n.1)).

Meaning "to entertain with food and drink without expense to the recipient by way of compliment or kindness (or bribery)" is recorded from c. 1500. Sense of "deal with, handle, or develop in speech or writing" (early 14c.) led to the use in medicine "to attempt to heal or cure, to manage in the application of remedies" (1781). Related: Treated; treating.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "negotiate, bargain, deal with," 源自 古法语 traitier "deal with, act toward; set forth (in speech or writing)" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 tractare "manage, handle, deal with, conduct oneself toward," 原义为 "drag about, tug, haul, pull violently," 为 … 的反复体 trahere (past participle tractus) "to pull, draw" （参见 tract (n.1)). 义为 "to entertain with food and drink without expense to the recipient by way of compliment or kindness (or bribery)" 见于 约 1500 年. 义为 "deal with, handle, or develop in speech or writing" (14 世纪初) led to the use in medicine "to attempt to heal or cure, to manage in the application of remedies" (1781 年). 同源词：Treated; treating.

example.en: The nurse treated every patient with professional care and respect.

entries.etymology: 1560s, "conduct or behavior toward someone or something," from treat (v.) + -ment. In the medical sense, it is first recorded 1744.
entries.etymologyZh: 1560 年代, "conduct or behavior toward someone or something," 源自 treat （动） + -ment. In the medical sense, it is 首见于 1744 年.

example.en: Doctors recommended a new physical treatment for patients with chronic back pain.
example.zh: 医生为慢性背痛患者推荐了一种新的物理疗法。

entries.etymology:
Old English  treo, treow "tree" (also "timber, wood, beam, log, stake"), from Proto-Germanic *treuwaz- (source also of Old Frisian tre, Old Saxon trio, Old Norse tre, Gothic triu "tree"), from PIE *drew-o-, from *deru- "oak" (source also of Sanskrit dru "tree, wood," daru "wood, log;" Greek drys "oak," drymos "copse, thicket," doru "beam, shaft of a spear;" Old Church Slavonic drievo "tree, wood;" Serbian drvo "tree," drva "wood;" Russian drevo "tree, wood;" Czech drva; Polish drwa "wood;" Lithuanian derva "pine, wood;" Old Irish daur, Welsh derwen "oak," Albanian drusk "oak"). This is from PIE *drew-o-, a suffixed form of the root *deru- "to be firm, solid, steadfast" (see true), with specialized sense "wood, tree" and derivatives referring to objects made of wood.

The widespread use of words originally meaning "oak" in the sense "tree" probably reflects the importance of the oak to ancient Indo-Europeans. In Old English and Middle English also "thing made of wood," especially the cross of the Crucifixion and a gallows (such as Tyburn tree, famous gallows outside London). Middle English also had plural treen, adjective treen (Old English treowen "of a tree, wooden"). For Dutch boom, German Baum, the usual words for "tree," see beam (n.). Meaning "framework of a saddle" is from 1530s. Meaning "representation of familial relationships in the form of a tree" is from c. 1300. Tree-hugger, contemptuous for "environmentalist" is attested by 1989.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 treo, treow "tree" (also "timber, wood, beam, log, stake"), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *treuwaz- (source also of 古弗里西语 tre, 古撒克逊语 trio, 古北欧语 tre, Gothic triu "tree"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *drew-o-, 源自 *deru- "oak" (source also of 梵语 dru "tree, wood," daru "wood, log;" 希腊语 drys "oak," drymos "copse, thicket," doru "beam, shaft of a spear;" Old Church Slavonic drievo "tree, wood;" Serbian drvo "tree," drva "wood;" 俄语 drevo "tree, wood;" Czech drva; Polish drwa "wood;" Lithuanian derva "pine, wood;" Old 爱尔兰语 daur, Welsh derwen "oak," Albanian drusk "oak"). This 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *drew-o-, a suffixed form of the root *deru- "to be firm, solid, steadfast" （参见 true), with specialized sense "wood, tree" and derivatives referring to objects made of wood. The widespread use of words 原义为 意为 "oak" in the sense "tree" 可能 reflects the importance of the oak to ancient Indo-Europeans. In 古英语 and 中古英语 also "thing made of wood," 尤指 the cross of the Crucifixion and a gallows (such as Tyburn tree, famous gallows outside London). 中古英语 also had plural treen, 形容词 treen (古英语 treowen "of a tree, wooden"). For 荷兰语 boom, 德语 Baum, the usual words for "tree," 参见 beam （名）. 义为 "framework of a saddle" 始于 1530 年代. 义为 "representation of familial relationships in the form of a tree" 始于 约 1300 年. Tree-hugger, contemptuous for "environmentalist" is attested 截至 1989 年.

example.en: The old tree in the backyard provides shade during summer.
example.zh: 后院的那棵老树在夏天提供了遮阴。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "shake from fear, cold, etc.," from Old French trembler "tremble, fear" (11c.), from Vulgar Latin *tremulare (source also of Italian tremolare, Spanish temblar), from Latin tremulus "trembling, shaking, quaking," from tremere "to tremble, shiver, quake," from PIE *trem- "to tremble" (source also of Greek tremein "to shiver, tremble, to quake, to fear," Lithuanian trimu "to chase away," Old Church Slavonic treso "to shake," Gothic þramstei "grasshopper"). A native word for this was Old English bifian. Related: Trembled; trembling. The noun is recorded from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "shake from fear, cold, etc.," 源自 古法语 trembler "tremble, fear" (11 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *tremulare (source also of 意大利语 tremolare, 西班牙语 temblar), 源自 拉丁语 tremulus "trembling, shaking, quaking," 源自 tremere "to tremble, shiver, quake," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *trem- "to tremble" (source also of 希腊语 tremein "to shiver, tremble, to quake, to fear," Lithuanian trimu "to chase away," Old Church Slavonic treso "to shake," Gothic þramstei "grasshopper"). A 本族 word for this was 古英语 bifian. 同源词：Trembled; trembling. The 名词 见于 约 1600 年.

example.en: Her voice began to tremble as she faced the angry crowd.
example.zh: 面对愤怒的人群，她的声音开始颤抖。

entries.etymology: 1630s, "awful, dreadful, terrible," from Latin tremendus "fearful, to be dreaded, terrible," literally "to be trembled at," gerundive form of tremere "to tremble" (see tremble (v.)). Hyperbolic or intensive sense of "extraordinarily great or good, immense" is attested from 1812, paralleling semantic changes in terrific, terrible, dreadful, awful, etc. Related: Tremendously.
entries.etymologyZh: 1630 年代, "awful, dreadful, terrible," 源自 拉丁语 tremendus "fearful, to be dreaded, terrible," 字面义为 "to be trembled at," gerundive form of tremere "to tremble" （参见 tremble （动）). Hyperbolic or intensive 语义 "extraordinarily great or good, immense" 见于 1812 年, paralleling semantic changes in terrific, terrible, dreadful, awful, etc. 同源词：Tremendously.

example.en: The earthquake caused tremendous damage to the city's infrastructure.
example.zh: 这场地震对城市基础设施造成了巨大的破坏。

entries.etymology: 1590s, "to run or bend in a certain direction" (of rivers, coasts, etc.), from Middle English trenden "to roll about, turn, revolve," from Old English trendan "turn round, revolve, roll," from Proto-Germanic *trandijan (source also of Old English trinde "round lump, ball," Old Frisian trind, Middle Low German trint "round," Middle Low German trent "ring, boundary," Dutch trent "circumference," Danish trind "round"); origin and connections outside Germanic uncertain. Sense of "have a general tendency" (used of events, opinions, etc.) is first recorded 1863, from the nautical sense. Related: Trended; trending.
entries.etymologyZh: 1590 年代, "to run or bend in a certain direction" (of rivers, coasts, etc.), 源自 中古英语 trenden "to roll about, turn, revolve," 源自 古英语 trendan "turn round, revolve, roll," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *trandijan (source also of 古英语 trinde "round lump, ball," 古弗里西语 trind, Middle Low 德语 trint "round," Middle Low 德语 trent "ring, boundary," 荷兰语 trent "circumference," Danish trind "round"); origin and connections outside 日耳曼语 uncertain. 义为 "have a general tendency" (used of events, opinions, etc.) is 首见于 1863 年, 源自 nautical sense. 同源词：Trended; trending.

example.en: There is a growing trend toward working from home.
example.zh: 居家办公的趋势正在不断增长。

entries.etymology: mid-15c., "act or process of testing, a putting to proof by examination, experiment, etc.," from Anglo-French trial, noun formed from triet "to try" (see try (v.)). Sense of "examining and deciding of the issues between parties in a court of law" is first recorded 1570s; extended to any ordeal by 1590s. As an adjectival phrase, trial-and-error is recorded from 1806. Trial balloon (1826) translates French ballon d'essai, a small balloon sent up immediately before a manned ascent to determine the direction and tendency of winds in the upper air, though the earliest use in English is figurative.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, "act or process of testing, a putting to proof by examination, experiment, etc.," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 trial, 名词 formed 源自 triet "to try" （参见 try （动）). 义为 "examining and deciding of the issues between parties in a court of law" is 首见于 1570 年代; extended to any ordeal by 1590 年代. 作为 adjectival phrase, trial-and-error 见于 1806 年. Trial balloon (1826 年) translates 法语 ballon d'essai, a small balloon sent up immediately before a manned ascent to determine the direction and tendency of winds in the upper air, though the earliest use in English is figurative.

example.en: The defendant remained calm throughout the trial despite intense questioning.
example.zh: 尽管受到激烈盘问，被告在整个审判过程中保持冷静。

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Old French triangle (13c.), from Latin triangulum "triangle," noun use of neuter of adjective triangulus "three-cornered, having three angles," from tri- "three" (see tri-) + angulus "corner, angle" (see angle (n.)).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 triangle (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 triangulum "triangle," 为 … 的名词用法 neuter of 形容词 triangulus "three-cornered, having three angles," 源自 tri- "three" （参见 tri-) + angulus "corner, angle" （参见 angle （名）).

example.en: The area of a triangle can be calculated using the formula half base times height.
example.zh: 三角形的面积可以用底乘以高再除以二的公式来计算。

entries.etymology:
mid-13c., "one of the twelve divisions of the ancient Hebrews," from Old French tribu or directly from Latin tribus "one of the three political/ethnic divisions of the original Roman state" (Tites, Ramnes, and Luceres, corresponding, perhaps, to the Latins, Sabines, and Etruscans), later, one of the 30 political divisions instituted by Servius Tullius (increased to 35 in 241 B.C.E.), of unknown origin. Perhaps from tri- "three" + *bheue-, root of the verb be. Others connect the word with the PIE root *treb- "a dwelling" (see tavern).

In the Biblical sense, which was the original one in English, the Latin word translates Greek phyle "race or tribe of men, body of men united by ties of blood and descent, a clan" (see phylo-). Extension to modern ethnic groups or races of people is from 1590s, specifically "a division of a barbarous race of people, usually distinguishable in some way from their congeners, united into a community under a recognized head or chief" [Century Dictionary], but colloquially of any aggregate of individuals of a kind.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, "one of the twelve divisions of the ancient Hebrews," 源自 古法语 tribu or 直接源自 拉丁语 tribus "one of the three political/ethnic divisions of the original Roman state" (Tites, Ramnes, and Luceres, corresponding, 或许, to the Latins, Sabines, and Etruscans), later, one of the 30 political divisions instituted by Servius Tullius (increased to 35 in 241 B.C.E.), 来源不详. Perhaps 源自 tri- "three" + *bheue-, root of the 动词 be. Others connect the word with the 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *treb- "a dwelling" （参见 tavern). In the Biblical sense, which was the original one in English, the 拉丁语 word translates 希腊语 phyle "race or tribe of men, body of men united by ties of blood and descent, a clan" （参见 phylo-). Extension to modern ethnic groups or races of people 始于 1590 年代, specifically "a division of a barbarous race of people, usually distinguishable in some way from their congeners, united into a community under a recognized head or chief" [Century Dictionary], but colloquially of any aggregate of individuals of a kind.

example.en: The elders of the tribe gathered to discuss the future of their land.
example.zh: 部落的长老们聚集在一起商讨土地的未来。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "a judgement seat," from Old French tribunal "justice seat, judgement seat" (13c.) and directly from Latin tribunal "platform for the seat of magistrates, elevation, embankment," from tribunus "official in ancient Rome, magistrate," literally "head of a tribe" (see tribune). Hence, "a court of justice or judicial assembly" (1580s).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "a judgement seat," 源自 古法语 tribunal "justice seat, judgement seat" (13 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 tribunal "platform for the seat of magistrates, elevation, embankment," 源自 tribunus "official in ancient Rome, magistrate," 字面义为 "head of a tribe" （参见 tribune). Hence, "a court of justice or judicial assembly" (1580 年代).

definitionLines: n. 诡计，花招；恶作剧；窍门
entries.definition: n. 诡计，花招；恶作剧；窍门 vt.欺诈，哄骗
entries.etymology:
early 15c., "a cheat, a mean ruse," from Old North French trique "trick, deceit, treachery, cheating," from trikier "to deceive, to cheat," variant of Old French trichier "to cheat, trick, deceive," of uncertain origin, probably from Vulgar Latin *triccare, from Latin tricari "be evasive, shuffle," from tricæ "trifles, nonsense, a tangle of difficulties," of unknown origin.

Meaning "a roguish prank" is recorded from 1580s; sense of "the art of doing something" is first attested 1610s. Meaning "prostitute's client" is first attested 1915; earlier it was U.S. slang for "a robbery" (1865). To do the trick "accomplish one's purpose" is from 1812; to miss a trick "fail to take advantage of opportunity" is from 1889; from 1872 in reference to playing the card-game of whist, which might be the original literal sense. Trick-or-treat is recorded from 1942. Trick question is from 1907.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "a cheat, a mean ruse," 源自 Old North 法语 trique "trick, deceit, treachery, cheating," 源自 trikier "to deceive, to cheat," 为 … 的变体 古法语 trichier "to cheat, trick, deceive," 来源存疑, 可能 源自 通俗拉丁语 *triccare, 源自 拉丁语 tricari "be evasive, shuffle," 源自 tricæ "trifles, nonsense, a tangle of difficulties," 来源不详. 义为 "a roguish prank" 见于 1580 年代; 语义 "the art of doing something" is 最早见于 1610 年代. 义为 "prostitute's client" is 最早见于 1915 年; earlier it was U.S. 俚语 for "a robbery" (1865 年). To do the trick "accomplish one's purpose" 始于 1812 年; to miss a trick "fail to take advantage of opportunity" 始于 1889 年; 自 1872 年起 in reference to playing the card-game of whist, which might be the original literal sense. Trick-or-treat 见于 1942 年. Trick question 始于 1907 年.

example.en: The magician performed a trick that left the crowd amazed.
example.zh: 魔术师表演了一个让观众大为惊叹的把戏。

definitionLines: 少量，少许；小事，琐事；无价 值的东西
entries.definition: 少量，少许；小事，琐事；无价 值的东西
entries.etymology: c. 1200, trufle "false or idle tale," later "matter of little importance" (c. 1300), from Old French trufle "mockery," diminutive of truffe "deception," of uncertain origin. As a type of light confection from 1755.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, trufle "false or idle tale," later "matter of little importance" (约 1300 年), 源自 古法语 trufle "mockery," 为 … 的指小形式 truffe "deception," 来源存疑. 作为 type of light confection 自 1755 年起.

entries.definition: vt. 触发；引发，引起 n. 触发器；扳机
entries.etymology: "device by means of which a catch or spring is released and a mechanism set in action," 1650s, earlier tricker (1620s), from Dutch trekker "trigger," from trekken "to pull" (see trek). Tricker was the usual form in English until c. 1750. Trigger-happy is attested from 1942.
entries.etymologyZh: "device by means of which a catch or spring is released and a mechanism set in action," 1650 年代, earlier tricker (1620 年代), 源自 荷兰语 trekker "trigger," 源自 trekken "to pull" （参见 trek). Tricker was the usual form in English until 约 1750 年. Trigger-happy 见于 1942 年.

example.en: The loud noise outside seemed to trigger her anxiety attack.
example.zh: 外面的巨响似乎引发了她的焦虑发作。

entries.etymology: 1680s, from French trillion, from Italian trilione; see tri- + million. In the U.S., the fourth power of a thousand (one thousand billion, 1 followed by 12 zeroes); in Great Britain, the third power of a million (one million billion, 1 followed by 18 zeroes), which is the original sense. Compare billion.
entries.etymologyZh: 1680 年代, 源自 法语 trillion, 源自 意大利语 trilione; 参见 tri- + million. In the U.S., the fourth power of a thousand (one thousand billion, 1 followed by 12 zeroes); in Great Britain, the third power of a million (one million billion, 1 followed by 18 zeroes), which is the original sense. 对比 billion.

entries.etymology:
mid-15c., probably from Old English trymian, trymman "strengthen, fortify, confirm; comfort; incite; set in order, arrange, prepare, make ready; become strong," from trum "strong, stable," from Proto-Germanic *trum-, from PIE *dru-mo-, suffixed form of *deru- "to be firm, solid, steadfast" (see true). Examples in Middle English are wanting.

Original sense is preserved in nautical phrase in fighting trim (see trim (n.)); where the verb meant "distribute the load of a ship so she floats on an even keel" (1570s). Meaning "make neat by cutting" is first recorded 1520s; that of "decorate, adorn" is from 1540s. Sense of "reduce" is attested from 1966.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪中期, 可能 源自 古英语 trymian, trymman "strengthen, fortify, confirm; comfort; incite; set in order, arrange, prepare, make ready; become strong," 源自 trum "strong, stable," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *trum-, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *dru-mo-, suffixed form of *deru- "to be firm, solid, steadfast" （参见 true). Examples in 中古英语 are wanting. Original sense is preserved in nautical phrase in fighting trim （参见 trim （名）); where the 动词 meant "distribute the load of a ship so she floats on an even keel" (1570 年代). 义为 "make neat by cutting" is 首见于 1520 年代; that of "decorate, adorn" 始于 1540 年代. 义为 "reduce" 见于 1966 年.

example.en: She asked the barber to trim the sides of her hair.
example.zh: 她让理发师修剪她头发的两侧。

entries.etymology:
late 14c., "tread or step lightly and nimbly, skip, dance, caper," from Old French triper "jump around, dance around, strike with the feet" (12c.), from a Germanic source (compare Middle Dutch trippen "to skip, trip, hop; to stamp, trample," Low German trippeln, Frisian tripje, Dutch trappen, Old English treppan "to tread, trample") related to trap (n.).

The senses of "to stumble" (intransitive), "strike with the foot and cause to stumble" (transitive) are from mid-15c. in English. Meaning "to release" (a catch, lever, etc.) is recorded from 1897; trip-wire is attested from 1868. Related: Tripped; tripping.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "tread or step lightly and nimbly, skip, dance, caper," 源自 古法语 triper "jump around, dance around, strike with the feet" (12 世纪), 源自 a 日耳曼语 source (对比 Middle 荷兰语 trippen "to skip, trip, hop; to stamp, trample," Low 德语 trippeln, Frisian tripje, 荷兰语 trappen, 古英语 treppan "to tread, trample") related to trap （名）. The senses of "to stumble" (intransitive), "strike with the foot and cause to stumble" (transitive) 始于 15 世纪中期 in English. 义为 "to release" (a catch, lever, etc.) 见于 1897 年; trip-wire 见于 1868 年. 同源词：Tripped; tripping.

example.en: I'm just popping out for a quick trip to the supermarket; I'll be back soon.
example.zh: 我只是出去快速跑一趟超市，很快就回来。

entries.definition: a.三倍的 vi.增至三倍 vt. 使成三倍
entries.etymology: late 14c., from Medieval Latin triplare "to triple," from Latin triplus "threefold, triple," from tri- "three" (see tri-) + -plus "-fold" (see -plus). Related: Tripled; tripling.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 中古拉丁语 triplare "to triple," 源自 拉丁语 triplus "threefold, triple," 源自 tri- "three" （参见 tri-) + -plus "-fold" （参见 -plus). 同源词：Tripled; tripling.

entries.definition: n. 胜利，成功 vi. 得胜，战胜
entries.etymology: late 14c., "success in battle, conquest," also "spiritual victory" and "a procession celebrating victory in war," from Old French triumphe (12c., Modern French triomphe), from Latin triumphus "an achievement, a success; celebratory procession for a victorious general or admiral," from Old Latin triumpus, probably via Etruscan from Greek thriambos "hymn to Dionysus," a loan-word from a pre-Hellenic language.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "success in battle, conquest," also "spiritual victory" and "a procession celebrating victory in war," 源自 古法语 triumphe (12 世纪, 现代法语 triomphe), 源自 拉丁语 triumphus "an achievement, a success; celebratory procession for a victorious general or admiral," 源自 Old 拉丁语 triumpus, 可能 经由 Etruscan 源自 希腊语 thriambos "hymn to Dionysus," a loan-word 源自 a pre-Hellenic language.

example.en: The team celebrated their triumph over the defending champions with great joy.
example.zh: 球队欢欣鼓舞地庆祝他们战胜卫冕冠军的胜利。

entries.etymology:
"ordinary" (1580s); "insignificant, trifling" (1590s), from Latin trivialis "common, commonplace, vulgar," literally "of or belonging to the crossroads," from trivium "place where three roads meet," in transferred use, "an open place, a public place," from tri- "three" (see three) + via "road" (see via). The sense connection is "public," hence "common, commonplace."

The earliest use of the word in English was early 15c., a separate borrowing in the academic sense "of the trivium" (the first three liberal arts -- grammar, rhetoric, and logic); from Medieval Latin use of trivialis in the sense "of the first three liberal arts," from trivium, neuter of the Latin adjective trivius "of three roads, of the crossroads." Related: Trivially. For sense evolution to "pertaining to useless information," see trivia.
entries.etymologyZh: "ordinary" (1580 年代); "insignificant, trifling" (1590 年代), 源自 拉丁语 trivialis "common, commonplace, vulgar," 字面义为 "of or belonging to the crossroads," 源自 trivium "place where three roads meet," in transferred use, "an open place, a public place," 源自 tri- "three" （参见 three) + 经由 "road" （参见 经由). The sense connection is "public," hence "common, commonplace." The earliest use of the word in English was 15 世纪初, a separate borrowing in the academic sense "of the trivium" (the first three liberal arts -- grammar, rhetoric, and logic); 源自 中古拉丁语 use of trivialis in the sense "of the first three liberal arts," 源自 trivium, neuter of the 拉丁语 形容词 trivius "of three roads, of the crossroads." 同源词：Trivially. For sense evolution to "pertaining to useless information," 参见 trivia.

definitionLines: n. （一）群，（一）队；（pl.）部 队，军队
entries.definition: n. （一）群，（一）队；（pl.）部 队，军队
entries.etymology: 1540s, "body of soldiers," 1540s, from Middle French troupe, from Old French trope "band of people, company, troop, crowd" (13c.), of uncertain origin, perhaps from Frankish *throp "assembly, gathering of people" or another Germanic source, perhaps related to Old English ðorp, Old Norse thorp "village" (see thorp). OED derives the French word from Latin troppus "flock," which is of unknown origin but also might be from the proposed Germanic source. Of groups of animals from 1580s. Specifically as "a subdivision of a cavalry force" from 1580s; of Boy Scouts from 1908. Troops "armed forces" is from 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 1540 年代, "body of soldiers," 1540 年代, 源自 中古法语 troupe, 源自 古法语 trope "band of people, company, troop, crowd" (13 世纪), 来源存疑, 或源自 Frankish *throp "assembly, gathering of people" or another 日耳曼语 source, 或许 related to 古英语 ðorp, 古北欧语 thorp "village" （参见 thorp). OED derives the 法语 word 源自 拉丁语 troppus "flock," which is 来源不详 but also might be 源自 proposed 日耳曼语 source. Of groups of animals 源自 1580 年代. Specifically as "a subdivision of a cavalry force" 源自 1580 年代; of Boy Scouts 自 1908 年起. Troops "armed forces" 始于 1590 年代.

example.en: Government troops were deployed to the border to prevent further clashes.
example.zh: 政府军队被派往边境以防止进一步冲突。

entries.etymology: 1520s, "pertaining to the celestial tropics," from tropic + -al (1). In reference to the torrid zones of the earth, from 1690s. Meaning "hot and lush like the climate of the tropics" is first attested 1834.
entries.etymologyZh: 1520 年代, "pertaining to the celestial tropics," 源自 tropic + -al (1). In reference to the torrid zones of the earth, 源自 1690 年代. 义为 "hot and lush like the climate of the tropics" is 最早见于 1834 年.

example.en: The island is home to a wide variety of tropical plants and wildlife.
example.zh: 这座岛屿拥有种类繁多的热带植物和野生动物。

definitionLines: n. 苦恼，麻烦，困难；疾病； 故障；辛苦，费心；纷争，动 乱
entries.definition: n. 苦恼，麻烦，困难；疾病； 故障；辛苦，费心；纷争，动 乱 vt. 麻烦，打扰 vi. 费神，费力
entries.etymology: c. 1200, from Old French trubler, metathesis of turbler, torbler "to trouble, disturb; make cloudy, stir up, mix" (11c.), from Vulgar Latin *turbulare, from Late Latin turbidare "to trouble, make turbid," from Latin turbidus (see turbid). Related: Troubled; troubling.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, 源自 古法语 trubler, metathesis of turbler, torbler "to trouble, disturb; make cloudy, stir up, mix" (11 世纪), 源自 通俗拉丁语 *turbulare, 源自 晚期拉丁语 turbidare "to trouble, make turbid," 源自 拉丁语 turbidus （参见 turbid). 同源词：Troubled; troubling.

example.en: The broken engine caused a lot of trouble for the whole team.
example.zh: 损坏的引擎给整个团队带来了很多麻烦。

definitionLines: a. 麻烦的，讨厌的，棘手的
entries.definition: a. 麻烦的，讨厌的，棘手的
entries.etymology: 1540s, from trouble (n.) + -some (1). Troublesomeness.

entries.etymology: "garment for men, covering the lower body and each leg separately," 1610s, earlier trouzes (1580s), extended from trouse (1570s), with plural ending typical of things in pairs, from Gaelic or Middle Irish triubhas "close-fitting shorts," of uncertain origin. The unexplained intrusive second -r- is perhaps by influence of drawers or other words in pairs ending in -ers.

definitionLines: a. 真实，不假的；忠实，可靠的； 准确的，正确无误的
entries.definition: a. 真实，不假的；忠实，可靠的； 准确的，正确无误的
entries.etymology:
Old English triewe (West Saxon), treowe (Mercian) "faithful, trustworthy, honest, steady in adhering to promises, friends, etc.," from Proto-Germanic *treuwaz- "having or characterized by good faith" (source also of Old Frisian triuwi, Dutch getrouw, Old High German gatriuwu, German treu, Old Norse tryggr, Danish tryg, Gothic triggws "faithful, trusty"), from PIE *drew-o-, a suffixed form of the root *deru-/*dreu- "be firm, solid, steadfast" (source also of Lithuanian drutas "firm," Welsh drud, Old Irish dron "strong," Welsh derw "true," Old Irish derb "sure"), with specialized sense "wood, tree" and derivatives referring to objects made of wood (see tree (n.)).

Sense of "consistent with fact" first recorded c. 1200; that of "real, genuine, not counterfeit" is from late 14c.; that of "conformable to a certain standard" (as true north) is from c. 1550. Of artifacts, "accurately fitted or shaped" it is recorded from late 15c. True-love (n.) is Old English treowlufu. True-born (adj.) first attested 1590s. True-false (adj.) as a type of test question is recorded from 1923. To come true (of dreams, etc.) is from 1819.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 triewe (West Saxon), treowe (Mercian) "faithful, trustworthy, honest, steady in adhering to promises, friends, etc.," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *treuwaz- "having or characterized by good faith" (source also of 古弗里西语 triuwi, 荷兰语 getrouw, 古高地德语 gatriuwu, 德语 treu, 古北欧语 tryggr, Danish tryg, Gothic triggws "faithful, trusty"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *drew-o-, a suffixed form of the root *deru-/*dreu- "be firm, solid, steadfast" (source also of Lithuanian drutas "firm," Welsh drud, Old 爱尔兰语 dron "strong," Welsh derw "true," Old 爱尔兰语 derb "sure"), with specialized sense "wood, tree" and derivatives referring to objects made of wood （参见 tree （名）). 义为 "consistent with fact" 首见于 约 1200 年; that of "real, genuine, not counterfeit" 始于 14 世纪晚期; that of "conformable to a certain standard" (as true north) 始于 约 1550 年. Of artifacts, "accurately fitted or shaped" it 见于 15 世纪晚期 True-love （名） is 古英语 treowlufu. True-born （形） 最早见于 1590 年代. True-false （形） 作为 type of test question 见于 1923 年. To come true (of dreams, etc.) 始于 1819 年.

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "reliance on the veracity, integrity, or other virtues of someone or something; religious faith," from Old Norse traust "help, confidence, protection, support," from Proto-Germanic abstract noun *traustam (source also of Old Frisian trast, Dutch troost "comfort, consolation," Old High German trost "trust, fidelity," German Trost "comfort, consolation," Gothic trausti "agreement, alliance"), from Proto-Germanic *treuwaz-, source of Old English treowian "to believe, trust," and treowe "faithful, trusty" (see true (adj.)).

from c. 1300 as "reliability, trustworthiness; trustiness, fidelity, faithfulness;" from late 14c. as "confident expectation" and "that on which one relies." From early 15c. in legal sense of "confidence placed in a one who holds or enjoys the use of property entrusted to him by its legal owner;" mid-15c. as "condition of being legally entrusted." Meaning "businesses organized to reduce competition" is recorded from 1877. Trust-buster is recorded from 1903.

From 15 世纪初 in legal 语义 "confidence placed in a one who holds or enjoys the use of property entrusted to him by its legal owner;" 15 世纪中期 as "condition of being legally entrusted." 义为 "businesses organized to reduce competition" 见于 1877 年. Trust-buster 见于 1903 年.

definitionLines: n. 真实，真相；真实性；真理
entries.definition: n. 真实，真相；真实性；真理
entries.etymology:
Old English triewð (West Saxon), treowð (Mercian) "faith, faithfulness, fidelity, loyalty; veracity, quality of being true; pledge, covenant," from triewe, treowe "faithful" (see true (adj.)), with Proto-Germanic abstract noun suffix *-itho (see -th (2)).

Sense of "something that is true" is first recorded mid-14c. Meaning "accuracy, correctness" is from 1560s. English and most other IE languages do not have a primary verb for for "speak the truth," as a contrast to lie (v.). Truth squad in U.S. political sense first attested in the 1952 U.S. presidential election campaign.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 triewð (West Saxon), treowð (Mercian) "faith, faithfulness, fidelity, loyalty; veracity, quality of being true; pledge, covenant," 源自 triewe, treowe "faithful" （参见 true （形）), with 原始日耳曼语 abstract 名词 suffix *-itho （参见 -th (2)). 义为 "something that is true" is 首见于 14 世纪中期 义为 "accuracy, correctness" 始于 1560 年代. English and most other IE languages do not have a primary 动词 for for "speak the truth," 作为 contrast to lie （动）. Truth squad in U.S. political sense 最早见于 in the 1952 年 U.S. presidential election campaign.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "examine judiciously, discover by evaluation, test;" mid-14c., "sit in judgment of," also "attempt to do," from Anglo-French trier (13c.), from Old French trier "to pick out, cull" (12c.), from Gallo-Roman *triare, of unknown origin. The ground sense is "separate out (the good) by examination." Sense of "subject to some strain" (of patience, endurance, etc.) is recorded from 1530s. To try on "test the fit of a garment" is from 1690s; to try (something) on for size in the figurative sense is recorded by 1946. Try and instead of try to is recorded from 1680s.

entries.etymology: 1610s, from Middle French tube (15c.), from Latin tubus "tube, pipe," of unknown origin. The London subway was christened the Twopenny Tube (H.D. Browne, in the "Londoner" of June 30, 1900) before it even opened; tube for "cylindrical railway tunnel" is attested from 1847. The meaning "TV as a medium" is from 1959, short for cathode ray tube or picture tube. Tube top as a women's clothing style is attested from 1972. Tube steak is attested from 1963 as "frankfurter," slang meaning "penis" is recorded by mid-1980s.

entries.etymology: 1860, "disease characterized by tubercules," a medical Latin hybrid, from Latin tuberculum "small swelling, pimple," diminutive of tuber "lump" (see tuber) + -osis, a suffix of Greek origin. So called in reference to the tubercules which form in the lungs. Originally in reference to any disease characterized by tubercules; since the discovery in 1882 of the tubercule bacillus by German bacteriologist Robert Koch (1843-1910) restricted to disease caused by this. Abbreviation T.B. attested from 1912.

entries.etymology:
third day of the week, Old English tiwesdæg, from Tiwes, genitive of Tiw "Tiu," from Proto-Germanic *Tiwaz "god of the sky," the original supreme deity of ancient Germanic mythology, differentiated specifically as Tiu, ancient Germanic god of war, from PIE *deiwos "god," from root *dyeu- "to shine" (see diurnal). Compare Old Frisian tiesdei, Old Norse tysdagr, Swedish tisdag, Old High German ziestag.

The day name (second element dæg, see day) is a translation of Latin dies Martis (source of Italian martedi, French Mardi) "Day of Mars," from the Roman god of war, who was identified with Germanic Tiw (though etymologically Tiw is related to Zeus), itself a loan-translation of Greek Areos hemera. In cognate German Dienstag and Dutch Dinsdag, the first element would appear to be Germanic ding, þing "public assembly," but it is now thought to be from Thinxus, one of the names of the war-god in Latin inscriptions.
entries.etymologyZh: third day of the week, 古英语 tiwesdæg, 源自 Tiwes, 属格 of Tiw "Tiu," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *Tiwaz "god of the sky," the original supreme deity of ancient 日耳曼语 mythology, differentiated specifically as Tiu, ancient 日耳曼语 god of war, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *deiwos "god," 源自 root *dyeu- "to shine" （参见 diurnal). 对比 古弗里西语 tiesdei, 古北欧语 tysdagr, Swedish tisdag, 古高地德语 ziestag. The day name (second element dæg, 参见 day) is a translation of 拉丁语 dies Martis (source of 意大利语 martedi, 法语 Mardi) "Day of Mars," 源自 Roman god of war, who was identified with 日耳曼语 Tiw (though etymologically Tiw is related to Zeus), itself a loan-translation of 希腊语 Areos hemera. In 同源 德语 Dienstag and 荷兰语 Dinsdag, the first element would appear to be 日耳曼语 ding, þing "public assembly," but it is 现在 thought to be 源自 Thinxus, one of the names of the war-god in 拉丁语 inscriptions.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "protection, care, custody," from Anglo-French tuycioun (13c.), Old French tuicion "guardianship," from Latin tuitionem (nominative tuitio) "a looking after, a caring for, watching over, protection, guardianship," from tuitus, past participle of tueri "to look after" (see tutor (n.)). Meaning "action or business of teaching pupils" is recorded from 1580s. The meaning "money paid for instruction" (1828) probably is short for tuition fees, in which tuition refers to the act of teaching and instruction (a sense attested from 1580s).

entries.definition: n. 隧道，地道 vt.挖地道/隧道
entries.etymology:
early 15c., "funnel-shaped net for catching birds," from Middle French tonnelle "net," or tonel "cask," diminutive of Old French tonne "tun, cask for liquids," possibly from the same source as Old English tunne (see tun).

Sense of "tube, pipe" (1540s) developed in English and led to sense of "underground passage" (1660s). This sense subsequently has been borrowed into French (1878). The earlier native word for this was mine (n.). Meaning "burrow of an animal" is from 1873. Tunnel vision first recorded 1912. The amusement park tunnel of love is attested from 1911 (in reference to New York's Luna Park). The figurative light at the end of the tunnel has been seen since 1882.

entries.definition: 1，翻，旋转，转动；机会，轮替； 变化，改变；转折点 v. 转动；翻，翻转；改变方向；
entries.etymology:
late Old English turnian "to rotate, revolve," in part also from Old French torner "to turn away or around; draw aside, cause to turn; change, transform; turn on a lathe" (Modern French tourner), both from Latin tornare "to polish, round off, fashion, turn on a lathe," from tornus "lathe," from Greek tornos "lathe, tool for drawing circles," from PIE root *tere- (1) "to rub, rub by turning, turn, twist" (see throw (v.)). Transitive sense in English is from c. 1300. Related: Turned; turning.

Use in expression to turn (something) into (something else) probably retains the classical sense of "to shape on a lathe." To turn up "arrive, make an appearance" is recorded from 1755. Turn about "by turns, alternately" is recorded from 1640s. To turn (something) loose "set free" is recorded from 1590s. Turn down (v.) "reject" first recorded 1891, American English. Turn in "go to bed" is attested from 1690s, originally nautical. To turn the stomach "nauseate" is recorded from 1620s. To turn up one's nose as an expression of contempt is attested from 1779.

Turning point is attested by 1640s in a figurative sense "point at which a decisive change takes place;" literal sense "point on which a thing turns; point at which motion in one direction ceases and that in another or contrary direction begins" is from 1660s.

To turn up "arrive, make an appearance" 见于 1755 年. Turn about "by turns, alternately" 见于 1640 年代. To turn (something) loose "set free" 见于 1590 年代. Turn down （动） "reject" 首见于 1891 年, American English. entries.etymology: late 14c., "guardian, custodian," from Old French tuteor "guardian, private teacher" (13c., Modern French tuteur), from Latin tutorem (nominative tutor) "guardian, watcher," from tutus, variant past participle of tueri "watch over," of uncertain origin, perhaps from PIE *teue- (1) "pay attention to" (see thews). Specific sense of "senior boy appointed to help a junior in his studies" is recorded from 1680s.

entries.etymology:
late 14c., with -th (1), altering Middle English twelfte, from Old English twelfta, from twelf ((see twelve). The earlier form is cognate with Old Norse tolfti, Danish tolvte, Old Frisian twelefta, Dutch twaalfde, Old High German zwelifto, German zwölfte .

As a noun meaning "a twelfth part," from 1550s. Twelfth Night is Old English twelftan niht "Twelfth Night," the eve of Epiphany, which comes twelve days after Christmas, formerly an occasion of social rites and a time of merrymaking.

The earlier form is 与 … 同源 古北欧语 tolfti, Danish tolvte, 古弗里西语 twelefta, 荷兰语 twaalfde, 古高地德语 zwelifto, 德语 zwölfte . 作名词时 意为 "a twelfth part," 源自 1550 年代. Twelfth Night is 古英语 twelftan niht "Twelfth Night," the eve of Epiphany, which comes twelve days after Christmas, formerly an occasion of social rites and a time of merrymaking.

entries.etymology: Old English twelf "twelve," literally "two left" (over ten), from Proto-Germanic *twa-lif-, a compound of the root of two + *lif-, root of the verb leave (see eleven). Compare Old Saxon twelif, Old Norse tolf, Old Frisian twelef, Middle Dutch twalef, Dutch twaalf, Old High German zwelif, German zwölf, Gothic twalif. Outside Germanic, an analogous formation is Lithuanian dvylika, with second element -lika "left over."
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 twelf "twelve," 字面义为 "two left" (over ten), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *twa-lif-, a 由 … 复合而成 the root of two + *lif-, root of the 动词 leave （参见 eleven). 对比 古撒克逊语 twelif, 古北欧语 tolf, 古弗里西语 twelef, Middle 荷兰语 twalef, 荷兰语 twaalf, 古高地德语 zwelif, 德语 zwölf, Gothic twalif. Outside 日耳曼语, an analogous formation is Lithuanian dvylika, with second element -lika "left over."

entries.etymology:
Old English twentig "group of twenty," from twegen "two" (see two) + -tig "group of ten" (see -ty (1)). Cognate with Old Saxon twentig , Old Frisian twintich, Dutch twintig, Old High German zweinzug, German zwanzig. Gothic twai tigjus is even more transparent: literally "two tens."

The card game twenty-one (1790) is from French vingt-et-un (1781). Twenty-twenty hindsight is first recorded 1962, a figurative use of the Snellen fraction for normal visual acuity, expressed in feet. The guessing game of twenty questions is recorded from 1786.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 twentig "group of twenty," 源自 twegen "two" （参见 two) + -tig "group of ten" （参见 -ty (1)). Cognate with 古撒克逊语 twentig , 古弗里西语 twintich, 荷兰语 twintig, 古高地德语 zweinzug, 德语 zwanzig. Gothic twai tigjus is even more transparent: 字面义为 "two tens." The card game twenty-one (1790 年) 始于 法语 vingt-et-un (1781 年). Twenty-twenty hindsight is 首见于 1962 年, a figurative use of the Snellen fraction for normal visual acuity, expressed in feet. The guessing game of twenty questions 见于 1786 年.

entries.etymology:
late Old English twies, from Old English twiga, twigea "two times," from Proto-Germanic *twiyes (source also of Old Frisian twia, Old Saxon tuuio), from PIE *dwis-, adverbial form of *dwo- "two" (see two). Spelling with -ce reflects the voiceless pronunciation.

Think twice, then speak was an "old Prouerbe" by 1623. At twice, though less common than at once, means "at two distinct times; by two distinct operations."
entries.etymologyZh: late 古英语 twies, 源自 古英语 twiga, twigea "two times," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *twiyes (source also of 古弗里西语 twia, 古撒克逊语 tuuio), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *dwis-, adverbial form of *dwo- "two" （参见 two). Spelling with -ce reflects the voiceless pronunciation. Think twice, 之后 speak was an "old Prouerbe" 截至 1623 年. At twice, though less common than at once, means "at two distinct times; by two distinct operations."

entries.etymology: Old English twinn "consisting of two, twofold, double, two-by-two," from Proto-Germanic *twisnjaz "double" (source also of Old Norse tvinnr "double, twin," Old Danish tvinling, Dutch tweeling, German zwillung), from PIE *dwisno- (source also of Latin bini "two each," Lithuanian dvynu "twins"), from *dwi- "double," from root *dwo- "two" (see two). Minneapolis and St. Paul in Minnesota have been the Twin Cities since 1883, but the phrase was used earlier of Rock Island and Davenport (1856).

entries.etymology:
mid-14c., "flat part of a hinge" (now obsolete), probably from Old English -twist "divided object; fork; rope" (as in mæsttwist "mast rope, stay;" candeltwist "wick"), from Proto-Germanic *twis-, from PIE root *dwo- (see two). Original senses suggest "dividing in two" (source also of cognate Old Norse tvistra "to divide, separate," Gothic twis- "in two, asunder," Dutch twist, German zwist "quarrel, discord," though these senses have no equivalent in English), but later ones are of "combining two into one," hence the original sense of the word may be "rope made of two strands."

Meaning "thread or cord composed of two or more fibers" is recorded from 1550s. Meaning "act or action of turning on an axis" is attested from 1570s. Sense of "beverage consisting of two or more liquors" is first attested c. 1700. Meaning "thick cord of tobacco" is from 1791. Meaning "curled piece of lemon, etc., used to flavor a drink" is recorded from 1958. Sense of "unexpected plot development" is from 1941.

The popular rock 'n' roll dance craze is from 1961, so called from the motion involved, but twist was used to describe popular dances in 1894 and again in the 1920s. To get one's knickers in a twist "be unduly agitated" is British slang first attested 1971.

Original senses suggest "dividing in two" (source also of 同源 古北欧语 tvistra "to divide, separate," Gothic twis- "in two, asunder," 荷兰语 twist, 德语 zwist "quarrel, discord," though these senses have no equivalent in English), but later ones are of "combining two into one," hence the original 语义 the word may be "rope made of two strands." 义为 "thread or cord composed of two or more fibers" 见于 1550 年代. 义为 "act or action of turning on an axis" 见于 1570 年代. 义为 "beverage consisting of two or more liquors" is 最早见于 约 1700 年. 义为 "thick cord of tobacco" 始于 1791 年. 义为 "curled piece of lemon, etc., used to flavor a drink" 见于 1958 年. 义为 "unexpected plot development" 始于 1941 年. The popular rock 'n' roll dance craze 始于 1961 年, so called 源自 motion involved, but twist was used to describe popular dances 于 1894 年 and again in the 1920 年代. To get one's knickers in a twist "be unduly agitated" is British 俚语 最早见于 1971 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English twa "two," fem. and neuter form of twegen "two" (see twain), from Proto-Germanic *twa (source also of Old Saxon and Old Frisian twene, twa, Old Norse tveir, tvau, Dutch twee, Old High German zwene, zwo, German zwei, Gothic twai), from PIE *duwo, variant of dwo "two" (source also of Sanskrit dvau, Avestan dva, Greek duo, Latin duo, Old Welsh dou, Lithuanian dvi, Old Church Slavonic duva "two," first element in Hittite ta-ugash "two years old").

Two-fisted is from 1774. Two cheers for _____, expressing qualified enthusiasm first recorded 1951 in E.M. Forster's title "Two Cheers for Democracy." Two-dimensional is recorded from 1883; figurative sense of "lacking substance or depth" is attested from 1934.

Two-dimensional 见于 1883 年; figurative 语义 "lacking substance or depth" 见于 1934 年.

entries.etymology:
late 15c., "symbol, emblem," from Latin typus "figure, image, form, kind," from Greek typos "a blow, dent, impression, mark, effect of a blow; figure in relief, image, statue; anything wrought of metal or stone; general form, character; outline, sketch," from root of typtein "to strike, beat," from PIE *tup-, variant of root *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" (see steep (adj.)).

Extended 1713 to printing blocks with letters carved on them in relief. The meaning "general form or character of some kind, class" is attested in English from 1843, though it had that sense in Latin and Greek. To be (someone's) type "be the sort of person that person is attracted to" is recorded from 1934.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪晚期, "symbol, emblem," 源自 拉丁语 typus "figure, image, form, kind," 源自 希腊语 typos "a blow, dent, impression, mark, effect of a blow; figure in relief, image, statue; anything wrought of metal or stone; general form, character; outline, sketch," 源自 root of typtein "to strike, beat," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *tup-, 为 … 的变体 root *(s)teu- (1) "to push, stick, knock, beat" （参见 steep （形）). Extended 1713 年 to printing blocks with letters carved on them in relief. The 意为 "general form or character of some kind, class" is 见于 English 自 1843 年起, though it had that sense in 拉丁语 and 希腊语. To be (someone's) type "be the sort of person that person is attracted to" 见于 1934 年.

entries.etymology:
mid-13c., uglike "frightful or horrible in appearance," from a Scandinavian source, such as Old Norse uggligr "dreadful, fearful," from uggr "fear, apprehension, dread" (perhaps related to agg "strife, hate") + -ligr "-like" (see -ly (1)). Meaning softened to "very unpleasant to look at" late 14c. Extended sense of "morally offensive" is attested from c. 1300; that of "ill-tempered" is from 1680s.

Among words for this concept, ugly is unusual in being formed from a root for "fear, dread." More common is a compound meaning "ill-shaped" (such as Greek dyseides, Latin deformis, Irish dochrud, Sanskrit ku-rupa). Another Germanic group has a root sense of "hate, sorrow" (see loath). Ugly duckling (1877) is from the story by Hans Christian Andersen, first translated from Danish to English 1846. Ugly American "U.S. citizen who behaves offensively abroad" is first recorded 1958 as a book title.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪中期, uglike "frightful or horrible in appearance," 源自 a Scandinavian source, such as 古北欧语 uggligr "dreadful, fearful," 源自 uggr "fear, apprehension, dread" (或许 related to agg "strife, hate") + -ligr "-like" （参见 -ly (1)). 义为 softened to "very unpleasant to look at" 14 世纪晚期 Extended 语义 "morally offensive" 见于 约 1300 年; that of "ill-tempered" 始于 1680 年代. Among words for this concept, ugly is unusual in being formed 源自 a root for "fear, dread." More common is a 复合词 意为 "ill-shaped" (such as 希腊语 dyseides, 拉丁语 deformis, 爱尔兰语 dochrud, 梵语 ku-rupa). Another 日耳曼语 group has a root 语义 "hate, sorrow" （参见 loath). Ugly duckling (1877 年) 始于 the story by Hans Christian Andersen, first translated 源自 Danish to English 1846 年. entries.etymology:
"hand-held portable canopy which opens and folds," c. 1600, first attested in Donne's letters, from Italian ombrello, from Late Latin umbrella, altered (by influence of umbra) from Latin umbella "sunshade, parasol," diminutive of umbra "shade, shadow" (see umbrage).

A sunshade in the Mediterranean, a shelter from the rain in England; in late 17c. usage, usually as an Oriental or African symbol of dignity. Said to have been used by women in England from c. 1700; the use of rain-umbrellas carried by men there traditionally is dated to c. 1750, first by Jonas Hathaway, noted traveler and philanthropist. Figurative sense of "authority, unifying quality" (usually in a phrase such as under the umbrella of) is recorded from 1948.

A sunshade in the Mediterranean, a shelter 源自 rain in England; in 17 世纪晚期 usage, 通常 作为 Oriental or African symbol of dignity. Said to have been used by women in England 源自 约 1700 年; the use of rain-umbrellas carried by men there traditionally is dated to 约 1750 年, first by Jonas Hathaway, noted traveler and philanthropist. Figurative 语义 "authority, unifying quality" (通常 in a phrase such as under the umbrella of) 见于 1948 年.

entries.etymology:
late 13c., from Old French oncle, from Latin avunculus "mother's brother" ("father's brother" was patruus), literally "little grandfather," diminutive of avus "grandfather," from PIE root *awo- "grandfather, adult male relative other than one's father" (source also of Armenian hav "grandfather," Lithuanian avynas "maternal uncle," Old Church Slavonic uji "uncle," Welsh ewythr "uncle").

Replaced Old English eam (usually maternal; paternal uncle was fædera), which represents the Germanic form of the root (source also of Dutch oom, Old High German oheim "maternal uncle," German Ohm "uncle").

Also from French are German, Danish, Swedish onkel. As a familiar title of address to an old man, attested by 1793; in the U.S. South, especially "a kindly title for a worthy old negro" [Century Dictionary]. First record of Dutch uncle (and his blunt, stern, benevolent advice) is from 1838; Welsh uncle (1747) was the male first cousin of one's parent. To say uncle as a sign of submission in a fight is North American, attested from 1909, of uncertain signification.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, 源自 古法语 oncle, 源自 拉丁语 avunculus "mother's brother" ("father's brother" was patruus), 字面义为 "little grandfather," 为 … 的指小形式 avus "grandfather," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *awo- "grandfather, adult male relative other than one's father" (source also of Armenian hav "grandfather," Lithuanian avynas "maternal uncle," Old Church Slavonic uji "uncle," Welsh ewythr "uncle"). Replaced 古英语 eam (通常 maternal; paternal uncle was fædera), which represents the 日耳曼语 form of the root (source also of 荷兰语 oom, 古高地德语 oheim "maternal uncle," 德语 Ohm "uncle"). Also 源自 法语 are 德语, Danish, Swedish onkel. 作为 familiar title of address to an old man, attested 截至 1793 年; in the U.S. South, 尤指 "a kindly title for a worthy old negro" [Century Dictionary]. To say uncle 作为 sign of submission in a fight is North American, attested 自 1909 年起, of uncertain signification.

definitionLines: vt. 懂，理解，领会；获悉，听说
entries.definition: vt. 懂，理解，领会；获悉，听说
entries.etymology:
Old English understandan "comprehend, grasp the idea of," probably literally "stand in the midst of," from under + standan "to stand" (see stand (v.)). If this is the meaning, the under is not the usual word meaning "beneath," but from Old English under, from PIE *nter- "between, among" (source also of Sanskrit antar "among, between," Latin inter "between, among," Greek entera "intestines;" see inter-). Related: Understood; understanding.

That is the suggestion in Barnhart, but other sources regard the "among, between, before, in the presence of" sense of Old English prefix and preposition under as other meanings of the same word. "Among" seems to be the sense in many Old English compounds that resemble understand, such as underniman "to receive," undersecan "examine, investigate, scrutinize" (literally "underseek"), underðencan "consider, change one's mind," underginnan "to begin." It also seems to be the sense still in expressions such as under such circumstances.

Perhaps the ultimate sense is "be close to;" compare Greek epistamai "I know how, I know," literally "I stand upon." Similar formations are found in Old Frisian (understonda), Middle Danish (understande), while other Germanic languages use compounds meaning "stand before" (German verstehen, represented in Old English by forstanden "understand," also "oppose, withstand"). For this concept, most Indo-European languages use figurative extensions of compounds that literally mean "put together," or "separate," or "take, grasp" (see comprehend). Old English oferstandan, Middle English overstonden, literally "over-stand" seem to have been used only in literal senses. For "to stand under" in a physical sense, Old English had undergestandan.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 understandan "comprehend, grasp the idea of," 可能 字面义为 "stand in the midst of," 源自 under + standan "to stand" （参见 stand （动）). If this is the 意为, the under is not the usual word 意为 "beneath," but 源自 古英语 under, 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *nter- "between, among" (source also of 梵语 antar "among, between," 拉丁语 inter "between, among," 希腊语 entera "intestines;" 参见 inter-). 同源词：Understood; understanding. That is the suggestion in Barnhart, but other sources regard the "among, between, before, in the presence of" 语义 古英语 prefix and preposition under as other meanings of the same word. "Among" seems to be the sense in many 古英语 compounds that resemble understand, such as underniman "to receive," undersecan "examine, investigate, scrutinize" (字面义为 "underseek"), underðencan "consider, change one's mind," underginnan "to begin." It also seems to be the sense still in expressions such as under such circumstances. Perhaps the ultimate sense is "be close to;" 对比 希腊语 epistamai "I know how, I know," 字面义为 "I stand upon." Similar formations are found in 古弗里西语 (understonda), Middle Danish (understande), while other 日耳曼语 languages use compounds 意为 "stand before" (德语 verstehen, represented in 古英语 by forstanden "understand," also "oppose, withstand"). For this concept, most Indo-European languages use figurative extensions of compounds that 字面义为 mean "put together," or "separate," or "take, grasp" （参见 comprehend). 古英语 oferstandan, 中古英语 overstonden, 字面义为 "over-stand" seem to have been used only in literal senses. For "to stand under" in a physical sense, 古英语 had undergestandan.

entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 understanding "comprehension," verbal 名词 源自 understand （动）. 义为 "mutual agreement" 见于 1803 年.

example.zh: 她那位能体谅人的老板从不因为她犯诚实的错误而责怪她。

definitionLines: vt. 接收，承担；约定，保证； 着手，从事
entries.definition: vt. 接收，承担；约定，保证； 着手，从事
entries.etymology: c. 1200, "to entrap;" c. 1300, "to set about (to do)," from under + take (v.). Similar formation in French entreprendre "to undertake," from entre "between, among" + prendre "to take." The under in this word may be the same one that also may form the first element of understand. Old English had underniman "to trap, accept" (cognate with Dutch ondernemen, German unternehmen).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "to entrap;" 约 1300 年, "to set about (to do)," 源自 under + take （动）. Similar formation in 法语 entreprendre "to undertake," 源自 entre "between, among" + prendre "to take." The under in this word may be the same one that also may form the first element of understand. 古英语 had underniman "to trap, accept" (与 … 同源 荷兰语 ondernemen, 德语 unternehmen).

example.en: She agreed to undertake the responsibility of leading the research team.
example.zh: 她同意承担领导研究团队的责任。

entries.etymologyZh: 1749 年, of ships, "having begun to move," 源自 under + way （名）. In reference to projects, activities, etc., it 见于 1935 年.

entries.etymology: Old English undon "to unfasten and open" (a window or door), "to unfasten by releasing from a fixed position; to cancel, discharge, abrogate, reverse what has been done, put back in a former condition; bring to ruin, destroy," from un- (2) "opposite of" + do (v.). entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 undon "to unfasten and open" (a window or door), "to unfasten by releasing from a fixed position; to cancel, discharge, abrogate, reverse what has been done, put back in a former condition; bring to ruin, destroy," 源自 un- (2) "opposite of" + do （动）. 同源词：Undone; undoing.

example.en: She is undoubtedly the most talented musician in the entire school.
example.zh: 她无疑是整所学校最有才华的音乐家。

entries.etymology: late 13c., "not comforting, causing trouble," from un- (1) "not" + easy (adj.). Meaning "disturbed in mind" is attested from 1670s. Related: Uneasily; uneasiness.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "not comforting, causing trouble," 源自 un- (1) "not" + easy （形）. 义为 "disturbed in mind" 见于 1670 年代. 同源词：Uneasily; uneasiness.

entries.etymology: 1600, "at leisure, not occupied," from un- (1) "not" + past participle of employ (v.). Meaning "temporarily out of work" is from 1660s. The noun meaning "unemployed persons collectively" is from 1782.
entries.etymologyZh: 1600 年, "at leisure, not occupied," 源自 un- (1) "not" + 为 … 的过去分词 employ （动）. 义为 "temporarily out of work" 始于 1660 年代. The 名词 意为 "unemployed persons collectively" 始于 1782 年.

example.en: The factory closure left hundreds of workers unemployed.
example.zh: 工厂关闭使数百名工人失业。

entries.etymology: 1887, from un- (1) "not" + employment.
entries.etymologyZh: 1887 年, 源自 un- (1) "not" + employment.

example.en: Rising unemployment forced the government to introduce new job programs.
example.zh: 不断上升的失业率迫使政府推出新的就业计划。

entries.etymology: 1580s, from un- (1) "not" + past participle of expect (v.). Related: Unexpectedly.

example.zh: 这支球队的胜利完全出乎意料，因为他们本赛季此前每场比赛都输了。

entries.etymology: Old English unfægr "unlovely, not beautiful, deformed, hideous, unlovable," from un- (1) "not" + fair (adj.). Similar formation in Old Norse ufagr, Gothic unfagrs. Meaning "wicked, evil, bad" is recorded from c. 1300. Sense of "not equitable, unjust" is first recorded 1713. Related: Unfairly.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 unfægr "unlovely, not beautiful, deformed, hideous, unlovable," 源自 un- (1) "not" + fair （形）. Similar formation in 古北欧语 ufagr, Gothic unfagrs. 义为 "wicked, evil, bad" 见于 约 1300 年. 义为 "not equitable, unjust" is 首见于 1713 年. 同源词：Unfairly.

example.zh: 许多工人认为新的薪资政策极为不公平。

Similar formation in Middle Dutch ontvouden, German entfalten. Intransitive sense is attested from late 14c. Related: Unfolded; unfolding.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 unfealdan, "to open or unwrap the folds of," also figuratively, "to disclose, reveal, explain," 源自 un- (2) "opposite of" + fold （动）. Similar formation in Middle 荷兰语 ontvouden, 德语 entfalten. Intransitive sense 见于 14 世纪晚期 同源词：Unfolded; unfolding.
