entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 victorious and 直接源自 晚期拉丁语 victoriosus "having many victories," 源自 victoria "victory" （参见 victory). 同源词：Victoriously; victoriousness.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "military supremacy, victory in battle or a physical contest," from Anglo-French and Old French victorie (12c.) and directly from Latin victoria "victory," from past participle stem of vincere (see victor). V.E. ("victory in Europe") and V.J. ("victory in Japan") days in World War II were first used Sept. 2, 1944, by James F. Byrne, U.S. director of War Mobilization ["Washington Post," Sept. 10, 1944].
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "military supremacy, victory in battle or a physical contest," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 and 古法语 victorie (12 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 victoria "victory," 源自 past participle stem of vincere （参见 victor). V.E. ("victory in Europe") and V.J. ("victory in Japan") days in World War II were first used Sept. 2, 1944 年, by James F. Byrne, U.S. director of War Mobilization ["Washington Post," Sept. 10, 1944 年].

example.en: The team celebrated their victory with a parade through the city.
example.zh: 球队用一场穿越全市的游行庆祝了他们的胜利。

definitionLines: a. 电视的，视频的；录像的
entries.definition: n. 电视，视频，录像 a. 电视的，视频的；录像的
entries.etymology:
1935, as visual equivalent of audio, from Latin video "I see," first person singular present indicative of videre "to see" (see vision). As a noun, "that which is displayed on a (television) screen," 1937.

video game is from 1973.
entries.etymologyZh: 1935 年, as visual equivalent of audio, 源自 拉丁语 video "I see," first person singular present indicative of videre "to see" （参见 vision). 作名词时, "that which is displayed on a (television) screen," 1937 年. video game 始于 1973 年.

example.en: She posted a short video of her cooking skills on social media.
example.zh: 她在社交媒体上发布了一段展示烹饪技能的短视频。

definitionLines: n. 观察，视域，眼界；观点， 见解，看法；景色，风景
entries.definition: n. 观察，视域，眼界；观点， 见解，看法；景色，风景
entries.etymology: early 15c., "formal inspection or survey" (of land); mid-15c., "visual perception," from Anglo-French vewe "view," Old French veue "light, brightness; look, appearance; eyesight, vision," noun use of fem. past participle of veoir "to see," from Latin videre "to see" (see vision). Sense of "manner of regarding something" attested from early 15c. Meaning "sight or prospect of a landscape, etc." is recorded from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "formal inspection or survey" (of land); 15 世纪中期, "visual perception," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 vewe "view," 古法语 veue "light, brightness; look, appearance; eyesight, vision," 为 … 的名词用法 fem. 为 … 的过去分词 veoir "to see," 源自 拉丁语 videre "to see" （参见 vision). 义为 "manner of regarding something" attested 源自 15 世纪初 义为 "sight or prospect of a landscape, etc." 见于 约 1600 年.

example.en: From her view, the proposal ignored long-term environmental risks.
example.zh: 从她的角度来看，这份提案忽视了长期环境风险。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "civic official responsible for surveying property," agent noun from view (v.). Meaning "watcher of television" first recorded 1935, in place of earlier suggestion looker-in (1927).
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "civic official responsible for surveying property," agent 名词 源自 view （动）. 义为 "watcher of television" 首见于 1935 年, in place of earlier suggestion looker-in (1927 年).

example.en: The documentary attracted millions of viewers across the country.
example.zh: 这部纪录片吸引了全国数百万名电视观众。

entries.etymology: 1856, of mental positions; 1858 in a physical sense, from view + point (n.).
entries.etymologyZh: 1856 年, of mental positions; 1858 年 in a physical sense, 源自 view + point （名）.

example.en: From my viewpoint, the proposed policy will hurt small businesses the most.
example.zh: 在我看来，这项拟议政策对小企业的伤害最大。

definitionLines: a. 有力的；精力充沛的
entries.definition: a. 有力的；精力充沛的
entries.etymology: c. 1300 (early 13c. as a surname), from Anglo-French vigrus, Old French vigoros "strong, robust, powerful" (12c., Modern French vigoreux), from Medieval Latin vigorosus, from Latin vigere "be lively, flourish, thrive" (see vigor). Related: Vigorously.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年 (13 世纪初 作为 surname), 源自 盎格鲁-法语 vigrus, 古法语 vigoros "strong, robust, powerful" (12 世纪, 现代法语 vigoreux), 源自 中古拉丁语 vigorosus, 源自 拉丁语 vigere "be lively, flourish, thrive" （参见 vigor). 同源词：Vigorously.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "inhabited place larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town," from Old French vilage "houses and other buildings in a group" (usually smaller than a town), from Latin villaticum "farmstead" (with outbuildings), noun use of neuter singular of villaticus "having to do with a farmstead or villa," from villa "country house" (see villa). As an adjective from 1580s. Village idiot is recorded from 1825. Related: Villager (1560s).
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "inhabited place larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town," 源自 古法语 vilage "houses and other buildings in a group" (通常 smaller than a town), 源自 拉丁语 villaticum "farmstead" (with outbuildings), 为 … 的名词用法 neuter singular of villaticus "having to do with a farmstead or villa," 源自 villa "country house" （参见 villa). 作形容词时 源自 1580 年代. Village idiot 见于 1825 年. 同源词：Villager (1560 年代).

example.en: She grew up in a small village surrounded by mountains and rice fields.
example.zh: 她在一个四周被山脉和稻田环绕的小村庄长大。

entries.etymology: early 14c., from Old French vinaigre "vinegar," from vin "wine" (from Latin vinum; see wine (n.)) + aigre "sour" (see eager). In Latin, it was vinum acetum "wine turned sour;" compare Greek oxos "wine vinegar," which is related to oxys "sharp" (see acrid). Related: Vinegary; vinegarish.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪初, 源自 古法语 vinaigre "vinegar," 源自 vin "wine" (源自 拉丁语 vinum; 参见 wine （名）) + aigre "sour" （参见 eager). In 拉丁语, it was vinum acetum "wine turned sour;" 对比 希腊语 oxos "wine vinegar," which is related to oxys "sharp" （参见 acrid). 同源词：Vinegary; vinegarish.

example.en: She added a splash of vinegar to the salad dressing to give it a tangy flavor.
example.zh: 她在沙拉酱中加了一点醋，使其带有酸爽的味道。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "to break" (an oath, etc.), from Latin violatus, past participle of violare "treat with violence, dishonor, outrage" (see violation). Sense of "ravish" is first recorded mid-15c. Related: Violated; violating.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "to break" (an oath, etc.), 源自 拉丁语 violatus, 为 … 的过去分词 violare "treat with violence, dishonor, outrage" （参见 violation). 义为 "ravish" is 首见于 15 世纪中期 同源词：Violated; violating.

definitionLines: n. 强暴，暴力；暴行；激烈，猛烈
entries.definition: n. 强暴，暴力；暴行；激烈，猛烈
entries.etymology: late 13c., "physical force used to inflict injury or damage," from Anglo-French and Old French violence (13c.), from Latin violentia "vehemence, impetuosity," from violentus "vehement, forcible," probably related to violare (see violation). Weakened sense of "improper treatment" is attested from 1590s.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "physical force used to inflict injury or damage," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 and 古法语 violence (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 violentia "vehemence, impetuosity," 源自 violentus "vehement, forcible," 可能 related to violare （参见 violation). Weakened 语义 "improper treatment" 见于 1590 年代.

example.en: Experts warn that media exposure increases tolerance for violence.
example.zh: 专家警告称，媒体接触会增加对暴力的容忍度。

definitionLines: 《.猛烈的，强烈的，剧烈的； 强暴的，由暴力引起的
entries.definition: 《.猛烈的，强烈的，剧烈的； 强暴的，由暴力引起的
entries.etymology: mid-14c., from Old French violent or directly from Latin violentus, related to violare (see violation). In Middle English the word also was applied in reference to heat, sunlight, smoke, etc., with the sense "having some quality so strongly as to produce a powerful effect." Related: Violently.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 violent or 直接源自 拉丁语 violentus, related to violare （参见 violation). In 中古英语 the word also was applied in reference to heat, sunlight, smoke, etc., with the sense "having some quality so strongly as to produce a powerful effect." 同源词：Violently.

example.en: The violent storm destroyed several homes along the coast.
example.zh: 猛烈的风暴摧毁了沿海几处住宅。

entries.definition: n. 紫罗兰 a. 紫罗兰色的
entries.etymology: small wild plant with purplish-blue flowers, c. 1300, from Old French violete (12c.), diminutive of viole "violet," from Latin viola "the violet, a violet color," cognate with Greek ion (see iodine), probably from a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean language. The color sense (late 14c.) developed from the flower.
entries.etymologyZh: small wild plant with purplish-blue flowers, 约 1300 年, 源自 古法语 violete (12 世纪), 为 … 的指小形式 viole "violet," 源自 拉丁语 viola "the violet, a violet color," 与 … 同源 希腊语 ion （参见 iodine), 可能 源自 a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean language. The color sense (14 世纪晚期) developed 源自 flower.

entries.etymology: 1570s, from Italian violino, diminutive of viola (see viola). The modern form of the smaller, medieval viola da braccio.
entries.etymologyZh: 1570 年代, 源自 意大利语 violino, 为 … 的指小形式 viola （参见 viola). The modern form of the smaller, medieval viola da braccio.

definitionLines: a.处女的；纯洁的；处于原始状 态的
entries.definition: n. 处女 a.处女的；纯洁的；处于原始状 态的
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "unmarried or chaste woman noted for religious piety and having a position of reverence in the Church," from Anglo-French and Old French virgine "virgin; Virgin Mary," from Latin virginem (nominative virgo) "maiden, unwedded girl or woman," also an adjective, "fresh, unused," probably related to virga "young shoot," via a notion of "young" (compare Greek talis "a marriageable girl," cognate with Latin talea "rod, stick, bar").

Meaning "young woman in a state of inviolate chastity" is recorded from c. 1300. Also applied since early 14c. to a chaste man. Meaning "naive or inexperienced person" is attested from 1953. The adjective is recorded from 1550s in the literal sense; figurative sense of "pure, untainted" is attested from c. 1300. The Virgin Islands were named (in Spanish) by Columbus for St. Ursula and her 11,000 martyred virgin companions.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "unmarried or chaste woman noted for religious piety and having a position of reverence in the Church," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 and 古法语 virgine "virgin; Virgin Mary," 源自 拉丁语 virginem (主格 virgo) "maiden, unwedded girl or woman," also an 形容词, "fresh, unused," 可能 related to virga "young shoot," 经由 a 概念 "young" (对比 希腊语 talis "a marriageable girl," 与 … 同源 拉丁语 talea "rod, stick, bar"). 义为 "young woman in a state of inviolate chastity" 见于 约 1300 年. Also applied 自 14 世纪初 to a chaste man. 义为 "naive or inexperienced person" 见于 1953 年. The 形容词 见于 1550 年代 in the literal sense; figurative 语义 "pure, untainted" 见于 约 1300 年. The Virgin Islands were named (in 西班牙语) by Columbus for St. Ursula and her 11,000 martyred virgin companions.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "influencing by physical virtues or capabilities, effective with respect to inherent natural qualities," from Medieval Latin virtualis, from Latin virtus "excellence, potency, efficacy," literally "manliness, manhood" (see virtue). The meaning "being something in essence or effect, though not actually or in fact" is from mid-15c., probably via sense of "capable of producing a certain effect" (early 15c.). Computer sense of "not physically existing but made to appear by software" is attested from 1959.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "influencing by physical virtues or capabilities, effective with respect to inherent natural qualities," 源自 中古拉丁语 virtualis, 源自 拉丁语 virtus "excellence, potency, efficacy," 字面义为 "manliness, manhood" （参见 virtue). The 意为 "being something in essence or effect, though not actually or in fact" 始于 15 世纪中期, 可能 经由 语义 "capable of producing a certain effect" (15 世纪初). Computer 语义 "not physically existing but made to appear by software" 见于 1959 年.

example.en: Students can take a virtual tour of ancient Rome without leaving the classroom.
example.zh: 学生们无需离开教室就能进行一次虚拟的古罗马之旅。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "as far as essential qualities or facts are concerned;" from virtual + -ly (2). Sense of "in effect, as good as" is recorded from c. 1600.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "as far as essential qualities or facts are concerned;" 源自 virtual + -ly (2). 义为 "in effect, as good as" 见于 约 1600 年.

example.en: The new policy has virtually changed the way people commute.
example.zh: 这项新政策实际上已经彻底改变了人们的通勤方式。

entries.etymology:
c. 1200, vertu, "moral life and conduct; a particular moral excellence," from Anglo-French and Old French vertu "force, strength, vigor; moral strength; qualities, abilities" (10c. in Old French), from Latin virtutem (nominative virtus) "moral strength, high character, goodness; manliness; valor, bravery, courage (in war); excellence, worth," from vir "man" (see virile).

Especially (in women) "chastity, sexual purity" from 1590s. Phrase by virtue of (early 13c.) preserves alternative Middle English sense of "efficacy." Wyclif Bible has virtue where KJV uses power. The seven cardinal virtues (early 14c.) were divided into the natural (justice, prudence, temperance, fortitude) and the theological (hope, faith, charity). To make a virtue of a necessity (late 14c.) translates Latin facere de necessitate virtutem [Jerome].
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, vertu, "moral life and conduct; a particular moral excellence," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 and 古法语 vertu "force, strength, vigor; moral strength; qualities, abilities" (10 世纪 in 古法语), 源自 拉丁语 virtutem (主格 virtus) "moral strength, high character, goodness; manliness; valor, bravery, courage (in war); excellence, worth," 源自 vir "man" （参见 virile). Especially (in women) "chastity, sexual purity" 源自 1590 年代. Phrase by virtue of (13 世纪初) preserves alternative 中古英语 语义 "efficacy." Wyclif Bible has virtue where KJV uses power. The seven cardinal virtues (14 世纪初) were divided into the natural (justice, prudence, temperance, fortitude) and the theological (hope, faith, charity). To make a virtue of a necessity (14 世纪晚期) translates 拉丁语 facere de necessitate virtutem [Jerome].

example.en: Honesty is considered a virtue that every leader should possess.
example.zh: 诚实被认为是每位领导者都应具备的美德。

entries.etymology: c. 1300, "characterized by vigor or strength; having qualities befitting a knight; valiant, hardy, courageous;" from Old French vertuos "righteous; potent; of good quality; mighty, valiant, brave" (12c.), from Late Latin virtuosus "good, virtuous," from Latin virtus (see virtue). From mid-14c. in English as "having beneficial or efficacious properties;" late 14c. (of persons) as "having excellent moral qualities; conforming to religious law." Related: Virtuously; virtuousness.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "characterized by vigor or strength; having qualities befitting a knight; valiant, hardy, courageous;" 源自 古法语 vertuos "righteous; potent; of good quality; mighty, valiant, brave" (12 世纪), 源自 晚期拉丁语 virtuosus "good, virtuous," 源自 拉丁语 virtus （参见 virtue). From 14 世纪中期 in English as "having beneficial or efficacious properties;" 14 世纪晚期 (of persons) as "having excellent moral qualities; conforming to religious law." 同源词：Virtuously; virtuousness.

entries.etymology: 1831, "official signature or endorsement on a passport," from French visa, from Modern Latin charta visa "verified paper," literally "paper that has been seen," from fem. past participle of Latin videre "to see" (see vision). Earlier visé (1810), from French past participle of viser "to examine, view." The credit card of this name was introduced 1976, replacing BankAmericard.
entries.etymologyZh: 1831 年, "official signature or endorsement on a passport," 源自 法语 visa, 源自 现代 拉丁语 charta visa "verified paper," 字面义为 "paper that has been seen," 源自 fem. 为 … 的过去分词 拉丁语 videre "to see" （参见 vision). Earlier visé (1810 年), 源自 法语 为 … 的过去分词 viser "to examine, view." The credit card of this name was introduced 1976 年, replacing BankAmericard.

example.en: She needed to apply for a visa before traveling to China next month.
example.zh: 她需要在下个月去中国之前申请签证。

entries.etymology: c. 1400, "condition of being visible," from Late Latin visibilitatem (nominative visibilitas) "condition of being seen; conspicuousness," from visibilis (see visible). Meaning "range of vision under given conditions" is from 1914. Sense of "prominence, fame, public attention" is recorded from 1958.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1400 年, "condition of being visible," 源自 晚期拉丁语 visibilitatem (主格 visibilitas) "condition of being seen; conspicuousness," 源自 visibilis （参见 visible). 义为 "range of vision under given conditions" 始于 1914 年. 义为 "prominence, fame, public attention" 见于 1958 年.

entries.etymology: mid-14c., from Old French visable, visible "perceptible" (12c.) and directly from Latin visibilis "that may be seen," from visus, past participle of videre "to see" (see vision). An Old English word for this was eagsyne. Related: Visibly.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪中期, 源自 古法语 visable, visible "perceptible" (12 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 visibilis "that may be seen," 源自 visus, 为 … 的过去分词 videre "to see" （参见 vision). An 古英语 word for this was eagsyne. 同源词：Visibly.

example.en: The warning label on the bottle was clearly visible even without reading glasses.
example.zh: 即使不戴老花镜，瓶子上的警告标签也清晰可见。

definitionLines: n. 视觉，视力；幻想，幻影； 眼力，想像力，远见
entries.definition: n. 视觉，视力；幻想，幻影； 眼力，想像力，远见
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "something seen in the imagination or in the supernatural," from Anglo-French visioun, Old French vision "presence, sight; view, look, appearance; dream, supernatural sight" (12c.), from Latin visionem (nominative visio) "act of seeing, sight, thing seen," noun of action from past participle stem of videre "to see."

This is from the productive PIE root *weid- "to know, to see" (source also of Sanskrit veda "I know;" Avestan vaeda "I know;" Greek oida, Doric woida "I know," idein "to see;" Old Irish fis "vision," find "white," i.e. "clearly seen," fiuss "knowledge;" Welsh gwyn, Gaulish vindos, Breton gwenn "white;" Gothic, Old Swedish, Old English witan "to know;" Gothic weitan "to see;" English wise, German wissen "to know;" Lithuanian vysti "to see;" Bulgarian vidya "I see;" Polish widzieć "to see," wiedzieć "to know;" Russian videt' "to see," vest' "news," Old Russian vedat' "to know").

The meaning "sense of sight" is first recorded late 15c. Meaning "statesman-like foresight, political sagacity" is attested from 1926.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1300 年, "something seen in the imagination or in the supernatural," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 visioun, 古法语 vision "presence, sight; view, look, appearance; dream, supernatural sight" (12 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 visionem (主格 visio) "act of seeing, sight, thing seen," 名词 of action 源自 past participle stem of videre "to see." This 始于 the productive 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *weid- "to know, to see" (source also of 梵语 veda "I know;" Avestan vaeda "I know;" 希腊语 oida, Doric woida "I know," idein "to see;" Old 爱尔兰语 fis "vision," find "white," i.e. "clearly seen," fiuss "knowledge;" Welsh gwyn, Gaulish vindos, Breton gwenn "white;" Gothic, Old Swedish, 古英语 witan "to know;" Gothic weitan "to see;" English wise, 德语 wissen "to know;" Lithuanian vysti "to see;" Bulgarian vidya "I see;" Polish widzieć "to see," wiedzieć "to know;" 俄语 videt' "to see," vest' "news," Old 俄语 vedat' "to know"). The 意为 "sense of sight" is 首见于 15 世纪晚期 义为 "statesman-like foresight, political sagacity" 见于 1926 年.

example.en: The leader had the vision to anticipate market changes years in advance.
example.zh: 这位领导者有远见，能够提前数年预测市场变化。

entries.definition: a. 梦想的；幻影的 n.空想家；梦想者
entries.etymology: "able to see visions," 1650s (earlier "perceived in a vision," 1640s), from vision + -ary. Meaning "impractical" is attested from 1727. The noun is attested from 1702, from the adjective; originally "one who indulges in impractical fantasies."
entries.etymologyZh: "able to see visions," 1650 年代 (earlier "perceived in a vision," 1640 年代), 源自 vision + -ary. 义为 "impractical" 见于 1727 年. The 名词 见于 1702 年, 源自 形容词; 原义为 "one who indulges in impractical fantasies."

entries.etymology: c. 1200, "come to (a person) to comfort or benefit," from Old French visiter "to visit; inspect, examine; afflict" (12c.) and directly from Latin visitare "to go to see, come to inspect," frequentative of visere "behold, visit" (a person or place), from past participle stem of videre "to see, notice, observe" (see vision). Originally of the deity, later of pastors and doctors (c. 1300), general sense of "pay a call" is from mid-13c. Meaning "come upon, afflict" (in reference to sickness, punishment, etc.) is recorded in English from mid-14c. Related: Visited; visiting.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "come to (a person) to comfort or benefit," 源自 古法语 visiter "to visit; inspect, examine; afflict" (12 世纪) and 直接源自 拉丁语 visitare "to go to see, come to inspect," 为 … 的反复体 visere "behold, visit" (a person or place), 源自 past participle stem of videre "to see, notice, observe" （参见 vision). Originally of the deity, later of pastors and doctors (约 1300 年), general 语义 "pay a call" 始于 13 世纪中期 义为 "come upon, afflict" (in reference to sickness, punishment, etc.) is recorded in English 源自 14 世纪中期 同源词：Visited; visiting.

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Anglo-French visitour, Old French visiteor "visitor, inspector," from visiter (see visit (v.)). Sports sense is from 1900.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, 源自 盎格鲁-法语 visitour, 古法语 visiteor "visitor, inspector," 源自 visiter （参见 visit （动）). Sports sense 始于 1900 年.

example.en: The museum welcomed over a million visitors last year.
example.zh: 博物馆去年接待了逾百万名参观者。

entries.etymology: early 15c., "pertaining to the faculty of sight;" also "coming from the eye or sight" (as a beam of light was thought to do), from Late Latin visualis "of sight," from Latin visus "a sight, a looking; power of sight; things seen, appearance," from visus, past participle of videre "to see" (see vision). Meaning "perceptible by sight" is from late 15c; sense of "relating to vision" is first attested c. 1600. The noun meaning "photographic film or other visual display" is first recorded 1944.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "pertaining to the faculty of sight;" also "coming from the eye or sight" (作为 beam of light was thought to do), 源自 晚期拉丁语 visualis "of sight," 源自 拉丁语 visus "a sight, a looking; power of sight; things seen, appearance," 源自 visus, 为 … 的过去分词 videre "to see" （参见 vision). 义为 "perceptible by sight" 始于 late 15c; 语义 "relating to vision" is 最早见于 约 1600 年. The 名词 意为 "photographic film or other visual display" is 首见于 1944 年.

example.en: The presentation relied heavily on visual aids to explain the data.
example.zh: 这场演讲大量借助视觉辅助手段来解释数据。

definitionLines: a. 极其重要的，致命的；生命 的，有生机的
entries.definition: a. 极其重要的，致命的；生命 的，有生机的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "of or manifesting life," from Latin vitalis "of or belonging to life," from vita "life," related to vivere "to live," from PIE root *gweie- (1) "to live" (see bio-). The sense of "necessary or important" is from 1610s, via the notion of "essential to life" (late 15c.). Vital capacity recorded from 1852. Related: Vitally.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "of or manifesting life," 源自 拉丁语 vitalis "of or belonging to life," 源自 vita "life," related to vivere "to live," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *gweie- (1) "to live" （参见 bio-). The 语义 "necessary or important" 始于 1610 年代, 经由 the 概念 "essential to life" (15 世纪晚期). Vital capacity recorded 自 1852 年起. 同源词：Vitally.

example.en: The nurse checked the patient's vital signs every fifteen minutes after surgery.
example.zh: 手术后，护士每十五分钟检查一次病人的生命体征。

entries.etymology: 1920, originally vitamine (1912) coined by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk (1884-1967), from Latin vita "life" (see vital) + amine, because they were thought to contain amino acids. The terminal -e formally was stripped off when scientists learned the true nature of the substance; -in was acceptable because it was used for neutral substances of undefined composition. The lettering system of nomenclature (Vitamin A, B, C, etc.) was introduced at the same time (1920).
entries.etymologyZh: 1920 年, 原义为 vitamine (1912 年) coined by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk (1884 年-1967 年), 源自 拉丁语 vita "life" （参见 vital) + amine, because they were thought to contain amino acids. The terminal -e formally was stripped off when scientists learned the true nature of the substance; -in was acceptable because it was used for neutral substances of undefined composition. The lettering system of nomenclature (Vitamin A, B, C, etc.) was introduced at the same time (1920 年).

example.en: Orange juice is a great source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system.
example.zh: 橙汁是维生素C的重要来源，有助于增强免疫系统。

definitionLines: a.生动的，栩栩如生的，鲜艳的
entries.definition: a.生动的，栩栩如生的，鲜艳的
entries.etymology: 1630s, from French vivide and perhaps also directly from Latin vividus "spirited, animated, lively, full of life," from vivus "alive," from PIE *gweie- (1) "to live" (see bio-). Extension to colors is from 1660s. Sense of "strong, distinct" (as of memories, etc.) is from 1680s; that of "very active or intense" (as of imagination, interest, etc.) is from 1853. Related: Vividly; vividness.
entries.etymologyZh: 1630 年代, 源自 法语 vivide and 或许 also 直接源自 拉丁语 vividus "spirited, animated, lively, full of life," 源自 vivus "alive," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *gweie- (1) "to live" （参见 bio-). Extension to colors 始于 1660 年代. 义为 "strong, distinct" (as of memories, etc.) 始于 1680 年代; that of "very active or intense" (as of imagination, interest, etc.) 始于 1853 年. 同源词：Vividly; vividness.

example.en: The author uses vivid language to bring the characters to life on the page.
example.zh: 作者用生动的语言让书页上的人物栩栩如生。

entries.etymology: 1530s, "list of words with explanations," from Medieval Latin vocabularium "a list of words," from Latin vocabulum "word, name, noun," from vocare "to name, call" (see voice (n.)). Meaning "range of words in the language of a person or group" is first attested 1753.
entries.etymologyZh: 1530 年代, "list of words with explanations," 源自 中古拉丁语 vocabularium "a list of words," 源自 拉丁语 vocabulum "word, name, noun," 源自 vocare "to name, call" （参见 voice （名）). 义为 "range of words in the language of a person or group" is 最早见于 1753 年.

example.en: Reading widely is one of the best ways to expand your vocabulary.
example.zh: 广泛阅读是扩大词汇量的最佳方法之一。

definitionLines: a. 声音的，有声的；歌唱的
entries.definition: a. 声音的，有声的；歌唱的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "spoken, oral," from Old French vocal (13c.), from Latin vocalis "sounding, sonorous, speaking," as a noun, "a vowel," from vox (genitive vocis) "voice" (see voice (n.)). In reference to music (as opposed to instrumental), first recorded 1580s; meaning "outspoken" first attested 1871. Vocal cords is from 1872; see cord.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "spoken, oral," 源自 古法语 vocal (13 世纪), 源自 拉丁语 vocalis "sounding, sonorous, speaking," 作名词时, "a vowel," 源自 vox (属格 vocis) "voice" （参见 voice （名）). In reference to music (as opposed to instrumental), 首见于 1580 年代; 意为 "outspoken" 最早见于 1871 年. Vocal cords 始于 1872 年; 参见 cord.

entries.etymology: early 15c., "spiritual calling," from Old French vocacion "call, consecration; calling, profession" (13c.) or directly from Latin vocationem (nominative vocatio), literally "a calling, a being called" from vocatus "called," past participle of vocare "to call" (see voice (n.)). Sense of "one's occupation or profession" is first attested 1550s.
entries.etymologyZh: 15 世纪初, "spiritual calling," 源自 古法语 vocacion "call, consecration; calling, profession" (13 世纪) or 直接源自 拉丁语 vocationem (主格 vocatio), 字面义为 "a calling, a being called" 源自 vocatus "called," 为 … 的过去分词 vocare "to call" （参见 voice （名）). 义为 "one's occupation or profession" is 最早见于 1550 年代.

entries.etymology:
late 13c., "sound made by the human mouth," from Old French voiz "voice, speech; word, saying, rumor, report" (Modern French voix), from Latin vocem (nominative vox) "voice, sound, utterance, cry, call, speech, sentence, language, word" (source also of Italian voce, Spanish voz), related to vocare "to call," from PIE root *wekw- "give vocal utterance, speak" (source also of Sanskrit vakti "speaks, says," vacas- "word;" Avestan vac- "speak, say;" Greek eipon (aorist) "spoke, said," epos "word;" Old Prussian wackis "cry;" German er-wähnen "to mention").

Replaced Old English stefn. Meaning "ability in a singer" is first attested c. 1600. Meaning "expression of feeling, etc." (in reference to groups of people, etc., such as Voice of America) is recorded from late 14c. Meaning "invisible spirit or force that directs or suggests" (especially in the context of insanity, as in hear voices in (one's) head) is from 1911.
entries.etymologyZh: 13 世纪晚期, "sound made by the human mouth," 源自 古法语 voiz "voice, speech; word, saying, rumor, report" (现代法语 voix), 源自 拉丁语 vocem (主格 vox) "voice, sound, utterance, cry, call, speech, sentence, language, word" (source also of 意大利语 voce, 西班牙语 voz), related to vocare "to call," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *wekw- "give vocal utterance, speak" (source also of 梵语 vakti "speaks, says," vacas- "word;" Avestan vac- "speak, say;" 希腊语 eipon (aorist) "spoke, said," epos "word;" Old Prussian wackis "cry;" 德语 er-wähnen "to mention"). Replaced 古英语 stefn. 义为 "ability in a singer" is 最早见于 约 1600 年. 义为 "expression of feeling, etc." (in reference to groups of people, etc., such as Voice of America) 见于 14 世纪晚期 义为 "invisible spirit or force that directs or suggests" (尤指 in the context of insanity, as in hear voices in (one's) head) 始于 1911 年.

example.en: Her voice trembled as she delivered the emotional speech.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "roll of parchment containing writing; a bound book," from Old French volume "scroll, book; work, volume; girth, size" (13c.) and directly from Latin volumen (genitive voluminis) "roll (of a manuscript); coil, wreath," literally "that which is rolled," from volvere "to turn around, roll" (see volvox). Generalized sense of "bulk, mass, quantity" (1620s) developed from that of "bulk or size of a book" (1520s), again following the sense evolution in the French word.

example.en: Please turn down the volume on the TV — I can barely hear myself think.

definitionLines: a. 志愿的；自愿的；自发的

entries.etymology: late 14c., from Latin voluntarius "willing, of one's free will," from voluntas "will," from the ancient accusative singular present participle of velle "to wish" (see will (v.)). Originally of feelings, later also of actions (mid-15c.). Related: Voluntarily.

example.en: Participation in the program is entirely voluntary and no one is forced to join.
example.zh: 参与该项目完全出于自愿，没有人被强迫加入。

Non-military sense is first recorded 1630s. As an adjective from 1640s. Tennessee has been the Volunteer State since the Mexican War, when a call for 2,800 volunteers brought out 30,000 men.

example.en: She signed up as a volunteer to help distribute food at the homeless shelter every weekend.
example.zh: 她报名成为志愿者，每周末在无家可归者收容所帮助分发食物。

example.en: All eligible citizens are urged to vote in tomorrow's presidential election.
example.zh: 所有合格的公民被敦促在明天的总统大选中投票。

example.en: It was a small wooden ship, yet it survived a perilous voyage around the Cape of Good Hope.

definitionLines: a. 粗俗的；通俗的；本土的
entries.definition: a. 粗俗的；通俗的；本土的
entries.etymology: late 14c., "common, ordinary," from Latin vulgaris, volgaris "of or pertaining to the common people, common, vulgar, low, mean," from vulgus "the common people, multitude, crowd, throng," perhaps from a PIE root *wel- "to crowd, throng" (source also of Sanskrit vargah "division, group," Greek eilein "to press, throng," Middle Breton gwal'ch "abundance," Welsh gwala "sufficiency, enough") [not in Watkins]. Meaning "coarse, low, ill-bred" is first recorded 1640s, probably from earlier use (with reference to people) with meaning "belonging to the ordinary class" (1530). Related: Vulgarly.
entries.etymologyZh: 14 世纪晚期, "common, ordinary," 源自 拉丁语 vulgaris, volgaris "of or pertaining to the common people, common, vulgar, low, mean," 源自 vulgus "the common people, multitude, crowd, throng," 或源自 a 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *wel- "to crowd, throng" (source also of 梵语 vargah "division, group," 希腊语 eilein "to press, throng," Middle Breton gwal'ch "abundance," Welsh gwala "sufficiency, enough") [not in Watkins]. 义为 "coarse, low, ill-bred" is 首见于 1640 年代, 可能 源自 earlier use (with reference to people) with 意为 "belonging to the ordinary class" (1530 年). 同源词：Vulgarly.

entries.definition: n.（pL.）工资，报酬 wag（p）on n.运货马车，运货车
entries.etymology:
c. 1300, "a payment for services rendered, reward, just deserts;" mid-14c., "salary paid to a provider of service," from Anglo-French and Old North French wage (Old French gage) "pledge, pay, reward," from Frankish *wadja- or another Germanic source (compare Old English wedd "pledge, agreement, covenant," Gothic wadi "pledge"), from Proto-Germanic *wadi- (see wed (v.)).

Also from mid-14c., "a pledge, guarantee, surety" (usually in plural), and (c. 1400) "a promise or pledge to meet in battle." The "payment for service" sense by late 14c. extended to allotments of money paid at regular intervals for continuous or repeated service. Traditionally in English wages were payment for manual or mechanical labor and somewhat distinguished from salary or fee. Modern French cognate gages (plural) means "wages of a domestic," one of a range of French "pay" words distinguished by class, such as traitement (university professor), paye, salaire (workman), solde (soldier), récompense, prix. The Old English word was lean, related to loan and representing the usual Germanic word (Gothic laun, Dutch loon, German lohn). Wage-earner attested from 1871.

Also 源自 14 世纪中期, "a pledge, guarantee, surety" (通常 in plural), and (约 1400 年) "a promise or pledge to meet in battle." The "payment for service" sense by 14 世纪晚期 extended to allotments of money paid at regular intervals for continuous or repeated service. Traditionally in English wages were payment for manual or mechanical labor and somewhat distinguished 源自 salary or fee. 现代法语 同源 gages (plural) means "wages of a domestic," one of a range of 法语 "pay" words distinguished by class, such as traitement (university professor), paye, salaire (workman), solde (soldier), récompense, prix. The 古英语 word was lean, related to loan and representing the usual 日耳曼语 word (Gothic laun, 荷兰语 loon, 德语 lohn). Wage-earner attested 自 1871 年起.

entries.etymology: late 14c., "middle part of the body," also "part of a garment fitted for the waist, portion of a garment that covers the waist" (but, due to fashion styles, often above or below it), probably from Old English *wæst "growth," hence, "where the body grows," from Proto-Germanic *wahs-tu- (source also of Old English wæstm, Old Norse vöxtr, Swedish växt, Old High German wahst "growth, increase," Gothic wahstus "stature," Old English weaxan "to grow" see wax (v.)), from PIE *wegs-, extended form of root *aug- (1) "to increase" (see augment).

entries.definition: v. 等候；伺候 n.等候，等待时间
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "to watch with hostile intent, lie in wait for, plot against," from Anglo-French and Old North French waitier "to watch" (Old French gaitier "defend, watch out, be on one's guard; lie in wait for;" Modern French guetter), from Frankish *wahton or another Germanic source, from Proto-Germanic *waht- (source also of Dutch wacht "a watching," Old High German wahten, German wachten "to watch, to guard;" Old High German wahhon "to watch, be awake," Old English wacian "to be awake;" see wake (v.)). General sense of "remain in some place" is from late 14c.; that of "to see to it that something occurs" is late 14c. Meaning "to stand by in attendance on" is late 14c.; specific sense of "serve as an attendant at a table" is from 1560s. Related: Waited; waiting.

To wait (something) out "endure a period of waiting" is recorded from 1849. Waiting room is attested from 1680s. Waiting list is recorded from 1841; the verb wait-list "to put (someone) on a waiting list" is recorded from 1960. Waiting game is recorded from 1835, originally in horse-racing.

General 语义 "remain in some place" 始于 14 世纪晚期; that of "to see to it that something occurs" is 14 世纪晚期 义为 "to stand by in attendance on" is 14 世纪晚期; specific 语义 "serve as an attendant at a table" 始于 1560 年代. 同源词：Waited; waiting. To wait (something) out "endure a period of waiting" 见于 1849 年. Waiting room 见于 1680 年代. Waiting list 见于 1841 年; the 动词 wait-list "to put (someone) on a waiting list" 见于 1960 年. Waiting game 见于 1835 年, 原义为 in horse-racing.

example.en: Customers had to wait over forty minutes just to get a table at the restaurant.
example.zh: 顾客不得不在餐厅等候超过四十分钟才能入座。

entries.etymology: late 14c., "attendant, watchman," agent noun from wait (v.). Sense of "attendant at a meal, servant who waits at tables" is from late 15c., originally in reference to household servants; in reference to inns, eating houses, etc., it is attested from 1660s.

definitionLines: vt. 醒来，唤醒；使觉悟，激发， 引起
entries.definition: vt. 醒来，唤醒；使觉悟，激发， 引起 vi. 醒来
entries.etymology: "to become awake," a Middle English merger of Old English wacan "to become awake, arise, be born, originate," and Old English wacian "to be or remain awake," both from Proto-Germanic *waken (source also of Old Saxon wakon, Old Norse vaka, Danish vaage, Old Frisian waka, Dutch waken, Old High German wahhen, German wachen "to be awake," Gothic wakan "to watch"), from PIE root *weg- (2) "to be strong, be lively" (source also of Sanskrit vajah "force, strength; swiftness, speed," vajayati "drives on;" Latin vigil "watchful, awake,"  vigere "be lively, thrive," velox "fast, lively," vegere "to enliven;" vigil "awake, wakeful," vigor "liveliness, activity"). Causative sense "to rouse from sleep" is attested from c. 1300. Related: Waked; waking.
entries.etymologyZh: "to become awake," a 中古英语 merger of 古英语 wacan "to become awake, arise, be born, originate," and 古英语 wacian "to be or remain awake," both 源自 原始日耳曼语 *waken (source also of 古撒克逊语 wakon, 古北欧语 vaka, Danish vaage, 古弗里西语 waka, 荷兰语 waken, 古高地德语 wahhen, 德语 wachen "to be awake," Gothic wakan "to watch"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *weg- (2) "to be strong, be lively" (source also of 梵语 vajah "force, strength; swiftness, speed," vajayati "drives on;" 拉丁语 vigil "watchful, awake," vigere "be lively, thrive," velox "fast, lively," vegere "to enliven;" vigil "awake, wakeful," vigor "liveliness, activity"). Causative sense "to rouse from sleep" 见于 约 1300 年. 同源词：Waked; waking.

example.en: The alarm clock failed to wake him from his unusually deep sleep that morning.
example.zh: 那天早上闹钟未能将他从异常深沉的睡眠中唤醒。

entries.definition: vt. 唤醒；使觉醒 vi. 醒来；觉醒
entries.etymology: "to become awake, cease to sleep," Old English wæcnan, wæcnian "to rise, awake; spring from, come into being," from the same source as wake (v.). OED regards the ending as the -n- "suffix of inchoative verbs of state," but Barnhart rejects this and says it is simply -en (1). Figurative sense was in Old English. Transitive sense of "to rouse (someone or something) from sleep" is recorded from c. 1200. Related: Wakened; wakening.
entries.etymologyZh: "to become awake, cease to sleep," 古英语 wæcnan, wæcnian "to rise, awake; spring from, come into being," 源自 same source as wake （动）. OED regards the ending as the -n- "suffix of inchoative verbs of state," but Barnhart rejects this and says it is simply -en (1). Figurative sense was in 古英语. Transitive 语义 "to rouse (someone or something) from sleep" 见于 约 1200 年. 同源词：Wakened; wakening.

entries.definition: vi. /n. 步行，散步 n. 人行道，散步场所
entries.etymology:
"travel on foot," c. 1200, a merger of two verbs, 1. Old English wealcan "to toss, roll, move round" (past tense weolc, past participle wealcen), and 2. wealcian "to roll up, curl," from Proto-Germanic *welk- (source also of Old Norse valka "to drag about," Danish valke "to full" (cloth), Middle Dutch walken "to knead, press, full" (cloth), Old High German walchan "to knead," German walken "to full"), perhaps ultimately from PIE root *wel- (3) "to turn, roll" (see volvox).

The shift in sense is perhaps from a colloquial use of the Old English word or via the sense of "to full cloth" (by treading on it), though this sense does not appear until after the change in meaning. In 13c. it is used of snakes and the passage of time, and in 15c. of wheeled carts. "Rarely is there so specific a word as NE walk, clearly distinguished from both go and run" [Buck]. Meaning "to go away" is recorded from mid-15c. Transitive meaning "to exercise a dog (or horse)" is from late 15c.; meaning "to escort (someone) in a walk" is from 1620s. Meaning "move (a heavy object) by turning and shoving it in a manner suggesting walking" is by 1890. To walk it off, of an injury, etc., is from 1741. Related: Walked; walking.
entries.etymologyZh: "travel on foot," 约 1200 年, a merger of two verbs, 1. 古英语 wealcan "to toss, roll, move round" (past tense weolc, past participle wealcen), and 2. wealcian "to roll up, curl," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *welk- (source also of 古北欧语 valka "to drag about," Danish valke "to full" (cloth), Middle 荷兰语 walken "to knead, press, full" (cloth), 古高地德语 walchan "to knead," 德语 walken "to full"), 或许 最终源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *wel- (3) "to turn, roll" （参见 volvox). The shift in sense is 或源自 a 口语 use of the 古英语 word or 经由 the 语义 "to full cloth" (by treading on it), though this sense does not appear until after the change in 意为. In 13 世纪 it is used of snakes and the passage of time, and in 15 世纪 of wheeled carts. "Rarely is there so specific a word as NE walk, clearly distinguished from both go and run" [Buck]. 义为 "to go away" 见于 15 世纪中期 Transitive 意为 "to exercise a dog (or horse)" 始于 15 世纪晚期; 意为 "to escort (someone) in a walk" 始于 1620 年代. 义为 "move (a heavy object) by turning and shoving it in a manner suggesting walking" is 截至 1890 年. To walk it off, of an injury, etc., 始于 1741 年. 同源词：Walked; walking.

example.en: It only takes ten minutes to walk from here to the train station.
example.zh: 从这里步行到火车站只需十分钟。

entries.etymology:
Old English weall, Anglian wall "rampart, dike, earthwork" (natural as well as man-made), "dam, cliff, rocky shore," also "defensive fortification around a city, side of a building," an Anglo-Frisian and Saxon borrowing (Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Middle Low German, Middle Dutch wal) from Latin vallum "wall, rampart, row or line of stakes," apparently a collective form of vallus "stake," from PIE *walso- "a post." Swedish vall, Danish val are from Low German.

Meaning "interior partition of a structure" is mid-13c. In this case, English uses one word where many languages have two, such as German Mauer "outer wall of a town, fortress, etc.," used also in reference to the former Berlin Wall, and wand "partition wall within a building" (compare the distinction, not always rigorously kept, in Italian muro/parete, Irish mur/fraig, Lithuanian muras/siena, etc.). The Latin word for "defensive wall" was murus (see mural).

Anatomical use from late 14c. To give (someone) the wall "allow him or her to walk on the (cleaner) wall side of the pavement" is from 1530s. To turn (one's) face to the wall "prepare to die" is from 1570s. Phrase up the wall "angry, crazy" is from 1951; off the wall "unorthodox, unconventional" is recorded from 1966, American English student slang. To go over the wall "escape" (originally from prison) is from 1933. Wall-to-wall (adj.) recorded 1939, of shelving, etc.; metaphoric use (usually disparaging) is from 1967.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 weall, Anglian wall "rampart, dike, earthwork" (natural as well as man-made), "dam, cliff, rocky shore," also "defensive fortification around a city, side of a building," an Anglo-Frisian and Saxon borrowing (古撒克逊语, 古弗里西语, Middle Low 德语, Middle 荷兰语 wal) 源自 拉丁语 vallum "wall, rampart, row or line of stakes," 似乎 a collective form of vallus "stake," 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *walso- "a post." Swedish vall, Danish val 始于 Low 德语. 义为 "interior partition of a structure" is 13 世纪中期 In this case, English uses one word where many languages have two, such as 德语 Mauer "outer wall of a town, fortress, etc.," used also in reference to the former Berlin Wall, and wand "partition wall within a building" (对比 the distinction, not always rigorously kept, in 意大利语 muro/parete, 爱尔兰语 mur/fraig, Lithuanian muras/siena, etc.). The 拉丁语 word for "defensive wall" was murus （参见 mural). Anatomical use 源自 14 世纪晚期 To give (someone) the wall "allow him or her to walk on the (cleaner) wall side of the pavement" 始于 1530 年代. To turn (one's) face to the wall "prepare to die" 始于 1570 年代. Phrase up the wall "angry, crazy" 始于 1951 年; off the wall "unorthodox, unconventional" 见于 1966 年, American English student 俚语. To go over the wall "escape" (原义为 源自 prison) 始于 1933 年. Wall-to-wall （形） recorded 1939 年, of shelving, etc.; metaphoric use (通常 disparaging) 始于 1967 年.

Meaning "flat case for carrying paper money" is first recorded 1834, American English.

entries.etymology:
late Old English wyrre, werre "large-scale military conflict," from Old North French werre "war" (Old French guerre "difficulty, dispute; hostility; fight, combat, war;" Modern French guerre), from Frankish *werra, from Proto-Germanic *werz-a- (source also of Old Saxon werran, Old High German werran, German verwirren "to confuse, perplex"), from PIE *wers- (1) "to confuse, mix up". Cognates suggest the original sense was "to bring into confusion."

Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian guerra also are from Germanic; Romanic peoples turned to Germanic for a "war" word possibly to avoid Latin bellum because its form tended to merge with bello- "beautiful." There was no common Germanic word for "war" at the dawn of historical times. Old English had many poetic words for "war" (wig, guð, heaðo, hild, all common in personal names), but the usual one to translate Latin bellum was gewin "struggle, strife" (related to win (v.)).

First record of war time is late 14c. Warpath (1775) is originally in reference to North American Indians, as are war-whoop (1761), war-paint (1826), and war-dance (1757). War crime first attested 1906 (in Oppenheim's "International Law"). War chest is attested from 1901; now usually figurative. War games translates German Kriegspiel (see kriegspiel).

There was no common 日耳曼语 word for "war" at the dawn of historical times. 古英语 had many poetic words for "war" (wig, guð, heaðo, hild, all common in personal names), but the usual one to translate 拉丁语 bellum was gewin "struggle, strife" (related to win （动）). First record of war time is 14 世纪晚期 Warpath (1775 年) is 原义为 in reference to North American Indians, as are war-whoop (1761 年), war-paint (1826 年), and war-dance (1757 年). War crime 最早见于 1906 年 (in Oppenheim's "International Law"). War chest 见于 1901 年; 现在 通常 figurative. War games translates 德语 Kriegspiel （参见 kriegspiel).

entries.etymology: Old English weard "a guarding, protection; watchman, sentry, keeper," from Proto-Germanic *wardaz "guard" (source also of Old Saxon ward, Old Norse vörðr, Old High German wart), from PIE *war-o-, from root *wer- (4) "perceive, watch out for" (source also of Latin vereri "to observe with awe, revere, respect, fear;" Greek ouros "a guard, watchman," and possibly horan "to see;" Hittite werite- "to see"). Used for administrative districts (at first in the sense of guardianship) from late 14c.; of hospital divisions from 1749. Meaning "minor under control of a guardian" is from early 15c. Ward-heeler is 1890, from heeler "loafer, one on the lookout for shady work" (1870s).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 weard "a guarding, protection; watchman, sentry, keeper," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wardaz "guard" (source also of 古撒克逊语 ward, 古北欧语 vörðr, 古高地德语 wart), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *war-o-, 源自 root *wer- (4) "perceive, watch out for" (source also of 拉丁语 vereri "to observe with awe, revere, respect, fear;" 希腊语 ouros "a guard, watchman," and possibly horan "to see;" Hittite werite- "to see"). Used for administrative districts (at first in the 语义 guardianship) 源自 14 世纪晚期; of hospital divisions 自 1749 年起. 义为 "minor under control of a guardian" 始于 15 世纪初 Ward-heeler is 1890 年, 源自 heeler "loafer, one on the lookout for shady work" (1870 年代).

entries.etymology: early 14c., "room where wearing apparel is kept," earlier "a private chamber" (c. 1300), from Old North French warderobe, wardereube (Old French garderobe) "dressing-room, place where garments are kept," from warder "to keep, guard" (see ward (v.)) + robe "garment" (see robe (n.)). Meaning "a person's stock of clothes for wearing" is recorded from c. 1400. Sense of "movable closed cupboard for wearing apparel" is recorded from 1794. Meaning "room in which theatrical costumes are kept" is attested from 1711. Wardrobe malfunction is from 2004.

entries.definition: a. 暖，温暖；热忱，热心 v. 使暖
entries.etymology:
Old English wearm "warm," from Proto-Germanic *warmaz (source also of Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Middle Dutch, Old High German, German warm, Old Norse varmr, Gothic warmjan "to warm"), of uncertain origin. On one guess it is from PIE *gwher- (source also of Sanskrit gharmah "heat;" Old Persian Garmapada-, name of the fourth month, corresponding to June/July, from garma- "heat;" Armenian jerm "warm;" Greek thermos "warm;" Latin formus "warm," fornax "oven;" Old Irish fogeir "heated;" Hittite war- "to burn"). On another guess it is connected to the source of Old Church Slavonic goriti "to burn," varŭ "heat," variti "to cook, boil;" and Lithuanian vérdu "to seethe."

The use of distinct words, based on degree of heat, for warm and hot is general in Balto-Slavic and Germanic, but in other languages one word often covers both (Greek thermos; Latin calidus, French chaud, Spanish caliente). In reference to feelings, etc., attested from late 15c. Of colors from 1764. Sense in guessing games first recorded 1860, from earlier hunting use in reference to scent or trail (1713). Warm-blooded in reference to mammals is recorded from 1793. Warm-hearted first recorded c. 1500.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 wearm "warm," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *warmaz (source also of 古撒克逊语, 古弗里西语, Middle 荷兰语, 古高地德语, 德语 warm, 古北欧语 varmr, Gothic warmjan "to warm"), 来源存疑. On one guess it 始于 原始印欧语 (PIE) *gwher- (source also of 梵语 gharmah "heat;" Old 波斯语 Garmapada-, name of the fourth month, corresponding to June/July, 源自 garma- "heat;" Armenian jerm "warm;" 希腊语 thermos "warm;" 拉丁语 formus "warm," fornax "oven;" Old 爱尔兰语 fogeir "heated;" Hittite war- "to burn"). On another guess it is connected to the source of Old Church Slavonic goriti "to burn," varŭ "heat," variti "to cook, boil;" and Lithuanian vérdu "to seethe." The use of distinct words, based on degree of heat, for warm and hot is general in Balto-Slavic and 日耳曼语, but in other languages one word 常 covers both (希腊语 thermos; 拉丁语 calidus, 法语 chaud, 西班牙语 caliente). In reference to feelings, etc., attested 源自 15 世纪晚期 Of colors 自 1764 年起. Sense in guessing games 首见于 1860 年, 源自 earlier hunting use in reference to scent or trail (1713 年). Warm-blooded in reference to mammals 见于 1793 年. Warm-hearted 首见于 约 1500 年.

example.en: She gave us a warm welcome by hugging each of us at the door.

entries.etymology: Old English warnian "to give notice of impending danger," also intransitive, "to take heed," from Proto-Germanic *warnon (source also of Old Norse varna "to admonish," Old High German warnon "to take heed," German warnen "to warn"), from PIE *wer- (5) "to cover" (see weir). Related: Warned; warning.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 warnian "to give notice of impending danger," also intransitive, "to take heed," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *warnon (source also of 古北欧语 varna "to admonish," 古高地德语 warnon "to take heed," 德语 warnen "to warn"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *wer- (5) "to cover" （参见 weir). 同源词：Warned; warning.

definitionLines: n. 证明；保证；许可证；授权
vt. 保证；担保；辩解；批准
entries.definition: n. 证明；保证；许可证；授权 vt. 保证；担保；辩解；批准
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "protector, defender," from Old North French warant "defender; surety, pledge; justifying evidence" (Old French garant), from Frankish *warand, from Proto-Germanic *war- "to warn, guard, protect" (source also of Old High German werento "guarantor," noun use of present participle of weren "to authorize, warrant;" German gewähren "to grant"), from PIE root *wer- (5) "to cover" (see weir).

Sense evolved via notion of "permission from a superior which protects one from blame or responsibility" (early 14c.) to "document conveying authority" (1510s). A warrant officer in the military is one who holds office by warrant (as from a government department), rather than by commission (from a head of state).
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "protector, defender," 源自 Old North 法语 warant "defender; surety, pledge; justifying evidence" (古法语 garant), 源自 Frankish *warand, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *war- "to warn, guard, protect" (source also of 古高地德语 werento "guarantor," 为 … 的名词用法 为 … 的现在分词 weren "to authorize, warrant;" 德语 gewähren "to grant"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) root *wer- (5) "to cover" （参见 weir). Sense evolved 经由 概念 "permission from a superior which protects one from blame or responsibility" (14 世纪初) to "document conveying authority" (1510 年代). A warrant officer in the military is one who holds office by warrant (as 源自 a government department), rather than by commission (源自 a head of state).

example.en: The evidence does not warrant such a drastic response from the authorities.

entries.definition: v./n. 洗，冲洗 v.（浪涛）冲刷，拍打 n. 洗涤物，衣服
entries.etymology:
Old English wascan "to wash, cleanse, bathe," transitive sense in late Old English, from Proto-Germanic *watskan "to wash" (source also of Old Norse vaska, Middle Dutch wasscen, Dutch wassen, German waschen), from stem *wed- "water, wet" (see water (n.1)). Related: Washed; washing.

Used mainly of clothes in Old English (the principal verb for washing the body, dishes, etc. being þwean). Old French gaschier "to stain, soil; soak, wash" (Modern French gâcher) is from Frankish *waskan, from the same Germanic source. Italian guazzare also is a Germanic loan-word. To wash (one's) hands of something id 1550s, from Pilate in Matt. xxvii.24. To wash up "clean utensils after a meal" is from 1751. Washed up "no longer effective" is 1923, theater slang, from notion of washing up at the end of a job.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 wascan "to wash, cleanse, bathe," transitive sense in late 古英语, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *watskan "to wash" (source also of 古北欧语 vaska, Middle 荷兰语 wasscen, 荷兰语 wassen, 德语 waschen), 源自 stem *wed- "water, wet" （参见 water (n.1)). 同源词：Washed; washing. Used mainly of clothes in 古英语 (the principal 动词 for washing the body, dishes, etc. being þwean). 古法语 gaschier "to stain, soil; soak, wash" (现代法语 gâcher) 始于 Frankish *waskan, 源自 same 日耳曼语 source. 意大利语 guazzare also is a 日耳曼语 loan-word. To wash (one's) hands of something id 1550 年代, 源自 Pilate in Matt. xxvii.24. To wash up "clean utensils after a meal" 始于 1751 年. Washed up "no longer effective" is 1923 年, theater 俚语, 源自 概念 washing up at the end of a job.

example.en: She told the kids to wash their muddy boots at the door before entering.
example.zh: 她让孩子们进门前在门口把泥靴子洗干净。

entries.definition: a.荒废的，没用的 vt./n. 浪费，消耗 n.废物，废品
entries.etymology:
c. 1200, "devastate, ravage, ruin," from Anglo-French and Old North French waster "to waste, squander, spoil, ruin" (Old French gaster; Modern French gâter), altered (by influence of Frankish *wostjan) from Latin vastare "lay waste," from vastus "empty, desolate, waste" (see vain). Related: wasted; wasting.

The Germanic word also existed in Old English as westan "to lay waste, ravage." Spanish gastar, Italian guastare also are from Germanic. Meaning "to lose strength or health; pine; weaken" is attested from c. 1300; the sense of "squander, spend or consume uselessly" is first recorded mid-14c.; meaning "to kill" is from 1964. Waste not, want not attested from 1778.
entries.etymologyZh: 约 1200 年, "devastate, ravage, ruin," 源自 盎格鲁-法语 and Old North 法语 waster "to waste, squander, spoil, ruin" (古法语 gaster; 现代法语 gâter), altered (by influence of Frankish *wostjan) 源自 拉丁语 vastare "lay waste," 源自 vastus "empty, desolate, waste" （参见 vain). 同源词：wasted; wasting. The 日耳曼语 word also existed in 古英语 as westan "to lay waste, ravage." 西班牙语 gastar, 意大利语 guastare also 始于 日耳曼语. 义为 "to lose strength or health; pine; weaken" 见于 约 1300 年; the 语义 "squander, spend or consume uselessly" is 首见于 14 世纪中期; 意为 "to kill" 始于 1964 年. Waste not, want not attested 自 1778 年起.

example.en: It would be a waste to throw away all that perfectly good food.
example.zh: 把那些完好的食物都扔掉真是一种浪费。

entries.etymology: Old English wæccan "keep watch, be awake," from Proto-Germanic *wakjan, from PIE *weg- (2) "to be strong, lively;" essentially the same word as Old English wacian "be or remain awake" (see wake (v.)); perhaps a Northumbrian form of it. Meaning "be vigilant" is from c. 1200. That of "to guard (someone or some place), stand guard" is late 14c. Sense of "to observe, keep under observance" is mid-15c. Related: Watched; watching.

entries.etymology: Old English weax "substance made by bees," from Proto-Germanic *wahsam (source also of Old Saxon, Old High German wahs, Old Norse vax, Dutch was, German Wachs), from PIE root *wokso- "wax" (source also of Old Church Slavonic voskŭ, Lithuanian vaškas, Polish wosk, Russian vosk "wax" (but these may be from Germanic). definitionLines: n. 道路，路程；方法，手段，方式； 习惯，作风；状态，情况
entries.definition: n. 道路，路程；方法，手段，方式； 习惯，作风；状态，情况
entries.etymology:
Old English weg "road, path; course of travel; room, space, freedom of movement;" also, figuratively, "course of life" especially, in plural, "habits of life" as regards moral, ethical, or spiritual choices, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz (source also of Old Saxon, Dutch weg, Old Norse vegr, Old Frisian wei, Old High German weg, German Weg, Gothic wigs "way"), from PIE *wegh- "to move" (see weigh).

From c. 1300 as "manner in which something occurs." Adverbial constructions attested since Middle English include this way "in this direction," that way "in that direction," both from late 15c.; out of the way "remote" (c. 1300). In the way "so placed as to impede" is from 1560s.

From the "course of life" sense comes way of life (c. 1600), get (or have) one's way (1590s), have it (one's) way (1709). From the "course of travel" sense comes the figurative go separate ways (1837); one way or (the) other (1550s); have it both ways (1847); and the figurative sense of come a long way (1922).

Adverbial phrase all the way "completely, to conclusion" is by 1915; sexual sense implied by 1924. Make way is from c. 1200. Ways and means "resources at a person's disposal" is attested from early 15c. Way out "means of exit" is from 1926. Encouragement phrase way to go is short for that's the way to go.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 weg "road, path; course of travel; room, space, freedom of movement;" also, figuratively, "course of life" 尤指, in plural, "habits of life" as regards moral, ethical，或spiritual choices, 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wegaz (source also of 古撒克逊语, 荷兰语 weg, 古北欧语 vegr, 古弗里西语 wei, 古高地德语 weg, 德语 Weg, Gothic wigs "way"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *wegh- "to move" （参见 weigh). From 约 1300 年 as "manner in which something occurs." Adverbial constructions attested 自 中古英语 include this way "in this direction," that way "in that direction," both 源自 15 世纪晚期; out of the way "remote" (约 1300 年). In the way "so placed as to impede" 始于 1560 年代. From the "course of life" sense comes way of life (约 1600 年), get (or have) one's way (1590s), have it (one's) way (1709 年). From the "course of travel" sense comes the figurative go separate ways (1837 年); one way or (the) other (1550 年代); have it both ways (1847 年); and the figurative 语义 come a long way (1922 年). Adverbial phrase all the way "completely, to conclusion" is 截至 1915 年; sexual sense implied 截至 1924 年. Make way 始于 约 1200 年. Ways and means "resources at a person's disposal" 见于 15 世纪初 Way out "means of exit" 始于 1926 年. Encouragement phrase way to go is short for that's the way to go.

entries.etymology:
Old English we, first person plural pronoun, "I and another or others," from Proto-Germanic *wiz (source also of Old Saxon wi, Old Norse ver, Danish vi, Old Frisian wi, Dutch wij, Old High German and German wir, Gothic weis "we"), from PIE *we- (source also of Sanskrit vayam, Old Persian vayam, Hittite wesh "we," Old Church Slavonic ve "we two," Lithuanian vedu "we two").

The "royal we" (use of plural pronoun to denote oneself) is at least as old as "Beowulf" (c.725); use by writers to establish an impersonal style is also from Old English; it was especially common 19c. in unsigned editorials, to suggest staff consensus, and was lampooned as such since at least 1853 (see wegotism).
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 we, first person plural pronoun, "I and another or others," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wiz (source also of 古撒克逊语 wi, 古北欧语 ver, Danish vi, 古弗里西语 wi, 荷兰语 wij, 古高地德语 and 德语 wir, Gothic weis "we"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *we- (source also of 梵语 vayam, Old 波斯语 vayam, Hittite wesh "we," Old Church Slavonic ve "we two," Lithuanian vedu "we two"). The "royal we" (use of plural pronoun to denote oneself) is at least as old as "Beowulf" (约 725 年); use by writers to establish an impersonal style is 亦源自 古英语; it was 尤指 common 19 世纪 in unsigned editorials, to suggest staff consensus, and was lampooned as such 自 at least 1853 年 （参见 wegotism).

entries.etymology:
c. 1300, from Old Norse veikr "weak," cognate with Old English wac "weak, pliant, soft," from Proto-Germanic *waikwa- "yield" (source also of Old Saxon wek, Swedish vek, Middle Dutch weec, Dutch week "weak, soft, tender," Old High German weih "yielding, soft," German weich "soft"), from PIE root *weik- (4) "to bend, wind" (see vicarious).

Sense of "lacking authority" is first recorded early 15c.; that of "lacking moral strength" late 14c. In grammar, denoting a verb inflected by regular syllabic addition rather than by change of the radical vowel, from 1833. Related: Weakly. Weak-kneed "wanting in resolve" is from 1870.

Weak-kneed "wanting in resolve" 始于 1870 年.

entries.etymology:
Old English werian "to clothe, put on, cover up," from Proto-Germanic *wazjan (source also of Old Norse verja, Old High German werian, Gothic gawasjan "to clothe"), from PIE *wos-eyo-, from root *wes- (4) "to clothe" (source also of Sanskrit vaste "he puts on," vasanam "garment;" Avestan vah-; Greek esthes "clothing," hennymi "to clothe," eima "garment;" Latin vestire "to clothe;" Welsh gwisgo, Breton gwiska; Old English wæstling "sheet, blanket;" Hittite washshush "garments," washanzi "they dress").

The Germanic forms "were homonyms of the vb. for 'prevent, ward off, protect' (Goth. warjan, O.E. werian, etc.), and this was prob. a factor in their early displacement in most of the Gmc. languages" [Buck]. Shifted from a weak verb (past tense and past participle wered) to a strong one (past tense wore, past participle worn) in 14c. on analogy of rhyming strong verbs such as bear and tear. Secondary sense of "use up, gradually damage" (late 13c.) is from effect of continued use on clothes. To wear down (transitive) "overcome by steady force" is from 1843. To wear off "diminish by attrition or use" is from 1690s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 werian "to clothe, put on, cover up," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wazjan (source also of 古北欧语 verja, 古高地德语 werian, Gothic gawasjan "to clothe"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *wos-eyo-, 源自 root *wes- (4) "to clothe" (source also of 梵语 vaste "he puts on," vasanam "garment;" Avestan vah-; 希腊语 esthes "clothing," hennymi "to clothe," eima "garment;" 拉丁语 vestire "to clothe;" Welsh gwisgo, Breton gwiska; 古英语 wæstling "sheet, blanket;" Hittite washshush "garments," washanzi "they dress"). The 日耳曼语 forms "were homonyms of the vb. for 'prevent, ward off, protect' (Goth. warjan, O.E. werian, etc.), and this was prob. a factor in their early displacement in most of the Gmc. languages" [Buck]. Shifted 源自 a weak 动词 (past tense and past participle wered) to a strong one (past tense wore, past participle worn) in 14 世纪 on analogy of rhyming strong verbs such as bear and tear. Secondary 语义 "use up, gradually damage" (13 世纪晚期) 始于 effect of continued use on clothes. To wear down (transitive) "overcome by steady force" 始于 1843 年. To wear off "diminish by attrition or use" 始于 1690 年代.

entries.etymology:
Old English weder "air, sky; breeze, storm, tempest," from Proto-Germanic *wedram "wind, weather" (source also of Old Saxon wedar, Old Norse veðr, Old Frisian, Middle Dutch, Dutch weder, Old High German wetar, German Wetter "storm, wind, weather"), from PIE *we-dhro-, "weather" (source also of Lithuanian vetra "storm," Old Church Slavonic vedro "good weather"), from root *we- "to blow" (see wind (n.1)). Alteration of -d- to -th- begins late 15c., though such pronunciation may be older (see father (n.)).

In nautical use, as an adjective, "toward the wind" (opposed to lee). Greek had words for "good weather" (aithria, eudia) and words for "storm" and "winter," but no generic word for "weather" until kairos (literally "time") began to be used as such in Byzantine times. Latin tempestas "weather" (see tempest) also originally meant "time;" and words for "time" also came to mean weather in Irish (aimsir), Serbo-Croatian (vrijeme), Polish (czas), etc. Weather-report is from 1863. Weather-breeder "fine, serene day which precedes and seems to prepare a storm" is from 1650s.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 weder "air, sky; breeze, storm, tempest," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wedram "wind, weather" (source also of 古撒克逊语 wedar, 古北欧语 veðr, 古弗里西语, Middle 荷兰语, 荷兰语 weder, 古高地德语 wetar, 德语 Wetter "storm, wind, weather"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *we-dhro-, "weather" (source also of Lithuanian vetra "storm," Old Church Slavonic vedro "good weather"), 源自 root *we- "to blow" （参见 wind (n.1)). Alteration of -d- to -th- begins 15 世纪晚期, though such pronunciation may be older （参见 father （名）). In nautical use, 作形容词时, "toward the wind" (opposed to lee). 希腊语 had words for "good weather" (aithria, eudia) and words for "storm" and "winter," but no generic word for "weather" until kairos (字面义为 "time") began to be used as such in Byzantine times. 拉丁语 tempestas "weather" （参见 tempest) also 原义为 meant "time;" and words for "time" also came to mean weather in 爱尔兰语 (aimsir), Serbo-Croatian (vrijeme), Polish (czas), etc. Weather-report 始于 1863 年. Weather-breeder "fine, serene day which precedes and seems to prepare a storm" 始于 1650 年代.

entries.etymology:
Old English webb "woven fabric, woven work, tapestry," from Proto-Germanic *wabjam "fabric, web" (source also of Old Saxon webbi, Old Norse vefr, Dutch webbe, Old High German weppi, German gewebe "web"), from PIE *webh- "to weave" (see weave (v.)).

Meaning "spider's web" is first recorded early 13c. Applied to the membranes between the toes of ducks and other aquatic birds from 1570s. Internet sense is from 1992, shortened from World Wide Web (1990). Web browser, web page both also attested 1990.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 webb "woven fabric, woven work, tapestry," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wabjam "fabric, web" (source also of 古撒克逊语 webbi, 古北欧语 vefr, 荷兰语 webbe, 古高地德语 weppi, 德语 gewebe "web"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *webh- "to weave" （参见 weave （动）). 义为 "spider's web" is 首见于 13 世纪初 Applied to the membranes between the toes of ducks and other aquatic birds 源自 1570 年代. Internet sense 始于 1992 年, shortened 源自 World Wide Web (1990 年). Web browser, web page both also attested 1990 年.

entries.etymology: Old English weddung "state of being wed; pledge, betrothal; action of marrying," verbal noun from wed (v.). Meaning "nuptials, ceremony of marriage" is recorded from early 13c.; the usual Old English word for the ceremony was bridelope, literally "bridal run," in reference to conducting the bride to her new home. Wedding ring is from late 14c.; wedding cake is recorded from 1640s, as a style of architecture from 1879. Wedding-dress attested from 1779; wedding-reception from 1856.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 weddung "state of being wed; pledge, betrothal; action of marrying," verbal 名词 源自 wed （动）. 义为 "nuptials, ceremony of marriage" 见于 13 世纪初; the usual 古英语 word for the ceremony was bridelope, 字面义为 "bridal run," in reference to conducting the bride to her new home. Wedding ring 始于 14 世纪晚期; wedding cake 见于 1640 年代, 作为 style of architecture 自 1879 年起. Wedding-dress attested 自 1779 年起; wedding-reception 自 1856 年起.

example.en: They chose a small church for their wedding ceremony.

entries.etymology: Old English wecg "a wedge," from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz (source also of Old Norse veggr, Middle Dutch wegge, Dutch wig, Old High German weggi "wedge," dialectal German Weck "wedge-shaped bread roll"), of uncertain origin; perhaps related to Latin vomer "plowshare." From 1610s in reference to other things shaped like a wedge. Of women's shoes or shoe-heels, from 1939. Wedge issue is attested from 1999.

entries.etymology:
fourth day of the week, Old English wodnesdæg "Woden's day," a Germanic loan-translation of Latin dies Mercurii "day of Mercury" (compare Old Norse Oðinsdagr, Swedish Onsdag, Old Frisian Wonsdei, Middle Dutch Wudensdach). For Woden, see Odin.

Contracted pronunciation is recorded from 15c. The Odin-based name is missing in German (mittwoch, from Old High German mittwocha, literally "mid-week"), probably by influence of Gothic, which seems to have adopted a pure ecclesiastical (i.e. non-astrological) week from Greek missionaries. The Gothic model also seems to be the source of Polish środa, Russian sreda "Wednesday," literally "middle."
entries.etymologyZh: fourth day of the week, 古英语 wodnesdæg "Woden's day," a 日耳曼语 loan-translation of 拉丁语 dies Mercurii "day of Mercury" (对比 古北欧语 Oðinsdagr, Swedish Onsdag, 古弗里西语 Wonsdei, Middle 荷兰语 Wudensdach). For Woden, 参见 Odin. Contracted pronunciation 见于 15 世纪 The Odin-based name is missing in 德语 (mittwoch, 源自 古高地德语 mittwocha, 字面义为 "mid-week"), 可能 by influence of Gothic, which seems to have adopted a pure ecclesiastical (i.e. non-astrological) week 源自 希腊语 missionaries. The Gothic model also seems to be the source of Polish środa, 俄语 sreda "Wednesday," 字面义为 "middle."

entries.definition: n. 杂草，野草 v. 除草，锄草
entries.etymology: "plant not valued for use or beauty," Old English weod, uueod "grass, herb, weed," from Proto-Germanic *weud- (source also of Old Saxon wiod, East Frisian wiud), of unknown origin. Also applied to trees that grow abundantly. Meaning "tobacco" is from c. 1600; that of "marijuana" is from 1920s. The chemical weed-killer is attested by 1885.

entries.etymology:
Old English wucu, wice, etc., from Proto-Germanic *wikon (source also of Old Norse vika, Old Frisian wike, Middle Dutch weke, Old High German wecha, German woche), probably originally with the sense of "a turning" or "succession" (compare Gothic wikon "in the course of," Old Norse vika "sea-mile," originally "change of oar," Old English wican "yield, give way"), from PIE root *weik- (4) "to bend, wind" (see vicarious). The vowel sound seems to have been uncertain in Old and Middle English and -e-, -i-, -o-, -u-, -y-, and various diphthongs are attested for it.

"Meaning primarily 'change, alteration,' the word may once have denoted some earlier time division, such as the 'change of moon, half month,' ... but there is no positive evidence of this" [Buck]. No evidence of a native Germanic week before contact with the Romans. The seven-day week is ancient, probably originating from the 28-day lunar cycle, divisible into four periods of seven day, at the end of each of which the moon enters a new phase. Reinforced during the spread of Christianity by the ancient Jewish seven-day week.

As a Roman astrological convention it was borrowed by other European peoples; the Germanic tribes substituting their own deities for those of the Romans, without regard to planets. The Coligny calendar suggests a Celtic division of the month into halves; the regular Greek division of the month was into three decades; and the Romans also had a market week of nine days.

Phrase a week, as in eight days a week recorded by 1540s; see a- (1).

The vowel sound seems to have been uncertain in Old and 中古英语 and -e-, -i-, -o-, -u-, -y-, and various diphthongs are attested for it. "Meaning primarily 'change, alteration,' the word may once have denoted some earlier time division, such as the 'change of moon, half month,' ... but there is no positive evidence of this" [Buck]. No evidence of a 本族 日耳曼语 week before contact with the Romans. The seven-day week is ancient, 可能 originating 源自 28-day lunar cycle, divisible into four periods of seven day, at the end of each of which the moon enters a new phase. Reinforced during the spread of Christianity by the ancient Jewish seven-day week. 作为 Roman astrological convention it was borrowed by other European peoples; the 日耳曼语 tribes substituting their own deities for those of the Romans, without regard to planets. The Coligny calendar suggests a Celtic division of the month into halves; the regular 希腊语 division of the month was into three decades; and the Romans also had a market week of nine days. Phrase a week, as in eight days a week recorded by 1540 年代; 参见 a- (1).

entries.etymology: also week-end, 1630s, from week + end (n.). Originally a northern word (referring to the period from Saturday noon to Monday morning); it became general after 1878. As an adjective, "only on weekends," it is recorded from 1935. Long weekend attested from 1900; in reference to Great Britain in the period between the world wars, 1944.

example.en: The team holds a weekly meeting every Monday morning.

entries.etymology: Old English wepan "shed tears, cry; bewail, mourn over; complain" (class VII strong verb; past tense weop, past participle wopen), from Proto-Germanic *wopjan (source also of Old Norse op, Old High German wuof "shout, shouting, crying," Old Saxon wopian, Gothic wopjan "to shout, cry out, weep"), from PIE *wab- "to cry, scream" (source also of Latin vapulare "to be flogged;" Old Church Slavonic vupiti "to call," vypu "gull"). Of water naturally forming on stones, walls, etc., from c. 1400. Related: Wept; weeping; weeper.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 wepan "shed tears, cry; bewail, mourn over; complain" (class VII strong 动词; past tense weop, past participle wopen), 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wopjan (source also of 古北欧语 op, 古高地德语 wuof "shout, shouting, crying," 古撒克逊语 wopian, Gothic wopjan "to shout, cry out, weep"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *wab- "to cry, scream" (source also of 拉丁语 vapulare "to be flogged;" Old Church Slavonic vupiti "to call," vypu "gull"). definitionLines: vt. 称，量；重，重达；考虑，权衡
entries.definition: vt. 称，量；重，重达；考虑，权衡 vi. 重……
entries.etymology:
Old English wegan (class V strong verb, past tense wæg, past participle wægon) "find the weight of, measure; have weight; lift, carry, support, sustain, bear; move," from Proto-Germanic *wegan (source also of Old Saxon wegan, Old Frisian wega, Dutch wegen "to weigh;" Old Norse vega, Old High German wegan "to move, carry, weigh;" German wiegen "to weigh," bewegen "to move, stir"), from PIE *wegh- "to move" (source also of Sanskrit vahati "carries, conveys," vahitram "vessel, ship;" Avestan vazaiti "he leads, draws;" Greek okhos "carriage;" Latin vehere "to carry, convey;" Old Church Slavonic vesti "to carry, convey;" Lithuanian vežu "to carry, convey;" Old Irish fecht "campaign, journey").

The original sense was of motion, which led to that of lifting, then to that of "measure the weight of." The older sense of "lift, carry" survives in the nautical phrase weigh anchor. Figurative sense of "to consider, ponder" (in reference to words, etc.) is recorded from mid-14c. To weigh in in the literal sense is from 1868, originally of jockeys; figurative meaning "bring one's influence to bear" is from 1909.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 wegan (class V strong 动词, past tense wæg, past participle wægon) "find the weight of, measure; have weight; lift, carry, support, sustain, bear; move," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wegan (source also of 古撒克逊语 wegan, 古弗里西语 wega, 荷兰语 wegen "to weigh;" 古北欧语 vega, 古高地德语 wegan "to move, carry, weigh;" 德语 wiegen "to weigh," bewegen "to move, stir"), 源自 原始印欧语 (PIE) *wegh- "to move" (source also of 梵语 vahati "carries, conveys," vahitram "vessel, ship;" Avestan vazaiti "he leads, draws;" 希腊语 okhos "carriage;" 拉丁语 vehere "to carry, convey;" Old Church Slavonic vesti "to carry, convey;" Lithuanian vežu "to carry, convey;" Old 爱尔兰语 fecht "campaign, journey"). The original sense was of motion, which led to that of lifting, 之后 to that of "measure the weight of." The older 语义 "lift, carry" survives in the nautical phrase weigh anchor. Figurative 语义 "to consider, ponder" (in reference to words, etc.) 见于 14 世纪中期 To weigh in in the literal sense 始于 1868 年, 原义为 of jockeys; figurative 意为 "bring one's influence to bear" 始于 1909 年.

example.en: Before signing, you should weigh the pros and cons of each option.

definitionLines: n. 重量，体重；砝码，秤砣； 重压，负担；重要性，价值
entries.definition: n. 重量，体重；砝码，秤砣； 重压，负担；重要性，价值
entries.etymology:
Old English gewiht "weighing, weight, downward force of a body, heaviness," from Proto-Germanic *wihti- (source also of Old Norse vætt, Danish vegt, Old Frisian wicht, Middle Dutch gewicht, German Gewicht), from *weg- (see weigh).

Figurative sense of "burden" is late 14c. To lose weight "get thinner" is recorded from 1961. Weight Watcher as a trademark name dates from 1960. To pull one's weight (1921) is from rowing. To throw (one's) weight around figuratively is by 1922. Weight-training is from 1945. Weight-lifting is from 1885; weight-lifter (human) from 1893.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 gewiht "weighing, weight, downward force of a body, heaviness," 源自 原始日耳曼语 *wihti- (source also of 古北欧语 vætt, Danish vegt, 古弗里西语 wicht, Middle 荷兰语 gewicht, 德语 Gewicht), 源自 *weg- （参见 weigh). Figurative 语义 "burden" is 14 世纪晚期 To lose weight "get thinner" 见于 1961 年. Weight Watcher 作为 trademark name dates 自 1960 年起. To pull one's weight (1921) is from rowing. To throw (one's) weight around figuratively is 截至 1922 年. Weight-training 始于 1945 年. Weight-lifting 始于 1885 年; weight-lifter (human) 自 1893 年起.

entries.definition: a. 受欢迎的 vt./n./ int. 欢迎
entries.etymology: Old English wilcuma "welcome!" exclamation of kindly greeting, from earlier wilcuma (n.) "welcome guest," literally "one whose coming suits another's will or wish," from willa "pleasure, desire, choice" (see will (n.)) + cuma "guest," related to cuman (see come). Similar formation in Old High German willicomo, Middle Dutch wellecome. Meaning "entertainment or public reception as a greeting" is recorded from 1530. The adjective is from Old English wilcuma. You're welcome as a formulaic response to thank you is attested from 1907. Welcome mat is from 1908; welcome wagon is attested from 1940.
entries.etymologyZh: 古英语 wilcuma "welcome!" exclamation of kindly greeting, 源自 earlier wilcuma （名） "welcome guest," 字面义为 "one whose coming suits another's will or wish," 源自 willa "pleasure, desire, choice" （参见 will （名）) + cuma "guest," related to cuman （参见 come). You're welcome 作为 formulaic response to thank you 见于 1907 年. Welcome mat 始于 1908 年; welcome wagon 见于 1940 年.

entries.etymology: c. 1300, from Old English wel faran "condition of being or doing well," from wel (see well (adv.)) + faran "get along" (see fare (v.)). Similar formation in Old Norse velferð. Welfare state is recorded from 1941.
